# PHASE 011:

# Phase 011 — Create the ids-discovery crate: Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Status:** Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.

## 1. Executive Summary

Phase 011 creates **`ids-discovery`**, a new IDS crate providing **gossip-based membership discovery without a central coordinator**. Every node maintains a local membership table and periodically exchanges state with a small random subset of peers; membership facts (join, leave, suspect, confirm, dead, heartbeat) spread epidemically until the cluster converges on a shared view. The crate is carrier-agnostic: all traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` datagrams) with zero dependencies on `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh stacks.

**Scope (research-verified):** rumor mongering (push/pull/push-pull epidemic dissemination), anti-entropy reconciliation with compact digests, aggregate gossip (state summarization before transmission), membership convergence, discovery propagation, discovery expiration/refresh (TTL tombstones), and churn handling (join/leave/suspect/confirm/dead lifecycle with failure detection). Suspicion/refutation and indirect probes follow the SWIM pattern (Scalable Weakly-consistent Infection-style Process Group Membership Protocol, Cornell DSN 2002); failure detection is modeled on Chandra-Toueg incomplete/weak accuracy failure detectors; phi-accrual suspicion (Hayashibara et al. 2004) provides adaptive thresholds; Cassandra-style vector clocks `(generation, version)` order per-member state; Merkle/sha256-blake3 digests bound anti-entropy bandwidth to O(log n) convergence rounds with per-node O(fanout) traffic independent of cluster size.

**Key engineering decisions:** (1) gossip and failure detection are separate concerns, piggybacked on the same datagrams but rate-tunable independently (memberlist pattern); (2) all state merges are idempotent, commutative, associative — message loss, duplication, and reordering are harmless; (3) expiration is time-basis-driven via `ids-time` ticks, never wall-clock; (4) allowed crypto only — ed25519 signatures for authenticated gossip envelopes, sha256/blake3 for digests, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 optional for envelope confidentiality; (5) `ids-000-aa` is the master crate: `NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, and all sealed trait contracts come from there verbatim.

## 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-discovery` sits above `ids-carrier` and below `ids-membership`/application layers. It is not a transport: it produces and consumes opaque datagrams through `ids-carrier::Endpoint::send_datagram`/`receive_datagram`.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-membership                     │
│              membership state (join/leave/active/dead), events      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 011: ids-discovery (NEW CRATE)             │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Membership Table│ │ Rumor Mongering  │ │ Anti-Entropy Engine │  │
│  │ (local view,    │ │ push/pull/push-  │ │ (digest exchange,   │  │
│  │  TTL entries)   │ │  pull gossip)    │ │  merkle/sha256)     │  │
│  └────────┬────────┘ └────────┬─────────┘ └──────────┬───────────┘  │
│           │                   │                      │              │
│  ┌────────▼───────────────────▼──────────────────────▼────────┐   │
│  │            Aggregate Gossip + Epidemic Broadcast             │   │
│  │  state summarization, hop-limited dissemination, fanout K    │   │
│  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │       Failure Detection (SWIM suspicion/refutation, indirect │   │
│  │       probes, ping/ping-req/ack, phi-accrual suspicion)      │   │
│  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │            Churn + Expiration/Refresh (TTL tombstones)       │   │
│  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌──────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  Wire / Security: envelope (ed25519 sig), digest (sha256/    │   │
│  │  blake3), optional xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305        │   │
│  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │ ids-carrier::Endpoint (CarrierType + Vec<u8>)
└─────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┘
│             ids-carrier (opaque datagrams, no IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/etc.)│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow (gossip round):** each gossip tick, the node selects K random peers from its membership table, builds an aggregate gossip envelope (delta + digest + heartbeat), signs it (ed25519), and sends via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. The receiver verifies, merges into its membership table (idempotent LWW-style merge keyed on `(member, generation, version)`), and may reply with missing entries. Suspicion: no ack within suspicion interval → mark suspect → indirect probe via K intermediaries (ping-req) → refute if any ack returns → confirm dead otherwise. Expiration: entries without refresh beyond TTL become tombstones, then are garbage-collected.

**Convergence:** with fanout K and N members, any membership fact reaches all correct nodes within O(log_K N) gossip rounds with high probability; per-node traffic is O(K) datagrams per round regardless of N (no O(N²) mesh).

## 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

### 3.1 Rumor Mongering (Epidemic Dissemination)

Source pattern: Demers et al., "Epidemic Algorithms for Replicated Database Maintenance" (PODC 1987) — the seminal push/pull/push-pull rumor mongering model. Each membership update becomes a "hot rumor"; the holder periodically contacts a random peer and pushes the rumor; the recipient merges and becomes a new spreader; nodes lose interest after K contacts (counter-based) or with probability 1/K (coin-based), or only when the peer already knows the rumor (feedback). Blind variants keep spreading regardless. Result: information infects the whole population in O(log n) rounds; each node sends O(1) messages per round. IDS adaptation: membership facts (join/leave/suspect/confirm/dead/heartbeat) are rumors; each gossip datagram carries a bounded delta (bounded size is a gossip defining property — bounded-size information exchange with reliable-not-assumed channels).

### 3.2 Anti-Entropy Reconciliation

Source pattern: anti-entropy (Demers et al.; Cassandra; Dynamo). Periodically, two peers exchange compact digests of their membership tables instead of full state: each entry summarized as `(member_id, generation, version)` hashed into a blake3/sha256 Merkle-like digest or version-vector summary. Equal digests ⇒ tables in sync (O(1) agreement check); differing digests trigger recursive descent to locate divergent entries, exchanging only deltas. Keeps typical gossip messages under ~1 KB even in clusters of thousands of nodes. Anti-entropy interval is much longer than the gossip round (e.g., gossip every 200 ms–1 s; anti-entropy every 30–120 s) to bound bandwidth while healing missed updates and partition drift. IDS adaptation: digest computed over canonical blake3/sha256 encoding of the local membership view; reconciliation exchanges only divergent `(member, generation, version)` entries; last-write-wins merge by `(generation, version)`.

### 3.3 Aggregate Gossip

Aggregate gossip summarizes state before transmission: instead of sending the full membership table each round, nodes send (a) their own delta since last exchange, (b) a compact digest/hash summary, and (c) piggybacked rumors pending forwarding. This bounds per-datagram size and respects the MTU-ish constraints of `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams (opaque Vec<u8>; carrier may impose its own size limits, unknown to the crate). Aggregation is applied locally; merge remains idempotent so duplicated aggregates are harmless.

### 3.4 Epidemic Broadcast

Epidemic (rumor-mongering) broadcast for discovery events: when a node learns of a new member or a state change (join/leave/dead), it injects the event into the gossip stream with a monotonically increasing sequence/version; every recipient forwards to K random peers not known to have it, with hop-count/TTL damping and duplicate suppression by `(origin, seq)`. Broadcast is probabilistic — eventual delivery with high probability, not guaranteed — matching the carrier-agnostic, unreliable-datagram model (no retransmission guarantees assumed from ids-carrier).

### 3.5 Membership Convergence

Each node's local view: map `NodeId → MembershipEntry { generation, version, state (alive/suspect/confirm/dead), heartbeat, ttl, metadata }`. Merge rule: for each `NodeId`, keep the entry with the highest `(generation, version)`; state transitions obey the lifecycle (alive → suspect → confirm/dead; confirm dead is terminal unless re-join with bumped generation). Convergence criterion: all correct nodes holding the same set of updates reach the same view (strong eventual consistency of the membership table) because merge is a join-semilattice over `(generation, version)` with idempotent, commutative, associative LUB. Convergence time O(log_K N) rounds with fanout K.

### 3.6 Discovery Propagation

New nodes bootstrap by knowing at least one existing endpoint (contact/seed), advertised via configuration or out-of-band (IDS provisioning channel — not DNS). The joiner sends a join rumor; recipients propagate it epidemically. Departures: explicit leave rumor (signed, ed25519) or implicit via heartbeat expiry. Discovery events carry origin `NodeId` + signature so forged join/leave for another identity is detectable.

### 3.7 Discovery Expiration / Refresh

Every membership entry carries a TTL keyed to the `ids-time` tick basis (IDS proprietary time, not wall-clock, not HLC). A live member refreshes its entry via heartbeat gossip each round. Entries not refreshed before TTL expiry enter tombstone state; tombstones are retained for a grace window (so a late leave/suspect can still be processed) and then garbage-collected. This prevents a silent node from lingering forever in views while avoiding premature eviction of slow-but-alive members (false-positive suppression via suspicion interval, SWIM pattern).

### 3.8 Churn Handling

Churn = continuous joins, leaves, failures, recoveries. Mechanisms: (1) generation bump on re-join after dead, so stale entries resurrecting from old gossip lose to the new generation; (2) suspect → indirect probe → confirm/dead state machine to distinguish transient loss from real failure; (3) tombstone grace windows so departed members' `dead` rumors still propagate after local GC; (4) fanout and gossip interval tuned so convergence outpaces expected churn rate; (5) bounded tables (max entries, LRU/tombstone eviction) so membership memory stays O(1) per node under unbounded churn.

### 3.9 Failure Detection (SWIM + Phi Accrual)

Direct probe: ping → ack within suspicion interval. On timeout: indirect probe — ping-req to K random intermediaries, each pings the target; any ack refutes suspicion. If no ack by end of protocol period, mark confirm/dead and gossip `dead`. Phi-accrual overlay: suspicion level φ computed from sliding window of heartbeat inter-arrival times; configurable threshold trades detection latency vs false positives (φ=1 ≈ 10% error, φ=2 ≈ 1%, φ=3 ≈ 0.1%, default ~8–10). Chandra-Toueg properties: strong/weak completeness (eventually suspect every crashed process) and strong/weak accuracy (bounded false suspicions) are probabilistic here — the detector is unreliable by design, consistent with eventual-consistency membership.

## 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
|| Forged join/leave/suspect for another node | ed25519 signature over `(origin NodeId, seq, event type, payload)` in every gossip envelope; unverified envelopes dropped before merge ||
|| Replay of old gossip (resurrecting departed nodes) | Monotonic per-origin sequence + `(generation, version)` LWW merge; older generations lose; tombstones retained through grace window ||
|| Duplicate / reordered datagrams (unreliable carrier) | Idempotent semilattice merge; loss/dup/reorder harmless by design ||
|| Sybil / eclipse (fake identities flood views) | ed25519-bound identities; per-peer entry budgets; view size caps; bootstrap trust provisioned out of band (no DNS, no central coordinator) ||
|| Gossip denial-of-service (oversized datagrams, digest bombs) | Bounded datagram size; max delta entries per envelope; digest depth limits; reject-and-drop oversized envelopes before merge ||
|| False positives (healthy node marked dead under loss/slow processing) | Suspicion + indirect probe + refutation; phi-accrual adaptive threshold; suspicion interval ≫ expected RTT variance; never hard-evict on single timeout ||
|| Flapping (rapid suspect/revive oscillations) | Hysteresis: confirm/dead requires sustained silence; re-join requires new generation; grace window before rejoining views ||
|| Partition healing divergence | Anti-entropy digest exchange reconciles divergent views after partition heals; `(generation, version)` LWW merge converges ||
|| Traffic analysis / metadata leakage | Optional xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 envelope encryption (allowed crypto only); no sender/receiver addresses in clear beyond carrier-mandated opaque routing ||
|| Compromised node broadcasting conflicting states | Per-origin sequence monotonicity; equivocation (same seq, different payload) detected and flagged; origin's subsequent gossip down-weighted pending evidence ||
|| Long-term table growth under churn | TTL tombstones + GC; bounded view size; eviction policy (oldest tombstone first) ||
|| No central coordinator = no single source of truth | Every node computes its own view locally; convergence is eventual, not immediate; applications read membership with explicit staleness tolerance via ids-consistency profiles ||

## 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role in Phase 011 ||
||-------|-------------------|-------------------|
|| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: `NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `OpState`, sealed trait contracts, versioning, error contracts — all types used verbatim ||
|| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), `Datagram`, `send_datagram`/`receive_datagram` — the ONLY traffic boundary; all discovery traffic is opaque datagrams ||
|| `ids-crypto` | ed25519 sign/verify (envelope authentication), sha256/blake3 (digests), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (optional envelope encryption), nonce/key management ||
|| `ids-time` | Proprietary tick basis for TTL/expiration/heartbeat timing — never wall-clock, never std::net timers ||
|| `ids-topology` | Failure-domain-aware peer selection (gossip targets spread across power/facility/network/operator/geographic domains when known) ||
|| `ids-failure-detector` | Chandra-Toueg completeness/accuracy properties frame the suspicion/confirm semantics; SWIM suspicion maps onto it ||
|| `ids-membership` | Consumer of discovery events (node states: candidate/validating/active/degraded/draining/failed/retired); discovery emits join/leave/dead, membership applies admission policy ||
|| `ids-consistency` | Consistency profiles govern how fresh a discovery view must be for reads/writes (bounded staleness on membership) ||

**Integration points:** `ids-discovery` depends only on `ids-000-aa`, `ids-carrier`, `ids-crypto`, `ids-time`; it is consumed by `ids-membership` (and optionally `ids-topology` for domain-aware peer sampling). It imports nothing from `ids-carrier` beyond `Endpoint`/`Datagram` — no sockets, no addresses, no carrier-specific code. If all networking disappeared, `ids-discovery` remains coherent (local table maintenance continues; datagrams simply queue).

## 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

### 7.1 Membership view (join-semilattice)

```
MembershipView = Map<NodeId, MembershipEntry>
MembershipEntry = { generation: u64, version: u64, state: alive|suspect|confirm|dead,
                    heartbeat: Tick, ttl: Tick, metadata: Bytes }

merge(local, remote):
  for (id, entry) in remote:
    if id not in local or (entry.generation, entry.version) > local[id].(generation, version):
      local[id] = entry                       // last-write-wins by (generation, version)
  laws: commutative, associative, idempotent  // join = LUB; SEC by Shapiro et al. 2011
```

### 7.2 Rumor mongering round

```
every gossip_tick:
  peers = sample_k(view.alive, K)             // K = fanout (2–4 typical)
  for peer in peers:
    envelope = aggregate(delta(view), digest(view), heartbeat)
    sign(ed25519, envelope)
    ids-carrier::Endpoint.send_datagram(peer.endpoint, envelope.bytes)
  on receive(envelope):
    verify(ed25519, envelope)                 // drop if invalid
    merge(view, envelope.delta)
    forward pending rumors per fanout/damping
```

### 7.3 SWIM suspicion / refutation

```
direct probe: ping(target); await ack within suspicion_interval
on timeout: indirect probe — ping-req(target) to K intermediaries → each pings target
any ack → refute suspicion, stay alive
no ack by end of protocol period → confirm/dead, gossip dead rumor
phi-accrual: φ = -log10(1 - F(time_since_last_heartbeat)); F = normal CDF over
sliding window of inter-arrival times; threshold φ (default ~8–10) triggers suspicion
```

### 7.4 Anti-entropy digest exchange

```
digest = blake3/sha256(canonical(view_snapshot))        // or Merkle root over entries
on mismatch: recursively compare subtree digests; exchange only divergent
  (member, generation, version) entries; merge via §7.1 LWW
interval: anti_entropy_tick ≫ gossip_tick (e.g. 30–120 s vs 200 ms–1 s)
cost: equal digests → O(1) bytes; k divergent entries → O(k) bytes, not O(view size)
```

### 7.5 Expiration / refresh

```
entry.ttl = heartbeat_tick + TTL
every refresh: entry.heartbeat = now_tick; entry.version += 1
expire sweep: if now_tick > entry.ttl → state = tombstone (retain grace_window)
GC: drop tombstones older than grace_window; bounded view eviction (oldest tombstone first)
```

### 7.6 Convergence bound

With fanout K and N members, rumor reaches all correct nodes in O(log_K N) rounds w.h.p.; per-node traffic O(K) datagrams/round, independent of N (verified in gossip literature: Demers et al. 1987; memberlist/Cassandra production behavior).

## 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

|| # | Criterion | Measurement ||
||---|-----------|-------------|
|| AC-011.1 | No central coordinator | Discovery runs with zero designated nodes; join via any known endpoint only ||
|| AC-011.2 | Carrier-agnostic | Compiles and behaves identically with zero imports of std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS; all traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint ||
|| AC-011.3 | Allowed crypto only | Envelope auth = ed25519; digests = sha256/blake3; optional encryption = xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305; nothing else ||
|| AC-011.4 | Convergence time | Membership fact reaches all correct nodes in O(log_K N) gossip rounds; measured in simulation for N ∈ {10, 100, 1000}, K ∈ {2, 3, 4} ||
|| AC-011.5 | Per-node traffic bound | O(K) datagrams per gossip round regardless of N; bytes/round bounded by configured max envelope size ||
|| AC-011.6 | Idempotent merge | View merge commutative/associative/idempotent; property test 100k+ iterations ||
|| AC-011.7 | Loss/dup/reorder tolerance | Convergence under randomized loss/duplication/reordering (chaos test) ||
|| AC-011.8 | Suspect → confirm/dead | Direct ping timeout → indirect probe (K intermediaries) → refute on any ack → dead after protocol period ||
|| AC-011.9 | Expiration correctness | Entry without refresh past TTL → tombstone; dropped only after grace window ||
|| AC-011.10 | Churn handling | Join/leave/rejoin storms converge; re-join bumps generation; stale resurrections lose ||
|| AC-011.11 | Anti-entropy | Equal digests → no transfer; divergent entries repaired with O(k) bytes ||
|| AC-011.12 | Authentication | Unsigned/tampered envelopes dropped before merge; forged origin rejected ||
|| AC-011.13 | Replay resistance | Monotonic per-origin sequence + (generation, version) LWW; old generations lose ||
|| AC-011.14 | Bounded memory | View size capped; tombstone GC; eviction under sustained churn ||
|| AC-011.15 | Determinism | Same seed + event sequence → identical views across nodes (seeded simulation) ||

## 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Bootstrap without a coordinator:** the crate assumes at least one known endpoint per joiner (configured/provisioned out of band); a fully seedless bootstrap (e.g., local multicast-style discovery) is not specified and conflicts with the carrier-agnostic mandate (no broadcast primitives assumed).
2. **Failure-detector parameters:** suspicion interval, phi threshold, indirect-probe fanout, and grace window are workload-dependent; defaults are placeholders pending deployment measurement.
3. **Signed vs unsigned gossip:** ed25519 envelope signing is specified, but whether signing is mandatory or configurable per-carrier-trust-model is unresolved; signing costs CPU on every gossip datagram.
4. **Interaction with ids-membership states:** discovery emits raw join/leave/dead; the mapping to `ids-membership` node states (candidate/validating/active/…/retired) and admission-control gating lives in ids-membership, not here — interface contract TBD.
5. **Digest design:** plain blake3/sha256 whole-view digest vs Merkle tree over entries — Merkle gives O(divergent) localization but more implementation surface; decision deferred.
6. **Table eviction policy under churn:** oldest-tombstone-first vs LRU vs generation-based — unresolved; affects memory vs accuracy trade-off.
7. **Cross-carrier endpoint semantics:** `Endpoint` carries `CarrierType + Vec<u8>`; how discovery maps NodeId → CarrierType + opaque address for send_datagram depends on ids-carrier/ids-000-aa contracts not yet finalized.
8. **Encryption overhead:** optional xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 envelope encryption doubles datagram size roughly; whether default-on or opt-in is a product decision.

## 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| Separate crate `ids-discovery` | User mandate: separate crates for new capabilities; keeps ids-carrier/ids-000-aa focused ||
|| Gossip + failure detection as separate layers, piggybacked datagrams | memberlist pattern: gossip rate tunable independently of failure-detection rate; shared datagrams save bandwidth ||
|| Rumor mongering push/pull/push-pull | O(log n) convergence, O(1) per-node traffic, robust to loss/dup/reorder (Demers et al. 1987) ||
|| (generation, version) LWW merge | Idempotent semilattice → strong eventual consistency without reliable channels (Shapiro et al. 2011) ||
|| SWIM suspicion + indirect probes + refutation | Distinguishes transient loss from real failure; bounds false positives (Cornell DSN 2002; HashiCorp memberlist) ||
|| Phi-accrual suspicion | Adaptive threshold tracks observed heartbeat intervals; φ threshold tunes false-positive vs detection-latency trade-off (Hayashibara et al. 2004) ||
|| Anti-entropy digest exchange (blake3/sha256) | Heals missed partitions/divergence; O(1) equal check, O(k) repair; interval ≫ gossip interval bounds bandwidth (Cassandra/Dynamo pattern) ||
|| TTL expiration keyed to ids-time ticks | IDS proprietary time basis; never wall-clock; grace-window tombstones prevent premature eviction ||
|| All traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint (CarrierType + Vec<u8>) | Carrier-agnostic mandate; no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS ||
|| ed25519 envelope signatures | Authenticated origin within allowed crypto set; forged join/leave/suspect detectable ||
|| ids-000-aa as master type crate | NodeId, Endpoint, CarrierType, sealed traits used verbatim; no type duplication ||
|| Reject op-based reliable broadcast as primary | Requires exactly-once causal delivery — contradicts carrier-agnostic unreliable-datagram model ||
|| Bounded view size + tombstone GC | Memory stays O(1) under unbounded churn ||

# PHASE 012:

## Phase 012 — Create the ids-protocol crate: HX-241-style native frame format, self-defined, carrier-agnostic

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

Note on numbering: prompts.txt entry 12 is ids-protocol ("Create the ids-protocol crate: HX-241-style native frame format, self-defined, carrier-agnostic."). Entry 13 (ids-write) is a separate phase.

---\n### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 012 creates `ids-protocol`, the IDS native wire/message format crate. It defines a self-defined, HX-241-style carrier-agnostic frame format: every unit of traffic is a `Frame` carrying a frame header, frame body, sequencing, acknowledgements, fragmentation/reassembly metadata, delivery-semantics flags, flow-control credits, loss-detection state, and retransmission markers. `ids-protocol` knows nothing about the transport: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), making the crate usable over any carrier — reliable, unreliable, datagram, stream, store-and-forward, or opaque.

Contents per prompts.txt entry 12 and CRATES.md §12: frame header, frame body, framing, sequencing, acknowledgements, fragmentation/reassembly, delivery semantics, stream/session semantics, flow control, loss detection, retransmission, protocol invariants. All crypto is confined to the allowed set only: ed25519 (signatures), xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 (AEAD), sha256 and blake3 (hashing/checksums). `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract; `ids-protocol` depends on `ids-000-aa` for frame types (`FrameId`, `SeqNum`, `FrameType`, `DeliverySemantics`, `Checksum`, `Signature`, `Endpoint`) and only consumes type surface from `ids-crypto` (no runtime dep, preserving the no-cycle rule).

`ids-protocol` does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-protocol/`. This plan specifies creation from scratch; no source modifications are made in this phase. Research basis: 30 parallel searches covering length-prefixed framing (tokio-util `LengthDelimitedCodec`, krot-proto postcard framing), SCALE codec (Parity), protobuf length-delimited varints, SSH binary packet protocol (RFC 4253), AMQP 1.0 frame header (8-byte fixed header), MQTT 5.0 variable-byte-integer remaining length, gRPC length-prefixed message over HTTP/2, Yamux credit-based flow control, QUIC loss detection (RFC 9002), QUIC stream credit-based flow control (RFC 9000), TCP sliding window / PAWS (RFC 7323/1323), selective-repeat ARQ, QUIC ACK scheduling, Kafka at-least-/exactly-once semantics, TLA+/IC3 distributed protocol verification, Rust `nom` zero-copy binary parsing, `bytes::BytesMut` zero-copy buffers, Cap'n Proto / FlatBuffers zero-copy comparison, UDT reliable-over-UDP, OSI session layer (stream vs datagram semantics), Merkle/MMR synchronization, XChaCha20-Poly1305 (libsodium), Ed25519 RFC 8032, BLAKE3.

---\n### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-protocol` is the wire-format and reliability layer for all IDS inter-node traffic. It is not a transport: it serializes application/control messages into carrier-agnostic `Frame`s that `ids-carrier::Endpoint` ships. Reliability (sequencing, acks, retransmission, flow control) is implemented inside the frame format itself so that any carrier — reliable or unreliable — can carry IDS traffic without change.

CARRIER BOUNDARY (non-negotiable): `ids-carrier::Endpoint` is the sole address and envelope type. `ids-protocol` never imports `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any carrier-specific crate.

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- Self-defined native frame format: header + body, length-prefixed or varint-delimited, checksummed per frame (blake3 or sha256 — CRC not in allowed crypto).
- Sequencing: monotonic `SeqNum` per session/endpoint; ACKs carried in-frame (piggybacked) or as pure ACK frames.
- Acknowledgements: cumulative + selective (SACK-style bitmask) to tolerate reordering/loss without RTT-bound timers.
- Fragmentation/reassembly: per-frame MTU-aware splitting with fragment ID + offset + total; reassembly deadline keyed to creation time (never RTT).
- Delivery semantics: `AtMostOnce`, `AtLeastOnce`, `ExactlyOnce` per frame (idempotency via frame dedup window).
- Stream/session semantics: ordered byte-stream sessions and datagram sessions coexist; stream reassembly preserves order within a session.
- Flow control: credit-based (per-session credit window), no RTT dependence.
- Loss detection: packet/time thresholds per QUIC RFC 9002 (per-packet-number-space loss detection, PTO probe), keyed to monotonic clocks, never raw wall-clock validity.
- Retransmission: selective retransmit of unacked frames after loss detection or PTO expiry; new frame number on retransmit (QUIC-style) to avoid retransmission ambiguity.
- Protocol invariants: frame length bounded; checksum verified before any semantic processing; sequencing gaps bounded; dedup window bounded; no frame ever carries carrier addressing.
- Allowed crypto only: ed25519 (frame signature), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (frame AEAD encryption), sha256/blake3 (frame checksum). No other crypto.

---\n### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Frame Header & Frame Body (native wire format)
Every `Frame` = fixed/variable header + opaque body. Header fields: frame type (u8), flags (u8), version (u8), `FrameId` (u64, globally unique per origin), `SeqNum` (u64 per session), ACK field (cumulative ack + SACK bitmask), length (varint or fixed u32), checksum (blake3/sha256 over header+body), optional signature (ed25519 over canonical encoding), optional crypto block (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 nonce + ciphertext tag). Body = opaque `Vec<u8>` payload. Reference layouts: SSH binary packet protocol (RFC 4253: packet_length/padding_length/payload/padding/MAC), AMQP 1.0 frame header (8-byte fixed: SIZE u32, DOFF, TYPE, channel), MQTT 5.0 fixed header (packet type/flags + variable-byte-integer remaining length), gRPC length-prefixed message (1-byte compressed flag + 4-byte big-endian length + message). tokio-util `LengthDelimitedCodec` and krot-proto postcard framing confirm varint length prefixes are standard and safe when max-frame-size is enforced. SCALE codec (Parity/Substrate) shows a compact little-endian aggregate encoding suitable when self-describing framing is unnecessary.

#### 3.2 Framing (length-prefix vs varint vs delimiter)
Length-prefixed framing solves "where does one message end" on byte streams. Options: fixed-width length (1/2/4/8 bytes, wire_codec `LengthPrefixed`), varint length (LEB128, protobuf/gRPC/krot-proto style), delimiter (newline/0xCE, AMQP 0-9-1 frame end). For carrier-agnostic `Vec<u8>` payloads over possibly-datagram carriers, length-prefix + max-frame-size bound is safest: receiver reads length, then exactly N bytes, bounds memory against framing bombs. Varint (protobuf base-128 varints) compact for small frames; fixed u32 simpler for hardware/ASCII boundaries. Decision: u32 little-endian length prefix + varint option as feature, max frame size configurable (default 1 MiB), checksum appended per frame (wire_codec `Checksummed` decorator pattern adapted to blake3/sha256).

#### 3.3 Sequencing & Acknowledgements
Per-session `SeqNum` (u64) monotonic, assigned at frame creation. Sender tracks unacked frames in a send buffer; receiver tracks highest in-order seq and a SACK bitmask of received out-of-order frames. ACK frames carry cumulative ack + selective bitmask (TCP SACK / QUIC ACK frame pattern). Cumulative ACK acknowledges everything up to N; SACK bitmask covers received-but-not-cumulative frames. Receiver sends ACKs on data frames (piggyback) and as pure ACK frames when no outbound data (QUIC ack-eliciting packet pattern, ack-frequency guidance). QUIC loss detection (RFC 9002): packet declared lost if unacked, in flight, and sent prior to an acked packet; packet threshold kPacketThreshold=3 or time threshold; PTO timer per packet-number-space sends probe packets. IDs-protocol adapts: loss detection per session, PTO per session, no RTT-bound timeouts (absolute deadlines keyed to frame creation time).

#### 3.4 Fragmentation & Reassembly
Frames exceeding carrier MTU (or configured max) are fragmented: fragment header carries `FragId` (u64, per original frame), `FragOffset` (u32, multiple of 8 like IP), `FragTotal` (u16), `MoreFragments` flag. Reassembly buffer per `FragId` with creation-time-keyed expiry (IP-style reassembly timer, but keyed to creation time not RTT). Incomplete reassembly at deadline = discard fragment set (never guess). IP fragmentation precedent (ID/flags/offset, destination-only reassembly, multiples-of-8 offsets) adapted to frame-internal framing rather than network layer.

#### 3.5 Delivery Semantics
Three per-frame delivery semantics: `AtMostOnce` (send once, no retry, may be lost), `AtLeastOnce` (retry until acked, dedup at receiver), `ExactlyOnce` (idempotent apply via frame dedup window + apply-once marker, Kafka idempotent-producer / RIFL exactly-once pattern). Dedup: receiver keeps seen `FrameId`s within a bounded window; duplicate = drop, re-ack prior result. Window expiry = duplicate-admission event, not silent cleanup (Machine-Checked Dual-Write Recovery pattern). Idempotency key = `FrameId` (origin + seq). Exactly-once requires sender+receiver cooperation (Kafka principle).

#### 3.6 Stream / Session Semantics
Two session types: stream sessions (ordered byte stream, like TCP stream / QUIC STREAM: offsets reassemble in order, frame boundaries not preserved) and datagram sessions (message boundaries preserved, like UDP datagram / QUIC datagram extension). Stream session state: next-expected offset, receive buffer for out-of-order data, flow-control credit per stream. Session ID in frame header binds frames to a session; sessions created via SYN/SYN-ACK handshake (yamux-style SYN flag on new stream) and torn down with FIN/GOAWAY. OSI session-layer precedent: dialog control, synchronization points/checkpoints, half/full-duplex. IDs-protocol keeps session state minimal: ID, type, next offset/seq, credit, open/closed state.

#### 3.7 Flow Control (credit-based)
Credit-based flow control (QUIC stream + connection level, HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, yamux Window Update): receiver advertises credit (bytes it can buffer); sender may not send beyond outstanding unacked bytes ≤ credit. Receiver sends Window Update frames as buffer drains. Two levels: per-session credit and per-frame (connection) credit. Yamux: 256KiB initial stream window, no session window; window updates sent regularly to avoid stalls. IDs-protocol: credit carried in frame header flags/field or dedicated credit frame; no RTT dependence; credit exhaustion = backpressure (sender waits), distinct from carrier backpressure.

#### 3.8 Loss Detection & Retransmission
Loss detection per QUIC RFC 9002: track sent frames per packet-number-space-equivalent (session); frame declared lost when (a) unacked, in flight, sent prior to an acked frame, and (b) kPacketThreshold=3 packets after an ack or time threshold elapsed. PTO timer per session: on expiry send at least one ack-eliciting probe frame (up to two datagrams). Retransmission: lost frame re-sent with a NEW `SeqNum` (QUIC removes retransmission ambiguity — new frame number means an ACK cannot be confused about which transmission is acknowledged). Original frame data identical; only seq number changes. Reordering tolerance via SACK bitmask; spurious retransmit detection if original later acked (increase reordering threshold). No RTT-estimate timers; absolute deadlines keyed to frame creation time.

#### 3.9 Protocol Invariants & Safety
- Frame length ≤ max_frame_size (reject oversized before allocation — framing bomb guard).
- Checksum (blake3/sha256) verified before any semantic processing; mismatch = drop frame, count error, never act on corrupt frame.
- `SeqNum` monotonic per session; wraparound handled by modular comparison (TCP PAWS protects against old duplicates after wrap; timestamps monotone non-decreasing).
- Dedup window bounded; oldest evicted on pressure (LRU + TTL).
- Reassembly buffers bounded per `FragId`; expiry by creation-time deadline.
- Credit never exceeded by sender; receiver enforces.
- Crypto confined to allowed set; no frame carries plaintext keys.
- Invariant: an ACKed frame is never retransmitted; a lost frame is retransmitted at most N times before session error.
- Fail-closed: on invariant violation, session enters error state, not silent corruption.

---\n### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Framing bomb / oversized length prefix exhausts memory | Enforce max_frame_size before allocating; reject-and-count per peer |
| Corrupt frame acted on | Per-frame blake3/sha256 checksum verified before semantics; mismatch = drop |
| Replay of old frame | Dedup window on FrameId; monotonic SeqNum; PAWS-style timestamp rejection of old duplicates |
| Retransmission ambiguity (old vs new transmission confused) | New SeqNum on retransmit (QUIC-style); ACK cannot be confused |
| Sequence number wraparound | Modular comparison + monotone timestamps (PAWS) |
| Flow-control credit exceeded | Sender bounded by advertised credit; receiver enforces |
| Reassembly never completes | Creation-time-keyed deadline; discard incomplete set |
| Dedup window DoS | Bounded LRU + TTL eviction; per-peer quota |
| Disallowed crypto in frame | Dependency audit bans non-allowed crates; only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3 |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (std::net etc.) | Endpoint sole address type; source grep assertion in tests |
| Session stall (credit never replenished) | Window update frames sent regularly (yamux pattern); stall detection |
| Unbounded send buffer | Bound unacked bytes; apply backpressure / reject new frames |

---\n### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Frame encode/decode** — length prefix (u32 LE or varint LEB128) + header + body + checksum; max_frame_size enforced before allocation. Sources: tokio-util `LengthDelimitedCodec`, protobuf base-128 varints, gRPC length-prefixed message.
2. **Sequence number space** — u64 `SeqNum` per session; modular comparison for wraparound; monotonic timestamps (PAWS) reject old duplicates. Sources: TCP PAWS (RFC 1323/7323), QUIC packet numbers (RFC 9000).
3. **Cumulative + SACK acknowledgement** — cumulative ack (everything up to N) + selective bitmask for out-of-order received frames; piggybacked on data frames or pure ACK frames. Sources: TCP SACK, QUIC ACK frame (RFC 9000).
4. **Loss detection (QUIC RFC 9002)** — frame lost if unacked, in flight, sent prior to an acked frame, and past packet threshold (k=3) or time threshold; PTO per session sends probe frames. Source: RFC 9002 §6.
5. **Selective retransmit with new SeqNum** — retransmitted frame gets a new `SeqNum` to remove retransmission ambiguity; data identical. Source: QUIC retransmission (RFC 9000).
6. **Dedup window (exactly-once)** — bounded FrameId → seen map; duplicate = drop + re-ack; window expiry = duplicate-admission event. Sources: Kafka idempotent producer, RIFL exactly-once, Machine-Checked Dual-Write Recovery.
7. **Fragmentation/reassembly** — FragId + offset + total + MoreFragments; reassembly buffer per FragId; creation-time-keyed deadline; discard incomplete. Source: IP fragmentation (ID/flags/offset), adapted frame-internal.
8. **Credit-based flow control** — receiver advertises credit; sender bounded by outstanding ≤ credit; Window Update frames replenish. Sources: QUIC stream/connection flow control, HTTP/2 WINDOW_UPDATE, yamux.
9. **Stream session reassembly** — next-expected offset + receive buffer; out-of-order data buffered; delivered in order. Source: QUIC STREAM frames, TCP byte stream.
10. **Datagram session** — message boundaries preserved; no reassembly ordering beyond seq. Source: QUIC datagram, UDP datagram semantics.
11. **Checksum per frame** — blake3 (preferred speed) or sha256; CRC32C not used (not in allowed crypto). Sources: BLAKE3 spec, NIST FIPS 180-4.
12. **Protocol invariants** — length bound, checksum-before-semantics, seq monotonic, credit bound, dedup bounded; fail-closed on violation.

`ids-protocol/Cargo.toml`:

- `blake3 = "1.5"` — frame checksum (preferred)
- `sha2 = "0.10"` — SHA-256 frame checksum (alternative)
- `thiserror = "2.0"` — `ProtocolError` enum
- `serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }` — frame serialization
- `bytes = "1"` — `BytesMut` zero-copy buffers for decode
- `serde_json = "1"` (dev-dependency) — test serialization

**No** `std::net`, `tokio`, `tokio::net`, `libp2p`, `hyper`, `reqwest`, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh dependencies. No async runtime. No networking stack. `ids-protocol` does NOT depend on `ids-crypto` at runtime (consumes `Checksum`/`Signature` type surface from `ids-000-aa` only, preserving the no-cycle rule).

Downstream dependents (all on `ids-000-aa`, plus `ids-protocol` where they consume frames): `ids-session`, `ids-rpc`, `ids-pubsub`, `ids-replication`, `ids-sync`, `ids-carrier` consumers — all send/receive `Vec<u8>` frames via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

---\n### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

| Uncertainty | Impact | Resolution path |
|---|---|---|
| Length prefix: fixed u32 vs varint LEB128 | Frame size overhead, simplicity | u32 LE default; varint as feature-gated option; bench both |
| Checksum: blake3 vs sha256 default | Record size, speed | blake3 default (speed), sha256 option; configurable per session |
| Whether signature is per-frame or per-session | Overhead vs handshake cost | Per-frame optional signature; session-level signature as future optimization |
| Dedup window size | Memory vs outage survival | Sized from longest intended outage; expiry = duplicate-admission event |
| Whether flow control is per-session or per-connection | Granularity of backpressure | Both levels supported; per-session default |
| Whether sessions need explicit handshake | Session setup latency | SYN/SYN-ACK handshake (yamux-style); datagram sessions may skip |
| PTO initial value without RTT | Probe timing | Conservative fixed initial; adaptive after first RTT sample (not used for validity) |
| Max frame size default | Memory vs large payloads | 1 MiB default; configurable; enforced before allocation |
| Whether crypto block (AEAD) is per-frame | Encryption overhead | Optional per-frame AEAD block; session-level encryption as future optimization |

---\n### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| `ids-protocol` as separate crate (not folders in existing crate) | Matches user directive: separate crates, not more folders |
| Self-defined native frame format (header + body, length-prefixed) | HX-241-style; carrier-agnostic; no reliance on existing wire formats |
| Length-prefix framing with max_frame_size bound | Solves stream framing; bounds memory against framing bombs |
| blake3/sha256 checksum per frame (no CRC32C) | Checksum restricted to allowed crypto set |
| Monotonic `SeqNum` per session + modular wraparound | Total order per session; survives u64 wrap via modular comparison |
| Cumulative + SACK ACKs | Tolerates reordering/loss without RTT-bound timers |
| QUIC-style loss detection (packet/time thresholds, PTO) | Proven loss/retransmission over unreliable carriers |
| New `SeqNum` on retransmit | Removes retransmission ambiguity (QUIC pattern) |
| Fragmentation keyed to creation time, not RTT | Correct over arbitrary delays; avoids TCP-style timeout misfire (RFC 3449) |
| Credit-based flow control | Bounded receiver buffer; backpressure without RTT dependence |
| Stream + datagram session types | Ordered byte stream and message-boundary sessions coexist |
| Delivery semantics per frame (at-most/at-least/exactly-once) | Flexible reliability; exactly-once via idempotent dedup |
| Dedup window expiry = duplicate-admission event | Avoids silent cleanup and duplicate-admission hazards |
| No `ids-crypto` runtime dependency | Preserves no-cycle rule (`ids-crypto` does not depend on `ids-000-aa`); type surface only |
| `saturating`/modular arithmetic on all seq/tick arithmetic | No overflow panics in distributed sequencing |
| Cargo workspace member at `C:/idfs/ids-protocol/` | Matches existing workspace layout |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 013 creates `ids-write`, the IDS write engine and write-ahead log. It owns the durable write path: `received → ordered → executing → committed → synchronized`. Contents per CRATES.md §13 and prompts.txt entry 13: WAL, append-only log, durable write path, write fan-out (up to ~30 databases simultaneously), idempotent writes, operation references, ordering positions, durability conditions, commit acknowledgements, write-order management, concurrent-write resolution.

The crate is carrier-agnostic: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-write` only consumes hashing/signing type surface from `ids-000-aa`). `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract; `ids-write` depends on `ids-000-aa` only (plus `ids-crypto` types, no `ids-crypto` runtime dep since crypto is type-level here — aligned to the rule that `ids-crypto` does not depend on `ids-000-aa` to avoid cycles).

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned ARIES WAL (Mohan et al., 1992) analysis/redo/undo, log sequence number (LSN) semantics and idempotent replay (`record_lsn > page_lsn`), group commit / batched fsync amortizing flush cost, segment rotation + checkpoint + truncation + garbage collection (Kudu LogGCOp, Prometheus TSDB checkpoint, Grafana Loki truncation), torn-tail recovery (truncate corrupt tail, never guess), CRC/checksummed frames (RocksDB WAL record format: CRC32C + length + type + payload; adapted here to blake3/sha256 since CRC32C is not in the allowed crypto list), physical vs logical logging, write concern / durability acknowledgement levels (MongoDB w/j), high-watermark/commit-index separation (Martin Fowler distributed patterns; Raft commit index), idempotency keys for exactly-once semantics (RIFL, Stripe, Kafka dedup windows), multi-writer / fan-out replication (TiCDC, Cassandra CommitLog idempotent mutations, DynamoDB Global Tables operation-ID dedup), backpressure under WAL load (ClickHouse WAL backpressure cgroups, Loki disk-full throttle), low-latency cloud logging (BtrLog quorum replication, LSN windowing), and Rust WAL primitives (wal-db lock-free append, wal-engine fsync policies + group commit, nano-wal lock-free segment rotation).

A skeleton `ids-write` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-write/`. This plan specifies creation from scratch; no source modifications are made in this phase.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-write` is the durability and ordering layer for all IDS writes. Every write crosses five lifecycle states defined in `ids-000-aa::OpState`: `received → ordered → executing → committed → synchronized`. `ids-write` owns the WAL (durable, append-only, checksummed, segmented), the ordering position allocator (monotonic `OrderingPos`), the op-reference (`OpRef`) binder for idempotency, the durability-condition evaluator, commit-ack tracking, write-order management, concurrent-write resolution, and fan-out to up to ~30 downstream databases/replicas.

```
│  submit(op with OpRef idempotency key)                              │

                               │ Endpoint (ids-carrier, opaque)
┌──────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐

│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │  receive    │ │  order       │ │  execute        │ │ commit  │ │
│  │  (OpRef     │ │  (OrderingPos│ │  (durable write │ │  ack    │ │
│  │   dedup)    │ │   allocator) │ │   path + WAL)   │ │  tracker│ │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │

┌──────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐
│              REPLICAS / DOWNSTREAM DBs (via ids-carrier)            │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CARRIER BOUNDARY (no std::net / tokio::net): ids-carrier::Endpoint only
```

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- WAL is append-only, segmented, checksummed (blake3/sha256 per record), with torn-tail recovery on restart.
- Every record gets a monotonically increasing LSN/`OrderingPos`; recovery is idempotent (`record_lsn > applied_lsn` skips already-applied).
- Durability = fsync/equivalent before ack, with group commit (one flush per batch) to amortize cost.
- Idempotency via `OpRef` (9-byte alphanumeric, 36^9 namespace) + dedup window; duplicate OpRef = no-op, return prior result.
- Write fan-out to up to ~30 databases simultaneously; each fan-out target tracks its own commit ack.
- Durability conditions (local / quorum / regional / cross-region) evaluated per `ids-durability-policy`; commit vs synchronization distinguished.
- Concurrent writes to the same key resolved by write-order (last writer wins by ordering position) or domain-scoped conflict rule.
- No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, or any networking stack; `Endpoint` is the sole address type.
- Crypto surface: `Checksum([u8;32])` (blake3/sha256), `Signature` (ed25519) from `ids-000-aa`; no direct `ids-crypto` runtime dependency.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Write-Ahead Log (WAL) — Append-Only, Segmented, Checksummed

Core principle: describe a change durably *before* applying it (ARIES WAL rule; log first, data second). Each WAL record: fixed header (LSN/u64, record type u8, length u32, flags u8, checksum u32/blake3 or sha256) + variable payload. Records grouped into fixed-size segments; segment rolls at size threshold; new segment file created per segment sequence number. Checksum per record enables corruption detection; a checksum mismatch or truncated tail marks the logical end of the log (torn-tail recovery: truncate at last complete record, never guess). Sources: ARIES paper (Stanford cs345d), RocksDB WAL file format (CRC32C + size + type + payload, 32KB blocks), Prometheus TSDB WAL checkpoint, Kudu WAL segment GC, Grafana Loki WAL truncation/checkpoint, CMU 15-721 physical vs logical logging, BtrLog low-latency cloud logging.

Record types (logical logging, aligned to idempotent ops): `BEGIN_OP`, `WRITE_RECORD` (op payload + OpRef + ordering position), `COMMIT_OP`, `ABORT_OP`, `CHECKPOINT`, `TRUNCATE_MARKER`, `FANOUT_ACK`. Logical (not physical) records keep entries small and support idempotent replay; physical page-level logging is explicitly rejected (IDS has no buffer pool/page concept in this phase).

#### 3.2 Log Sequence Number / Ordering Position

Every WAL record receives a monotonically increasing `OrderingPos` (u64) — the LSN. Assigned at append time, before durability sync. `OrderingPos::next()`/`prev()` with saturating arithmetic (from `ids-000-aa`). LSN makes replay idempotent: on recovery, skip records whose LSN <= already-applied LSN (`record_lsn > applied_lsn`). LSNs coordinate checkpoints, fan-out ack progress, and the oldest retained position for truncation. Sources: ARIES, CMU 15-445 logging notes, wal-db (LSN = byte offset, atomic reservation).

#### 3.3 Durable Write Path & Commit Acknowledgement

Write path: (1) receive op + OpRef; (2) check idempotency (seen OpRef → return cached result, no-op); (3) allocate OrderingPos; (4) append WAL record(s); (5) fsync/flush per durability policy + fsync policy (Always / EveryN / Interval / Never — wal-engine); (6) apply to executing state; (7) write COMMIT_OP to WAL + fsync; (8) send commit ack via ids-carrier::Endpoint; (9) fan-out to replicas; (10) track synchronized state when replicas ack. A transaction is committed only when all its log records + COMMIT record are on stable storage (ARIES rule #2). Durability levels: local-persisted, quorum-persisted, regionally-durable, cross-region-durable (from `ids-durability-policy`, ids-consistency-profile). Commit vs synchronization distinguished: commit = durable locally; synchronized = durably replicated to required fan-out targets. Sources: MongoDB write concern (w/j), SQL Server transaction log architecture, CMU 15-445 recovery, Martin Fowler high-watermark/commit index.

#### 3.4 Group Commit & Batching

Concurrent commits coalesce into one `write()` + one `fdatasync()`/`fsync()` (group commit) to amortize the fixed flush cost. Release rule: flush after timer T, after K pending records, or adaptive. Ack is held until the group flush returns. Off-lock fsync lets new appends proceed during an in-flight flush. Sources: Group Commit Self-Clocks (arxiv 2606.27051), wal-engine `append_batch`, Happy Engineering WAL & group commit (off-lock fsync, commit tokens in ticket order), toyMQ batched-fsync ADR.

#### 3.5 Idempotent Writes & Operation References

`OpRef` = exactly 9 ASCII alphanumeric bytes (36^9 namespace, from `ids-000-aa`). Client supplies idempotency key; `ids-write` binds OpRef → result. Duplicate OpRef within the dedup window returns the prior result without re-execution. Dedup state persisted in WAL (commit idempotency key + outcome). Window sized from longest survivable outage; window expiry = duplicate-admission event, not silent cleanup (Machine-Checked Dual-Write Recovery). RIFL converts at-least-once to exactly-once via idempotent ops; DynamoDB Global Tables uses operation ID + origin ID + dedup window (~10 min). Idempotency guarantees exactly-once application even with retries/replays. Sources: RIFL (Stanford rifl.pdf), Stripe idempotency keys, Kafka idempotent-producer dedup, Machine-Checked Dual-Write Recovery (arxiv 2608.00501), scirs2-io exactly-once WAL.

#### 3.6 Segment Rotation, Checkpoint, Truncation, GC

WAL grows unbounded unless bounded. Segments roll at size threshold; a background `LogGCOp`-style task deletes segments no longer needed for durability (all replicas acked past them, checkpoint taken). Before truncation, a checkpoint (filtered WAL / snapshot of committed state) is taken named after the last retained segment; replay = load checkpoint + replay subsequent segments. Idempotent replay tolerates re-applying already-checkpointed ops. Loki: delete all but last segment at checkpoint interval, advance WAL segments first. Prometheus: checkpoint after head truncation, resume replay from segment after checkpoint. Kudu: fixed-size segments, LogGCOp background GC. RocksDB: variable-length records padded to block size, trailer skipped. Sources: Grafana Loki WAL design doc, Prometheus TSDB WAL blog, Kudu WAL GC docs, RocksDB WAL file format wiki.

#### 3.7 Torn-Tail & Corruption Recovery

On restart, scan WAL forward; a torn/partial final record (interrupted write) or CRC mismatch = logical end of log; truncate the tail at last complete record (never repair/guess). Damage in a sealed (non-tail) segment = hard corruption error, never silent data loss (wal-engine design). Every record checksummed independently so a batch crash can leave a valid prefix. fsync before ack ensures acked records survive power loss. Sources: wal-engine torn-tail recovery, raft-wal commit frame CRC, SQLite/LMDB/BoltDB assumptions (powersafe overwrites).

#### 3.8 Write Fan-Out (~30 Databases)

A write fans out to up to ~30 downstream databases/replicas simultaneously. Each target: independent `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; ordered/versioned stream; per-target ack cursor; lag observability; resumable delivery from cursor. Multi-leader/multi-writer fan-out: concurrent writers produce independent histories merged by ordering position; each event carries origin identity so forwarding preserves origin (no replication loops). Fan-out rate model: cross-region egress ≈ W·B·(M−1); balanced ingress ≈ W·B·(M−1)/M. Idempotent application at targets (OpRef dedup) tolerates at-least-once redelivery. Sources: TiCDC multi-writer CDC, Cassandra CommitLog (idempotent mutations, shared segments), system-design-patterns multi-leader replication commit/ship/apply.

#### 3.9 Write-Order Management & Concurrent-Write Resolution

Concurrent writes to the same key/partition are totally ordered by `OrderingPos` (assigned at append). Last writer wins by ordering position, or domain-scoped conflict rule from `ids-consistency` / `ids-crdt`. Optimistic concurrency: prepare against current version; commit advances version conditionally (OCC, Apache Iceberg pattern) — if another writer committed first, discard and retry. Write-order management preserves per-key serialization; cross-key ordering left to `ids-ordering-domain` (dataset-scoped, no global master). Sources: Iceberg optimistic concurrency control, Apache Cassandra commit log ordering, CMU 15-445 logging.

#### 3.10 Backpressure & Flow Control

When writes arrive faster than the WAL can fsync, apply backpressure: reject/throttle new writes once unflushed bytes exceed a ceiling (Service Fabric `MaxWriteQueueDepthInKB`, ClickHouse WAL backpressure cgroup caps, Loki disk-full threshold 90%, replay memory ceiling). WAL backpressure is distinct from carrier backpressure; `ids-write` exposes credit-based signals only through `ids-carrier::Endpoint` payloads (no network stack). Sources: ClickHouse WAL backpressure, Service Fabric throttling guidelines, Grafana Loki WAL disk-full throttle, OpenData backpressure on unflushed deltas.

#### 3.11 Crypto Surface & Integrity

Allowed crypto only: ed25519 (signatures), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (AEAD), sha256 and blake3 (hashing/checksums). WAL record integrity: blake3 or sha256 checksum per record (not CRC32C — CRC32 not in allowed list; blake3 preferred for speed). OpRef/signing surface from `ids-000-aa` (`Signature`, `KeyId`, `Checksum`). No `ids-crypto` runtime dependency (crypto crate does not depend on `ids-000-aa`; `ids-write` consumes type surface only). Sources: RFC 8032 Ed25519, RFC 7539 ChaCha20-Poly1305, libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305, NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256, BLAKE3 spec.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||---|---|---|
|| Unacked write lost on power loss | fsync before ack; group commit fence; durable LSN published only after flush ||
|| Torn/partial WAL record on crash | Per-record blake3/sha256 checksum; torn-tail truncation at last complete record ||
|| Silent corruption in sealed segment | Hard error on checksum mismatch in non-tail segment; never guess ||
|| Duplicate apply after replay/restart | Idempotent replay (`record_lsn > applied_lsn`); OpRef dedup window ||
|| OpRef collision / replay attack | 36^9 namespace; allocator uniqueness; collision variant in error contract ||
|| Write fan-out target lost / lagging | Per-target ack cursor; resumable delivery; bounded backoff retries; lag observability ||
|| Write storm exhausts WAL disk | Backpressure throttle at unflushed-byte ceiling; disk-full threshold reject ||
|| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (`std::net`, IP, etc.) | `ids-carrier::Endpoint` sole address; dependency audit bans networking crates ||
|| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 ||
|| Ordering position overflow | `saturating_add`/`saturating_sub`; MAX constants ||
|| Commit vs synchronization confusion | Separate commit ack (local durable) from synchronized ack (replicas applied) ||

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **WAL append** — reserve byte range atomically (LSN = start offset), write length-prefixed checksummed record, `durable_lsn()` tracks highest synced LSN. Source: wal-db lock-free append.
2. **Group commit** — concurrent `sync` calls coalesce into one `write()` + one `fdatasync()`; commit tokens resolve in enqueue/ticket order; ack held until group flush returns. Sources: wal-engine `append_batch`, Happy Engineering off-lock fsync, toyMQ batched-fsync.
3. **Torn-tail recovery** — scan forward; CRC mismatch or partial final record = logical EOF; truncate at last complete record; sealed-segment corruption = hard error. Source: wal-engine torn-tail recovery, raft-wal commit CRC.
4. **Idempotent replay** — `record_lsn > applied_lsn` skips already-applied; replay restarts after crash safely (CLR-style undo not needed for logical ops; abort records discard uncommitted ops). Sources: ARIES, CMU 15-445, Duke CompSci 516.
5. **Checkpoint + truncation** — checkpoint named after last retained segment; delete prior segments; resume replay from segment after checkpoint. Sources: Loki truncation, Prometheus TSDB checkpoint, Kudu LogGCOp.
6. **OpRef idempotency** — 9-byte alphanumeric; `OpRef → result` binding; duplicate = cached no-op; dedup window expiry = duplicate-admission event. Sources: RIFL, Stripe, Machine-Checked Dual-Write Recovery.
7. **Ordering position** — monotonic u64 `OrderingPos`; `next()`/`prev()` with saturating arithmetic; per-key total order; cross-key ordering deferred to `ids-ordering-domain`.
8. **Durability condition evaluation** — level 1–6 (local/quorum/regional/cross-region); `meets(required)` gates commit ack; commit vs synchronization distinguished.
9. **Fan-out manager** — per-target `Endpoint`, ack cursor, lag observability, resumable delivery, bounded backoff; idempotent apply at targets. Source: TiCDC, Cassandra CommitLog, multi-leader replication.
10. **Concurrent-write resolution** — last-writer-wins by `OrderingPos`; OCC version-conditioned commit (discard + retry on conflict). Sources: Iceberg OCC, CMU logging.
11. **Backpressure** — throttle/reject when unflushed bytes exceed ceiling; credit-based signal via `Endpoint` payload only. Sources: ClickHouse WAL backpressure, Service Fabric, Loki disk-full.
12. **Checksum per record** — blake3 (preferred speed) or sha256; CRC32C explicitly not used (not in allowed crypto list). Sources: BLAKE3, NIST FIPS 180-4.

`ids-write/Cargo.toml`:

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

|| Uncertainty | Impact | Resolution path ||
||---|---|---||
|| fsync primitive on Windows (target host) | `fdatasync`/`fsync` semantics differ | Use `std::fs::File::sync_all` + platform-appropriate flush; document per-platform behavior ||
|| Whether WAL record checksum is blake3 or sha256 by default | Record size, speed | blake3 default (speed), sha256 option; configurable per dataset ||
|| Logical vs physical record choice | Recovery complexity, record size | Logical records only (IDS has no buffer pool/page concept in this phase) ||
|| Whether group commit release rule is timer/K-counted/adaptive | Commit latency vs throughput | Start timer + count; adaptive evaluated in bench phase (ids-bench) ||
|| Dedup window size for OpRef | Memory vs outage survival | Sized from longest intended outage; expiry = duplicate-admission event ||
|| Whether fan-out is synchronous (blocking) or asynchronous | Write latency | Asynchronous fan-out with per-target cursor; synchronous only for cross-region durability policy ||
|| Whether `ids-write` owns `OpRef` generation or `ids-operation-ref` does | Allocator visibility | `ids-operation-ref` (Phase 056) generates; `ids-write` binds/validates ||
|| Whether concurrent-write resolution is LWW-only or domain-scoped | Conflict semantics | LWW by OrderingPos default; domain-scoped rule from `ids-consistency`/CRDT phases ||

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||---|---|---|
|| `ids-write` crate for write engine + WAL (not folders in existing crate) | Matches user directive: separate crates, not more folders ||
|| WAL = append-only, segmented, checksummed (blake3/sha256) | Durable, crash-recoverable, corruption-detectable; checksum restricted to allowed crypto ||
|| Logical (not physical) WAL records | IDS has no buffer pool/page concept; logical records are smaller and idempotent-replay-friendly ||
|| `OrderingPos` (u64 LSN) assigned at append, before sync | Monotonic total order; enables idempotent replay (`record_lsn > applied_lsn`) ||
|| fsync before ack; group commit batching | Durability guarantee; amortizes fixed flush cost across concurrent commits ||
|| OpRef (9-byte, 36^9) idempotency + dedup window | Exactly-once application under retries/replays; window expiry = duplicate-admission, not cleanup ||
|| Commit ≠ synchronization (local durable vs replicas applied) | Matches `ids-durability-policy` and `ids-consistency-profile` semantics; commit vs synchronization distinction explicit in CRATES.md ||
|| Fan-out via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only, per-target cursor | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; resumable ordered delivery; lag observability ||
|| Backpressure at unflushed-byte ceiling | Prevents unbounded WAL memory/disk growth under write storms ||
|| No `ids-crypto` runtime dependency | Preserves rule that `ids-crypto` does not depend on `ids-000-aa` (no cycles); type surface only ||
|| `saturating_add`/`saturating_sub` on all position/tick arithmetic | No overflow panics in distributed ordering/commit ||
|| Cargo workspace member at `C:/idfs/ids-write/` | Matches existing workspace layout (`ids-000-aa` at `C:/idfs/ids-000-aa/`) ||

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 014 creates a new, separate crate `ids-read` for the IDS project: distributed reads with replica-aware selection and fallback. It is **not** a folder inside an existing crate — per the IDS convention, new capabilities land in separate crates with subfolder organization. `ids-read` owns the full read lifecycle: issuing a read, selecting the closest/most fresh replica, enforcing a consistency profile (strong, bounded-staleness, session, eventual), fanning out parallel reads, aggregating scattered results, repairing stale replicas on the read path, and falling back through hinted-handoff holders when preferred replicas are unreachable. All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (opaque `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); there are zero direct networking dependencies (no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh). Allowed cryptography only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305. `ids-000-aa` remains the master crate holding all canonical types and sealed trait contracts; `ids-read` depends on it, `ids-carrier`, and `ids-crypto`-equivalent primitives, and is carrier-agnostic by construction.

The read design is Dynamo/Cassandra-lineage: N replicas per key, tunable read quorum R, quorum intersection R + W > N for freshness under normal operation, sloppy quorum + hinted handoff for availability during replica failure, read repair that merges divergent versions and writes back to stale replicas, and Merkle-tree anti-entropy as the periodic backstop. Session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, writes-follow-reads, monotonic-writes from Bayou) and causal visibility (vector clocks / version vectors / hybrid logical clocks) sit on top for clients that need ordering. PACELC frames the latency-consistency trade-off: in the absence of partitions the crate chooses between latency and consistency via the consistency profile; under partition it degrades to available stale reads or fails closed per profile.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-read` sits between the application/query layer and the carrier/transport layer, below any query decomposition (ids-query, Phase 015) and above `ids-carrier`/`ids-000-aa`. It is a local read orchestrator — it never opens a socket; it hands `Vec<u8>` read requests to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` and receives `Vec<u8>` responses.

```
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 014: ids-read (NEW CRATE)                  │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐     │

│  │  (digest/full,  │ │  fallback holders│ │  ness (VC/VV/HLC)│     │
│  │   write-back)   │ │  (sloppy quorum) │ │                  │     │

│  │  Ordered-read   │ │  Session state   │ │  Merkle anti-en- │     │

└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a single read:**
1. Application submits `Read { key, consistency_profile, read_quorum_R, session_token }`.
2. Read lifecycle validates the request, loads the replica preference list (N homes for the key) from `ids-000-aa` canonical types.
3. Replica selector ranks candidates by freshness (version vector / HLC) and proximity, picks the read quorum R (closest/freshest first), and identifies hinted-handoff fallback holders for any unreachable home.
4. Parallel reads fan out to R replicas (plus fallbacks) over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` as `Vec<u8>` payloads; each request carries the read's causal context (session vector clock).
5. Replies carry version stamps; the coordinator applies read repair: if digests/versions disagree, it performs a full read from the disagreeing replicas, merges by LWW/causal rule, and writes the merged value back to stale replicas before returning.
6. Scatter-gather aggregation merges partial results (for multi-key/range reads) into one answer; ordered-read visibility checks the session vector clock so reads never move backward.
7. Consistency profile enforcement gates the answer: strong waits for R with R + W > N; bounded-staleness accepts within the staleness bound; session enforces read-your-writes/monotonic-reads; eventual returns the first reply.
8. The merged, repaired, visibility-checked answer is returned to the application.

**No end-to-end path assumption:** a read may be served by any reachable replica; unreachable homes are handled by sloppy-quorum fallback to hinted-handoff holders, not by blocking.
