### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Read lifecycle and quorum intersection (R + W > N)

**Quorum reads/writes (Dynamo, Cassandra):** each key is replicated on N homes. A write succeeds after W homes ack; a read succeeds after R homes respond. Setting R + W > N guarantees the read quorum overlaps every recent write quorum, so at least one responding replica holds the latest acknowledged write under normal conditions (no sloppy quorum, no concurrent conflicting write). Latency is dictated by the slowest of the R (or W) responders, so R and W are normally < N to tolerate slow/unavailable nodes and cut the tail of the delay distribution.

**Decision for ids-read:** expose R and W as configurable per-read (or per-profile) parameters; default R + W > N for strong reads; allow R = 1 / W = N (read-one/write-all) and R = N / W = 1 (read-all/write-one) as profile extremes. Never wait for all N. A read contacts all N homes in parallel and returns as soon as R valid replies arrive (the others are cancelled/drained), matching Dynamo-style tail-latency behavior.

**Edge cases where R + W > N still yields stale reads (documented, not eliminated):** sloppy quorum (writes land outside the N homes), concurrent writes with divergent versions, write/read race (write reflected on only some replicas), partial-write success on fewer than W replicas, and restore-from-old-replica scenarios. These are handled by read repair, version stamps, and consistency-profile gating rather than by stronger quorum alone.

#### 3.2 Closest-replica selection and fallback (hinted handoff / sloppy quorum)

**Replica selection:** rank the N home replicas by a composite score: freshness (version-vector/HLC stamp relative to the read's causal context), observed RTT/latency history, and load. Select the R highest-scoring reachable homes as the read quorum. Unreachable homes are not retried synchronously; the coordinator proceeds with the reachable subset if it still meets R, otherwise falls back.

**Sloppy quorum (Dynamo/Cassandra/ScyllaDB):** when a home replica is down, reads/writes proceed on the first N *healthy* nodes from the preference list, which may fall outside the key's N homes. This preserves availability but breaks the R + W > N overlap guarantee globally: a read to home replicas may miss a write that landed on a sloppy (fallback) node.

**Hinted handoff (Cassandra default max_hint_window 3h):** when a preferred replica A is unreachable, the coordinator stores the write locally on a fallback D tagged with a hint naming A as the intended recipient. When A recovers, D replays the hint to A and deletes its local copy. If A stays down beyond the hint window, hints stop accumulating and full anti-entropy repair is required. ScyllaDB bounds hint disk usage to avoid hint-holder disk exhaustion.

**Decision for ids-read:** read path supports sloppy-quorum reads: if fewer than R homes respond, the read quorum may include hinted-handoff holders (temp nodes holding values for homes), with the read marked "sloppy" and freshness degraded. A hint record = {target_home_replica, key, value, version, write_timestamp, hint_ttl}; fallback holders retain hints and replay them to the home on recovery; hints expire after a configurable window (default aligned to 3h Cassandra precedent) after which full repair (Merkle anti-entropy, §3.9) reconciles. Hint accumulation is bounded per holder to prevent DoS; exceeding the bound rejects new hints and triggers repair.

#### 3.3 Ordered-read visibility and session guarantees

**Session guarantees (Bayou; four per-session guarantees):** read-your-writes (a write becomes visible to subsequent reads in the same session), monotonic reads (successive reads in a session observe monotonically non-decreasing versions), writes-follow-reads (a write after a read causally depends on that read), monotonic-writes (writes in a session complete in session order). Causal consistency = conjunction of the four session guarantees.

**Implementation sketch:** each session holds a session vector clock (highest-read VC + highest-write VC). A read tags its request with the session's read VC; a replica only serves versions whose dependencies are ≤ that VC (causal delivery). On receiving a reply, the session advances its read VC to the entry-wise max of its current VC and the reply's version VC (monotonic reads). A write carries the session's write VC and bumps the session's own entry; subsequent reads include it (read-your-writes). Writes-follow-reads is enforced by making a write's dependency vector include the versions read in the session.

**Hybrid logical clocks (Okapi; "Session Guarantees with Raft and HLC"):** HLC = (physical_time, logical_counter, replica_id) gives causality-respecting timestamps with low latency and tolerance to clock skew; never raw wall-clock for validity. Used as the per-version stamp and for tie-breaking concurrent versions. HLC eliminates write-delay for session guarantees while bounding skew.

**Decision for ids-read:** ordered-read visibility is session-scoped via a session vector clock / HLC carried on every read request and returned on every reply. Replicas enforce causal visibility before serving. Total order for concurrent versions is provided by LWW on (HLC, replica_id) — see §3.6.

#### 3.4 Replica freshness and consistency profile enforcement

**Freshness:** each replica tracks, per key, a version stamp (version vector or HLC). A read coordinator collects (value, version) from R replicas and selects the freshest version (dominates in VC, or higher HLC). Versions that neither dominate nor are dominated are concurrent → conflict → resolved by consistency profile / LWW / read repair.

**Consistency profiles (tunable per read):**
- **Strong:** wait for R replies with R + W > N; return the freshest version; guarantees no stale read under normal conditions.
- **Bounded staleness:** return a version no older than K versions or T time behind the latest (Cosmos DB bounded-staleness; Skybridge-style bounded-staleness target ~2s for 99.99998% of writes). Reads may be served by any replica whose lag ≤ bound.
- **Session:** enforce read-your-writes + monotonic reads via session VC; reads may go to a nearby replica as long as session causality holds.
- **Eventual (consistent prefix):** return the first reply; reads may lag and may be non-monotonic without session guarantees; consistent-prefix reads never appear out of order (reads lag writes but never reorder).

**PACELC framing:** in the absence of partitions, strong/profile reads trade latency for consistency (choose L or C); under partition the crate degrades to available stale reads (sloppy quorum + hinted handoff) or fails closed per profile — a PA/EL-style choice made per profile.

**Freshness leases (optional):** a freshness lease from a replica guarantees the replica will not serve a version older than the lease bound for the lease duration; reduces coordinator-side version comparison. Deferred — leases require clock synchronization assumptions the carrier-agnostic design avoids unless explicitly configured.

#### 3.5 Parallel reads, scatter-gather, and query aggregation

**Parallel fan-out/fan-in:** reads are sent to all N homes (or the R selected quorum) in parallel; the coordinator waits for the first R valid replies and treats the rest as best-effort (cancel or drain). This is the Dynamo/Cassandra "reads and writes always sent to all N replicas; R/W determine how many we wait for" model — it absorbs slow nodes and reduces tail latency.

**Scatter-gather (Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse, MongoDB):** for a multi-key or range read, the coordinator decomposes the read into per-replica/per-partition sub-reads, fans them out in parallel, each replica computes a local partial result, and the coordinator merges partial results into the final answer (gather). Fan-out is bounded by the replica set holding the needed keys; the more servers participate, the higher tail latency (straggler problem) — so replica selection and adaptive routing (route within a replica group / mirror set to avoid slow servers) matter.

**Aggregation:** partial results are merged per the query's aggregation kind (count → sum, sum → sum, min/max → min/max, group-by → merge groups, filter → union, sort → merge-sort). Aggregation is pure/local; no cross-replica state mutation during gather. Read repair applies per-key before aggregation.

**Decision for ids-read:** scatter-gather for multi-key reads: fan out one sub-read per replica shard holding any requested key, gather partial results, merge. Single-key reads use the read-quorum path (§3.1). Aggregation operators supported: count, sum, min, max, group-by, filter, sort (merge-sort). Fan-out degree is capped; slow replicas are skipped after a deadline keyed to read start time (no RTT-bound timers).

#### 3.6 Conflict resolution and version merge (last-writer-wins, MV-register)

**Concurrent versions:** when two versions are concurrent (neither VC-dominates), the coordinator must pick or keep both. Options:
- **Last-writer-wins (LWW-Register):** keep the version with the highest (HLC, replica_id) stamp; concurrent writes — one is silently lost. Acceptable when losing a concurrent write is tolerable (user profiles, config).
- **Multi-value register (MV-Register):** keep all concurrent values; return the set to the application/session to resolve (Dynamo shopping cart, Riak siblings). No silent data loss; shifts conflict resolution to the reader.
- **Vector-clock-based "sibling" detection:** return multiple concurrent values with their version vectors; read repair reconciles.

**Decision for ids-read:** support both LWW-Register (default, single answer) and MV-Register (no loss, reader resolves), selectable per consistency profile / per key. LWW uses HLC + replica_id tie-break, never raw wall-clock. MV-register returns siblings with version vectors; the client or a repair pass picks the winner.

#### 3.7 Read repair (digest + full read, write-back)

**Cassandra read repair:** on a read, the coordinator issues one full read to the fastest replica and digest reads (CL-1) to the rest. If digests disagree, it upgrades to full reads, merges by timestamp (LWW), and writes the merged value back to stale replicas *before* returning. Read repair happens on every read at the configured consistency level; background read repair (CL=ONE) does not help the current request.

**Anti-entropy vs read repair:** read repair is passive (fixes what a read touches); anti-entropy (Merkle tree, §3.9) is periodic and proactive (fixes everything, including never-read keys). They complement: read repair heals the hot path quickly; anti-entropy is the safety net for cold keys and long partitions.

**Decision for ids-read:** read repair on every quorum read: compare version stamps across the R replies; on disagreement, fetch full versions from disagreeing replicas, merge (LWW or MV-register sibling set), write-back the merged value to stale replicas before returning. Read repair is bounded (only replicas in the read quorum) so it never amplifies into a storm; a separate anti-entropy job handles full-key-space healing.

#### 3.8 Hinted handoff on the read path

When a read's preferred home is unreachable and the read quorum cannot be filled from homes, the coordinator may read from a hinted-handoff holder (a temp node that accepted a write for the down home). The returned value is tagged as "from hinted handoff" and treated as potentially stale relative to the home; read repair, when the home recovers, reconciles. Reads from hinted holders are allowed only for eventual/session profiles (not strong), since strong requires R + W > N overlap which sloppy quorum breaks.

#### 3.9 Read anti-entropy (Merkle tree) — periodic backstop

**Merkle-tree anti-entropy (Dynamo/Cassandra/Riak):** each replica builds a Merkle tree over its key range; peers exchange root hashes; equal roots ⇒ equal state (O(1) agreement check). On mismatch, descend only into differing subtrees (O(d·k) for k divergent keys out of n), exchanging only divergent keys. Cassandra divides key ranges into segments, computes per-segment hashes, exchanges ~32KB for 1M keys vs 1GB full comparison. Riak Active Anti-Energy uses persistent on-disk hash trees, updated in real time, regenerated weekly. Trade-off: anti-entropy cycles are slow (30–120s) → max staleness of that duration; it complements read repair/gossip, never replaces them.

**Decision for ids-read:** periodic Merkle anti-entropy as the convergence backstop: fixed-shape Merkle tree over the keyspace (bucketized by hashed key so two replicas build identical tree shapes regardless of which keys each holds); beacon ships bucket digests; diff descends into differing buckets; repair re-sends only drifted entries. BLAKE3 for hashing (allowed crypto). Runs on a schedule, independent of reads; bounds staleness for cold keys.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Stale read despite R + W > N (sloppy quorum, concurrent writes, partial writes) | Read repair + version stamps; consistency-profile gating; sloppy reads tagged/degraded; strong profile requires strict quorum overlap |
| Hint loss if hint-holder crashes before replay | Bound hint window; full Merkle anti-entropy reconciles after expiry; per-holder hint disk quota |
| Read-repair storm / amplification | Read repair bounded to replicas in the current read quorum; no cascading repair; separate scheduled anti-entropy |
| Version-vector / HLC clock skew corrupts ordering | HLC never raw wall-clock; HLC bounded skew; causality, not wall time, decides validity |
| Concurrent conflicting versions silently lost (LWW) | Offer MV-register per key/profile; siblings returned to reader for resolution |
| Read from unreplica/freshness-lagged replica | Freshness scoring (VC/HLC + latency + load); bounded-staleness profile rejects replicas beyond lag bound |
| Replay of old read responses | Nonce per read request; signed read envelopes (ed25519) over (coordinator, key, causal context, nonce) |
| Metadata bomb / oversized read request | Size/depth budgets before parsing; per-key and per-read request caps |
| Carrier-level DoS via read flood | Per-peer read rate limits; read-quorum R caps fan-out; no unbounded parallelism |
| Hinted-handoff holder serves stale value as fresh | Tag hint-sourced reads; strong profile disallows hint sources; read repair reconciles on recovery |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

Phase 014 depends on and integrates with:

| Crate | Role in Phase 014 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types (NodeID, ReplicaId, Key, Value, Version, CarrierType), sealed trait contracts; read preference list (N homes per key) |
| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` (CarrierType + Vec<u8>) — the only traffic boundary; all read requests/responses ride as `Vec<u8>` |
| `ids-crypto` (allowed set) | ed25519 signing/verification of read envelopes; sha256/blake3 for version/digest hashing; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 if read payloads are encrypted |
| `ids-query` (Phase 015, future) | Consumer — query decomposition feeds multi-key scatter-gather reads to ids-read |
| `ids-storage` (future/local) | Local replica store backend for the replica this node hosts; read repair write-back targets local storage |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-carrier::Endpoint` is the sole carrier boundary — `ids-read` never imports `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any carrier-specific type; opaque `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` only, preserving I-CARR-001 carrier-agnostic stance.
- Read requests and responses carry a canonical envelope: {coordinator, key, read_quorum_R, consistency_profile, session_VC, nonce, version_stamp, payload, ed25519_sig}.
- Replica preference list (N homes per key) is supplied by `ids-000-aa` canonical types; `ids-read` does not own topology.
- Read repair write-back targets the local replica's store (`ids-storage`) via the same carrier envelope when the stale replica is remote.
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS — works over any `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

### 6. Proposed File Structure (~90–1000 files in subfolders)

**Crate:** `ids-read` (new crate; depends on `ids-000-aa`, `ids-carrier`, allowed-crypto primitives; `serde`, `thiserror`, `blake3`, `bytes`, `parking_lot`, `dashmap`, `proptest`/`bolero`, `criterion`). Target ~400–700 production-grade files, all under `src/` in subfolders; crate-root files (`Cargo.toml`, `lib.rs`, `constants.rs`, `error.rs`) directly in `src/`.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Read quorum (R + W > N)
```
Read { key, R, profile, session_VC, nonce }
homes = preference_list(key)   // N homes from ids-000-aa
candidates = rank(homes) by freshness(score = VC/HLC, latency, load)
quorum = top R reachable candidates
if |reachable| < R: quorum += hinted_handoff_holders (sloppy; mark degraded)
fan out Read to quorum in parallel over ids-carrier::Endpoint
wait for first R valid replies (deadline = read_start + timeout)
return freshest version among replies; apply read repair on disagreement
```

#### 7.2 Closest-replica selection
```
score(replica) = w_fresh * freshness(replica, key)
               + w_lat  * (1 / observed_latency(replica))
               + w_load * (1 / replica_load(replica))
freshness = 1 if replica.version[key] >= session_VC else decay(lag)
select top R by score among reachable
```

#### 7.3 Read repair (digest + full read + write-back)
```
replies = [(value_i, version_i, replica_i)] for i in quorum
if all versions equal: return value
else:
  full = fetch full value+version from disagreeing replicas
  merged = merge(full)   // LWW: max(HLC, replica_id); MV-register: sibling set
  write_back(merged) to stale replicas (before returning)
  return merged
```

#### 7.4 Consistency profile gating
```
strong:    accept iff R replies received AND quorum overlap (R + W > N) holds
bs(K,T):   accept iff version.lag <= K versions OR age <= T
session:   accept iff version >= session.read_VC (read-your-writes, monotonic reads)
eventual:  accept first valid reply (may be stale, non-monotonic)
```

#### 7.5 Session guarantees (VC / HLC)
```
read(request):  tag with session.read_VC; replica serves versions deps <= session.read_VC
on reply: session.read_VC = entrywise_max(session.read_VC, reply.version_VC)
write:  session.write_VC[own] += 1; write carries session.write_VC as deps
subsequent reads include session.write_VC (read-your-writes)
writes_follow_reads: write.deps ⊇ versions read in session
```

#### 7.6 Version merge (LWW / MV-register)
```
LWW:  winner = version with max (HLC, replica_id)  // tie-break by replica_id
MV:   keep all concurrent versions; return sibling set with version vectors
concurrent(a, b):  !(a.VC <= b.VC) && !(b.VC <= a.VC)
```

#### 7.7 Hinted handoff
```
hint = {target_home, key, value, version, write_time, ttl}
on write failure to home A: store hint on fallback D; ack write (sloppy)
on A recovery: D replays hint to A; D deletes local copy
if now - write_time > ttl (default 3h): drop hint; full anti-entropy reconciles
bound hint store per holder; reject new hints when full
```

#### 7.8 Merkle anti-entropy
```
tree = MerkleTree over hashed keyspace (fixed 2^depth buckets)
beacon = bucket_digests (sparse, non-empty buckets only)
diff(ours, theirs): descend differing buckets; O(d·k) for k divergent keys
repair: re-send only drifted entries; full-state sync avoided
hash = blake3
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Replica preference list source:** the N homes per key come from `ids-000-aa` canonical types, but the exact topology/membership API (how homes are discovered and updated) is undefined; `ids-read` consumes it read-only.
2. **Local storage backend:** read repair write-back targets a local store; whether `ids-storage` exists or a local KV trait is needed is undecided (Phase-local, not part of this crate).
3. **Read timeout value:** the per-read deadline is keyed to read start time (no RTT timers), but the absolute timeout default is workload-dependent and unquantified.
4. **Hint window default:** Cassandra precedent is 3h; the IDS default hint TTL and per-holder hint disk quota need product decision.
5. **LWW vs MV-register default:** which conflict policy is default per key is undecided; profile-keyed selection is the mechanism, the default is a product choice.
6. **Session clock size:** unbounded session VC growth under many replicas; compaction/pruning policy for session state unresolved.
7. **Encryption of read payloads:** xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 are allowed but whether read envelopes are encrypted by default is undecided (ed25519 signatures are mandatory for integrity).
8. **Anti-entropy interval:** periodic Merkle anti-entropy cycle length (30–120s precedent) trades staleness vs bandwidth; default unmeasured.
9. **HLC skew bound:** HLC tolerates clock skew but liveness (session staleness detection timeouts) needs deployment tuning; never used for validity.
10. **Cross-region read routing:** proximity scoring uses observed latency; multi-region topology awareness (local-quorum style) is future work.

-- -

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-read` crate, not subfolder | IDS convention: new capabilities in separate crates with subfolder organization; keeps existing crates focused |
| Read quorum R + W > N for strong reads | Guarantees read quorum overlaps every recent write quorum → no stale reads under normal conditions (Dynamo/Cassandra) |
| Sloppy quorum + hinted handoff for availability | Preserves read/write progress during replica failure; breaks strict overlap → reads tagged sloppy/degraded, reconciled via read repair + anti-entropy |
| Read repair on every quorum read | Heals the hot path quickly (digest/full/merge/write-back); anti-entropy is the cold-key backstop |
| Session VC / HLC for ordered reads | Bayou session guarantees (ryw, mr, mw, wfr); HLC avoids wall-clock validity and write-delay (Okapi precedent) |
| LWW default, MV-register optional | LWW single answer for most keys; MV-register keeps concurrent siblings where no loss is tolerable; per-key/profile selectable |
| Parallel fan-out to all N, wait for R | Absorbs slow nodes, cuts tail latency (Dynamo model) |
| Merkle anti-entropy backstop | Locates divergence in O(d·k) vs O(n) full-state; bounded staleness for cold keys (Riak/Cassandra precedent) |
| All traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint | Carrier-agnostic; zero std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |
| Allowed crypto: ed25519, sha256, blake3, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305 only | Matches IDS crypto policy; no x25519; ed25519 signatures mandatory on read envelopes |
| Deadlines keyed to read start time, not RTT | Correct over any latency; avoids RTT-bound timeout misfire |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 015 creates `ids-query`, the IDS crate for distributed query planning and execution. It owns the query path: **plan a query, decompose it into per-partition/per-node/per-region fragments, execute via scatter-gather, combine intermediate results, and return a final result**. Contents per CRATES.md §15 and prompts.txt entry 15: query planner, targeted query execution, partition maps, indexes, predicates, ownership metadata, scatter-gather execution, distributed aggregation (count, sum, min, max, group, filter, sort), cross-regional queries, intermediate result combination.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned Citus coordinator/worker fragment planning and result merge, MongoDB mongos targeted vs scatter-gather routing, Aerospike scatter-gather streaming, Dremel serving-tree execution with parallel aggregation on the way up, Drill foreman/fragment model, Presto coordinator/tasks/stages, Calcite optimizer framework, Volcano/Cascades cost-based optimization, Spanner split-region execution plans, CockroachDB per-node planning, two-phase aggregation (local partial + final combine), HyperLogLog approximate distinct count, consistent hashing/vnodes/token ranges for partition ownership, semi-join data reduction, function vs data shipping, top-k threshold algorithms, speculative execution/straggler speculation, graceful partial-result degradation, continuous queries.

A skeleton `ids-query` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-query/`. This plan specifies creation from scratch; no source modifications are made in this phase.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-query` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors) and `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram send/receive). It is layered so planning, decomposition, execution, and combination are independent modules that compose:

```

│                 Phase 015: ids-query (THIS CRATE)                   │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │\n│  │   planner   │ │  decomposer  │ │   fragment      │ │ scatter │ │
│  │ (SQL/DSL →  │ │ (partition-  │ │   executor      │ │ gather  │ │
│  │  logical/   │ │  aware       │ │ (per-Endpoint   │ │ executor│ │
│  │  physical   │ │  fragment    │ │  fragment +     │ │ (merge) │ │
│  │  plan)      │ │  plan)       │ │  predicate push)│ │         │ │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │

│  │  (count,    │ │  result      │ │  query          │ │ lookup  │ │
│  │   sum, min, │ │  combination │ │  (region routing│ │ (planner│ │

│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                               │ Endpoint (ids-carrier, opaque)
┌──────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐
│              PARTITION / NODE / REGION ENDPOINTS (via ids-carrier)  │
│  ids-read · ids-write · ids-storage · region replicas · …          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CARRIER BOUNDARY (no std::net / tokio::net): ids-carrier::Endpoint only
```

**Data flow:** client submits a query → planner produces a logical plan → decomposer maps plan fragments to partitions/nodes/regions via ownership metadata + partition maps → scatter executor dispatches fragments to target Endpoints → each target executes locally (predicate pushdown, index use, local aggregation) → results stream back as opaque `Vec<u8>` → gather executor combines intermediate results (partial-aggregate merge, k-way sorted merge, top-k reduction) → final result returned to client.

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- Query decomposition is partition/node/region aware; a fragment targets one or more Endpoints.
- Predicates are pushed down to the fragment's owner so only results (not raw rows) cross Endpoints (function shipping preferred over data shipping).
- All inter-Endpoint traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-query` never addresses by IP/port.
- Crypto: signatures over query fragments (ed25519), result confidentiality (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305), fragment/result integrity (blake3/sha256). No other algorithms.
- Distributed aggregation uses two-phase: local partial aggregate per fragment + final combine at the coordinator/gatherer; approximate distinct count via HyperLogLog over blake3/sha256 hashes when exactness is not required.
- Cross-regional queries route through region-aware planning; residency constraints are hard filters (fail closed if no in-region Endpoint).
- Partial results / graceful degradation: return partial coverage rather than total failure when a region is unreachable (configurable).
- Idempotent query fragments (re-dispatch on straggler/timeout to an alternate Endpoint); speculative execution for tail-latency.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Query decomposition — coordinator/fragment model

Citus-style decomposition: a coordinator holds shard/partition metadata, partitions each query into independent fragments per shard, assigns fragments to workers, oversees execution, and merges results. Each fragment runs independently on its shard; no inter-fragment coordination during execution; result merge happens on the way up. Dremel's serving tree generalizes this: a root routes queries down a tree; intermediate servers perform parallel aggregation of partial results on the way up; leaves scan local tablets. Drill's foreman model: the node receiving a query drives it end-to-end, distributing work across cluster for data locality.

**Decision for ids-query:** adopt a coordinator/decomposer model where one Endpoint (or a designated planner Endpoint) owns decomposition, fragments target data-owner Endpoints, and results merge on the way up through a gatherer. Planner may be co-located with the client or a dedicated Endpoint.

#### 3.2 Targeted vs scatter-gather execution

MongoDB mongos: queries including the shard key route to specific shards (targeted); queries without the shard key become scatter-gather broadcast to all shards, then results merged. Scatter-gather is efficient for full-collection scans but inefficient for routine targeted lookups. Aerospike clients execute scatter-gather in parallel across nodes with chunked streaming and cursors.

**Decision for ids-query:** support both — targeted execution when the predicate references a partition/ownership key (route to owning Endpoint only), scatter-gather when it does not (broadcast fragment to all relevant Endpoints, merge results). Ownership metadata decides which.

#### 3.3 Partition maps and ownership metadata

Every partitioned system must answer "which machine owns this key" via routing metadata. Stale routing (one epoch behind) sends requests to a node that already handed the range away, causing divergence; ownership epochs convert racy handoffs into detectable errors. Cassandra uses consistent hashing token ranges; vnodes split each node's range into many small ranges for better balance and minimal movement on topology change. Rendezvous hashing scores every server per key (good for small server sets, no ring).

**Decision for ids-query:** partition map = mapping from `PartitionId` → set of owning `Endpoint`s with an epoch; ownership metadata versioned with epochs so stale maps cause detectable errors, not silent divergence. Consistent hashing (with vnodes) as the default partitioning scheme, pluggable.

#### 3.4 Indexes and predicate pushdown

Distributed indexes have PARTITION (distributes index rows), CLUSTERING (orders rows within partition), INCLUDE (covering columns to avoid table round-trips). Local secondary indexes are async/eventual; global indexes require distributed maintenance. Predicate pushdown pushes selection operators as close to the data source as possible, reducing transmission/computation cost. Partition pruning uses partition metadata to skip irrelevant partitions.

**Decision for ids-query:** index module helps the planner choose indexes and prune partitions; predicates are pushed into fragments so only matching results cross Endpoints. Index lookups themselves target partition-scoped Endpoints.

#### 3.5 Distributed aggregation — two-phase combine

Two-phase aggregation: local partial aggregate per partition/node (map), then hash-redistribute partial states on GROUP BY keys and final total-aggregate (reduce). R2 SQL scatter-gather aggregations compute pre-aggregates on workers and combine at coordinator; shuffling aggregations add HAVING/ORDER BY via local finalization + k-way merge. SkyWalking BanyanDB: map on data nodes, reduce on liaison nodes.

**Decision for ids-query:** aggregation module implements two-phase combine for count/sum/min/max (decomposable, duplicate-insensitive → trivial combine); average requires (sum, count) pairs; group-by uses hash redistribution of partial states on the group keys; filter and sort are embarrassingly parallel per partition with a final k-way merge for sort.

#### 3.6 Approximate distinct count

Exact COUNT(DISTINCT) does not scale across workers (overlapping records; pulling all distinct to one machine doesn't scale). Options: HyperLogLog / HyperLogLog++ sketches with provable error bounds, fixed memory (~c*8 bytes for precision threshold c), ~1.62% relative error at default precision. Elasticsearch cardinality aggregation and Snowflake HLL both use this. Combine is associative (HLL_COMBINE merges states), making it distributed-friendly.

**Decision for ids-query:** offer exact count/sum/min/max and an approximate distinct-count via HyperLogLog over blake3/sha256 hashes, with a configurable error/precision trade-off. Allowed hashes only.

#### 3.7 Cross-regional queries and data residency

Cross-region latency dominates query time; the goal is to minimize data movement — route queries to the region where data lives and avoid cross-region shuffles. Locality-aware optimization incorporates cross-region latency as a first-class cost input to prefer local plans. Data residency/domiciling constrains replicas to approved geographies; region-locked routing sends each request only to endpoints inside the allowed region, covering fallback/load-balancing (fail closed if no in-region endpoint).

**Decision for ids-query:** cross-region module adds region-aware planning: prefer local-region execution, only consult remote regions if needed; residency is a hard filter; all cross-region fragment dispatch is via Endpoint, region metadata from ids-routing/ids-000-aa.

#### 3.8 Intermediate result combination

Intermediate results combine via partial-aggregate merge (sum of counts, max of maxes, etc.) or k-way sorted merge of result streams (coordinator reads row-by-row from each worker, picks winner by sort order, supports early LIMIT termination). Vectorwise-style recycling reuses materialized intermediate results across queries with subsumption and proactive rewriting; materialization vs pipelining is a workload trade-off.

**Decision for ids-query:** gather module combines intermediate results per operator: aggregate merge for group-by, k-way merge for sort, top-k reduction (keep top-k per partition then merge). Optional intermediate-result caching keyed by fragment hash.

#### 3.9 Fault tolerance — stragglers, speculation, partial results

BigQuery/Dremel: deterministic and idempotent tasks allow restarts; straggler detection re-executes slow tasks redundantly past a threshold. Cassandra speculative execution: pre-emptively re-send idempotent queries to another node after a p99.9 latency threshold; whichever replies first wins. Vespa graceful degradation: return partial results with degraded coverage rather than total failure when a query can't complete in time.

**Decision for ids-query:** fragments are idempotent (re-dispatch on straggler/timeout to an alternate Endpoint); speculative re-execution for tail latency; graceful degradation returns partial coverage when regions are unreachable (configurable coverage threshold).

#### 3.10 Query shipping vs data shipping

Function shipping (worker executes query, returns result) vs data shipping (coordinator reads raw data, executes locally) is a fundamental trade-off: function shipping minimizes data movement but needs compute at data; data shipping is simpler but moves more data. Data locality favors shipping the function to the data.

**Decision for ids-query:** default to function shipping (fragments execute at data-owner Endpoints, only results return); data shipping available as an opt-in for small result sets where shipping raw data is cheaper.

#### 3.11 Top-k execution

Distributed top-k uses threshold algorithms (TA, NRA) and variants (TPUT three-phase uniform threshold); KLEE trades result quality vs performance/bandwidth. Massively parallel top-k: local top-k per partition (bounded to k), then merge reduces candidate sets; sorted index access ~20× faster than random access for large lists.

**Decision for ids-query:** sort+limit pushed to fragments as local top-k; gatherer merges per-partition top-k streams into a global top-k (k-way merge with early termination).

#### 3.12 Continuous queries

Continuous queries run over dynamic (streaming) tables and never terminate, producing dynamic results semantically equivalent to batch re-execution on snapshots (Flink dynamic tables, BigQuery continuous queries, Hazelcast stream SQL). Distinct from batch; long-running, backpressured, restartable.

**Decision for ids-query:** continuous-query support is a documented future dimension (out of scope for Phase 015 MVP); the planner/fragment/executor structure is designed to be extensible to streaming.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Fragment interception/tampering in transit | ed25519 signature over fragment + payload; blake3/sha256 integrity; verification at target before execution |
| Result confidentiality | xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 encryption of result payloads between Endpoints |
| Replay of a fragment | Nonce + per-Endpoint sequence; replay cache bounded with TTL eviction |
| Stale partition map → wrong owner | Ownership epochs; epoch mismatch is a detectable error, triggers map refresh |
| Straggler/timeout stalls query | Idempotent fragment re-dispatch to alternate Endpoint; speculative execution; configurable timeouts |
| Partial region failure → total failure | Graceful degradation: return partial coverage rather than fail; configurable coverage threshold |
| Distinct-count accuracy | HyperLogLog approximate with explicit error bounds; exact mode available |
| Metadata bomb in partition map | Size/depth budgets on ownership metadata before parsing |
| Cross-region data residency violation | Region is a hard filter; fail closed if no in-region Endpoint |
| Unauthorized query execution | Query fragment signed by client key; target verifies signature + grant (ed25519) |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

| Crate | Role in Phase 015 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `PartitionId`, `RecordId`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, sealed trait contracts, invariants, errors — reused verbatim |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); all traffic rides here; no direct socket/transport imports |
| `ids-crypto` | ed25519 sign/verify, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3 — type-level + primitive IDs; no new algorithms |
| `ids-read` | Local read path consumed by fragments executing at data-owner Endpoints |
| `ids-write` | Not a dependency (query is read-only); write path out of scope |
| `ids-routing` | Region-aware / locality-aware Endpoint resolution for cross-regional and targeted routing |
| `ids-broadcast` | Future: reliable/causal/total-order delivery of fragments if needed |
| `ids-durability-policy` | Future: durability conditions per query |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-query` produces fragment payloads (opaque `Vec<u8>`) dispatched via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; targets execute locally using `ids-read`.
- Partition maps and ownership metadata derive from `ids-000-aa` types (`PartitionId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, epochs).
- Region routing for cross-regional queries delegates to `ids-routing`; no `ids-query` knowledge of geography beyond `RegionId`.
- All fragment/result signing and encryption uses `ids-crypto` primitives only.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Query plan & fragment

```
Query { id: PlanId, sql/dsl, logical_plan, physical_plan }
PlanFragment { id: FragmentId, operator_tree, target_endpoints: Vec<Endpoint>,
               predicate_pushdown: bool, idempotent: bool, nonce: [u8;32] }
FragmentResult { fragment_id, partial_state: Vec<u8>, coverage: f32, blake3_digest }
```

#### 7.2 Partition map & ownership (epoch-versioned)

```
PartitionMap { entries: Map<PartitionId, PartitionOwnership> }
PartitionOwnership { endpoints: Vec<Endpoint>, epoch: u64, version: u64 }
// lookup(partition) -> owning Endpoint set; epoch mismatch → detectable error → refresh
```

#### 7.3 Two-phase aggregation combine

```
// Phase 1 (per fragment): partial = aggregate(local_rows)
// Phase 2 (gatherer): combined = combine(partial_1, …, partial_n)
// count: sum; sum: sum; min: min; max: max; avg: (sum,count) → sum/count
// group-by: hash-redistribute partial states on group keys, then total aggregate
// distinct: HLL_COMBINE(partial sketches) → HLL_ESTIMATE
```

#### 7.4 Scatter-gather vs targeted routing

```
// targeted: predicate references partition key → route fragment to owning Endpoint only
// scatter-gather: no partition key → broadcast fragment to all relevant Endpoints,
//                 gatherer merges results (dedup if overlapping replicas)
```

#### 7.5 K-way sorted merge (sort + top-k)

```
// each fragment returns its local top-k sorted stream
// gatherer opens a stream per fragment, compares current row by sort order,
// emits winner, advances that stream; early termination on LIMIT
```

#### 7.6 Speculative re-execution

```
// fragment dispatched to primary Endpoint; if no response by p99.9 threshold,
// re-dispatch idempotent fragment to alternate Endpoint; first valid result wins;
// cancelled request still executes at primary (idempotent, no side effects)
```

#### 7.7 Graceful degradation

```
// coverage = fraction of target Endpoints that returned valid results
// if coverage >= threshold → return partial result with degraded coverage flag
// else → fail the query (configurable)
```

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-015.1 | Query decomposition | A query referencing a partition key decomposes into one fragment targeting the owning Endpoint; non-partitioned queries become scatter-gather over all relevant Endpoints (unit test) |
| AC-015.2 | Targeted execution | Query with partition-key predicate executes only at the owner; no broadcast to unrelated Endpoints (trace assertion) |
| AC-015.3 | Scatter-gather merge | Full-collection query returns combined results from all Endpoints; duplicates from overlapping replicas deduped (integration test) |
| AC-015.4 | Predicate pushdown | Only matching rows/results cross Endpoints; raw rows are not shipped unless data-shipping opt-in (integration test) |
| AC-015.5 | Two-phase aggregation | count/sum/min/max combine correctly across fragments under reorder/loss/dup (property test, 100k iterations) |
| AC-015.6 | Group-by | Distributed group-by matches single-node result on identical data (integration test) |
| AC-015.7 | Approximate distinct count | HyperLogLong result within configured error bound of exact count (unit test) |
| AC-015.8 | Cross-region routing | Query prefers local-region execution; residency constraint fails closed when no in-region Endpoint (unit test) |
| AC-015.9 | Sort + top-k | Distributed sort produces globally sorted stream; top-k early termination returns k rows (integration test) |
| AC-015.10 | Fault tolerance | Idempotent fragment re-dispatched to alternate Endpoint on straggler/timeout; first valid result wins (chaos test) |
| AC-015.11 | Speculative execution | Tail-latency query completed by speculative replica; cancelled primary still executes idempotently (chaos test) |
| AC-015.12 | Graceful degradation | Partial result returned with degraded coverage when a region is unreachable, above threshold (chaos test) |
| AC-015.13 | Security | Fragment signed ed25519; target verifies before execution; tampered fragment rejected; result encrypted xchacha20poly1305 (security test) |
| AC-015.14 | Replay resistance | Replayed fragment rejected by nonce+sequence replay cache (bounded, TTL) (security test) |
| AC-015.15 | Carrier agnosticism | `ids-query` compiles and behaves identically with zero direct dependencies on TCP/IP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, libp2p; all traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (build + audit) |
| AC-015.16 | Crypto constraint | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3 used; no other algorithms (dependency audit) |
| AC-015.17 | Determinism | Same query + same partition map → identical result (determinism test) |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Query language scope:** Which DSL/SQL subset does `ids-query` support natively (SELECT/WHERE/GROUP BY/ORDER BY/LIMIT vs full SQL)? Defer detailed grammar to implementation; planner designed to be extensible.
2. **Planner Endpoint selection:** Is the planner co-located with the client, a dedicated Endpoint, or elected? All three work; decision deferred to deployment topology.
3. **Continuous queries:** Streaming/continuous query support is out of scope for Phase 015 MVP; the fragment/executor structure is designed to be extensible but not specified here.
4. **Intermediate cache eviction:** Optional cached intermediate results keyed by fragment hash; eviction policy (size/age/ttl) unresolved.
5. **Coverage threshold default:** The graceful-degradation coverage threshold is workload-dependent; default is a placeholder pending measurement.
6. **HLL precision default:** Approximate distinct-count precision threshold (memory vs error trade-off) needs workload tuning.
7. **Join support:** Distributed joins (broadcast join vs shuffle join) are documented as a future dimension; not in Phase 015 contents.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Coordinator/decomposer + gatherer model (Citus/Dremel/Drill) | Decomposition is coordinator-driven; workers scan local partitions in parallel; results merge on the way up; matches IDS partition/node/region model |
| Targeted execution when partition-key predicate present; scatter-gather otherwise | MongoDB mongos precedent: targeted is efficient, scatter-gather is the fallback for unkeyed scans |
| Predicate pushdown / function shipping default | Minimizes data movement across Endpoints; only results cross the carrier boundary |
| Two-phase aggregation (partial + combine) | count/sum/min/max/group decomposable; combine is associative; bounded coordinator memory |
| Approximate distinct count via HyperLogLog (blake3/sha256) | Exact COUNT(DISTINCT) doesn't scale across workers; HLL has fixed memory and provable error bounds |
| Epoch-versioned partition map + ownership metadata | Stale maps cause detectable errors, not silent divergence; consistent hashing with vnodes as default partitioning |
| Region-aware planning + hard residency filter | Cross-region latency is a first-class cost input; residency fails closed |
| Idempotent fragments + speculative re-execution + graceful degradation | Fault tolerance for stragglers, timeouts, and partial region failure without total query failure |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule (CRATES.md §9); no IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/libp2p |
| Crypto restricted to ed25519 / xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 / sha256 / blake3 | Allowed-crypto mandate (CRATES.md; prompts.txt) |
| New `ids-query` crate, not subfolder | Separate crate per IDS convention (CRATES.md §15); keeps existing crates focused |

# PHASE 016:

## Phase 016 — Create the ids-routing crate: Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

Note on numbering: prompts.txt entry 16 is ids-routing ("Create the ids-routing crate: Data-aware request resolution, not network packet routing."). plan-016.md covers the ids-routing crate.

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 016 creates `ids-routing`, the IDS data-aware request routing crate. Purpose per prompts.txt entry 16 and CRATES.md §16: **data-aware request resolution, not network packet routing**. Contents: Request resolver, locality-aware routing (geography, health, load, freshness, capacity, ownership, consistency), replica-aware routing, near-to-far routing, adaptive routing, routing tables, path selection, loop prevention.

The crate is **carrier-agnostic**: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-routing` consumes hashing/signing type surface from `ids-000-aa`, no direct `ids-crypto` runtime dep where it would create a cycle — aligned to the rule that `ids-crypto` does not depend on `ids-000-aa`). `ids-000-aa` is the master crate with all canonical types and sealed trait contracts; `ids-routing` depends on `ids-000-aa`.

Routing here is **application-layer request resolution**: given a request keyed by object/entity id plus routing hints, select one or more candidate replicas/endpoints and order the attempt sequence. It is explicitly *not* IP/packet forwarding, BGP/OSPF, or any network-layer concern. Routing decisions are driven by data locality (which replica holds/shards the key), health, load, freshness, capacity, ownership, and consistency requirements — signals that live above the carrier.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned locality-aware request distribution (LARD, ACM SIGPLAN), content-based distribution, replica-aware/sticky routing (ClickHouse Cloud), near-to-far and prefix-affinity routing (Ray Serve / vLLM / NVIDIA Dynamo KV-aware routing), topology-aware routing (Kubernetes), capacity-aware load balancing (Google global LB), consistency-aware read routing (FLAIR NSDI'20, MongoDB read preference / nearest), gossip-based routing table dissemination and finite-time convergent gossiping, loop-free distance vector with sequence numbers (DSDV/AODV), application-layer routing requirements (Pamela Zave), DHT/Kademlia application-level lookup (libp2p Kad-DHT, XOR distance, k-buckets, iterative FIND_NODE), TiKV replica selection (leader/follower/mixed strategies, store health/liveness, label matching for data locality), request coalescing / single-flight (deduplicate identical in-flight requests), Merkle Search Trees for efficient state-based sync in open networks, vector clocks / Lamport clocks for causal ordering, blake3 content-addressed identifiers (iroh blobs), ed25519-signed routing metadata, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 AEAD encrypted routing envelopes, failover and health-check routing, adaptive path selection (DARD), and Merkle-tree routing-table synchronization.

A skeleton `ids-routing` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-routing/`. This plan specifies creation from scratch; no source modifications are made in this phase.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-routing` is the request-resolution layer for all IDS inbound requests. It receives a request (key + optional routing hints + consistency requirement) from `ids-client`/`ids-gateway` and returns an ordered list of candidate endpoints (each an `ids-carrier::Endpoint`) to try, plus a routing decision record. It owns: the request resolver, routing tables (locality, replica, health, load, freshness, capacity, ownership, consistency indexes), near-to-far candidate ordering, adaptive path selection, loop prevention (hop count + visited set + sequence numbers), replica selection (leader/follower/mixed/prefer-leader/learner), request coalescing (single-flight per key), and routing-table gossip/dissemination.

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- Routing is data-aware, application-layer: selects endpoint(s) by key/ownership/locality, not by IP or packet header.
- All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS or any carrier import.
- Routing table entries keyed by blake3/sha256 content hash of the request key (content-addressed routing keys).
- Locality signals: geography (zone/region), health (reachable/healthy/unhealthy), load (queue depth / in-flight), freshness (last update / staleness bound), capacity (headroom vs quota), ownership (which replica owns the shard/key), consistency (read preference: leader / follower / nearest / any with staleness bound).
- Near-to-far: order candidates by a composite cost score (locality + load + health + freshness + capacity), try nearest first, fail over on error.
- Adaptive path selection: cost weights adjust from observed latency/success/failure telemetry (feedback loop).
- Loop prevention: per-request hop-count TTL + visited-endpoint set + routing sequence numbers; discard/return error on loop detection.
- Replica selection strategies: leader-only, follower-prefer, mixed, prefer-leader, learner (TiKV-pattern), with store health/liveness gating.
- Request coalescing: identical in-flight requests for the same key coalesce into one leader + waiters (single-flight), protecting downstream under thundering herd.
- Routing-table dissemination: gossip-based epidemic sync (finite-time convergent gossiping) so every node builds a convergent local view without central coordination; Merkle digest anti-entropy optional for table reconciliation.
- Crypto surface: `Checksum([u8;32])` (blake3/sha256), `Signature` (ed25519) from `ids-000-aa`; optional AEAD envelope (xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305) for encrypted routing metadata; no direct `ids-crypto` runtime dependency.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Data-Aware Request Resolution vs Network Packet Routing

The foundational distinction (Pamela Zave, "Requirements for Routing in the Application Layer"): network-layer routing decides which node receives a packet based on addresses in headers; application-layer routing is a coordination mechanism that decides which server/application handles a message based on message content and application state. ids-routing is the latter. It resolves a request key to candidate endpoints using data locality and runtime signals — the carrier merely delivers opaque `Vec<u8>` payloads between them. Implication: no IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS assumptions; routing decisions survive re-framing by any carrier; the resolver is pure over `(RequestKey, RoutingHints, ConsistencyReq, LocalView) -> OrderedCandidateList`.

#### 3.2 Locality-Aware Routing — Geography, Health, Load, Freshness, Capacity, Ownership

**Content-based / locality-aware request distribution** (LARD, ACM SIGPLAN Notices): a front-end directs requests to back-ends using requested content plus back-end load, improving cache locality and partitioning storage. ids-routing adopts the same principle keyed on blake3/sha256(request key).

Signals maintained per endpoint (in the locality routing table):
- **Geography**: zone/region of the endpoint; prefer same-zone/region (Kubernetes Topology Aware Routing pattern; LARS latency-aware route servers).
- **Health**: healthy / degraded / unhealthy / unknown, from health checks and carrier-level liveness; unhealthy endpoints excluded until recovered.
- **Load**: current in-flight count / queue depth / recent latency; lower load preferred (least-loaded / power-of-two-choices).
- **Freshness**: staleness of the endpoint's replica relative to the key's latest write; consistency-aware reads filter by max staleness (FLAIR consistency-aware routing; MongoDB maxStalenessSeconds).
- **Capacity**: headroom vs configured quota; near-saturated endpoints deprioritized (capacity-aware load balancing, Google global LB).
- **Ownership**: which endpoint owns the shard/range containing the key (shard ownership, Uber Shard Manager pattern); ownership is the primary filter — only owners (or allowed followers) are candidates.

Candidate score = weighted sum of normalized signals; weights adaptive (Section 3.6). The resolver returns candidates sorted ascending by score (near-to-far).

#### 3.3 Replica-Aware Routing — Leader / Follower / Mixed / Learner

TiKV replica selection (client-go): each region has multiple replicas with one leader. Read types: leader-only, follower-prefer, mixed (any leader/follower), prefer-leader, learner. Selection considers: leader status, store health/slowness, label matching for data locality, previous attempt history, learner status. Writes always go to the leader; reads may route to followers to balance load (read preference primary/secondary/nearest, MongoDB).

ids-routing maps this: `ReplicaReadStrategy { LeaderOnly, FollowerPrefer, Mixed, PreferLeader, Learner }`. Consistency requirement picks the strategy:
- Strong/linearizable read → leader only.
- Stale-acceptable read → follower / mixed / nearest with staleness bound.
- Session/read-after-write → sticky to the replica that served the prior write (replica-aware routing / sticky sessions, ClickHouse Cloud; best-effort, remapped on rescale).

Store health/liveness gating: track reachable/unreachable/unknown per endpoint; exclude unreachable until recovered; request forwarding (leader-unreachable → follower proxies to leader) as optional fallback.

#### 3.4 Near-to-Far Routing and Adaptive Path Selection

**Near-to-far**: candidates ordered by composite locality cost; try nearest first; on failure/circuit-breaker, fall back to next. Ray Serve PrefixCacheAffinityRouter and NVIDIA Dynamo KV-aware routing combine cache/locality overlap with active load: a cache-hot but overloaded worker can lose to a colder worker with lower projected total cost (cache locality + remaining prefill/decode work). ids-routing's cost model: `cost = w_locality·geo + w_load·queue + w_health·penalty + w_freshness·staleness + w_capacity·saturation`, weights tuned adaptively from telemetry.

**Adaptive path selection** (DARD, ICFEM adaptive routing): move traffic from overloaded paths to underloaded paths without central coordination; converges to a Nash equilibrium. ids-routing adapts: each node updates local weights from observed success/failure/latency; gossip disseminates weight deltas; routing converges under stable load. Reinforcement-learning / SLA-based path selection (arxiv adaptive path selection) noted as future enhancement; baseline is deterministic weighted cost + feedback.

#### 3.5 Routing Tables, Path Selection, and Dissemination

Routing tables: per-node bounded view of endpoints + signals (DHT principle: limited links, bounded state; Pastry neighborhood set / leaf set; Kademlia k-buckets organized by XOR proximity of blake3(key) — usable as a *logical* proximity index for locality grouping without any network addressing). Tables updated via **gossip-based dissemination**: epidemic broadcast of table deltas; finite-time convergent gossiping (each node tracks a small neighbor set, exchanges state periodically, converges globally without central coordinator). Merkle Search Trees (Auvolat & Taïani, SRDS 2019) provide efficient state-based reconciliation of routing tables over unreliable channels (causal broadcast not required) — aligned with carrier-agnostic unknown-membership model.

Path selection: given ordered candidates, choose first healthy eligible candidate; mark attempted; on error advance. Path selection is deterministic given (request, local view) so all nodes that see the same view make the same choice — supports convergence and idempotent retries.

#### 3.6 Loop Prevention

Loop-free distance-vector principles (DSDV: per-destination sequence numbers; bad news lower sequence; AODV sequence-number duplicate detection) and exact-hop-count (decrement TTL, discard at zero/on re-visit). ids-routing loop prevention:
- Per-request `hop_count` TTL (u8), decremented at each hop; discard at 0.
- `visited` endpoint set (blake3(endpoint id)); reject/return error if candidate already visited.
- Per-route sequence numbers: routing-table entries carry a monotonic sequence; prefer higher sequence on conflict (DSDV rule), preventing stale loops.
- Deterministic ordering + visited set guarantees no infinite forwarding; bounded retries configurable.

#### 3.7 Request Coalescing (Single-Flight)

Identical in-flight requests for the same key coalesce: one leader performs the resolution + dispatch, waiters reuse the result (Atlas request coalescing / Go singleflight / Varnish proxy_cache_lock / bunny.net). Coalescing key = blake3(request key + consistency req). Per-instance (per-endpoint) coalescing; fleet-wide dedup requires distributed lock (out of scope, noted). Reduces downstream load during thundering herd / cache-miss storms.

#### 3.8 Cryptographic Surface

Allowed only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- blake3/sha256: content-addressed routing keys, endpoint ids, checksums.
- ed25519: sign routing-table deltas and routing decisions for authentication (authenticated gossip, no transport trust).
- xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305: optional AEAD envelope for encrypted routing metadata envelopes.
- `ids-routing` consumes type surface from `ids-000-aa`; no direct `ids-crypto` runtime dep (avoid cycles).

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
|| Stale routing table causes mis-routed requests | Gossip convergence + sequence numbers + per-request TTL + read-your-writes sticky fallback; error + retry with refreshed view |
|| Routing loop (misconfiguration / partition) | Hop-count TTL, visited-endpoint set, sequence numbers; deterministic fail-close |
|| Unhealthy/overloaded endpoint selected | Health gating, load in cost score, circuit-breaker on repeated failure, fail over to next candidate |
|| Thundering herd on hot key | Request coalescing (single-flight) per key; bounded waiters, waiter timeout |
|| Inconsistent reads from stale replica | Consistency requirement filters candidates by freshness/staleness bound; leader-only for strong reads |
|| Routing-table poisoning / fake advertisements | ed25519-signed table deltas; verify origin before applying (decentralized identity, no trusted third party) |
|| Carrier re-framing / untrusted relay | Routing decisions are content-addressed, carrier-independent; payload opaque; no carrier header trust |
|| Key space / endpoint id exhaustion | blake3 256-bit ids; bounded k-bucket-style tables; eviction policy (LRU/least-recently-used) |
|| Adaptive weight oscillation | Damping, min/max weight bounds, change-rate limits; converge-only-on-stable-observations |

**Security risks:** forged routing ads (mitigated by ed25519 signatures), replay of old table deltas (sequence numbers + TTL), routing-table DoS (bounded table size, per-peer quota), cache-poisoning via false health reports (signed health attestations), timing dependence (never use wall-clock for validity; HLC/Lamport only).

**Integration points:**
- `ids-client`/`ids-gateway` call `ids_routing::resolve(request) -> OrderedCandidates`; dispatch via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.
- `ids-read`/`ids-write`/`ids-replication` consume candidate lists for replica-aware dispatch.
- Routing-table gossip rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (opaque bytes), zero carrier imports.
- Crypto only via `ids-000-aa` types (`Checksum`, `Signature`); `ids-crypto` not a direct runtime dep of `ids-routing` to preserve the no-cycle rule (`ids-crypto` does not depend on `ids-000-aa`).
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS — carrier-agnostic by design (I-CARR-001 equivalent).

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Request Resolution (core)
```
resolve(key, hints, consistency, local_view) -> OrderedCandidates
  1. key_id = blake3(key)   // content-addressed routing key
  2. owner = ownership_filter(key_id, local_view)  // endpoints owning the shard
  3. candidates = owner ∪ allowed_followers (by consistency strategy)
  4. filter: health == healthy; staleness <= consistency.max_staleness; capacity headroom
  5. score(c) = w_geo·geo(c) + w_load·queue(c) + w_health·penalty(c) + w_fresh·staleness(c) + w_cap·saturation(c)
  6. order = sort(candidates, ascending score)   // near-to-far
  7. apply loop guard (hop TTL, visited set, sequence numbers)
  8. coalescing: if in-flight for key_id, join as waiter; else become leader
  9. return OrderedCandidates { order, routing_decision, hop_budget }
```

#### 7.2 Composite Score & Adaptive Weights
```
score(c) = Σ w_i · norm_i(c)   // each norm in [0,1], lower is better
weights adapt from telemetry: observed latency/success/failure per endpoint
damping: Δw bounded per interval; min/max clamp; change-rate limit
convergence: under stable load, weights settle; routing choice deterministic given (request, view)
```

#### 7.3 Replica Selection (TiKV-pattern)
```
strategy LeaderOnly   -> candidates = {leader} (writes, strong reads)
strategy FollowerPrefer -> candidates = followers sorted by score, leader last
strategy Mixed        -> candidates = all replicas sorted by score
strategy PreferLeader -> candidates = leader first, then followers by score
strategy Learner      -> candidates = learner replicas
gate: store health != unreachable; staleness <= maxStaleness for non-leader reads
sticky: best-effort route to replica that served prior write (remapped on rescale)
```

#### 7.4 Loop Prevention
```
hop_count-- at each hop; if hop_count == 0 -> error LoopDetected
if endpoint in visited_set -> error LoopDetected
else visited_set.add(endpoint)
route entry sequence: accept update only if seq > stored seq (DSDV rule)
bounded retries: max_attempts configurable; return Unroutable when exhausted
```

#### 7.5 Gossip-Based Routing-Table Dissemination
```
each node tracks small neighbor set; periodically exchange table deltas
view ← merge(local_view, received_view)   // semilattice merge (union + higher-seq wins)
finite-time convergence: under reliable eventual delivery, all views equal
Merkle digest anti-entropy: exchange root hashes; descend only differing branches; O(d·log n) divergence location
```

#### 7.6 Request Coalescing (single-flight)
```
coalesce_key = blake3(request_key + consistency_req)
if coalesce_map.contains(key):
    register waiter on existing leader's result channel
else:
    become leader; perform resolution; broadcast result to all waiters; remove entry
waiter timeout configurable; on leader failure, waiters re-resolve independently
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Cost-weight calibration:** Initial weights for geo/load/health/freshness/capacity and adaptive tuning rules are workload-dependent; unquantified without production telemetry.
2. **Sticky-session semantics:** Best-effort replica affinity (ClickHouse pattern) remaps on rescale — read-after-write guarantees need explicit consistency binding, not implicit affinity.
3. **Table size vs churn:** Bounded routing-table eviction (LRU) under high churn may evict still-relevant entries; eviction policy and retention bounds need deployment tuning.
4. **Merkle anti-entropy adoption:** Optional; adds complexity. Decide during implementation based on table size and gossip bandwidth.
5. **Encrypted envelope adoption:** xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 AEAD for routing metadata — optional, deferred unless threat model requires encrypted routing metadata.
6. **Formal verification scope:** TLA+/PlusCal spec for routing-table convergence and loop freedom is additional effort beyond core classes.
7. **Cross-region consistency routing:** Routing across regions with consistency requirements (read-your-writes, session consistency) needs explicit session-sticky binding design.

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| Application-layer data-aware routing (not packet routing) | Prompts.txt purpose; Zave requirements; content-addressed keys, carrier-independent |
|| `ids-carrier::Endpoint` sole transport | Carrier-agnostic (I-CARR-001); no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |
|| blake3/sha256 content-addressed routing keys | Fixed-size, collision-resistant, content-based (LARD principle; iroh blobs pattern) |
|| Composite score + near-to-far ordering | Locality + load + health + freshness + capacity; cache-hot overloaded worker can lose to colder worker (Dynamo/KV-aware) |
|| TiKV-style replica strategies (leader/follower/mixed/prefer-leader/learner) | Production-verified (TiKV, MongoDB read preference); consistency maps cleanly to strategy |
|| Gossip-based table dissemination | Convergent without central coordinator; matches unknown-membership carrier-agnostic model |
|| Merkle Search Trees optional anti-entropy | Efficient state-based reconciliation over unreliable channels (no causal broadcast needed) |
|| Loop prevention: hop TTL + visited set + sequence numbers | Bounded retries, deterministic fail-close, DSDV sequence rule prevents stale loops |
|| Request coalescing (single-flight) | Protects downstream under thundering herd; per-instance coalescing |
|| Logical clocks only (Lamport/HLC), never wall-clock validity | Causality without clock-drift hazards |
|| Crypto via ids-000-aa types only | Preserve no-cycle rule (ids-crypto does not depend on ids-000-aa) |
|| New separate crate ids-routing | Per prompts.txt directive "use separate crates instead of more folders"; clean dependency boundary |
