```
│              Phase 020: ids-broadcast (THIS CRATE)                  │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐   │
│  │ reliable    │ │ FIFO        │ │ causal      │ │ total order │   │
│  │ broadcast   │ │ broadcast   │ │ broadcast   │ │ (atomic)    │   │
│  │ (Bracha)    │ │ (per-sender │ │ (vector     │ │ (consensus │   │
│  │ INIT/ECHO/  │ │ seq + buffer│ │ clock + dep │ │ slot: Paxos/ │   │
│  │ READY)      │ │ reassembly) │ │ set + buf)  │ │ Raft/Zab)   │   │
│  └─────────────┘ └─────────────┴───────────────┴─────────────┘   │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ FIFO-total order · SMR executor · delivery buffer · gap repair │  │
│  │ Dolev-Strong authenticated broadcast (Byzantine, ed25519)    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             CARRIER BOUNDARY (ids-carrier::Endpoint only)           │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, Vec<u8>≤1024}, &[u8])          │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                             │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- One canonical definition per type; canonical types (`NodeId`, `OrderingPos`, `OpRef`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, `ConsistencyProfile`, `FailureDomain`) imported from `ids_000_aa::X`, never redefined.
- `ids-broadcast` implements the sealed `trait Broadcast` from `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/broadcast.rs`; downstream crates use it as a trait bound, cannot implement it.
- All message transport is datagram-based via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` enum: Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom(u16) + opaque `Vec<u8>` capped at 1024 bytes). No IP addresses, ports, sockets.
- Crypto surface: ed25519 signatures (authentication/Dolev-Strong chains), sha256/blake3 (message digests, sequence commitments), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (optional payload encryption). All ops in `ids-crypto`; this crate declares only usage boundaries.
- Ordering is dataset-scoped via `ids-ordering-domain` (crate 55); no global master (invariant `no_global_master` in `ids-000-aa`).
- Operation lifecycle reuses `ids-000-aa` `OpState` (`received → ordered → executing → committed → synchronized → verified → failed`) and `CommitState`.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Broadcast Hierarchy and Guarantees

| Layer | Guarantee | Source |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| Reliable broadcast | Validity (correct sender → all correct deliver), Agreement (one correct delivers → all correct deliver), Integrity (no duplication, only broadcast messages delivered) | Bracha 1987; decentralizedthoughts.github.io/2020-09-19-living-with-asynchrony-brachas-reliable-broadcast |
| FIFO broadcast | Reliable + per-sender FIFO order (sender's messages delivered in broadcast order) | Purdue ECE 60872 DistributedPrimitives; ETH distsys ch.18 |
| Causal broadcast | Reliable + happens-before order (causally related messages delivered in order; concurrent unordered) | arXiv 2206.14767 (verified causal broadcast); Yale Aspnes Broadcast wiki |
| Total order broadcast (= atomic broadcast) | Reliable + uniform total order (all processes deliver same messages in same order) | Hadzilacos & Toueg 1994; Wikipedia Atomic broadcast; CMU atomic-broadcast.pdf |
| FIFO-total order | Total order + per-sender FIFO preserved within the total order | ACM total-order taxonomy 10.1145/1041680.1041682; Southampton causal+total order paper |

Key distinction (from research): total order alone does NOT imply FIFO or causal order; FIFO-total order and causal-total order are strict strengthenings. Atomic broadcast ≡ consensus in asynchronous crash-failure systems (Chandra-Toueg).

#### 3.2 Reliable Broadcast — Bracha Algorithm

The foundational primitive. A designated sender broadcasts value `v`; protocol uses three message classes: INIT (sender → all), ECHO (forwarded on first INIT), READY (sent on f+1 ECHOs or n-f READY conditions). Delivery when n-f READYs received for the same `v`. Tolerates up to f < n/3 Byzantine faults for agreement; crash-only variant needs no authentication. Properties:
- **Validity**: if the sender is non-faulty and broadcasts, all correct processes eventually deliver.
- **Agreement**: if any correct process delivers a message, all correct processes eventually deliver it.
- **Integrity**: every correct process delivers at most one message, and only a message that was broadcast.

For `ids-broadcast`: generic Bracha core parameterized by `n` and `f`, driven by `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams; retransmission on timeout via endpoint re-send; duplicate suppression via message IDs.

#### 3.3 FIFO Broadcast

Built on reliable broadcast: each sender tags messages with a per-sender sequence number; receivers buffer out-of-order messages in a per-sender reassembly buffer and deliver in sequence order (`next[q]` cursor). No cross-sender ordering constraints. Research source: Purdue FIFO broadcast algorithm (msgBag + next[q] while-loop delivery).

#### 3.4 Causal Broadcast

Built on FIFO broadcast plus dependency tracking: each message carries a vector clock (or dependency set) of causally preceding broadcasts; a message is delivered only after all its dependencies have been delivered (delivery buffer + dependency-resolution loop). Implies single-source FIFO but not total order. Research: arXiv 2206.14767 (causal delivery = buffer until all causally preceding messages applied; vector clock metadata); Yale pinewiki (causal ⇒ single-source FIFO but not total). Vector clocks come from `ids-vector-clock` (crate 66); timestamps from `ids-hlc` (crate 67) optional.

#### 3.5 Total Order Broadcast / Atomic Broadcast

All correct processes deliver the same set of messages in the same total order. Uniform variants (apply also to faulty processes): Uniform Total Order, Uniform Agreement, Uniform Integrity. Plus Validity and Termination. Consensus equivalence: atomic broadcast is reducible to consensus and vice versa (Chandra-Toueg 1996); cannot be implemented in purely asynchronous systems with even one crash failure (FLP) — needs eventual synchrony or a failure detector (eventually strong ⋄P / ⋄S).

Implementation approaches for `ids-broadcast`:
- **Sequencer-based**: dataset-scoped leader assigns monotonically increasing sequence numbers (`OrderingPos`) from `ids-ordering-domain`; all replicas deliver in sequence order. Simplest, matches "no global master" since leadership is per ordering domain.
- **Consensus-slot-based**: one consensus instance per sequence slot (Multi-Paxos / Raft / Zab). Delegated to sibling crates: `ids-total-order-broadcast` (68), `ids-flexible-paxos` (71), `ids-bft-consensus` (72).
- **Leaderless**: EPaxos-style dependency graph (arXiv 2511.02743) — commands order collaboratively via predecessor agreement.

#### 3.6 Atomic Broadcast Properties (Uniform)

From Hadzilacos & Toueg / CMU atomic-broadcast.pdf:
- **Validity**: if a correct process broadcasts m, it eventually delivers m.
- **Uniform Agreement**: if any process (correct or faulty) delivers m, all correct processes eventually deliver m.
- **Uniform Integrity**: every process delivers m at most once, and only if m was previously broadcast by sender(m).
- **Uniform Total Order**: if p and q both deliver m and m′, then p delivers m before m′ iff q delivers m before m′.

Validity + Agreement + Integrity ⇒ reliable broadcast. Total order + agreement ⇒ atomic broadcast.

#### 3.7 State Machine Replication (SMR)

Broadcast is the ordering substrate for SMR: clients submit commands → total order broadcast assigns a position → every replica applies commands in that same order → deterministic state machine ⇒ identical state across replicas. Sources: Lamport "Paxos made simple" / replicated state machines; Raft (raft.github.io/raft.pdf); Zab (ZooKeeper ACM 1529974.1529978 — reliable delivery, total order, causal order); Viewstamped Replication (Oki & Liskov — viewstamps, totally ordered view IDs + timestamps). `ids-broadcast` defines the SMR integration surface (command log, deterministic apply hook); actual executor lives in `ids-write`/`ids-consistency` (crates 13/19).

#### 3.8 Ordering Mechanisms (metadata on broadcast messages)

- **Lamport logical clocks**: partial order, tie-broken by process ID (CMU 04-clocks.pdf; Yale LogicalClocks).
- **Vector clocks**: exact causality detection; concurrent when neither VC ≤ other (systemoverflow vector clocks guide). Consumed from `ids-vector-clock` (crate 66).
- **Hybrid Logical Clock (HLC)**: causality like logical clocks, stays close to NTP physical time (Kulkarni HLC paper, UChicago). Consumed from `ids-hlc` (crate 67).
- **IDS standard time** (`ids-time`, crate 5): proprietary tick basis (`Idstime`), not wall-clock — commit/ordering timestamps.

#### 3.9 Byzantine / Authenticated Broadcast

- **Dolev-Strong (1983)**: authenticated broadcast tolerating any t < n with PKI; signature chains; t+1 rounds; O(n²t) words; lower bound f+1 rounds for deterministic Byzantine broadcast (decentralizedthoughts.github.io/2019-12-22-dolev-strong; UMD lecture 26).
- **PBFT** (Castro & Liskov SOSP 1999): 3f+1 replicas, pre-prepare/prepare/commit three-phase, view changes, tolerates f Byzantine (cs.utah.edu pbft.pdf).
- **HotStuff**: view-by-view recipe, optimistic responsiveness, linear view change (arXiv 2305.13556).
`ids-broadcast` references `ids-authenticated-broadcast` (crate 73, Dolev-Strong) and `ids-bft-consensus` (crate 72); ed25519 (from `ids-crypto`) signs broadcast messages and signature chains.

#### 3.10 Quorum and Consensus Building Blocks

- **Flexible Paxos** (arXiv 1608.06696): only cross-phase quorum intersection (Q1 ∩ Q2 ≠ ∅) is required; within-phase quorums need not intersect. Enables small commit quorums, large election quorums. Sibling crate: `ids-flexible-paxos` (71).
- **Fast Paxos** (MSR TR 2005-112): learn in 2 message delays; collisions fall back to classic Paxos.
- **EPaxos** (arXiv 2511.02743): leaderless, dependency-graph ordering, command coordinator per command, failure recovery.
- **Chandra-Toueg failure detectors**: completeness (strong/weak) + accuracy (strong/weak, eventual); consensus and atomic broadcast are reducible to each other; ⋄S is the weakest failure detector for consensus (cs.princeton.edu cos518 unreliable.pdf). `ids-failure-detector` (crate 7) supplies suspicion; `ids-broadcast` consumes it for liveness.

#### 3.11 Gossip / Epidemic and Reliable Multicast

- **Gossip broadcast**: periodic random peer exchange; O(log N) rounds to reach all nodes w.h.p.; probabilistic reliability (ACM 1317379.1317383; HyParView IEEE 4272993 — fanout tuning for 99%+ reliability). Useful for anti-entropy and dissemination in `ids-broadcast` when carrier topology is sparse/multi-hop.
- **SRM reliable multicast** (IEEE 650139): eventual delivery without enforced order; ordering machinery layered on top.
- **Atomic multicast** (ACM taxonomy 10.1145/1041680.1041682; arXiv 1406.7540): broadcast generalized to destination groups; atomic broadcast = single-group atomic multicast; genuine atomic multicast involves only addressed processes. `ids-broadcast` covers all-replicas broadcast; partitioning/group variants deferred to later phases.

#### 3.12 Delivery Buffer, Gap Detection, and Retransmission

All broadcast flavors need: per-sender sequence space, delivery buffer (out-of-order holdback), gap detection (missing sequence numbers), duplicate suppression (delivered-set), and retransmission requests. Since there is no network stack, retransmission is expressed as re-sending a datagram via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` to the same endpoint — carrier decides how to deliver. This keeps `ids-broadcast` fully carrier-agnostic.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
| Reordering in carrier (datagrams may arrive out of order) | Per-sender sequence numbers + delivery buffer + gap detection before delivery |
| Duplicate datagrams | Delivered-set (message ID dedup); Uniform Integrity (at-most-once delivery) |
| Lost datagrams / carrier packet loss | Retransmission via endpoint re-send on timeout; Bracha ECHO/READY quorum masks loss |
| Byzantine sender sending conflicting values | Dolev-Strong signature chains / PBFT authentication via ed25519 from ids-crypto |
| Byzantine equivocation (sender sends m to some, m′ to others) | Uniform Agreement + Uniform Integrity; authenticated broadcast (crate 73) |
| Replica crash mid-broadcast | Uniform Agreement forces all correct replicas to deliver if any did; Termination under eventual synchrony |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (`std::net`, `tokio::net`, IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/…) | `Endpoint` sole address type; dependency audit bans networking crates; clippy/CI rule; test greps source for prohibited symbols |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305; `ids-crypto` enforces at implementation layer |
| Version skew / wire incompatibility between replicas | `ProtocolVersion` + `EdgeCaseBits` from ids-000-aa; broadcast message frames version-tagged; mismatched peers reject before delivery |
| Ordering stall if domain leader fails | Failure detector (`ids-failure-detector`) triggers view/epoch change; Flexible Paxos quorum reconfiguration |
| Memory growth of delivery buffers | Bounded buffer with gap watermark; backpressure via `ids-fault` circuit breakers (crate 27) |
| Causal delivery deadlock (missing dependency never arrives) | Timeout-based dependency resolution with retransmission requests; eventual delivery under carrier liveness |

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Bracha reliable broadcast state machine** — INIT(sender, v, msg_id) → ECHO on first INIT → READY on f+1 matching ECHOs or n-f READYs; deliver on n-f READYs for same `v`; quorum counters per (msg_id, v); duplicate suppression by msg_id.
2. **Per-sender FIFO sequencing** — each sender increments a per-destination sequence number; receiver holds `next[q]` cursor and a per-sender `msgBag` buffer; deliver when `msgBag` contains `next[q]` from `q`, then increment (Purdue algorithm).
3. **Causal delivery with dependency sets** — message carries vector clock / dependency set; delivery buffer holds messages until all dependencies delivered; dependency-resolution loop after each delivery; implies FIFO but not total order.
4. **Dataset-scoped sequencer (total order)** — ordering domain leader (from `ids-ordering-domain`, crate 55) assigns next `OrderingPos`; all replicas deliver broadcast messages in `OrderingPos` order; leadership is per-domain, no global master (invariant `no_global_master`).
5. **Consensus slot per sequence position** — Multi-Paxos / Raft / Zab slot decides the message at each sequence number; uniform total order + uniform agreement; delegated to `ids-total-order-broadcast` (68), `ids-flexible-paxos` (71), `ids-bft-consensus` (72).
6. **Uniform atomic broadcast** = reliable broadcast + uniform total order + uniform agreement + uniform integrity + validity + termination (Hadzilacos & Toueg 1994).
7. **FIFO-total order** — global total order with per-sender FIFO as an intra-order constraint; tie-break by sender ID for deterministic total order among concurrent messages.
8. **SMR command log** — broadcast command → total order position → deterministic apply → identical replica state; executor hook lives in `ids-write`/`ids-consistency`.
9. **Dolev-Strong authenticated broadcast** — signature chains of distinct signers; t+1 rounds; t < n tolerated with PKI; ed25519 signatures from `ids-crypto`; message content signed, chain verified hop-by-hop.
10. **Delivery buffer + gap detection** — generic holdback buffer for all layers; gap = missing sequence from any sender/domain; retransmission request re-sent via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; watermark advances on contiguous delivery.
11. **Gossip fanout dissemination** — on broadcast, send to `fanout` random/configured endpoints; first-time receivers re-gossip; O(log N) rounds to reach all nodes w.h.p.; used for anti-entropy and sparse carrier topologies.
12. **Message digest** — sha256/blake3 digest over `(sender, seq_no, domain, payload)` for dedup and integrity; committed-prefix tracking reuses `ids-consistency`.

# PHASE 021:

## Phase 021 — Create the ids-quorum crate (quorum intersection for consistency): Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 021 creates `ids-quorum`, a new separate crate (not folders inside existing crates), organized into subfolders by subsystem. It implements quorum intersection for consistency across the IDS workspace: read quorum, write quorum, quorum intersection (r + w > n), majority quorums, Flexible Paxos quorum intersection, quorum capacity, quorum fault tolerance, read/write fault tolerance, and quorum system optimization. It depends on `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed trait contracts), speaks only over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), and uses only the allowed crypto set (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305). No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh.

**Core algorithmic choice:** A strict read-write quorum system `(R, W)` over a replica set of size `N` where every read quorum intersects every write quorum (`∀ r ∈ R, w ∈ W : r ∩ w ≠ ∅`), reducible to the size rule `r + w > N` for uniform quorum sizes. Majority quorums (`r = w = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1`) are the symmetric default, tolerating `f = ⌊(N-1)/2⌋` crash failures. Flexible Paxos weakens this to cross-phase intersection only (phase-1 election quorum intersects phase-2 replication quorum; quorums within a phase may be disjoint). Grid quorums offer `√N − 1` resilience with smaller quorums. Byzantine quorum systems require intersection size `2f + 1` to mask `f` Byzantine nodes. Quorum capacity/load/fault-tolerance tradeoffs follow Naor & Wool (capacity = 1/load).

**Decision:** Create a new separate crate `ids-quorum`, carrier-agnostic, depending only on `ids-000-aa` types/contracts and `ids-carrier::Endpoint` for any datagram transport of quorum messages. All quorum state is local and deterministic; the crate produces bytes to ship over whatever carrier IDS is using.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-quorum` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed contracts) and below any consumer crate that needs replicated consistency (e.g. a future `ids-replica`, `ids-store`, `ids-crdt`). It is **not** a network protocol — it is a local, deterministic quorum calculator and intersection enforcer that produces bytes to ship over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CONSUMER ids-* CRATES                    │
│  ids-replica · ids-store · ids-crdt · ids-broadcast · …     │
│  (consume QuorumCalculator, QuorumSystem, QuorumIntersection)│
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 021: ids-quorum (NEW CRATE)              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  quorum system model: (R, W) over replica set N     │   │
│  │  r + w > N · majority · Flexible Paxos · grid ·     │   │
│  │  Byzantine masking (2f+1) · weighted voting         │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  quorum intersection enforcement                    │   │
│  │  read/write fault tolerance · capacity · optimization│   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │  wire format: versioned, checksummed quorum envelopes│   │
│  │  (CBOR/bincode over ids-carrier::Endpoint bytes)     │   │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              ids-000-aa (master crate, canonical types)     │
│  NodeId · RegionId · … · sealed trait Carrier · Quorum trait │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             CARRIER BOUNDARY (no std::net / tokio::net)      │
│  ids-carrier::Endpoint = CarrierType + Vec<u8>               │
│  trait Carrier: send_datagram(Endpoint, &[u8]) / receive     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a quorum decision:**
1. Consumer asks `ids-quorum` whether a read/write quorum is satisfiable given current replica roster `N` and desired `r`, `w`.
2. `ids-quorum` checks `r + w > N` (strict) or custom quorum-set intersection (Flexible Paxos / grid / weighted).
3. On fault injection, `ids-quorum` recomputes read fault tolerance, write fault tolerance, and overall resilience; reports which quorums remain available.
4. Consumer ships quorum proposals/votes as `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams; `ids-quorum` only defines the versioned, checksummed envelope — never the transport.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Read Quorum, Write Quorum, Quorum Intersection (r + w > N)

Given `N` replicas, a read quorum `r` and a write quorum `w` must satisfy `r + w > N` (equivalently `r > N − w` and `w > N − r`). By the pigeonhole principle, any `r`-sized subset and any `w`-sized subset of `N` elements overlap in at least one node, guaranteeing a read always sees at least one replica that participated in the last write — preventing stale reads. This is the foundational strict quorum rule (Gifford 1979; Naor & Wool 1998; UCSD CSE291 lecture; Cassandra/Dynamo `R + W > RF`).

**Three canonical tunings (strong consistency, all satisfy r + w > N):**
- `W = N, R = 1`: writes to all, read from one — fast reads, slow writes, no fault tolerance for writes.
- `W = 1, R = N`: write to one, read from all — fast writes, slow reads.
- `W = R = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1` (majority): symmetric, tolerates `f = ⌊(N-1)/2⌋` failures; two majorities always overlap.

Caveat: `R + W > N` prevents stale reads but does not, by itself, prevent write-write conflicts; version numbers/timestamps (or a leader/lease) are needed to order concurrent writes (UCSD lecture rule 4).

#### 3.2 Majority Quorums and Fault Tolerance

Majority quorum = `⌊N/2⌋ + 1` of `N`. A cluster of 5 needs quorum 3, tolerating 2 failures; cluster of 3 needs 2, tolerating 1. General rule: to tolerate `f` crash failures, cluster size `N = 2f + 1`. Majority quorums achieve optimal fault tolerance `⌊(N−1)/2⌋` but throughput caps at ~2× a single node regardless of cluster size (Naor & Wool), because every access touches a majority. Majority is the best-availability quorum when per-node failure probability < 0.5.

#### 3.3 Flexible Paxos Quorum Intersection

Flexible Paxos (Howard, Malkhi, Spiegelman, arxiv:1608.06696) weakens "all quorums intersect" to "quorums from different phases intersect." Phase-1 (election/prepare) quorum `Q1` and phase-2 (replication/accept) quorum `Q2` must satisfy `Q1 ∩ Q2 ≠ ∅` for every pair; quorums within a phase may be disjoint. For uniform sizes, `Q1 + Q2 > N`. This permits smaller replication quorums (better write throughput) at the cost of larger election quorums, and vice versa. WPaxos applies flexible quorums per-object-partition across WAN. Fast Flexible Paxos further relaxes fast-round intersection (fast quorums need ≥ 3/4 of nodes).

#### 3.4 Quorum Capacity, Load, and Fault Tolerance

Quorum-system quality metrics (Naor & Wool; Read-Write Quorum Systems Made Practical, arxiv:2104.04102; ETH Zurich Distributed Computing):
- **Load** `L(S)`: minimal max per-node access probability over all access strategies; the busiest node is the throughput bottleneck.
- **Capacity** `Cap(S) = 1 / L(S)`: max quorum accesses per time unit; directly proportional to max throughput.
- **Work** `W(Q) = |Q|`: nodes accessed per quorum.
- **Resilience** `R(S)`: max `f` such that after any `f` failures some quorum survives; `R(S) < min quorum size`.
- Majority quorum: load `1/2`, capacity `2`, resilience `⌊(N−1)/2⌋`.
- Grid quorum (`√N × √N`; quorum = full row + full column): resilience `√N − 1`, smaller quorums (~2√N), lower load than majority for large N.

`f`-resilient strategies trade capacity for resilience continuously (not binary). Quoracle (arxiv:2104.04102) quantifies these tradeoffs per deployment/workload via integer programming.

#### 3.5 Read / Write Fault Tolerance

Read fault tolerance = max `f` such that despite any `f` node failures, some read quorum remains available. Write fault tolerance defined similarly. Overall fault tolerance = min(read, write). Example grid `Q(2×3)`: read FT = 1, write FT = 2, overall FT = 1. Asymmetric read/write workloads can tune `R` and `W` independently (subject to `R + W > N`) to match workload skew — e.g., read-heavy: small `R`, large `W`.

#### 3.6 Quorum System Optimization

Optimization dimensions: quorum size (smaller = lower latency/load but lower resilience), access strategy (probabilistic selection over quorums to balance load), workload skew (read fraction vs write fraction), node heterogeneity (read capacity ≠ write capacity per node), and replica placement across failure domains. Probabilistic / ε-intersecting quorum systems relax intersection to `Pr[Q1 ∩ Q2 = ∅] ≤ ε`, improving availability at small inconsistency risk (used by Dynamo-style eventual-consistency systems). For IDS, strict intersection (`r + w > N`) is the default; probabilistic is an explicit opt-in with bounded `ε`.

#### 3.7 Byzantine Quorum Systems

Under crash faults, non-empty intersection suffices. Under Byzantine faults, two quorums may intersect only in faulty nodes, which can equivocate and break consistency. Masking quorum systems (Malkhi & Reiter) require every pair of quorums to intersect in `2f + 1` nodes to mask `f` Byzantine nodes, requiring `N > 4f` (or `N ≥ 3f + 1` for dissemination quorum systems with a correct quorum). Heterogeneous quorum systems (Stellar/Ripple style, per-node quorum slices) additionally require quorum subsumption + intersection + availability for consensus. IDS default is crash-fault model; Byzantine is a documented opt-in with `2f + 1` intersection.

#### 3.8 Leases and Bounded-Clock Quorum Reads

Leader leases (LeaseGuard, arxiv:2512.15659) allow a leader to serve linearizable local reads for a lease period without a quorum round-trip, requiring bounded-uncertainty clocks. Leases extend via committed log entries; a new leader cannot commit until the old lease expires. This trades a bounded-clock assumption for zero-RTT consistent reads. IDS may layer leases atop quorum reads as an optimization; the quorum core remains clock-free.

#### 3.9 Dynamic Quorum Reconfiguration

Changing `N`, `R`, `W`, or the quorum set itself must preserve intersection across the transition. Joint consensus (Raft joint configuration: new config committed only after old config agrees; quorums from both configs must intersect during the window) is the standard safe pattern. Flexible Paxos joint quorums: `c01.read` contains a `c0.read` and a `c1.read` quorum; same for write. Reconfiguration must never create a window where two disjoint quorums can both decide.

#### 3.10 Formal Verification

Quorum intersection is the safety-critical invariant: any two quorums overlap at a correct process, so information passes from one operation to the next. TLA+/PlusCal specifications model-check quorum intersection (Flexible Paxos TLA+ spec model-checked; etcd `IsQuorum` = `2*|votes ∩ config| > |config|`; `IntersectingQuorums` checks config pairs). Mechanized proofs (Ivy, TLA+) confirm leader uniqueness via quorum intersection. IDS should specify quorum intersection in TLA+/PlusCal (housed in a future `ids-state-machine` crate) and property-test the crate.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
|| Stale read (read quorum misses last write) | Enforce `r + w > N`; version/timestamp reads to pick newest; majority or Flexible Paxos cross-phase intersection ||
|| Write-write conflict (two disjoint write quorums) | Require write quorum intersection (`w + w > N`) or a single leader/lease serializer; version ordering ||
|| Split-brain / two leaders | Quorum intersection ensures any two election quorums share a voter; single winner per term ||
|| Node failures disable all quorums | Resilience ≥ `f`; choose quorum size > `f`; grid/majority tuned to expected failure rate ||
|| Uneven load (hot node) | Probabilistic access strategy over quorums; load-balanced quorum selection; capacity-aware tuning ||
|| Byzantine intersection in faulty nodes only | Byzantine opt-in: intersection size `2f + 1`, `N > 4f`; content/identity trust decoupling ||
|| Reconfiguration creates disjoint quorum window | Joint consensus; old+new config quorums must intersect during transition ||
|| Clock skew corrupts lease/quorum reads | Bounded-uncertainty clocks only for lease optimization; quorum core never trusts wall clock ||
|| Carrier/transport failure between replicas | Carrier-agnostic; quorum decisions are local; retries handled by consumer over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` ||
|| Disallowed dependency (std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/etc.) | Dependency audit bans networking crates; clippy/CI rule; `Endpoint` is sole address type ||
|| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 enforced at implementation layer ||

---

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role in Phase 021 ||
||-------|-------|-------------------|
|| `ids-000-aa` | Canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, …), sealed trait contracts (`trait Quorum` declared here), invariants including `QuorumIntersection`, versioning, errors ||
|| `ids-quorum` (this crate) | Quorum system model, intersection enforcement, capacity/fault-tolerance, wire envelopes ||
|| `ids-carrier` | Concrete `Endpoint` transport for quorum datagrams; depends on `ids-000-aa`; `ids-quorum` imports `Endpoint` type only ||
|| Future `ids-replica` / `ids-store` | Consumers — replicated state built on quorum reads/writes ||
|| Future `ids-crdt` | May layer quorum-based convergence on top ||
|| Future `ids-state-machine` | TLA+/PlusCal quorum intersection specification ||

**Integration points:**
- `ids-000-aa` declares `trait Quorum` (sealed) and `src/invariants/quorum_intersection.rs` — `ids-quorum` is the implementation crate for these contracts.
- Quorum messages travel as versioned, checksummed envelopes over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); `ids-quorum` defines the envelope format but no transport implementation.
- No dependency on `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS — all traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (I-CARR-001 carrier-agnostic stance).
- Cargo workspace: `ids-quorum = { path = "../ids-quorum" }`, depends on `ids-000-aa` only (plus allowed crypto/serialization crates).

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Quorum System Model
```
QuorumSystem<N> {
    replicas: ReplicaSet<NodeId>,       // size N
    reads:   QuorumFamily,              // family of valid read quorums
    writes:  QuorumFamily,              // family of valid write quorums
}
// invariant: ∀ r ∈ reads, w ∈ writes : r ∩ w ≠ ∅
```

#### 7.2 Size Rule (strict quorum)
```
satisfiable(r, w, N) = (r + w > N) ∧ (1 ≤ r ≤ N) ∧ (1 ≤ w ≤ N)
// equivalently: r > N − w  and  w > N − r
```

#### 7.3 Majority Quorum
```
majority(N) = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1
resilience(N) = ⌊(N − 1) / 2⌋   // max crash failures tolerated
N = 2f + 1   // to tolerate f failures
```

#### 7.4 Flexible Paxos Cross-Phase
```
// Q1 (election) and Q2 (replication) may be disjoint within a phase
// but every Q1 must intersect every Q2:
∀ q1 ∈ Q1, q2 ∈ Q2 : q1 ∩ q2 ≠ ∅
// uniform sizes: |Q1| + |Q2| > N
```

#### 7.5 Grid Quorum
```
// √N × √N matrix; quorum = one full row + one full column
// any row+column quorum intersects any other at exactly one cell
// resilience = √N − 1
```

#### 7.6 Byzantine Masking (opt-in)
```
// any two quorums intersect in ≥ 2f + 1 nodes to mask f Byzantine
// requires N > 4f (dissemination: N ≥ 3f + 1 with one correct quorum)
```

#### 7.7 Capacity / Load
```
// Load L(S) = min over access strategies of max per-node access probability
// Capacity Cap(S) = 1 / L(S)
// Work W(Q) = |Q| (nodes per quorum access)
// Resilience R(S) = max f such that some quorum survives any f failures
// R(S) < min quorum size
```

#### 7.8 Wire Envelope
```
QuorumEnvelope {
    version: ProtocolVersion,
    payload: Vec<u8>,        // QuorumProposal / QuorumVote / QuorumAck
    checksum: [u8; 32],      // sha256 or blake3 of payload
    signature: Option<[u8; 64]>, // ed25519 over canonical encoding (optional)
}
// shipped as ids-carrier::Endpoint datagram bytes; no transport in crate
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Quorum set representation:** Uniform size-based (`r + w > N`) vs arbitrary quorum families (explicit subsets). Size-based is simpler and sufficient for majority/Flexible Paxos; arbitrary families needed for grid/heterogeneous. Decision: start size-based, add family support for grid/weighted.
2. **Read-your-writes / session guarantees:** `r + w > N` prevents stale reads across clients but not read-your-writes within a session after a write to a minority. Needs session tracking or version gating — deferred to consumer crate.
3. **Version ordering for concurrent writes:** Intersection prevents stale reads but not write-write conflicts; needs vector clocks, Lamport/HLC timestamps, or a leader/lease. Deferred to `ids-time`/`ids-lease` integration.
4. **Wire format:** CBOR (deterministic, self-describing) vs bincode vs protobuf. CBOR favored for compactness/schema evolution; crate decision pending.
5. **Byzantine scope:** Default crash-fault model; Byzantine `2f+1` masking is opt-in with `N > 4f`; threat model and acceptance criteria assume crash faults unless opted in.
6. **Dynamic reconfiguration frequency:** Joint consensus adds latency; how often quorum configs change is workload-dependent.
7. **Formal verification scope:** TLA+/PlusCal quorum intersection spec (future `ids-state-machine`) proves intersection; property tests cover the rest — extent of mechanized proof unresolved.
8. **Integration consumer:** No existing IDS crate yet consumes `ids-quorum`; integration points (ids-replica/ids-store) are future phases — API surface may evolve.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| New separate crate `ids-quorum` | User requires separate crates for new capabilities; keeps `ids-000-aa` focused on types/contracts ||
|| Strict `r + w > N` default | Fundamental read-write intersection; prevents stale reads; well-understood (Gifford, Cassandra/Dynamo) ||
|| Majority quorum `⌊N/2⌋+1` default symmetric | Optimal crash fault tolerance `⌊(N−1)/2⌋`; simplest, best availability when p(failure) < 0.5 ||
|| Flexible Paxos cross-phase intersection | Smaller replication quorums possible (better write throughput); Q1+Q2 > N ||
|| Grid quorums as alternative | Smaller quorums (~2√N), resilience √N − 1; good for large N ||
|| Byzantine 2f+1 masking opt-in | Required for Byzantine faults; N > 4f; not default (crash model assumed) ||
|| Capacity/load/resilience metrics | Naor & Wool; enables quorum-system tuning per workload (Quoracle-style) ||
|| Joint-config reconfiguration | Preserves intersection across config changes; prevents split-brain ||
|| Lease optimization for reads | Zero-RTT consistent reads with bounded-uncertainty clock (LeaseGuard pattern); optional ||
|| Wire envelope versioned + checksummed | Forward compatibility; integrity over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` bytes ||
|| Carrier-agnostic; no transport | `ids-quorum` produces bytes; consumer ships via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; preserves I-CARR-001 ||
|| Allowed crypto only | ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305; enforced at implementation layer ||
|| Reject "all quorums intersect" within a phase | Flexible Paxos result: only cross-phase intersection required; more efficient ||

# PHASE 022:

## Phase 022 — Create the ids-crdt crate: Optimistic replication with deterministic convergence. Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 022 creates **ids-crdt**, a new standalone crate in the IDS repository providing conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) for optimistic replication with deterministic convergence. CRDTs are the natural substrate for IDS's carrier-agnostic, masterless replication model: any replica can accept local updates at any time, and replicas that have received the same set of updates reach identical state regardless of delivery order, duplication, or delay — strong eventual consistency (SEC) (Shapiro et al., 2011; strong eventual consistency).

**Scope of CRDT classes (research-verified):**
- **G-Counter** — grow-only counter; per-replica increment counts; merge = pointwise max; value = sum of all entries. Only replica `r` writes entry `r`, and it only grows, so the max of entry `r` is the most recent count from `r` anyone has seen. The addition happens once, at read time, never in the merge.
- **PN-Counter** — positive/negative counter = pair of G-Counters (increments, decrements); value = pos − neg; merge joins each half independently. Both halves only grow, so decrements are never silently undone.
- **G-Set** — grow-only set; add-only; merge = set union; anonymous (no replica IDs needed). Trivially convergent because add is an idempotent inflation.
- **2P-Set** — two-phase set = pair of G-Sets (added, removed/tombstones); element present iff in added \ removed; once removed, never re-addable (remove-wins / remove-bans). Unbounded tombstone growth is the known shortcoming.
- **LWW-Register** — last-writer-wins register = (value, stamp); merge keeps the higher stamp; stamps must be unique, totally ordered, and consistent with causality (Lamport clock / hybrid logical clock + replica-id tie-breaker). Raw wall-clock time is unsafe: clock drift, NTP jumps, and VM pauses lose concurrent writes.
- **OR-Set** — observed-remove / add-wins set; each add creates a fresh unique tag (dot = replica, seq); remove tombstones only the tags this replica has observed; element is present iff it has at least one live (untombstoned) tag. A remove can only kill adds it has seen; a concurrent add on another replica creates a tag the remover could not have seen, so the add wins — add-wins semantics.
- **Operation-based vs state-based tradeoffs** — state-based (CvRDT) ships full state and merges via a join-semilattice; operation-based (CmRDT) ships operations and requires reliable exactly-once causal delivery. For IDS, state-based is the safer primary mechanism because it tolerates lost, reordered, stale, and duplicate messages over an unknown carrier.
- **Merge laws** — commutativity, associativity, idempotency of merge; local updates inflationary; merge computes the least upper bound. Together these are the sufficient condition for strong eventual consistency.

**Key engineering decisions:**
- **State-based (CvRDT) + δ-CRDT hybrid as primary:** full-state merge for simplicity and weak-network tolerance; δ-mutators ship small incremental states instead of full state (Almeida, Shoker, Baquero, 2018). State-based needs no ordering guarantees from the carrier — essential for IDS's carrier-agnostic, unknown-membership model where all traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` opaque bytes. Op-based CRDTs are rejected as the primary mechanism because they require reliable exactly-once causal broadcast, which IDS does not provide and which contradicts its carrier-agnostic design.
- **Join-semilattice merge:** every CRDT state forms a join-semilattice; merge = least upper bound; merge is commutative, associative, idempotent; local updates are inflationary. This is the sufficient condition for strong eventual consistency (SEC).
- **Persistence via snapshots + delta journal (WAL):** periodic full snapshots (versioned, checksummed) plus an append-only delta journal; recovery = load latest snapshot + replay journal. Tombstones compacted only at causal stability (all peers have acked past a version).
- **New crate `ids-crdt`**, carrier-agnostic, depends only on `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed trait contracts), `ids-carrier` (`Endpoint` = `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), and allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305). Zero `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh dependencies.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

The CRDT layer sits between the application/IDS metadata layer and the sync layer. It is **not** a network protocol — it is a local, deterministic merge engine that produces bytes to be shipped over whatever carrier IDS is using, exclusively through `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / IDS LAYER                      │
│  CRDT metadata, content-addressed objects, local replica state  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    ids-sync (sync engine)                       │
│  anti-entropy, gossip, delta exchange, acks over ids-carrier    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             Phase 022: ids-crdt (NEW CRATE)                     │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  CRDT classes: GCounter, PNCounter, GSet, TwoPSet,     │    │
│  │  LWWRegister, ORSet                                    │    │
│  │  δ-mutators, join-semilattice merge, ACI laws          │    │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  persistence: snapshot + delta journal (WAL)           │    │
│  │  tombstone GC (causal stability)                       │    │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐    │
│  │  wire format: versioned CBOR, deterministic encoding   │    │
│  │  Merkle digest anti-entropy, state-vector exchange     │    │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              ids-storage (key-value, snapshots, compression)   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│           ids-000-aa  ·  ids-carrier  ·  ids-crypto            │
│  NodeId, ReplicaId, Endpoint · CarrierType + Vec<u8> ·          │
│  ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a local update + merge:**
1. Local client invokes a mutator (e.g. `counter.increment(replica_id)` or `orset.add(element)`).
2. The δ-mutator produces a small delta-state `δ = mδ(X)` and the local state advances: `X′ = X ⊔ δ`.
3. The delta is appended to the local delta journal (WAL) and queued for shipping.
4. Periodically (or on demand), ids-sync ships deltas (or full state on join) to peers; each peer merges `X = X ⊔ δ`. Idempotence means duplicates and reordering are harmless.
5. Anti-entropy: peers exchange Merkle digests/state vectors; divergent keys are repaired by shipping only the missing deltas.
6. Snapshots are taken periodically; once all peers have acked past a snapshot, tombstones and journal entries before it are compacted.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 CRDT Classes — Counters (G-Counter, PN-Counter)

**G-Counter (grow-only counter):** state is a map `ReplicaId → u64`; only the owning replica increments its own entry; merge = pointwise max; `value = sum of all entries`. Convergence proof: join = pointwise max over natural numbers, which is commutative, associative, idempotent; updates are inflations. Verified in Coq (G-Counter merge lemmas); production implementations include Hazelcast PN counter and the `delta-stream` Rust crate. (Shapiro et al. 2011; CMU 17-350 CRDT lecture.)

**PN-Counter (positive-negative counter):** composition of two G-Counters: `PNCounter = GCounter × GCounter` (increments, decrements); `value = pos − neg`; `merge = join each half independently`. Both halves only grow, so decrements are never silently undone — a single G-Counter cannot decrement because `max` would resurrect the old value. A pair of lattices joined componentwise is a lattice: the first example of CRDT composition. Maps naturally to `ids-000-aa::ReplicaId`-keyed `BTreeMap<u64>`. Merge cost O(replicas seen). No tombstones — no GC needed.

#### 3.2 CRDT Classes — Sets (G-Set, 2P-Set, OR-Set)

**G-Set:** state = set; add-only; merge = set union. Anonymous CRDT — no replica identifiers needed. Useful as a building block (accumulating search results, capability sets). Add is idempotent: adding the same element multiple times equals adding it once.

**2P-Set (two-phase set):** state = pair of G-Sets `(A added, R removed/tombstones)`; element present iff `e ∈ A \ R`; `add(e) → A ∪ {e}`; `remove(e) → R ∪ {e}` (guarded: only if `e ∈ A`); merge = union of both halves. Remove-wins / remove-bans semantics: once removed, an element can never be re-added. Shortcoming: unbounded tombstone growth; removed elements are permanently banned. Implemented in `crdt_kit`, `lattice_sets`; verified in Coq (Two-Part Set). Riak DT sets use similar add/remove-set pairs behind the scenes.

**OR-Set (observed-remove / add-wins set):** state = map `element → set of tags` plus tombstone set of removed tags. Each `add(e)` creates a globally unique tag (dot = replica, seq); `remove(e)` tombstones only the tags this replica has observed for `e`; element present iff it has at least one live (untombstoned) tag. Merge = union of tag sets, union of tombstones. This preserves sequential set semantics while allowing concurrent add/remove: a concurrent add creates a tag the remover could not have seen, so the add wins. Optimized OR-Set drops tombstones in favor of a version vector of every tag ever seen (Riak DT / Akka Pekko DData ORSet; `riak_dt_orswot`-inspired, no tombstones, version-vector based; in production Erlang, QuickCheck tested). Tombstone GC: a tombstone is only needed while it might suppress a not-yet-propagated tag; once no live element carries the tag and the removal is causally stable, the tombstone is safe to discard (`compact_tombstones` local GC; `compact_tombstones_all` only when all peers converged).

#### 3.3 CRDT Classes — Registers (LWW-Register)

**LWW-Register:** state = `(value, stamp)`; `assign(v)` stamps with a new, larger stamp; merge keeps the value with the higher stamp (tie broken by replica id). Stamps must be unique, totally ordered, and consistent with causality — a wall clock alone is insufficient (drift, NTP jumps, VM pauses lose concurrent writes). Use a Lamport clock / hybrid logical clock: `(counter, replica_id)` compared lexicographically, where the counter is raised above every stamp seen on merge. Semantics: last write wins; concurrent writes — one is silently lost. Acceptable when the choice among concurrent values does not matter (user profiles, config). Multi-writer needs read-modify-write care (use a counter CRDT for counts instead). Implemented in `crdt_kit::LWWRegister` (HybridTimestamp) and Pekko `LWWRegister` (vector-address tie-break; `reverseClock` for first-write-wins).

#### 3.4 Operation-based vs State-based Tradeoffs

**State-based (CvRDT):** replicas gossip entire state; merge reconciles via join-semilattice. Needs no guarantees from the communication channel: messages may be dropped, duplicated, and reordered. Downside: shipping full state is costly as state grows. Convergence guaranteed if every replica eventually receives every state (eventual transitive delivery of the latest state).

**Operation-based (CmRDT):** replicas gossip operations, not state. Execution splits into `prepare` (local, side-effect free, produces a message) and `effect` (applied at every replica on delivery). Requires reliable causal broadcast: exactly-once delivery, and concurrent operations must commute. If delivered without causal order, all operations must commute; if operations may be delivered more than once, all operations must be idempotent. Most op-based designs require exactly-once and causal delivery. Expressive power is greater, but the middleware assumptions conflict with IDS's carrier-agnostic model.

**IDS decision:** state-based as the primary mechanism; op-based considered only as a future layered option where a causal-delivery substrate exists. δ-CRDTs (delta-state CRDTs) bridge the gap: small incremental states shipped over unreliable channels, with idempotent join tolerating loss/duplication/reordering — the best of both worlds for IDS.

#### 3.5 Merge Laws and Convergence Proofs

**Strong Eventual Consistency (SEC, Shapiro et al. 2011):** safety = strong convergence (any two replicas that received the same set of updates are in the same state); liveness = eventual delivery (every update eventually reaches every replica). SEC = eventual consistency + immediate convergence.

**Sufficient condition for state-based (CvRDT) convergence:** (i) states form a join-semilattice (partial order + least-upper-bound join `⊔` that is commutative, associative, idempotent); (ii) local updates are inflations (`s ≤ update(s)`); (iii) merge computes the join (LUB). Then replicas that have seen the same updates meet at the same state — the LUB of all states involved. Three propositions: semilattice ordering; merge = LUB; monotonicity. Combined with eventual delivery → safety + liveness = SEC.

**Op-based (CmRDT) convergence:** operations delivered via reliable causal broadcast; concurrent effector operations must commute; exactly-once delivery (or idempotent ops). If delivered without causal order, all ops must commute.

**State ↔ op equivalence:** always possible to emulate one with the other (Shapiro et al. 2011): state-based as op-based by broadcasting `merge(st)`; op-based as state-based by lattice `(P(Op × Ts), ⊆, ∪)` (set of timestamped ops).

**Verification:** mechanized proofs in Isabelle ("Verifying Strong Eventual Consistency in δ-CRDTs"), Coq (G-Counter merge lemmas; Add-Wins Set 103 spec/228 proof, Remove-Wins Set 99/386, LWW Register 54/136, MV-Register 35/195, Grow-Only Set 22/57, PN-Counter 88/108). Type-checking CRDT convergence (2023) guarantees commutativity/associativity/idempotence via a type system.

**Randomized/convergence testing:** go-crdt proves convergence by randomized sessions with late/reordered/duplicated delivery and by enumerating every permutation of small histories; Ditto tests CRDTs in Rust from theory to practice (property-based convergence tests, adversarial interleavings).

#### 3.6 δ-CRDT: Efficient Merge over Unreliable Channels

**Problem:** state-based CRDTs ship the entire state on every sync — cost grows with state size.

**δ-CRDT (Delta State CRDT, Almeida/Shoker/Baquero 2018):** δ-mutators return a small delta-state `δ = mδ(X)` such that `m(X) = X ⊔ δ`; deltas are joined into local and remote states; shipped individually or coalesced into delta-groups. Convergence guaranteed if every delta reaches every replica; idempotent join tolerates loss, duplication, and reordering over unreliable channels — unlike op-based CRDTs, which demand exactly-once delivery. Anti-entropy ensures causal consistency via delta-intervals + causal delta-merging condition. Preserves commutativity/associativity/idempotence.

**Join decomposition:** decompose state into join-irreducible elements to ship minimal deltas; avoids redundant delta propagation on multi-path network graphs.

**Merkle anti-entropy:** exchange root hashes; equal roots ⇒ equal state (O(1) agreement check); descend only differing branches; locate k changed leaves in O(d·k); bandwidth O(d·log n). Merkle Search Trees preserve key order (important for sequences/maps) vs plain Merkle trees. Scuttlebutt = vector-clock anti-entropy (clock grows linearly with node count — bad for churn/large networks).

**ConflictSync (2025):** digest-driven sync for state-based CRDTs; reduce sync to set reconciliation of irredundant join decompositions; Bloom filters + rateless IBLTs; up to 18× less data transfer vs full-state sync; Bloom prefiltering cuts overhead up to 50% at low similarity.

#### 3.7 Persistence (snapshots, journal, compaction)

Two durable storage patterns:
1. **Log of changes (WAL/journal):** after every change, append the delta bytes; load = replay all deltas. Simple but recovery time grows with history (one production case: 55K ops / 276MB replayed 27+ minutes on restart).
2. **Whole-document snapshot:** `save()` → full serialized state; `load()` → restore. Fast recovery but full-state rewrite on every save (write amplification).
3. **Hybrid (recommended):** periodic full snapshot + append-only delta journal anchored by state vector; recovery = load latest snapshot + replay journal since snapshot. Compaction threshold (size, op count, age, tombstone ratio).

**Correctness rules (non-negotiable):** no partial replay on corruption; no out-of-order journal persistence; fail closed on hash mismatch; tombstones compacted only after **all** replicas acknowledge (causal stability) or deleted records resurrect ("zombie records"); offline/never-acking members block GC — requires membership management or a grace/quarantine window.

#### 3.8 Sequence CRDTs (out of scope for v1, noted for completeness)

Sequence CRDTs (RGA, Logoot, LSEQ, Treedoc, YATA/Yjs, ESBT) solve ordered lists / collaborative text. Each element gets a unique, immutable position identifier defining its logical position on every replica; new elements are placed relative to existing elements (not by index, since positions shift under concurrent edits); concurrent inserts merge deterministically; SEC. Tombstones accumulate and need GC (retained until causally stable, then re-parented before removal to avoid corrupting order). ESBT (2025) bounds identifier growth and is formally proven unique, totally ordered, convergent, SEC — best current answer to unbounded identifier growth. Not in the Phase 022 contents list; flagged as a future extension.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
|| Concurrent writes silently lost (LWW-Register) | Document per-field semantics; offer multi-value register where no loss is tolerable; use counter CRDT for counts |
|| Tombstone / metadata growth unbounded | GC at causal stability; snapshot compaction; tombstone ratio/count thresholds; incremental GC |
|| Wall-clock skew corrupts LWW ordering | Hybrid logical clock / Lamport `(counter, replica_id)` stamps; never raw `SystemTime` |
|| Late/duplicate/reordered deltas break convergence | Idempotent, commutative, associative join; δ-CRDT tolerates unreliable channels |
|| Offline replica blocks tombstone GC | Membership-aware causal stability; grace/quarantine window; evict dead nodes deliberately, never by timeout |
|| Resurrected deleted data (zombie records) | Never compact before all peers ack; causal-stability gate; tombstone kept while any op pending for its key |
|| Corrupt snapshot/journal | Checksums (SHA-256) on every payload; fail closed on mismatch; keep multiple historical snapshots |
|| Identifier exhaustion (sequence CRDTs) | ESBT bounded identifiers; periodic renaming/compaction; Logoot/LSEQ as bounded alternatives |
|| Byzantine/malicious metadata | Out of scope for Phase 022 (deferred to synchronization security phase); authenticate deltas at trust boundary |

---

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

Phase 022 depends on and integrates with:

|| Crate | Role in Phase 022 ||
||-------|-------|-------------------|
|| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types and sealed trait contracts (`NodeId`, `ReplicaId`, `Endpoint` surface, invariants) |
|| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` = `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`; all CRDT traffic bytes ride this opaque endpoint — zero carrier assumptions |
|| `ids-crypto` | Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (signatures, commitments, content addressing, authenticated encryption) |
|| `ids-storage` | Key-value persistence (sled/memory), snapshots, compression |
|| ids-sync | Sync engine — consumes CRDT deltas for gossip/anti-entropy, drives acks back for causal-stability GC |

**Integration points:**
- ids-sync becomes the delta/anti-entropy transport for ids-crdt: ids-crdt produces `δ` bytes; ids-sync gossips them over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` and reports acks back for causal-stability GC.
- ids-storage persists CRDT snapshots + delta journal; ids-crdt defines the snapshot/journal formats (versioned, checksummed, SHA-256).
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS — ids-crdt works over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` opaque bytes, preserving the carrier-agnostic architecture.
- No `std::net` / `tokio::net` anywhere in the crate; enforced by `ids-000-aa`'s prohibited-dependency list, build.rs lint, and cargo-deny CI.

---

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

| Component | Algorithm / data structure | Convergence basis |
|-----------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| G-Counter | `Map<ReplicaId, u64>`; per-replica max on merge; value = sum | Pointwise max over ℕ is a join-semilattice |
| PN-Counter | Pair of G-Counters (pos, neg); value = pos − neg | Componentwise lattice join |
| G-Set | Set; merge = set union | Union is a join-semilattice; add is idempotent inflation |
| 2P-Set | Pair of G-Sets (added, removed); membership = added \ removed | Remove-wins; tombstones grow unboundedly |
| OR-Set | `Map<Element, Set<Tag>>` + tombstone set; tags = dots `(replica, seq)` | Add-wins: a remove tombstones only observed tags; concurrent adds survive |
| LWW-Register | `(value, stamp)`; stamp = `(counter, replica_id)` HLC; merge keeps higher stamp | Total order on stamps; tie-broken by replica id |
| δ-mutator | `mδ(X) → δ` with `m(X) = X ⊔ δ` | Delta join idempotent; tolerates loss/dup/reorder |
| Anti-entropy | Merkle digest exchange + state-vector comparison | O(1) agreement check on equal roots; repair only divergent branches |
| Persistence | Versioned snapshot + append-only delta journal (WAL) | Fail-closed on hash mismatch; replay from latest snapshot |
| Tombstone GC | Causal stability = min over all peer frontiers | Compact only after all peers ack past a version |

---

### 8. Dependencies

**Permitted (per IDS policy):**
- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types, sealed trait contracts, prohibited-dependency enforcement
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); all traffic bytes
- `ids-crypto` — ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 only
- `serde`, `thiserror`, `bytes`, `blake3`, `hkdf` — serialization/error handling/crypto primitives (allowed set)
- `proptest` / `bolero` — property-based testing (test-only)

**Prohibited (enforced by `ids-000-aa` build.rs lint + cargo-deny CI):**
`std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, mio, socket2, cid, multihash, ipld-core, reqwest, hyper, url, rustls, webpki — and, per IDS phase policy: IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, mesh. No concrete networking stack may appear in the dependency graph of `ids-crdt` or its transitive dependencies.

---

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

- **Merge laws:** property tests verify merge is commutative, associative, and idempotent for every CRDT class (1000+ random cases per class).
- **Convergence:** randomized sessions with late, duplicated, and reordered delta delivery converge to identical state on all replicas; every permutation of small histories enumerated and checked.
- **Per-class semantics:** G-Counter value = sum of per-replica counts; PN-Counter = pos − neg; G-Set/2P-Set/OR-Set match published add/remove semantics (add-wins for OR-Set: concurrent add beats remove).
- **δ-CRDT correctness:** `m(X) = X ⊔ δ` for every δ-mutator; delta-group join equals sum of individual delta joins.
- **Persistence:** snapshot + journal round-trip survives corruption injection; fail-closed on SHA-256 mismatch; recovery = latest snapshot + journal replay.
- **GC safety:** tombstones compacted only after all-peer ack (causal stability); no zombie records; offline members block GC until grace/quarantine window expires.
- **Carrier-agnostic:** crate compiles with zero networking dependencies; `cargo-deny` and build.rs lint pass on prohibited-dependency list.
- **Allowed crypto only:** any cryptographic primitive used is limited to ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **Op-based adoption:** whether a future op-based layer (requiring exactly-once causal delivery) is ever justified for IDS, given the carrier-agnostic mandate. Currently rejected as primary.
- **Tombstone GC with offline members:** causal-stability GC blocks on never-acking peers; membership management or quarantine window policy still to be decided.
- **LWW clock bounds:** hybrid logical clocks bound skew loosely, but liveness under extreme clock drift needs workload tuning.
- **Sequence CRDTs:** RGA vs ESBT tradeoff, tombstone GC complexity, identifier exhaustion — deferred to a later phase; not in Phase 022 contents.
- **Composed types (LWW-Map, OR-Map, JSON-like CRDT):** semantics of nested merges and conflict resolution need per-use-case decisions.
- **Byzantine metadata:** authenticated deltas and equivocation handling deferred to the synchronization security phase.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| State-based (CvRDT) + δ-CRDT hybrid as primary | Tolerates lost/dup/reordered messages over unknown carrier; no ordering guarantees needed from `ids-carrier::Endpoint` |
| Op-based rejected as primary | Requires reliable exactly-once causal broadcast — unavailable and contrary to carrier-agnostic design |
| Join-semilattice merge (ACI + inflationary updates) | Sufficient condition for strong eventual consistency (Shapiro et al. 2011) |
| HLC / Lamport stamps for LWW-Register | Raw wall clock loses concurrent writes under drift; `(counter, replica_id)` is total, unique, causal |
| OR-Set add-wins with tombstones (+ optimized tombstone-free variant) | Preserves sequential set semantics under concurrent add/remove; version-vector variant trades tombstones for per-replica state |
| PN-Counter = two G-Counters | Decrements never silently resurrected; composition of lattices is a lattice |
| Hybrid persistence (snapshot + delta journal) | Bounded recovery time; write amplification controlled by compaction thresholds |
| Tombstone GC only at causal stability | Prevents zombie records; offline members handled via grace/quarantine window |
| ids-crdt as separate crate (not folders in existing crates) | Follows IDS separate-crates pattern; clean dependency boundary on `ids-000-aa` / `ids-carrier` / `ids-crypto` |

---

- Shapiro, Preguiça, Baquero, Zawirski, "Conflict-free Replicated Data Types," 2011 (INRIA RR-7687 / "A comprehensive study of Convergent and Commutative Replicated Data Types") — state-based and op-based approaches, G-Counter, PN-Counter, G-Set, 2P-Set, LWW-Register, OR-Set, semilattice convergence condition, SEC.
- Almeida, Shoker, Baquero, "Delta State Replicated Data Types," 2018 (arxiv:1603.01529) — δ-CRDT framework, delta-mutators, anti-entropy, convergence over unreliable channels.

- arxiv:1608.03960 — JSON CRDT (Automerge foundation): automatic convergence, no lost updates, permutation equivalence.
- arxiv:2607.28101 — ESBT: bounded identifier sequence CRDT; 50–75% lower identifier memory vs Logoot/LSEQ; proven SEC.
- docs.rs `crdt_kit`, `delta-stream` (PN-Counter, GCounter Rust implementations), `merkle-search-tree` (Merkle Search Tree anti-entropy).
- `crdt-graph` (op-based 2P2P-Graph, prepare/downstream phases), `yrs`/`y-crdt` (Yjs Rust port, delta-state sequence), Automerge (JSON CRDT, production).

# PHASE 023:

## Phase 023 — Create the ids-erasure crate (reconstruction-based redundancy with storage efficiency): Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 023 creates `ids-erasure`, the IDS crate for reconstruction-based redundancy with storage efficiency. It implements erasure coding across the redundancy spectrum: Reed-Solomon (n,k) codes in systematic form, Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) codes, regenerating codes, locally recoverable codes (LRC), erasure-code reconstruction, decode-latency optimization, fragment placement across failure domains, and partial parallel repair (PPR). `ids-erasure` is an umbrella crate that composes sibling specialized crates — `ids-reed-solomon` (84), `ids-regenerating-codes` (85), `ids-locally-recoverable-codes` (86), `ids-ppr-reconstruction` (87) — rather than folding them into existing crates, matching the user directive "try to use separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones."

Crate: `ids-erasure` (CRATES.md entry 23). Purpose: Reconstruction-based redundancy with storage efficiency. Contents per prompts.txt entry 23: Reed-Solomon (n,k) codes, systematic form, maximum distance separable (MDS), regenerating codes, locally recoverable codes (LRC), erasure-code reconstruction, decode latency, fragment placement across failure domains, partial parallel repair (PPR).

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- One canonical definition per type; canonical types (`NodeId`, `DatasetId`, `FragmentId`, `FragmentPlacement`, `RedundancyMode`, `FailureDomain`, `Checksum`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Epoch`, `Version`) imported from `ids_000_aa::X`, never redefined.

- Crypto surface: ed25519 (fragment authentication), sha256/blake3 (fragment integrity, content addressing), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (optional fragment encryption at rest/in-transit). All ops in `ids-crypto`; this crate declares only usage boundaries.
- `ids-crypto` does NOT depend on `ids-000-aa` (dependency rule from CRATES.md); `ids-erasure` depends on both.
- `ids-erasure` composes `ids-reed-solomon`, `ids-regenerating-codes`, `ids-locally-recoverable-codes`, `ids-ppr-reconstruction` as path dependencies; code-family selection is per-dataset redundancy policy.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Reed-Solomon (n,k) Codes — Foundation MDS Code

Reed-Solomon codes are the standard erasure-coding design choice for distributed storage. An (n,k) RS code divides data into k equal-sized chunks, encodes them into n coded chunks of equal size such that any k out of n coded chunks suffice to reconstruct the original data. RS codes are Maximum Distance Separable (MDS): they achieve optimal fault tolerance for minimum storage overhead — any n−k chunk failures can be tolerated without data loss. RS codes are defined over Galois Fields GF(2^w), most commonly GF(256) where each field element is one byte; systematic form places the original k data chunks uncoded among the n chunks (generator matrix top k×k block is identity), so normal reads avoid decoding entirely.

For `ids-erasure`: RS (n,k) encoder/decoder over GF(256) with Vandermonde or Cauchy generator matrices, systematic encoding (identity top block), decoding via Gaussian elimination over GF(256) selecting k surviving fragment rows and inverting the sub-matrix. Decoding requires at least k available fragments; fewer → `InsufficientFragments` error.

#### 3.2 Systematic Form — Data Preserved Uncached

Systematic codes keep the original k data chunks unchanged after encoding; they can be accessed without a decoding process by reading the systematic blocks directly. This preserves read performance in normal operations (the common case) and only incurs decode cost on degraded reads (missing/unavailable fragments). Systematic encoding also means parity chunks are linear combinations of data chunks with coding coefficients, each parity `P_j = sum(alpha_{i,j} * D_i)` over GF(2^w).

For `ids-erasure`: systematic encoding as default mode; `is_systematic` flag on `ErasureConfig`; reads prefer k data fragments, fall back to decode only when data fragments are unavailable; parity-only recovery path documented.

#### 3.3 Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) Codes — Optimal Redundancy-Reliability Tradeoff

MDS codes attain the Singleton bound: minimum distance d = n − k + 1, tolerating exactly n−k erasures. Among linear codes, MDS codes (Reed-Solomon principal example) provide optimal storage efficiency — expansion factor n/k, overhead (n−k)/k — for a given fault tolerance f = n−k. For example RS(10,4) tolerates 4 failures at 1.4× storage overhead vs 3× for triple replication. Facebook's f4 uses RS(10,4); HDFS-EC ships RS(6,3), RS(3,2), RS(2,1).

For `ids-erasure`: `RedundancyMode::ErasureCoded { k, n }` exposes `failure_tolerance()` = n−k and `expansion_factor()` = n/k; MDS property verified via `any k columns of generator matrix are linearly independent`; non-MDS options (LRC) documented as trade-off (extra storage for locality).

#### 3.4 Regenerating Codes — Bandwidth-Efficient Node Repair

Regenerating codes (Dimakis et al., IEEE Trans. IT 2010) address the core RS weakness: repairing a single failed node traditionally requires downloading k full chunks (the whole data) to regenerate one. Regenerating codes let a replacement node download functions (β symbols) from d helper nodes instead of full chunks (α symbols), drastically reducing repair bandwidth. The fundamental tradeoff between per-node storage α and repair bandwidth γ = d·β is characterized by a cut-set bound. Two extremal points: Minimum-Storage Regenerating (MSR) codes (α = M/k, MDS-optimal storage, reduced bandwidth) and Minimum-Bandwidth Regenerating (MBR) codes (minimum repair bandwidth at slightly higher storage). Exact repair (replica identical to failed node) vs functional repair (information-equivalent). Clay codes (MSR, FAST'18) achieve exact repair with up to 2.9× less repair traffic; Simple Regenerating Codes achieve exact repair via XOR-only packet operations at rates up to 2/3.

For `ids-erasure`: `ids-regenerating-codes` (crate 85) implements MSR/MBR parameterization; exact-repair default; repair bandwidth γ vs storage α tradeoff exposed via `RegeneratingParams`; `ids-crypto` not involved in regenerating math (pure GF arithmetic); helper-node selection minimizes distinct-node reads.

#### 3.5 Locally Recoverable Codes (LRC) — Locality-Aware Repair

LRCs (Papailiopoulos & Dimakis, ISIT 2012; deployed in Windows Azure Storage, Facebook HDFS-Xorbas) introduce repair locality r: each code symbol can be recovered by accessing at most r other symbols (vs trivial locality k in MDS codes). Small r reduces network bandwidth and disk I/O during single-node repair. Trade-off: non-trivial locality necessarily increases storage overhead beyond MDS (distance penalty d ≤ n − k − ceil(k/r) + 2 for optimal LRC). Availability t: multiple disjoint repair sets per symbol. LRC = local parities (within small groups) + global parities (MDS across groups). Facebook Xorbas (10,6,5) LRC: 10 data blocks → RS(10,4) global parities + local XOR parities; ~2× less repair disk I/O and network traffic vs RS-only, at 14% more storage.

For `ids-erasure`: `ids-locally-recoverable-codes` (crate 86) implements (n,k,r) LRC with locality groups; local repair path (contact r nodes) preferred over global RS decode (contact k nodes); global fallback when locality group is itself damaged; availability t = number of disjoint repair sets.

#### 3.6 Erasure-Code Reconstruction — Decode from k of n

Reconstruction recreates lost data from any k surviving fragments. RS decoding: (1) remove erased rows from generator matrix, (2) select k surviving rows to form k×k sub-matrix, (3) invert sub-matrix over GF(256), (4) multiply by surviving data/parity values to recover erased elements. Any square submatrix of a Vandermonde generator matrix is invertible, so decoding is always possible from any k surviving shards. Decoding is the latency-critical path — degraded reads and failed-node repair both wait on it. Integrity verification (blake3/sha256 per fragment) must precede decode to avoid reconstructing from corrupted fragments.

For `ids-erasure`: `reconstruct(dataset, available, missing_indices)` via GF(256) matrix inversion; decode-latency optimization (parallel fragment fetch, SIMD GF multiplication, precomputed inverse matrices per erasure pattern); `decode(dataset, fragments)` returns original data from ≥k fragments; checksum verification before use.

#### 3.7 Decode Latency — Reconstruction Performance

Decode latency dominates degraded-read and repair tail latency. RS (n,k) decode contacts k nodes and performs O(k²·fragment_size) GF operations; LRC reduce to O(r·fragment_size) for local repairs; regenerating codes reduce transferred bytes to d·β < k·α. Optimization levers: precompute inverse matrices per erasure pattern, parallel fragment retrieval across helpers, SIMD-accelerated GF(256) multiplication (table lookups), fragment-size alignment to cache lines, read-repair vs full-decode choice based on availability. Intel ISA-L achieves ~5 GB/s RS EC on server Xeon via SSE/ASM; pure-Rust crates (reed-solomon-erasure, tape-reed-solomon) fall back to portable Rust with runtime SIMD selection.

For `ids-erasure`: decode-latency benchmarks target (p50/p95/p99) per erasure pattern; inverse-matrix cache keyed by (n,k,erasure-set); parallel fragment fetch with per-helper timeouts; SIMD feature flag; no dependency on ISA-L C code in research phase (documented integration option).

#### 3.8 Fragment Placement Across Failure Domains — Correlated Failure Awareness

Placement determines effective fault tolerance. An (n,k) layout tolerates m = n−k fragment losses only if no single failure domain holds more than m fragments of a stripe. Placement across servers, racks, datacenters, regions: each fragment of a stripe on a distinct fault domain at the required level. f4 (Facebook) lays RS(10,4) blocks across different racks within one datacenter, XOR coding wide-area for datacenter resilience. Scality layouts: k+m splits, rule "no fault domain may hold more than m fragments of any stripe"; minimum cluster shape derived per failure level (server, rack, DC). Correlated failures (power, network segment, operator, jurisdiction) modeled via `FailureDomain` hierarchy from `ids-000-aa` (`topology_diversity`, `correlated_failure` invariants).

For `ids-erasure`: `place_fragments(dataset, fragments, nodes)` respects failure-domain constraints; `FragmentPlacement` records node + domain; placement validator rejects layouts where any domain holds > (n−k) fragments; `ids-topology` (crate 6) supplies domain map; `ids-placement` (crate 9) supplies capacity-aware node selection.

#### 3.9 Partial Parallel Repair (PPR) — Distributed Reconstruction Scheduling

PPR (EuroSys 2016, Purdue) divides reconstruction into small partial operations scheduled across multiple nodes already involved in reconstruction, then progressively combines partial results via a reduction tree. For a (k,m) RS code, conventional repair transfers k fragments sequentially; PPR completes network transfer in ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ time vs k time, reducing network pressure and repair time significantly, compatible with existing erasure codes with no additional storage overhead. m-PPR scheduling handles concurrent failures; partial results aggregated through a reduction tree (each node combines two partial results per round).

For `ids-erasure`: `ids-ppr-reconstruction` (crate 87) implements PPR partial-operation scheduling, reduction-tree aggregation, m-PPR for concurrent failures; integrated into `repair()` path; PPR optional flag on `ErasureConfig`; repair-time benchmarks compare sequential vs PPR.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Correlated failure wipes > m fragments of a stripe (same domain holds too many fragments) | Placement validator enforces ≤ (n−k) fragments per domain; `FailureDomain` overlap check; multi-domain placement policy |
| Fragment corruption (bit rot) silently decodes into wrong data | blake3/sha256 checksum per fragment; verify before decode; `verify_fragment()` gate; corrupted fragments excluded from decode set |
| Insufficient fragments available (available < k) | `InsufficientFragments` error; `detect_loss()` reports reconstructability before attempting decode; auto-repair triggered when below threshold |
| Decode latency spike on degraded reads | Precomputed inverse matrices, parallel fragment fetch, SIMD GF ops, LRC local-repair fast path, PPR reduction tree |
| Repair bandwidth explosion (RS full-chunk download) | Regenerating codes (MSR/MBR) download β < α per helper; LRC contact only r nodes; PPR distributes load |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (std::net, tokio::net, IP/TCP/UDP/…) | `ids-carrier::Endpoint` sole address type; dependency audit bans networking crates; CI grep for prohibited symbols |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305; `ids-crypto` enforces at implementation layer |
| Version skew / wire incompatibility between replicas | `ProtocolVersion` + `EdgeCaseBits` from ids-000-aa; erasure frame format version-tagged |
| Storage overhead too high for cold data | Lenient configs (k=2,n=3) vs strict (k=8,n=16); redundancy policy selects per dataset; `expansion_factor()` exposed |
| Reconstruction from wrong/fragment-set ambiguity | Fragment index + `FragmentId` + `Version` + `Epoch` on every `ErasureFragment`; decode set validated against expected indices |

- Cargo workspace: `ids-erasure = { path = \"../ids-erasure\" }` in each dependent crate; sibling crates 84–87 as path dependencies.
