### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Reed-Solomon (n,k) systematic encoding** — data split into k equal fragments; generator matrix G (n×k) over GF(256) with top k×k = identity (systematic); parity rows from Vandermonde/Cauchy matrix pre-multiplied by inverse of top k×k sub-matrix so any k×k submatrix of G is invertible; output = [data, parity]. Any k of n fragments reconstruct original.

2. **GF(256) arithmetic** — log/exp tables (256 + 512 entries), primitive polynomial 0x11d; mul/div/pow/inv via table lookup; SIMD-accelerated option; constant-time not required (erasure coding is not secret-handling).

3. **RS decoding via matrix inversion** — select k surviving fragment rows; form k×k sub-matrix of G; Gaussian elimination over GF(256) to invert; multiply inverse by surviving values to recover erased fragments; O(k²·fragment_size).

4. **Regenerating code repair** — replacement node contacts d helpers, downloads β symbols each (not full α); γ = d·β < k·α repair bandwidth; MSR keeps α = M/k (MDS-optimal storage); exact repair reproduces lost fragment identically.

5. **LRC local repair** — lost symbol recovered from r locality-mates (r ≪ k); local parity = linear combination of group symbols; global MDS parities survive multi-group failures; availability t = disjoint repair sets.

6. **PPR reduction-tree repair** — reconstruction split into partial ops; ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ communication rounds vs k sequential; reduction tree combines partial results pairwise; m-PPR for concurrent failures; zero extra storage.

7. **Fragment placement validator** — for each failure domain, count fragments of stripe; reject if any domain holds > (n−k) fragments; uses `ids-topology::FailureDomain` overlap check (power/facility/network/operator/geographic).

8. **Integrity gate** — blake3/sha256 checksum per fragment computed at encode; verified before decode and before serving; corrupted fragments excluded, counted in `ErasureLossReport.corrupted_indices`.

9. **Erasure state machine** — stripe lifecycle: `encoded → protected → degraded (available < n) → repairing → restored`; terminal `lost` if available < k (unreconstructable); transitions guarded by `can_transition_to`.

10. **Reconstruction strategy selection** — data-fragments-first (systematic read) → LRC local repair (r nodes) → PPR reduction tree (log rounds) → full RS decode (k nodes, matrix inversion) → report `InsufficientFragments` if < k available.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

|| Uncertainty | Impact | Resolution path ||
|-------------|---------|----------------|
| GF field size: GF(256) vs GF(2^16) | n ≤ 256 for GF(256); larger n needs GF(2^16) | GF(256) default (n ≤ 256 sufficient for most layouts); GF(2^16) option for wide stripes |
| Code-family selection per dataset | Affects `ErasureConfig.mode` and which sibling crate is used | Redundancy policy (RS/LRC/regenerating) per dataset; decided at configure time |
| PPR integration maturity | PPR is a 2016 research technique; production adoption limited | PPR optional flag; sequential repair as default; PPR enabled via config |
| Regenerating code exact vs functional repair | Exact repair keeps code coefficients; functional allows coefficient change | Exact repair default (simpler system maintenance); functional documented option |
| LRC storage overhead trade-off | 14%+ overhead vs MDS for locality benefit | Per-dataset policy chooses MDS (max efficiency) vs LRC (faster repair) |
| SIMD GF multiplication | Pure-Rust GF(256) table lookup vs SIMD/ISA-L | Portable Rust default; `simd` feature flag for runtime SIMD selection; ISA-L C integration deferred |
| Fragment size alignment | Unequal fragment sizes complicate GF matrix ops | Equal-size fragments enforced; padding documented |
| Checksum algorithm choice | blake3 (fast) vs sha256 (FIPS) | Both allowed; blake3 default for fragment integrity; sha256 option for compliance |
| n upper bound for RS | GF(256) limits n ≤ 256 (including parity) | n ≤ 256 validated in config; larger n requires multi-stripe or GF(2^16) |
| Interaction with ids-recovery (crate 25) | Erasure reconstruction is a recovery mechanism | `ids-recovery` consumes `ids-erasure::reconstruct()`; integration point documented |

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Umbrella `ids-erasure` crate composing siblings 84–87 | Matches user directive \"separate crates instead of more folders\"; each code family independently versioned and tested |
| RS (n,k) GF(256) systematic as default | MDS-optimal storage; systematic reads avoid decode in common case; industry-standard (HDFS-EC, f4, Xorbas) |
| LRC for locality-sensitive deployments | Local repair r ≪ k reduces repair bandwidth/I/O; 14% overhead accepted where repair speed matters |
| Regenerating codes (MSR/MBR) for bandwidth-constrained repair | γ < k·α; MSR keeps MDS storage optimality |
| PPR for distributed repair scheduling | ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ rounds vs k; reduces network pressure; zero extra storage |
| Fragment placement ≤ (n−k) per failure domain | Preserves effective fault tolerance under correlated failures; uses `ids-topology::FailureDomain` |
| blake3 default checksum, sha256 option | blake3 fast for integrity; sha256 for FIPS compliance; both in allowed set |
| `ids-carrier::Endpoint` sole transport | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no networking stack |
| Allowed crypto: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | IDS policy; `ids-crypto` implements, this crate declares usage boundaries |
| No code in this phase | Research only per prompts.txt entry 23 |

# PHASE 024:

## Phase 024 — Create the ids-lease crate: Time-bounded authority to prevent split-brain.

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

## 1. Executive Summary

Phase 024 creates a **new separate crate `ids-lease`** (not folders inside an existing crate), organized into subfolders by subsystem. `ids-lease` implements time-bounded authority grants to prevent split-brain in the IDS distributed system: a lease is a time-limited grant of exclusive authority (to be leader, to own a key range, to write to a resource) that auto-expires if not renewed, so a crashed, paused, or partitioned holder cannot block the system indefinitely.

The crate enforces safety through **fencing tokens** (monotonically increasing per-grant sequence numbers checked by the protected resource), **lease expiry with guard periods** (the holder stops acting before the grantor considers the lease expired), **leadership epochs** (term-based authority that invalidates stale holders), and **STONITH integration** (fencing the previous holder before any failover). All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); the crate is carrier-agnostic and depends on `ids-000-aa` (master crate holding all canonical types and sealed trait contracts, including `trait Lease` and the `fencing_stonith` invariant) and `ids-carrier`.

Key engineering decisions:
- **New crate `ids-lease`**, separate from `ids-000-aa` and all other crates, per the IDS principle of separate crates over folders.
- **Lease grant / renewal / expiry** as core operations, each carrying a monotonically increasing fencing token issued by the grantor.
- **Guard period**: holder treats lease as expiring `T − ε` (safety margin for clock drift and scheduling pauses), eliminating the split-brain window between holder-expiry and grantor-expiry.
- **Epoch-based authority**: every lease grant increments a leadership epoch; the protected resource rejects any operation carrying a stale epoch.
- **STONITH/fencing before failover**: the new holder must confirm the old holder is fenced (powered down or isolated) before assuming active authority.
- **Premature leadership loss prevention**: renewal scheduled at `⅓ of TTL` with jitter, exponential backoff retries, and an immediate step-down on renewal failure.
- **Carrier-agnostic**: zero `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh; all frames carried via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.
- **Allowed crypto only**: ed25519 (lease signatures, fencing token authentication), xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 (lease payload encryption), sha256 and blake3 (lease content addressing, epoch commitment digests).
- **ids-000-aa** holds `trait Lease` (sealed contract), `LeaseId`, `FencingToken`, `Epoch`, `LeaseState`, and the `fencing_stonith` invariant; `ids-lease` implements the contract.

---

## 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-lease` sits above `ids-carrier` and below the application / coordinator layer, bridging the gap between "who is leader" (decided by consensus or a lease grantor) and "who may act" (enforced by fencing at the resource). It never opens sockets or speaks IP/TCP/UDP directly; it produces `Frame` payloads shipped as `Vec<u8>` over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤

├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             ids-000-aa (master crate, sealed contracts)         │
│  trait Lease, LeaseId, FencingToken, Epoch, fencing_stonith     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a lease lifecycle:**
1. **Grant**: holder requests a lease from the grantor (a quorum-backed lease service or the current coordinator). Grantor checks no live lease exists (quorum intersection), issues `LeaseId`, `FencingToken = last_token + 1`, `Epoch = last_epoch + 1`, TTL, and expiry `now + TTL` on grantor's monotonic clock. Grant is signed (ed25519) and optionally encrypted.
2. **Holder activation**: holder records the lease, sets its local deadline to `T − ε` (guard period), and begins acting as authority. Every protected operation carries `(lease_id, fencing_token, epoch)`.
3. **Renewal**: holder renews at `TTL/3` with jitter, exponential backoff on failure. Each renewal re-issues or extends the fencing token and epoch.
4. **Expiry / step-down**: if renewal fails for `RenewDeadline` (typically `TTL − ε`), holder steps down immediately and stops admitting new work. If the holder is paused/partitioned and its lease expires, the grantor may grant to a new holder with a higher token/epoch.
5. **Fencing at the resource**: the protected resource persists the highest fencing token/epoch seen and rejects any operation carrying a lower or equal value — this is the safety backstop even if the old holder is still alive and unaware.
6. **STONITH**: before the new holder assumes active write authority, it confirms the previous holder is fenced (isolated / powered down) per the `fencing_stonith` invariant in ids-000-aa.

**Split-brain prevention argument:** quorum-backed grant ensures at most one valid lease per resource at any instant; guard period ensures the holder stops before the grantor can reassign; fencing tokens ensure even a paused holder that wakes late cannot overwrite the new holder's writes.

---

## 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

### 3.1 Lease fundamentals (time-bounded authority)

A lease is a lock with a built-in expiration: the holder may act as owner only until the lease expires, and the grantor refuses conflicting grants until its exclusion interval ends. Unlike an indefinite lock, a crashed holder's lease auto-expires, converting a liveness problem (waiting for a dead client to release) into a bounded performance problem (unavailable for at most the lease duration). (Sources: sanzgiri/patterns lease block; Aicassindra leases article; Martin Kleppmann DDIA process pauses; lease definition literature.)

**TTL trade-offs** (sanzgiri patterns):
- Short TTL (1–5 s): fast recovery; aggressive heartbeating; sensitive to network blips (false expiry).
- Medium TTL (5–30 s): production sweet spot; tolerates ordinary GC pauses and brief network issues.
- Long TTL (5+ min): stable, low overhead; long unavailability window on real holder death.

### 3.2 Grant / renew / expire mechanics

- **Grant**: atomic compare-and-set at the grantor (create-if-not-exists or CAS on an expired lease). Exactly one grantor (quorum-backed) can issue a live lease for a resource at any time.
- **Renew**: holder sends `KeepAlive`/`Renew` before expiry; grantor extends TTL. etcd uses a bidirectional keep-alive stream; Kubernetes Lease renews `renewTime` every `leaseDurationSeconds / 2`; Consul renews sessions periodically with a default 15 s TTL.
- **Expire**: no renewal within TTL → grantor releases automatically; attached state (lock, leadership, cached data) is invalidated. Chubby: session expiry invalidates cached copies; Consul: session invalidation releases or deletes held locks.
- **Revoke**: explicit early termination by grantor or operator; holder must step down immediately.

### 3.3 Fencing tokens (monotonic per-grant sequence)

Each grant returns a strictly increasing fencing token. The protected resource persists the highest token seen and rejects any operation carrying a lower/equal token. This moves safety from the holder (which may be paused and unaware) to the resource (which enforces ordering independently). etcd revision numbers and ZooKeeper zxids serve as natural fencing tokens; Chubby provides sequence numbers; DynamoDB lock client generates monotonic tokens. Without fencing tokens, Redlock-style schemes are unsafe under pauses/partitions (Kleppmann critique). (Sources: sanzgiri fencing; systemoverflow fencing tokens; Kleppmann Redlock analysis; redis distributed locks; various fencing-token explanations.)

### 3.4 Epoch / term-based authority

Every leadership term carries a monotonically increasing epoch (Raft "term", Paxos ballot, Chubby master epoch). A new leader invalidates all prior epochs; followers and storage reject operations tagged with stale epochs. Raft terms: each server stores `current_term`; votes only once per term; at most one winner per term (election safety). OpenRaft CheckQuorum: leader steps down if it cannot reach a quorum within `leader_lease`. LeaseGuard: new leader defers commits until the deposed leader's prior-term entry is `Δ` old. (Sources: Raft paper/lectures; CockroachDB replication layer; openraft check_quorum; LeaseGuard arxiv 2512.15659.)

### 3.5 Guard period and clock safety

The holder assumes its lease expires at `T − ε` (safety margin) so it stops before the grantor is entitled to reassign. Spanner TrueTime gives bounded-uncertainty timestamps; classical leases assume bounded clock drift. Monotonic clocks (not wall-clock) measure lease durations — wall-clock NTP steps backwards have caused real split-brain (2-second NTP step during VM migration gave node A 2 extra seconds of lease, overlapping with node B's lease). LeaseGuard requires clocks with bounded uncertainty for inherited-lease reads; timers suffice for deferred-commit writes. (Sources: sanzgiri clock-skew danger; michal-drozd clock step split-brain; distributedrequest clock skew; empty squa.re timers; arxiv PaxosLease relativistic frames.)

### 3.6 Renewal scheduling and failure modes

- **Renewal cadence**: `TTL/3` is a common convention (one failed renewal is survivable, two indicate real loss). Kubernetes leaderelection: retry period with jitter; `RenewDeadline` < `LeaseDuration`.
- **Jitter**: randomizes renewal times to avoid thundering herds (ExpressVPN incident: fixed 5 s interval across 12 k leases overwhelmed a single etcd node during a partition; adding 100–500 ms jitter cut expiry events by 99.8%).
- **Backoff**: exponential backoff on renewal retry (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, capped at 5 s).
- **Step-down**: on renewal failure for `RenewDeadline`, holder stops acting immediately; does not wait for lease expiry.
- **Pause resilience**: a long GC pause or VM freeze can outlive the lease; the holder must not resume writes after waking without re-verifying authority (fencing tokens catch this at the resource).
- **Clock jumps**: NTP step backwards extends apparent lease validity; forward steps expire leases early. Monotonic time for durations; wall-clock only for external display. (Sources: etcd lease.go; kubernetes leaderelection.go; consul sessions; ExpressVPN incident; aerospike jitter article; systemoverflow critical failure modes.)

### 3.7 STONITH / fencing before failover

STONITH ("Shoot The Other Node In The Head") isolates a suspected failed node (power off / reboot) so it cannot access shared storage. Pacemaker/SUSE/RedHat HA: STONITH must never report false positives; reset must complete before returning control. Linux-HA: a STONITH plugin that reports a node down must be correct. Chubby master failover: new master generates a new epoch larger than all previous, waits for existing sessions to expire or fail-over messages to be acked, then responds to operations. Consul lock-delay (default 15 s) gives the potentially-still-live leader time to detect invalidation and stop. (Sources: Wikipedia fencing/STONITH; Oracle fencing config; RedHat Pacemaker STONITH; Linux-HA STONITH; SUSE fencing; Chubby papers/slides; Consul sessions internals.)

### 3.8 Premature leadership loss prevention

A leader that loses its lease must step down before a new leader is elected, so their active windows never overlap. Timeline (Kubernetes one-nought-one module): T=0 partition; T=10 leader attempts renewal, cannot reach service; T=25 retries exhausted, enters guard period, stops acting; T=30 lease expires at service; T=31 new holder acquires. Key insight: old holder stops **before** new holder is elected → never two active leaders. Recovery: when partition heals, old holder discovers it is no longer leader and becomes follower. (Sources: onenoughtone leader election lease-based; various leader-lease explanations.)

### 3.9 Quorum-backed grant (split-brain prevention at the grantor)

At most one partition can hold a majority; quorum intersection (any two majorities share ≥1 node) prevents two independent grants for the same resource. Chubby: Paxos elects master for a lease period; new master accepted only if old master's lease has expired. Raft: majority vote elects one leader per term. PaxosLease: quorum of acceptors grants time-bounded ownership; no durable acceptor lease state; quarantine after acceptor restart. (Sources: Chubby slides/papers; Raft paper; Rutgers consensus notes; arxiv PaxosLease revisited 2609.14640.)

### 3.10 did:crdt / signed deltas relevance

did:crdt (arxiv 2606.16223): signed CRDT deltas with HLC timestamps, causal delivery, Ed25519 signatures over canonical content, BLAKE3-256 content addressing — a model for authenticated, carrier-agnostic authority transfers that `ids-lease` can mirror for signed lease grants. Decoupling Trust in Byzantine CRDTs (arxiv 2606.31759): decouples identity trust from content trust; post-compromise handling without breaking causality — relevant when a lease holder's key is compromised mid-lease. (Sources: did:crdt arxiv; Decoupling Trust arxiv.)

---

## 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Split brain: two holders believe they have valid leases simultaneously | Quorum-backed grant (at most one grantor, quorum intersection); guard period `T − ε`; fencing tokens checked by resource |
| Stale holder resumes after pause/partition (zombie leader) | Fencing token: resource rejects writes with token < highest seen; epoch check |
| Clock skew between holder and grantor | Holder uses `T − ε`; monotonic clocks for durations; never trust wall-clock for lease arithmetic |
| NTP step backwards extends apparent lease | Monotonic time; alert on clock steps > 50 ms; fencing tokens as backstop |
| Long GC pause / VM freeze outlives lease | Renewal at TTL/3 with jitter; step-down on renewal failure; fencing at resource |
| Renewal thundering herd overwhelms grantor | Jitter (10–20% of interval, capped 500 ms); exponential backoff; circuit breakers |
| Grantor unavailability during partition | Holder steps down after `RenewDeadline`; no new grants until quorum heals |
| STONITH false positive (isolating a live node) | STONITH must never report false positives; reset confirmed before control returns; lock-delay grace window |
| Revoked key / compromised holder mid-lease | Epoch-based revocation; new grant invalidates old epoch; did:crdt-style decoupling of content/identity trust |
| Replay of old lease grant messages | Nonce + per-grant fencing token; grantor rejects duplicate/out-of-order grants; signed grants prevent forgery |
| Carrier-level interception / injection | All lease traffic signed (ed25519) and optionally encrypted (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); carrier provides no security (per I-CARR-016/I-CARR-018) |

## 5. Integration with Existing Crates

`ids-lease` depends on and integrates with:

| Crate | Role in Phase 024 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: `trait Lease` (sealed contract), `LeaseId`, `FencingToken`, `Epoch`, `LeaseState`, `Endpoint`/`CarrierType` re-exported via `ids-carrier`, `fencing_stonith` invariant, sealed error contracts |
| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); all lease traffic rides opaque datagrams over `Endpoint`; no direct carrier dependency |
| `ids-coordinator` (domain-scoped leadership, fencing/STONITH) | Consumer: lease grants back domain leadership; STONITH hook before failover |
| `ids-storage` | Durable persistence of lease journal, epoch watermark, fencing-token high-water mark |
| `ids-crypto` | ed25519 signatures, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 encryption, sha256/blake3 hashing (only allowed primitives) |
| `ids-membership` | Join/leave/lifecycle context for lease holders |
| `ids-quorum` | Quorum intersection for grant safety |
| `ids-broadcast` | Reliable/causal broadcast of lease grants and revocations |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-coordinator` consumes `ids-lease` for domain-scoped leadership: a domain leader holds a lease; on lease loss it steps down and triggers STONITH/fencing before a new leader assumes authority.
- `ids-storage` persists the lease journal, epoch high-water mark, and fencing-token high-water mark durably so a restarted holder/grantor cannot regress tokens.
- All lease traffic is `ids-carrier::Endpoint` frames (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); `ids-lease` never imports `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any carrier-specific crate.
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS — carrier-agnostic by design (I-CARR-001).

## 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

**LeaseGrant** = `{ lease_id: LeaseId, holder: NodeId, fencing_token: FencingToken, epoch: Epoch, ttl_ms: u64, granted_at: Instant, expires_at: Instant, signature: ed25519::Signature }`

**FencingToken / Epoch**: monotonic `u64` counters incremented on every grant at the grantor; persisted durably (high-water mark) so restarts cannot regress.

**Guard period**: `local_deadline = grant_received_at + ttl − ε` where `ε` covers clock drift + scheduling pause + message delay. Holder stops acting at `local_deadline`, not at grantor's `expires_at`.

**Renewal scheduler**: fire at `ttl / 3` + jitter; on failure, exponential backoff (1s → 2s → 4s, cap 5s); if `RenewDeadline` (typically `ttl − ε`) elapses without success → `step_down()` immediately.

**FencedRegister** (at protected resource): `highest_token: u64`; `write(token, op)` → reject if `token <= highest_token`; else `highest_token = token; apply(op)`. Atomic check-and-apply prevents TOCTOU.

**Authority state machine**: `Acquired → Active → Jeopardy (renewal failing) → Expired | Revoked | SteppedDown`; transitions only on valid grant/renew/revoke/stepdown events.

**Quorum-backed grant**: grantor accepts a new grant only if (a) no live lease exists, or (b) the existing lease's expiry has passed; quorum intersection ensures at most one grantor can decide this consistently.

**STONITH-before-failover**: new holder confirms previous holder fenced (isolation confirmed via carrier messages, power-cycle confirmed via plugin) before entering `Active` write state.

## 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

1. **Exclusivity:** At most one valid lease per resource at any instant (quorum-backed grant); verified by split-brain simulation test: 0 split-brain events across 5000 simulated rounds with partitions/pauses (cf. PRIMUS validation: 0.0 vs 794.5 without fencing).
2. **Fencing:** Resource rejects every operation carrying `fencing_token <= highest_seen`; stale-holder write rejected even if holder is still alive and unaware (unit test: token 41 rejected after token 42 accepted).
3. **Guard period:** Holder stops acting at `T − ε` before grantor's `T`; verified by clock-skew test (±5 s steps, no split-brain).
4. **Renewal:** Renewal fires at `TTL/3` + jitter; jitter spread ≥ 100 ms across concurrent leases (anti-thundering-herd); exponential backoff on failure.
5. **Step-down:** On `RenewDeadline` expiry without successful renewal, holder stops admitting new work within one tick (no waiting for lease expiry).
6. **Epoch invalidation:** New grant with `epoch = n+1` invalidates all operations tagged `epoch <= n`; storage rejects stale-epoch writes.
7. **STONITH ordering:** New holder enters `Active` write state only after confirming previous holder fenced; verified by ordering test (fencing confirmed before first write).
8. **Expiry auto-release:** Crashed holder's lease expires after TTL without renewal; another holder can acquire (no manual intervention).
9. **Carrier agnosticism:** `ids-lease` compiles and behaves identically with zero direct dependencies on TCP/IP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, libp2p, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh; all traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.
10. **Crypto compliance:** Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3 used; no other cryptographic primitives.
11. **Durability:** Epoch and fencing-token high-water marks survive grantor/holder restart; no token regression after restart (quarantine interval applied).
12. **Performance:** Grant + sign + verify ≤ 1 ms on reference hardware; fencing-token check is a single integer comparison per operation.

---

## 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **STONITH implementation mechanism:** The crate defines the fencing hook and ordering guarantee, but the concrete fencing action (power-cycle via carrier message vs. hardware plugin) is deployment-specific and deferred to the STONITH plugin layer.
2. **Grantor election:** `ids-lease` assumes a quorum-backed grantor per resource; electing the grantor itself may reuse a separate consensus crate (to be determined).
3. **ε sizing:** The guard-period margin must be derived from measured clock drift and pause distributions; `TTL/3` renewal is a convention, not a proof.
4. **Lease duration policy:** TTL values (short/medium/long) are workload-dependent; no single default is mandated by this plan.
5. **Revocation propagation latency:** Epoch revocation takes effect after causal convergence; the acceptable compromise window is unquantified.
6. **Offline lease allowance:** Preallocated offline authority for partitioned holders (bounded offline finality) is a possible extension, not in scope.
7. **Fencing-token persistence crash window:** If the resource crashes after accepting token `n` but before durably recording `n+1`, a stale `n` could be re-accepted; write-ahead logging of the high-water mark mitigates but adds latency.

---

## 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| New separate crate `ids-lease` (not folders in `ids-000-aa`) | IDS principle: separate crates over folders; `ids-000-aa` holds only the sealed `trait Lease` contract |
| Fencing tokens on every grant | Safety backstop independent of holder awareness; moves enforcement to the resource |
| Guard period `T − ε` on holder side | Holder stops before grantor can reassign; eliminates split-brain window |
| Monotonic clocks for durations, never wall-clock | Wall-clock NTP steps have caused real split-brain; monotonic is immune |
| Renewal at `TTL/3` + jitter + exponential backoff | One failed renewal survivable; jitter prevents thundering herd |
| Immediate step-down on `RenewDeadline` | Old holder stops before new holder elected → never two active leaders |
| STONITH/fencing before failover | Confirms old holder isolated before new holder writes; per `fencing_stonith` invariant |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Carrier-agnostic; no `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh |
| Crypto limited to ed25519 / xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 / sha256 / blake3 | Per IDS allowed-crypto policy |
| Epoch-based authority invalidation | New grant invalidates stale holders; term-based authority like Raft terms |
| Durable high-water marks for token + epoch | Prevents token regression after restart |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 025 creates `ids-recovery`, the IDS crate for multi-level failure recovery across nodes, H-units, and regions. It owns the recovery lifecycle: failure detection (heartbeat timeouts), recovery planning (per-scope step graphs), plan execution (replica reconstruction, erasure repair, replica copy, ownership transfer), quarantine/release of suspect scopes, state reconciliation, redundancy restoration, and recovery verification via cryptographic proofs. Recovery is organized into four scope levels — Node, HUnit, Region, and RegionWide — each with its own escalation path and repair strategy. All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` opaque datagrams; `ids-recovery` never opens a socket or references any transport-specific type. Recovery proofs are verified with BLAKE3/SHA-256 checksums and authenticated with ed25519; optional payload encryption uses XChaCha20-Poly1305/ChaCha20-Poly1305. Capacity bounds govern concurrent recovery to prevent thundering-herd rebuild storms. The crate is research-only in this phase; no code or source modifications are produced.

**Scope (from prompts.txt entry 25 and CRATES.md §25):** node failure recovery, H-unit failure compensation, cross-H-unit recovery, regional failure compensation, regional failure isolation, replica-based recovery, erasure-code reconstruction, capacity-bounded recovery, ownership-aware recovery, recovery verification, redundancy restoration, multi-level recovery state machine.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-recovery` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed `trait Recovery` contract + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is layered so each recovery concern — detection, planning, execution, verification, quarantine, redundancy — is an independent module:

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER                            │
│  (dataset owners request redundancy restoration, verification, rebalance)│
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 025: ids-recovery (THIS CRATE)                 │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │\n│  │ detection    │ │ planning     │ │ execution    │ │ verification │ │\n│  │ (heartbeat)  │ │ (per-scope   │ │ (reconstruct,│ │ (proofs,     │ │\n│  │ node/hunit/  │ │  step graph) │ │  copy, erase)  │ │  checksums)  │ │\n│  │ region)      │ └──────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘ │\n│  └──────────────┘                                                    │\n│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │\n│  │ quarantine   │ │ redundancy   │ │ capacity     │ │ state machine│ │\n│  │ / release    │ │ restoration  │ │ bounding     │ │ (multi-level)│ │\n│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘ │\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only               │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, Vec<u8>}, payload: &[u8])          │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                 │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- One canonical definition per type; canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `HUnitId`, `DatasetId`, `PartitionId`, `OrderingPos`, `Capacity`, `FailureEvent`, `FailureEventType`, `RecoveryScopeLevel`, `RecoveryAction`, `RecoveryProof`, `RedundancyMode`, `DurabilityCondition`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `Checksum`, `FragmentId`, `FragmentPlacement`, `IdsTime`) imported from `ids_000_aa::X`, never redefined.
- `ids-recovery` implements the sealed `trait Recovery` from `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/recovery.rs`; downstream crates use it as a trait bound, cannot implement it.
- All message transport is datagram-based via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` enum: Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom(u16) + opaque `Vec<u8>`). No IP addresses, ports, sockets.
- Crypto surface: ed25519 signatures (recovery proof authentication, quarantine attestation), sha256/blake3 (fragment and state checksums, content addressing), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (optional recovery payload encryption). All ops in `ids-crypto`; this crate declares only usage boundaries.
- Recovery scope levels: Node (1), HUnit (2), Region (3); escalation proceeds upward when lower-level repair is insufficient.
- Operation lifecycle reuses `ids-000-aa` `RecoveryPhase` (Detection → Planning → Execution → Verification → Completion) and `RecoveryAction` (ReconstructErasure, CopyReplica, TransferOwnership, RestoreRedundancy, VerifyIntegrity, QuarantineNode).
- Repair strategy priority (per `RepairPlanner`): CopyReplica (1) → RestoreRedundancy (2) → ReconstructErasure (3) → TransferOwnership (4).
- No global recovery master (invariant `no_global_master` in `ids-000-aa`); each domain manages its own recovery context.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Multi-Level Recovery Scope Hierarchy (Node / HUnit / Region / RegionWide)

Research basis: hierarchical fault domains (zone/region two-level awareness, Mesos/DC-OS fault domain awareness; Google Cloud building blocks of reliability — regions contain zones; independent failure domains). Failure domain isolation restricts the effect of a failure to a limited number of components; components outside the boundary are unaffected.

- **Node level:** single NodeId fails (crash, disk failure, power failure). Repair: CopyReplica from surviving peers, or ReconstructErasure from erasure-coded fragments. Fastest, most local recovery.
- **HUnit level:** hardware unit (rack/chassis grouping within a region) fails; all nodes in the HUnit are unreachable. Repair: restore redundancy by re-placing replicas to other HUnits in the same region; cross-H-unit recovery if intra-region capacity is insufficient.
- **Region level:** entire RegionId fails (regional outage, network partition isolating a region). Repair: cross-region recovery — fail over to replicas in surviving regions, restore redundancy region-wide, update placement decisions.
- **Region-wide level:** correlated failure spanning multiple regions or the whole deployment. Repair: last-resort erasure-code reconstruction from globally dispersed fragments, ownership transfer, capacity-bounded staged restoration.

Decision: model scope as `RecoveryScope { Node(NodeId) | HUnit(HUnitId) | Region(RegionId) }` (already in `ids-000-aa`); add a `RegionWide` virtual scope concept for cross-region correlated failures handled by the `RegionalRecoveryCoordinator`. Escalation: node → hunit → region → region-wide, each with increasing repair cost and slower convergence.

#### 3.2 Failure Detection (Heartbeat Timeouts + Failure Event Classification)

Research basis: gossip-style failure detection (Cornell "Gossip Style Failure Detection" — random gossiping scales well, resilient to message loss; false-report probability independent of member count); heartbeat-based detection with timeout thresholds; Chandra-Toueg failure detectors (consensus reducible to atomic broadcast). Detection classifies failures into `FailureEventType`: NodeFailure, HUnitFailure, RegionalFailure, NetworkPartition, DiskFailure, PowerFailure.

Decision: heartbeat timeouts per scope (node/hunit/region) recorded via `FailureDetector` (already in `ids-000-aa`, default 30s timeout); a missed heartbeat emits a `FailureEvent` with `ids_time` (IDS standard time, not wall-clock); detection feeds the `RecoveryCoordinator` state machine (Detection → Planning → ...). No timeout-based eviction — eviction is deliberate, never automatic.

#### 3.3 Recovery Planning (Per-Scope Step Graphs)

Research basis: two-level/multi-level distributed recovery schemes (ACM "A case for two-level distributed recovery schemes" — differentiate probable vs. improbable failures, lower overhead for common cases); Derecho reliable efficient recovery (view changes, epoch termination, restart quorum); Raft reconfiguration (joint consensus, learner promotion, add-then-remove ordering).

Decision: `RecoveryPlan` (already in `ids-000-aa`) holds plan_id, failure_event, scope, ordered `Vec<RecoveryStep>`, status (Pending/InProgress/Completed/Failed/Cancelled), timestamps. Each `RecoveryStep` carries a `RecoveryAction`, scope level, target, attempt/max_attempts, status. Planner selects strategy by scope level: Node→CopyReplica, HUnit→RestoreRedundancy, Region→ReconstructErasure. Plan execution advances step-by-step; failed steps retry up to max_attempts then fail the plan.

#### 3.4 Replica-Based Recovery (Copy Replica / Restore Redundancy)

Research basis: replication-based fault tolerance (DSN 2014 — checkpoint-based recovery; reload state from last checkpoint); replica-based recovery copies a healthy replica to a replacement node; read quorum (R=1 in Derecho shards) lets any up-to-date replica serve state.

Decision: `CopyReplica` action copies full dataset state from a healthy donor node to a replacement node via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams; `RestoreRedundancy` re-establishes the target replication factor by placing new replicas on healthy nodes selected by capacity (`Capacity.can_serve`) and failure-domain placement (`PlacementDecision`). Donor selection prefers same-region, different-HUnit nodes to limit blast radius.

#### 3.5 Erasure-Code Reconstruction (k-of-n Fragment Repair)

Research basis: regenerating codes (Dimakis et al. — minimize repair bandwidth; exact minimum-repair-bandwidth cooperative regenerating codes); robust repair of Reed-Solomon codes under erroneous helper responses; fragment distribution across data owner/parity owner nodes; rebuilding lost data via computation from a recovery strip set.

Decision: `ReconstructErasure` action reconstructs lost fragments from surviving k-of-n erasure-coded fragments; helper nodes return fragment hashes (BLAKE3) first to detect erroneous responses before full fragment transfer; reconstruction writes to a new node and updates `FragmentPlacement`. Tolerates up to n−k simultaneous fragment losses. Verification via BLAKE3/SHA-256 checksum of reconstructed data against the original content hash.

#### 3.6 Ownership-Aware Recovery (Transfer Ownership)

Research basis: Raft group reconfiguration (add learners first, promote one at a time, remove after sync); ReCraft (wait-free membership changes, quorum overlap); Khepri failure recovery (Raft-driven, new leader elected, rejoining node catches up from common log point).

Decision: `TransferOwnership` action reassigns dataset leadership/ownership from a failed node to a healthy replica; ownership transfer requires the target to be caught up to the current `OrderingPos`; fencing epoch increment prevents split-brain; transfer is ownership-only, no data movement unless combined with CopyReplica.

#### 3.7 Capacity-Bounded Recovery (Throttling / Resource Limits)

Research basis: SRE throttling design pattern (coordinated overload rejection, per-caller quotas); token pools / DRB (bounded resource entitlements, fair-share convergence); recovery load bounded — clearing a backlog cannot exceed downstream safe capacity; bounded backoff with jitter.

Decision: `RecoveryResourceManager` (already in `ids-000-aa`) bounds concurrent active recoveries by `resource_limit`; excess recoveries are queued/rejected; per-recovery capacity requirements (`Capacity`) checked against donor node `can_serve` before starting; bounded exponential backoff between retry attempts; no unbounded parallel rebuilds that could saturate carrier bandwidth or donor capacity.

#### 3.8 Recovery Verification (Proofs + Checksums)

Research basis: content-addressed storage verification (BLAKE3 blob hashing, verified streaming via bao); recovery proof = dataset_id + recovered_fragments + checksum + ids_time (already `RecoveryProof` in `ids-000-aa`); integrity verification result per node (Checksum, verified flag, anomaly).

Decision: `VerifyIntegrity` action recomputes BLAKE3/SHA-256 checksum over recovered/replicated data and compares to the recorded content hash; a `RecoveryProof` is issued only when checksums match; mismatches trigger `Anomaly` (ByteMismatch, ChecksumFailure, StateCorruption, ReplicaDrift) and quarantine. Verification is mandatory before a plan reaches Completion.

#### 3.9 Quarantine and Release (Suspected Failure Isolation)

Research basis: Byzantine node isolation/quarantine; exclusion as last resort; identity-bound exclusion (not unauthenticated peer handles); post-compromise handling without breaking causality (decouple content trust from identity trust).

Decision: `QuarantineManager` (already in `ids-000-aa`) isolates a scope (node/hunit/region) with a `QuarantineReason` (SuspectedFailure, CorruptionDetected, Unresponsive, PolicyViolation); quarantined scopes are excluded from donor/recipient selection; release requires successful `VerifyIntegrity`; quarantine is deliberate, never timeout-based.

#### 3.10 Multi-Level Recovery State Machine

Research basis: multi-level recovery schemes (common case fast, worst case covered); recovery phase state machine (Detection, Planning, Execution, Verification, Completion — already `RecoveryPhase` in `ids-000-aa`); transition ordering enforced (can_transition requires order_index increase).

Decision: `RecoveryCoordinator` (already in `ids-000-aa`) drives the phase machine per active scope; `RegionalRecoveryCoordinator` handles cross-region recovery initiation; `NodeRecoveryTracker`/`HUnitRecoveryTracker` track per-node/hunit recovery state (Healthy, Degraded, Recovering, Failed, Quarantined); `RecoveryTimeline` records failure_detected → plan_created → plan_started → step_completed/failed → plan_completed/failed → quarantined/released/reconciled/reconstructed.

#### 3.11 Regional Failure Compensation and Isolation

Research basis: cell-based architecture (AWS — fault isolated boundaries limit blast radius; bulkheads contain hull breaches); region outage failover (Spanner failover — independent failure domains with separate Paxos quorums); regional load balancer failover; drain-a-region traffic shifting.

Decision: regional failure compensation redirects traffic/ownership to surviving regions before repair begins; regional failure isolation prevents the failed region's nodes from being selected as donors or recipients; cross-region recovery re-establishes redundancy in surviving regions; region health tracked (Healthy/Degraded/Critical/Failed — already `HealthStatus`).

#### 3.12 Cross-H-Unit Recovery

Decision: when an HUnit fails, cross-H-unit recovery places replacement replicas in other HUnits within the same region (intra-region, low latency); if intra-region capacity is insufficient, escalate to region-level recovery. Placement respects failure domain (different HUnit from surviving copies to avoid correlated loss).

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
| Rebuild storm (thundering herd) saturates carrier/donor capacity | Capacity-bounded recovery (`RecoveryResourceManager`); per-donor capacity check; bounded backoff; staged restoration |
| Donor node fails mid-rebuild | Retry with alternate replica; step-level max_attempts; plan-level failure escalation to higher scope |
| Corrupt replica used as donor | Verify integrity (BLAKE3/SHA-256) before and after copy; `VerifyIntegrity` action; quarantine corrupt donors |
| Erasure reconstruction with erroneous helper responses | Fragment hash pre-check (BLAKE3) before full transfer; robust repair tolerates e erroneous helpers |
| Split-brain during ownership transfer | Fencing epoch increment; target must be caught up to current `OrderingPos`; no global master |
| Quarantine blocks all donors (insufficient replicas) | `InsufficientReplicas` error; escalate scope (node→hunit→region→region-wide); alert for manual intervention |
| Recovery never completes (offline/permanent failure) | Deliberate eviction only, never timeout-based; quarantine with release condition; membership management required |
| Zombie/resurrected stale data | Recovery proofs bind to `ids_time` and content checksum; stale replicas rejected by `OrderingPos` comparison |
| Carrier loss during recovery datagrams | Carrier-agnostic datagrams may be lost; recovery is idempotent at step level; retransmission handled by caller/retry manager |
| Resource exhaustion from concurrent recoveries | `RecoveryResourceManager` hard limit; queued/rejected overflow; per-recovery capacity budgets |
| Region-wide correlated failure | Cross-region recovery; restore redundancy in surviving regions; failover before repair |

**Critical failure modes:** (1) donor exhaustion — all healthy replicas also fail during rebuild; mitigated by scope escalation and `InsufficientReplicas` error. (2) Erasure code below k survivors — data unrecoverable; mitigated by proactive redundancy restoration before hitting threshold. (3) Quarantine of a majority region — remaining regions cannot form quorum; mitigated by deliberate membership management, never automatic eviction.

| `ids-broadcast` (Phase 020) | Ordered delivery of recovery coordination messages (optional) |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-recovery` implements `ids-000-aa::Recovery` sealed trait; downstream crates call `detect_failures`, `create_plan`, `execute_plan`, `quarantine`, `restore_redundancy`, `reconcile_state`.
- Failure events flow from `FailureDetector` (heartbeats) → `RecoveryCoordinator` (phase machine) → `RepairPlanner` (strategy) → step execution → `StateReconciler`/`ReplicaReconstructor` → `QuarantineManager`/`VerifyIntegrity` → `RecoveryStats`/`RecoveryTimeline`.
- All inter-node recovery traffic (fragment copy, parity transfer, state sync) uses `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams; no direct carrier imports beyond `Endpoint` and `CarrierType`.
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS — preserves carrier-agnostic architecture.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Multi-Level Recovery State Machine
```
RecoveryPhase: Detection(0) → Planning(1) → Execution(2) → Verification(3) → Completion(4)
can_transition(from, to) = from.order_index() < to.order_index() || from == to
Per active scope: RecoveryCoordinator drives phase transitions; RecoveryTimeline records each event.
```

#### 7.2 Failure Detection
```
record_heartbeat(scope_id, at_ms) → store last heartbeat
detect_failures(now_ms) → for each scope: if now_ms - last_hb > timeout_ms → FailureEvent
FailureEventType: NodeFailure | HUnitFailure | RegionalFailure | NetworkPartition | DiskFailure | PowerFailure
Default heartbeat_timeout_ms: 30000 (from ids-000-aa FailureDetector::default)
```

#### 7.3 Repair Strategy Selection by Scope
```
Node     → CopyReplica      (priority 1)
HUnit    → RestoreRedundancy (priority 2)
Region   → ReconstructErasure (priority 3)
RegionWide → TransferOwnership (priority 4)
Escalation: if lower-level repair yields InsufficientReplicas, escalate to next scope level.
```

#### 7.4 Erasure-Code Reconstruction (k-of-n)
```
Given n fragments, any k suffice to reconstruct.
Failure tolerance = n − k simultaneous losses.
Helper validation: each helper sends BLAKE3(fragment_hash) first; mismatch → exclude helper.
Reconstruct from k valid helpers; write to replacement node; verify BLAKE3(content_hash) matches original.
```

#### 7.5 Capacity-Bounded Recovery
```
acquire(plan_id) → reject if active_count >= resource_limit
donor_selection(candidate) → candidate.Capacity.can_serve(required) && !candidate.quarantined
backoff(delay) = base * multiplier^attempt, clamped to max_delay_ms, plus jitter
```

#### 7.6 Recovery Verification
```
checksum = BLAKE3(data) or SHA-256(data)
VerifyIntegrity: recompute checksum over recovered data; compare to recorded content_hash
match → issue RecoveryProof { dataset_id, recovered_fragments, checksum, ids_time }
mismatch → Anomaly (ByteMismatch/ChecksumFailure/StateCorruption/ReplicaDrift) → quarantine
Plan reaches Completion only after VerifyIntegrity passes.
```

#### 7.7 Ownership Transfer with Fencing
```
target must be caught up to current OrderingPos (target.pos >= current.pos)
fencing_epoch += 1; record fencing_epoch in transfer
no global master — transfer is per-dataset, coordinated via RecoveryCoordinator
```

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

|| # | Criterion | Measurement ||
|---|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-025.1 | Node failure recovery | Single node failure → CopyReplica restores replica; verify via IntegrityResult.verified == true |
| AC-025.2 | H-unit failure compensation | HUnit failure → RestoreRedundancy places replicas in other HUnits; placement satisfies failure_domain |
| AC-025.3 | Cross-H-unit recovery | Intra-region capacity insufficient → escalate to Region scope; cross-region placement |
| AC-025.4 | Regional failure compensation | Region failure → fail over to surviving regions before repair; regional isolation excludes failed region |
| AC-025.5 | Regional failure isolation | Failed region's nodes never selected as donors/recipients during regional recovery |
| AC-025.6 | Replica-based recovery | CopyReplica from healthy donor → target state matches donor (checksum equality) |
| AC-025.7 | Erasure-code reconstruction | k-of-n fragment reconstruction tolerates up to n−k helper failures; output checksum matches original |
| AC-025.8 | Capacity-bounded recovery | Concurrent active recoveries never exceed resource_limit; excess queued/rejected |
| AC-025.9 | Ownership-aware recovery | TransferOwnership only to target caught up to current OrderingPos; fencing_epoch incremented |
| AC-025.10 | Recovery verification | RecoveryProof issued only when BLAKE3/SHA-256 checksum matches; mismatch → Anomaly + quarantine |
| AC-025.11 | Redundancy restoration | Post-recovery, dataset replication factor restored to target; verify via redundancy report |
| AC-025.12 | Multi-level recovery state machine | Phase transitions strictly ordered Detection→Planning→Execution→Verification→Completion; no backward transitions |
| AC-025.13 | No timeout-based eviction | Quarantine/release is deliberate; no automatic eviction after heartbeat timeout |
| AC-025.14 | Carrier agnosticism | Zero direct dependencies on std::net, tokio::net, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, mesh; all traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint |
| AC-025.15 | Allowed crypto only | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 used; no other algorithms |
| AC-025.16 | File structure | ~90–150 files, all production-grade, organized in subfolders, no stubs |
| AC-025.17 | Property tests | proptest/bolero properties across all subsystems; 100k+ iterations |
| AC-025.18 | Adversarial tests | Donor failure mid-rebuild, corrupt replica donor, region-wide failure — all pass/fail defined |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Region-wide recovery scope:** CRATES.md and prompts mention "region-wide failure recovery" but `ids-000-aa` `RecoveryScope` only has Node/HUnit/Region. Need to decide whether RegionWide is a virtual scope handled by `RegionalRecoveryCoordinator` or a fourth enum variant added to `ids-000-aa` (contract change, requires master-crate coordination).
2. **Recovery heartbeat transport:** Heartbeats are recorded via `FailureDetector` but the transport mechanism (who sends heartbeats, over which `ids-carrier::Endpoint`) is not specified in `ids-000-aa`; must be designed without assuming any carrier semantics.
3. **Erasure-code library:** No erasure-coding crate is currently in the IDS dependency set; selection of a Reed-Solomon/regenerating-code implementation (pure Rust, no networking) is pending.
4. **Checkpoint integration:** `ids-snapshot` (Phase 026) will provide checkpoints as recovery restore points; the exact restore-from-checkpoint flow in `ids-recovery` is undefined until Phase 026 is planned.
5. **Cross-region failover trigger:** What triggers regional failover vs. in-region repair (threshold of failed nodes in a region, or region health == Critical/Failed) is a product decision.
6. **Recovery proof format:** `RecoveryProof` exists in `ids-000-aa` but the checksum algorithm (BLAKE3 vs SHA-256 vs both) and fragment inclusion rules need final specification.
7. **Capacity accounting:** How `Capacity` is measured per node (storage vs memory vs CPU vs network_bps) and refreshed during recovery is not yet defined.
8. **Quarantine release policy:** Release requires successful `VerifyIntegrity`, but who authorizes release (automatic vs manual) and appeal windows are policy decisions.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Separate `ids-recovery` crate | Keeps recovery as a distinct concern; `ids-000-aa` holds the sealed `trait Recovery` contract; implementation lives downstream |
| Multi-level scope model (Node/HUnit/Region/RegionWide) | Matches CRATES.md §25 and prompts.txt entry 25; hierarchical fault domains limit blast radius (AWS cell-based, Google Cloud failure domains) |
| Repair priority: CopyReplica → RestoreRedundancy → ReconstructErasure → TransferOwnership | Follows `RepairPlanner` in `ids-000-aa`; cheapest first, escalating cost/scope |
| Capacity-bounded recovery (`RecoveryResourceManager`) | Prevents rebuild storms; bounded backoff with jitter (SRE throttling pattern) |
| No timeout-based eviction | Eviction is deliberate, never automatic; quarantine requires deliberate release after `VerifyIntegrity` |
| Verification before Completion | `VerifyIntegrity` mandatory; `RecoveryProof` binds `ids_time` + content checksum; prevents zombie/resurrected data |
| Erasure-code helper hash pre-check | BLAKE3 fragment hash before full transfer; robust repair tolerates erroneous helpers |
| Carrier-agnostic over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Preserves IDS carrier-agnostic stance; no TCP/IP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/libp2p |
| Allowed crypto only: ed25519/sha256/blake3/xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 | Matches IDS crypto policy (implemented in `ids-crypto`) |
| `ids-000-aa` as master crate | All canonical types and sealed trait contracts defined once; `ids-recovery` imports, never redefines |

# PHASE 026:

## Phase 026 — Create the ids-snapshot crate: Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 026 creates **`ids-snapshot`**, a new separate crate in the IDS workspace (C:/idfs) providing **consistent global state for checkpointing and recovery**. The crate implements the Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshot algorithm (marker messages, consistent cuts, in-flight/channel message recording), stable property detection, global snapshots, savepoints, checkpoints, incremental checkpoints, and state restoration — all carrier-agnostic, riding only `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), with zero direct network dependencies.

**Scope of ids-snapshot (research-verified):**
- **Chandy–Lamport global snapshot algorithm** — any node can initiate; initiator records local state, sends marker messages on all outgoing logical channels, begins recording inbound messages; on first marker received a node records its local state, marks the incoming channel as empty, forwards markers on all outgoing channels, and records subsequent messages on that channel as in-flight channel state; on a second marker received on a channel it records that channel's captured messages as channel state. Produces a consistent cut (if event `e` is captured, all events that happened-before `e` are also captured). Termination when every node has recorded its state and a marker on every incoming channel. (Chandy & Lamport 1985, "Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems"; MIT 6.852J; Princeton COS418; UIUC ECE428/CS425.)
- **Marker messages** — special control messages distinct from application messages, FIFO-ordered on logical channels, barrier between pre-snapshot and post-snapshot traffic; guarantee zero loss + zero duplication of recorded channel state.
- **Consistent global state / consistent cut** — a cut `C` is consistent iff for every pair of events `e, f`, if `f ∈ C` and `e → f` (happens-before) then `e ∈ C`. A global state is consistent iff it corresponds to a consistent cut. Vector clocks (Fidge/Mattern) provide the causality test: cut is consistent iff `∀i, V(i) = V_i(i)` (no one knows more about a node than that node knows about itself).
- **In-flight message recording** — messages sent before the sender's state is recorded but received after the receiver's state is recorded are captured as channel state; this is what makes the cut consistent (no orphan receive without its matching send).
- **Stable property detection** — a predicate `y` is stable if once true it remains true; record a consistent global state `S*` and evaluate `y(S*)`; correctness follows from `S*` reachable from start and end reachable from `S*`. Examples: computation terminated, deadlock detected, token lost. Unstable predicates cannot be detected by snapshots alone.
- **Global snapshot, savepoint, checkpoint** — snapshot = consistent global state captured at runtime; savepoint = a named, exportable consistent state image for stop-and-resume/fork/update; checkpoint = a durable point-in-time state used for rollback recovery.
- **Incremental checkpoint** — differential snapshots capturing only state changed since the last checkpoint/base checkpoint; tiered checkpointing keeps lightweight differential checkpoints locally/peer-side and migrates heavyweight base checkpoints to durable storage.
- **State restoration** — restore from latest checkpoint + replay journal/delta entries since the checkpoint (snapshot + WAL pattern); recovery = load snapshot + replay journal; fail closed on hash mismatch; never partial replay on corruption.

**Key engineering decisions:**
- **New separate crate `ids-snapshot`**, not folders inside existing crates (per IDS rule: separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones). Depends only on `ids-000-aa`, `ids-carrier` (endpoint/opaque bytes), `ids-crypto`-allowed primitives; carrier-agnostic over `Endpoint`.
- **Chandy–Lamport over logical channels** — snapshot state is captured over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams; marker messages are opaque `Vec<u8>` payloads distinguished by a message-type tag, sent via `carrier.send_datagram(endpoint, &[u8])`. No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh.
- **Consistent cut via marker barrier** — FIFO ordering of markers relative to app messages on each logical channel is the consistency mechanism; no wall-clock or global snapshot coordinator required.
- **Vector-clock causality tracking** — each node maintains a vector clock (one entry per known node) tagged on state and markers; consistent-cut validation via the Mattern/Fidge max-vector rule.
- **Persistence: checkpoint + delta journal** — periodic full checkpoints (versioned, checksummed, bincode/CBOR, optional compression) plus append-only delta journal; recovery = load latest checkpoint + replay journal since checkpoint. Tombstones/compaction gated on causal stability (all nodes acked past a checkpoint).
- **Allowed crypto only**: ed25519 (snapshot signing/integrity), xchacha20poly1305 + chacha20poly1305 (at-rest snapshot encryption), sha256 and blake3 (content addressing, checksums, Merkle roots).
- **ids-000-aa is the master crate** — `Snapshot` sealed trait, `NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `DatasetId`, `SnapshotError`, etc. live there; `ids-snapshot` implements downstream.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

The ids-snapshot crate sits between the application/state layer and the carrier layer, below `ids-recovery`/`ids-replication` and above `ids-carrier`. It is **not** a network protocol — it is a local, deterministic consistent-state capture engine that produces bytes shipped over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              APPLICATION / ids-state                        │
│  local mutable state to be snapshotted                      │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             ids-recovery / ids-replication                  │
│  rollback recovery, checkpoint triggers, restore requests   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│         Phase 026: ids-snapshot (NEW CRATE)                 │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  snapshot engine: Chandy-Lamport, marker messages     │  │
│  │  consistent cut, channel/in-flight recording          │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  vector clock + causality / consistent-cut validation │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  checkpoint / savepoint / incremental checkpoint      │  │
│  │  versioned, checksummed, compressed (blake3/sha256)   │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  state restoration: checkpoint + delta journal replay │  │
│  │  fail-closed on hash mismatch                         │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  stable property detection (termination, deadlock)    │  │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │  wire: marker + snapshot chunks over ids-carrier::Endpoint│ │
│  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              ids-carrier (Endpoint opaque bytes)            │
│  CarrierType + Vec<u8>; send_datagram / receive_datagram    │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             ids-000-aa (master, sealed traits)              │
│  NodeId, Endpoint, CarrierType, DatasetId, Snapshot trait   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a coordinated snapshot:**
1. Initiator `i` records local state `S_i`, tags with vector clock `VC_i`, sends a marker on every outgoing logical `Endpoint`, begins recording inbound messages on all incoming channels.
2. On receiving a marker on channel `c` from `k`: if first marker seen — record local state `S_j`, mark channel `c` state as empty, forward markers on all outgoing channels, begin recording inbound messages on all other incoming channels. If marker already seen — record channel `c` state as all messages received since local state was recorded (the in-flight messages).
3. Termination: every node has recorded local state and a marker on every incoming channel. The collection of local states + channel states forms a consistent global snapshot.
4. The snapshot is serialized (versioned, BLAKE3/SHA-256 checksummed, optional XChaCha20-Poly1305/ChaCha20-Poly1305 encrypted), written as a checkpoint/savepoint; a delta journal records subsequent changes.
5. Recovery: load latest checkpoint, replay delta journal; fail closed on hash/checksum mismatch; never partial replay on corruption.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Chandy–Lamport Global Snapshot Algorithm

The foundational algorithm (Chandy & Lamport, 1985). System model: `n` processes, two unidirectional FIFO channels per ordered pair, all messages arrive intact and unduplicated, no failures, any process may initiate.

**Marker-sending rule (process p):** For each outgoing channel `c`, p sends one marker along `c` after p records its own state and before p sends further messages along `c`. The marker is a special control message with no effect on the underlying computation.

**Marker-receiving rule (process q):** On receiving a marker along channel `c`:
- if q has not recorded its state: q records its state; q records state of `c` as the empty sequence.
- else: q records the state of `c` as the sequence of messages received along `c` after q's state was recorded and before q received the marker along `c`.

**Termination:** All processes have recorded their state; all processes have received a marker on all incoming channels. A central collector (or each node locally) assembles the global snapshot from local states + channel states.

**Properties:** Any run creates a consistent cut — if event `e` happens-before `f` (`e → f`) and `f` is in the cut, then `e` is also in the cut. Proof: by FIFO ordering, markers on each link precede regular application messages, so a receive recorded in the snapshot implies its matching send is also recorded. Works with multiple initiators; decentralized — any process may start a snapshot.

#### 3.2 Consistent Cuts and Global State

A cut `C` selects a prefix of each process's local event history. `C` is consistent iff it is closed under happens-before: `f ∈ C ∧ e → f ⟹ e ∈ C`. Equivalently, every received message in the cut has its matching send in the cut; no orphan receives.

Vector-clock consistency test (Mattern/Fidge): let `V_i` be node `i`'s vector clock at its cut point, and `V = componentwise_max(V_1..V_n)`. The cut is consistent iff `∀i, V(i) = V_i(i)` — no node knows more about any node than that node knows about itself at its cut point. This rules out a node receiving a message (learning more about the sender) before its cut point while the sender's cut point is earlier.

The recorded global state may never have actually occurred during the real execution, but it is reachable by reordering only events within the snapshot window — it is sequentially consistent with a real state.

#### 3.3 Marker Messages and In-Flight Message Recording

Markers are special messages distinct from application messages, carried as opaque `Vec<u8>` payloads over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` with a message-type tag. They act as a barrier: messages sent by `p` before `p` records its state on channel `c` are "before the marker"; messages sent after are "after". Because channels are FIFO, the marker cleanly separates the two classes at the receiver.

In-flight message recording: a message `m` sent by `p` to `q` where `send(m)` is before `p`'s recorded state but `recv(m)` is after `q`'s recorded state is captured as part of channel `c`'s state. Without recording channel state, the snapshot would contain a receive without its matching send (an inconsistent cut / orphan message). The channel state is either "empty" (first-marker case) or the sequence of messages received between local-state recording and marker receipt (second-marker case).

#### 3.4 Stable Property Detection

A predicate `y` over global states is **stable** if `y(S) ⟹ y(S')` for all `S'` reachable from `S` (once true, stays true). Examples: computation terminated, system deadlocked, all tokens disappeared, no in-flight messages.

Detection algorithm: record a consistent global state `S*` via Chandy–Lamport; compute `definite = y(S*)`. Correctness: `S*` is reachable from the start state `S_i`; the termination state `S_f` is reachable from `S*`; by stability, `y(S*) ⟹ y(S_f)` and `¬y(S*) ⟹ ¬y(S_i)`. Unstable predicates cannot be detected by snapshots — a sequence of snapshots may have gaps exactly where the unstable predicate holds.

IDS relevance: stable-property detection underpins termination/quiescence checks before taking checkpoints, and deadlock detection across the carrier-agnostic logical topology.

#### 3.5 Checkpointing, Savepoints, and Incremental Checkpoints

- **Checkpoint:** durable point-in-time consistent state used for rollback recovery. Coordinated checkpointing (Chandy–Lamport markers) guarantees a consistent global checkpoint; uncoordinated/independent checkpoints risk inconsistent cuts and orphan messages, requiring rollback to older consistent checkpoints (domino effect).
- **Savepoint:** a named, exportable consistent state image for stop-and-resume, fork, or upgrade (Apache Flink savepoint pattern: directory of binary state files + small metadata file of pointers; can resume from savepoint, dispose of savepoint).
- **Incremental checkpoint / differential checkpoint:** captures only state changed since the last base checkpoint; tiered designs keep lightweight differential checkpoints local/peer-side and migrate heavyweight base checkpoints to durable storage (TierCheck pattern). Reduces I/O and write amplification vs full-state snapshots.
- **Persistence pattern (recommended):** periodic full checkpoint + append-only delta journal (WAL); recovery = load latest checkpoint + replay journal entries after the checkpoint checkpoint version. Compaction after all nodes ack past a checkpoint version. Avoids full-history replay (observed production case: 55K ops / 276MB replayed 27+ minutes — snapshot+journal bounds recovery to seconds).

#### 3.6 State Restoration

Restoration loads the latest checkpoint to initialize state, then replays the delta journal since the checkpoint version to reach the current state. Correctness rules: no partial replay on corruption; fail closed on hash/checksum mismatch; keep multiple historical checkpoints; tombstones compacted only after all nodes acknowledge (causal stability) to avoid "zombie records" (resurrected deleted data). Offline/never-acking nodes block GC — requires membership management or a grace/quarantine window.

#### 3.7 Vector Clocks and Causality for Snapshot Coordination

Vector clocks (one entry per known node) tag each node's local state and each marker. They enable consistent-cut validation without a global clock. Causal delivery: a node applies a marker/snapshot only after its causal dependencies are satisfied; gaps are tracked and requested. Never use wall-clock for validity decisions; HLC/Lamport may be used as a secondary bounded-skew timestamp but never as authority.

#### 3.8 Snapshot Serialization and Versioning

Snapshot payloads must be versioned for schema evolution. A magic number + format version header precedes the serialized body; a format change bumps the major version; backward compatibility via `#[serde(default)]`, `#[serde(alias)]`, or explicit versioned structs with migration `From`/`TryFrom` impls. Checksums (BLAKE3/SHA-256) on every payload; fail closed on mismatch. Firecracker snapshot versioning pattern (magic_id + MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH format version, independent of binary version) is a reference design.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|------------|
| Inconsistent cut / orphan receive (receive without matching send) | Chandy–Lamport marker barrier over FIFO logical channels; consistent-cut validation via vector clocks |
| Non-FIFO or reordered marker/app messages break consistency | Logical FIFO channel guarantee required from ids-carrier layer; markers tagged with sequence per (sender, channel) |
| Lost or duplicated marker messages | Retransmit markers until acked; idempotent state recording tolerates duplication |
| Snapshot never terminates (node never records / channel never marked) | Per-node completion tracking; timeout-based retry; dead/quarantined nodes handled by ids-recovery |
| Corrupt snapshot/journal payload | BLAKE3/SHA-256 checksum on every chunk/payload; fail closed on mismatch; multiple historical checkpoints |
| Zombie records / resurrected deleted data after GC | Tombstone compaction only after causal stability (all nodes ack); gate GC on all-peer ack |
| Offline node blocks tombstone GC / compaction | Membership-aware causal stability; grace/quarantine window; deliberate eviction, never by timeout |
| Wall-clock skew corrupts causality ordering | Vector clocks / Lamport clocks only; never raw `SystemTime` for validity |
| Unauthorized snapshot/restore | ed25519 signatures on snapshot commitments; integrate with ids-security |
| Snapshot encryption at rest | XChaCha20-Poly1305 / ChaCha20-Poly1305 only (allowed crypto set) |
| Carrier-specific assumptions leaking in | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; zero `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

`ids-snapshot` depends on and integrates with:

| Crate | Role in Phase 026 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: `NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `DatasetId`, `SnapshotError`, sealed `Snapshot` trait, canonical types |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); all marker/snapshot traffic via `send_datagram`/`receive_datagram` |
| `ids-crypto` (allowed subset) | ed25519 signing, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 encryption, sha256/blake3 hashing |
| `ids-recovery` | Consumer: checkpoints/savepoints feed multi-level node/H-unit/region recovery |
| `ids-replication` | Consumer: consistent snapshots for replica state synchronization |
| `ids-state` / application layer | Source of local mutable state to be snapshotted/restored |
| `ids-fault` | Integration: circuit breakers/bulkheads protect snapshot triggers |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-snapshot` produces marker + snapshot-chunk bytes; `ids-carrier` ships them over opaque `Endpoint`s; `ids-snapshot` never imports a carrier implementation.
- `ids-000-aa`'s sealed `Snapshot` trait is implemented by `ids-snapshot`'s `SnapshotEngine`; downstream crates call through the trait, zero downstream edits on contract change.
- `ids-recovery` consumes checkpoints/savepoints for rollback recovery; `ids-replication` consumes consistent snapshots for replica sync.
- Carrier-agnostic by design (I-CARR-001 equivalent): compiles and behaves identically over Loopback/Serial/Optical/Radio/Custom carriers.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Chandy–Lamport Snapshot (coordinated, marker-based)

```
initiate(p):
    record local state S_p tagged with VC_p
    for each outgoing channel c: send Marker on c  (after state, before further app msgs)
    begin recording inbound messages on all incoming channels

on receive Marker on channel c from k at q:
    if q has not recorded state:
        record local state S_q tagged VC_q
        record channel c state = empty
        for each outgoing channel c': send Marker on c'
        begin recording inbound on all incoming channels except c
    else:
        record channel c state = messages received since q recorded state
        stop recording on c

terminate: all nodes recorded state + marker on all incoming channels
```

#### 7.2 Consistent Cut Validation (vector clocks)

```
V_i = node i's vector clock at its cut point
V = componentwise_max(V_1..V_n)
cut consistent ⟺ ∀i: V(i) == V_i(i)
```

Happens-before: `e → f` iff `VC(e) < VC(f)` (all components ≤, at least one strict).

#### 7.3 In-Flight Message Recording

```
channel_state(c) = empty                    if c was first-marker channel
                 = [m | recv(m) after state_recorded ∧ recv(m) before marker_recv]
```

#### 7.4 Checkpoint + Delta Journal Recovery

```
Checkpoint { version, state_bytes, vector_clock, checksum, created_at }
Journal: append-only (seq, delta_bytes, checksum)
recover: load latest checkpoint, replay journal entries with seq > checkpoint.version
compact: after all-peer ack past checkpoint version, prune journal + tombstones before it
```

#### 7.5 Stable Property Detection

```
record consistent global state S* via Chandy-Lamport
definite = y(S*)
correctness: S* reachable from start S_i; end S_f reachable from S*; y stable ⟹ y(S*) ⟹ y(S_f)
```

#### 7.6 Causal Stability / GC Gate

```
stable_frontier[i] = min over all known peers of frontier[i]
version v stable ⟺ ∀ replicas r: frontier[r] >= v   (MVV componentwise min)
tombstone t GC-able ⟺ t's remove op is causally stable
```

| `xchacha20poly1305` / `chacha20poly1305` | At-rest snapshot encryption |
| `thiserror` | Error types |
| `proptest` / `bolero` | Property-based testing |
| `criterion` | Benchmarks |

No networking crates (libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS) — `ids-snapshot` is transport-agnostic over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
