### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
| Separate `ids-saga` crate (not folders inside `ids-000-aa`) | Matches "try to use separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones"; single control point per concern |
| Implement sealed `trait Saga` from `ids-000-aa` | Canonical contract already defined; downstream uses as bound, cannot implement |
| Both choreography and orchestration in one crate | prompts.txt entry 29 lists both; shared state machine, retry, idempotency, compensation code |
| Compensation = new forward transaction, not rollback | Semantic compensation per Garcia-Molina & Salem / Azure; original effect stays auditable |
| Reverse compensation order, idempotent + retriable compensations | Required by saga correctness (IBM, Azure, Temporal, Cloudflare Workflows) |
| Bounded exponential backoff + jitter for retries | AWS Architecture Blog; prevents retry storms and thundering herds; bounded attempts guarantee termination |
| Idempotency keys + dedup inside local transaction; outbox for events | Exactly-once effect over at-least-once carrier; no dual-write window |
| Saga-level wait-for graph + victim abort for deadlocks | Distributed deadlock detection (Purdue/ACM); steps hold no cross-service locks, so cycle detection is saga-local |
| Randomized backoff + bounded attempts + circuit breaker for livelock | Classic livelock prevention; converts potential livelock into bounded delay or failure |
| `ids-carrier::Endpoint` sole address type; no networking crates | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule (IDS policy) |
| Crypto: ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 only via `ids-crypto` | IDS allowed-crypto policy; `ids-saga` consumes type surface only |
| Durable saga log + checkpoints on every transition | Crash recovery without re-executing completed steps (Eventuate Tram, Temporal) |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 030 creates `ids-integrity`, the IDS crate for data integrity verification and bit rot detection. It owns end-to-end checksums, content hashes, Merkle trees, version comparisons, replica audits, partition-level integrity verification, continuous integrity scrubbing, silent bit rot detection, checksum mismatch handling, and ZFS-style end-to-end protection. Every stored record, partition, and replica is checksummed; background scrubs recompute checksums against stored values to find silent corruption before reads hit it; mismatches are reported, reconstructed from redundant copies, and rewritten to healthy media.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`, max 1024-byte address). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-integrity` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-integrity` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-integrity/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types `Checksum` (`src/types.rs:1973`), `Anomaly` / `AnomalyType` (`src/types.rs:1934` — ByteMismatch, ReplicaDrift, ChecksumFailure, StateCorruption), plus `SnapshotId`, `FragmentId`, `RecoveryProof` — all referenced by this crate but never redefined. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned ZFS end-to-end checksums (Bonwick 2005; OpenZFS docs; UWisc FAST'10 fault injection), ZFS/Btrfs scrub and self-healing, Merkle trees as self-validating block-pointer trees, anti-entropy Merkle reconciliation (Dynamo/Cassandra/ScyllaDB; Merkle Search Trees IEEE 9049566), dm-verity/fs-verity block-level integrity, end-to-end argument (Saltzer/Reed/Clark 1984), silent data corruption studies (CERN Xyratex; NetApp 1.5M drives/41 months/400k+ mismatches; Bairavasundaram et al. SOSP), bit half-life and petabyte-scale integrity, content-addressable storage (Git SHA-1/SHA-256), content-defined chunking (Rabin fingerprint; restic), SHA-256 vs CRC32 collision probability, T10 DIF/DIX end-to-end data integrity field, fixity checking / digital preservation auditing, fs-verity, cold-storage bit rot scrubbing, erasure coding (Reed-Solomon) repair.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-integrity` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is layered so each concern — checksums, content hashes, Merkle trees, version comparison, replica audit, partition verification, scrubbing, bit rot detection, mismatch handling — is an independent module:

│  │              │ │ sha256)      │ │ record/part)│ │ Version)     │    │ │
│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┘    │ │

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▼───────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                  │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, Vec<u8>≤1024}, payload: &[u8])        │

**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- One canonical definition per type; canonical types (`NodeId`, `DatasetId`, `PartitionId`, `RecordId`, `OrderingPos`, `Version`, `SnapshotId`, `Checksum`, `Anomaly`, `AnomalyType`, `FragmentId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`) imported from `ids_000_aa::X`, never redefined.
- `ids-integrity` implements the sealed `trait Integrity` contract from `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/` (checksums, scrub, audit, verify) as declared in the master crate; downstream crates use it as a trait bound, cannot implement it.
- All integrity metadata (checksums, digests, proofs) is transported as opaque bytes via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No IP addresses, ports, sockets.
- Crypto surface: sha256/blake3 for content hashes and checksums; ed25519 (optional) for signing integrity proofs/audit records; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 only if checksum payloads need encryption (integrity crate does not encrypt by default). All ops in `ids-crypto`; this crate declares only usage boundaries.
- Integrity is dataset-scoped; no global integrity master (invariant `no_global_master` in `ids-000-aa`).
- Operation lifecycle reuses `ids-000-aa` `OpState` and `CommitState`; integrity findings are `Anomaly` records raised through `ids-000-aa` error/annex channels.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Silent Data Corruption and Bit Rot

Bit rot = random bit flips on storage media with no announced error. Research basis:
- CERN/Xyratex study (Kelemen 2007): ~3000 nodes, ~5 weeks, 500 errors on 100 nodes; 80% were 64K-region corruptions correlated with disk drop-out; single-bit errors correlated with ECC memory errors. Silent corruption is a fact of life.
- NetApp study (Bairavasundaram et al., SOSP): 1.53M disk drives over 41 months; >400,000 checksum mismatches; 8.5% of nearline drives and 1.9% of enterprise drives developed corruption; a large fraction went undetected until RAID restoration.
- Bit half-life model ("Keeping Bits Safe", CACM): at current enterprise storage error rates (~1e-9 bytes corrupted per 6 months at CERN), reaching petabyte-for-a-century durability requires ~1e9 improvement — hence checksums + scrubbing + redundancy are mandatory.
- Silent corruption is invisible to SMART/URE reporting; only application-level or filesystem-level checksums detect it. RAID scrub alone cannot identify which copy is correct.

#### 3.2 End-to-End Checksums (ZFS-style)

Research basis:
- ZFS end-to-end data integrity (Bonwick 2005; OpenZFS docs; UWisc FAST'10): checksums stored in parent block pointers, not with the block itself — fault isolation between data and checksum. Every block checksummed by its parent; the whole pool is a self-validating Merkle tree rooted at the uberblock. Detects bit rot, phantom writes, misdirected reads/writes, DMA parity errors, driver bugs.
- On every read: recompute block checksum, compare to parent-block-pointer checksum. On mismatch with redundancy (mirror/RAID-Z), fetch good copy, return it, rewrite bad block. Without redundancy: detect and report exactly which file/block is affected.
- Scrub walks all data, verifies each block checksum, repairs where redundancy allows. Finds latent corruption in unread (cold) data.

#### 3.3 Content Hashes

Research basis:
- Content-addressable storage (Git; IPFS; Nix; Docker): object address = hash of content. Same content → same hash → dedup + integrity. Git uses SHA-1 (transitioning to SHA-256); if content doesn't match its name, corruption detected.
- Allowed IDS hashes: sha256 (FIPS 180-4), blake3 (tree hash, incremental, fast, 256-bit default output). CRC32 is weaker (1/(2^32) undetected error probability) and not in the allowlist; sha256/blake3 give cryptographic-strength accidental-corruption detection.

#### 3.4 Merkle Trees

Research basis:
- Merkle tree = binary hash tree; leaves = data block/content hashes; internal nodes = hash of children. Root match ⇒ whole dataset matches (collision-resistant assumption); root mismatch ⇒ descend into differing branches; locate k divergent leaves in O(k·log n) bandwidth vs O(n) full transfer.
- Dynamo/Cassandra/ScyllaDB anti-entropy: Merkle trees per replica; compare roots; descend only mismatching subtrees; stream only divergent ranges. Cassandra uses depth-15 compact trees (2^15 leaves).
- Merkle Search Trees (IEEE 9049566): preserve key order for sequences/maps; important when integrity verification must align with ordered key spaces.
- dm-verity/fs-verity (Linux kernel): block device / file Merkle trees verified on every read; root hash as trust anchor; EIO/SIGBUS on mismatch. Read-only authenticity model.

#### 3.5 Version Comparisons

Every record carries `OrderingPos` (u64, monotonic per dataset domain) and `Version` (u64, MVCC) from `ids-000-aa`. Integrity verification compares versions across replicas: divergent `OrderingPos`/`Version` for the same `RecordId` indicates replica drift; checksum comparison on top detects whether the drift is silent corruption or legitimate concurrent update.

#### 3.6 Replica Audits

An audit compares replica states for a dataset/partition: exchange checksum roots or Merkle roots; mismatch triggers per-range descent to locate corrupted records; `Anomaly` records (ByteMismatch, ReplicaDrift, ChecksumFailure, StateCorruption) raised per `ids-000-aa`. Audit scope: full replica, partition subset, or record range. Audit results are reproducible and version-pinned.

#### 3.7 Partition-Level Integrity Verification

Dataset is partitioned (`PartitionId`). Integrity verification runs per partition: each partition has a checksum root and per-record/content hashes. Verification can target a single partition (fast, scoped) or the whole dataset. Partition checksums feed a dataset-level Merkle-like aggregation for O(log partitions) divergence location.

#### 3.8 Continuous Integrity Scrubbing

Research basis:
- ZFS scrub (OpenZFS docs): walks all pool data, verifies checksums, repairs via redundancy. Recommended monthly for pools with unread data.
- Btrfs scrub (btrfs docs): per-device validation pass; detects checksum mismatch, superblock errors, header errors, disk read errors; repairs from redundant copies.
- Ceph scrubbing (IBM Ceph docs): daily light scrub (metadata comparison across PG replicas), weekly deep scrub (bit-for-bit object comparison).
- SeaweedFS EC Bitrot Scrub: verifies cold parity shards against per-block checksums; catches corruption before rebuild.
- Scrub is continuous/throttled background work; completes a full pass over a defined period (weeks/quarter); competes with client traffic — rate-limited.
- Scrub cycle = maximum undetected corruption window for cold data; shorter cycles cost more I/O.

#### 3.9 Silent Bit Rot Detection

Detection = recomputed checksum ≠ stored checksum on read or scrub. No error announced by drive/firmware; only checksum mismatch reveals it. Detection surfaces `Anomaly{anomaly_type: ChecksumFailure, description, node_id, ids_time}`. Detection without repair only tells you what you lost; repair requires redundancy (replica/erasure/parity).

#### 3.10 Checksum Mismatch Handling

Research basis:
- ZFS: transient mismatch → retry read; persistent mismatch with redundancy → fetch good copy, return to app, rewrite bad block, count error in pool status.
- Scality object storage: transfer checksum (upload), per-block checksum (read), background scrub (all data), application-level fixity check (end-to-end). On mismatch: treat fragment as missing, reconstruct from good copies/fragments, verify result, write to healthy media, log event (cluster of mismatches on one drive = early hardware-failure warning).
- Handling steps: detect → quarantine affected record/block → reconstruct from redundant copy or erasure fragments → verify reconstructed checksum → rewrite to healthy media → record anomaly → alert. If no redundancy: report only, never silently return bad data (fail closed).

#### 3.11 ZFS-Style End-to-End Protection

Data and checksum stored separately (checksum in parent block pointer). Entire structure self-validating to the root. Protects against bit rot, phantom writes, misdirected reads/writes, DMA parity errors, driver bugs, accidental overwrite. Limitation: page-cache/memory corruption not covered by on-disk checksums (UWisc FAST'10 observation); memory-side protection (ECC RAM) is orthogonal and out of scope for this crate beyond documenting the boundary.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
| Silent bit rot on media (unannounced bit flips) | End-to-end checksums per block/record; continuous scrubbing recomputes and compares |
| Checksum stored with data (self-consistent corruption) | Checksum stored separately (parent/pointer or sidecar metadata), not inline with data |
| Corruption in cold/unread data | Periodic scrub reads everything; scrub cycle bounds undetected window |
| No redundancy to repair from | Detect and report (fail closed); never return bad data; anomaly logged |
| Checksum mismatch on read | Retry once (transient); on persistent mismatch with redundancy, reconstruct from good copy, verify, rewrite |
| Replica drift masquerading as corruption | Version/OrderingPos comparison before checksum verdict; drift ≠ corruption |
| Corrupted checksum metadata itself | Checksum-of-checksums / Merkle root; sidecar redundancy; multiple historical roots |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (`std::net`, `tokio::net`, IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/…) | `Endpoint` sole address type; dependency audit bans networking crates; CI grep for prohibited symbols |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305; `ids-crypto` enforces at implementation layer |
| Scrub storms / I/O contention | Throttled continuous scrub; configurable rate; window-based full-pass scheduling |
| Undetected hash collision (accidental) | sha256/blake3: ~1/(2^256) accidental collision — negligible vs cosmic-ray bit-flip odds |
| Version skew / wire incompatibility | `ProtocolVersion` + `EdgeCaseBits` from ids-000-aa; integrity frames version-tagged; mismatched peers reject before verification |
| Memory-side corruption (page cache) | Documented boundary: on-disk checksums do not cover RAM; ECC RAM recommended (out of crate scope) |
| Erasure fragment corruption undetected until rebuild | Per-fragment checksums; EC scrub verifies cold parity shards |

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 End-to-End Checksum (ZFS-style)
```
block.data → sha256/blake3(block.data) = block.checksum
block.checksum stored in parent block pointer / sidecar — NOT with block.data
on read(block): recompute sha256/blake3(block.data); compare to stored block.checksum
on mismatch: retry once (transient); persistent → reconstruct from redundancy, verify, rewrite
```
Fault isolation: data and checksum never stored together, so firmware bugs that corrupt both together are still detectable (they'd have to corrupt both consistently).

#### 7.2 Content Hash
```
object.address = sha256(object.content) or blake3(object.content)
same content → same hash → dedup + integrity
verification: recompute hash of retrieved content; compare to address
```

#### 7.3 Merkle Tree
```
leaf_i = hash(block_i)
internal_j = hash(left_child || right_child)
root = hash of root internal node
replica A root == replica B root ⇒ datasets match
roots differ → descend only differing subtrees → locate k divergent leaves in O(k·log n)
inclusion proof: path from leaf to root (sibling hashes at each level)
```

#### 7.4 Version Comparison (Drift Detection)
```
record R on replica A: (OrderingPos_A, Version_A)
record R on replica B: (OrderingPos_B, Version_B)
OrderingPos_A != OrderingPos_B ⇒ replica drift (legitimate or corruption)
checksum(R_A) == checksum(R_B) ⇒ drift is legitimate concurrent update
checksum(R_A) != checksum(R_B) ⇒ silent corruption / ByteMismatch anomaly
```

#### 7.5 Replica Audit Descent
```
exchange roots (checksum root or Merkle root) between replicas
roots match → audit passed, no descent
roots differ → descend into child ranges; compare per-range hashes
leaf mismatch → raise Anomaly{ChecksumFailure | ByteMismatch}, quarantine record
```

#### 7.6 Continuous Scrub
```
schedule: throttled, full-pass over window W (weeks/quarter)
walk: for each block/record, recompute checksum, compare to stored
mismatch → mismatch handling pipeline (quarantine → reconstruct → verify → rewrite)
progress: bytes scrubbed, mismatches found, repairs done, rate (bytes/sec)
```

#### 7.7 Mismatch Handling Pipeline
```
detect(mismatch) → quarantine(record) → reconstruct(from redundant copy or EC fragments)
→ verify(reconstructed.checksum == expected) → rewrite(healthy media)
→ log_anomaly(Anomaly{node_id, anomaly_type, description, ids_time})
→ if cluster of mismatches on one node/disk → hardware-failure warning
if no redundancy: fail closed, report only, never return bad data
```

#### 7.8 Data Structures
```
ChecksumRecord { record_id: RecordId, checksum: Checksum, algorithm: Algo, ids_time: IdsTime }
ContentHash { hash: [u8; 32], algorithm: Algo, content_len: u64 }
MerkleRoot { root: [u8; 32], leaf_count: u64, depth: u32, ids_time: IdsTime }
IntegrityScope { dataset_id: DatasetId, partition_id: Option<PartitionId>, record_range: Option<(RecordId, RecordId)> }
ScrubState { state, bytes_scrubbed, mismatches, repairs, rate_bps, started_at, ids_time }
MismatchVerdict { transient, persistent, repairable, unrepairable }
Anomaly { node_id, anomaly_type: AnomalyType, description, ids_time }  // from ids-000-aa
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

|| Uncertainty | Impact | Resolution path ||
||-------------|--------|-----------------|
| Checksum granularity (block vs record vs partition) | Affects `src/checksum/` design and overhead | Block-level for large objects, record-level for fine-grained; partition-level aggregation |
| Persistence backend for checksum stores | Which crate owns durable checksum metadata | Delegate to `ids-scrub`/storage crate; adapter pattern |
| Repair source selection (which replica/fragment is correct) | Determines reconstruction correctness | Version/OrderingPos comparison + quorum of checksums; majority vote among redundant copies |
| Scrub rate vs client traffic trade-off | Performance impact | Configurable rate limiter; window-based full pass; benchmarks in implementation |
| Memory-side corruption boundary | Checksums don't cover RAM/page cache | Document boundary; ECC RAM recommended out-of-crate |
| ed25519-signed integrity proofs: mandatory or optional | Authenticity vs accidental-corruption scope | Optional layer; core integrity is accidental-corruption detection |
| Merkle Search Tree vs plain Merkle tree | Order-preserving verification for sequences | Plain Merkle for blocks/records; MST option for ordered key spaces |
| Erasure-coded fragment integrity | Per-fragment checksums + EC scrub | Follow `ids-erasure` crate boundaries (deferred phase) |

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-integrity` crate (not folders inside existing crates) | Matches user directive "try to use separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones"; single-responsibility boundary |
| Checksum stored separately from data (parent pointer / sidecar) | ZFS end-to-end principle: fault isolation between data and checksum; detects self-consistent corruption |
| sha256 + blake3 as allowed hashes | IDS crypto allowlist; cryptographic-strength accidental-corruption detection; blake3 for incremental/tree hashing |
| Merkle trees for scalable reconciliation | O(k·log n) divergence location vs O(n) full transfer; Dynamo/Cassandra lineage |
| Continuous throttled scrubbing | Finds latent bit rot in cold data; bounds undetected window; ZFS/Btrfs/Ceph precedent |
| Version/OrderingPos comparison before checksum verdict | Distinguishes legitimate replica drift from silent corruption |
| Fail-closed mismatch handling | Never return bad data; reconstruct from redundancy or report only |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule |
| Allowed crypto: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | IDS policy; `ids-crypto` implements, this crate declares usage boundaries |
| No code in this phase | Research only per prompts.txt entry 30 |

# PHASE 031:

## Phase 031 — Create the ids-security crate: Security across complete infrastructure.

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---\n

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 031 creates a **new separate crate `ids-security`** (not folders inside an existing crate), organized into subfolders by subsystem. It is the IDS security layer implementing mutual authentication (mutual), dataset/operation/identity-level authorization, data encryption in transit + at rest, key management (generation, rotation, revocation, distribution, recovery), regional security boundaries, auditability, and tamper-evident audit records. The crate is strictly carrier-agnostic: all traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh anywhere. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.

`ids-security` depends on `ids-000-aa` (master crate, canonical types + sealed trait contracts) and `ids-crypto` (leaf crate, allowed primitives). It implements the sealed `Security` trait contract defined in `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/security.rs`. There is no global security master — each dataset/region manages its own security context. The design is research-only: this plan specifies architecture, interfaces, data structures, algorithms, dependencies, integration points, acceptance criteria, and file structure; zero code and zero source modifications result from this phase.

---\n

**Design principles:**
- **Domain wrapper, not raw exposure:** every primitive is wrapped in IDS-specific newtypes (`Ed25519SigningKey`, `XChaCha20Poly1305SealKey`, `Blake3Digest`, `Sha256Digest`, `Nonce`, `KeyHandle`) so allowed-algorithm policy is enforced at the type boundary, key material is zeroized on drop, and the crate can swap implementations without touching the other 99 crates.
- **Zeroize discipline:** every key-holding type implements `zeroize::Zeroize` and `Drop` that zeroes memory on scope exit. No secret material survives beyond the lifetime of its wrapper type.
- **No RNG inside the crate:** key generation and nonce generation accept caller-provided entropy via a `CryptoRng`-like trait parameter. The caller (e.g. ids-security) supplies entropy.
- **Fail-closed semantics:** revoked keys, missing tokens, failed authorization, zero nonces, all-zeros ephemeral keys, oversized endpoint addresses all reject by default. Recoverable vs. unrecoverable errors are categorized.
- **No global security master:** each dataset/region manages its own security context through its own key material and policy.

---\n

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Mutual Authentication (ed25519 challenge-response)

Authentication is mutual: both parties prove possession of their ed25519 private keys. The verifier issues a fresh nonce (32 bytes, caller-supplied entropy via `getrandom`-adjacent trait), the claimant signs `(nonce || domain_separator || identity)` with its ed25519 key, and the verifier checks the signature against the enrolled public key. Domain separation strings (e.g. `ids-security/v1/auth`) bind signatures to this subsystem to prevent cross-protocol replay. `AuthManager` tracks sessions by `AuthToken` (blake3 hash of credential), enforces TTL, rejects empty and all-zeros credentials, and rotates out the previous token for an identity on re-authentication. Reference pattern: ed25519 challenge-response as used in `aegis-auth`, `identikey_auth`, `Ironseal`, and `krot-proto` — all Rust implementations signing a nonce-bound challenge payload and verifying with `ed25519-dalek::verify_strict`.

#### 3.2 Authorization (dataset/operation/identity-level permissions)

Authorization is token-based and dataset-scoped. An `AuthzGrant` binds `(AuthToken, DatasetId)` to a `Permission` derived from `OpType` (Read, Write, Delete, Replicate, Recover, Admin), with optional TTL. Admin grants subsume all permissions on a dataset. The evaluation is `(token, dataset, op) → allow/deny` with fail-closed default. `AuthzManager` tracks grant counts, denial rates, expiry, and supports revocation of individual grants. Design reference: Cedar policy language (default deny, explicit permit/forbid, ABAC attributes) and casbin-rs `{subject, object, action}` enforcement — ids-security adopts a simpler grant-table model appropriate to its sealed-trait boundary, with Cedar-style default-deny semantics and optional future ABAC extension.

#### 3.3 Data Encryption in Transit + At Rest (xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305)

Encryption uses only the two allowed AEADs: `XChaCha20Poly1305` (192-bit/24-byte nonce, random nonce safe, no counter persistence needed) and `ChaCha20Poly1305` (96-bit/12-byte nonce, requires monotonic counter persistence to avoid reuse). `EncryptionManager` registers keys by `KeyId`, validates key size (32 bytes) and rejects all-zeros key material, and produces `EncryptedPayload { ciphertext, nonce, algorithm, key_id, encrypted_at_ms }`. For XChaCha20, random nonce generation is the documented default (birthday bound 2^96 messages per key). For ChaCha20, nonce counter persistence (monotonic u64 with overflow detection) is a downstream caller responsibility owned by ids-security/ids-session. Both algorithms are implemented in `chacha20poly1305` (RustCrypto, RFC 8439).

#### 3.4 Key Management (generation, rotation, revocation, distribution, recovery)

`KeyManager` owns the key lifecycle: `KeyState { Pending, Active, Rotating, Revoked, Expired }`, `KeyInfo` (key_id, state, timestamps, usage_count, max_usage, algorithm), `create_key`, `rotate_key` (derives new KeyId via blake3 of old key_id), `revoke_key`, `expire_key`, `increment_key_usage` with usage-limit expiry. `KeyRotationManager` holds `RotationSchedule` entries (next rotation at ms, interval, max rotations) and supports idle-time rotation execution with due/missed tracking. `KeyRevocationManager` maintains a grow-only revocation map of `RevocationEntry { key_id, revoked_at_ms, reason, revoked_by }` with fail-closed `is_revoked` checks. Key distribution and recovery are out-of-band concerns (enrollment key distribution via ids-security/admission; recovery keys sealed under dataset-level master keys).

#### 3.5 Regional Security Boundaries

`RegionalBoundary` checks `(source: RegionId, target: RegionId)` against a configured allowlist of region pairs, rejecting cross-region traffic not on the list. There is no global master — each region manages its own boundary policy. This is a configuration-level control enforced at the security layer before any encryption/authentication operation crosses regions.

#### 3.6 Nonce Management, Replay Protection, Zero Nonce Rejection

`NonceManager` generates nonces as `blake3_hash_32(context)`, rejects zero nonces, tracks used nonces with eviction at capacity. `ReplayProtection` wraps a `ReplayWindow` (HashSet of `[u8; 9]` op refs) with window eviction at capacity, plus `NonceManager` for `[u8; 32]` nonces. `check_op_ref` returns `Err(ReplayDetected)` on duplicate. All nonce operations are fail-closed: unknown nonce → replay detected; zero nonce → `ZeroNonceRejected`.

#### 3.7 Channel Binding (constant-time comparison)

`ChannelBinding` stores per-node bindings and verifies with `constant_time_eq` (XOR-accumulate, no early exit) to prevent timing attacks on binding comparison. Reference: `subtle` crate's `ct_eq`, and the existing `constant_time_eq` already present in `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/security.rs`.

#### 3.8 Ephemeral Key Validation, Address Limits, Zero Nonce Validation

`EphemeralKeyValidator` rejects all-zeros 32-byte public keys, weak high-bit-only keys, and duplicate validations. `AddressLimitValidator` enforces a 1024-byte maximum endpoint address size. `ZeroNonceValidator` rejects any `[u8; 32]` that is all zeros. These are lightweight preconditions that run before any cryptographic operation on untrusted input.

#### 3.9 Tamper-Evident Audit Records

`AuditManager` maintains an append-only hash chain: each `AuditEvent { event_id, node_id, event_type, detail, timestamp_ms, sequence_number, previous_hash, event_hash }` commits to the previous event's hash via `blake3_hash_32`. `verify_chain` walks the chain and fails on any broken link. Reference: `airframe_audit` (SHA-256 hash chain, RFC 6962-style), `pamoja-audit`, `Quipu-Log`, and `settled` (Merkle-tree inclusion/consistency proofs). ids-security uses a simpler hash chain (per the sealed trait contract in ids-000-aa) with optional future Merkle-tree upgrade. Audit entries are signed-context aware: the caller's `node_id` and `event_type` are bound into the hash.

#### 3.10 Security Stats & Monitoring

`SecurityStats` aggregates `auth_count`, `authz_count`, `encrypt_count`, `decrypt_count`, failure rates, denial rates, replay rates, mismatch rates, and zero-nonce rejection counts. These feed observability and alerting without exposing secrets.

---\n

### 4. Threat Model

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Credential theft / impersonation | Mutual ed25519 challenge-response; nonce-bound signatures; short TTL auth tokens; fail-closed on invalid credential |
| Replay of auth tokens / operations | `ReplayWindow` + `NonceManager` tracking; per-op `[u8; 9]` refs; fail-closed on duplicate |
| Replay of sealed ciphertext | Nonce uniqueness enforced (XChaCha random 192-bit; ChaCha monotonic counter); replay protection at ids-security/ids-session layer |
| Key compromise | Key rotation (time- and volume-based), revocation grow-only set, fail-closed `is_revoked`, key derivation via blake3 |
| Authorization bypass | Default-deny grant table; Admin subsumes all; token+dataset+op triple checked; denial counting |
| Tampering of audit records | Hash-chained audit entries; `verify_chain` detects any modification/reordering/deletion |
| Timing attacks on comparisons | `constant_time_eq` for channel binding and all secret comparisons |
| All-zeros / weak ephemeral keys | `EphemeralKeyValidator` rejects all-zeros and high-bit-only weak keys |
| Oversized endpoint addresses | `AddressLimitValidator` 1024-byte cap, fail-closed |
| Zero nonce reuse | `reject_zero_nonce` everywhere nonces are consumed |
| Cross-region data leakage | `RegionalBoundary` allowlist, enforced before any cross-region operation |
| Insider key misuse | Audit logging of every auth/authz/encrypt/decrypt/rotate/revoke event; per-node attribution |
| Entropy exhaustion | Caller-supplied entropy via trait parameter; no OS RNG inside the crate; testable with deterministic entropy |

Critical failure modes: revoked-key acceptance (mitigated by fail-closed `is_revoked` check before every operation), nonce reuse under ChaCha20 (mitigated by monotonic counter persistence requirement documented for callers), audit chain truncation (mitigated by bounded ring buffer with max_events and tamper detection counting).

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Mutual Authentication (ed25519 challenge-response)

```
challenge = random_32_bytes(caller_entropy)
payload   = domain_separator || nonce || claimant_identity
signature = ed25519_sign(claimant_private_key, payload)
valid     = ed25519_verify(claimant_public_key, payload, signature)  // verify_strict
token     = blake3_hash_32(credential)                               // AuthToken
session   = AuthSession{identity, token, state, ttl}
```

#### 7.2 Authorization (grant table)

```
AuthzGrant = {token, dataset_id, permission, granted_at_ms, expires_at_ms, grant_count}
authorize(token, dataset, op, at_ms):
  grant = grants[(token, dataset)]
  allow iff grant.valid(at_ms) && (grant.permission == Admin || grant.permission == op)
  default: deny (AuthorizationDenied)
```

#### 7.3 Encryption (xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305)

```
encrypt(data, key_id):
  key = keys[key_id]  // 32 bytes, validated non-zero
  nonce = random_24_bytes()        // XChaCha20
       or counter_12_bytes()        // ChaCha20 (caller persists counter)
  ciphertext = AEAD_seal(key, nonce, data)
  return EncryptedPayload{ciphertext, nonce, algorithm, key_id, at_ms}

decrypt(payload, key_id):
  key = keys[key_id]
  plaintext = AEAD_open(key, payload.nonce, payload.ciphertext)
```

#### 7.4 Key lifecycle state machine

```
Pending → Active (create_key) → Rotating (rotate_key, derives new KeyId via blake3)
Active → Revoked (revoke_key) → terminal
Active → Expired (expire_key or usage_limit) → terminal
Rotating → Active (new key activated)
is_revoked(key_id) → fail-closed check against grow-only revocation set
```

#### 7.5 Audit hash chain

```
AuditEvent = {event_id, node_id, event_type, detail, timestamp_ms, sequence_number,
              previous_hash, event_hash}
event_hash = blake3_hash_32(node_id || event_type || detail || timestamp_ms || sequence_number)
event_id   = blake3_hash_16(event_hash)
verify_chain: for each event, event.previous_hash == prior event_hash; else tamper detected
```

#### 7.6 Constant-time comparison

```
constant_time_eq(a, b):
  if len(a) != len(b): return false
  result = 0
  for (x, y) in zip(a, b): result |= x ^ y
  return result == 0
```

#### 7.7 Replay protection

```
check_op_ref(op_ref: [u8; 9]):
  if op_refs.contains(op_ref): return Err(ReplayDetected)
  evict half window if at capacity
  op_refs.insert(op_ref); return Ok(true)
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Nonce counter persistence for ChaCha20Pol1305:** The monotonic u64 counter must persist across restarts to avoid nonce reuse; storage ownership (ids-security vs. ids-session) and persistence mechanism are undefined.
2. **Key distribution and recovery:** Out-of-band enrollment key distribution and recovery key sealing are referenced but not designed; deferred to integration with ids-identity/admission.
3. **Audit storage backend:** In-memory ring buffer (per sealed trait contract) vs. durable append-only store; durability requirements for multi-day audit retention undefined.
4. **Merkle-tree upgrade for audit:** Hash chain is the baseline; Merkle inclusion/consistency proofs (RFC 6962 style) are a future enhancement, not in this phase.
5. **Regional boundary configuration source:** Static config vs. exchanged out-of-band vs. learned; all must be supported behind one interface, source undecided.
6. **Authentication session storage:** `RefCell<HashMap>` baseline is single-threaded; `Arc<DashMap>` or `parking_lot` for multi-threaded deployment is a deployment decision.
7. **ChaCha20 vs. XChaCha20 default:** XChaCha20 (random 192-bit nonce) is safer by default; ChaCha20 (counter nonce) requires counter persistence. Default algorithm selection for `EncryptionManager` is undecided.
8. **Formal verification scope:** No mechanized proof of the security contract planned for this phase; property tests are the verification mechanism.

---\n

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| New separate crate `ids-security`, not subfolder | User requires separate crates for new capabilities; keeps `ids-000-aa` focused on types/contracts |
| Implements sealed `Security` trait from `ids-000-aa` | Single canonical contract; downstream crates program to the trait, not the crate |
| Depends on `ids-crypto` (leaf, no ids-000-aa) | Avoids circular dependency; `ids-crypto` is the only crate not depending on `ids-000-aa` |
| Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3 | Matches ids-crypto allowed-primitive policy; no algorithm agility beyond the set |
| Carrier-agnostic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only | No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh |
| Caller-supplied entropy (no RNG inside crate) | Pure, testable, runtime-agnostic; caller supplies entropy |
| Zeroize on all key-holding types | Key material wiped on Drop; no secret survives wrapper lifetime |
| Default-deny authorization | Explicit permit required; fail-closed on missing grant |
| Hash-chained audit (not Merkle yet) | Matches sealed trait contract in ids-000-aa; Merkle upgrade deferred |
| XChaCha20 random nonce default; ChaCha20 counter nonce caller-persisted | XChaCha20 avoids nonce-reuse risk; ChaCha20 counter persistence is downstream concern |
| Fail-closed everywhere: revoked keys, zero nonces, all-zeros ephemeral keys, oversized addresses | Security defaults to rejection, not acceptance |
| No global security master | Each dataset/region manages its own security context |

# PHASE 032:

## Phase 032 — Create the ids-resource crate: Resource tracking and workload protection.

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 032 creates **ids-resource**: the IDS crate for resource tracking and workload protection. It provides storage/CPU/memory/network monitoring, latency/queue/utilization/health measurements, per-client/per-dataset/per-operator/per-region quotas, workload isolation, backpressure, resource reservations, committed capacity optimization, and resource exhaustion prevention.

**Scope (from prompts.txt entry 32):**
- Crate: `ids-resource`
- Purpose: Resource tracking and workload protection.
- Contents: Storage/CPU/memory/network monitoring, latency/queue/utilization/health measurements, per-client/per-dataset/per-operator/per-region quotas, workload isolation, backpressure, resource reservations, committed capacity optimization, resource exhaustion prevention.
- Guideline: try to use separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones → `ids-resource` is its own crate, not a folder inside another crate.

**Architectural constraints (non-negotiable, from prompts.txt):**
- Carrier-agnostic: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).
- Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `ids-000-aa` is the master crate with all canonical types and sealed trait contracts.
- Research only — no code, no source modifications, only the plan document.

**Key engineering decisions (preview, justified in §11):**
- `ids-resource` depends only on `ids-000-aa`, `ids-carrier`, `ids-crypto`, `ids-storage`; it is not a network crate.
- Quota enforcement: token bucket (rate), leaky bucket (steady shaping), escrow bounded counter (distributed capacity quotas, Σ grants ≤ limit, Δ = 0 strict → no overshoot without per-write round trip).
- Workload isolation: bulkhead concurrency pools per workload, weighted fair queuing / max-min fairness, cell-based fault isolation.
- Backpressure: bounded queues, reject-newest with Retry-After derived from queue depth / drain rate, circuit breaker for saturated dependencies.
- Reservations: Borg-style allocs + admission control; idempotent reserve/commit/release ledger for exactly-once resource accounting.
- Exhaustion prevention: PSI-based early detection, graceful feature degradation, load shedding triggered by p99 latency vs SLO.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-resource` sits below the orchestrator/scheduler and above `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. It is **not** a network protocol — it is a local resource accounting and admission engine that emits bytes to ship over whatever carrier IDS uses.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              ORCHESTRATOR / ids-scheduler                   │
│  admits, defers, or rejects work based on ids-resource      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              Phase 032: ids-resource (NEW CRATE)            │
│  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐       │
│  │ monitor  │ │ measure  │ │   quota  │ │ isolate  │       │
│  │ storage  │ │ latency  │ │ token    │ │ bulkhead │       │
│  │ cpu      │ │ queue    │ │ bucket   │ │ wfq      │       │
│  │ memory   │ │ util     │ │ leaky    │ │ cell     │       │
│  │ network  │ │ health   │ │ escrow   │ │ slice    │       │
│  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘       │
│  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐       │
│  │ backpress│ │ reserve  │ │ exhaust  │ │ carrier  │       │
│  │ sheduler │ │ alloc    │ │ oom guard│ │ endpoint │       │
│  │ breaker  │ │ capacity │ │ degrade  │ │ adapter  │       │
│  └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘ └──────────┘       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             ids-000-aa (master crate, sealed traits)        │
│  ResourceId, QuotaId, WorkloadId, ClientId, DatasetId,      │
│  OperatorId, RegionId + sealed trait contracts              │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              ids-carrier::Endpoint                          │
│  CarrierType + Vec<u8>  (the ONLY traffic channel)          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              ids-crypto / ids-storage                       │
│  ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256,      │
│  blake3 | quota ledger, reservation journal, snapshots      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a work item:**
1. Scheduler asks `ids-resource` for an admission decision before admitting work for client `c`, dataset `d`, operator `o`, region `r`, workload `w`.
2. `monitor` samples current storage/CPU/memory/network usage (network = bytes handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`, no sockets).
3. `measure` updates latency/queue/utilization/health gauges and histograms (sharded atomic counters on the hot path).
4. `quota` evaluates per-axis quotas (token bucket for rate, escrow for capacity); hierarchical charges are all-or-none across bucket/tenant/root.
5. `isolate` checks the workload's bulkhead concurrency cap and WFQ share.
6. `backpressure` applies block/drop/signal; if the queue is full, reject with Retry-After derived from queue depth / drain rate.
7. `reserve` checks committed capacity (allocation = reserved resource set); admits iff Σ reserved + demand ≤ capacity on every resource dimension.
8. `exhaust` guards against resource exhaustion (hard caps, PSI-based early warning, graceful degradation).
9. Decision (admit / defer / reject + reason) is returned to the scheduler; control-plane traffic between nodes travels only via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Resource Monitoring — Storage / CPU / Memory / Network

**USE method** (Brendan Gregg): for every resource, monitor **U**tilization (% time busy), **S**aturation (queue depth / work waiting), and **E**rrors (error event count). CPU: `1 − avg(rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}))`; Memory: used/total with available-bytes headroom; Disk/Storage: iops and bytes; Network: bytes in/out as observed at the `ids-carrier::Endpoint` boundary (byte counts only — no sockets, no protocol parsing).

**Pressure Stall Information (PSI)** (Linux kernel, cgroup v2): `some` pressure = some tasks stalled on a resource (early contention indicator); `full` pressure = all non-idle tasks stalled (severe shortage). Metrics `avg10`/`avg60`/`avg300` moving averages plus cumulative `total` in microseconds, for CPU, memory, and IO. `systemd-oomd` uses PSI to kill a cgroup before the kernel OOM killer fires — the model for ids-resource's early exhaustion guard. Cross-platform caveat: PSI requires Linux cgroup v2; on other platforms ids-resource falls back to poll-based utilization sampling (TBD, see §10).

**Sharded metrics:** hot-path counters/gauges/histograms use thread-sharded atomics (cache-line padded, aggregate on read) to avoid cross-core cache-line bouncing (fast-telemetry pattern). OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for instrument names and attributes (counter/gauge/histogram with labeled dimensions: client, dataset, operator, region, workload).

#### 3.2 Latency / Queue / Utilization / Health Measurements

- **Latency histograms:** fixed exponential buckets (e.g. 100µs … 100ms), streaming quantiles (summary with ~2% relative error), percentiles p50/p95/p99 reported per resource and per workload.
- **Queue depth:** number of pending work items per workload/queue; saturation signal = queue depth × service time vs drain rate; worst-case wait = queue depth / drain rate.
- **Utilization:** per-resource busy fraction over moving windows (10s/60s/300s), matching PSI averaging windows.
- **Health:** composite signal from utilization + saturation + error rate; drives load shedding as utilization approaches the hard limit (early rejection, not abrupt cutoff).

#### 3.3 Quotas — Per-Client / Per-Dataset / Per-Operator / Per-Region

Four quota axes, each independently configurable with rate + capacity + concurrency dimensions (Golem-style quota model):

- **Rate** — refills `value` tokens every `period`; capped at `max`. For API call rates, requests/sec per client.
- **Capacity** — fixed pool of tokens; consumed, never refilled. For storage budgets, byte quotas per dataset/region.
- **Concurrency** — pool of tokens returned on release. For parallel operation limits per operator.

**Algorithms:**
- **Token bucket (lock-free):** atomic CAS token accounting; tokens accumulate from elapsed monotonic time (scaled integer arithmetic, sub-token precision); burst = bucket capacity; admit iff tokens ≥ cost. 10M+ ops/sec achievable with lock-free sharding (tokio-rate-limit / leaky-bucket research).
- **Leaky bucket:** requests add to a finite-level bucket; leaks at a constant drain rate; overflow → reject. Strict output pacing; smooths bursts; pairs with bounded queue + backpressure.
- **Escrow bounded counter** (arxiv 1503.09052, `bcounter` design): global budget `Quota` lends local grants to nodes; a node admits locally iff `net_used + amount ≤ granted`; invariant `Σ grants ≤ limit` guarantees `Σ used ≤ limit` with no overshoot and no per-write round trip. `Δ = 0` gives strict enforcement; `Δ > 0` permits bounded overshoot (≤ Δ) for fewer false denials. False denials (node out of grant while others are idle) are accepted and healed by grant rebalancing.
- **Hierarchical quotas (`bcounter::BCounterMap`):** one counter per scope (bucket / tenant / root); a single write charges the whole path all-or-none — every level checked before any is charged; on shortage the scope is named and nothing is charged; server tops up from the scope's quota and retries.
- **Fenced, expiring leases** over a gossip/repair tree (Plumtree-style): grantor takes back a grant only after the holder relinquishes it slightly before the lease TTL, so take-back never double-lends (no overshoot); lease TTL longer than tree-repair time reclaims dead subtrees automatically; outstanding-grant ledger is durable so leader changes never re-lend budget.
- **Minimum viable quota:** if a quota is below `Y_min` for its workload, refuse it rather than enforce badly; options: raise `Y`, loosen the target (show tightest band reachable at `f_max`), or accept a soft best-effort limit.

**Enforcement actions:** `reject` (Err with optional estimated wait time), `throttle` (suspend until capacity available), `terminate` (kill with failure message). Acquisition tokens carry idempotency keys; `split`/`merge` guard against child-expected-use exceeding parent.

#### 3.4 Workload Isolation

- **Bulkhead pattern:** separate concurrency pool per workload (per-client/dataset/operator/region slice). A semaphore-like permit cap per pool; failure or latency in one pool never starves another (noisy-neighbor protection). Timeout + cancellation wrapper releases permits on hang/cancel.
- **Cell-based architecture / fault isolation:** partition into independent cells that do not share state; a failure in one cell affects only that cell's requests (AWS well-architected bulkhead/cell guidance).
- **Weighted Fair Queuing (WFQ) / max-min fairness:** each workload `i` with weight `w_i` receives `w_i / Σw` of capacity; guarantees proportional shares and isolation — a workload cannot affect others beyond its share. Virtual finish time ordering selects the next queue to serve.
- **cgroups-style slices:** workload slice = reserved set of CPU/memory/storage with MIN/MAX caps per dimension (SQL Server Resource Governor model: resource pools + workload groups, `MIN_CPU_PERCENT`/`MAX_CPU_PERCENT`, classification of sessions into groups).
- **Gang / co-scheduling:** co-allocated workloads reserve resources together; BoPF (Bounded Priority Fairness) gives latency-sensitive jobs short-term guarantees while preserving long-term fairness for throughput-sensitive jobs (arxiv 1912.03523).

#### 3.5 Backpressure

Bounded buffer + explicit signaling when full (block / drop / signal):

- **Block:** producer waits until buffer has space (blocks the caller — acceptable only when callers can absorb latency).
- **Drop:** reject-newest (tail-drop) with `429` + `Retry-After`; or drop-oldest (head-drop) for real-time feeds where stale data is worthless; or dead-letter routing for work that must not be lost.
- **Signal:** consumer requests exactly `n` items (pull-based flow control).

**Retry-After:** derived live from queue depth / drain rate, plus jitter, to avoid synchronized retry waves (thundering herd). `429 Too Many Requests` = this caller exceeded its allowance; `503 Service Unavailable` = system-wide saturation. `Retry-After` must never be a fixed constant.

**Circuit breaker:** FSM with Closed / Open / Half-Open states; trips after failure/latency threshold within a monitoring window; open state short-circuits calls immediately (fail fast, protects threads/connections); half-open admits a limited trial to test recovery (Azure pattern, Martin Fowler).

#### 3.6 Resource Reservations & Committed Capacity

- **Allocs (Borg model):** an alloc is a reserved set of resources on a machine, assigned whether or not used; used to hold resources between task stop/start and to pack tasks onto machines. Admission control + efficient task-packing + overcommitment + machine sharing with process-level performance isolation (Google Borg paper).
- **Kubernetes ResourceQuotas:** constraints limiting aggregate resource consumption per namespace; object-count limits by API kind; enforced at admission (k8s docs).
- **Committed capacity optimization:** track committed vs reserved vs used capacity; admission rejects when Σ reserved + demand > capacity on any dimension; overcommitment policy per workload class (how much overcommit is safe).

**Reservation ledger:** idempotent reserve → commit → release. Double-entry style: every reservation writes a matched reserve/commit pair; append-only journal; balance invariant (Σ reservations ≤ capacity) checked on commit; idempotency key prevents double-application on retry (open-ledger / idempotent-ledger patterns).

#### 3.7 Resource Exhaustion Prevention

- **Early OOM detection:** PSI memory `some`/`full` pressure triggers guards before the kernel OOM killer; `systemd-oomd` model selects a cgroup to terminate when limits are exceeded, rather than letting the kernel choose.
- **CWE-400 mitigations** (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption): design-in throttling, admission control, per-user rate limits, maximum connection/load limits, absolute timeouts (OWASP DoS cheat sheet).
- **Load shedding:** as utilization approaches the hard limit, reject a growing fraction of requests; trigger on p99 latency vs SLO, not average utilization (average can look healthy while p99 has already breached — Azure throttling pattern).
- **Graceful feature degradation:** turn off nonessential features so essential ones keep resources.
- **Connection/session limits:** max ingress data rate, absolute connection timeout, session inactivity timeout.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

||| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
| Noisy neighbor monopolizes CPU/memory/storage | Per-tenant quotas (4 axes) + bulkhead concurrency caps + cgroups-style hard MIN/MAX caps per slice |
| Unbounded queue growth → memory exhaustion | Bounded queues bounded by count AND bytes; reject-newest with Retry-After; queue depth as health metric; sustained growth = capacity mismatch |
| Cascading failure via saturated dependency | Circuit breaker (fail fast) + bulkheads isolate failure domains; never block on a dependency without timeout |
| Quota-splitting evasion (spread writes across clients/regions/nodes) | Hierarchical quotas charged all-or-none; `Σ grants ≤ limit` escrow invariant; `Δ = 0` strict path for hard billing/abuse limits; refuse quota below `Y_min` |
| Replay / double-charge of reservations | Idempotency keys on reserve/commit/release; append-only ledger; unique constraint on idempotency key; replay returns original result |
| Clock skew corrupting rate-limit windows | Monotonic steady clock for token-bucket refill; never wall-clock; HLC/Lamport only where ordering matters |
| Resource exhaustion DoS (CWE-400) | Admission control, throttling, hard caps, per-session/connection limits, load shedding on p99 vs SLO |
| Offline member blocks quota reclamation / GC | Fenced expiring leases with TTL > repair time; deliberate eviction, never timeout-only reclamation |
| Compromised workload reads another's metrics | Workload-scoped metric labels; no cross-tenant visibility into counters/gauges |
| Crypto outside allowlist | Only ed25519 (quota attestation signatures), xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 (encryption), sha256 / blake3 (hashing, content addressing); dependency + grep audit |

---

|| `ids-crypto` | ed25519 signatures, xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 encryption, sha256 / blake3 hashing |

|| `ids-telemetry` | Metrics emission: counters, gauges, histograms with labeled dimensions |
|| `ids-scheduler` | Admission control — consults `ids-resource` before admitting work |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-resource` implements the sealed traits from `ids-000-aa`; the scheduler calls `admit(client, dataset, operator, region, workload, demand)` and receives `Admit / Defer(retry_after) / Reject(reason)`.
- All inter-node traffic (quota grant rebalancing, lease renewal, saturation signals) goes over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); zero use of `std::net`, `tokio::net`, or any networking crate.
- Quota decisions may be signed with ed25519 where attestation across trust boundaries is required.
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh — preserving carrier-agnostic architecture (I-CARR-001).

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Token Bucket (rate quota)
```
state = (tokens: scaled u64, last_refill: Instant)
refill(now): tokens = min(capacity, tokens + (now − last_refill) × rate); last_refill = now
consume(cost): refill(); admitted ⟺ tokens ≥ cost; if admitted: tokens −= cost
```
Lock-free via atomic CAS on the token cell; sub-token precision with scaled integer arithmetic.

#### 7.2 Leaky Bucket (steady shaping + backpressure)
```
level += cost on arrival; if level > capacity → reject (overflow)
drain continuously at drain_rate; worst-case wait = level / drain_rate
```

#### 7.3 Escrow Bounded Counter (distributed capacity quota)
```
acquire(node, amount) admitted ⟺ node.net_used + amount ≤ node.granted
invariant: Σ grants ≤ limit (+ Δ); Δ = 0 ⇒ strict, overshoot-free enforcement
rebalance: grantor transfers grant to grantee via fenced, expiring lease (Plumtree tree)
```

#### 7.4 Hierarchical Charge (all-or-none)
```
charge(path scopes, amount): for each scope s in path: check s.granted ≥ s.used + amount
  if all pass: charge every scope; else: name the short scope, charge nothing, top up and retry
```

#### 7.5 Weighted Fair Queuing (isolation)
```
flow i share = w_i / Σw × capacity
virtual finish time F_i = max(now, last_F_i) + cost_i / w_i   (GPS-style)
serve next: flow with smallest F_i
isolation: flow i cannot exceed w_i/Σw of capacity regardless of others' behavior
```

#### 7.6 Backpressure Controller
```
queue_depth ≥ capacity → overflow policy:
  reject-newest: 429 + Retry-After(queue_depth / drain_rate + jitter)
  drop-oldest: evict head, admit tail (real-time feeds)
  dead-letter: durable replay queue (must-not-lose work)
circuit breaker: failures ≥ threshold in window → Open (short-circuit) → Half-Open (trial) → Closed
```

#### 7.7 Reservation Admission
```
admit(demand): for each resource dimension r:
  Σ reserved[r] + demand[r] ≤ capacity[r]  else reject
reserve → commit → release journal; idempotency key dedups retries
```

#### 7.8 Early Exhaustion Guard
```
PSI memory full > threshold → trigger guard
utilization ≥ hard limit → shed load (reject growing fraction, trigger on p99 vs SLO)
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Quota rebalancing cadence:** event-driven early top-up (node lease runs low ahead of schedule) vs periodic sweep; lease TTL vs tree-repair time trade-off (escrow design, bcounter).
2. **Hierarchical depth:** how many levels (bucket → tenant → root) before rebalancing overhead dominates grant moves.
3. **Overcommitment policy:** how much committed-capacity overcommit is safe per workload class; measured empirically during implementation.
4. **PSI portability:** pressure stall information requires Linux cgroup v2; cross-platform fallback to poll-based utilization sampling is TBD.
5. **Wire format for quota signals over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`:** CBOR vs bincode vs plain scalar encoding; TBD.
6. **Scheduler integration:** synchronous quota check in the admission path vs async deferral with a durable timer (denied call releases its slot and waits — arxiv 2611.02926 backpressure gate pattern).
7. **Formal verification scope:** TLA+/PlusCal spec for quota invariants and backpressure contracts; sequence of verification effort TBD.
8. **Idempotency key retention window** for the reservation ledger (bounded retention vs replay safety).

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

||| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| Separate `ids-resource` crate | Prompt guideline: separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones |
|| Carrier-agnostic; `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only | I-CARR-001 architecture; no networking crates |
|| Token bucket + leaky bucket + escrow | Covers rate limiting, steady shaping, and distributed capacity quotas without per-write round trips |
|| Escrow `Σ grants ≤ limit`, Δ = 0 | Overshoot-free enforcement (bcounter, arxiv 1503.09052) |
|| Bulkhead per workload | Failure isolation; noisy-neighbor protection |
|| WFQ / max-min fairness | Proportional capacity sharing with per-workload weights |
|| Idempotent reserve/commit/release ledger | Exactly-once resource accounting under retries |
|| PSI-based early exhaustion detection | `systemd-oomd` pattern; act before kernel OOM |
|| Circuit breaker for saturation | Fail fast on failing/saturated dependencies |
|| Reject-newest + Retry-After from queue depth | Backpressure without thundering herd |
|| Allowed crypto: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3 | Prompt allowlist |

## Phase 033 — Create the ids-lifecycle crate: Dataset lifecycle: creation → active → archive → expiry → retention → legal hold → deletion → reclamation.

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 033 creates **ids-lifecycle**: the IDS crate for dataset lifecycle management across creation → active → archive → expiry → retention → legal hold → deletion → reclamation. It owns lifecycle policies, retention periods, legal holds, expiry enforcement, deletion coordination, reclamation, tombstone management, space amplification reduction, and snapshot compatibility.

**Scope (from prompts.txt entry 33):**
- Crate: `ids-lifecycle`
- Purpose: Dataset lifecycle: creation → active → archive → expiry → retention → legal hold → deletion → reclamation.
- Contents: Lifecycle policies, retention periods, legal holds, expiry, deletion coordination, reclamation, tombstone management, space amplification reduction, snapshot compatibility.
- Guideline: try to use separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones → `ids-lifecycle` is its own crate, not a folder inside another crate.

**Architectural constraints (non-negotiable, from prompts.txt):**
- Carrier-agnostic: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).
- Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `ids-000-aa` is the master crate with all canonical types and sealed trait contracts.
- Research only — no code, no source modifications, only the plan document.

**Key engineering decisions (preview, justified in §11):**
- `ids-lifecycle` depends only on `ids-000-aa`, `ids-carrier`, `ids-crypto`, `ids-storage`; it is not a storage engine or network crate.
- Lifecycle modeled as a deterministic state machine (creation → active → archive → expiry → retention → legal hold → deletion → reclamation) with guard conditions on every transition; illegal transitions rejected, never silently coerced.
- Legal hold overrides every disposition: an active hold suspends expiry/deletion/reclamation regardless of retention state (verified by retention-enforcement research — legal hold evaluated first, overrides everything).
- Tombstones used for deletion (LSM/CRDT-style): deletion writes a tombstone, propagated before permanent drop during compaction; tombstone GC only after all peers acknowledge past the deletion (causal stability), preventing zombie resurrection.
- Space amplification reduction via tombstone compaction/reclaim sweep bounded by quota; reclamation marks blocks free but does not delete snapshot-referenced content (content-addressed storage, snapshot compatibility).
- Snapshot compatibility: every snapshot holds an implicit GC hold on referenced CAS blocks; deleting a snapshot releases its hold; snapshots immovable during lifecycle transitions that touch referenced data.
- Retention enforcement is deterministic and reversible-by-review: the evaluator emits disposition actions (RETAIN/REVIEW/PURGE/ARCHIVE) and routes purges through a delayed queue — never deletes directly.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-lifecycle` sits below the orchestrator/scheduler and above `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. It is **not** a storage engine — it is a local lifecycle policy engine that evaluates dataset state transitions and emits bytes to ship over whatever carrier IDS uses.

**Data flow of a lifecycle decision:**
1. Scheduler (or time-driven sweeper) asks `ids-lifecycle` to evaluate dataset `d` against its policy.
2. `state machine` reads current state (creation/active/archive/expiry/retention/hold/deletion/reclamation).
3. `policy engine` evaluates lifecycle rules + guard conditions for the candidate transition.
4. `retention` checks retention period vs reference event (created/published/last_accessed) and computes disposition date.
5. `hold` checked FIRST: if a legal hold is active, disposition is forced to RETAIN regardless of retention state (legal hold overrides expiry/deletion/reclamation).
6. `expiry` checks deadline (`creation_time + lifetime` keyed to creation time, never RTT); expired → candidate for disposition.
7. `deletion` coordinator requires consent gate: no active holds, retention elapsed, no snapshot references blocking; writes tombstone before permanent drop.
8. `tombstone` manager propagates tombstone; GC only after causal stability (all peers acked past the deletion).
9. `reclaim` sweep reclaims space bounded by quota; snapshot-referenced content never reclaimed (snapshot compatibility).
10. Decision (transition / hold / retain / review / purge / reject + reason) returned; control-plane traffic between nodes travels only via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Lifecycle State Machine — creation → active → archive → expiry → retention → legal hold → deletion → reclamation

Each dataset exists in exactly one lifecycle state at any time; all transitions follow deterministic guard rules. Based on SDLP-style lifecycle research (seven-state deterministic object lifecycle), every transition has explicit preconditions and postconditions; illegal transitions are rejected, never silently coerced.

- **creation** — dataset being provisioned/ingested; mutable; creation timestamp recorded (all deadlines keyed to creation time, never measured RTT).
- **active** — dataset in regular use for analysis/operations; receives writes; retention clock may start at creation, publish, or last_accessed (reference event configurable per policy).
- **archive** — data no longer actively used but retained for legal/regulatory/business reasons; moved to cheaper storage tier; read-only or restricted-write.
- **expiry** — dataset passed its expiry deadline; data no longer useful; candidate for disposition but not yet deleted.
- **retention** — minimum retention period enforced from reference event; data kept until disposition date + grace window.
- **legal hold** — suspends all disposition (expiry, deletion, reclamation) until explicitly released; evaluated first and overrides every other rule.
- **deletion** — permanent removal; requires consent gate (no active hold, retention elapsed, no blocking snapshot references); tombstone written before drop.
- **reclamation** — space reclamation sweep; reclaims tombstoned/expired blocks not referenced by snapshots; bounded by quota.

Research confirms lifecycle is nonlinear: data may be revived from archive back to active use, and states are not strictly linear (National Academies data lifecycle: "data may move from one state to another in a nonlinear manner"). The state machine must allow active ← archive revival.

#### 3.2 Retention Periods & Policy Enforcement

Retention defined per data category (e.g., transaction records: 7 years; session logs: 30 days), applied consistently across every system holding that data. Based on retention-enforcement research (policy-as-code model):

| Field | Meaning | Drives |
|-------|---------|--------|
| `policy_id` | Stable rule identifier, cited in audit log | ties every action to its rule |
| `category` | Data class the rule matches | selects datasets |
| `retention_period` | Minimum duration from reference event | disposition date |
| `reference_event` | Clock start: created / published / last_accessed | which timestamp |
| `disposition` | Action after period: RETAIN / REVIEW / PURGE / ARCHIVE | emitted action |
| `legal_hold` | Hold reference freezing disposition | forces RETAIN when active |
| `grace_days` | Buffer after disposition date before action | prevents same-day churn |

Enforcement is **deterministic** (same dataset + same policy → same action, auditable/reproducible) and **reversible-by-review** (evaluator emits a disposition action and routes purges through a delayed queue — never deletes directly; a misconfigured rule surfaces as a flagged review, not silent data loss).

Retention clocks observed in production systems: Google Cloud Datastore TTL (deleted within ~24h of expiry, non-instantaneous, lower priority), Firestore TTL, Spanner TTL (within 72h), Azure Blob lifecycle (daily runs, delete after daysAfterModificationGreaterThan), Snowflake storage lifecycle policies (archive to COOL/COLD then expire), OpenSearch Serverless (24h–3650d retention). TTL does not immediately invalidate data — expired-but-not-yet-deleted data remains visible until the sweep runs, matching ids-lifecycle's tombstone approach.

#### 3.3 Legal Hold

A legal hold (litigation hold) preserves data relevant to anticipated/ongoing litigation; once a duty to preserve exists, routine retention/destruction schedules must be suspended. Based on legal-hold research (Zubulake v. UBS Warburg standard; Exterro legal-hold guidance):

- Hold placed by legal authority; covers all records or a scoped subset (e.g., invoices only).
- Hold remains until explicitly released; release requires pre-determined authority, confirmation no other hold covers the data, and legal sign-off.
- Release lifts the suspension on routine disposition — it does not delete anything. Retention obligations underneath still apply after release.
- Overlapping holds merge into one continuous protection stretch; a dataset under any active hold is retained regardless of retention state.
- FRCP Rule 37(e) governs sanctions when preserved information is lost.

Implementation rule: `hold_active(dataset)` evaluated before every disposition; if true → RETAIN, disposition suspended; hold release returns dataset to its underlying retention schedule.

#### 3.4 Expiry & Archive Tiering

Expiry is keyed to creation time (`creation_time + lifetime`), never to measured RTT — matching delay-tolerant research (lifetime = ms past creation; no RTT-bound timers). Archive tiering moves data to cheaper storage (cool → cold → archive) based on age/access patterns:

- Azure Blob: tier to cool after 30 days, archive after 90 days; archive minimum 180 days or early-deletion charge; rehydration up to 15 hours.
- Oracle Object Storage: move to Archive tier after N days, delete after M days; up to 1000 rules per bucket.
- Snowflake: archive to COOL (instant retrieval) or COLD (up to 48h retrieval); archive period before expiry.
- Microsoft Fabric OneLake: conditions on daysAfterCreationGreaterThan / daysAfterModificationGreaterThan / daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan; actions tier to cool/cold/archive or delete.

ids-lifecycle models expiry as a deadline queue; expired datasets are candidates for disposition (archive / retain / purge) subject to hold and retention gates.

#### 3.5 Deletion Coordination & Tombstone Management

Distributed deletion does not immediately drop data; instead a tombstone marks the deletion and is propagated to replicas before permanent removal during compaction. Based on Cassandra/DSE tombstone research and Lethe (delete-aware LSM engine):

- Delete inserts a tombstone invalidating older instances of the key.
- Tombstone propagates to replicas before permanent drop during compaction/sweep.
- Tombstone GC only after causal stability (all peers acked past the deletion) — prevents "zombie records" (deleted data resurrecting when an offline peer replays old state).
- Offline/never-acking members block GC — requires membership management or a grace/quarantine window.
- Tombstone GC must re-parent survivors before removing stable tombstones to avoid corrupting order (sequence-CRDT GC lesson applied to dataset tombstones).

Deletion coordination: a deletion is consented only when (a) no active legal hold, (b) retention period elapsed, (c) no snapshot references the data, (d) expiry deadline passed. Consent is recorded in the deletion journal before the tombstone is written.

#### 3.6 Reclamation & Space Amplification Reduction

Space amplification = ratio of physical bytes used to logical live data. Tombstones and old versions inflate space until reclaimed. Based on LSM compaction research:

- Compaction merges sorted runs, drops tombstoned/deleted entries, reduces read and space amplification at the cost of write amplification.
- KV-separated LSM-trees (WiscKey, BlobDB, Titan, TerakDB) reduce index size but increase storage overhead; compaction overhead is a key trade-off.
- Scavenger+ revisits space-time tradeoffs in KV-separated LSM-trees.

Reclamation sweep: marks tombstoned blocks free, runs within quota bounds; snapshot-referenced content excluded (content-addressed storage — mark-and-sweep GC enumerates all snapshots, collects reachable blocks, sweeps unreached). Reclamation is bounded (quota-enforced) to prevent unbounded I/O spikes during sweeps.

#### 3.7 Snapshot Compatibility

Snapshots are point-in-time, immutable, content-addressed views. Based on dittofs/cloudstic research:

- Every snapshot holds an implicit GC hold on referenced CAS blocks (manifest-on-disk = held).
- Deleting a snapshot releases its hold; blocks reclaimed only when unreferenced by all snapshots.
- Snapshot state transitions: creating → ready (or creating → failed); failed snapshots are retained for inspection, not silently swept.
- Restore creates a pre-restore safety snapshot first; restore-in-progress marker survives crashes for automatic rollback.

Lifecycle rule: no deletion/reclamation may remove data referenced by any existing snapshot. Snapshot compatibility is a hard guard condition on the deletion consent gate.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Premature deletion under active legal hold | Hold evaluated FIRST before every disposition; hold forces RETAIN; hold release requires authority + no-other-hold check + legal sign-off |
| Zombie records (deleted data resurrected by offline peer) | Tombstone GC only after causal stability (all-peer ack); quarantine/grace window for dead members |
| Illegal state transition coerced silently | Deterministic state machine; every transition has guard conditions; illegal transitions rejected, never coerced |
| Retention period bypassed | Retention enforced per data category, consistently across systems; disposition actions logged before action |
| Space amplification unbounded (tombstone bloat) | Bounded reclamation sweep with quota; tombstone compaction thresholds; GC at causal stability |
| Snapshot data deleted by reclamation | Snapshot implicit GC hold; reclamation excludes snapshot-referenced blocks; snapshot compatibility guard on deletion consent |
| Clock skew corrupting expiry | Deadlines keyed to dataset creation time, never RTT or wall-clock validity; monotonic clock for internal scheduling |
| Replay of stale lifecycle actions | Action IDs + dedup log; idempotency keys on lifecycle operations; nonce/replay cache bounded with TTL |
| Unauthorized lifecycle mutation | ed25519-signed lifecycle actions; capability/grant check before state transition; audit log append-only |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

Phase 033 depends on and integrates with:

| Crate | Role in Phase 033 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | `DatasetId`, `DatasetState`, `LifecyclePolicyId`, `RetentionId`, `HoldId`, `TombstoneId`, `SnapshotId` + sealed trait contracts |
| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) — sole traffic channel for lifecycle signals between nodes |
| `ids-crypto` | ed25519 signatures on lifecycle actions; sha256/blake3 for content addressing; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 for encrypted lifecycle metadata |
| `ids-storage` | Lifecycle journal, tombstone log, snapshot index, disposition queue persistence |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-carrier::Endpoint` is the only carrier boundary — lifecycle state transitions and disposition signals are shipped as `Vec<u8>` payloads, carrier-agnostic.
- `ids-000-aa` provides canonical types and sealed trait contracts that `ids-lifecycle` implements; no type duplication.
- `ids-storage` persists the lifecycle journal, tombstone log, snapshot index, and disposition queue; recovery replays the journal.
- `ids-crypto` signs lifecycle actions (ed25519) and hashes content (sha256/blake3) for snapshot/tombstone addressing.
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS — `ids-lifecycle` is carrier-agnostic over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Lifecycle State Machine
```
state ∈ {creation, active, archive, expiry, retention, hold, deletion, reclamation}
transition(from, to, guard) admitted ⟺ guard(dataset, policy, now) = true
illegal transitions rejected, never silently coerced
nonlinear: active ← archive revival permitted
```

#### 7.2 Retention Enforcement (legal hold evaluated first)
```
evaluate(dataset, policy, today):
  if hold_active(dataset): return RETAIN, "legal hold active"
  anchor = reference_date(dataset, policy.reference_event)
  disposition_date = anchor + policy.retention_period
  effective_date = disposition_date + policy.grace_days
  if today < effective_date: return RETAIN
  return policy.disposition   // REVIEW / PURGE / ARCHIVE
```
Reversible-by-review: PURGE routed through delayed queue, never deleted directly.

#### 7.3 Deletion Consent Gate
```
consent(dataset):
  hold_active(dataset)      → reject (hold)
  retention_not_elapsed     → reject (retention)
  snapshot_references(data) → reject (snapshot compatibility)
  expiry_not_passed         → reject (expiry)
  else: write consent to deletion journal, issue tombstone
```

#### 7.4 Tombstone GC (causal stability)
```
stable_frontier[r] = min over all peers of frontier[r]
version v stable ⟺ ∀ replicas: frontier[replica] ≥ v   // MVV componentwise min
tombstone t GC-able ⟺ t's deletion is causally stable
offline member blocks GC → quarantine/grace window
```

#### 7.5 Reclamation (space amplification reduction)
```
reclaim(quota):
  candidates = tombstoned blocks NOT referenced by any snapshot
  reclaim up to quota bytes; mark free
  snapshot-referenced content excluded (implicit GC hold)
```

#### 7.6 Expiry Deadline (creation-time keyed)
```
expiry(dataset) = dataset.creation_time + dataset.lifetime
expired ⟺ now >= expiry(dataset)
// No RTT appears in any deadline; absolute deadline keyed to creation time.
```

| Reclamation bounded | within quota; space amplification reduced | bench |
