**Design rules (non-negotiable):**
- One canonical definition per type; canonical types (`RegionId`, `HUnitId`, `NodeId`, `DatasetId`, `PartitionId`, `PlacementDecision`, `RedundancyMode`, `FailureDomain`, `FailureEvent`, `RecoveryScope`, `RecoveryPlanId`, `RecoveryStepId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `HUnitState`, `HUnitInfo`, `RegionInfo`, `NodeInfo`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, `DurabilityCondition`, `Capacity`, `FailureEventType`, `RecoveryAction`, `RepairStrategy`) imported from `ids_000_aa::X`, never redefined.
- `ids-selfreorg` implements the sealed `trait SelfReorg` contract from `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/` (membership, placement, replica, recovery-assignment, regional-responsibility revision) as declared in the master crate; downstream crates use it as a trait bound, cannot implement it.
- All reorganisation metadata (membership deltas, placement decisions, replica maps, recovery assignments) transported as opaque bytes via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No IP addresses, ports, sockets.
- Crypto surface: sha256/blake3 for membership/placement decision hashes and integrity; ed25519 (optional) for signing reorganisation decisions/proofs; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 only if decision payloads need encryption (this crate does not encrypt by default). All ops in `ids-crypto`; this crate declares only usage boundaries.
- Reorganisation is dataset/region-scoped; no global reorganisation master (invariant `no_global_master` in `ids-000-aa`).
- Operation lifecycle reuses `ids-000-aa` `OpState` and `CommitState`; reorganisation findings are raised through `ids-000-aa` error/annex channels.
- Logical identity remains stable across physical placement changes; metadata updated through controlled transition with epoch versions.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 H-Unit Membership Revision

H-units are intermediate subclusters between regions and nodes (IDS hierarchy: Region → regional database cluster → H-unit → node). Membership revision covers adding a node to an H-unit, creating a new H-unit, removing an H-unit, and changing H-unit state (`Forming` → `Operational` → `Degraded` → `Compensating` → `Retired` per `ids-000-aa` `HUnitState`). Research basis:
- Raft Add/RemoveServer (single-member change, quorum overlap preserved) vs joint consensus (multi-member change, two-phase) — CRaft/ReCraft generalize to arbitrary membership deltas while maintaining quorum overlap between consecutive configurations.
- SWIM failure detection: randomized peer-to-peer probing separates failure detection from membership dissemination; large-scale process groups with sub-linear detection time.
- Akka cluster membership: CRDT-based gossip state with monotonic merge; leader determined deterministically after gossip convergence; member status (joining/up/leaving/exiting/removed/down) transitions.
- H-unit capacity (`Capacity` type in ids-000-aa) constrains admission: a node joins an H-unit only if residual capacity admits it; capacity advertisement via discovery.

#### 3.2 Placement Revision

Placement revision recomputes which region/H-unit/node holds each dataset, partition, replica, or fragment when membership, capacity, or topology changes. Research basis:
- Consistent hashing with virtual nodes (tokens): each node claims ~Q/N shards of hash space; join "steals" shards consistently; leave redistributes shards to remaining nodes; deterministic so all nodes compute the same partition map; minimizes movement on view changes.
- Aerospike partition assignment: replication list = permutation of cluster succession list; first node = master, subsequent = replicas; objectives: deterministic, uniform distribution, minimized partition movement on view change.
- HDFS rack-aware placement: replicas spread across racks for fault tolerance; one replica local rack, others remote racks; re-replication when factor drops below target; block placement policy prefers same-rack writer then remote rack.
- Cassandra NetworkTopologyStrategy + virtual nodes: per-datacenter independent replica placement; vnodes automatically rebalance token ranges on join/leave/failure; dead node rebuild faster due to vnode granularity.
- CockroachDB replication zones + locality-aware rebalancing: replica allocator maintains configured replica count per range; locality or placement constraints can keep counts uneven to preserve survivability across zones; load-based rebalancing coexists with load-based splitting.
- Zone-aware replica placement and impact-free rebalancing (Pinot): mirror server sets across replica groups; placement repair preserves mirror sets, accommodates replacement nodes from arbitrary racks.

#### 3.3 Replica/Fragment Revision

Replica/fragment revision adjusts replica counts, fragment groups, redundancy mode (`FullReplica` / `ErasureCoded{k,n}` / `Hybrid` per ids-000-aa `RedundancyMode`), and fragment placement across failure domains. Research basis:
- Dynamic replication factor changes: Aerospike AP namespaces allow dynamic replication factor with `recluster`; SC mode requires quorum; TigerGraph repartition changes replication factor without adding/removing nodes; ScyllaDB cloud resize adds/removes nodes in multiples of replication factor.
- Erasure-coded fragment integrity: per-fragment checksums; EC scrub verifies cold parity shards before rebuild (SeaweedFS EC Bitrot Scrub); Reed-Solomon repair bandwidth optimization.
- Replica placement constraints: CockroachDB replica placement constraints and zones keep replica counts uneven where needed for survivability; locality-aware placement trades some load balance for failure-domain diversity.
- Hinted handoff (Cassandra): temporary node failure — missed writes stored by coordinator with target ID, replayed on recovery; anti-entropy Merkle tree repair as backstop for divergent replicas.

#### 3.4 Recovery Assignment Revision

Recovery assignment revision reassigns recovery owners and plans after failures (node/H-unit/region). Research basis:
- `trait Recovery` sealed contract in ids-000-aa: `detect_failures`, `create_plan`, `execute_plan`, `quarantine`, `restore_redundancy`, `reconcile_state`; `RepairStrategy` enum (CopyReplica, RestoreRedundancy, ReconstructErasure, TransferOwnership) with priority ordering; `RecoveryScope` (Node/HUnit/Region); `RecoveryPlan` with steps and status; `FailureEvent` typed by `FailureEventType`.
- Regional recovery coordinator: cross-region recovery, regional failure counting, region health tracking.
- Repair planner selects strategy by scope level: node→CopyReplica, H-unit→RestoreRedundancy, region→ReconstructErasure; resource-bounded active recoveries.
- Revision triggers recovery re-planning when placement changes invalidate current owners: new owner assumes in-flight recovery plans, quarantine releases restore redundancy.

#### 3.5 Regional Responsibility Revision

Regional responsibility revision moves responsibilities (dataset ownership, replica mastership, recovery coordination) between regions. Research basis:
- CockroachDB joint consensus for region failure: intermediate joint configuration requires agreement of both old and new configs, preventing split-brain during region outages; survives individual region outage.
- ReCraft split/merge: subclusters split into disjoint members and data ranges; joint configuration C_joint requires quorums from each subcluster; merge via 2PC among subclusters.
- ids-mobility (crate 38): preferred/authoritative region changes, logical identity preservation, controlled handoff between old/new owners, cutover verification — ids-selfreorg consumes mobility handoff outputs.
- Kubernetes topology spread constraints: spread pods across failure domains (regions, zones, nodes) with maxSkew/minDomains; ids-selfreorg's regional responsibility revision is the storage-layer analog.

#### 3.6 Invariant Preservation During Reorganisation

Invariant preservation ensures safety properties hold throughout reorganisation steps. Research basis:
- Quorum overlap property: Raft joint consensus maintains quorum overlap between C_old and C_new (AR-RPC one-node difference; JC two-phase). Generalized Raft reconfiguration (P2' proof) underlies ReCraft's wait-free multi-node changes.
- OpenRaft adaptive config change: skips joint consensus when old/new quorums already overlap (single entry); otherwise joint → uniform (two entries).
- Invariant synthesis via IC3 (arxiv 2605.24619): inductive invariants for distributed protocols incl. dynamic Raft reconfiguration; verifies safety across reconfiguration transitions.
- Grace period member removal: synchrony assumptions bound how long a removed member can still act; stale-metadata windows guarded by epoch versions.
- Durability conditions: `DurabilityCondition` in ids-000-aa gates replica/fragment changes; redundancy floor never breached mid-revision.

#### 3.7 Topology Change Handling

Topology change handling covers node join/leave, H-unit formation/retirement, region split/merge, link degradation, and carrier changes. Research basis:
- Fault-tolerant active rings for structured P2P overlays: neighbor pointers updated immediately on join/leave; active topology maintenance (Li/Misra/Plaxton) ensures immediate consistency of neighbor links.
- SWARM+ hierarchical multi-agent consensus: topology descriptor specifies hierarchy level, group id, peer set, parent reference; quorum q(t) = ceil((n_live(t)+1)/2) adapts dynamically without explicit reconfiguration.
- HyParView: active view + passive view; gossip-based broadcast; passive view promoted on active view failure; peer-to-peer periodic randomized probing.
- Gluster volume rebalance: expand/shrink volumes online; rebalance migrates data to new bricks; remove-brick triggers automatic rebalance.
- Cross-datacenter replica placement latency optimization: WAN-limited bandwidth trades replication for locality; GeoLayer layered graph for low-latency geo-distributed placement.
- Self-healing (Kubernetes): automatic replacement of failed pods/rescheduling on node unavailability; desired-state reconciliation.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Node/H-unit/region failure mid-revision | Epoch-versioned decisions; recovery assignment revision re-plans on failure; `trait Recovery` quarantine + restore_redundancy |
| Split brain during membership change | Quorum overlap (joint consensus when quorums don't overlap); single-entry transition when overlap exists; `ids-000-aa` sealed trait enforces at contract layer |
| Redundancy floor breached (too few replicas during revision) | `DurabilityCondition` gating; redundancy floor check before every revision step; abort if below floor |
| Stale topology/membership views | Gossip sequence numbers + timestamps; epoch versions on placement decisions; stale entries expired via `DiscoveryExpiration` |
| Replica/fragment data loss during movement | Reconstruct from redundant copies or erasure fragments before removing source; verify checksum (ids-integrity) before rewrite |
| Capacity overcommit on H-unit join | `Capacity` check against `HUnitInfo.available_capacity()`; admission control rejects over-full H-units |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (`std::net`, `tokio::net`, IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/…) | `Endpoint` sole address type; dependency audit bans networking crates; CI grep for prohibited symbols |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305; `ids-crypto` enforces at implementation layer |
| Revision storms / oscillation | Decision recorder with epoch log; cooldown windows; policy-driven thresholds; concurrent-request serialization |
| Reorganisation without observable completion | `RecoveryPlanId`-scoped plan tracking; completion conditions exposed; completion condition verified before next revision |
| Logical identity instability across physical moves | Dataset/partition `RecordId`/`OrderingPos` unchanged; only physical location (RegionId/HUnitId/NodeId) updated via `PlacementDecision` |
| Memory growth of decision/epoch logs | Bounded epoch log with TTL eviction; periodic compaction |

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Membership Revision (H-unit add/remove/retire)
```
delta = {add: [NodeId], remove: [NodeId], retire_hunit: [HUnitId]}
validate: admission check (capacity), lifecycle state (Forming/Operational/Degraded/Compensating/Retired)
apply: DiscoveryEngine.register_node/deregister_node/register_hunit; emit MembershipDelta via Endpoint
serialization: membership_scheduler serializes concurrent deltas; epoch versioned
```

#### 7.2 Placement Revision (consistent hashing + virtual nodes)
```
hash_space = 2^m; Q shards; T tokens per node
node claims ~Q/N shards; join steals shards consistently; leave redistributes to remaining nodes
deterministic partition map: all nodes compute identical RegionId/HUnitId/NodeId per (DatasetId, PartitionId)
rack-aware: spread replicas across failure domains; zone-aware: locality-aware uneven counts for survivability
movement minimization: Aerospike replication-list permutation minimizes moved partitions on view change
```

#### 7.3 Replica/Fragment Revision
```
replica_count = f(RedundancyMode): FullReplica→N copies; ErasureCoded{k,n}→n fragments, k needed; Hybrid→per-policy
transition: increase → allocate new replicas/fragments; decrease → remove excess after redundancy floor re-checked
fragment placement: across H-units/regions per failure-domain constraints; hinted_handoff for temporary failure
```

#### 7.4 Recovery Assignment Revision
```
on placement change: RecoveryOwnerRevision reassigns RecoveryPlan owners
plan_revision: in-flight RecoveryPlan steps retargeted to new owner; owner_transfer via Endpoint datagrams
quarantine_release: release scope, restore_redundancy via ids-recovery trait
```

#### 7.5 Regional Responsibility Revision (joint consensus + split/merge)
```
region split: disjoint members + data ranges per subcluster; C_joint requires quorums from each subcluster
region merge: 2PC among subclusters; C_new committed after all agree; data exchange then new leader
quorum overlap: if old/new quorums already overlap → single-entry transition; else joint→uniform (two entries)
handoff: controlled old→new owner with cutover verification (ids-mobility)
```

#### 7.6 Invariant Preservation
```
pre-revision: quorum_overlap_ok(old, new) ∧ redundancy_floor_ok() ∧ durability_condition_met()
post-revision: same invariants re-checked; epoch_validator rejects stale views
grace period: removed member retains read-only access for bounded window; no write authority
```

#### 7.7 Topology Change Handling
```
node join/leave: SWIM-style randomized probing; gossip CRDT merge (monotonic); leader deterministic after convergence
link degradation: carrier-agnostic — detected via Endpoint reachability, not IP/TCP; alternate CarrierType
self-healing: automatic replacement of failed responsibilities; desired-state reconciliation
dynamic quorum: q(t) = ceil((n_live(t)+1)/2) adapts without explicit reconfiguration (SWARM+)
```

#### 7.8 Data Structures
```
SelfReorgDecision { decision_id, epoch, revision_type, scope, payload_hash (sha256/blake3), signature (ed25519 opt), ids_time }
RevisionEpoch { epoch: u64, decided_at_ms: u64, decided_by: NodeId }
MembershipDelta { add_nodes: Vec<NodeId>, remove_nodes: Vec<NodeId>, retire_hunits: Vec<HUnitId>, epoch }
PlacementRevision { dataset_id, partition_id, old: PlacementDecision, new: PlacementDecision, epoch }
ReplicaFragmentRevision { partition_id, old_redundancy: RedundancyMode, new_redundancy: RedundancyMode, epoch }
RecoveryAssignmentRevision { plan_id: RecoveryPlanId, old_owner, new_owner, scope: RecoveryScope, epoch }
RegionalResponsibilityRevision { region_from, region_to, responsibilities, joint_config_opt, epoch }
CompletionCondition { decision_id, satisfied: bool, verified_at_ms, integrity_result }
```

`ids-selfreorg/Cargo.toml` (proposed):

- `ids-crypto = { path = \"../ids-crypto\" }` — sha256, blake3, ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305 (consumed only)

- `ids-recovery = { path = \"../ids-recovery\" }` — recovery plans, failure detection, reconstruction

- `ids-placement = { path = \"../ids-placement\" }` — partition maps, distribution across nodes/H-units/regions
- `ids-replication = { path = \"../ids-replication\" }` — replica/fragment sources and targets
- `ids-mobility = { path = \"../ids-mobility\" }` — region handoff outputs for regional responsibility revision
- `ids-integrity = { path = \"../ids-integrity\" }` — checksum verification of moved/reconstructed data
- `ids-time = { path = \"../ids-time\" }` — `IdsTime` tick basis
- `ids-ordering-domain = { path = \"../ids-ordering-domain\" }` — dataset-scoped ordering stability
- `thiserror = \"2.0\"` — error enum derive
- `serde = { version = \"1\", features = [\"derive\"] }` — decision message serialization
- `blake3 = \"1.5\"` — content hashing (type-level/use only)

**No** `std::net`, `tokio`, `tokio::net`, `libp2p`, `hyper`, `reqwest`, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh dependencies. No async runtime required; datagram-driven. `cargo tree` must show zero networking crates. Sibling infra crates referenced via adapters; persistence delegation is a design option, not a hard dependency in this phase.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

| Uncertainty | Impact | Resolution path |
|-------------|--------|-----------------|
| `trait SelfReorg` not yet declared in `ids-000-aa` | `src/contract.rs` cannot reference it until declared | Declaration deferred to master crate phase; plan assumes its existence per sealed-contract pattern |
| Membership/placement revision trigger source | Whether revisions are event-driven (failure detected) or policy-driven (periodic evaluation) | Both specified; trigger router in `membership_scheduler`/`decision_recorder` |
| Consistent hashing token count T and shard count Q defaults | Affects rebalance granularity and movement | Configurable via `PlacementConfig`; tuned at implementation |
| Redundancy floor vs erasure-coded k/n during transition | Breaking floor mid-revision risks data loss | `DurabilityCondition` gate before every step; abort-and-retry on violation |
| Region split/merge data movement volume | Large moves can stall reorganisation | Movement minimizer + phased transfer; cutover verification via ids-mobility |
| Grace period duration for removed members | Too short → split-brain risk; too long → stale authority | Configurable; bounded by epoch version + heartbeat timeout from `ids-time` |
| Integration ordering with ids-mobility/ids-recovery | Regional responsibility revision depends on mobility handoff | Plan assumes ids-mobility (crate 38) and ids-recovery exist before this phase |
| Whether revision decisions are signed by default | Authenticity vs accidental-change scope | ed25519 signing optional; core revision is policy-driven state transition |

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-selfreorg` crate (not folders inside existing crates) | Matches user directive \"try to use separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones\"; single-responsibility boundary |
| H-unit membership, placement, replica/fragment, recovery assignment, regional responsibility as separate modules | Matches prompts.txt entry 39 contents exactly; each independently testable |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule (CRATES.md, prompts.txt entry 39) |
| Allowed crypto: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | IDS policy; `ids-crypto` implements, this crate declares usage boundaries |
| Quorum overlap (joint consensus when quorums don't overlap) | Raft joint consensus safety; generalized Raft reconfiguration (ReCraft/P2') |
| Consistent hashing + virtual nodes for placement | Deterministic partition map; minimal movement on view change (Aerospike/Dynamo lineage) |
| Epoch-versioned decisions + completion condition | Observable reorganisation; stale-view rejection; measurable acceptance |
| Logical identity stable across physical moves | Dataset/partition `RecordId`/`OrderingPos` unchanged; only physical location updated |
| No code in this phase | Research only per prompts.txt entry 39 |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 040 creates `ids-immutable`, the IDS crate that protects selected records against modification and deletion. It owns immutable record protection, retention-period enforcement, legal-hold enforcement, enforcement across replicas/fragments/derived copies, tamper detection, and retention expiry. The design follows the WORM (write-once, read-many) model with two independent, composable controls: (a) a retention period with a retain-until-date after which a record may be modified/deleted, and (b) a legal hold with no expiration that blocks deletion/modification until explicitly released. A legal hold always takes precedence over retention. Every protection decision is recorded in an append-only, hash-chained audit trail with signed checkpoints so any modification, deletion, truncation, or reordering is detectable.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`, max 1024-byte address; `CarrierType` ∈ {Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom}). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-immutable` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-immutable` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-immutable/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types `RecordId` (`src/types.rs:262`), `SnapshotId` (`src/types.rs:1329`), `FragmentId` (`src/types.rs:1889`), `RecoveryProof` (`src/types.rs:1905`), `Checksum` (`src/types.rs:1975`), `AnomalyType` ∈ {ByteMismatch, ReplicaDrift, ChecksumFailure, StateCorruption} (`src/types.rs:1951`), `NodeId` (`src/types.rs:21`), `RegionId` (`src/types.rs:68`), `IdsTime`, and `CarrierType` (`src/types.rs:394`) — all referenced by this crate but never redefined. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-immutable` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is layered so each concern — record protection, retention, legal hold, replica/fragment/derived-copy enforcement, tamper detection, expiry — is an independent module. `ids-immutable` is a guard layer: it does not store records itself; it vetoes or stamps mutating operations issued by `ids-store`, `ids-fragment`, `ids-replication`, and `ids-reclaim` (Phase 041) before they take effect.

**Data flow of a protected mutation:**
1. A mutation issuer (`ids-store` write/delete, `ids-reclaim` compaction, `ids-replication` replica update) submits a `RecordId` + intended operation to `ids-immutable`'s guard entrypoint.
2. The protection module resolves the record's `ProtectionLevel`: `None` → allow; `Retention` → check `retain_until_date` against `IdsTime` (monotonic); `Hold` → reject; `Compliance` → reject with no override path.
3. The policy engine evaluates all matching retention/hold rules (max-duration-wins; legal hold checked first and short-circuits every disposition) and emits a disposition (`retain` / `review` / `purge` / `archive`) recorded to the append-only audit log.
4. If allowed, the mutation proceeds and is stamped into the tamper-detection hash chain/Merkle log with a `Checksum` (BLAKE3/SHA-256) and optional ed25519 signature; a signed checkpoint (Signed Tree Head) anchors periodically.
5. Deletion of an expired/retained record does not erase history: it writes a tombstone (sequence range, Merkle root, signed checkpoint) that survives forever, so verifiers can distinguish "expired-but-retained" from an unexplained gap. Tombstones are removable only after every replica has acknowledged compaction past them (MTRO/MCCO-style).
6. All cross-node protection metadata travels as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-immutable` never touches a carrier directly.

**Protection levels:**
- `None` — no constraint; normal mutable record.
- `Retention` — record is immutable until `retain_until_date`; after expiry it may be modified/deleted per disposition (unless also held).
- `Hold` — legal hold; immutable and undeletable until explicitly released; independent of retention, no expiration.
- `Compliance` — WORM: immutable and undeletable for the retention period with no override (not even root); mirrors SEC 17a-4 compliance mode.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Immutable record protection model (WORM, versioning, append-only)

Records are protected at the `RecordId` granularity by wrapping the record in an immutable envelope: content-addressed by `Checksum` (BLAKE3 or SHA-256 over canonical bytes), versioned by monotonic sequence, and linked into a per-stream hash chain so each version binds the previous version's digest. A protected record can be read and replicated but never overwritten in place; a "modification" of a retained record is rejected by the guard, and a new version is only creatable once retention has expired or been lawfully superseded under the audit-trail alternative (SEC 17a-4: the system must permit recreation of the original if modified/deleted, with a complete time-stamped audit trail naming actor, date-time, and all modifications)[^4][^5]. This matches the WORM requirement of non-rewriteable, non-erasable storage [^1][^2] and the audit-trail alternative's time-stamped, actor-attributed change log. Content-addressing (SHA-256/BLAKE3 keyed by content hash) gives integrity for free: any alteration breaks the digest, and identical content is stored once [^25][^24]. The envelope carries a `ProtectionLevel` and `retain_until_date`, both monotonic (retention may only be extended, never shortened — mirroring the irreversibility of a locked bucket retention policy)[^3].

#### 3.2 Retention period enforcement (fixed/variable retention, retain-until-date, policy engine)

Each protected record or record class carries a retention period with an absolute retain-until-date or a duration from a reference event (created/published/last-accessed). The enforcement engine runs periodically (background sweep, e.g. every N minutes like InfluxDB's retention service[^10]) and evaluates every record against its category policy. When multiple policies match a record, max-duration-wins applies: the longest retention period is honored, so any policy requiring longer retention prevails [^18]. A grace period buffers after the disposition date to prevent same-day churn [^18]. Retention can be extended (retain-until-date moved later) but never reduced once locked, consistent with Google Cloud's locked bucket policy (irreversible; cannot delete bucket while objects remain under retention)[^3]. Rows/records become ineligible for modification or deletion while within the retention period; after expiry they become eligible for disposition but are not physically removed until a compaction/reclaim pass (Phase 041 `ids-reclaim`) runs and the guard signs off [^10][^13]. This mirrors row-level TTL (CockroachDB/Spanner/Doris): expiration is checked at query time; physical reclamation is a separate background step with no fixed deletion deadline [^2][^10].

#### 3.3 Legal hold enforcement (indefinite, overrides retention, explicit release)

A legal hold is independent of retention: it has no expiration and remains in force until explicitly released [^1][^2]. When a record is under an active hold, all disposition (delete/modify) is suspended regardless of how far past its retention date it is — the hold is evaluated first and short-circuits every other rule [^18]. Hold and retention can coexist: a record under both a retention period and a hold is not deleted when retention expires; it is retained until the hold is lifted [^19][^3]. Holds are targeted to specific records, record classes, or custodians (e-discovery/litigation model) rather than applied organization-wide blindly [^19]. Release of a hold is a controlled, audited action recorded in the append-only audit log so the transition from "preserved" to "eligible for disposition" is traceable [^18][^19]. This implements the Microsoft 365/Box principle that preservation for a legal matter always takes precedence over routine retention [^19].

#### 3.4 Tamper detection (hash chains, Merkle trees, append-only verification, anchoring)

Every protected mutation is appended to an append-only, hash-chained audit ledger: each entry SHA-256- or BLAKE3-chains to the previous entry's digest over its canonical fields, so any modification, insertion, deletion, or reordering invalidates all subsequent hashes and is detected on verification (recomputation of the chain)[^21][^20][^24]. Periodic Merkle batching produces a Signed Tree Head (STH) — a Merkle root over the ledger signed with ed25519 — enabling compact inclusion and consistency proofs that the ledger is append-only between any two STHs (Certificate Transparency / Trillian model)[^8]. STHs are anchored (checkpointed) at intervals so an off-ledger verifier can confirm the ledger was not rewritten; anchoring itself is chained so removing an anchor is detectable [^21][^14]. IBM's Logging for Compliance demonstrates a provably immutable log rotated after retention, with signed checkpoints committed to a distributed ledger to eliminate truncation/elongation attacks[^14]. Authenticated Append-Only Skip Lists give a malicious-maintainer-resistant variant: one-way digests plus succinct inclusion proofs, with proofs that data cannot be invented or equivocated after a digest is published[^20]. Verification is offline: given the disclosed payload and Merkle proof, any verifier checks independently without trusting the logger [^21].

#### 3.5 Enforcement across replicas/fragments/derived copies (tombstones, convergent deletion)

Protection must be uniform across every replica, fragment, and derived copy of a record. A delete of an expired record does not erase the record everywhere immediately; it writes a tombstone (sequence range + Merkle root + signed checkpoint) that is replicated like any other entry, so offline/lagging replicas learn of the deletion when they reconnect [^17][^12]. Tombstone removal (garbage collection) is gated on causal stability: a tombstone is eligible for physical removal only after it is expired and its timestamp range does not overlap any live data on any replica (ScyllaDB/Cassandra `gc_grace_seconds`, default 10 days; repair-based GC sets the expiry threshold per token range so no replica can resurrect the data)[^11]. Kafka's MTRO/MCCO pattern is the precise convergent rule: per-replica maximum-cleanly-compacted offset (MCCO) only moves forward; the tombstone-removal offset (MTRO) is the minimum MCCO across the replica set, including unavailable replicas, so a tombstone below MTRO is safe to remove because every replica has compacted past it [^12]. Derived copies (fragment shards, replicas, caches) inherit the protection level of their source; a derived copy may not outlive its source's retention/hold, and compaction of a fragment must consult the guard before dropping any retained/held record. This keeps enforcement convergent under any delivery order, duplication, or delay — matching the carrier-agnostic, unknown-membership model [^12][^11].

#### 3.6 Retention expiry and disposition (retain / review / purge / archive, expired-but-retained)

When retention expires, the guard emits a disposition: `retain` (keep), `review` (human/approver gate before any destructive action), `purge` (permanent deletion via tombstone), or `archive` (move to cold/immutable storage)[^18]. The enforcer never deletes directly: it records the disposition in the immutable audit log and routes purges through a delayed queue or human review so a misconfigured rule causes a flagged review, not silent data loss[^18]. Expired data is not immediately erased; the ciphertext/blob may be removed but the tombstone row (sequence range, Merkle root, signed checkpoint) survives forever, and verifiers report the range as "expired-but-retained" — verifiable by the retained signed checkpoint — rather than as a false gap[^17]. ATL's approach of deleting the payload while retaining the hash (right-to-erasure compatible: the hash remains as a mathematical constant but no longer links to personal data)[^15] is relevant where GDPR erasure conflicts with an immutable audit trail. Elasticsearch ILM shows rollover + time-based delete phases for append-only indices[^13].

#### 3.7 Compliance frameworks (SEC 17a-4, FINRA 4511, CFTC 1.31, GDPR, legal hold precedence)

- SEC Rule 17a-4: electronic records preserved exclusively in non-rewriteable, non-erasable (WORM) format, or via the audit-trail alternative (complete time-stamped audit trail of all modifications/deletions with actor identity, permitting recreation of the original)[^4][^5]. FINRA Rule 4511 and CFTC Regulation 1.31 impose equivalent WORM/audit-trail obligations on financial records [^1][^2]. `ids-immutable` supports both pathways: `Compliance` protection = WORM; `Retention` + append-only signed audit chain = audit-trail alternative.
- GDPR: storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) — keep no longer than necessary, justified per purpose; right to erasure (Art. 17) — non-absolute, with exceptions for legal obligation, public interest, archiving/research/statistics, and legal claims[^6][^7]. Tension: retention (keep) vs erasure (delete). Resolution: a legal hold or statutory retention obligation is a lawful basis to refuse erasure; once retention expires and no hold applies, purge via tombstone; backups held "beyond use" until replaced on schedule[^6][^7]. EDPB's 2025 sweep found organizations struggle to define and implement retention periods and to delete data in backups — the plan addresses both with a policy engine and expired-but-retained tombstones[^7].
- Legal hold always takes precedence over retention (Microsoft 365/Box principle)[^19].

#### 3.8 Cryptographic commitment & anchoring (allowed primitives only)

Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 are used:
- ed25519: signs audit entries and Signed Tree Heads/checkpoints (origin authentication, non-repudiation).
- sha256 / blake3: record content hashes (`Checksum`), hash-chain links, Merkle tree nodes, receipt-chain references (JCS-canonicalized, self-verifiable without network)[^24].
- xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305: encrypt record payloads at rest when confidentiality is required; retention deletes ciphertext while the hash/tombstone remains (ATL right-to-erasure pattern)[^15].
- Crypto-agility / renewal: because records may be retained for years, the audit chain supports re-time-attestation of prior entries under a fresh chain before an algorithm weakens (EP-EVIDENCE-RECORD / RFC 4998 Evidence Record Syntax renewal chain; RFC 3161 timestamps for offline existence proof)[^16]. SHA-256/BLAKE3 only — no SHA-3/Post-quantum primitives, per the allowed-crypto rule.

### Threat Model

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Unauthorized modification or deletion of a protected record | Record integrity/immutability | Guard vetoes all writes/deletes against `ProtectionLevel`; `Compliance`/`Hold` reject unconditionally; every decision signed and chained |
| Insider / root-key override of a WORM record | Compliance (SEC 17a-4 compliance mode) | `Compliance` level has no override path, not even root; retention only extendable, never shortenable once locked |
| Replica divergence / data resurrection across replicas | Convergent deletion | Tombstones replicated like entries; removal gated on all-peer compaction (MTRO/MCCO) + `gc_grace_seconds` overlap checks |
| Truncation / elongation of the audit ledger | Audit trail integrity | Hash chain + Merkle STHs + signed checkpoints; any gap/reorder/edit breaks verification and names the entry |
| Rollback to a pre-protection state | Protection guarantee | Checkpoints are chained; reverting to an older state breaks the chain and fails verification against the latest anchored root |
| Signing-key compromise | Authenticity of proofs | Signed key-rotation handoff (old key seals the chain, new key continues); old public keys retained forever for verification |
| Clock manipulation to force early expiry | Retention correctness | `retain_until_date` evaluated against monotonic `IdsTime`, not wall clock; retention only extensible |
| Retention sweep / hold storm causing denial of service or mass deletion | Availability | Dispositions queued through review/purge gates; holds short-circuit and block mass purge; bounded per-peer metadata budgets |

The carrier is never trusted: protection metadata is signed over payload bytes, so it survives re-framing by any carrier, and the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **ProtectionLevel** ∈ {None, Retention, Hold, Compliance}: resolved per `RecordId`; `Hold`/`Compliance` reject mutation unconditionally; `Retention` checks `retain_until_date` vs monotonic `IdsTime`; `None` permits.
- **Retain-until-date**: monotonic; set at protection time; extendable only (never shortened); once locked (compliance mode) immutable for the period.
- **Legal hold**: boolean + hold reference + placed/released timestamps + releasing actor; indefinite; checked first, short-circuits every disposition.
- **Policy engine**: for each record, collect all matching retention/hold rules; apply max-duration-wins; legal hold short-circuits to `RETAIN`; emit disposition {retain, review, purge, archive} with grace days; record to audit log.
- **Hash chain**: each audit entry = SHA-256/BLAKE3(entry || prev_digest || seq); verification replays the chain; any edit/gap/reorder breaks and names the entry.
- **Merkle tree + STH**: periodic Merkle root over the ledger, ed25519-signed; inclusion/consistency proofs prove append-only between any two STHs.
- **Tombstone**: {sequence range, Merkle root, signed checkpoint, deleted_at, retention/hold reason}; survives forever; verifiers report "expired-but-retained".
- **Tombstone removal**: eligible only after expired AND no overlap with live data on any replica (gc_grace threshold) AND removal offset ≤ min(MCCO across replica set) — MTRO/MCCO rule.
- **Signed checkpoint**: ed25519 signature over Merkle root + seq range + prev checkpoint; chained so removing an anchor is detectable; old public keys retained for rotation verification.

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`RecordId`, `FragmentId`, `SnapshotId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Checksum`, `AnomalyType`, `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait for opaque datagram transport only.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `serde` — serialization of protected envelopes, audit entries, checkpoints.
No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list.

### Measurable Acceptance Criteria

1. While a record's retention period is active, 100% of write/modify/delete attempts against it are rejected by the guard; after expiry, disposition governs.
2. An active legal hold blocks 100% of modify/delete attempts regardless of retention state; release is the only clearing path and is audited.
3. `Compliance` (WORM) level rejects modification/deletion with no override path (not even root) for the full retention period.
4. Tamper detection catches 100% of single-record modifications, insertions, deletions, and reorderings in the audit ledger; verification names the offending entry.
5. A tombstone is physically removed only after (a) expiry, (b) no overlap with live data on any replica, and (c) removal offset ≤ min(MCCO across the replica set) — zero premature removals under any replica lag/partition.
6. Retention can only be extended, never shortened, once set; a locked retention policy is irreversible.
7. Every protection decision (place hold, set/extend retention, dispose, release hold) is recorded in the append-only, hash-chained, signed audit log with actor + `IdsTime`.
8. All protection metadata is carried as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS in the crate.
9. Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 appear in the crate's crypto surface.
10. Expired-but-retained records are reported by verifiers via retained signed checkpoints (not false gaps); payload deletion leaves a verifiable tombstone.

---

### Remaining Uncertainties

- Clock source for `retain_until_date`: monotonic `IdsTime` vs loosely-synced wall time; monotonic avoids manipulation but complicates cross-node absolute deadlines without a network clock.
- Interaction of key compromise/revocation with an active legal hold or compliance record: rotation preserves verifiability, but a compromised signing key's past checkpoints remain valid (content trust ≠ identity trust) — revocation policy is out of scope for this crate.
- Cross-replica tombstone convergence under long partitions: MTRO stalls with an unavailable replica (correct but may delay reclamation); acceptable trade-off, needs operational tuning of `gc_grace_seconds`.
- Performance of per-record hash chain at high write throughput; Merkle batching interval and anchor frequency are tunable parameters to be validated.
- Interaction with Phase 041 `ids-reclaim`: compaction must not violate retention/hold; the exact guard-reclaim handshake (eligibility proof) is defined here but validated at integration.

---

### Engineering Decisions Summary

- Separate crate `ids-immutable` (not a folder inside an existing crate), organized into subfolders/files by subsystem — one file per concern.
- Two independent controls (retention + legal hold); hold always wins; compliance/WORM has no override.
- Retention is extendable-only and irreversible once locked (mirrors locked bucket policy).
- Deletion never erases history: tombstones (sequence range, Merkle root, signed checkpoint) survive forever; "expired-but-retained" is verifiable, not a gap.
- Convergent deletion across replicas via tombstone + MTRO/MCCO + `gc_grace_seconds` overlap checks.
- Tamper detection via SHA-256/BLAKE3 hash chain + Merkle STHs + ed25519-signed checkpoints, verifiable offline.
- Only allowed crypto; carrier-agnostic boundary via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; no network stack.

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 041 creates `ids-reclaim`, the IDS crate that compacts fragmented storage and reclaims eligible space. It owns fragmented-storage compaction, obsolete-version removal, tombstone expiry, eligible-data expiration, space-amplification reduction, snapshot/retention compatibility, compaction scheduling, and reclamation verification. `ids-reclaim` is a **guard-and-sweep layer**: it does not own storage; it evaluates eligibility, schedules compactions, and verifies reclamation, coordinating with `ids-immutable` (Phase 040 guard) so retained/held records are never reclaimed. It operates out-of-place (copy-live-forward, never overwrite-in-place), keeping old versions visible to concurrent snapshots until compaction commits atomically.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (consumed from `ids-crypto`/`ids-000-aa`).

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned RocksDB tiered/leveled/FIFO compaction and compaction scoring (level fill factor, tombstone threshold, TTL)[^1][^4]; LSM compaction design space and delete-aware file picking (tombstone count/age)[^5]; WiscKey key/value separation with separate value-log GC[^4]; Cassandra/ScyllaDB STCS/LCS/ICS/TWCS tombstone thresholds (`tombstone_threshold` default 0.2, `tombstone_compaction_interval` default 1 day)[^6][^7]; leanstore-style page compaction and B-tree[^8]; Pebble compaction kinds incl. delete-only/tombstone-density/rewrite[^9]; TigerBeetle incremental LSM compaction and move-table optimization[^10]; SQLite VACUUM full rebuild / auto_vacuum incremental[^11]; WiredTiger cooperative Btree+BlockManager compaction with checkpoint prerequisite[^12]; Apache Iceberg `expire_snapshots` + orphan-file removal[^13]; Delta Lake `OPTIMIZE` bin-packing + `VACUUM` tombstoned-file deletion[^14]; Sprite LFS segment cleaning (live-block copy-forward, cost/benefit segment selection)[^15]; log-structured storage GC write-amplification model (invalid vs valid block rewrites)[^16]; MVCC old-version garbage collection bottleneck[^2]; Delta Lake small-file compaction and checkpoint log compaction[^14]; space/reclamation metrics (logical vs physical bytes, reclaimed per pass)[^14]. This document is the research blueprint only — no code written, no files modified.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-reclaim` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a **compaction-and-reclamation service**: it evaluates fragment/file eligibility, selects compaction victims, schedules and runs compactions out-of-place, and verifies reclaimed bytes. It defers to `ids-immutable` (Phase 040) for retention/hold vetoes — `ids-reclaim` never reclaims a record under an active legal hold or unexpired retention.

**Data flow of a compaction cycle:**
1. **Eligibility evaluation:** each fragment/file is scored for tombstone density, obsolete-version ratio, expired TTL, and snapshot/retention safety. `ids-immutable` vetoes any record under retention/hold/compliance.
2. **Victim selection:** cost/benefit model picks candidates (highest reclaimable bytes per unit of rewrite I/O), respecting concurrent-snapshot pinning (versions visible to any open snapshot are retained).
3. **Compaction scheduling:** out-of-place copy-live-forward into new fragment files; old fragment files become obsolete only after the new set is durably committed and the manifest atomically swaps.
4. **Reclamation verification:** post-compaction byte delta (bytes_before − bytes_after) is recorded to an append-only, hash-chained reclamation audit log; obsolete physical files are deleted only after verification and after no reader/snapshot can reference them.
5. All compaction metadata travels as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-reclaim` never touches a carrier directly.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Fragmented storage compaction (out-of-place copy-live-forward)
Fragmentation arises from out-of-place updates/deletes: newer versions shadow older ones, deletes leave tombstones, and small incremental writes create many small fragments. Compaction rewrites overlapping fragments into fewer, larger ones, dropping shadowed/obsolete versions and expired tombstones [^1][^15]. The copy-live-forward pattern (read live blocks, write to new segment, free old segment) mirrors Sprite LFS segment cleaning [^15] and is crash-safe because old files remain intact until the new set is atomically published [^2][^14].

#### 3.2 Obsolete version removal (MVCC garbage collection)
Out-of-place engines retain multiple versions per key for snapshot isolation; obsolete versions are reclaimed only when no open snapshot/reader can reference them [^2][^22]. Version-chain GC is a known HTAP bottleneck [^2]; the reclaimer must pin versions by oldest-active-snapshot sequence and drop versions strictly older than every retained snapshot's read point [^22]. `ids-reclaim` treats snapshot pins as hard retention: versions visible to any pinned snapshot are never removed, preserving snapshot/retention compatibility.

#### 3.3 Tombstone expiry
Deletes are recorded as tombstones rather than in-place removal [^6][^9][^16]. A tombstone is droppable only when (a) its delete is visible at all levels below (no older value can be resurrected), (b) it is older than the tombstone expiry / `gc_grace_seconds` window, and (c) every replica has compacted past it (MTRO/MCCO-style convergent rule [^12]). ScyllaDB uses a `tombstone_threshold` (default 0.2 tombstone density) plus `tombstone_compaction_interval` (default 1 day) to trigger single-SSTable tombstone compaction [^6][^7]; `ids-reclaim` adopts the same threshold + interval pattern.

#### 3.4 Eligible data expiration (TTL / retention sweep)
Records past their retention expiry (from `ids-immutable`) or TTL become eligible for disposition (retain/review/purge/archive) [^23][^24]. The eligibility evaluator consults `ids-immutable`'s policy engine; only records with an approved `purge` disposition enter compaction candidates. Expired-but-retained records keep a tombstone row (sequence range, Merkle root, signed checkpoint) forever — never a false gap [^24].

#### 3.5 Space amplification reduction
Space amplification = physical bytes / logical bytes [^1][^16]. Compaction reduces it by dropping obsolete versions and tombstones and coalescing small fragments. The cost/benefit score for a victim fragment = reclaimable_bytes / rewrite_io_bytes; candidates exceeding the threshold are compacted [^1][^5]. Temporary space overhead during compaction (old + new files coexist) is bounded by compacting one fragment set at a time [^1][^2].

#### 3.6 Snapshot / retention compatibility
Compaction must not break open snapshots: any version visible to a pinned snapshot (sequence ≤ snapshot read point) is retained even if obsolete [^2][^22]. `ids-immutable` retention/hold/compliance levels are hard vetoes: held/compliant records are never reclaimed; retention-only records are reclaimed only after `retain_until_date` passes [^23]. This matches Iceberg `expire_snapshots` (data files deleted only when unreferenced by any retained snapshot) [^13].

#### 3.7 Compaction scheduling
Compactions run as background jobs with configurable priority, rate limits, and write-stall backpressure (RocksDB-style: slowdown/stop thresholds on pending compaction bytes) [^1][^9]. Scheduling strategies: time-based (periodic sweep), threshold-based (tombstone density / space-amp / fragment-count triggers), and event-based (post-reclaim queue drain). Compaction is never allowed to starve foreground writes; backpressure stalls writes when pending work exceeds a hard cap [^1][^9].

#### 3.8 Reclamation verification
Each compaction run records bytes_before, bytes_after, tombstones_dropped, versions_dropped, and fragments_merged into an append-only, hash-chained (SHA-256/BLAKE3) reclamation audit log with an ed25519-signed checkpoint [^24]. Verification recomputes the chain and confirms `reclaimed_bytes == bytes_before − bytes_after` and that no live/retained version was removed. Physical deletion of obsolete fragment files happens only after the signed checkpoint is durable.

---

### 4. Threat Model

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Reclaiming a retained/held/compliant record | Data durability / compliance | Hard veto via `ids-immutable` guard; hold/compliance unconditional; retention until `retain_until_date` |
| Resurrecting deleted data across replicas | Convergent deletion | Tombstone removal gated on MTRO/MCCO (all replicas compacted past) + `gc_grace_seconds` overlap |
| Removing a version visible to an open snapshot | Snapshot correctness | Oldest-snapshot pinning; versions ≤ any pinned read point are retained |
| Truncation / falsification of reclamation audit log | Audit integrity | SHA-256/BLAKE3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints; verification recomputes chain |
| Compaction crash leaving half-built fragments | Crash safety | Out-of-place copy-live-forward; atomic manifest swap; old files kept until new set durable |
| Unbounded compaction I/O stalling writes | Availability | Rate limits, backpressure (slowdown/stop thresholds), one fragment set at a time |
| Reclaim storm deleting too much too fast | Availability | Disposition gates (retain/review/purge/archive), grace days, per-cycle byte caps |
| Carrier re-framing / tampering of compaction metadata | Integrity of sweep decisions | Metadata signed over payload bytes; opaque `Endpoint` datagrams survive re-framing |

The carrier is never trusted: compaction decisions and reclamation proofs are signed over payload bytes, so they survive re-framing by any carrier.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **Eligibility score:** `score = reclaimable_bytes / rewrite_io_bytes` per fragment; inputs = tombstone density, obsolete-version ratio, expired TTL, snapshot-pin status, ids-immutable veto. Victim picked when score ≥ threshold and no veto.
- **Out-of-place compaction:** read live (non-shadowed, non-expired) records from N input fragments → merge-sort → write to M new fragment files → atomic manifest swap → old fragments marked obsolete → physical deletion after verification + no reader pin.
- **Obsolete version removal:** version `v` droppable iff `v < oldest_pinned_snapshot_read_point` and a newer visible version exists for the same key; tombstone `t` droppable iff `t` expired + `t` ≤ min(MCCO across replicas) + `gc_grace_seconds` elapsed.
- **Tombstone expiry trigger:** `tombstone_threshold` (default 0.2 tombstone density) × `tombstone_compaction_interval` (default 1 day) — ScyllaDB/Cassandra pattern.
- **Space amplification:** `space_amp = physical_bytes / logical_bytes`; compaction target reduces it toward 1.0.
- **Hash chain + signed checkpoint:** each reclamation record SHA-256/BLAKE3-chained to previous digest; periodic ed25519-signed checkpoint anchors; verification recomputes chain and confirms reclaimed-byte delta.
- **Backpressure:** slowdown threshold on pending compaction bytes; stop threshold halts new compaction jobs until pending work drains.

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-41.1 | Retained/held/compliant records never reclaimed | 100% of reclaim attempts on held/retention-active/compliance records rejected by ids-immutable veto |
| AC-41.2 | Tombstone removal only after expiry + grace + MTRO/MCCO | Zero premature tombstone removals under replica lag/partition (adversarial test) |
| AC-41.3 | Snapshot-pinned versions never removed | Versions ≤ any pinned snapshot read point retained across compaction runs |
| AC-41.4 | Reclamation verification detects byte-delta fraud | `reclaimed == before − after` verified; mismatches fail closed and are audit-logged |
| AC-41.5 | Audit chain integrity | 100% of single-record insert/delete/reorder in reclamation log detected; verification names offending entry |
| AC-41.6 | Space amplification reduced | Compaction run reduces `physical/logical` bytes; measured pre/post per fragment set |
| AC-41.7 | Out-of-place crash safety | Interrupted compaction leaves old fragments intact; recovery resumes or rolls back without data loss |
| AC-41.8 | Backpressure bounds | Writes stalled only when pending compaction bytes ≥ hard threshold; resume below slowdown threshold |
| AC-41.9 | Carrier-agnostic | Zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS; all traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` |
| AC-41.10 | Allowed crypto only | ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 appear in crypto surface; nothing else |

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Compaction granularity:** whole-fragment vs sub-fragment range compaction — trade-off between rewrite I/O and reclaim precision; unquantified for IDS fragment sizes.
2. **Tombstone grace window tuning:** `gc_grace_seconds` default (ScyllaDB 10 days) balances resurrection safety vs metadata bloat; IDS deployment-specific tuning needed.
3. **Compaction vs snapshot tension:** long-running snapshots pin versions and block reclamation, risking space exhaustion; snapshot lease/timeout policy undefined.
4. **Physical file deletion timing:** delete obsolete files immediately after commit vs deferred (reclaim-only-when-space-pressure) — affects write amplification during space crises.
5. **Cross-replica MTRO stall:** an unavailable replica stalls tombstone removal (correct but delays reclamation); operational eviction policy for dead replicas is out of scope.
6. **Compaction scheduling defaults:** time-based vs threshold-based vs event-based triggers; rate-limit and backpressure thresholds are placeholders pending measurement.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-reclaim` (not a subfolder) | User directive: separate crates instead of more folders; keeps reclamation concerns isolated |
| Out-of-place copy-live-forward compaction | Crash-safe; old fragments intact until atomic manifest swap; matches Sprite LFS / RocksDB / Iceberg patterns |
| Tombstone + obsolete version removal gated by snapshot pins | Prevents snapshot corruption and data resurrection; matches Iceberg `expire_snapshots` unreferenced-file rule |
| ids-immutable hard veto (retention/hold/compliance) | Guarantees compliance (SEC 17a-4 WORM) and legal-hold precedence over reclamation |
| MTRO/MCCO convergent tombstone removal | All replicas must compact past a tombstone before removal — prevents cross-replica resurrection (Kafka pattern) |
| Threshold-based compaction trigger (tombstone density 0.2, 1-day interval) | ScyllaDB/Cassandra proven pattern; simple and predictable |
| Hash-chained audit log + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Tamper-evident reclamation proof; offline verifiable; matches Phase 040 audit design |
| Only allowed crypto; carrier-agnostic `Endpoint` boundary | Complies with IDS carrier-agnostic and crypto allowlist rules |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 042 creates `ids-backup`, the IDS crate that owns recovery points and incremental backup histories. It provides point-in-time recovery: every backup is a complete, consistent, point-in-time snapshot (never a partial file copy), with a recovery-point history (full backup anchor + incremental deltas) that can be replayed to any point covered by the history. Restore verification confirms each recovery point is byte-identical and restorable before it is trusted. Backup copies are tracked separately from serving replicas — a backup copy is an independent, retention-protected copy that a compromised production node cannot alter or delete.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`; `CarrierType` ∈ {Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom}). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-backup` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-backup` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-backup/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types `RecordId` (`src/types.rs:262`), `SnapshotId` (`src/types.rs:1329`), `FragmentId` (`src/types.rs:1889`), `RecoveryProof` (`src/types.rs:1905`), `Checksum` (`src/types.rs:1975`), `RecoveryAction::RestoreRedundancy` (`src/types.rs:2455`), `OrderingPosSnapshot` (`src/types.rs:2355`), `IdsTime` (`src/types.rs:1069`), `CarrierType` (`src/types.rs:394`) — all referenced by this crate but never redefined. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned PostgreSQL continuous archiving / PITR (base backup + archived WAL replayed to any target time or named restore point; timeline IDs prevent WAL overwrite across recoveries)[^1][^2]; WAL archiving with off-site archive before segment recycling, `archive_timeout` bounding RPO on quiet systems[^2][^3]; Veeam / NAKIVO backup-chain models — forward incremental with periodic synthetic/active fulls as "chain breakers," forever-forward-incremental with synthetic-full merge, reverse-incremental (deprecated, incompatible with immutability)[^4][^5][^6]; synthetic full built from prior full + incrementals without reading the source again[^5]; chain fragility — one missing/corrupt incremental breaks the whole chain, requiring a new full backup[^29]; crash-consistent vs application-consistent snapshots (VSS writers flush pending I/O; crash-consistent = on-disk state as of power loss)[^18]; changed block tracking (CBT / Hyper-V Resilient Change Tracking) — bitmaps record changed blocks since a reference point so incrementals read only changed blocks; chain reset if tracking state is lost[^22][^23]; content-defined chunking (FastCDC / Rabin / Gear rolling hash; boundaries content-derived, so insertions shift only local boundaries; ~10–20% more dedup than fixed-size)[^20]; restic / Proxmox Backup / kit-msgvault repository models — content-addressed blobs, immutable append-only packs (~32 MB, sealed once, never modified), snapshot manifest written last (crash-safe), index rebuild from pack footers, prune+GC with grace period for concurrent writers[^24][^25][^26]; continuous data protection (CDP) — journal-based near-real-time change capture for near-zero RPO vs scheduled snapshots[^7]; RPO/RTO targets — RPO drives backup frequency, RTO drives recovery architecture; interval + run time ≤ RPO[^8]; immutable/air-gapped backup copies — logically air-gapped vaults, WORM, compliance vs governance mode, separate administrative boundary so compromised production identities cannot delete backups[^9][^10][^11]; restore verification / restore drills — automated periodic restore to isolated sandbox + checksum + data-usability assertions (AWS Well-Architected REL09-BP04, AWS Backup restore testing)[^13]; GFS grandfather-father-son tiered retention (weekly/monthly/yearly full backups as retention anchors)[^21]; backup checksums / pg_verifybackup — manifest-first verification: signature over canonical manifest proves digest authenticity, then per-artifact re-hash proves stored bytes still reproduce trusted digests; fail-closed on missing/invalid signature[^12][^13]; fsfreeze / LVM snapshot — filesystem freeze flushes dirty pages and journals for a consistent on-disk image before capture[^19]; differential vs incremental — incremental since last backup (smaller, slower restore chain) vs differential since last full (larger, faster restore)[^22].

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-backup` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a backup/recovery subsystem: it does not serve live traffic. It coordinates snapshot capture, incremental history, point-in-time replay, restore verification, and independent backup-copy tracking. Backup copies are tracked separately from serving replicas — a backup copy's lifecycle (retention, immutability, deletion) is governed by `ids-backup` alone, never by the replica that produced the source data.

│  ids-store, ids-snapshot, ids-replication — request backup/recovery ops      │
