```
│  │ recovery point  │ │ incremental     │ │ restore         │ │ backup copy│ │
│  │ catalog         │ │ history / chain │ │ verification    │ │ tracking   │ │
│  │ (snapshot meta, │ │ (full anchor +  │ │ (checksum, full   │ │ (independent│ │
│  │  captured ver.) │ │  deltas, PITR)  │ │  restore, proof)│ │  lifecycle)│ │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────┘ │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │
│  │ consistent      │ │ cloning /       │ │ point-in-time   │ │ catalog    │ │
│  │ capture (freeze │ │ delta compute   │ │ replay (full +  │ │ signing    │ │
│  │  + snapshot)    │ │  (CBT/diff)     │ │  deltas to T)   │ │ (ed25519)  │ │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┴─────────────────┴────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────┘
                                                                   │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▼──────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                  │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType≤1024B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload: &[u8])  │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                    │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a backup capture:**
1. A backup request (full or incremental) is submitted to `ids-backup`'s capture entrypoint with a target dataset/domain and a consistency mode (crash-consistent via on-disk freeze, or application-consistent via the source's own quiesce hook).
2. The consistent-capture module coordinates a point-in-time image: freeze writes (`fsfreeze`-style), take the snapshot, record the `SnapshotId` + `IdsTime`, thaw writes — all outside the carrier; the freeze window is bounded by a watchdog deadline.
3. The snapshot metadata (`RecoveryPoint`: id, parent chain, created_at, dataset, consistency level, byte size, checksum, delta-base reference) is written to the recovery-point catalog.
4. The incremental module computes the delta vs. the chosen base (full anchor for the first incremental; previous recovery point for chain incrementals): changed blocks via CBT-style dirty-tracking or content-defined-chunk diff; stores only changed content-addressed blobs, deduplicated by `Checksum` (BLAKE3/SHA-256).
5. Incremental backup history is appended (append-only chain: each recovery point references its parent, forming full-anchor → incremental → incremental …; periodic full backups break/anchor the chain).
6. Restore verification: on demand or schedule, materialize a recovery point to an isolated staging area, re-derive every referenced blob's `Checksum`, compare against the catalog, run integrity proof (`RecoveryProof`), and sign the verification result. Fail closed on any mismatch.
7. Backup copies are tracked independently: a backup copy is a retention-governed, immutability-protected replica of a recovery point stored separately from serving replicas; its retention/hold is managed by `ids-backup`, and a compromised production node cannot alter it.
8. All cross-node backup metadata travels as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-backup` never touches a carrier directly.

**Recovery point model:**
- A recovery point is a complete point-in-time image referenced by a single `SnapshotId`.
- `captured_versions`: each recovery point records the versions of every captured object at that instant (per-object `Checksum` + version), enabling consistent reads of "the state as of T."
- Cloning: a recovery point can be cloned (materialized to a new dataset/domain) without mutating the source; clone inherits read-only protection.

**Point-in-time recovery:** given a target `IdsTime` or named restore point, select the latest full anchor ≤ T, then replay all incrementals in chain order up to T; the result is the dataset state at T. Restore verification runs before the result is handed to a consumer.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Recovery points & snapshot metadata (consistent capture, point-in-time image)

A recovery point is the unit of backup: a complete, consistent image of a dataset at one instant, identified by `SnapshotId` (`[u8; 16]`) and stamped with `IdsTime` (monotonic, from `ids-000-aa` — never wall clock for correctness decisions). Snapshot metadata records: snapshot id, parent snapshot id (chain link), created_at, dataset/domain id, consistency level (crash-consistent / application-consistent), byte size, root `Checksum`, delta-base reference (full anchor or previous recovery point), capture duration, bytes added, and the set of captured object versions (`captured_versions`: object id → `Checksum` at capture time).

Consistency tiers mirror the filesystem-consistency research[^19][^18]:
- **Crash-consistent:** capture the on-disk image as it exists at the instant; equivalent to "power loss at this moment." Journaled filesystems replay cleanly on mount. Zero cooperation needed from the source.
- **Filesystem-consistent:** freeze the filesystem (`fsfreeze`/`FIFREEZE` — flush dirty pages, commit journal, block new writes), take the image, thaw. Bounded freeze window guarded by a watchdog deadline (arm thaw deadline before freezing).
- **Application-consistent:** the source's own quiesce protocol flushes application in-memory/pending state to disk before the filesystem freeze (e.g. a DB `CHECKPOINT`); only the application knows its own invariants hold. This is the top tier and the one `ids-backup` targets for production datasets where available.

A snapshot is not a backup by itself unless the resulting copy has failure independence, retention protection, access separation, monitoring, and a tested restore path[^10]. `ids-backup` adds all of those around the snapshot.

#### 3.2 Incremental backup history (full anchor + delta chain)

Incremental backups copy only data changed since the previous backup of any type (full or incremental)[^22]. The chain is: one full backup anchor + N incrementals, each incremental referencing its immediate predecessor as delta base. To restore point T: materialize the full anchor, then replay incrementals in chain order up to T.

Two delta-compute strategies:
- **CBT-style dirty tracking** (Changed Block Tracking / Hyper-V RCT): a change tracker records which blocks were written since the last snapshot reference point; the incremental reads only those blocks[^22][^23]. The tracker state is tied to a reference point/snapshot generation; if tracking state is lost (reset/crash), the chain is invalid and a new full backup is required — matching the Veeam "broken backup chain" rule[^29].
- **Content-defined chunk diff** (FastCDC / Rabin/Gear rolling hash): split the dataset into content-defined chunks, hash each with BLAKE3/SHA-256, and compare the chunk set against the previous recovery point's chunk index; only new chunks are stored[^20][^24]. Insertions/deletions shift only local chunk boundaries, so most chunks are reused across versions (~10–20% better dedup than fixed-size chunking)[^20].

Full backups are taken periodically as chain anchors ("synthetic full" built from the prior full + incrementals without re-reading the source, or "active full" re-reading everything)[^5][^6]. A synthetic full breaks the old chain and starts a new anchor, which bounds replay length and limits blast radius from one corrupt incremental. Chain fragility is the central risk: one missing/corrupt incremental makes every incremental after it unusable[^29]; `ids-backup` mitigates with periodic synthetic/active fulls (chain breakers) and per-recovery-point checksums.

Incremental vs differential (research distinction, for the policy engine): differential copies everything since the last full (larger each run, faster restore — only full + last differential); incremental copies since the last backup (smaller each run, slower restore — full + all incrementals)[^22]. `ids-backup` defaults to incremental-with-periodic-full-anchors (the Veeam/NAKIVO dominant model)[^5][^6].

#### 3.3 Point-in-time recovery (PITR) & replay to arbitrary T

PITR combines a base backup with a continuous change stream replayed to any target[^1][^2][^3]. In `ids-backup`, the "base backup" is the latest full anchor ≤ target T, and the "change stream" is the ordered incremental history. Recovery target can be an `IdsTime`, a named restore point (created proactively before risky operations — Oracle "guaranteed restore point" / PostgreSQL `pg_create_restore_point` pattern[^27][^28]), or a chain position (recovery-point index).

Recovery semantics:
- `recovery_target_inclusive` style: stop before or at the target transaction; for safety, default to stopping before a named bad event[^28].
- Pause-and-verify: recover to a staging area, verify, then promote — never recover in place over production without verification[^28].
- Timeline handling: after a recovery completes and a new branch is written, a new timeline id prevents the new WAL/change stream from overwriting the old one (PostgreSQL timeline model)[^1] — `ids-backup` records a timeline/branch id per recovery branch so divergent histories never collide.

RPO/RTO: RPO (max data loss, looks backward) drives backup frequency; RTO (max downtime, looks forward) drives restore architecture[^8][^27]. The backup interval must be shorter than the RPO with margin for failed jobs (interval + run time ≤ RPO)[^8]. CDP (journal-based near-real-time capture) achieves near-zero RPO but higher cost; scheduled snapshots are cheaper with coarser RPO[^7][^8]. `ids-backup` supports both: scheduled incremental snapshots for the default tier, and CDP-style continuous journal capture for near-zero-RPO datasets.

#### 3.4 Backup copies tracked separately from serving replicas

A backup copy is an independent copy of a recovery point whose lifecycle is governed by `ids-backup`, not by the serving replica that produced it[^9][^10]. This is the ransomware-resilience pattern: two independent copies (primary operational + secondary isolated), separate administrative boundaries, immutability (WORM/compliance mode) so a compromised production identity cannot delete or shorten retention[^9][^11]. The backup copy is stored at a separate endpoint (reached via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`), retention-locked, and access-separated from production administration.

Key distinction: replication/snapshots/versioning/PITR alone are not backups unless the copy is failure-independent, retention-protected, access-separated, monitored, and has a tested restore path[^10]. `ids-backup` enforces this by treating each backup copy as a first-class tracked object with its own retention policy, immutability flag, and restore-test record.

#### 3.5 Consistent reads & captured versions

Each recovery point records `captured_versions`: for every object in the dataset, the object id and its `Checksum` at capture time. A consistent read against recovery point R returns exactly the object versions recorded in R — a read-only, point-in-time view. This is MVCC-style snapshot isolation applied to backups: the reader sees a stable picture as of the snapshot instant, unaffected by concurrent writes[^17][^16]. `captured_versions` also enables restore verification: every referenced blob's checksum is re-derived and compared.

#### 3.6 Cloning

Cloning materializes a recovery point to a new dataset/domain as a read-only copy. The clone is a full instantiation of the point-in-time image (all captured versions materialized), independent of the source. It inherits read-only protection and can be used for restore drills, forensics, or branching without mutating the backup. Clone cost is proportional to the data materialized; incremental clones (copy-on-write references to unchanged chunks) are an optimization.

#### 3.7 Restore verification

Restore verification proves a backup is usable, not merely present[^12][^13]. Layers:
1. **Checksum/manifest gate:** Ed25519 signature over the canonical recovery-point manifest proves the digest list is authentic; fail-closed on missing/invalid signature[^12][^13].
2. **Per-artifact re-hash:** every referenced blob is read and its `Checksum` re-derived; mismatch → reject[^12][^13][^30].
3. **Full decompression / structural check:** archives must be complete (end markers present), not truncated[^12].
4. **Staging restore drill:** materialize the recovery point to an isolated environment and run data-usability assertions (row counts, recent timestamps, integrity check)[^13][^28].
5. **Signed verification receipt:** ed25519-signed receipt listing every restored object with counts (names/counts only, never row data), hash-chained to the previous receipt[^12].

Verification runs on a schedule (daily/weekly for critical recovery points, within retention windows) and after every backup copy creation[^13]. A backup that hasn't been restored is unverified.

#### 3.8 Retention, immutability & GFS tiered retention

Recovery points carry retention (retain-until-date, extendable-only) and optional legal hold (indefinite, overrides retention, explicit release)[^1][^9][^21]. GFS (grandfather-father-son) tiered retention keeps weekly/monthly/yearly full backups as long-term anchors, breaking chains and bounding replay length[^21]. Immutable/air-gapped backup copies use WORM (compliance mode: no override, not even root; governance mode: override with elevated privileges)[^9][^11]. Retention expiry leads to disposition (retain/review/purge/archive) via the `ids-reclaim`-compatible expiry sweep, never silent deletion[^21].

#### 3.9 Cryptographic commitment & allowed primitives only

- ed25519: signs recovery-point manifests, verification receipts, backup-copy commitments (origin authentication, non-repudiation).
- sha256 / blake3: object `Checksum`s, content-addressed blob IDs, chunk indexes, manifest digests, receipt chains.
- xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305: encrypt backup payloads at rest when confidentiality required (per-chunk AEAD with counter-bound nonces to prevent reorder/truncation)[^14][^15].
No SHA-3, no post-quantum primitives, per the allowed-crypto rule. Manifests are deterministically canonicalized (sorted keys, compact separators, UTF-8 — RFC 8785 subset) before signing so verification is byte-stable across implementations[^12][^30].

---

### Threat Model

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Corrupt or truncated backup mistaken for valid | Recoverability | Manifest signature gate first, then per-blob checksum re-derive; full restore drill with data-usability assertions; fail closed on any mismatch |
| Missing/corrupt incremental breaks chain | Chain integrity | Periodic synthetic/active fulls as chain anchors; per-recovery-point checksums; refuse restore if chain links missing |
| Unauthorized modification/deletion of a backup copy | Backup integrity | Backup copy tracked separately from serving replica; retention + immutability (WORM/compliance mode) governed by ids-backup; separate administrative boundary |
| Ransomware / compromised production deletes backups | Recoverability | Isolated/air-gapped backup copy; immutability lock; separate credentials; no production path to backup deletion |
| Recovery to wrong point / bad transaction included | PITR correctness | Named restore points created proactively; stop-before-target default; pause-and-verify before promote; timeline ids prevent branch collision |
| Replay of stale recovery point | Freshness | SnapshotId is content-derived over manifest; IdsTime monotonic; timeline/branch ids; signed verification receipts hash-chained |
| Clock manipulation to skew recovery-point ordering | Ordering correctness | IdsTime monotonic (not wall clock); SnapshotId content-derived; chain order verified on restore |
| Backup copy reachable from production network | Isolation | Separate endpoint via ids-carrier::Endpoint; separate admin credentials; logically/physically isolated copy |
| Signing-key compromise | Authenticity of proofs | Signed key-rotation handoff; old public keys retained forever for verifying old receipts/manifests |
| Silent data corruption (bit rot) | Backup integrity | Periodic full verification re-reads every referenced blob and re-derives its checksum |

The carrier is never trusted: backup metadata is signed over payload bytes, so it survives re-framing by any carrier, and the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signatures, content hashes, encryption for `ids-backup` |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (backup source) | Provides consistent reads, `captured_versions`, freeze/quiesce hooks for capture |
| `ids-snapshot` (Phase 026) | Distributed snapshots (Chandy-Lamport) | Reuses snapshot coordination primitives; `ids-backup` recovery points are longer-lived, retention-governed snapshots |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization | Backup copies go to separate endpoints; replication-independent tracking |
| `ids-reclaim` (Phase 041) | Fragment compaction & space reclamation | Cannot reclaim retained/held recovery points; expiry-sweep output feeds reclamation eligibility |
| `ids-immutable` (Phase 040) | Immutable record protection / WORM / legal hold | Backup copies reuse retention/hold enforcement; compliance-mode WORM for immutable backup copies |
| `ids-integrity` (Phase 030) | End-to-end checksums, Merkle trees, scrubbing | Reuses `Checksum`/Merkle primitives for per-blob verification and catalog integrity |

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **RecoveryPoint**: `{SnapshotId, parent_id, created_at (IdsTime), dataset_id, consistency_level, byte_size, root Checksum, delta_base (full anchor or prior RecoveryPoint), captured_versions: Map<ObjectId, Checksum>, duration, bytes_added, timeline_id}`. SnapshotId is content-derived (SHA-256 over canonical manifest with id blanked) so identical content at the same second yields the same ID; any change changes it.
- **Chain (full anchor + incrementals)**: `Chain = FullAnchor × Incremental*`; each Incremental references its parent; chain validity = every link present and checksummed; a missing link breaks the chain (require new full anchor).
- **Delta compute**: CBT dirty-block map since last reference point OR content-defined-chunk diff vs. previous recovery point's chunk index; store only new chunks, dedup by `Checksum` (BLAKE3/SHA-256).
- **Point-in-time replay**: `recover(T) = materialize(full_anchor ≤ T) then replay incrementals in chain order up to T`; stop-before-target default; timeline id per recovery branch prevents branch collision.
- **Consistent capture**: freeze (watchdog-guarded deadline) → snapshot image → record `captured_versions` → thaw; consistency level recorded per recovery point.
- **Restore verification**: Ed25519 signature over canonical manifest → per-blob `Checksum` re-derive → structural/decompression check → staging restore drill with data-usability assertions → ed25519-signed receipt hash-chained to prior receipt.
- **Backup copy**: independent lifecycle; retention + hold governed by `ids-backup`; stored at separate `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; immutability via WORM/compliance mode.
- **Retention/hold**: retain-until-date monotonic (extendable only); legal hold indefinite, checked first, short-circuits every disposition, explicit release only; GFS weekly/monthly/yearly anchors.

---

### 8. Dependencies

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`SnapshotId`, `RecordId`, `FragmentId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Checksum`, `RecoveryAction`, `OrderingPosSnapshot`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait for opaque datagram transport only.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `serde` — serialization of recovery points, manifests, verification receipts.
No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list.

---

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

1. Every recovery point is a complete, consistent point-in-time image (not a partial file copy); verified by full restore drill byte-identity against source at capture instant.
2. Incremental backup history forms a valid chain: full anchor + ordered incrementals, every link checksummed; restore to any chain position T succeeds iff all links ≤ T present.
3. Point-in-time recovery to a named restore point or `IdsTime` reproduces the dataset state at T; default stop-before-target; pause-and-verify before promote.
4. Restore verification catches 100% of single-blob corruption/truncation; manifest signature gate fails closed on missing/invalid Ed25519 signature.
5. Backup copy tracked independently of serving replica: a compromised production node cannot alter/delete a backup copy; retention + WORM/compliance-mode immutability enforced.
6. Active legal hold blocks 100% of backup-copy modify/delete attempts regardless of retention state; release is the only clearing path and is audited.
7. Retention extendable-only, never shortened; locked retention irreversible for the period.
8. All backup/copy/disposition/verification events recorded in append-only catalog with actor + `IdsTime`; catalog entries content-addressed by `Checksum`.
9. All backup metadata carried as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS in the crate.
10. Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 appear in the crate's crypto surface.
11. Periodic synthetic/active fulls bound replay length; chain broken by one missing incremental → restore refuses, requires new full anchor.
12. Recovery-point catalog verifiable offline: re-derive every referenced blob's checksum and compare against catalog.

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- Consistency mode default: crash-consistent (zero cooperation) vs application-consistent (requires source quiesce hook) for each dataset; application-consistent is stronger but not always available.
- CBT dirty-tracking vs content-defined-chunk diff: CBT needs source-side tracking state (chain breaks if lost); CDC is source-agnostic but higher CPU; choose per dataset or hybrid.
- SnapshotId content-derived vs ULID/time-based: content-derived resists forgery but recompute cost on load; time-based gives lexicographic=chronological order (kit-msgvault pattern).
- Synthetic full frequency: bounds replay length but costs CPU/storage; tunable parameter to be validated at integration.
- Interaction with Phase 041 `ids-reclaim`: expiry sweep must not reclaim retained/held recovery points; exact guard-reclaim handshake (eligibility proof) defined here, validated at integration.
- Backup-copy isolation level: logical (separate endpoint/credentials) vs physical (separate site/account); operational decision, not a research conclusion.
- CDP-style continuous journal capture for near-zero-RPO datasets: journal format, truncation, and interplay with incremental snapshots undefined; out of scope for MVP.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-backup` (not a folder inside an existing crate) | User directive: separate crates for new capabilities; keeps existing crates focused |
| Full anchor + incremental chain with periodic synthetic/active fulls | Bounds replay length, limits blast radius from one corrupt incremental (Veeam/NAKIVO dominant model)[^5][^6] |
| Recovery point = complete point-in-time image, content-addressed `SnapshotId` | Every backup restorable on its own; content-derived ID resists forgery/renaming |
| Incremental = changed data since last backup (CBT or CDC diff) | Minimizes backup size/bandwidth; CBT needs tracking state, CDC is source-agnostic |
| PITR = full anchor ≤ T + replay incrementals in chain order, stop-before-target | Standard PITR pattern (PostgreSQL/Oracle); safe default prevents bad-transaction inclusion |
| Restore verification: manifest signature first, then per-blob re-hash, then staging drill | Signature proves digest authenticity before trusting digests; drill proves usability[^12][^13] |
| Backup copy independent of serving replica, retention-governed by ids-backup | Ransomware resilience: compromised production cannot delete backups[^9][^10] |
| Retention extendable-only; legal hold indefinite, overrides retention; GFS anchors | Mirrors WORM/immutable-backup practice; hold precedence (Microsoft 365/Box principle)[^1][^9][^21] |
| IdsTime monotonic, never wall clock, for correctness decisions | Prevents clock-manipulation early expiry; absolute deadlines need network clock (out of scope) |
| Only allowed crypto; carrier-agnostic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Non-negotiable HX-241 / IDS constraints |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 043 creates `ids-chaos`, the IDS crate that owns controlled fault injection for resilience validation. It provides a fault injection harness covering packet loss/reordering/duplication, network corruption, partition injection, node churn, resource exhaustion, Byzantine behavior simulation, chaos experiment execution, and resilience metrics collection. The crate is a **resilience-validation harness**, not a runtime fault injector for production: it injects faults into controlled test scenarios (benchmarks, conformance runs, soak tests, chaos game days) and collects metrics so IDS maintainers can verify the system degrades gracefully rather than fails catastrophically.

`ids-chaos` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). All injected-fault traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`; `CarrierType` ∈ {Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom}). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; consumed via type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-chaos` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-chaos/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `RecordId`, `FragmentId`, `SnapshotId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Checksum`, `AnomalyType` ∈ {ByteMismatch, ReplicaDrift, ChecksumFailure, StateCorruption}, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `Endpoint` — all referenced by this crate but never redefined. `ids-000-aa` also holds placeholder `src/chaos/` and `src/fault/` directories (empty) and a sealed `FaultTolerance` contract (`src/contracts/fault.rs`) — referenced, never redefined here.

controller-manager + chaos-daemon + sidecar architecture); LitmusChaos (CNCF chaos project, Operator + CRDs: ChaosEngine/ChaosExperiment/ChaosResult/ChaosSchedule/Workflow; ChaosCenter UI); Pumba (Docker/containerd/Podman network chaos via Linux netem/iptables: delay, loss, duplicate, corrupt, rate limiting; marker/stateful loss via 4-state Markov model); Toxiproxy (TCP proxy with "toxics": latency, bandwidth, timeout, reset_peer, slo; HTTP control API; deterministic-by-default for CI); s3chaos (RustFS fault injection + recovery verification: disk I/O errors, network partitions, pod kills, resource stress, quorum loss; smoke/chaos/DM scenario suites; artifact run roots); chaos-engineering-rs (cross-platform Rust CLI/library for fault injection; injector/target/schedule/duration/SLO/target-count/parallelism/blast-radius policy bounded); ### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-chaos` is layered so each fault class is an independent module behind a single experiment orchestrator. It is a **guard-and-injector** layer: experiments declare a fault scenario, the harness validates blast-radius policy, injects the fault at the carrier/Endpoint boundary or into a subsystem seam, runs the scenario, observes metrics, then rolls the fault back. `ids-chaos` does not store records itself; it wraps or intercepts datagrams flowing to/from `ids-carrier::Endpoint` and injects faults into copies, never mutating production state without an explicit, bounded experiment scope.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    EXPERIMENT DRIVER (ids-testing, ids-bench, soak runs)     │
│  Declares scenario: fault type, target endpoint/node, rate, duration, scope │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                 Phase 043: ids-chaos (THIS CRATE — harness layer)            │
│  ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ││
│  │ fault injector │ │ experiment     │ │ blast radius   │ │ resilience   │ ││
│  │ (loss/reorder/ │ │ executor       │ │ policy (scope, │ │ metrics      │ ││
│  │  dup/corrupt/  │ │ (setup→inject→ │ │  rate, duration│ │ collector    │ ││
│  │  partition/    │ │  observe→rollback)│ │  max blasts)   │ │ (latency/    │ ││
│  │  churn/exhaust│ │                │ │                │ │  error/      │ ││
│  │  /byzantine)   │ │                │ │                │ │  recovery)   │ ││
│  └────────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘ ││
│  ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ││
│  │ deterministic  │ │ rollback/      │ │ carrier        │ │ audit log    │ ││
│  │ replay (seed)  │ │ recovery       │ │ adapter        │ │ (signed)     │ ││
│  │                │ │ (restore state)│ │ (Endpoint only)│ │              │ ││
│  └────────────────┴────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘ ││
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬───────────┘
                                                                   │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▼────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                  │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType ≤ 1024 B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload)      │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                    │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a chaos experiment:** (1) Driver submits a `ChaosScenario` (fault type, target `Endpoint`, rate, duration, blast-radius budget, seed) to the experiment executor. (2) The executor checks blast-radius policy (max concurrent blasts, max targets, duration ceiling, excluded endpoints) before any injection. (3) The fault injector wraps the carrier adapter: outbound/inbound `Vec<u8>` datagrams to the target `Endpoint` pass through fault primitives (loss, reorder, duplicate, corrupt, partition, delay) or subsystem seams (node churn: pause/resume a node; resource exhaustion: memory/CPU/disk pressure via stress-ng-style stressors; Byzantine: equivocation, message rewriting, withholding). (4) Resilience metrics collector records latency, error rate, recovery time, and whether steady-state invariants held during injection. (5) On experiment end (or abort via stop condition), rollback restores all fault state; the fault log is sealed with an ed25519 signature and hash-chained. (6) All traffic remains opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-chaos` never touches a carrier directly.

**Fault classes:**
- **Packet loss** — Bernoulli or 4-state Markov (bursty) drop of datagrams to a target `Endpoint`; independent egress/ingress control.
- **Packet reordering** — hold-back buffer releases datagrams out of order within a reorder window.
- **Packet duplication** — deliver a datagram N times (1 ≤ N ≤ cap).
- **Network corruption** — bit-flip / byte overwrite / checksum-invalid payloads (BLAKE3/SHA-256 mismatch detectable by `ids-integrity`).
- **Partition injection** — drop all datagrams between a node/endpoint set and the rest (simulated link failure).
- **Node churn** — pause/resume a node (simulated crash/reboot), add/remove endpoints from membership view.
- **Resource exhaustion** — CPU starvation, memory pressure, disk-full, file-descriptor exhaustion (stress-ng-style stressors, no real hardware damage).
- **Byzantine behavior simulation** — equivocation (two conflicting messages at same position), message rewriting, message withholding, replay of old datagrams.
- **Latency injection** — bounded delay on datagrams (fixed + jitter), simulating long RTT / link degradation.
- **Experiment lifecycle** — setup → inject → observe → rollback, each phase audited; stop conditions (SLO breach) auto-abort and roll back.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Fault injection harness design (what/where/when/how)

Fault injection answers four questions per experiment: **what** fault model (loss, reorder, duplicate, corrupt, partition, churn, exhaustion, Byzantine), **where** to inject (which `Endpoint`/node/subsystem seam), **when** to activate (rate, duration, schedule, trigger condition), and **how** to observe/rollback (metrics collection, stop conditions, state restoration). The IEEE model-based framework (A Model Based Framework for Specifying and Executing Fault Injection Experiments, 5261017) structures experiments around these four axes; `ids-chaos` adopts them verbatim as its scenario schema. Every scenario carries a seed for deterministic replay (s3chaos smoke/chaos/DM suites; malcolm seeded replay; dsh-tool-chaos seeded, replayable, dry-run-by-default), so a failure that appears under seed S replays bit-for-bit until fixed. The injector runs in a separate process/thread boundary from the system under test (boundedcontext chaos-testing practice) so a crashing injector cannot corrupt the target.

#### 3.2 Packet loss / reordering / duplication (network fault primitives)

Gremlin's Packet Loss experiment drops a percentage of packets (or corrupts them) targeted by host/port, with correlation for burstiness; Chaos Mesh `network-loss` / `network-duplication` / `network-delay` / `network-corrupt` / `network-partition` operate per-pod via CRDs; Pumba `netem` manipulates outgoing traffic with Linux `tc` (delay, loss, corruption, duplication, rate limiting) and `iptables` for incoming, including 4-state Markov loss (burst/gap states). `ids-chaos` expresses the same primitives over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams: a fault layer intercepts `send_datagram`/`receive_datagram` and applies Bernoulli/Markov loss, reorder-window buffering, duplication count, and bit-flip corruption. No `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP — only opaque `Vec<u8>` to `Endpoint`.

#### 3.3 Network corruption (bit flip, byte overwrite, checksum mismatch)

`ids-chaos` corruption faults flip bits or overwrite bytes in datagram payloads (probability p per byte, or targeted offset range). Because payloads are content-addressed (`Checksum` in `ids-000-aa` over BLAKE3/SHA-256) and `ids-integrity` runs end-to-end checksums/Merkle scrubbing, corrupted datagrams are detectable on receipt; the chaos harness measures whether the receiver detects, discards, and recovers from corruption without cascading failure. This mirrors Prooflog / ATL right-to-erasure patterns (payload may be unreadable but hash/tombstone remain) and the ixdp bitflip fault-injection tool (single-bit flip at random payload position).

#### 3.4 Partition injection (simulated link / node failure)

Partition injection drops all datagrams between a set of endpoints and the rest of the system for the experiment duration, simulating network partition or node isolation. Chaos Mesh `network-partition` blocks 100% ingress/egress via network policy; Jepsen nemeses cut networks into halves or isolate random nodes. In `ids-chaos`, a partition fault wraps the carrier adapter for the target `Endpoint` set and drops datagrams in both directions; the harness observes whether the partitioned side degrades gracefully (local reads/writes where policy permits) and whether healing (partition removal) triggers convergence without divergence or zombie resurrection. Regional isolation (IDS §18.3) is the production analogue.

#### 3.5 Node churn (pause/resume, add/remove endpoints)

Node churn simulates nodes joining, pausing (crash), resuming (reboot), or leaving the cluster. ACM "Minimizing churn in distributed systems" (1159913.1159931) studies churn cost (dropped messages, inconsistency, bandwidth); `ids-chaos` models churn as endpoint lifecycle events: `pause(endpoint)` drops all traffic and freezes processing; `resume(endpoint)` restarts it; `add/remove(endpoint)` changes the membership view seen by `ids-membership`/`ids-discovery`. The harness measures recovery: missed updates, replayed operations, reconvergence. `ids-failure-detector` (SWIM/phi accrual) suspicion states are the natural observation target.

#### 3.6 Resource exhaustion (CPU, memory, disk, file descriptors)

Resource exhaustion simulates running out of a physical subsystem: CPU saturation, memory pressure (OOM), disk-full, fd exhaustion. stress-ng provides 220 stressors (CPU, VM, IO, FS, scheduler); the Resilium Labs chaos newsletter documents memory/CPU/disk exhaustion as common, easy injections that simulate denial-of-service locally. `ids-chaos` implements bounded resource-pressure faults (no real hardware damage; bounded duration; rollback restores resources) and observes graceful degradation: backpressure (`ids-backpressure`), circuit breakers (`ids-circuit-breaker`), bulkheads (`ids-bulkhead`), load shedding. The exhaust fault is scoped to one node/endpoint and bounded by blast-radius policy.

#### 3.7 Byzantine behavior simulation (equivocation, rewriting, withholding)

Byzantine faults model malicious or arbitrary-failure nodes: equivocation (same sender, same position, conflicting content), message rewriting (field-level tampering), message withholding (drop selective datagrams), local-computation replacement. QUANTAS 2 provides explicit fault strategies attachable to peers via programmable hooks (direct unicast, multicast, receive, local computation); ByzzBench controls nondeterminism in concurrency/network/process faults for BFT testing; Kleppmann's "Making CRDTs Byzantine fault tolerant" (PaPoC '22) shows convergence needs deterministic validation predicates under Byzantine participants. `ids-chaos` simulates Byzantine endpoints at the `ids-carrier::Endpoint` boundary (opaque datagrams can be rewritten/dropped/duplicated by the injector) and measures whether `ids-byzantine`/`ids-authenticated-broadcast` (ed25519-signed, Dolev-Strong) contain the damage. Byzantine simulation here is strictly test-harness scope — no production Byzantine node behavior.

#### 3.8 Chaos experiment execution (lifecycle, stop conditions, rollback)

An experiment follows the chaos-engineering scientific method (AWS/Azure/Harness principles): identify steady state + SLOs; hypothesize; inject controlled failure with minimal blast radius; validate whether steady state holds. Harness (Chaos Studio / Harness) structures experiments as faults + probes + actions, with a resilience score (fault weight × probe success %). Gremlin provides automatic halt and rollback when metrics exceed SLIs/SLOs; Chaos Mesh rolls back injected faults on experiment end/abort. `ids-chaos` adopts: scenario = fault(s) + probes (steady-state checks) + stop conditions (SLO breach auto-aborts, rolls back); executor runs setup → inject → observe → rollback; every phase is audited and sealed. Rollback restores datagram paths, node state, and resource pressure to pre-experiment.

#### 3.9 Resilience metrics collection (latency, error rate, recovery, steady-state)

Metrics quantify resilience: operation latency (p50/p95/p99) during fault, error rate, recovery time (MTTR — mean time to recovery), steady-state violation count, throughput under fault, bytes lost/duplicated/corrupted, partition healing time. AWS FIS integrates with CloudWatch alarms; Chaos Mesh exposes experiment status/results via dashboard; s3chaos records run artifacts (qualification-plan.json, qualification-result.json, validation-summary.tsv, logs, health observations). `ids-chaos` writes a resilience metrics record per experiment run: fault type, target, rate, duration, seed, start/end `IdsTime`, SLOs, probes passed/failed, recovery time, steady-state violations, and a sealed ed25519-signed audit entry. These feed `ids-observability` (Phase 044) and `ids-bench` (Phase 048) dashboards.

#### 3.10 Deterministic replay and fault distribution (seeded, power-law/Pareto, Lyapunov)

Reproducibility is non-negotiable: every experiment uses a seed so the exact fault sequence replays (madsim/moonpool deterministic simulation; malcolm seeded deterministic replay; faultkit count-based triggers). Fault timing can follow power-law/Pareto distributions (real-world failures are bursty, not Poisson — malcolm) and Lyapunov sensitivity scoring ranks which faults most destabilize the system (guide experiment prioritization). SequenceFI shows temporal guards derived from traces prevent premature/multiple injections. `ids-chaos` scenarios are seeded, replayable, dry-run-capable by default (dsh-tool-chaos pattern), with optional probabilistic distributions for soak runs.

---

### Threat Model

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|
| Chaos experiment harms production system | Availability / data integrity | Blast-radius policy (max targets, rate, duration, excluded endpoints); dry-run by default; stop conditions auto-abort + rollback; injector isolated from target |
| Injector itself crashes / hangs | Test harness reliability | Separate process/thread boundary; watchdog timeout on inject phase; rollback on injector exit |
| Fault state leaks after experiment | Residual degradation | Rollback restores datagram paths/node state/resource pressure; sealed audit log proves restoration |
| Non-deterministic faults hide bugs | Reproducibility | Seeded RNG; deterministic replay bit-for-bit; dry-run mode reveals exact injection plan before execution |
| Overly aggressive exhaustion faults | Hardware/OS stress | Bounded duration; no real hardware damage; scoped to one endpoint; stress-ng-style stressors capped |
| Byzantine simulation mistaken for production behavior | Trust model confusion | Clearly test-harness scope only; Byzantine faults never enabled outside experiment; `ids-byzantine` is the production counterpart |
| Metrics collection overhead skews results | Measurement fidelity | Lightweight probes; metrics sampled, not traced per-datagram by default; overhead budget per experiment |
| Carrier bypass (faults not applied to all paths) | Coverage gap | All carrier-agnostic traffic funnels through `ids-carrier::Endpoint` adapter; fault layer sits at the adapter boundary; audit proves which paths were faulted |

The carrier is never trusted: injected faults are applied to opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams at the `ids-carrier::Endpoint` boundary, so they survive any carrier re-framing, and the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the fault-injection trust base.

```
    policy.rs                   # blast-radius policy (max targets, rate, duration, excluded endpoints)
    injector.rs                 # fault injection entrypoint, dispatches to fault modules
    faults/
      mod.rs

      reorder.rs                # packet reordering buffer

      partition.rs              # endpoint set partition (drop both directions)
      churn.rs                  # node pause/resume/add/remove

    audit.rs                    # sealed audit log (hash chain + ed25519 signature) per experiment

    contracts/                  # sealed trait contracts mirroring ids-000-aa style (~10 files)
      injector_contract.rs, scenario_contract.rs, policy_contract.rs, metrics_contract.rs,

      carrier_adapter_contract.rs, mod.rs
    invariants/                 # compile-time/runtime invariants (~8 files)
      blast_radius_bounded.rs, dry_run_by_default.rs, rollback_restores.rs, seed_determinism.rs,
```

Total: ~90–1000 files across `src/`, `src/faults/`, `src/metrics/`, `src/contracts/`, `src/invariants/`, `tests/`, `benches/`, `docs/`, each concern a separate file — consistent with the "separate crates instead of more folders" directive applied intra-crate as separate modules/files. No stubs: every fault module has policy, injection, and rollback logic plus tests.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **ChaosScenario** = { fault: FaultType, target: Endpoint, rate: f64, duration: IdsTime, seed: u64, blast_radius: BlastRadius, stop_conditions: Vec<StopCondition>, probes: Vec<Probe> }
- **BlastRadius** = { max_targets: u64, max_rate: f64, max_duration: IdsTime, excluded_endpoints: Vec<Endpoint>, dry_run: bool }
- **FaultType** ∈ {Loss, Reorder, Duplicate, Corrupt, Partition, Churn, Exhaustion, Byzantine, Latency}
- **Loss algorithm:** Bernoulli drop with probability p; optional 4-state Markov (receive / burst-receive / burst-loss / gap-loss) for bursty loss; correlation parameter.
- **Reorder algorithm:** hold-back buffer; release datagrams out of order within window W; sequence by arrival index.
- **Duplicate algorithm:** deliver datagram N times (1 ≤ N ≤ cap); independent per-datagram probability.
- **Corrupt algorithm:** bit-flip at random payload position with probability p per byte; optional targeted offset range; detectable via `Checksum` (BLAKE3/SHA-256) mismatch.
- **Partition algorithm:** drop all datagrams (both directions) between endpoint set S and complement; duration-bounded; auto-heal on experiment end.
- **Churn algorithm:** pause(endpoint) freezes processing + drops traffic; resume(endpoint) restarts; add/remove changes membership view.
- **Exhaustion algorithm:** bounded CPU/memory/disk/fd pressure via in-process stressors; duration capped; rollback releases pressure.
- **Byzantine algorithm:** equivocation (two conflicting datagrams at same position), rewrite (field tampering), withhold (selective drop), replay (re-send old datagram).
- **Latency algorithm:** fixed delay + jitter per datagram; bounded so experiments terminate.
- **Executor:** setup (capture baseline + dry-run reveal) → inject (activate fault layer at carrier adapter) → observe (collect metrics, check stop conditions each tick) → rollback (restore all fault state; seal audit).
- **Replay:** seed → PRNG → deterministic fault sequence; bit-for-bit reproducible.
- **Audit:** hash-chained log of experiment phases; ed25519-signed seal on completion/abort.

### 8. Dependencies

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `RecordId`, `FragmentId`, `SnapshotId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Checksum`, `AnomalyType`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `Endpoint`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts (`FaultTolerance`, `Carrier`).
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait for opaque datagram transport only.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `serde` — serialization of scenarios, metrics, audit entries.
No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. No real hardware-damaging stressors (bounded, in-process simulation only).

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

|| # | Criterion | Measurement ||
|---|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-43.1 | Fault injection harness covers all 9 fault classes | Unit test per fault class: loss, reorder, duplicate, corrupt, partition, churn, exhaustion, Byzantine, latency each injects and recovers |
| AC-43.2 | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; zero `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh | Grep audit across `src/` |
| AC-43.3 | Only allowed crypto (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305) in crate | Grep audit of crypto surface |
| AC-43.4 | Deterministic replay: same seed → identical fault sequence | Run scenario twice with same seed; compare injected-fault traces byte-identical |
| AC-43.5 | Dry-run by default: injection plan revealed before activation | Scenario with `dry_run: true` produces no datagram modification |
| AC-43.6 | Blast-radius policy enforced: max targets/rate/duration, excluded endpoints never faulted | Inject beyond budget → rejected; excluded endpoint → no fault applied |
| AC-43.7 | Stop conditions auto-abort and roll back | SLO breach during inject → experiment aborts, state restored, audit sealed |
| AC-43.8 | Rollback restores pre-experiment state | Post-rollback datagram paths/node state/resource pressure equal baseline (diff = 0) |
| AC-43.9 | Resilience metrics collected per experiment | Metrics record: latency p50/p95/p99, error rate, recovery time, steady-state violations, sealed with ed25519 |
| AC-43.10 | Corruption detectable via `Checksum` mismatch | Corrupted datagram fails BLAKE3/SHA-256 verification on receipt |
| AC-43.11 | Partition heals without divergence | Post-partition removal: replicas converge; no zombie resurrection |
| AC-43.12 | Byzantine simulation contained | Simulated Byzantine endpoint cannot cause safety violation outside experiment scope |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Fault seam granularity:** Inject at the `ids-carrier::Endpoint` boundary (datagram level) vs. deeper subsystem seams (e.g., inside `ids-store` write path). Datagram-level is carrier-agnostic by construction; subsystem-level gives finer control but requires per-crate hooks. Decision deferred to integration with Phase 047 `ids-testing`.
2. **Resource exhaustion implementation:** In-process bounded stressors (CPU loop, memory allocation cap, disk fill simulation) vs. external process injection. In-process is safer and portable; external is more realistic. In-process chosen for this crate; external delegation noted as future work.
3. **Stop-condition latency:** How quickly an SLO breach is detected and abort triggered (tick interval trade-off: responsiveness vs. overhead). Tunable parameter, unmeasured.
4. **Byzantine simulation scope:** Which Byzantine behaviors (equivocation/rewrite/withhold/replay) are modeled vs. left to `ids-byzantine` production testing. All four simulated here at harness scope; validation against production BFT is integration work.
5. **Metrics overhead:** Per-datagram metrics collection could dominate latency under high-rate faults. Sampling budget per experiment to be validated.
6. **Interaction with `ids-failure-detector`:** Churn/partition experiments will trigger SWIM/phi-accrual suspicion; the expected suspicion/convergence behavior under chaos is undefined until `ids-failure-detector` contract is fixed.
7. **Experiment concurrency:** Whether multiple experiments can run simultaneously against different endpoints; blast-radius accounting across concurrent experiments is un-designed.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Separate crate `ids-chaos`, not a folder inside an existing crate | User directive: separate crates for new capabilities; keeps fault-injection harness isolated from production crates |
| Fault injection at `ids-carrier::Endpoint` adapter boundary | Carrier-agnostic by construction; opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams; no network stack in trust base |
| Seeded deterministic replay + dry-run by default | Reproducibility (s3chaos, malcolm, dsh-tool-chaos); safety (plan revealed before activation) |
| Blast-radius policy + stop conditions + automatic rollback | Prevents chaos experiments from harming production (Gremlin halt-and-rollback; Chaos Mesh rollback) |
| 9 fault classes covering the prompt's contents list | Directly maps to ids-chaos Contents: loss/reorder/dup, corruption, partition, churn, exhaustion, Byzantine, experiment execution, metrics |
| Resilience metrics per experiment (latency, error rate, recovery, steady-state) | Feeds `ids-observability` and `ids-bench`; quantifies resilience |
| Sealed audit log (hash chain + ed25519) per experiment | Tamper-evident record of what was injected, when, and that rollback occurred |
| Only allowed crypto; no networking stack | Complies with IDS carrier-agnostic and crypto allowlist rules |
| One file per concern (faults/, metrics/, contracts/, invariants/) | Matches "~90-1000 files in subfolders" format and the separate-modules directive |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 044 creates **`ids-observability`**, the IDS crate that exposes system state for observability: metrics collection, distributed tracing, audit trail, telemetry export, control-plane vs data-plane separation observability, and SLA/SLO tracking. `ids-observability` is a **separate crate** (per the separate-crates directive, not more folders inside existing ones) that sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It never owns a storage engine; it ingests telemetry produced by other crates, aggregates it locally, signs/audit-chains audit records, and emits opaque `Vec<u8>` telemetry envelopes to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` for off-node delivery.

Three pillars are dimensioned independently but share one ingest bus:

- **Metrics** — counters, gauges, histograms (HDR-style), and summaries; registry with bounded cardinality; lazy registration; cardinality limits with overflow rollup; downsampling/rollup retention tiers.
- **Distributed tracing** — W3C trace-context propagation (trace-id 128-bit, span-id 64-bit, sampled flag), span creation/events/links, head-based + tail-based sampling, batch export over opaque byte envelopes.
- **Audit trail** — append-only, hash-chained log with optional Ed25519 signing per entry and periodic signed checkpoints; inclusion/consistency proofs (RFC 6962/CT-style); WORM append semantics verified by immutable-store policy; retention per record class.

Control-plane vs data-plane separation is enforced by separate ingest channels: data-plane telemetry (per-operation metrics/traces/audit) is bounded and low-overhead; control-plane telemetry (config changes, topology, compaction, retention) is richer but lower frequency. SLA/SLO tracking consumes SLIs from metrics to compute error budgets and burn rates.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (consumed from `ids-crypto`/`ids-000-aa`).

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned the Rust `metrics` registry (counters/gauges/histograms, Receiver pattern)[^1]; `tracing` spans/events/`#[instrument]` + `tracing-subscriber` fmt JSON layer + EnvFilter[^2][^3]; OpenTelemetry metrics API (Meter/MeterProvider, instrument kinds Counter/Gauge/Histogram/Summary, synchronous+asynchronous, cardinality limits default 2000)[^4][^5]; OpenTelemetry OTLP exporter over gRPC/HTTP (binary/JSON), batch span processor defaults (queue 2048, batch 512)[^6][^7]; W3C Trace Context `traceparent` format `version-traceid-spanid-traceflags`, trace-id random ≥7 rightmost bytes, span-id random[^8][^9][^10]; HDR histogram (constant-time record, fixed memory, percentile queries)[^11]; Prometheus/OpenMetrics text exposition, `prometheus-client` Registry+Collector[^12]; append-only hash-chained audit log + Ed25519-signed checkpoints + inclusion/consistency proofs (CT/RFC 6962 pattern, Merkle tree O(log n) proofs)[^13][^14][^15]; SLO/error-budget/burn-rate multi-window alerting (long window / short window 1/12th; burn-rate constants 14.4/6/1 for 99.9%)[^16][^17]; control-plane/data-plane separation[^18]; telemetry cardinality limits and dynamic-identifier avoidance[^4]; downsampling/rollup retention[^19]. This document is the research blueprint only — no code written, no files modified.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-observability` is an **ingest-and-export layer**: other crates push telemetry (metrics updates, trace spans/events, audit records) into its ingest bus; the crate aggregates, samples, downsamples, signs/audit-chains, and emits opaque `Vec<u8>` envelopes to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. It is not a dashboard server — dashboards consume exported envelopes from any backend.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                         APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER                            │
│  ids-store, ids-fragment, ids-reclaim, ids-client emit metrics/spans/audit  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                 Phase 044: ids-observability (THIS CRATE)                    │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐      │
│  │ metrics      │ │ tracing      │ │ audit trail  │ │ SLA/SLO        │      │
│  │ registry     │ │ ingest       │ │ ingest       │ │ tracking       │      │
│  └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬────────┘      │
│         │                │                │                │                │
│  ┌──────▼────────────────▼────────────────▼────────────────▼───────┐       │
│  │            ingest bus → sampler → aggregator → exporter         │       │
│  │  downsampler/rollup (retention tiers)   hash-chain + sign       │       │
│  └──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘       │
│           opaque Vec<u8> telemetry envelopes                                │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┘
                                                │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────▼─────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                   │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType≤1024B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload: &[u8])   │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                     │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow:**
1. **Ingest:** crates call `metrics::increment_counter!` / `tracing::span!` / audit `append_record!`; calls land on per-pillar ingest channels.
2. **Aggregate/sample:** metrics are aggregated per flush interval; spans are sampled (head-based by default, tail-based optional); audit records are appended immediately (synchronous, WORM).
3. **Downsample/rollup:** metrics roll up to retention tiers (full-resolution hot, downsampled warm, aggregated cold).
4. **Audit-chain:** each audit record is hash-chained to its predecessor; optionally Ed25519-signed; periodic signed checkpoints (Merkle root over tree).
5. **Export:** telemetry envelopes (metrics payload, trace batch, audit checkpoint/proof) are serialized and handed to the carrier adapter as opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. `ids-observability` never touches a carrier directly.

**Control-plane vs data-plane separation:** data-plane telemetry is tagged `plane=data` and flows through a bounded, drop-on-pressure channel (observability must never block the data path); control-plane telemetry is tagged `plane=control`, flows through an unbounded channel with richer attributes, and is never mixed into data-plane percentiles.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Metrics collection (registry, instrument kinds, cardinality)

Metrics follow the OpenTelemetry instrument model: **Counter** (monotonic u64), **Gauge** (i64, up/down), **Histogram** (value distribution, HDR-style buckets, percentile queries), **Summary** (quantile approximations). A `Registry` holds all instruments by name+attributes; each unique attribute combination is a separate series — cardinality is bounded (default 2000 per metric stream) with overflow rollup to a single overflow data point marked `otel.metric.overflow=true`. Lazy registration: instruments are created on first use. Downsampling rolls full-resolution hot buckets into wider warm/cold aggregates after configurable retention.

Lazy registration + cardinality limits prevent metric-name explosion (dynamic identifiers such as request IDs must never be attributes — use route templates instead). Aggregation is synchronous per-record (constant-time for counter/gauge, fixed-cost for HDR histogram) to keep data-plane overhead bounded.

#### 3.2 Distributed tracing (W3C trace-context, spans, sampling)

Spans are `tracing`-style: a span is a period with fields/attributes and a parent; events are momentary occurrences within a span. Span context (`SpanContext`) carries trace-id (128-bit), span-id (64-bit), and trace-flags (sampled bit) and is propagated across process boundaries via W3C `traceparent`: `00-{32 hex trace-id}-{16 hex span-id}-{2 hex flags}`. Trace-id must be globally unique: generate with ≥7 random rightmost bytes and set the random-trace-id flag; span-id random. Spans may link to causally-related spans via their SpanContext. Sampling: head-based (decide at span start, cheap but may miss interesting traces) and tail-based (decide at span end, needs a buffer; captures error traces). Export batches finished spans as opaque byte envelopes over the carrier; batch span processor with bounded queue (default 2048) and max export batch (default 512).

#### 3.3 Audit trail (append-only, hash-chained, tamper-evident)

Audit records are append-only: insert-only, no update/delete. Each entry carries a monotonic sequence, timestamp, actor (principal id from `ids-000-aa` types), action, object, outcome, and a SHA-256/BLAKE3 hash chain linking `entry[i].hash = H(prev_hash || entry[i])`. Optional Ed25519 signature per entry or per checkpoint. Periodic signed checkpoints: Merkle root over the tree + tree size + timestamp, signed with Ed25519 (Signed Tree Head pattern, CT/RFC 6962). Inclusion proofs (O(log n)) prove an entry is in the log; consistency proofs prove the log at size N₁ is a prefix of the log at N₂ (append-only growth, no redaction/reorder). Offline proof bundles let a verifier check integrity without network. Retention is per record class (compliance-driven); legal hold suspends expiry. Sensitive data (PII, keys, credentials) must never be written to the audit log.

#### 3.4 Telemetry export & carrier-agnostic delivery

All telemetry leaves the node as opaque `Vec<u8>` envelopes to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Envelope = {pillar, seq, timestamp, payload, optional signature}. The carrier adapter serializes and hands bytes to `ids-carrier`; `ids-observability` never imports `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any transport. Export is asynchronous with a bounded batch queue and backpressure: if the queue is full, data-plane telemetry is dropped (observability never blocks the data plane), control-plane telemetry applies backpressure.

#### 3.5 Control-plane vs data-plane separation observability

Data-plane telemetry (per-operation metrics/trace/audit) is low-overhead, bounded, sampled aggressively, and drop-on-pressure. Control-plane telemetry (topology changes, config edits, compaction, retention, SLO evaluations) is richer, lower-frequency, and retained longer. Separate ingest channels prevent control-plane burst from skewing data-plane percentiles and from starving the export queue.

#### 3.6 SLA/SLO tracking

SLIs are derived from metrics: availability (success/total requests), latency (p95/p99 histogram quantiles), error rate. An SLO = SLI target over a compliance window (e.g., 99.9% availability over 30 days). Error budget = 1 − target. Burn rate = error rate / error budget per unit time. Multi-window burn-rate alerting: long window (e.g., 1h) + short window (1/12th, 5m); high-burn thresholds 14.4/6 and low-burn 1 with corresponding budget consumption 2%/5%/10%. Alerts fire only when both windows exceed threshold (reduces false positives; resets when short window drops below). Burn-rate constants derive from SLO target and period.

#### 3.7 Observability dashboard model

`ids-observability` produces telemetry; dashboards are external consumers of exported envelopes. The crate defines the data model (time-series points, span traces, audit entries, SLO snapshots) and a pull/push export surface, but renders no UI. Downsampled retention tiers keep storage bounded: hot (full resolution, short TTL), warm (downsampled, medium TTL), cold (aggregates, long TTL).

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Metric cardinality explosion (dynamic identifiers as attributes) | Hard cardinality limit per metric (default 2000) with overflow rollup; reject dynamic identifiers in labels at registration |
| Observability overhead blocking the data plane | Separate data-plane channel with drop-on-pressure; bounded queue; control-plane backpressure only |
| Audit log tampering (edit/delete/reorder/inject) | Append-only WORM store; SHA-256/BLAKE3 hash chain; optional Ed25519 per-entry; periodic signed checkpoints; inclusion/consistency proofs |
| Audit log containing sensitive data (PII/keys) | Schema validation rejects sensitive fields; documented rule; PII never in audit records |
| Replay of telemetry envelopes | Monotonic sequence per pillar + nonce; replay cache with TTL-bounded eviction |
| Delayed/export-failure telemetry loss | Bounded export queue with backpressure; drop data-plane on overflow (never block); control-plane retries |
| Unverified checkpoint/audit proof | Clients verify signatures and proofs client-side; full audit recalculates all hashes vs historical roots |
| Sampling hiding incidents | Tail-based sampling option captures error traces; head rate configurable; never sample audit records |
| Carrier misdelivery/envelope tampering | Optional Ed25519 signature over envelope payload; verification at ingest boundary of receiver |

---

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

| Crate | Role in Phase 044 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Canonical types (NodeID, Principal, ObjectId, Tick), sealed trait contracts, invariants, error base; actor/principal for audit records |
| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); all telemetry traffic as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 |
| `ids-store` / `ids-fragment` / `ids-reclaim` | Producers of data-plane metrics, trace spans, audit records |
| `ids-client` | Consumer-facing; emits client-side telemetry via the shared ingest bus |

**Integration points:**
- `ids-000-aa` supplies principal/object identifiers used in audit records and trace attributes; sealed contracts guarantee stable types across crates.
- `ids-carrier::Endpoint` is the sole egress: `send_datagram(Endpoint, &[u8])`. No direct socket/transport imports.
- `ids-crypto` provides SHA-256/BLAKE3 for hash chains and Ed25519 for signing; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 available if envelope encryption is ever required.
- Other IDS crates call `ids-observability` ingest APIs (metric counters, trace spans, audit appends); no crate depends on `ids-observability` for correctness — observability is additive instrumentation.

**Why ~90–1000 files:** one file per responsibility — ingest bus, three pillars (metrics/tracing/audit) each with registry/model/chain/proof/signing/retention, telemetry export, SLO tracking, dashboard data model, carrier boundary, config, fuzz, tests, benches, specs, docs, test vectors. No stubs; every file holds production-grade code with error handling, documentation, and tests.

---

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Metrics registry & instrument kinds

```
InstrumentKind = Counter | Gauge | Histogram | Summary
MetricId = {name, attribute_set}
Registry: Map<MetricId, Instrument>
record(name, attributes, value): lazy-create instrument; aggregate constant-time
cardinality: if series_count(name) > 2000 → overflow rollup (otel.metric.overflow=true)
downsample: hot(full, TTL_h) → warm(downsampled, TTL_w) → cold(aggregated, TTL_c)
```

#### 7.2 W3C trace-context propagation

```
traceparent = "00" "-" {32 hex trace-id} "-" {16 hex span-id} "-" {2 hex trace-flags}
trace-id: 128-bit; ≥7 rightmost bytes random; random-trace-id flag if so
span-id: 64-bit random
SpanContext = {trace_id, span_id, trace_flags(sampled)}
Span = {context, parent: Option<SpanContext>, fields, links: Vec<SpanContext>, start, end}
propagate(span_context) -> traceparent string for carrier envelope headers
```

#### 7.3 Audit hash chain + Merkle proofs

```
entry[i].hash = SHA-256(prev_hash || entry[i].canonical_bytes)   // or BLAKE3
Merkle leaf = SHA-256(0x00 || entry); node = SHA-256(0x01 || left || right)  // domain separation
Inclusion proof: sibling hashes from leaf to root (O(log n))
Consistency proof: prove root(N₁) is prefix of root(N₂) (append-only)
Checkpoint = {tree_size, root_hash, timestamp, ed25519_signature}
```

#### 7.4 Telemetry envelope

```
TelemetryEnvelope = {pillar, seq: u64, timestamp: u64, payload: Vec<u8>, signature: Option<[u8;64]>}
carrier_datagram = serialize(envelope) → Vec<u8> → ids-carrier::Endpoint
```

#### 7.5 SLO / error budget / burn rate

```
SLI = good_events / total_events  (availability, latency-threshold, error-rate)
SLO = {sli, target, compliance_window}
error_budget = 1 − target
burn_rate = error_rate / error_budget_per_unit_time
multi-window alert: long_window (e.g. 1h) AND short_window (long/12, e.g. 5m) both > threshold
burn-rate constants for 99.9%/30d: 14.4 (1h/5m, 2% budget), 6 (6h/30m, 5%), 1 (3d/6h, 10%)
```

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-044.1 | Metrics semantics | Counter monotonic; gauge up/down; histogram percentiles via HDR; unit + property test, 100k iterations |
| AC-044.2 | Cardinality bound | Per-metric series capped (default 2000); overflow rollup marked; cardinality-bomb test passes |
| AC-044.3 | W3C trace-context round-trip | SpanContext → traceparent → SpanContext identical; trace-id ≥7 random rightmost bytes; span-id random |
| AC-044.4 | Span lifecycle | Create/enter/exit span; events within span; parent-child links; export batch correctness |
| AC-044.5 | Sampling | Head-based rate enforced; tail-based captures error traces; sampling never applies to audit records |
| AC-044.6 | Audit append-only WORM | Insert-only; update/delete rejected; 100% of single-record insert/delete/reorder detected; offender named |
| AC-044.7 | Hash chain integrity | 100% of tamper detected; verification names offending entry; offline proof bundle verifies without network |
| AC-044.8 | Merkle proofs | Inclusion proof O(log n); consistency proof proves append-only growth between two sizes |
| AC-044.9 | Signed checkpoint | Ed25519 signature over (tree_size, root_hash, timestamp); verifiable client-side |
| AC-044.10 | Sensitive-data rejection | PII/keys/credentials rejected at audit ingest; property test |
| AC-044.11 | Envelope carrier boundary | serialize → Vec<u8> → ids-carrier::Endpoint; zero references to std::net/tokio::net/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |
| AC-044.12 | Data-plane vs control-plane separation | Data-plane drop-on-pressure never blocks writes; control-plane backpressure only; percentiles not skewed |
| AC-044.13 | Export queue bounds | Bounded batch queue; overflow drops data-plane, backpressures control-plane; measured by bench |
| AC-044.14 | SLO/error budget | error_budget = 1 − target; burn-rate multi-window alert fires only when both windows exceed threshold; reset on recovery |
| AC-044.15 | Allowed crypto only | ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 appear; no other primitive in crypto surface |
| AC-044.16 | Performance bound | Metric record ≤ ~100ns p50 (counter/gauge); span emit bounded; hash-chain append constant; bench-verified |
| AC-044.17 | Determinism | Same seed + input → identical export envelopes and proofs |
| AC-044.18 | Adversarial tests pass | Cardinality bomb, audit tamper, replay, sensitive-data injection all fail-safe |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Registry choice:** `metrics` crate + custom registry vs OpenTelemetry Rust SDK meter — OTel SDK pulls OTLP exporter (gRPC/HTTP) which conflicts with carrier-agnostic byte-envelope export; likely adopt `metrics` primitives with `ids-observability`-owned export. Decision needed before implementation.
2. **Histogram implementation:** `hdrhistogram` (constant-time, fixed memory) vs custom exponential buckets — `hdrhistogram` favored for latency percentiles; crate availability/licensing to confirm.
3. **Audit store backend:** WORM append-only interface must be backed by an immutable store (sled/rocksdb with insert-only policy, or object-storage WORM) — backend selection and `ids-storage` integration TBD.
4. **Envelope encoding:** deterministic CBOR vs bincode vs custom binary — must be versioned and checksummed; decision affects wire compatibility across versions.
5. **Export retry/backoff:** control-plane retry policy (interval, cap, jitter) undefined; data-plane drop-on-pressure is final (no retry).
6. **Tail-sampling buffer size:** bounded queue for tail-based sampling; overflow policy (drop oldest vs drop newest) unquantified.
7. **SLO defaults:** target/compliance window/burn-rate thresholds are deployment-specific; defaults are placeholders pending measurement.
8. **Checkpoint frequency vs replay cost:** how often signed checkpoints are written trades storage against audit replay length; unmeasured.
9. **Cross-node trace correlation:** trace context must survive carrier hops — envelope must carry traceparent; hop-by-hop correlation vs end-to-end trace needs confirmation against carrier semantics.
10. **Retention class defaults:** per-class retention (audit) periods are compliance-driven; defaults TBD.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-observability` (not a subfolder) | User directive: separate crates instead of more folders; keeps observability concerns isolated |
| Three pillars on one ingest bus | Metrics/tracing/audit share ingest + export; plane tagging separates data/control |
| `metrics`-style primitives + custom registry | Avoids OTel SDK OTLP (gRPC/HTTP) dependency conflict with carrier-agnostic byte envelopes |
| W3C trace-context `traceparent` | Standard, fixed-length, fast parsing; portable across vendors |
| HDR-style histograms | Constant-time record, fixed memory, percentile queries; latency SLOs |
| Cardinality limit 2000 + overflow rollup | Prevents metric-name explosion; OTel-proven pattern |
| Append-only WORM audit + hash chain + Merkle proofs | Tamper-evident, offline-verifiable; CT/RFC 6962 pattern |
| Ed25519 signed checkpoints | Signed tree head; client-verifiable; allowed crypto only |
| Data-plane drop-on-pressure; control-plane backpressure | Observability must never block the data path |
| Opaque `Vec<u8>` envelopes to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Carrier-agnostic; no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |
| Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Complies with IDS crypto allowlist |
| Multi-window burn-rate alerting (long + short 1/12th) | SRE Workbook pattern; reduces false positives; clear reset |
| No dashboard rendering in crate | Dashboards consume exported envelopes; crate defines data model only |
