---

### Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Proptest case count tuning:** 100,000 iterations is a starting point; expensive properties (stateful model, convergence) may need fewer cases with longer per-case timeouts; to be validated at implementation.
2. **Deterministic simulation harness implementation:** IDS has no confirmed workspace-wide deterministic simulation runtime; the chaos layer must simulate carrier/network/disk on logical time — design of this harness is provisional.
3. **Fuzzing toolchain on Windows/MSVC:** cargo-fuzz/libFuzzer requires nightly and toolchain support; MSVC linker complications for libFuzzer `main` noted in research — fallback to honggfuzz or in-process fuzz targets may be needed.
4. **Conformance test source of truth:** `ids-doc` (Phase 049) formal models/TLA+ specs may not yet exist; conformance test purposes must be derived from `ids-000-aa` sealed contracts until then.
5. **Differential testing implementation:** running two independent implementations requires a reference implementation to exist; may defer to property+model testing until a second implementation is available.
6. **Soak duration equivalence:** virtual-clock acceleration (iterations ≈ wall time) mapping to real-world duration is unquantified; thresholds (RSS bound, latency drift) are placeholders pending measurement.
7. **Cross-replica chaos under partitions:** deterministic simulation of multi-node partitions needs a simulated membership/failure detector; integration with `ids-failure-detector` semantics undefined.
8. **Test vector format:** JSON vs binary vs canonical serialization; digest algorithm (BLAKE3 vs SHA-256) choice for vector integrity.

---

### Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-testing` (not a folder inside an existing crate) | User directive: separate crates instead of more folders; keeps test code out of production dependency graph |
| `proptest` as primary property framework (per prompt) | Superior shrinking/composition vs quickcheck; state-machine testing via proptest-stateful |
| `cargo-fuzz` + `arbitrary` derive for fuzzing | De facto Rust fuzzing toolchain; structure-aware inputs keep fuzzer deep in the system |
| Deterministic simulation for chaos | Same seed ⇒ identical execution ⇒ reproducible bugs (FoundationDB/Antithesis pattern) |
| Conformance test purposes from `ids-doc`/`ids-000-aa` contracts | Conformance requires spec-specified assertions; ISO 9646-1 TP/abstract-test-case structure |
| Public API only; `ids-testing` never a production dependency | Prevents test code from coupling to/infecting production crates |
| All carrier traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; no network stack | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule (no exceptions) |
| Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305) | IDS crypto policy |
| Seeded runs + determinism oracle | Test reliability and reproducibility; CI can re-run failures bit-for-bit |
| One file per concern (~90–1000 files) | Matches IDS plan format and "separate crates instead of more folders" applied intra-crate |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 048 creates `ids-bench`, the IDS performance-benchmarking crate. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by measurement domain. `ids-bench` measures read/write latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput, cross-domain bytes transferred, recovery completion time, durability restoration time, storage amplification, repair bandwidth, control-plane traffic, metadata convergence time, intent-compilation time, resource utilisation, cost per byte, and energy per byte.

**Core design:** a criterion.rs-driven microbenchmark harness (warmup → measurement → statistical analysis → regression comparison) with `std::hint::black_box` to prevent optimization, HDR histogram / t-digest / DDSketch percentile sketches for tail latency, and optional divan benchmarks as a cross-check. Every measurement driver speaks only opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` address); `ids-bench` never touches a carrier directly and imports no networking crate. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` (ids-crypto does not depend on ids-000-aa to avoid the circular dependency; ids-bench depends on both).

**Scope boundary:** `ids-bench` measures; it does not tune. It produces reproducible numbers and regression signals for the implementation phases (ids-write, ids-read, ids-recovery, ids-erasure, ids-sync, ids-crdt, ids-query, …). Thresholds are configurable budgets, not hard-coded limits, so a slow platform degrades gracefully rather than failing the suite.

Skeleton `ids-bench` does NOT exist yet at `C:/idfs/ids-bench/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned criterion.rs (stats-driven microbenchmarks, black_box, outlier detection via Tukey IQR, 95% CI, bootstrap resampling, regression detection), divan (simpler harness, async support, instruction counting), bencher/libtest (nightly-only), HdrHistogram/hdrhistogram (p50/p95/p99, ~3–6 ns record cost, fixed memory, coordinated-omission correction), t-digest (MnO2; streaming, mergeable, tight tails), DDSketch (relative-error quantiles), ed25519-dalek criterion numbers (sign ~15 µs, verify ~40 µs), xchacha20poly1305 (~4.5 µs at 1 KiB, ~217 MiB/s), blake3 (~2–10 GiB/s), sha256 (~2.4 GiB/s), chacha20poly1305 (~1–3 GiB/s), sysinfo (process RSS/CPU), Welford online algorithm (streaming mean/variance), WAL-recovery benchmarks (~100–120 ms to replay 1M × 128 B records), LSM write amplification (10–30×), reed-solomon-simd (encode ~10 GiB/s, decode hundreds of MiB/s), clay codes MSR repair (37–67% repair-bandwidth savings vs Reed-Solomon), hotpath.rs CI regression guidance (wall-clock noise vs instruction-count stability), RAPL energy measurement, throughput-per-megabyte/energy-per-request methodology, rusty-comms IPC benchmark (p50/p95/p99, MiB/s per payload size).

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-bench` is a measurement layer above the IDS crates under test. It drives workloads through the public contracts declared in `ids-000-aa`, sends/receives only through `ids-carrier::Endpoint`, hashes/signs with `ids-crypto` primitives, and timestamps with `ids-time` (monotonic, never wall-clock for ordering). It does not store, route, or replicate data itself.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      BENCHMARK DRIVER (ids-bench, THIS CRATE)               │
│  cli.rs  ·  suite.rs  ·  workloads/  ·  reporters/  ·  config/              │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  latency/        throughput/     bytes/         recovery/     durability/   │
│  p50/p95/p99     MiB/s + ops/s   cross-domain   completion    restoration   │
│  HDR/t-digest    warmup          bytes_out==in   WAL replay    erasure       │
│  Welford stats   batch sizes     + acked         harness      reconstruction│
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  amplification/  repair-band/    control-plane/  metadata/     intent/     │
│  storage         bandwidth       traffic ratio   convergence   compilation │
│  phys vs logical bytes repaired  ctrl/data      post-heal     intent→plan   │
│  ratio                                 time                                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  resources/      cost-energy/    crypto-bench/   harness/      reports/    │
│  RSS/CPU/alloc   cost per byte   ed25519/xchacha criterion/divan  CSV/JSON │
│  per byte/energy blake3/sha256   chacha20poly1305 black_box      output    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                      ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                   │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload)      │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                     │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of one benchmark iteration:**
1. `suite.rs` selects a workload (read/write/repair/recovery/…), payload size, concurrency, duration; `workloads/` builds deterministic input (fixed seed, fixed byte patterns).
2. The driver submits operations through the crate-under-test's contract (e.g. `ids-store` write, `ids-read` get, `ids-erasure` encode/decode, `ids-recovery` replay). Each operation is timed with `ids-time` ticks.
3. Latency samples feed a concurrent HDR histogram (bounded range, fixed significant digits) plus a t-digest/DDSketch for mergeable cross-node aggregation; p50/p95/p99 extracted after warmup.
4. Byte counters record payload bytes + control-plane bytes per domain; cross-domain `bytes_transferred` checked against the `ids-000-aa` `out_eq_in` invariant (bytes-out == bytes-in + acked) within tolerance.
5. `resources/` samples process RSS and CPU% (sysinfo) and allocation counts; `cost-energy/` derives cost per byte and energy per byte (energy hooks optional, RAPL-style where available).
6. Crypto benches run ed25519 sign/verify, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 across payload sizes (64 B … 1 MiB).
7. `reporters/` emits CSV/JSON plus criterion comparison against the previous run (regression signal, 95% CI).

All cross-node benchmark traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-bench` never addresses IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS or any carrier by name.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Benchmark harness selection (criterion vs divan vs bencher)

**criterion.rs** — statistics-driven microbenchmarking (Rust port of Haskell Criterion). Four phases per benchmark: warmup (fill caches), measurement (repeated execution, timing samples), analysis (statistics), comparison (vs previous run, regression detection). Defaults: sample size 100, warm-up 3 s, measurement 5 s, bootstrap 100k resamples, 95% confidence, 5% significance, outlier classification via Tukey's IQR method. Works on stable Rust. De facto standard in the ecosystem; used by ed25519-dalek for its criterion benchmarks (signing ~15 µs, verification ~40 µs on an i7-10700K). `std::hint::black_box` prevents the compiler from constant-folding or deleting benchmarked work. `bench_with_input` / `BenchmarkId` detects O(n)/O(n²) complexity; `iter_batched` separates setup (unmeasured) from the operation under test.

**divan** — simpler harness with `#[divan::bench]`, `divan::black_box`, per-argument inputs, thread-contention (`threads` option), async benchmarks via a Tokio runtime inside the bench, allocation profiling, and hardware-adaptive measurement. Listed by CodSpeed as one of the three mainstream Rust harnesses alongside criterion and libtest-bench. Good as a cross-check harness because it measures differently (instruction-count-friendly, fast startup).

**bencher / libtest bench** — nightly-only (unstable `#[bench]`); neither actively developed. Rejected as the primary harness for an IDS crate targeting stable toolchains; usable only as a secondary, nightly-gated option.

**Verdict:** primary = criterion.rs (statistical rigor, regression detection, stable support); secondary = divan (cross-validation, async workloads, contention); nightly libtest bench not adopted.

#### 3.2 Latency histograms and percentiles (p50/p95/p99)

**HdrHistogram / hdrhistogram** — Gil Tene's HDR histogram port to Rust. Fixed log-linear buckets, constant-time `record` (~3–6 ns, no allocation per sample), fixed memory by dynamic range + significant digits, `value_at_percentile(0.50/0.95/0.99)`. Tail-accurate for bounded integer ranges (nanosecond latencies). Submillisecond cookbook numbers: record p99 ≈ 51 ns, percentile read ≈ 49 µs over ~20k populated counters for a 1 ns–1 ms range on EC2 t3.micro. Weakness: unbounded value ranges and merging across heterogeneous shapes need a sketch instead.

**t-digest (MnO2/t-digest; sketches)** — streaming quantile sketch; `record` O(1) amortised, quantile O(δ), mergeable across threads/nodes, tight at tails (p99/p99.9), compact state scales with compression factor not sample count. Use when value range is unbounded or percentiles must be merged across benchmark shards.

**DDSketch** — relative-error quantile sketch (logarithmic buckets); a 1% target means a true 100 ms p99 is estimated within [99, 101] ms; mergeable; good for cross-replica latency aggregation where relative error beats rank error.

**Coordinated omission** — on a fixed-rate load generator, one slow operation blocks every request that should have been issued during the stall; naive histograms report the tail the sampler saw, not the tail delivered. HDR's `record_with_expected_interval(value, interval)` backfills missing samples so percentiles reflect stalled requests. ids-bench must apply coordinated-omission correction for closed-loop drivers, or use open-loop drivers where it does not apply.

**Welford online algorithm** — single-pass, numerically stable running mean/variance (M2 update); O(1) memory, mergeable partitions (parallel → combine M2). Used for per-iteration statistics without storing every sample; complements histograms (not a replacement for percentiles).

**Verdict:** HDR histogram as the primary per-worker latency recorder (bounded ns–ms range, p50/p95/p99), t-digest/DDSketch as the mergeable cross-worker aggregation layer, Welford for streaming mean/variance, coordinated-omission correction on fixed-rate drivers.

#### 3.3 Throughput measurement

Throughput = bytes or operations per unit time, measured over the warmed-up steady state (not warmup), at multiple payload sizes (64 B, 256 B, 1 KiB, 4 KiB, 64 KiB, 256 KiB, 1 MiB, 4 MiB). Report MiB/s and ops/s per size, plus the size-throughput curve (knee detection). Reference patterns: rusty-comms IPC benchmark reports p50/p95/p99 plus MiB/s per message size; rustls reports bulk transfer MiB/s and handshakes/s; oxicrypto benchmarks AEAD/hash throughput at 1 KiB/64 KiB/1 MiB. ids-bench adopts the same per-size table format.

#### 3.4 Cross-domain bytes transferred

Counter every byte crossing a domain boundary (region → region, node → node, H-unit → H-unit): payload bytes and control bytes, sent and received. The `ids-000-aa` `out_eq_in` invariant (bytes-out == bytes-in + acked) gives a self-check: a benchmark run must account for every byte, or report the discrepancy as a measurement bug, not silence it. Cross-domain bytes transferred is reported per workload and per direction; amplification ratios (control bytes / payload bytes, repair bytes / logical bytes) derive from it.

#### 3.5 Recovery completion time and durability restoration time

**Recovery completion time:** time from failure detection signal to service resumption (replica caught up, WAL replayed, index rebuilt). Reference WAL-recovery benchmarks: ~78–122 ms to scan/replay 1M × 128 B records (~114 ms median), ~25M records/sec sequential WAL replay, group-commit append at hundreds of thousands of rec/s. ids-bench drives a crash/restart scenario (SIGKILL-style: truncate at last synced position) and measures replay time plus catch-up time.

**Durability restoration time:** time from failure to restored redundancy (re-replication or erasure reconstruction complete, quorum/region durability re-established). Measured for node, H-unit, and region failure scenarios with bounded recovery bandwidth (so recovery does not starve the data plane — ids-fault backpressure integration).

Both are absolute deadlines keyed to `ids-time` ticks, never RTT-derived.

#### 3.6 Storage amplification

Storage amplification = physical bytes stored / logical bytes ingested (includes WAL, replicas, erasure fragments, tombstones, index overhead, compaction headroom). Benchmark per workload: ingest N logical bytes, measure physical bytes on disk (via ids-store/ids-reclaim interfaces), compute ratio. Reference: LSM-trees suffer 10–30× write amplification under random workloads (repeated compaction); WAL-first engines trade amplification for durability. ids-bench reports amplification before/after compaction and after garbage collection so compaction efficacy is measurable.

#### 3.7 Repair bandwidth

Bytes transferred across the network to repair one failed node/fragment. Reed-Solomon (n,k) naive repair downloads k full chunks to reconstruct one; regenerating/MSR codes (clay codes) download a fraction per helper — measured 37–67% repair-bandwidth savings vs Reed-Solomon (configs (4,2,5), (9,3,11), (10,4,13)). reed-solomon-simd reference: encode ~10 GiB/s (32:32 shards), decode hundreds of MiB/s–1.4 GiB/s depending on shard count. ids-bench benchmarks single-node and concurrent-failure repair, reports bytes transferred and repair time, with repair bandwidth capped so foreground traffic is not starved (ids-fault/ids-backpressure integration).

#### 3.8 Control-plane traffic

Ratio of control-plane bytes (metadata, heartbeats, discovery gossip, Merkle digests, anti-entropy, replicas of control state) to data-plane bytes, measured per workload and per time window. Important because control traffic scales with node count and metadata volume, not payload size. ids-bench counts control bytes separately at the carrier boundary (opaque Vec<u8> frames tagged by frame type) and reports control/data ratio; a run is flagged if control traffic exceeds a configurable budget.

#### 3.9 Metadata convergence time and intent-compilation time

**Metadata convergence time:** after a partition heals or a node joins, time until all replicas agree on metadata (membership, placement, commit prefix). Driven through ids-membership/ids-sync/ids-crdt paths; measured as time-to-identical-state across replicas under controlled churn. Reference CRDT merge benchmarks: did:crdt criterion numbers — median merge latency 5–8 µs (small docs), 11–14 µs (medium), 70–88 µs (large), >140 K ops/s on small documents (Apple M2, criterion 0.5, release+LTO).

**Intent-compilation time:** from client `ids_submit(intent)` to compiled execution plan ready to execute (ids-query planning + ids-routing resolution). Measured end-to-end at the client handle; broken down into planning, routing, and validation sub-phases. Both metrics use deterministic inputs and fixed seeds so results are comparable across runs.

#### 3.10 Resource utilisation

Per-benchmark process RSS (peak and steady), CPU usage (% of one core and of machine), allocation counts, and (optionally) hardware events. sysinfo provides `Process::memory` (RSS) and `cpu_usage` (needs two refreshes). Allocation counting via `CountingAllocator`/dhat-style tools or a counting allocator wrapper for allocation-sensitive benches. Welford accumulates mean/variance of repeated runs. Resource numbers are reported per benchmark, never used as pass/fail without a configured budget (platform variance is high).

#### 3.11 Cost per byte and energy per byte

**Cost per byte:** derived from ids-accounting measurements — storage/bandwidth/compute/recovery effort attributed per byte written/read/transferred. ids-bench hooks the accounting counters and reports cost per byte per workload (write, read, repair, recovery).

**Energy per byte:** energy consumed per byte processed, measured where an energy interface exists (RAPL-style CPU/package energy, device energy where exposed; methodology from greensoftwarelab RAPL examples and throughput-per-megabyte studies measuring energy per request on Raspberry Pi 5). Reported as optional feature-gated benchmarks (`energy` feature) so the crate works on hosts without energy interfaces. NVMe energy-performance tools (nvme-energy-bench) show the storage-stack energy trade-off is real and workload-dependent; ids-bench reports it, does not prescribe targets.

#### 3.12 Crypto primitive benchmarks (allowed set only)

Within the allowed set — ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 — ids-bench measures sign/verify (ed25519), encrypt/decrypt throughput and latency at 64 B … 1 MiB (xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305), hash throughput (sha256, blake3). Indicative published numbers (hardware-dependent, to be re-measured on the target host): ed25519 sign ~15 µs / verify ~40 µs (i7-10700K, criterion); xchacha20poly1305 encrypt ~4.5 µs at 1 KiB (~217 MiB/s); blake3 ~2–10 GiB/s (parallel), ~2 GiB/s single-thread; sha256 ~2.4 GiB/s; chacha20poly1305 ~1–3 GiB/s. ids-bench records these per payload size and flags regressions vs the stored baseline; no other algorithm may be added without updating this plan and the crypto policy.

#### 3.13 Statistical methodology

- Warmup before measurement (criterion default 3 s; configurable).
- Sample size ≥ 100 measurements per bench; bootstrap CI at 95%.
- Outlier classification (Tukey IQR: samples < Q1 − 1.5·IQR or > Q3 + 1.5·IQR are outliers; mild/severe split).
- Regression detection: compare current sample vs stored previous run; report change with p-value (p ≤ 0.05 ⇒ significant).
- `black_box` on inputs and outputs to defeat constant folding and dead-code elimination; `iter_batched` to exclude setup.
- Determinism: fixed RNG seeds, fixed payload patterns, fixed contact/membership scenarios; same seed + same scenario → identical numbers (within measurement noise).
- Wall-clock noise warning: CI wall-clock can vary >2.5× on identical code; prefer instruction counts (Callgrind-style) or allocation counts for CI pass/fail, wall-clock for local trend (hotpath.rs finding).

#### 3.14 Determinism and reproducibility

Every bench writes a run manifest: Git revision + dirty state, Rust toolchain, OS/kernel, architecture, CPU model, logical CPU count, build profile, workload configuration, feature flags, and full results (schema-versioned JSON, camus-style). Results are comparable only on the same controlled host, device, build profile, and configuration — stated explicitly, no universal thresholds.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|--------|-----------|
| Optimized-away benchmark (compiler deletes the measured work) | `std::hint::black_box` on inputs/outputs; `iter_batched` setup exclusion; return values consumed |
| Warmup contamination (cold-start samples mixed into steady state) | Explicit warmup phase; discard warmup samples; report warmup vs measurement split |
| Coordinated omission hiding tail latency | `record_with_expected_interval` on fixed-rate drivers; open-loop drivers preferred |
| Wall-clock noise causing false regressions in CI | 95% CI + p-value; instruction-count/allocation metrics for pass/fail; wall-clock for trends only |
| Percentile sketch inaccuracy at tails | HDR for bounded ranges (significant digits), t-digest/DDSketch for unbounded/mergeable; accuracy targets stated per sketch |
| Cross-node percentile merge inconsistency | Same sketch type + same configuration on all nodes; merge before query |
| Byte accounting drift (lost bytes invisible) | `out_eq_in` invariant check at the end of every bytes-transfer bench; report discrepancy |
| Prohibited crate sneaking into the dependency tree | Dependency audit in CI; `cargo tree` check that no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/QUIC/HTTP/DNS crate appears; ids-bench imports no networking crate |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm added | ids-crypto is the sole crypto surface; ids-bench references only the five allowed primitive IDs; CI test asserts algorithm allowlist |
| Energy/cost numbers compared across heterogeneous hosts | Run manifest records host + config; numbers comparable only within identical manifest; no cross-host thresholds |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

| Crate | Role in Phase 048 |
|-------|-------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Canonical types (`NodeId`, `RecordId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, …), sealed trait contracts, invariants incl. `out_eq_in` (bytes-out == bytes-in + acked); master control point, zero downstream edits for contract changes |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 B address), `send_datagram`/`receive_datagram`; the only carrier boundary ids-bench touches |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305; ids-bench consumes primitive IDs, never implements crypto |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic IDS standard time source for all latency/deadline measurements (never wall-clock for ordering) |
| `ids-store`, `ids-read` | Read/write workloads under measurement (latency p50/p95/p99, throughput, storage amplification) |
| `ids-recovery` | WAL replay / recovery completion and durability restoration workloads |
| `ids-erasure`, `ids-regenerating-codes`, `ids-ppr-reconstruction` | Repair-bandwidth workloads (encode/decode/repair bytes) |
| `ids-sync`, `ids-crdt`, `ids-membership` | Metadata convergence workloads (post-heal time-to-agreement) |
| `ids-query`, `ids-routing` | Intent-compilation workloads (submit → compiled plan) |
| `ids-fault`, `ids-backpressure` | Bounded recovery/repair bandwidth so foreground traffic is not starved |
| `ids-accounting` | Cost-per-byte counters (storage/bandwidth/compute/recovery effort per byte) |
| `ids-observability` | Metric/trace sinks for benchmark telemetry (optional) |
| `ids-testing` | Reuses property-based/adversarial harness patterns (proptest); ids-bench is the measurement counterpart, not the test harness |

**Integration points:** ids-bench drives public contracts declared in ids-000-aa; it does not reach into crate internals. All cross-node traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on ids-discovery/ids-session/ids-cli beyond what the contracts expose.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Latency histogram (HDR)
```
HdrHistogram { significant_digits: 1..=5, low, high, buckets[] }
record(value): O(1), no allocation, bucket index from log2 bucket + linear sub-bucket
value_at_percentile(p): scan buckets cumulatively until count ≥ p·total
p50 = value_at_percentile(0.50), p95 = 0.95, p99 = 0.99
Coordinated omission: record_with_expected_interval(value, interval) backfills stall samples
```

#### 7.2 Mergeable quantile sketch (t-digest / DDSketch)
```
TDigest { centroids[], compression δ }
record(x): O(1) amortised; centroid weight grows near tails
quantile(q): O(δ); merge(digests): combine + re-centroid, O(δ₁+δ₂)
DDSketch: logarithmic buckets, relative error ε; true q within [(1−ε)·v, (1+ε)·v]
```
Used to aggregate percentiles across benchmark workers/nodes.

#### 7.3 Welford online statistics
```
state = (n, mean, M2)
push(x): n += 1; delta = x − mean; mean += delta/n; M2 += delta·(x − mean)
variance = M2 / n (population) or M2 / (n−1) (sample)
merge(a, b): combine two partitions in O(1) (parallel mean/variance)
```

#### 7.4 Throughput meter
```
Meter { window_start, bytes, ops }
record(bytes_count, op_count)
throughput = bytes / elapsed  (MiB/s), ops / elapsed (ops/s), steady-state only
```

#### 7.5 out_eq_in invariant check
```
bytes_out == bytes_in + bytes_acked   (per domain, per direction, tolerance ε)
violation → measurement bug flagged, run result marked inconsistent
```
From `ids-000-aa` invariant `out_eq_in`.

#### 7.6 Repair bandwidth
```
repair_bytes = Σ bytes fetched from helpers; repair_time = completion − start
MSR target: repair_bytes ≈ (d·β) where β < full chunk (clay codes: 37–67% vs Reed-Solomon)
cap: repair bandwidth ≤ configured budget so foreground traffic is protected
```

#### 7.7 Convergence / compilation timing
```
t_start = ids-time tick at intent submission / partition heal
t_end   = ids-time tick at plan-ready / state agreement across all replicas
elapsed = t_end − t_start   (ids-time ticks, monotonic, never wall-clock)
```

#### 7.8 Cost / energy per byte
```
cost_per_byte   = accounting_effort_units / logical_bytes_processed
energy_per_byte = package_energy_delta_joules / logical_bytes_processed   (optional feature)
```

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-48.1 | Read/write latency p50/p95/p99 reported per payload size (64 B … 1 MiB) | HDR histogram + sketch, post-warmup, 95% CI |
| AC-48.2 | Throughput reported in MiB/s and ops/s per payload size | Throughput meter, steady state after warmup |
| AC-48.3 | Cross-domain bytes transferred reported per direction/domain | Byte counters at carrier boundary |
| AC-48.4 | out_eq_in invariant holds: bytes-out == bytes-in + acked (tolerance ε) | Invariant check at end of every bytes-transfer bench; violations fail the run |
| AC-48.5 | Recovery completion time reported (crash → service resumed) | WAL replay + catch-up timing, ids-time keyed |
| AC-48.6 | Durability restoration time reported (node / H-unit / region failure) | Redundancy-restoration timing with bounded repair bandwidth |
| AC-48.7 | Storage amplification reported (physical / logical) per workload | Before/after compaction and GC |
| AC-48.8 | Repair bandwidth reported per failed node/fragment | Bytes transferred vs helpers; MSR target 37–67% savings vs naive RS (indicative) |
| AC-48.9 | Control-plane / data-plane byte ratio reported per workload | Frame-type-tagged byte meter |
| AC-48.10 | Metadata convergence time reported after partition heal / node join | Time-to-identical-state across replicas |
| AC-48.11 | Intent-compilation time reported (submit → plan ready) | Sub-phase breakdown: planning / routing / validation |
| AC-48.12 | Resource utilisation reported: peak RSS, CPU%, allocation counts | sysinfo sampler + counting allocator |
| AC-48.13 | Cost per byte and energy per byte reported (energy feature-gated) | ids-accounting counters; RAPL-style energy where available |
| AC-48.14 | Crypto benchmarks for ed25519 sign/verify, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 at 64 B … 1 MiB | Throughput + latency per payload size; indicative targets: sign ≤ ~20 µs, verify ≤ ~50 µs, sha256 ≥ ~2 GiB/s, blake3 ≥ ~2 GiB/s single-thread, AEAD ≥ ~1 GiB/s (re-measure on target host) |
| AC-48.15 | Statistical rigor: 95% CI, outlier classification, regression vs baseline with p-value | Criterion analysis; p ≤ 0.05 ⇒ significant change |
| AC-48.16 | Determinism: same seed + scenario ⇒ identical results | Determinism tests pass |
| AC-48.17 | Carrier agnosticism: compiles/behaves identically with zero direct dependencies on TCP/IP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, libp2p; all traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint | Dependency audit test (`cargo tree`) passes |
| AC-48.18 | Crypto allowlist: only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 reachable | Allowlist unit test passes |
| AC-48.19 | Run manifest emitted per run (git revision, dirty state, toolchain, host, config, results) | Schema-versioned JSON |

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Harness split between criterion and divan:** criterion is primary for statistical rigor; divan's exact role (async workloads only, or full cross-check) to be confirmed during implementation.
2. **Energy interface availability:** RAPL-style energy may not exist on target hosts; `energy` feature must degrade gracefully (feature off, not compile error).
3. **Baseline calibration:** indicative crypto/throughput numbers (ed25519 ~15 µs sign, sha256 ~2.4 GiB/s, etc.) are hardware-dependent and must be re-measured on the target host before any regression thresholds are set.
4. **out_eq_in tolerance ε:** the tolerance for byte-accounting discrepancies under loss/retransmission is workload-dependent; unquantified.
5. **Repair bandwidth caps:** MSR/clay-code savings (37–67%) are paper numbers; actual repair bandwidth under IDS topology constraints unmeasured.
6. **Storage amplification range:** depends on compaction/GC policy of ids-store/ids-reclaim; bench reports ratios, targets are product decisions.
7. **ids-time granularity:** monotonic tick resolution must be sufficient for sub-microsecond crypto benchmarks; clock source to be confirmed.
8. **Nightly libtest bench:** explicitly not adopted; revisited only if criterion/divan prove insufficient for a specific workload class.
9. **Cross-node sketch merge:** t-digest/DDSketch merge semantics across replicas need a single configured compression/ε; convergence of merged percentiles vs per-node percentiles untested.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-bench` crate, not a folder | Project rule: separate crates for new capabilities; keeps existing crates focused |
| criterion.rs as primary harness | Statistical confidence (CI, outliers, regression detection), stable Rust, ecosystem standard (ed25519-dalek uses it) |
| divan as optional cross-check | Different measurement style (fast startup, instruction-count-friendly, async, contention); guards against harness-specific bias |
| bencher/libtest bench rejected | Nightly-only, unmaintained; IDS targets stable toolchains |
| HDR histogram primary for p50/p95/p99 | Constant-time record (~3–6 ns), fixed memory, tail accuracy on bounded ranges; subms cookbook data |
| t-digest / DDSketch for cross-worker aggregation | Mergeable, tight tails (t-digest) or relative error (DDSketch) where HDR's fixed range is insufficient |
| Coordinated-omission correction on fixed-rate drivers | Prevents stall-masking tail illusions (subms cookbook / Gil Tene) |
| Welford online mean/variance | O(1) streaming stats without storing samples; mergeable partitions |
| All traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |
| Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | IDS crypto policy; consumed via ids-crypto primitive IDs, never implemented in ids-bench |
| ids-time monotonic for all deadlines | No wall-clock or RTT-derived timeouts; correct under arbitrary delays |
| out_eq_in invariant as self-check | bytes-out == bytes-in + acked from ids-000-aa; catches lost byte accounting |
| Run manifest per run (git, toolchain, host, config) | Numbers comparable only within identical manifest (no universal thresholds, per camus/hotpath findings) |
| Regression detection via criterion comparison + p-value | 95% CI; wall-clock noise >2.5× on identical code → instruction counts for CI pass/fail |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 049 creates `ids-doc`, the IDS crate that owns the **formal specification layer** of the IDS: the IDS Architecture Specification (natural-language + formal), TLA+ specifications for the session, stream, and wire layers, PlusCal algorithm models, formal invariants, a protocol conformance specification, determinism proofs, and a conformance suite generator. `ids-doc` is a specification-and-verification crate: it ships `.tla`/PlusCal sources and markdown specifications, checked with the TLA+ toolchain (TLC model checker, TLAPS proof system, Apalache symbolic model checker), not Rust implementation logic. It references canonical types and sealed trait contracts from `ids-000-aa` (the master crate) and models all traffic exclusively as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

The crate is organized in three horizontal layers matching the IDS data path:

1. **Session layer** — TLA+ spec + PlusCal model of the session state machine: session creation, expiration, session key management, state transitions, client affinity/stickiness, session token management, replay protection (Phase 050 `ids-session` implements this contract).
2. **Stream layer** — TLA+ spec + PlusCal model of stream reassembly, ordering, deduplication, exactly-once delivery, and overlap handling (IDS `ids-stream` implements this contract).
3. **Wire layer** — TLA+ spec + PlusCal model of wire framing, message types, and dispatch over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only.

Each layer has: a TLA+ module (`Init ∧ [][Next]_vars ∧ Liveness` pattern), an optional PlusCal algorithm model (translated to TLA+, checked by TLC), shared formal invariants, refinement mappings to an abstract IDS spec, determinism proofs, and conformance-suite coverage. Tooling: TLA+ syntactic analyzer, TLC model checker, TLAPS for proofs, Apalache for symbolic checking (state-explosion mitigation), VS Code TLA+ extension or TLA+ Toolbox as authoring environment.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh in `ids-doc` or any spec it references. All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 — any cryptographic primitive mentioned in a spec must come from this list.

A skeleton `ids-doc` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-doc/`. `ids-000-aa` declares canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `RecordId`, `FragmentId`, `SnapshotId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Checksum`, `AnomalyType`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts — all referenced by `ids-doc`, never redefined. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-doc` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is the formal contract layer: every IDS crate that owns a state machine (session, stream, wire) must have a corresponding TLA+/PlusCal spec in `ids-doc`, and its implementation must conform to that spec (verified by the conformance suite). `ids-doc` produces no runtime behavior itself — it produces specifications, models, invariants, proofs, and a conformance-suite generator.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    IDS IMPLEMENTATION LAYER (ids-* crates)                   │
│  ids-session (Phase 050), ids-stream, ids-wire — implement the formal specs  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                 Phase 049: ids-doc (FORMAL SPECIFICATION LAYER)              │
│  ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │\n│  │ IDS Arch.    │ │ TLA+ specs     │ │ PlusCal models │ │ Conformance  │ │\n│  │ Specification│ │ (session/      │ │ (session/      │ │ suite gen.   │ │\n│  │ (markdown)   │ │  stream/wire)  │ │  stream/wire)  │ │ (BFS + oracle│ │\n│  └────────────────┘ └────────────────┴────────────────┴── + refusals)  │ │\n│  ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │\n│  │ Formal         │ │ Protocol       │ │ Determinism    │ │ Tooling      │ │\n│  │ Invariants     │ │ Conformance    │ │ proofs         │ │ (TLC/TLAPS/  │ │\n│  │ (safety/liveness│ │ (refinement    │ │ (inductive     │ │  Apalache)   │ │\n│  │  invariants)   │ │  mappings)     │ │  invariants)   │ │              │ │\n│  └────────────────┘ └────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────┘ │ │\n└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────┘\n                                                                 │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams\n┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▼────────────┐\n│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                  │\n│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType ≤ 1024 B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload)      │\n│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                    │\n│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS    │\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Spec-to-implementation contract per layer:**
1. The TLA+ module defines `Init` (initial-state predicate), `Next` (next-state relation over unprimed/primed variables), and `Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Liveness`.
2. The PlusCal model (where used) encodes the same algorithm imperatively (labels = atomic steps, `await` for guards, `either` for nondeterminism) and is translated to TLA+ (translator inserts `BEGIN TRANSLATION`/`END TRANSLATION`).
3. TLC checks safety invariants and temporal properties over bounded constants; Apalache symbolically checks larger instances; TLAPS proves determinism/refinement theorems.
4. A refinement mapping (`INSTANCE Abstract WITH ...`) proves the concrete layer spec implements the abstract IDS spec (`Concrete!Spec => Abstract!Spec`).
5. The conformance suite is generated mechanically from the model: breadth-first tree over the reachable state space, one test per root-to-leaf path, refusal checks at every state, counterexample traces replayable against the live implementation.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 TLA+ language and toolchain (spec authoring + model checking)

TLA+ (Temporal Logic of Actions, Leslie Lamport) is a formal specification language based on untyped ZF set theory, first-order logic, and temporal logic of actions. A system is specified as allowed behaviors — sequences of states — via `Init` (initial-state predicate) and `Next` (next-state relation: unprimed variables = pre-state, primed = post-state). A typical spec has the form `Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Liveness`, where stuttering steps (unchanged variables) are allowed so specs are stutter-invariant and composable. Specifications are organized in modules that `EXTEND` other modules (e.g. `Integers`, `Sequences`, `TLC`, `FiniteSets`).

Toolchain:
- **TLA+ syntactic analyzer** — parses modules; the VS Code TLA+ extension (TLA+ Foundation) or TLA+ Toolbox runs "Parse module". Requires a JVM (Java ≥ 11) for the underlying `tla2tools.jar`.
- **TLC model checker** — exhaustively explores all reachable states of a finite instantiation (bounded constants), checks invariants (safety) and temporal properties (liveness), produces counterexample traces on violation. Modes: model checking (exhaustive) and simulation (random, incomplete). Supports symmetry sets (permutes model values, reduces state space ~n!, safety-only — incompatible with liveness checks), constraint bindings, and worker parallelism.
- **TLAPS (TLA+ Proof System)** — interactive proof assistant for theorems asserted in modules (determinism, refinement mappings, inductive invariants), with automatic backends (SMT, provers, propositional temporal logic decision procedure).
- **Apalache** — symbolic model checker for TLA+, complements TLC when state explosion bounds TLC; checks bounded executions without enumerating all states.
- Authoring: VS Code TLA+ extension (Ctrl+T translates PlusCal; runs TLC; visualizes results) or TLA+ Toolbox (GUI, `Translate PlusCal Algorithm` Ctrl+T, `TLC Model Checker` run).

PlusCal (2009, Lamport) is an algorithm language embedded as a comment in a TLA+ module (`(* --algorithm name { ... } *)`), with C-like (c-syntax) and Pascal-like (p-syntax) variants. It translates to human-readable TLA+ (`BEGIN TRANSLATION`/`END TRANSLATION` blocks with checksums). Features: simple imperative constructs, powerful TLA+ expressions, nondeterminism (`either`/`or`), labels marking atomic steps, `await` guards, `with`/`choose` for nondeterministic choice, `print`, `assert`, macros (compile-time inline, no labels/loops), procedures (runtime call stack, labels allowed, `call ... ;` then a label or `return`, recursion allowed, requires `Sequences`), processes (each process has its own `pc`), fair/fair+ processes (weak/strong fairness constraints on actions), label modifiers (`+`, `-`). The translation semantics is formal (a TLA+ spec of the translator itself, executable by TLC).

Sources: Lamport "Specifying Systems" book (lamport.org/tla/book.html); "Specifying and Verifying Systems With TLA+" (Lamport/Matthews, Init/Next/Liveness form); PlusCal paper (Microsoft Research); PlusCal Tutorial sessions (lamport.org/tla/tutorial); Learn TLA+ (learntla.com); tlaplus/Examples repo; vscode-tlaplus docs (Java requirement, install steps); PlusCal translator docs (Inria/TLA+ Toolbox); Distributed PlusCal paper (channels, send/receive primitives); p-manual (p-syntax/c-syntax, Euclid example).

#### 3.2 Session TLA+ specification (session state machine)

Scope: session creation, expiration, session key management, session state machine, client affinity/stickiness, session token management, session replay protection. Modeled as a TLA+ state machine: variables include `sessions` (map SessionId → SessionRecord), `state[session]` ∈ {Created, Active, Expired, Revoked}, `tokens`, `last_activity[session]`, `replay_cache` (nonce + per-peer sequence), `keys[session]` (ed25519-derived session keys from ids-000-aa canonical types). Actions: `CreateSession`, `BindToken`, `Renew`, `Expire`, `Revoke`, `AffinityAssign`, `ReplayCheck`. Fairness: weak fairness on expiry progress so sessions do not stall indefinitely under `fair process` semantics where sessions are modeled as processes. Invariants: at most one `Active` state per SessionId; a token binds to exactly one session; an expired session never transitions back to Active; replay cache rejects (peer, seq) duplicates within TTL. PlusCal model: one `fair process (s ∈ Sessions)` per session with labels for each action, atomic steps between labels, `await` on preconditions (e.g. `await state[self] = "Active"`).

Refs: Learn TLA+ state machines (either/await state machines); tiny-tlaplus-examples StateMachine.tla (fair algorithm, define block, Init/Next/Spec, WF_vars fairness); PlusCal tutorial session 2 (TLC models, constants); Distributed PlusCal (message send/receive channels for session messages over Endpoint).

#### 3.3 Stream TLA+ specification (stream reassembly / ordering)

Scope: stream reassembly, in-order delivery, deduplication, exactly-once semantics, overlap/conflict handling (relevant to NIDS-style stream reassembly where reassembly policy must match the receiver's; overlapping chunks modeled explicitly), carrier-agnostic delivery (loss, duplication, reordering tolerated — no TCP assumptions). Variables: `chunks` (map ChunkId → bytes), `reassembled[stream]` (sequence of bytes), `next_expected[stream]`, `dup_seen`, `gaps[stream]`, `delivery[stream]` (delivered offsets). Actions: `ReceiveChunk`, `Reassemble`, `DeliverInOrder`, `DropDuplicate`, `GapTimeout`. Invariants: delivered bytes form a prefix of the reassembled stream (no gaps in delivery); no byte delivered twice (exactly-once); chunks with overlapping ranges are resolved by a deterministic tie-break rule (e.g., earliest arrival wins, recorded in the spec); delivery order matches stream order on every replica regardless of arrival order. PlusCal model: processes per stream with labels `Receive`, `Reassemble`, `Deliver`; `await` on contiguity (`next_expected` present) before delivery. Determinism: given the same multiset of chunks, every replica reaches the same reassembled state (convergence under reorder/dup/loss — CRDT-style argument adapted to stream reassembly).

Refs: LogPlayer TLA+/PlusCal spec (exactly-once delivery under shard/LogPlayer failures); "Overlapping data in network protocols: bridging OS and NIDS reassembly gap" (overlap types via interval algebra, NIDS reassembly consistency); stream reassembly DPI literature (TCP sequence reassembly, drop repeats); CCF Raft TLA+ specs (TLC nightly + CLI runs).

#### 3.4 Wire TLA+ specification (wire framing + dispatch over Endpoint)

Scope: wire format, framing, message types, dispatch — modeled strictly over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), opaque datagrams, no network stack concepts. Variables: `outbound[Endpoint]` (queue of Vec<u8> frames), `inbound[Endpoint]` (received frames), `wire_state` (framing state machine: awaiting header / reading payload / complete), `msg_types` registry, `framing_errors`. Actions: `SendFrame(endpoint, bytes)`, `ReceiveFrame(endpoint, bytes)`, `ParseHeader`, `ParsePayload`, `Dispatch`, `DropMalformed`. Invariants: every dispatched message passes schema validation before any semantic effect (bomb guards: max frame size, max nesting depth before parse); the carrier is untrusted — messages are authenticated over payload bytes so they survive re-framing; no spec variable references IP/TCP/UDP/ports/DNS; `CarrierType` ∈ {Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom} (ids-000-aa canonical type) is the only carrier dimension. PlusCal model: a `process WireDispatcher` with labels per framing step and `await` guards on buffer completeness.

Refs: Practical TLA+ (wire transfer feature example, PlusCal processes); AgentConform / AgentRFC (protocol specs as TLA+ invariants with Protocol/Environment/Adversary action separation — wire layer modeled adversarially: environment = untrusted carrier); M2D2 formal data model for IDS alert correlation (IDS formal modeling precedent).

#### 3.5 PlusCal models (algorithm-level)

PlusCal is used where an imperative algorithm presentation aids review: session handshake, stream reassembly loop, wire dispatch loop. Each `.tla` module contains one or more `--algorithm` blocks inside comments; the translator (`pcal.trans` / VS Code Ctrl+T / Toolbox File → Translate PlusCal Algorithm) inserts the TLA+ translation below. Models use macros for recurring inline patterns (`send(to, msg)` appends to a network queue; `rcv(p, var)` blocks on a FIFO queue — these map directly to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagram send/receive), procedures for subroutines with local variables and `call ... ;` + label/return discipline, and `fair process` / `fair+` where liveness (progress) matters. Each PlusCal module carries its own TLC config (constants, invariants, properties). Translation integrity is an acceptance criterion: the inserted translation must round-trip (re-translation produces identical output).

Refs: PlusCal cheat sheet (pluscal.help; macros vs procedures table; call/return semantics); Learn TLA+ procedures and macros (stack representation, `Sequences` requirement); PlusCal translator docs (BEGIN/END TRANSLATION checksums, CTRL+T workflow); Distributed PlusCal (send/receive channels over networks — mapped to Endpoint datagrams); p-manual (c-syntax/p-syntax; Euclid; macro expansion rules).

#### 3.6 Formal invariants (safety + liveness)

Invariants are state predicates true in all reachable states; TLC checks `[]Inv` for each invariant entry. TLA+ has no special "invariant" construct — invariants are ordinary predicates checked by TLC as temporal properties — so `ids-doc` distinguishes: (a) type invariants (every variable is in its allowed domain — checked first, on every state), (b) safety invariants (bad things never happen: no double delivery, no expired session active, no replayed nonce accepted, no frame parsed beyond budget), (c) liveness properties (good things eventually: every session eventually expires or is revoked; every in-order complete stream eventually delivers; every sent frame is eventually dispatched or dropped) expressed with `<>` / `~>` / `[]<>` operators and checked as TLC temporal properties (separate config per invariant, since bundling stops TLC at the first violation). Stutter-invariance: all specs are stutter-invariant (no next-time operator); fairness constraints (`WF_vars`, `SF_vars`) on `fair process` actions rule out infinite stuttering where progress is required. Symmetry sets are used only for safety checks (never liveness) to tame state explosion.

Refs: Learn TLA+ temporal properties ([] / <> / ~> / stutter-invariance); Hillel Wayne weak & strong fairness; Lamport stutter-invariant temporal properties paper; AgentConform (per-invariant TLC configs, counterexample classification); "Specifying and Verifying Systems With TLA+" (safety = Inv, liveness = fairness conditions).

#### 3.7 Protocol conformance specification

Each concrete layer spec (session/stream/wire PlusCal/TLA+) is related to its abstract IDS spec by a refinement mapping: `Concrete!Spec => Abstract!Spec` expressed as `THEOREM Spec => HL!Spec` where `HL == INSTANCE AbstractSpec WITH ...` substitutes concrete variables/expressions for the abstract module's constants and variables (Abadi & Lamport refinement mapping existence; Lamport Specifying Systems Ch. 10; TLA+ Video Course Lecture 10; "Proving Safety" refinement-mapping note). The conformance specification additionally defines: the testable state space (bounded constants), the oracle (state after each action compared against the spec's allowed transitions), refusal checks (at every reachable state, every action the spec forbids must be refused by the implementation), and test generation: breadth-first tree over the reachable state space, one executable test per root-to-leaf path, each unused transition gets a short refusal test, prefix-subsumed tests dropped. This mirrors HoldSpec (machine-checked TLA+ model → conformance suite, 100% seeded-defect detection) and AgentConform (two-phase: model-check invariants, replay counterexample traces against live implementations).

Refs: "Proving Safety" refinement mapping note (Spec => HL!Spec); TLA+ Video Course lecture 10 (AB2 implements AB under refinement mapping); Hillel Wayne "Specification Refinement" (INSTANCE WITH mapping); HoldSpec (arxiv 2610.14419 — TLA+ state machine → conformance suite, BFS test tree, refusal checks, 100% seeded-defect detection); AgentRFC/AgentConform (TLA+ invariants as conformance spec; two-phase checker; counterexample replay against SDKs); Remix framework (conformance checking detects model↔implementation deviations); TraceFix (TLC counterexample → repair loop, replays against implementation).

#### 3.8 Determinism proofs

Determinism property: given the same initial state and the same sequence of inputs, every replica of the layer reaches the same state trajectory (state equivalence under any delivery order/duplication/delay — matching the carrier-agnostic unknown-membership model). Proven as TLAPS theorems: (a) the next-state relation is a deterministic function of (state, input) modulo commutative independent actions; (b) commutative actions commute (confluence); (c) fairness ensures progress. Inductive invariants (inference tools such as endive can discover candidate inductive invariants; TLAPS verifies them) establish that all reachable states satisfy determinism-relevant conditions (e.g., no two distinct states are observationally equivalent-but-divergent). TLC checks bounded instances exhaustively as a complement (not a substitute) to the proof. Determinism is proved separately for session, stream, and wire modules, then compositionally for the stack (refinement preserves determinism under the refinement mapping).

Refs: endive (inductive invariant inference for TLA+ protocols, verified with TLAPS, TwoPhase benchmark); MIT 6.826 concurrency lecture (invariant proofs by induction over atomic actions); PharOS determinacy proof in TLA+/TLAPS (determinacy = local states independent of scheduling order — directly applicable); "Specifying and Verifying Systems With TLA+" (assertional reasoning style); TLA+ Hyperbook (determinism/stuttering).

#### 3.9 TLA+ model checking & state explosion management

TLC state space grows with constants (sessions N, streams M, chunk sequences K). Mitigations researched: (1) symmetry sets over model values (reduces state space ~n!, safety checks only; never used with liveness; getchas: expensive on large sets, hidden asymmetry, no CHOOSE over symmetric sets); (2) constraint bindings (`TLCGet("level") < N`, `FastInit`/`FastNext` subsets); (3) Apalache symbolic checking for deeper bounds; (4) separate TLC config per invariant (per-invariant checking avoids early-stop masking); (5) simulation mode for rapid falsification before exhaustive runs. Acceptance: each spec must TLC-check within a bounded time budget at the configured constants; symmetry sets declared in config + `SYMMETRY` directive.

Refs: Learn TLA+ optimizing model checking (symmetry sets); "An introduction to symmetry in TLA+" (gotchas, liveness incompatibility); TLA+ By Example symmetry sets (57254 → 1647 states); Compositional Model Checking of Consensus Protocols (IPA abstraction for state explosion); CCF raft TLA+ (nightly TLC, CLI `tlc.sh`).

#### 3.10 IDS Architecture Specification (natural-language + formal)

The markdown specification in `spec/` defines: the three layers (session, stream, wire) and their responsibilities; the carrier boundary (`ids-carrier::Endpoint` only; opaque `Vec<u8>`; `CarrierType` ∈ {Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom}); the allowed-crypto allowlist (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305) and a rule that any spec mentioning crypto names only these primitives; the conformance method (refinement + generated suite); determinism requirement; type surface from `ids-000-aa` (never redefined: `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `RecordId`, `FragmentId`, `SnapshotId`, `RecoveryProof`, `Checksum`, `AnomalyType`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `Error`). The architecture spec is the human-readable companion to the TLA+/PlusCal modules; every claim in it must have a corresponding invariant, model, or proof obligation in `tla/`/`pluscal/`/`proofs/`.

### Threat Model

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|
| TLC state explosion hides real violations | Specification confidence | Symmetry sets (safety only), constraint bounds, per-invariant TLC configs, Apalache symbolic fallback; time budget per spec |
| Spec–implementation divergence | Conformance integrity | Conformance suite generated mechanically from the model (BFS test tree + refusal oracle); counterexample traces replayed against live implementations (HoldSpec/AgentConform pattern) |
| Nondeterminism masks bugs | Determinism guarantee | Explicit `either`/`with` nondeterminism in models; determinism proofs (TLAPS + inductive invariants); convergence under reorder/dup/loss |
| Infinite stutter breaks liveness | Liveness guarantees | Liveness checked separately from safety as temporal properties; `WF`/`SF` fairness on `fair process` actions; symmetry never enabled for liveness |
| Cross-layer inconsistency (session/stream/wire) | Specification coherence | Shared invariant module; refinement mappings between each concrete layer and the abstract IDS spec; common types from ids-000-aa |
| Conformance gaps (untested transitions) | Test completeness | Refusal checks at every reachable state; BFS covers all reachable states; prefix-subsumed tests dropped; unused transitions get short refusal tests |
| Carrier assumptions leak into specs | Carrier-agnostic integrity | Spec variables model only `Endpoint` datagrams; invariant: no IP/TCP/UDP/port/DNS symbols in any module; carrier treated as untrusted environment (AgentConform adversary pattern) |
| Crypto primitive misuse in specs | Allowed-crypto rule | Allowlist invariant: only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 named; reviewed per module |
| Refinement mapping unsound | Conformance soundness | Mapping proven as TLAPS theorem (`Spec => HL!Spec`); substitution documented in `WITH` clause; machine-checked |

### Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **TLA+ layer spec pattern (all three layers):**
```
---- MODULE session_spec ----
EXTENDS Integers, Sequences, TLC, FiniteSets
CONSTANTS Sessions, MaxTokens, ReplayTTL
VARIABLES state, tokens, last_activity, replay_cache, keys
TypeInvariant == /\ state \in [Sessions -> {"Created","Active","Expired","Revoked"}]
                /\ tokens \subseteq SessionId  \* etc.
Init == /\ state = [s \in Sessions |-> "Created"] /\ tokens = {} /\ ...
Next == \/ CreateSession \/ BindToken \/ Renew \/ Expire \/ Revoke \/ ReplayCheck
Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Liveness
```
Session Liveness example: `/\ \A s \in Sessions : <> (state[s] = "Expired" \/ state[s] = "Revoked")` (weak fairness on expiry actions).
- **PlusCal model pattern:** `--algorithm session { variables ...; process (s \in Sessions) { start: await ...; create: ...; goto start; } }` — translated to TLA+ with `pc` program counter; labels mark atomic steps; `fair process` adds `WF` constraints.
- **Refinement mapping:** `HL == INSTANCE abstract_ids_spec WITH sessions <- state, ...; THEOREM SessionSpec => HL!Spec`.
- **Conformance suite generation:** BFS over reachable states from `Init` via `Next`; emit one executable test per root-to-leaf path; for each state, refusal tests for every action `Next` forbids; drop prefix-subsumed tests; oracle compares post-state to spec-allowed transitions and runs refusal checks.
- **Determinism proof (TLAPS):** `Determinism == \A s1, s2, inp : ...` — given equal inputs, equal resulting states; proved via inductive invariants + confluence of independent actions; compositional across layers via refinement mapping preservation.
- **Replay cache model:** `replay_cache[peer] \in [Seq -> Bool]`; `Accept(peer, seq) == ~replay_cache[peer][seq]` then cache updated; bounded by TTL (stale entries evicted — modeled as nondeterministic eviction within TTL bound).

### Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Layer granularity:** Whether session/stream/wire suffice or a fourth "control-plane" TLA+ spec is needed (e.g., topology or membership) — decided when Phase 050 `ids-session` contract is written.
2. **PlusCal vs raw TLA+ split:** PlusCal is preferable for algorithm presentation (session handshake, stream loop) but cannot express everything raw TLA+ can (parameterized modules, advanced recursion limits); the boundary between PlusCal models and raw TLA+ specs is per-module, not yet fixed.
3. **TLC constants bounds:** Choosing bounded constants (Sessions, streams, chunk sequences) that falsify bugs without making model checking intractable — tuned per layer during implementation; symmetry-set gotchas (never with liveness) apply.
4. **TLAPS proof effort:** Determinism and refinement theorems require interactive proof work; the proportion provable automatically vs. requiring manual TLAPS steps is unknown until theorems are stated.
5. **Conformance runner implementation:** The suite generator produces executable tests, but the black-box runner hook into ids-* implementations (how an implementation is driven and observed) is defined here only at the design level; validated at integration with Phase 050+ crates.
6. **Apalache adoption:** Whether to adopt Apalache as a symbolic fallback for deeper bounds than TLC allows — toolchain maturity vs. benefit unmeasured.
7. **Tooling environment:** JVM requirement for TLA+ tools; authoring via VS Code extension vs. TLA+ Toolbox — team preference undecided; both documented in `src/tools/`.

---

### Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| TLA+ for layer specs (`Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ Liveness`) | Standard, tool-supported (TLC/TLAPS/Apalache); stutter-invariant and composable; industry-proven for distributed protocols |
| PlusCal for algorithm models | Imperative pseudocode feel eases review of session/stream/wire algorithms; translates to checkable TLA+; labels = atomic steps match carrier-agnostic datagram steps |
| Three layers: session / stream / wire | Mirrors the IDS data path; each has an owning implementation crate (ids-session Phase 050, ids-stream, ids-wire) with a formal contract |
| Refinement mapping per layer (`Spec => HL!Spec`) | Proves concrete layer implements the abstract IDS spec; properties flow downward automatically (Hillel Wayne refinement argument) |
| Determinism via TLAPS + inductive invariants | Determinism is a hyperproperty over execution pairs; TLC bounds it only finitely; TLAPS gives the general proof; endive-style invariant discovery as candidate source |
| Conformance suite generated mechanically (BFS + refusal oracle) | HoldSpec evidence: generated suite detects 100% of seeded defects vs 56–69% for random/hand-written suites; counterexamples replayable against implementations |
| Symmetry sets for safety only | ~n! state-space reduction; incompatible with liveness; never applied where liveness is checked |
| Carrier boundary = `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only | Preserves carrier-agnostic architecture; specs treat carrier as untrusted environment; messages authenticated over payload survive re-framing |
| Allowed-crypto allowlist as spec invariant | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 may appear in any spec; grep-enforced |
| ids-000-aa types never redefined | Single source of truth; specs reference canonical types and sealed trait contracts |

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 050 creates `ids-session`, the IDS crate that owns client-session binding and session state. It provides session creation, session expiration (idle + absolute timeouts), session key management, a session state machine, session recovery after disruption, client affinity, session stickiness, session token management, and session replay protection — all carrier-agnostic. `ids-session` does not open sockets or drive any transport directly; it binds a client to a session context, issues and validates session tokens, derives session keys, enforces a finite-state session lifecycle, and ships every protection-relevant message as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

Sessions are modeled as a small finite-state machine (Created → Bound → Active → [Idle → Expired | Suspended → Resuming → Active | Terminated]) keyed by a session token. Each session carries an ephemeral client-bound key pair (ed25519) used for proof-of-possession binding: every session-bound message carries an ed25519 signature proving the presenter holds the session's private key, preventing session-token theft and replay from a different client. Tokens are opaque random values (>=128 bits entropy per NIST SP 800-63B / OWASP ASVS 3.2.2) with a separate verification secret; revocation uses a bounded denylist (token rotation lineage or jti-based) checked server-side.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-session` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-session` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-session/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, plus sealed trait contracts and error types. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet (idle/absolute/renewal timeouts, ≥64 bits entropy session IDs, CSPRNG generation, server-side enforcement); NIST SP 800-63B Session Management (session secret ≥64 bits, opaque string, directly presented or cryptographically proven possession); OWASP ASVS V3 Session Management (3.2.2 ≥64 bits entropy; timeout aligned with NIST 800-63); MDN Web Docs session management (idle/absolute/renewal timeouts, 64-bit entropy minimum); OWASP WSTG Session Timeout testing (server-side idle/absolute timeouts, replay of old session ID must be rejected); RFC 4303 IPsec ESP anti-replay (per-SA 32-bit sequence number, sliding-window replay detection); RFC 8705 / RFC 9449 OAuth DPoP (proof-of-possession token binding to client key, `jti` replay detection, token substitution prevention); RFC 9700 OAuth 2.0 Security BCP (refresh token rotation with reuse detection OR sender-constraining via DPoP/mTLS); Device Bound Session Credentials (DBSC, W3C/webappsec-dbsc; Chrome origin trial) — hardware-bound private key proving session possession, short-lived cookies, proof on refresh; Hashicorp/Traefik/Envoy sticky sessions and consistent hashing (Ringhash/MagLev) for client affinity across backend churn; Socket.IO connection state recovery (session ID + last offset replay on reconnect, maxDisconnectionDuration, missed-packet restoration); WebSocket reconnection state sync (message sequence numbers, last-received tracking, gap replay); Signal double ratchet and Noise protocol handshake patterns (XX/IK/NK) for session key establishment and key evolution; EDHOC RFC 9528 + OSCORE RFC 8613 + ACE EDHOC/OSCORE profile (lightweight authenticated key exchange, OSCORE security context, replay protection via sequence numbers); DTLS 1.3 anti-replay (sliding-window bitmap per epoch, sequence-numbered records); mTLS / TLS-session-bound access tokens (binding tokens to a specific mTLS connection via exporter value); JWT blacklist/denylist patterns (Bloom filter, Redis TTL, streaming propagation, jti revocation); IPsec ESP replay window (RFC 4303 Section 3.4.3 sliding window).
