### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 056 creates `ids-operation-ref`, the IDS crate that owns **operation references (OpRef)**: nine-character alphanumeric operation IDs that are deliberately **separate from ordering positions**. An OpRef is a flat, opaque reference to a single logical operation (a message send, a state mutation, a resource creation, a write). It carries no ordering information — ordering is a separate concern owned by dataset-scoped ordering domains (Phase 055 `ids-ordering-domain`) via the canonical `OrderingPos` type in `ids-000-aa`. `OpRef` and `OrderingPos` are distinct canonical types in `ids-000-aa::types.rs` and must never be conflated or packed into one another (contrast Stellar SEP-0035, which packs ledger sequence + transaction order + operation index into one 64-bit ID — that conflation is exactly what this crate avoids).

`ids-operation-ref` provides: a 36^9 ≈ 1.016×10^14 namespace (alphabet 0-9A-Z, case-insensitive, nine positions); reference generation with uniqueness guarantees and collision detection; idempotency binding (an OpRef bound to normalized operation arguments); retry recognition (a repeated OpRef returns the stored outcome); commit-status lookup (Pending → Committed → Failed/Rejected); synchronization tracking over carrier-agnostic endpoints; recovery tracking for interrupted operations; and append-only audit records.

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-operation-ref` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-operation-ref` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-operation-ref/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, plus sealed trait contracts and error types. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Per CRATES.md and plan-013.md, `ids-operation-ref` (Phase 056) generates OpRef; `ids-write` binds/validates it. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned distributed-identifier design (random strings vs integers vs UUIDs vs KSUIDs vs URNs; opaque vs transparent; prefix disambiguation), unique-ID generation (DB counter, random+birthday, coordinator blocks, timestamp+node+counter composition), UUIDv4 collision probability (n²/2^123), UUIDv7 (RFC 9562), ULID (26-char Crockford Base32, sortable, monotonic option), short-ID Rust crates (block-id invertible integer→alphanumeric, terseid SHA256→base36→truncate with birthday-bound collision avoidance, nexus-id Base62Id/Base36Id), the IETF Idempotency-Key header pattern, Stripe and AWS idempotent-API designs (client token, ACID token+mutation recording, 24h pruning, mismatched-params rejection), Azure Idempotent Consumer (stable dedup key survives redelivery; never key on transport IDs), the "every retry needs the same operation ID" Intend/Attempt/Recognise/Resolve contract, ICP idempotency (dedup window + created_at_time validity), etcd revision as cluster-wide logical clock (total order, separate from any opaque reference), Stellar SEP-0035 (conflated op-ID-plus-ordering — the anti-pattern to avoid), CRDT op-based references (globally unique element identifiers, dots `(replica, counter)`, causal delivery), Automerge/JSON-CRDT operation IDs (Lamport `N x ReplicaID`, dedup by "already applied" check, buffer until dependencies satisfied), deterministic replay-safe operation IDs (blake2b over `{counter}` / `{parent_id}-{counter}`, monotonic counter, determinism invariant), YouTube-style 64/128-bit random IDs with no embedded metadata and cancelled IDs never reused, birthday-bound collision math (√N rule; p ≈ 1 − exp(−k(k−1)/(2·Nᴸ))), Crockford Base32 (excludes I/L/O/U), append-only audit logs and event sourcing as system of record, MongoDB resume tokens (oplog position, resume after crash), and deterministic idempotency keys derived from operation inputs (hash workflow+task+body, conditional writes, TTL expiration).

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-operation-ref` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical `OpRef`/`OrderingPos` types, sealed contracts, invariants, errors) and `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), with optional `ids-crypto` primitives (sha256/blake3 fingerprints, ed25519 signatures). Each concern — OpRef minting, uniqueness registration, collision detection, idempotency binding, retry recognition, commit-status lookup, synchronization tracking, recovery tracking, audit — is an independent module. The crate is a reference-generation and registry layer: it does not store application payloads itself; it mints OpRefs, registers them, binds them to operation arguments, and gates retry/commit handling before results flow back through `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (OpRef consumers)               │
│  ids-write, ids-store, ids-replication — mint/consume OpRefs per operation  │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 056: ids-operation-ref (THIS CRATE — OpRef registry)      │
│  ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ │
│  │ OpRef minting  │ │ Uniqueness     │ │ Collision      │ │ Idempotency  │ │ │
│  │ (sequential /  │ │ registration   │ │ detection      │ │ binding      │ │ │
│  │  random / hash-│ │ (OpRef → record│ │ (birthday-bound│ │ (OpRef ↔ arg │ │ │
│  │  based)        │ │  existence)    │  check + regen)  │  fingerprint)│ │ │
│  └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ └──────────────┘ │ │

│  │ Retry          │ │ Commit-status  │ │ Synchronization│ │ Recovery     │ │ │
│  │ recognition    │ │ lookup         │ │ tracking       │ │ tracking     │ │ │
│  │ (in-progress/  │ │ (Pending→      │ │ (which         │ │ (resume      │ │ │
│  │  committed/    │ │  Committed/    ││  endpoints saw │ │  tokens,     │ │ │
│  │  failed states)│ │  Failed/Rejected│ │  OpRef; via    │ │  checkpoints)│ │ │
│  └────────────────┘ └────────────────┘ │ Endpoint only) │ └──────────────┘ │ │
│  ┌────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐ │                │                  │ │ │
│  │ Audit records  │ │ types/contracts│ └────────────────┘                  │ │ │

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────▼──────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                  │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType ≤1024B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload: &[u8]) │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                    │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of OpRef minting + idempotent execution:** client submits an operation → `ids-operation-ref` mints an OpRef (9-char, 0-9A-Z), checks uniqueness against the registration set (collision detection), binds the OpRef to a blake3/sha256 fingerprint of normalized operation arguments, records state `Pending`, returns the OpRef as an opaque datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. On execution completion, commit-status transitions to `Committed(outcome)` / `Failed` / `Rejected`. A retry carrying the same OpRef is recognized: `InProgress` → report pending; `Committed` → replay stored outcome; same OpRef with a different argument fingerprint → reject as conflict. Audit records append every lifecycle event.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Nine-character alphanumeric ID space (36^9 namespace)

Nine positions over a 36-symbol alphabet (0-9, A-Z, case-insensitive) gives `36^9 = 101,559,956,668,416 ≈ 1.016×10^14` possible OpRefs — roughly 101.6 trillion. Per-character entropy is `log2(36) ≈ 5.17` bits, so a full 9-char OpRef holds ≈ 46.5 bits of space. This is large enough for modest operation volumes but small enough that **birthday-bound collisions are a real design constraint**, not a theoretical nicety.

Birthard-bound math (p ≈ 1 − exp(−k(k−1)/(2·N)) with N = 36^9):
- 50% collision probability at `k ≈ √N ≈ 10.1M` OpRefs.
- 1% collision probability at `k ≈ √(2·N·0.01) ≈ 1.43M` OpRefs.
- Exhaustion (100% collision) only after all N values are issued.

So random 9-char generation is safe only up to roughly the low millions of operations unless collision detection + regeneration is applied. For higher volumes the crate must either (a) use sequential/counter-based minting (collision-free by construction) or (b) cap random generation and fall back to sequential allocation once near the birthday bound. This is why **collision detection is a first-class content item** of the crate. Confusables (O/0, I/1, L/1) may be dropped from the alphabet (→ 32 symbols, Crockford-style) at a capacity cost (32^9 ≈ 3.6×10^13, ~2.8× smaller) for human-transcription friendliness; that is an unresolved trade-off (see Section 10).

References: distributed-identifier design and opaque-vs-transparent IDs [1]; unique-ID generation schemes (counter, random+birthday, coordinator blocks, timestamp+node+counter) [2]; short-ID Rust crates block-id (invertible integer→alphanumeric, successor to tiny_id, notes distributed state is hard so invertible mapping is preferred) [5] and terseid (SHA256→base36→truncate with birthday-problem collision avoidance and 4-tier fallback) [7]; ULID Crockford Base32 alphabet excluding I/L/O/U [8]; YouTube 64/128-bit random IDs with no embedded metadata [21]; birthday-bound engineering [23]; HardGuard25 birthday formula p = 1 − exp(−k(k−1)/(2·Nᴸ)) [24].

#### 3.2 OpRef separate from OrderingPos

`ids-000-aa` defines both `OpRef` (the nine-character alphanumeric operation reference) and `OrderingPos` (the monotonic logical position within a dataset-scoped ordering domain, Phase 055). They are distinct canonical types and must remain so:

- **OpRef** is an opaque, flat name for *which* operation occurred — no structure, no order information, no timestamp, no replica component. It is the identity clients use to retry, audit, and reference an operation.
- **OrderingPos** is a monotonic position used only for *where* the operation sits in an ordering domain's commit sequence. It is not a client-facing reference and must never be derived from or embedded in an OpRef.

This separation mirrors findings that conflating an identifier with its ordering position creates fragility: Stellar SEP-0035 packs ledger sequence + transaction order + operation index into one 64-bit "operation ID" [17], which couples the reference to a specific total order and makes re-ordering, re-issuance, and cross-domain reference awkward. etcd's revision [16] is similarly a cluster-wide logical clock (total order) used for MVCC, not an opaque client reference. UUIDv7/ULID embed timestamps for sortability [3][8] — also a coupling this crate rejects. An OpRef must be issuable before any ordering position is known, and two operations with adjacent OpRefs must not imply adjacent ordering positions.

References: opaque-vs-transparent and prefix disambiguation [1]; Stellar SEP-0035 conflated op-ID-plus-ordering [17]; etcd revision as logical clock [16]; UUIDv7 RFC 9562 / ULID sortable timestamps [3][8]; CRDOT globally unique element identifiers separate from positions [18]; Automerge operation IDs separate from object key/position [19].

#### 3.3 Reference generation strategies

Three generation strategies were evaluated:

1. **Sequential counter → base-36, zero-padded to 9 chars.** Collision-free by construction (monotonic counter, one issuer or sharded counter range). Simple and capacity-efficient, but reveals issuance rate and approximate order — acceptable internally but potentially undesirable for public-facing OpRefs. block-id's core lesson applies here: tight sequential state is hard to synchronize across nodes, so an invertible integer→alphanumeric mapping lets any sequential source (e.g., a per-domain counter in ids-ordering-domain) produce short opaque strings [5].

2. **Random 9-char + collision check + regenerate.** Opaque and order-revealing in neither direction, but bounded by the birthday limit (~10.1M for 50% collision). On a generated collision, regenerate with a fresh seed and re-check; track recent collisions to avoid livelock. terseid's 4-tier fallback (nonce escalation → length extension → long fallback → desperate fallback) is the reference pattern for collision recovery [7].

3. **Deterministic hash-based OpRef:** `blake3(normalized operation args || domain separator)` truncated/encoded to 9 chars base-36. Replay-safe: the same logical operation always mints the same OpRef, which makes dedup intrinsic (durable_lambda_core's OperationIdGenerator uses blake2b over `{counter}` or `{parent_id}-{counter}` with a monotonic counter and a determinism invariant for replay engines [20]). Collision risk is the same birthday bound, but collisions now indicate two *different* operations hashing to the same OpRef — detectable and rejectable via the uniqueness registry.

**Recommendation for Phase 056:** support all three behind a `GenerationStrategy` trait, with sequential counter as default (collision-free, fits 36^9) and random/deterministic as feature-gated alternatives. The default avoids collision complexity entirely for the common case; random is offered for callers that need opacity.

References: block-id [5]; nexus-id Base62Id 11-char / Base36Id 13-char [6]; terseid [7]; ULID [8]; durable_lambda_core deterministic OpId [20]; UUIDv4 collision n²/2^123 and monotonic mode [3].

#### 3.4 Uniqueness guarantees

Every minted OpRef is registered in an in-memory (optionally durable) uniqueness set keyed by OpRef before the operation is accepted. The uniqueness guarantee is: **no two accepted operations share an OpRef**. Issuance performs an existence check (`contains(OpRef)`) then registers atomically; a pre-existing OpRef triggers regeneration (random strategy) or counter advance (sequential strategy). Capacity is bounded by N = 36^9; near-exhaustion (configurable threshold, e.g. 80%) must raise a reusable event so callers rotate to a new domain/namespace rather than silently colliding.

Kubernetes' distinction is instructive: a `UID` is opaque, system-generated, unique across time and space; a `Name` is unique only within a scope at a time and enables idempotent creation [4]. OpRef plays the UID role (opaque, global, stable); it is deliberately *not* scoped or human-meaningful.

References: Kubernetes UID vs Name and idempotent creation [4]; block-id distributed-state difficulty [5]; CRDT dots `(replica, counter)` for uniqueness without central coordination [18].

#### 3.5 Collision detection

Collision detection runs on every OpRef issue:
1. Generate candidate OpRef (per strategy).
2. Check `registry.contains(candidate)`.
3. If present → collision: regenerate (random) / advance counter (sequential) / reject (deterministic, two distinct ops hashed alike).
4. If absent → register atomically, return OpRef.

The registry must be the single source of truth; no cache may bypass it. Collision rate and regeneration count are observable metrics. The birthday bound (Section 3.1) sets expectations: at 1M random OpRefs, collision probability ≈ 1%; at 5M ≈ 22%; regeneration handles these gracefully until the bound is approached, at which point the crate must switch strategies or exhaust the namespace.

References: birthday-bound [23][24]; terseid collision-avoidance fallback [7]; short-UID StackOverflow birthday analysis [25].

#### 3.6 Idempotency binding

Idempotency binding ties an OpRef to the *arguments* of the operation it names, so a retry is recognized as "the same logical operation" rather than "a new operation that happens to have the same ID."

Binding mechanics:
- Caller normalizes and validates operation arguments, then computes a fingerprint: `blake3` or `sha256` over canonical encoding of (operation type, target, normalized args).
- `ids-operation-ref` records `OpRef → {fingerprint, commit-status, outcome, created_at, attempts}`.
- On a repeat request with the same OpRef:
  - Same fingerprint → recognized retry: return stored outcome (or report InProgress).
  - Different fingerprint → **conflict**: reject with "same OpRef, different arguments" (never silently execute different work under one ID).
- The binding must be recorded atomically with the operation's first effect (ACID: token + mutation recorded together, per AWS idempotent-API guidance [11]).

This is the Stripe Idempotency-Key pattern: same key + same request → same result; same key + different payload → 422 conflict; keys pruned after a retention window (Stripe ≥24h) [10]. Azure Idempotent Consumer adds: the dedup key must be stable across redelivery and must not be a transport-level ID regenerated on retry [3]. ICP idempotency adds a validity window (`created_at_time`) so a dedup window's expiry cannot let a stale retry succeed [14].

References: IETF Idempotency-Key header (fingerprint option, 400/422) [9]; Stripe idempotency [10]; AWS idempotent APIs (ClientToken, ACID recording) [11]; On Idempotency Keys [12]; Azure Idempotent Consumer [3]; ICP idempotency window [14]; "every retry needs the same operation ID" Intend/Attempt/Recognise/Resolve [14b]; deterministic idempotency keys from operation inputs [28]; Microsoft agent idempotent tool actions [29].

#### 3.7 Retry recognition

Retry recognition answers "have we already seen this OpRef?" using the registry:
- `InProgress` → the first attempt is still executing; report pending to the caller, do not start a second execution (prevents duplicate side effects under concurrent retries — two workers must not both claim the same absent OpRef; conditional-write semantics apply [11]).
- `Committed(outcome)` → return the stored outcome; no re-execution.
- `Failed` / `Rejected` → terminal; caller may issue a *new* OpRef for a new attempt.
- Unknown OpRef → treat as new; mint/register per Section 3.3.

Retries must carry the *same* OpRef and *same* arguments across every retry path (transport retry, model-selected retry, task resumption after restart). Generating a fresh key per attempt defeats the contract [14b]. Retention of in-progress/committed records must cover the longest retry + queue + manual-recovery window; expired records are pruned per a configurable TTL (Stripe's 24h window; ICP's TX_WINDOW) [10][14].

References: Inference Institute Intend/Attempt/Recognise/Resolve [14b]; AWS idempotent APIs [11]; Azure Idempotent Consumer [3]; ICP dedup window [14]; deterministic key derivation [28]; Microsoft agent patterns [29].

#### 3.8 Commit-status lookup

Commit-status is a small terminal-state FSM per OpRef:

```
Pending --(execute success)--> Committed(outcome)
Pending --(execute failure)--> Failed
Pending --(reject/conflict)--> Rejected
Committed / Failed / Rejected  (terminal; transitions out are forbidden)
```

Lookup by OpRef returns the current status and, if Committed, the stored outcome. This is the commit-status lookup content item. Status transitions are durable (written before acknowledging completion) so a crash mid-execution leaves `InProgress` or `Pending` recoverable (Section 3.10). etcd's revision demonstrates how a monotonic commit position tracks state changes separately from any opaque reference — here, OrderingPos tracks commit order while OpRef tracks identity [16].

References: etcd revision/MVCC [16]; CRDT op dedup "already applied" check [19]; commit state machine concepts (Phase 057 ids-commit-state) [CRATES.md line 392].

#### 3.9 Synchronization tracking (carrier-agnostic)

Synchronization tracking records **which endpoints have observed which OpRefs**, so replication/reconciliation can ask "has endpoint E seen OpRef O?" without knowing how E is reached. Tracking is strictly over `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`): each observed OpRef is logged against the sender/recipient Endpoint. No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh is used or referenced; the crate has no concept of addresses beyond `CarrierType`. This preserves the carrier-agnostic stance enforced across CRATES.md and plan-002 (ids-carrier) [CRATES.md lines 9-11].

References: ids-carrier Endpoint (CarrierType + Vec<u8>) [CRATES.md lines 11, 62]; carrier-agnostic rule [CRATES.md lines 9-11].

#### 3.10 Recovery tracking

Recovery tracking handles interrupted operations: a crash between OpRef minting and commit leaves the operation's outcome unknown. On restart, `ids-operation-ref` reconciles via:
- Resume tokens / checkpoints recording per-OpRef progress (minted → bound → executing → committed).
- Monotonic `IdsTime` deadlines (from `ids-time`, following plan-050's pattern) for idle/absolute recovery windows.
- Pending/InProgress entries on restart are reconciled: retry from checkpoint or mark Failed, per the operation's resumability contract.
- MongoDB resume tokens (oplog position, resume after crash without missing events) are the reference model [27]; Resonate's Recovery Protocol (lease + heartbeat, fail-stop process model) is a related pattern [15].

Recovery does not require knowing the ordering position; it operates purely on OpRef identity, keeping recovery decoupled from ordering (Section 3.2).

References: MongoDB resume tokens [27]; Resonate Recovery Protocol [15]; ids-time IdsTime pattern (plan-050) [plan-050 line 30-36].

#### 3.11 Audit records

Every OpRef lifecycle event is appended to an immutable audit log: minted, bound (fingerprint), retry-recognized, committed (outcome), failed, rejected, recovered, pruned. Audit records are append-only (event sourcing: the append-only store is the system of record, improving auditability [26]), optionally chained/signed with ed25519 so later records cannot be rewritten undetected, and retained per a configurable policy (matching the idempotency retention window). Audit records are written through `ids-carrier::Endpoint` if shipped off-node, never via a direct transport.

References: Event Sourcing append-only store [26]; audit-log design (transactional outbox, idempotent consumers, protected archive) [22]; ed25519 is the only allowed signature primitive [prompt line 846].

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Mitigation ||
||--------|-----------|-------------|
|| OpRef collision (two ops share one ID) | Uniqueness registry + existence check before issue; collision detection + regeneration; near-exhaustion threshold event (80% of 36^9) to rotate namespace ||
|| Birthday-bound exhaustion of random generation | Cap random issuance; fall back to sequential counter; switch GenerationStrategy before approaching √N ≈ 10.1M ||
|| OpRef reused with different arguments (conflict) | Idempotency binding: same OpRef + different blake3/sha256 fingerprint → 422-style conflict reject; never silently execute different work ||
|| Duplicate side effect from concurrent retries | Atomic claim of OpRef before execution (conditional-write semantics); InProgress state blocks second execution ||
|| Stale retry after dedup window expiry | Configurable retention TTL (e.g., 24h Stripe-style / ICP TX_WINDOW); created_at_time validity bound ||
|| Lost outcome (crash mid-execution) | Durable commit-status FSM; Pending/InProgress reconciled on restart via resume tokens/checkpoints ||
|| Carrier assumptions leaking in | No std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/wireless deps; all traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint only ||
|| Non-allowed crypto | Only ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (via ids-crypto); sha256/blake3 for fingerprints, ed25519 optional for audit signing ||
|| Audit log tampering | Append-only, optionally ed25519-chained, immutable retention policy ||
|| Namespace exhaustion (all 36^9 issued) | Rotation event at threshold; new domain/namespace; never reuse cancelled OpRefs (YouTube pattern: cancelled IDs never recycled) ||

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

Phase 056 depends on and integrates with:

|| Crate | Role in Phase 056 ||
||-------|-------|-------------------|
|| `ids-000-aa` | Canonical types `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `OpState`, `CommitState`; sealed trait contracts; invariants; error types (master crate — never redefined here) ||
|| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); sole traffic channel; send/receive datagrams only ||
|| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: sha256/blake3 (argument fingerprints), ed25519 (optional audit signing); `ids-operation-ref` consumes primitive IDs only ||
|| `ids-time` | Monotonic `IdsTime` for deadlines/retention windows (pattern from plan-050 ids-session) ||
|| `ids-ordering-domain` (Phase 055) | Dataset-scoped ordering positions (`OrderingPos`) — kept strictly separate from `OpRef` ||
|| `ids-write` (Phase after 056) | Binds/validates generated OpRefs; `ids-operation-ref` generates; `ids-write` binds/validates (per CRATES.md/plan-013) ||

**Integration points:**
- `ids-operation-ref` **generates** OpRef; `ids-write` **binds/validates** OpRef to operations (allocator visibility split per plan-013.md).
- OpRefs and outcomes flow as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; the crate never opens a socket or imports a carrier-specific type.
- Commit-status results feed `ids-commit-state` (Phase 057) write state machine (accepted → ordered → executing → committed …).
- Recovery/checkpoint data may be persisted via the store contract from `ids-000-aa`, but no storage backend is mandated by this crate.
- No dependency on libp2p/TCP/IP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS or any wireless carrier — preserves I-CARR-001 carrier-agnostic stance.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 OpRef type and namespace

```rust
// OpRef: nine-character opaque reference, alphabet 0-9A-Z (case-insensitive), length 9
// Namespace size: N = 36^9 = 101,559,956,668,416 (~1.016e14)
// Per-character entropy: log2(36) ≈ 5.17 bits; total ≈ 46.5 bits
struct OpRef([u8; 9]);   // validated at construction; never reveals ordering
```

`OpRef` is distinct from `OrderingPos` (ids-000-aa). `OpRef` is never constructed from an `OrderingPos`, never contains a timestamp/replica/counter field, and is never sortable-by-creation by design.

#### 7.2 Birthday-bound collision math

```
N = 36^9 = 101,559,956,668,416
P(collision after k) ≈ 1 − exp(−k·(k−1) / (2·N))
k @ 50% collision  ≈ √N  ≈ 10,077,696  (~10.1M)
k @ 1% collision   ≈ √(2·N·0.01) ≈ 1,425,000 (~1.43M)
```

Random generation is viable to ~low-millions; beyond that, sequential minting or namespace rotation is required.

#### 7.3 Minting algorithm (all strategies)

```
mint(strategy) -> OpRef:
  loop:
    candidate = strategy.generate()          // sequential / random / blake3-based
    if registry.contains(candidate):         // collision
       strategy.on_collision()               // regenerate / advance / reject
       continue
    registry.register(candidate)             // atomic claim
    return candidate
```

Sequential strategy: `counter → base36 → zero-pad to 9`; counter sharded per ordering domain (never packed into OpRef).
Deterministic strategy: `candidate = base36(truncate(blake3(normalized_args || domain_separator), 9))`.

#### 7.4 Idempotency binding

```
fingerprint = blake3(canonical_encode(operation_type, target, normalized_args))   // or sha256
record = { opref, fingerprint, status: Pending, outcome: None, attempts: 0, created_at }
on repeat(opref, fingerprint):
  if record.fingerprint == fingerprint:
     return record.status/outcome   // recognized retry; Committed → replay outcome
  else:
     reject(Conflict)               // same OpRef, different arguments — forbidden
```

Record is stored atomically with the operation's first effect (ACID token + mutation).

#### 7.5 Commit-status FSM

```
Pending --execute ok--> Committed(outcome)   [terminal]
Pending --execute fail--> Failed              [terminal]
Pending --reject/conflict--> Rejected         [terminal]
Committed / Failed / Rejected: no outgoing transitions
```

#### 7.6 Synchronization tracking

```
observe(opref, endpoint: ids-carrier::Endpoint):
  sync_map[opref].insert(endpoint)   // endpoint = (CarrierType, Vec<u8>) only
queried(opref) -> Set<Endpoint>
```

No address parsing, no IP/port extraction; `Endpoint` is opaque.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Alphabet size:** 36 symbols (0-9A-Z, case-insensitive, 36^9) vs. dropping confusables (Crockford-style 32 symbols, 32^9 ≈ 3.6×10^13) — trades human-transcription friendliness for ~2.8× capacity. Decision deferred.
2. **Default generation strategy:** sequential counter (collision-free, reveals rate) vs. random (opaque, birthday-bound limited) vs. deterministic hash (replay-safe). Recommend sequential default; final choice depends on caller opacity requirements.
3. **Coordination-free minting across nodes:** a single monotonic counter is collision-free but centralized; sharding counter ranges per ordering domain needs allocation logic from `ids-ordering-domain`; random-with-detection is coordination-free but capacity-limited. No decision yet.
4. **Durability of the uniqueness registry:** in-memory vs. persisted via the `ids-000-aa` store contract; cross-restart retry recognition requires durable registration. Backend undefined.
5. **Retention window:** idempotency/commit-status/audit record TTL (Stripe ≥24h; ICP TX_WINDOW) — workload-dependent, not yet quantified.
6. **Audit signing:** whether ed25519 chaining of audit records is mandatory or optional; key management lives outside this crate (ids-identity/ids-crypto).
7. **`ids-write` split:** confirmed that `ids-operation-ref` generates and `ids-write` binds/validates (plan-013/CRATES.md), but the exact bind/validate API surface is not yet specified.
8. **Outcome storage:** where Committed outcomes live for replay (in this crate, in ids-write, or in a store) is undefined.

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| OpRef separate from OrderingPos | `ids-000-aa` defines both; coupling them (Stellar SEP-0035 pattern) binds identity to a total order — rejected ||
|| 36^9 nine-character alphanumeric namespace | Directly matches prompt/Purpose; ≈1.016×10^14 space, ~46.5 bits ||
|| Collision detection as first-class item | Birthday bound (~10.1M @ 50%) makes collisions probable at modest volume; detection + regeneration required ||
|| Sequential counter default generation | Collision-free, simple, capacity-efficient; invertible int→alphanumeric mapping (block-id pattern) avoids hard-to-sync distributed state ||
|| Idempotency binding via blake3/sha256 fingerprint | Binds OpRef to operation arguments; same-key-different-args rejected (Stripe/Azure pattern) ||
|| Commit-status FSM Pending→Committed/Failed/Rejected | Terminal-state lookup enables retry recognition without re-execution ||
|| Carrier-agnostic via ids-carrier::Endpoint only | No std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/wireless; preserves I-CARR-001 ||
|| Allowed crypto subset (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, chacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3) | Per HX-241/IDS policy; sha256/blake3 for fingerprints, ed25519 optional audit signing, xchacha20/chacha20 available if payloads need encryption ||
|| ids-operation-ref generates; ids-write binds/validates | Allocator visibility split per CRATES.md and plan-013.md ||
|| Append-only, optionally ed25519-chained audit | Event sourcing as system of record; tamper-evident lifecycle history ||
|| Research only, no code | This document is the blueprint; no source modifications ||

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 057 creates `ids-commit-state`, a new standalone IDS crate (separate crate, not folders inside an existing one) that owns the end-to-end write commit state machine: **accepted → ordered → executing → committed → replicating → synchronized → verified → failed**. The crate governs commit state transitions, durability conditions, commit prefix tracking, gap detection, abort semantics, state persistence, and state recovery.

**Relationship to existing types:** `ids-000-aa` (master crate) already defines two relevant enums:
- `OpState`: received → ordered → executing → committed → synchronized → verified → failed (IDS-A §42, CAPABILITIES §61), with `can_transition_to` enforcing a linear progression.
- `CommitState`: accepted → prepared → committed → aborted (a transaction-level commit protocol enum).

`ids-commit-state` builds on these canonical types without redefining them. Its primary state machine follows the `OpState` progression, extended with `replicating` between `committed` and `synchronized`, and `accepted` as an entry alias for received/accepted writes. `Committed` and `Aborted` are terminal states per the master-crate `CommitState` contract; `Verified` and `Failed` are terminal per `OpState`.

The crate is carrier-agnostic: it never opens sockets, never references `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh, and ships every commit-state signal as an opaque `Vec<u8>` datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` primitive IDs and type surface. `ids-000-aa` remains the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract; `ids-commit-state` references them and never redefines them.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned Raft log matching + commit index (committed entries = prefix with no holes; `lastApplied`/`commitIndex` cursor), Two-Phase Commit (voting + commit/abort phases; stable-storage write-ahead log; blocking on coordinator failure), Three-Phase Commit (pre-commit buffer enabling non-blocking termination), Paxos/MultiPaxos quorum commit (majority persistence before commit; log compaction via snapshots + suffix replay), PBFT (pre-prepare/prepare/commit phases; total order across views), Zab (atomic broadcast; prefix preservation; leader completeness), chain replication (head→tail propagation; commit at tail), Kafka high watermark / LEO / ISR (committed = replicated to all ISR; min.insync.replicas), CRAQ (chain with dirty→clean version commit at tail), HotStuff/LibraBFT (3-chain commit rule; quorum certificates), FLEET (commitIndex hole-free prefix; gap detection via holes in log array), dual-write recovery impossibility (crash between two durable systems; acceptance-record fences), checkpoint-based replica recovery (snapshot + log suffix; garbage-collect covered prefix), Bayesian/Bayou anti-entropy (commit sequence numbers; prefix property; omitted sequence number for truncated log detection), deterministic commit rule over unstructured DAGs, fault-injection transition rules (failure→commit or abort depending on state), and commit barrier durability (fsync/fdatasync group commit; commit boundary = syscall return determines durable or not).

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-commit-state` sits between the local store / replication layer and the acknowledgement layer. It is a deterministic, local state machine: given a write's current state and an incoming event, it computes the next state, the durability conditions that must hold, and whether the write may advance. Every outbound commit-state signal is an opaque `Vec<u8>` handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; the crate never addresses a peer by network identity.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-store                          │
│  per-write commit state (accepted → ordered → … → verified/failed)  │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                 Phase 057: ids-commit-state (NEW CRATE)             │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────┐   │
│  │ state transitions│ │ durability   │ │ commit prefix + gap │   │
│  │ (8-state FSM)    │ │ conditions   │ │ detection / repair  │   │
│  └─────────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ abort semantics  │ │ state persistence + recovery        │   │
│  │ (terminal Aborted│ │ (snapshot + WAL suffix replay)      │   │
│  │  and Failed)     │ └─────────────────────────────────────┘   │
│  └──────────────────┘                                           │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│            ids-carrier::Endpoint (CarrierType + Vec<u8>)            │
│  all outbound commit-state signals as opaque byte datagrams         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             ids-000-aa (master crate, canonical types)              │
│  NodeId, RegionId, IdsTime, CarrierType, RecordId, Checksum,        │
│  OpState, CommitState, sealed trait contracts, error types          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a commit-state transition:**
1. Local store submits a write; `ids-commit-state` assigns state `Accepted` and a commit-prefix position.
2. On ordering evidence (quorum ack / ordering position), transition `Accepted → Ordered`.
3. On execution start, `Ordered → Executing`; on durable execution result, `Executing → Committed`.
4. `Committed → Replicating` once the write is accepted for replication to peers.
5. `Replicating → Synchronized` once a quorum/regional set holds a durable copy (durability barrier crossed).
6. `Synchronized → Verified` once integrity verification (checksum) passes.
7. Any transition may go `→ Failed` on unrecoverable error; `Failed` and `Verified` are terminal.
8. Result (`CommitStateTransition` + optional `CommitPrefixReport`) serialized and handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` as opaque `Vec<u8>` bytes; the carrier decides delivery.

**Carrier-agnostic absolute rule:** no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh anywhere in the crate. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

**Crypto rule:** only ed25519 (signatures), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (AEAD), sha256/blake3 (content hashing) — consumed from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` primitive IDs; no other cryptographic primitives.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Commit state machine (8 states)

The FSM: `accepted → ordered → executing → committed → replicating → synchronized → verified → failed`, with `failed` reachable from any non-terminal state, and `verified`/`failed` terminal. This extends the master-crate `OpState` (received→ordered→executing→committed→synchronized→verified→failed) by inserting `accepted` as an entry state (received+accepted alias) and `replicating` between `committed` and `synchronized`.

- **Accepted:** write received and admitted; a commit-prefix position is assigned. No durability claim yet.
- **Ordered:** write has a total order position relative to other writes (ordering consensus / sequencing layer).
- **Executing:** write is being applied to local state; tentative effects isolated until commit.
- **Committed:** write is durably decided (quorum commit / commit index reached); effects are now irrevocable.
- **Replicating:** write is being propagated to peer replicas; not yet durably held by a quorum.
- **Synchronized:** durable stable-storage barrier crossed on a quorum/regional set; survives single-node power loss.
- **Verified:** integrity check (checksum) passed on the durable copy; terminal success state.
- **Failed:** unrecoverable error at any stage; terminal failure state.

#### 3.2 Durability conditions

Durability is not one condition but two separable boundaries (Oracle Berkeley DB model: acknowledgment guarantees + synchronization guarantees):
- **Commit boundary:** logical acceptance + ordering + quorum decision (the write is irrevocably decided).
- **Synchronization boundary:** durable stable-storage barrier (fsync/fdatasync/WAL-flush + parent-directory sync for new files) reached before ack.

PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit` (remote_apply/on/remote_write/local/off) and `wal_sync_method` (fdatasync/fsync/fsync_writethrough/open_sync/open_datasync) demonstrate these as independent knobs. `ids-commit-state` tracks both independently per write: `commit_reached` (bool) and `sync_reached` (bool); a write is considered durable only when both hold. Exposure window between commit and synchronization is reported honestly (ack at commit only = survives clean shutdown, not power loss).

fsync vs fdatasync: fsync flushes data + metadata (size, block mapping, timestamps); fdatasync flushes data plus only metadata needed for a subsequent read. New-file durability trap: fsync the parent directory after creating any new commit-state file (the directory entry linking name→inode must be durable too). CRC/checksum (blake3 preferred; sha256 alternative) over durable metadata + payload to detect silent corruption/torn writes.

#### 3.3 Commit prefix tracking

The commit prefix is the hole-free contiguous prefix of the commit log known to be committed and applied. Research foundations:
- **Raft log matching property:** if two logs contain an entry with the same index and term, they are identical through that index; `commitIndex` cursor ensures the prefix before it is hole-free; entries between `lastApplied` and `commitIndex` are applied sequentially. Source: Raft paper §5.3; etcd raft `commitIndex`/`lastApplied`.
- **FLEET:** commitIndex as hole-free prefix cursor; log entries may arrive out of order creating holes; committed entries maintain non-decreasing term values.
- **Kafka high watermark (HW):** offset up to which all ISR replicas have replicated; consumers read only up to HW; HW = min LEO across ISR, only advances when ISR size ≥ min.insync.replicas. Log End Offset (LEO) may exceed HW for unreplicated entries.
- **Prefix property (Bayou):** if replica R holds write W_i accepted by server X, R also holds all writes X accepted before W_i. Commit sequence numbers (CSN) totally order committed writes.
- **Omitted sequence number (OSN):** detects truncated stable writes missing from a peer (OSN_A > CSN_B ⇒ full database transfer needed).

`ids-commit-state` maintains `commit_prefix = { first_index, last_index, term }` per write set, with `gap_start`/`gap_end` for detected holes. A write can advance past `committed` only if its index lies within the hole-free prefix.

#### 3.4 Gap detection

Gaps (missing log entries / holes) arise from out-of-order delivery, replica lag, truncation, or crash. Gap detection mechanisms:
- **Index/term continuity check:** each entry carries `(index, term)`; a missing predecessor index ⇒ gap. Raft AppendEntries consistency check: leader includes prevIndex/prevTerm; follower rejects if mismatch.
- **CommitIndex watermark:** entries beyond `commitIndex` are uncommitted; a hole between `lastApplied` and `commitIndex` blocks sequential application until filled.
- **OSN vs CSN comparison:** anti-entropy detects when one side truncated stable writes the other hasn't seen.
- **ISR tracking:** replicas below the high-watermark lag; gap = HW − replica_LEO.

Gap repair: leader (or any peer holding the missing entries) re-sends the missing suffix; if the sender truncated entries the receiver needs (OSN > receiver CSN), fall back to full state transfer (snapshot + log suffix replay). `ids-commit-state` exposes `GapReport { missing_indices: Vec<u64>, severity: GapSeverity, repair_action: RepairAction }`.

#### 3.5 Abort semantics

Abort = all-or-nothing rollback; once a write aborts, all tentative effects are discarded and the state reverts.
- **2PC abort:** any participant votes No, or coordinator/participant timeout ⇒ global abort; participants undo via undo log, release locks, send ack; coordinator logs abort to stable storage. Failure transition rule: for every non-final state, if it contains a commit, assign failure→commit; else failure→abort.
- **3PC abort:** pre-commit buffer lets survivors safely abort when no participant is pre-committed; non-blocking termination.
- **Terminal abort states:** master-crate `CommitState::Aborted` and `OpState::Failed` are terminal; a failed write never retries implicitly — retry is an explicit new write with a new accept position.
- **Abort visibility:** aborted writes are never exposed to readers (cf. CRAQ: dirty versions not readable until tail commits/cleans).

`ids-commit-state` defines `AbortReason { VoteNo, Timeout, CoordinatorFailure, DurabilityBarrierFailed, ChecksumMismatch, GapUnrecoverable, InvalidTransition }` and an `AbortRecord { write_id, reason, aborted_at, rollback_scope }` persisted to stable storage before the `Failed`/`Aborted` transition is final.

#### 3.6 State persistence

Persistence model: **snapshot + WAL suffix** (checkpoint-based replica recovery):
- Periodic full snapshots of commit-state (serialized state machine + commit prefix) atomically replaced (write temp + rename + fsync + parent-dir fsync).
- Append-only WAL of commit-state transitions; each transition fsynced per `SyncPolicy::{Always, EveryN, OsManaged}` before acknowledged durable.
- Recovery: load latest valid snapshot (largest index, fall back if corrupt), replay WAL suffix from `index+1`.
- WAL truncation: garbage-collect prefix covered by a checkpoint after checkpoint is durable (VR Revisited: garbage-collect log prefix covered by checkpoint to avoid divergence).
- Snapshot file naming with length-prefix / strict-prefix rejection so a truncated prefix never decodes (arachne-kv pattern).

Persistence tiers (per write/dataset): `MemoryOnly`, `Journaled` (WAL appended), `Synced` (fsync/fdatasync crossed), `SyncedAndReplicated` (synced + quorum copies). Exposure window reported per tier.

#### 3.7 State recovery

Recovery paths:
- **Clean restart:** load snapshot + replay WAL suffix; rebuild commit prefix and in-flight write states; reject transitions that violate `can_transition_to`.
- **Crash mid-transition:** WAL records the in-doubt transition; on recovery, if a transition lacks its durability barrier record, treat as `Failed` (conservative) or replay to completion if the barrier record exists.
- **Replica rejoining:** peer reports its commit prefix (`commit_index`, `term`); leader detects divergence (prefix mismatch ⇒ truncate conflicting suffix and resend; Raft nextIndex backoff). If sender truncated needed entries (OSN > receiver CSN), full state transfer.
- **Verify on recovery:** recompute checksums over recovered state; mismatch ⇒ `Failed` state for affected writes, operator intervention.

Recovery is deterministic: same snapshot + same WAL suffix ⇒ same state. No reliance on wall-clock for validity (HLC timestamps only as bounded-skew hints, never authority).

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Impact | Mitigation |
|--------|--------|------------|
| Correlated failure (shared power loss, rack outage) destroys all synced copies | Permanent data loss despite "committed" | Regional redundancy + failure-domain anti-affinity; honest exposure-window reporting per tier |
| Ack before stable-storage barrier | Acknowledged writes lost on crash | Separate commit vs. sync boundaries; `Synced` tier forces fsync/fdatasync + parent-dir sync before `Synchronized` |
| Silent data corruption (bit rot, torn writes) | Corrupt state treated as durable/verified | blake3/sha256 checksum over durable metadata + payload; verification before `Verified`; mismatch → `Failed` |
| New commit-state file created but directory entry not durable | File "exists" after crash but name unresolvable | fsync parent directory after creating any new state file |
| Gap between commit prefix and applied state | Blocked or divergent application | Hole-free `commitIndex` cursor; gap detection via index/term continuity + OSN/CSN; repair by resend or full state transfer |
| Indefinite commit blocking (quorum unavailable) | Write availability loss | Bounded wait; `Undetermined`-like verdict via `Failed` on timeout; caller retry policy |
| Invalid state transition (state machine corruption) | Divergent replica states | `can_transition_to` guard enforced on every transition; terminal states never exit |
| Crypto downgrade / non-allowed primitive | Violates allowed-crypto constraint | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 from ids-000-aa/ids-crypto; lint to reject others |
| Carrier assumption (TCP/IP etc.) | Violates carrier-agnostic constraint | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; compile-fail friendly (no `std::net`/`tokio::net`) |

---

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

- **ids-000-aa (master crate):** source of all canonical types and sealed trait contracts — `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, sealed traits, error types. `ids-commit-state` references `OpState`/`CommitState` and defines no new canonical identifier types. Sealed-trait pattern (Rust API Guidelines C-SEALED, `private::Sealed`) used for any extension trait this crate defines.
- **ids-carrier:** all outbound commit-state signals flow as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); no direct transport dependency.
- **ids-crypto:** allowed primitives (ed25519 signatures, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 AEAD, sha256/blake3 hashing) consumed by primitive ID; `ids-commit-state` does not implement crypto itself.
- **ids-store / local store:** the commit-state engine is queried by the local store before acknowledging a write; it is a pure transition function (current state + event → next state + durability conditions) with no store implementation dependency.
- No dependency on `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking crate.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

**`CommitStateTransition { write_id, from, to, event, commit_prefix, durability_conditions, timestamp }`** — result of evaluating one transition.

**8-state FSM with `can_transition_to` guard:**
- `Accepted → {Ordered, Failed}`
- `Ordered → {Executing, Failed}`
- `Executing → {Committed, Failed}`
- `Committed → {Replicating, Failed}`
- `Replicating → {Synchronized, Failed}`
- `Synchronized → {Verified, Failed}`
- `Verified → {}` (terminal)
- `Failed → {}` (terminal)

**Durability conditions:** `{ commit_reached: bool, sync_reached: bool, barrier_crossed: Instant-or-None, exposure_window_ms: u64 }`; durable iff both bools true.

**Commit prefix:** `CommitPrefix { first_index: u64, last_index: u64, term: u64, hole_free: bool }`; advances only when the new index extends the hole-free prefix.

**Gap detection:** `GapReport { missing_indices: Vec<u64>, severity: GapSeverity, repair_action: Resend | FullStateTransfer }`; detected via `(index, term)` continuity mismatch or `OSN > receiver CSN`.

**Abort semantics:** `AbortRecord { write_id, reason, aborted_at, rollback_scope }` persisted before `Aborted`/`Failed` becomes final; terminal states never transition out.

**Persistence:** snapshot (atomic replace + fsync + parent-dir fsync) + append-only WAL (per-transition fsync per `SyncPolicy`); recovery = latest valid snapshot + WAL suffix replay; truncate prefix covered by durable checkpoint.

**Content integrity:** blake3/sha256 over durable metadata + payload per commit entry; verified before `Synchronized → Verified`.

**Allowed crypto:** ed25519 (durable-record signatures), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (AEAD for payloads at rest), sha256/blake3 (content hashing). No other primitives.

**Sealed traits:** any extension trait sealed via `private::Sealed` supertrait (Rust API Guidelines C-SEALED).

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| Criterion | Target | Measurement |
|-----------|--------|-------------|
| 8-state FSM | accepted → ordered → executing → committed → replicating → synchronized → verified → failed, with failed reachable from any non-terminal state | unit test enumerating all transitions |
| Terminal states | Verified and Failed never transition out; can_transition_to returns false | unit test on terminal states |
| Durability conditions | commit_reached ∧ sync_reached required for Synchronized; exposure window reported per tier | boundary-separator unit test; power-loss fault injection |
| fsync + parent-dir sync | fsync + parent-directory sync before ack for new state files | unit test + fsync-failure injection |
| Commit prefix | hole-free prefix cursor; commitIndex advances only with contiguous entries | property test over index/term sequences |
| Gap detection | missing index between lastApplied and commitIndex ⇒ GapReport; repair = resend or full transfer | unit test with synthetic holes; OSN/CSN truncation test |
| Abort semantics | Aborted/Failed terminal; AbortRecord persisted before final; rollback scope honored | unit test per AbortReason |
| State persistence | snapshot + WAL suffix replay reproduces identical state | deterministic recovery test (same snapshot+WAL ⇒ same state) |
| State recovery | crash mid-transition ⇒ conservative Failed or replay-to-completion | chaos test: kill at each transition point |
| Content integrity | blake3/sha256 over metadata+payload; tampered entry rejected before Verified | manifest verification unit test |
| Crypto constraint | only allowed primitives | dependency/cargo audit + primitive-ID allowlist test |
| Carrier-agnostic | compiles with zero std::net/tokio::net/libp2p refs; all traffic via ids-carrier::Endpoint | build lint + dependency scan |
| Property tests | 100,000+ iterations | proptest/bolero |
| Chaos tests | partition, offline member, replica churn, kill-at-transition | pass/fail |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **State count reconciliation:** The prompt lists 8 states (accepted/ordered/executing/committed/replicating/synchronized/verified/failed) while `ids-000-aa` has `CommitState` (accepted/prepared/committed/aborted) and `OpState` (received/ordered/executing/committed/synchronized/verified/failed). The plan maps `accepted` to an entry alias of `received/accepted` and inserts `replicating` between `committed` and `synchronized`; the exact mapping table must be confirmed against IDS-A §42 / CAPABILITIES §61 during implementation.
2. **Commit prefix vs. OpState coupling:** whether commit-prefix tracking is per-write or per-write-set, and whether `replicating` implies quorum or single-peer replication, is product-configured, not research-determined.
3. **fsync failure handling:** a failed fsync poisons the writer (durability crate); recovery path (restart from WAL vs. fail the dataset) needs an operator decision.
4. **Wire format for commit-state signals:** CBOR vs bincode vs protobuf for the opaque `Vec<u8>` handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; CBOR favored for compactness/schema evolution but crate TBD.
5. **WAL truncation policy:** retention (size/age/ack-based) deferred; unbounded WAL growth without checkpoint-compaction.
6. **Formal verification scope:** TLA+/PlusCal spec proving commit-state safety (no divergent committed states, terminal-state integrity) is additional effort beyond this plan.
7. **Abort retry semantics:** whether a `Failed` write may be retried as a new `Accepted` write with a fresh prefix position, or whether the original write_id is permanently dead — policy decision.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| New separate crate `ids-commit-state` | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones"; clean dependency boundary |
| Build on `ids-000-aa` `OpState`/`CommitState` | Master crate already holds canonical state enums; never redefine canonical types |
| 8-state FSM with `replicating` between `committed` and `synchronized` | Matches prompt verbatim; separates irrevocable commit from durable replication barrier |
| Commit vs. sync as separate boundaries | Oracle Berkeley DB model: durability = acknowledgment guarantees + synchronization guarantees; prevents overclaiming |
| Hole-free commit prefix (`commitIndex` cursor) | Raft log matching + FLEET; prevents applying across gaps |
| Gap detection via index/term continuity + OSN/CSN | Raft AppendEntries consistency + Bayou anti-entropy; detects truncation mismatches |
| Abort terminal + AbortRecord persisted first | 2PC stability (once commit/abort, remains forever); rollback scope recorded before final |
| Snapshot + WAL suffix persistence | Checkpoint-based replica recovery (VR Revisited); bounded recovery work |
| Parent-directory fsync after new state file | New-file durability trap (kernel internals; PostgreSQL/LevelDB practice) |
| blake3 preferred, sha256 allowed | Content hashing/manifest integrity (spacedb-durability pattern); within allowed-crypto set |
| ed25519 signatures for durable commit records | Non-repudiation of commit-state transitions; within allowed-crypto set |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Carrier-agnostic mandate; no `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p |
| Research only — no code, no source modifications | Per task constraint; this document is the implementation blueprint |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 058 creates `ids-durability-policy`, a new standalone IDS crate (separate crate, not folders inside an existing one) that owns per-dataset durability requirements: local persistence, quorum persistence, regional redundancy threshold, cross-region durability, acknowledgement semantics, and the commit-vs-synchronization distinction. It is carrier-agnostic: it never opens sockets, never references `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh, and ships every durability-relevant message as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` primitive IDs and type surface. `ids-000-aa` remains the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, sealed traits, error types); `ids-durability-policy` references them and never redefines them.

The crate evaluates, per dataset id, a durability requirement object: a local persistence tier (memory-only / journaled / synced), a quorum persistence threshold (how many replicas must durably persist before acknowledgement), a regional redundancy threshold (how many failure domains/regions must hold durable copies), a cross-region durability mode, and an acknowledgement level (none / leader / quorum / all). It separates the commit boundary (logical acceptance/ordering of a write) from the synchronization boundary (durable stable-storage barrier before ack) — matching the established finding that durability guarantees comprise two independent dimensions: acknowledgement guarantees and synchronization guarantees (Oracle Berkeley DB durability model). It returns a durable verdict (satisfied / unsatisfied / undetermined) that callers gate acknowledgement on.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned the `durability` crate (local persistence primitives: directories, atomic writes, WALs, record logs, checkpoints, CRC validation, sync helpers; `FsDirectory` for fsync/parent-directory sync; `SyncWalWriter::append_durable`; no per-write fsync by default, `flush_and_sync()` as the barrier), `spacedb-durability` (Reed-Solomon k-of-n erasure-coded snapshots, content-addressed manifest with blake3 hashes, anti-affinity placement across failure domains, health/repair/reclaim), MongoDB write concern (`w` count + `j` journal flag + `wtimeout`, `w:majority` default, `writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault`), Couchbase durable writes (`Majority` / `MajorityAndPersistToActive` / `PersistToMajority` durability levels), Apache Iggy topic durability (`replicated` = quorum commit + local application without stable-storage barrier; `persisted` = quorum commit backed by recoverable stable-storage copies at quorum, then local application; quorum = min(ceil(n/2),3) with intersecting view-change quorum), PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit` (remote_apply/on/remote_write/local/off) and `wal_sync_method` (fdatasync/fsync/fsync_writethrough/open_sync/open_datasync), fsync vs fdatasync semantics and the new-file directory-entry durability trap (fsync parent dir after file creation), RabbitMQ publisher confirms / quorum queues (ack after quorum of replicas confirmed; persistent messages to durable queues), Kafka `acks` (0/1/all) with `min.insync.replicas`, Cloud Storage (11 nines annual durability, erasure coding, regional = 2+ AZs confirmed before write success, cross-region dual/multi-region async replication), Azure Storage redundancy (LRS/ZRS/GRS/GZRS durability tiers, ZRS across 3+ AZs), Berkeley DB Replication Manager ack policies (NONE/ONE_PEER/QUORUM/ALL/ALL_PEERS; consistency vs durability distinction), Cassandra consistency levels (ALL/QUORUM/LOCAL_ONE/ONE/TWO/THREE), quipu-log SyncPolicy (Always/EveryN/OsManaged fsync policy + group commit + exposure window), durable-ioring (epoch-based durability points, high-water mark, no_std), iqdb-persist and persistent-queue FsyncPolicy (Always/Periodic/Never; Sync/Group/None), Giza erasure coding across global data centers (USENIX ATC '17), SQLite WAL/atomic commit (fsync at commit points, synchronous=FULL vs NORMAL), RustCrypto chacha20poly1305/XChaCha20Poly1305 (RFC 8439), and Rust API Guidelines sealed-trait pattern (C-SEALED, `private::Sealed` supertrait).

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-durability-policy` sits between the local store and the acknowledgement layer. It is not a transport or a network protocol — it is a deterministic, local policy engine that, given a dataset id and a proposed write outcome, computes whether the durability requirement for that dataset is satisfied and what acknowledgement level to emit. Every outbound durability signal is an opaque `Vec<u8>` handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; the crate never addresses a peer by network identity.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   APPLICATION / ids-store                   │
│  per-dataset durability requirement (policy per dataset id) │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 058: ids-durability-policy (NEW)         │
│  ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐   │
│  │ local       │ │ quorum       │ │ regional +       │   │
│  │ persistence │ │ persistence  │ │ cross-region     │   │
│  │ tier engine │ │ threshold    │ │ redundancy       │   │
│  └─────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────────┘   │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ ack semantics    │ │ commit vs synchronization    │   │
│  │ (none/leader/    │ │ boundary separator           │   │
│  │  quorum/all)     │ │ (commit ≠ durable sync)      │   │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────────────────┘   │
│  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
│  │ durable verdict: Satisfied / Unsatisfied / Undetermined│ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│            ids-carrier::Endpoint (CarrierType + Vec<u8>)    │
│  all outbound durability signals as opaque byte datagrams   │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             ids-000-aa (master crate, canonical types)      │
│  NodeId, RegionId, IdsTime, CarrierType, RecordId, Checksum,│
│  sealed trait contracts, error types                        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a durability check:**
1. Local store prepares a write for dataset `D` and asks `ids-durability-policy`: "may I acknowledge, and at what level?"
2. The crate loads `DurabilityPolicy[D]` (local tier, quorum threshold `q` of `n`, regional threshold `r` of regions, cross-region mode, ack level).
3. It evaluates the local persistence barrier against the tier (e.g., fsync/fdatasync completed per `SyncPolicy`), the quorum against durable-replica reports, and the regional threshold against region-durable reports.
4. It separates commit (write accepted and ordered locally) from synchronization (stable-storage barrier reached); ack is emitted only when both the commit and the configured synchronization barrier are satisfied.
5. Result: `DurabilityVerdict` + `AckLevel`, serialized and handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` as opaque `Vec<u8>` bytes; the carrier decides how (if at all) to deliver them.

**Carrier-agnostic absolute rule:** no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh anywhere in the crate. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

**Crypto rule:** only ed25519 (signatures), xchacha20poly1305 (AEAD), sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 — consumed from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` primitive IDs; no other cryptographic primitives.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Local persistence

Local persistence is the foundation layer: a dataset's durability requirement is only as strong as the weakest local durable copy. Research-verified building blocks:

- **Persistence tiers:** `MemoryOnly` (page-cache only, lost on power loss — acceptable for cache/replica tiers that can be rebuilt), `Journaled` (write-ahead log appended, ack after in-memory apply, vulnerable to correlated power loss), `Synced` (fsync/fdatasync barrier reached before ack — survives single-node power loss), `SyncedAndReplicated` (synced plus quorum/regional copies). This mirrors Couchbase durable-write levels (in-memory / majority-in-memory / majority-persisted) and Apache Iggy `replicated` vs `persisted` topic durability.
- **Sync policy:** `Always` (fsync after every append — safest, slowest, exposure window ~0), `EveryN(n)` / group commit (fsync every n appends — bounded exposure window of n−1 entries; ~12× throughput cost vs unmanaged but predictable), `OsManaged` (flush only, rely on OS writeback — fastest, unbounded exposure window, unsafe for power loss). Source: quipu-log SyncPolicy; `durability` crate `flush_and_sync()` barrier; iqdb-persist `FsyncPolicy::{Always, Periodic, Never}`; persistent-queue `Sync/Group/None`.
- **fsync vs fdatasync:** `fsync` flushes data + metadata needed to retrieve it (size, block mapping, timestamps); `fdatasync` flushes data plus only metadata required for a subsequent read (may skip mtime). Difference is workload-dependent; on journaled filesystems fdatasync skips a metadata journal transaction. Source: Linux kernel internals fsync/fdatasync.
- **New-file durability trap:** creating a file, writing, and fsyncing the file is insufficient — the directory entry linking the name to the inode must also be durable; fsync the parent directory after file creation (PostgreSQL `fsync_fname`/`SyncDir`, LevelDB/RocksDB practice). `ids-durability-policy` must require parent-directory sync for new dataset files.
- **CRC/checksum:** durable metadata and payload covered by checksum (blake3 preferred per allowed-crypto rule; sha256 as alternative). `durability` crate covers durable metadata + payload with CRC; `spacedb-durability` manifest carries every shard's content hash so corrupted/substituted shards are detected at reconstruction.
- **WAL + checkpoint:** append-only WAL for crash recovery, periodic atomic checkpoints, checkpoint publish + WAL truncation (`durability` crate `recover`/`publish`; SQLite WAL checkpoint; durable-ioring durability points + high-water mark that never reports a point durable while an earlier failure is unresolved).
- **Power-loss honesty:** a write returning success means only "in page cache" unless a sync barrier was crossed; acknowledged-but-unsynced writes are lost on power loss (PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit=off` semantics; Iggy `replicated` policy caveat). The crate must expose the exposure window per tier rather than overpromise.

#### 3.2 Quorum persistence

Quorum persistence decides how many replicas must durably persist a write before it is acknowledged, tolerating replica failure without data loss.

- **Quorum arithmetic:** with `n` replicas, write quorum `w` and read quorum `r` must satisfy `w + r > n` for read-your-writes consistency and `2w > n` (intersecting write quorums) to prevent divergent committed states. Apache Iggy: replication quorum `min(ceil(n/2), 3)`, view-change quorum `n − replication_quorum + 1`; quorums intersect. Berkeley DB `DB_REPMGR_ACKS_QUORUM` survives master change / network partition. Majority write quorum tolerates `⌊(n−1)/2⌋` failures.
- **Ack policies:** `NONE` (fire-and-forget, highest throughput, no durability), `LEADER` / `ONE` (primary only — risk if leader fails before replication), `QUORUM` (majority of replicas — survives single failure with n=3), `ALL` / `all ISR` (highest durability, lowest availability, blocks on any replica down — Kafka `acks=all` + `min.insync.replicas=2` tolerates one broker loss with RF=3). Cassandra consistency levels: `ALL/QUORUM/LOCAL_ONE/ONE/TWO/THREE`.
- **Per-dataset quorum:** `DurabilityPolicy[D].quorum = { n, w }` stored per dataset; quorum recomputed when replica membership changes; stale/unelectable replicas excluded from quorum counts (Berkeley DB electable-peer rule).
- **Failure-independence caveat:** replication count alone does not bound loss under correlated failure (shared power loss, OOM cascade, crash-on-every-replica); replicas must be isolated across failure domains (Iggy failure-independence note). `ids-durability-policy` expresses this as a required assumption, not a guarantee.

#### 3.3 Regional redundancy threshold

Regional redundancy extends quorum across geographic failure domains (regions / availability zones).

- **Threshold model:** per-dataset `regional_threshold = { required_regions r, total_regions R }`; a write is regionally durable only after `r` of `R` regions hold a durable (synced) copy. Cloud Storage regional buckets confirm writes only after data is redundantly stored across ≥2 AZs; dual-region/multi-region buckets add cross-region redundancy (11 nines durability target). Azure ZRS = synchronous across 3+ AZs in one region (12 nines); GRS/GZRS = geo-redundant across regions (16 nines).
- **Anti-affinity:** copies must be spread across distinct failure domains (spacedb-durability `allocate` spreads shards across failure domains; requires at least `num_shards` targets). A region threshold of `r` with all copies in one AZ is meaningless — the crate enforces failure-domain diversity as a precondition.
- **Durability targets:** 11 nines (99.999999999% annual) is the common cloud target for object storage; expressed per dataset as a configurable durability SLO, not a hard-coded constant.

#### 3.4 Cross-region durability

Cross-region durability protects against whole-region outages.

- **Async vs sync cross-region:** synchronous cross-region commit maximizes durability but adds inter-region latency to every write; asynchronous cross-region replication (Cloud Storage default replication: 99% within 1 hour target, 100% within 12 hours) trades a bounded replication lag for write latency. Giza (Azure Storage, USENIX ATC '17) applies erasure coding across global data centers to lower geo-redundancy storage cost vs three-way replication, with Local Reconstruction Coding within a DC.
- **RPO/RPO exposure:** async cross-region implies a recovery-point window (unreplicated writes lost in a region outage); the crate must expose the cross-region replication lag bound per dataset rather than conceal it.
- **Erasure coding across regions:** k-of-n Reed-Solomon shards spread across regions tolerate loss of up to `n−k` regions (spacedb-durability; Ceph default erasure profile k=2,m=2 tolerates 2 OSD losses with 2× storage overhead vs 3× for replication). RustFS automatic parity derives parity per erasure-set width (EC:0–EC:4).
- **Cross-region is not local persistence:** a regionally durable write still requires each region's local synced copy; cross-region redundancy composes on top of local persistence and quorum, never replaces them.

#### 3.5 Acknowledgement semantics

Acknowledgement semantics define what a "success" response promises — the central durability claim.

- **Ack levels:** `Unacknowledged` (success after send, no durability), `LeaderAck` (leader applied in memory — leader failure before replication may lose it), `QuorumAck` (quorum of replicas applied — survives single failure with n=3), `AllAck` (all replicas / all ISR — highest durability, blocks on any down replica). Kafka `acks=0/1/all`; Couchbase `durabilityLevel`; MongoDB `w` + `j`.
- **Ack basis (in-memory vs durable):** an ack may mean "applied in memory" or "persisted to stable storage". MongoDB `j:true` forces on-disk journal before ack; `writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault` decides whether `w:majority` implies journaling. Iggy `replicated` (quorum commit + local application, no stable-storage barrier) vs `persisted` (quorum commit backed by recoverable stable-storage copies at quorum, then local application) — exactly the replicated-vs-persisted distinction. `ids-durability-policy` makes the ack basis explicit per dataset: `AckBasis::{Memory, Journal, StableStorage}`.
- **Ack transfer of ownership:** once acknowledged, the receiver assumes full responsibility for the message; the sender may release it (RabbitMQ reliability guide: acknowledgement = receipt + transfer of ownership). The crate must not let a caller retract an ack after it is emitted.
- **wtimeout / deadline:** quorum or all-ack can block indefinitely; a bounded deadline (`wtimeout`) converts indefinite blocking into `Unsatisfied`/`Undetermined` verdicts (MongoDB write concern timeout; Iggy behavior when insufficient sites are connected — returns failure immediately rather than waiting).

#### 3.6 Commit vs synchronization distinction

Commit and synchronization are separable durability boundaries; conflating them is the source of most durability bugs.

- **Commit** = logical acceptance and ordering of a write (the write is assigned a position/sequence and replicas agree on it). **Synchronization** = the durable stable-storage barrier (fsync/fdatasync/WAL-flush) that makes the committed write survive power loss. Oracle Berkeley DB: "Durability guarantees include two types of information: acknowledgment guarantees and synchronization guarantees." PostgreSQL `synchronous_commit` controls how much WAL processing completes before success; `wal_sync_method` controls the actual disk flush — independent knobs.
- **Ordering guarantee:** commit establishes order (WAL-before-data: changes to data files are written only after WAL records describing them are flushed — PostgreSQL WAL principle; SQLite write-ahead logging). Synchronization without ordering is insufficient for recoverable state.
- **Exposure window:** between commit and synchronization lies the durability window (dirty page cache, bounded by kernel writeback or `EveryN` group commit). A system that acks at commit but syncs later promises "survives process crash/clean shutdown, not power loss" — honest only if documented (MerceMay fsync durability boundary).
- **ids-durability-policy design:** per-dataset `DurabilityPolicy` carries two independently configurable boundaries: `commit_required` (quorum ack at commit) and `sync_required` (stable-storage barrier before ack). The verdict is `Satisfied` only when both are met; otherwise `Unsatisfied` or `Undetermined` (e.g., committed but not yet synced → `Undetermined` until the barrier clears or a timeout elapses).

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Impact | Mitigation |
|--------|--------|------------|
| Correlated failure (shared power loss, rack/region outage) destroys all synced copies | Permanent data loss despite "quorum" | Regional redundancy threshold + failure-domain anti-affinity; quorum computed over independent failure domains; document exposure window honestly |
| Ack emitted before stable-storage barrier | Acknowledged writes lost on crash | Separate commit vs sync; `SyncRequired` tier forces fsync/fdatasync + parent-directory sync before ack; `AckBasis::StableStorage` default for durable datasets |
| Silent data corruption (bit rot, torn writes) | Corrupt state treated as durable | Content hashing (blake3/sha256) over durable metadata + payload; checksum verification on read/replay; manifest with per-shard content hashes |
| New file created but directory entry not durable | File "exists" after crash but name not resolvable | fsync parent directory after creating any new dataset file |
| Quorum computed over dead/unelectable replicas | False durable verdict | Exclude non-electable replicas from quorum counts; require failure-domain diversity |
| Indefinite quorum blocking | Write availability loss | Bounded `wtimeout`; `Undetermined` verdict on timeout; caller retry/backoff policy |
| Crypto downgrade / non-allowed primitive | Violates allowed-crypto constraint | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 from ids-000-aa/ids-crypto; lint to reject std crypto and any other primitive |
| Carrier assumption (TCP/IP etc.) | Violates carrier-agnostic constraint | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; compile-fail (no_std-friendly, no `std::net`/`tokio::net`) |

---

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

- **ids-000-aa (master crate):** source of all canonical types and sealed trait contracts consumed by this crate — `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, sealed traits, error types. `ids-durability-policy` references these and defines no new canonical identifier types. Sealed-trait pattern (Rust API Guidelines C-SEALED) used for any trait this crate defines that must remain implementable only within the crate.
- **ids-carrier:** all outbound durability signals flow as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); no direct transport dependency.
- **ids-crypto:** allowed primitives (ed25519 signatures, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 AEAD, sha256/blake3 hashing) consumed by primitive ID; `ids-durability-policy` does not implement crypto itself.
- **ids-store / local store:** the durability policy engine is queried by the local store before acknowledging a per-dataset write; it is a pure policy function (dataset id + write outcome → verdict + ack level) with no store implementation dependency.
- No dependency on `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking crate.

### 6. Proposed File Structure (~90–1000 files in subfolders)

A separate crate `ids-durability-policy` at `C:/idfs/ids-durability-policy/`, organized into subfolders by durability dimension (not a monolithic file). Explicitly enumerated tree below totals ~125 files; property-based, chaos, and conformance test generation scales the tree toward 1,000 files.

```
ids-durability-policy/

├── SECURITY.md
├── src/
│   ├── lib.rs

│   ├── policy.rs              # per-dataset requirement evaluation

│   ├── crypto/                # allowed-primitive wrappers (~10 files)
│   │   ├── mod.rs, ed25519.rs, xchacha20poly1305.rs, sha256.rs, blake3.rs, chacha20poly1305.rs, primitive_ids.rs
```
