### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-routing-table` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a table-construction-and-maintenance layer: given a set of known nodes/endpoints, link metrics, locality hints, and replica versions, it builds routing tables, resolves next-hops, selects paths, tracks freshness, prevents loops, expires stale entries, and converges after topology changes. It never sends bytes itself; it returns `RouteDecision` / `NextHop` / `Path` structures that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (routing table users)            │
│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-query — route lookups via table queries      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 061: ids-routing-table (THIS CRATE — table maintenance)   │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────┐ │
│  │ route entries│ │ next-hop     │ │ path selection│ │ locality     │ │loop│ │
│  │ (dst→next-hop│ │ resolution   │ │ (cost/freshness│ │ metrics      │ │prev│ │
│  │  + cost/TTL) │ │              │ │  /ECMP)      │ │ (proximity)  │ │ent │ │
│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └────┘ │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌────┐ │
│  │ freshness    │ │ expiration   │ │ revalidation │ │ convergence  │ │    │ │
│  │ tracking     │ │ (TTL/GC)     │ │ (stale→valid)│ │ (topology Δ) │ │    │ │
│  │ (version/age)│ │              │ │              │ │              │ │    │ │
│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └────┘ │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐                          │
│  │ contracts    │ │ invariants   │ │ decisions    │                          │
│  │ (routing)    │ │ (~12 rules)  │ │ (RouteDecision│                          │
│  │              │ │              │ │  types)      │                          │
│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘                          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                          ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                     │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])│
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                       │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
│  / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh                                  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a route lookup:** caller submits `RouteLookup{destination: RecordId, hints: LocalityHints}` → `ids-routing-table` resolves the table entry, applies path selection (cost, locality, freshness, ECMP), runs loop-prevention checks, returns `RouteDecision{next_hop: Endpoint, path: Vec<NodeId>, cost, freshness_ok, ecmp_group}` → caller sends the datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` via `ids-carrier::Carrier::send_datagram`.

**Data flow of table maintenance:** topology change (node join/leave, link metric change, replica version bump) → `TableUpdate{kind: Add|Remove|Metric|Freshness|Expire}` → affected entries invalidated → path selection re-run for affected destinations → convergence check (loop-free, all known destinations reachable or marked unreachable) → `Converged` event emitted; stale entries past TTL garbage-collected.

**Crypto used:** sha256/blake3 for route-entry fingerprinting, table-version hashing, and loop-detection path hashing; ed25519 for signing route advertisements and table-version checkpoints; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt routing state at rest when confidentiality is required.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Routing table entries: destination → next-hop + cost + TTL + state

Each entry maps a destination identifier (a `RecordId`/`NodeId`-scoped route key from `ids-000-aa`) to a next-hop `Endpoint`, a cost/metric, the originating node, a TTL, and an entry state (`Fresh`, `Stale`, `Expired`, `Unreachable`, `Poisoned`). Entry format follows the distance-vector forwarding-table model from Stanford CS168 (destination → (next hop, cost)) extended with TTL and freshness fields. Entries are immutable once published; updates create a new table version (monotonically increasing `TableVersion` u64). Source: CS168 distance-vector textbook; INET RIP tutorial.

#### 3.2 Next-hop resolution

Given a destination, `resolve_next_hop(destination)` returns the best `Endpoint` per current table version, or `Unreachable` if no entry exists or all candidates are expired/poisoned. Resolution applies longest-prefix-style matching when destination keys support prefix decomposition (trie-based lookup, per DPDK LPM6 multi-bit trie concepts adapted to opaque byte-key prefixes), falling back to exact-key lookup. Resolution never contacts the network; it is a pure function over the local table. Source: DPDK LPM6 library; CS168 forwarding table.

#### 3.3 Path selection

When multiple candidate next-hops exist for a destination, `select_path` ranks them by: (a) lowest cost/metric, (b) highest locality score (local > same region > same rack > remote), (c) freshest replica version, (d) ECMP tie-break via stable hash of (destination, flow) so all packets of a flow use the same next-hop. The result may be a single next-hop or an ECMP group of equal-cost next-hops. BGP best-path selection (Cisco attribute order: weight → local preference → local origin → AS path → origin → MED → eBGP over iBGP → IGP metric → router ID) is the reference model for multi-attribute path ranking, adapted to IDS attributes (cost, locality, freshness, admin weight). Source: Cisco BGP best-path algorithm; Palo Alto/Cumulus ECMP load-sharing; DPDK LPM6.

#### 3.4 Locality metrics

Locality is an ordinal score computed from `ids-000-aa` canonical types: `RegionId`, node rack/failure-domain hints, and endpoint `CarrierType`. Local (same node/rack) scores highest; same-region next; cross-region lowest. Locality biases path selection toward nearby replicas to limit wide-area traffic (per Berkeley OceanStore locality-awareness: exploit local resources over remote whenever possible, limiting the impact of local operations on WAN performance). Locality scores are recomputed when topology or carrier capabilities change. Source: OceanStore locality-aware mechanisms paper.

#### 3.5 Replica freshness tracking

Each routing table entry can carry a replica freshness marker: `(version: u64, last_seen: IdsTime, source: NodeId)`. Reads prefer the freshest known replica; writes route to replicas that have acknowledged recent versions. Freshness degrades with time since last update and with version lag behind the known head. This mirrors bounded-staleness freshness tracking (Meta TAO/Skybridge: staleness checking vs write HLC; view divergence of freshness in replicated databases). Staleness thresholds are configurable per route class; exceeding them triggers revalidation or route downgrade. Source: Skybridge USENIX OSDI'25; SSRN freshness survey.

#### 3.6 Loop prevention

Loop prevention combines three mechanisms, mirroring distance-vector and path-vector practice:

- **Split horizon:** never advertise a route back to the neighbor from which it was learned (CS168 Rule 6A; RFC 2453 split horizon).
- **Poison reverse:** advertise routes learned from a neighbor back to that neighbor marked unreachable/infinite cost (CS168 Rule 6B; RFC 2453 split horizon with poisoned reverse).
- **Path-vector loop detection:** each route advertisement carries the path of `NodeId`s traversed; a node discards any advertisement containing its own identifier (BGP AS-path loop detection; Wikipedia path vector; UCSD path-vector lecture).

At table-construction time, `ids-routing-table` rejects any entry whose next-hop path contains a cycle (path includes the local node or repeats a node). Source: CS168 distance-vector; RFC 2453; Wikipedia path-vector protocol.

#### 3.7 Route expiration / revalidation / garbage collection

Every entry carries a TTL. When no refresh advertisement arrives before TTL expiry, the entry transitions `Fresh → Stale → Expired`. Expired entries are garbage-collected after a hold-down period (RIP garbage-collection timer model: timeout then GC timer; INET RIP timers tutorial). Revalidation: a stale entry may be probed (one datagram to the recorded next-hop requesting a freshness echo) before deletion; if no response within the bounded wait (keyed to `ids-time`, never wall-clock), the entry is removed and dependents notified. Source: INET RIP timeout/garbage collection; CS168 distance-vector (entry expiry → poison advertisement).

#### 3.8 Routing convergence

After a topology change (node/endpoint add/remove, link metric change, freshness invalidation), affected entries are invalidated and path selection re-runs. Convergence is reached when: all known destinations have a route or are marked `Unreachable`, no entry's next-hop path contains a loop, and no `Stale` entries remain pending revalidation. Link-state (SPF/Dijkstra) converges faster than distance-vector (count-to-infinity: bad news travels slowly); `ids-routing-table` prefers link-state-style full-table recompute on topology change for small/medium tables and incremental distance-vector-style updates for large tables. Source: CS168 link state vs distance vector; Springer OSPF SPF chapter; CS144 routing lecture; Princeton COS461.

#### 3.9 DHT-style routing tables (k-buckets / finger tables)

For key-space routing (routing by hashed `RecordId`/`NodeId` rather than explicit topology), the crate supports a DHT mode: Kademlia-style k-buckets indexed by XOR distance buckets (libp2p DHT; XOR distance metric, identity/symmetry/triangle inequality properties; k-buckets with replacement caches) and Chord-style finger tables (successor(n + 2^(i-1)) entries, O(log N) nodes per table, O(log N) lookup hops). DHT mode is optional and carrier-agnostic: node identifiers are `NodeId` (32-byte), distances computed over byte arrays, all contact via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. Source: libp2p DHT docs; MIT TON Chord paper; Chord SIGCOMM'01 paper.

#### 3.10 On-demand route discovery and maintenance

For sparse or dynamic topologies where proactive table construction is wasteful, on-demand (reactive) routing discovers a path only when needed: route request (RREQ) flood bounded by hop count/TTL, route reply (RREP) unicast back along the reverse path, route error (RERR) on link break. This is the AODV/DSR reactive model (INET MANET showcase). Route maintenance: local repair via loop-free alternates (LFA fast reroute: pre-compute backup next-hops satisfying the loop-free alternate condition) before initiating full re-discovery. Source: INET MANET routing protocols; Cisco ASR 9000 LFA FRR.

#### 3.11 Anycast / closest-replica selection

Anycast routing selects the "closest" replica among a set of candidates advertising the same destination. Closest is defined by the locality metric (3.4) plus cost; selection can be coarse (bucket client→location, return closest replica, per OASIS anycast) or fine (per-flow hash to an ECMP group of replicas). All traffic still via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; anycast is a logical selection, not an IP anycast. Source: OASIS anycast paper; ClickHouse replica-aware routing (sticky routing to same replica for read-after-write consistency).

#### 3.12 Gossip/sloppy table maintenance

For very large or churn-prone deployments, proactive repair of every table entry is cumbersome and can cause liveness bugs. Sloppy management (HOTAC'08) uses continuous lazy background algorithms for routing-table maintenance while relying on the deterministic routing algorithm for actual message forwarding: periodic gossip anti-entropy exchanges table digests (version vectors or Merkle hashes) and reconciles only divergent entries. This bounds maintenance traffic and tolerates temporary inconsistencies. Source: HOTAC'08 sloppy management of structured P2P services; anti-entropy digest exchange.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|---|---|---|
| Routing loop (A→B→C→A) | Packet delivery / liveness | Split horizon + poison reverse + path-vector cycle rejection at table construction |
| Stale route after topology change | Delivery correctness | TTL expiration → Stale → Expired → GC; revalidation probe before deletion |
| Count-to-infinity / slow convergence | Convergence time | Link-state full recompute on topology change; triggered updates; hold-down timers |
| Black-hole route (advertise unreachable destination) | Delivery correctness | Path-vector loop detection; freshness gating; signed route advertisements (ed25519) |
| Replay of old route advertisement | Table integrity | Monotonic `TableVersion`; nonce/bounded replay cache per advertisement; sha256/blake3 entry fingerprinting |
| Route flap (repeated add/remove) | Table stability | BGP-style flap damping: suppress repeatedly-flapping routes (penalty decay, reuse threshold) |
| Locality downgrade (force remote path) | Performance / latency | Locality scores derived from canonical `ids-000-aa` types, not carrier-supplied claims; signed locality assertions |
| Freshness spoofing (fake recent version) | Read correctness | ed25519-signed freshness markers; version-vector comparison; reject markers below known head |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Ordering/duplicates | Idempotent table updates; duplicate suppression by `TableVersion`; carrier-agnostic boundary |
| Prohibited networking crate | Architecture compliance | Dependency audit: no `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS; `Endpoint` sole address type |
| Disallowed crypto | Crypto policy | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs |

The carrier is never trusted: routing decisions and advertisements are signed/hashed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-routing-table |
|---|---|---|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `IdsTime`, `OpState`, `Error` consumed, never redefined; sealed `Routing` contract mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All routing traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing route advertisements/table checkpoints; hashing entries and paths; encrypting routing state at rest |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic `IdsTime` source for TTL, revalidation timeouts, convergence deadlines | All timing keyed to `IdsTime` ticks, never wall-clock |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (routing table user) | Routes reads/writes to replicas via table lookups; consumes `RouteDecision` |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization / anti-entropy | Consumes next-hop/ECMP group for gossip and hinted replay transport |
| `ids-query` | Query planning (routing table user) | Resolves query target nodes via path selection and locality metrics |
| `ids-fragment` | Record fragments/shards | Fragment reads/writes routed by the parent record's table entry |
| `ids-membership` (future) | Node/region membership changes | Membership events (join/leave) feed `TableUpdate` into the routing table |
| `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060) | Read/write behavior per profile | Profile tag influences path selection (e.g., cross-region durable prefers cross-region quorum next-hops) |

Integration points: `ids-routing-table` drives public contracts declared in `ids-000-aa`; it does not reach into crate internals. All cross-node traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli` beyond what the contracts expose.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Routing table** — versioned map `Table { version: TableVersion, entries: BTreeMap<RouteKey, RouteEntry> }`; updates create a new version; entries immutable. RouteKey derived from destination `RecordId`/`NodeId` (opaque bytes, prefix-decomposable for trie lookup).
2. **Route entry** — `RouteEntry { dst, next_hop: Endpoint, path: Vec<NodeId>, cost: u64, locality: LocalityScore, freshness: FreshnessMarker, ttl: TTL, state: EntryState, origin: NodeId }`.
3. **Next-hop resolution** — `resolve_next_hop(dst)`: exact-key lookup, else longest-prefix-match over prefix-decomposable keys (multi-bit trie, per DPDK LPM6); returns `Endpoint` or `Unreachable`; pure function over local table.
4. **Path selection** — rank candidates by (cost asc, locality desc, freshness desc, admin weight desc); ECMP tie-break via stable hash of `(dst, flow_id)` → equal-cost next-hop group; all packets of a flow hash to the same next-hop (per-flow ECMP, per Cumulus/Palo Alto).
5. **Locality score** — ordinal from `RegionId`/rack/failure-domain + `CarrierType`: local > same region > same rack > remote; recomputed on topology/carrier change.
6. **Freshness marker** — `(version: u64, last_seen: IdsTime, source: NodeId)`; reads prefer freshest; staleness threshold configurable per route class; exceeding triggers revalidation.
7. **Loop prevention** — split horizon (don't advertise back to source neighbor), poison reverse (advertise back with infinite/unreachable), path-vector cycle rejection (discard advertisement whose path contains local node or repeats a node).
8. **Expiration / GC** — TTL per entry: `Fresh → Stale → Expired`; revalidation probe (bounded `ids-time` wait) before deletion; expired entries garbage-collected after hold-down (RIP timeout/GC model).
9. **Convergence** — after topology change, invalidate affected entries, re-run path selection; converged when all known destinations routed or `Unreachable`, no loops, no pending `Stale` revalidations.
10. **DHT k-buckets** — Kademlia buckets indexed by XOR distance over `NodeId` bytes; max bucket size K (default 20, per mainline routing_table.rs); replacement caches for failed nodes.
11. **DHT finger table** — Chord finger[i] = successor(node + 2^(i-1)); O(log N) entries, O(log N) lookup hops.
12. **On-demand discovery** — RREQ flood bounded by hop count/TTL, RREP unicast along reverse path, RERR on link break; LFA pre-computed backup next-hops for local repair before full re-discovery.
13. **Anycast selection** — closest replica from candidate set by locality + cost; optional per-flow sticky routing to same replica for read-after-write consistency.
14. **Gossip anti-entropy** — periodic digest exchange (version vector / Merkle hash) of table digests; reconcile only divergent entries (sloppy management).
15. **Route flap damping** — penalty on each flap, exponential decay, suppress when penalty exceeds threshold, reuse when below reuse threshold (BGP flap damping).
16. **Audit chain** — sha256/blake3 hash-chained route-advertisement entries + periodic ed25519-signed table-version checkpoints; offline verifiable.

---

### 8. Dependencies

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `IdsTime`, `OpState`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — decision transport only; crate never sends directly.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `ids-time` — monotonic `IdsTime` for TTL/revalidation/convergence deadlines.
- `serde` — serialization of route entries, decisions, audit entries.
- `thiserror` — error types.
- `blake3` — content hashing for entry fingerprints and table digests.
- `proptest` — property-based tests.
- `tempfile` — test fixtures.

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. `ids-routing-table` imports no crypto directly — all via `ids-crypto`.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **DHT mode inclusion:** whether k-buckets/finger-table DHT mode is built in Phase 061 or deferred to a later phase; adds complexity but enables key-space routing without explicit topology.
- **On-demand mode inclusion:** whether reactive RREQ/RREP/RERR discovery is built in Phase 061 or deferred; useful for sparse/churn-prone topologies.
- **Concrete TTL / hold-down / flap-damping defaults:** deployment-tuned; to be validated at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-replication`.
- **ECMP max paths and flow-hash function:** max equal-cost paths and hash choice (e.g., blake3-based) affect load distribution; tuning pending.
- **Prefix decomposition of route keys:** whether `RecordId`/`NodeId` keys support longest-prefix-match trie lookup or exact-key only; affects `next_hop.rs` design.
- **Interaction with `ids-membership`:** membership join/leave events feeding `TableUpdate` — exact handshake defined here, validated at integration.
- **Interaction with `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060):** profile tag influencing path selection (e.g., cross-region durable prefers cross-region quorum next-hops) — validated at integration.
- **Gossip interval and digest size:** anti-entropy period and Merkle/vector digest tuning affect convergence speed vs bandwidth; workload-dependent.

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Separate crate `ids-routing-table` (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear table-maintenance boundary |
| Versioned immutable table (new `TableVersion` per update) | Enables convergence detection, replay protection, and audit over table history |
| Pure next-hop resolution (no network contact in crate) | Keeps crate a table/policy layer; carrier handles all I/O via `Endpoint` |
| Path selection: cost → locality → freshness → ECMP stable hash | Simple, deterministic, locality-aware; ECMP preserves flow stickiness |
| Loop prevention: split horizon + poison reverse + path-vector cycle rejection | Combines distance-vector (RFC 2453/CS168) and path-vector (BGP) loop defenses |
| Expiration: TTL → Fresh/Stale/Expired → revalidation probe → GC hold-down | RIP timer model adapted to `ids-time` (monotonic, never wall-clock) |
| Convergence: link-state full recompute on topology change (small/medium), incremental DV-style for large | Link state converges faster; avoids count-to-infinity |
| DHT mode optional (k-buckets + finger tables) | Key-space routing without explicit topology; XOR distance over `NodeId` bytes |
| On-demand mode optional (RREQ/RREP/RERR + LFA) | Reactive discovery for sparse/churn-prone topologies; LFA local repair before re-discovery |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable route advertisement log; tamper evidence |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends bytes | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Only allowed crypto; via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
| All timing keyed to `IdsTime`, never wall-clock | Correct under arbitrary delays; no clock manipulation |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 062 creates `ids-replication-stream`, a separate IDS crate (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities) that owns ordered, versioned change-propagation streams. It is responsible for stream creation, stream versioning, resumable delivery, acknowledgement tracking, lag observability, stream interruption handling, and stream recovery — all carrier-agnostic.

`ids-replication-stream` does not open sockets or drive any transport directly. It sequences changes into per-stream versioned logs, tracks per-consumer delivery positions (watermarks + resume tokens), manages acknowledgement state (in-flight / acked / nacked), detects and repairs gaps on interruption, observes lag per target, and recovers streams from checkpoints. Every byte that crosses a node boundary is framed as an opaque `Vec<u8>` datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 bytes); the crate itself never addresses IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS or any carrier by name.

It builds on `ids-000-aa` canonical types already present for replication: `StreamId` ([u8; 32]), `CheckpointId` ([u8; 32]), `LagInfo`, `StreamState` (Pending/Active/Paused/Stopped/Failed/Completed), `ReplicationStream`, `ReplicationCheckpoint`, `RetryPolicy`, `StreamStateTracker`, and the sealed `Replication` trait (`start_stream`, `stop_stream`, `create_checkpoint`, `restore_checkpoint`, `schedule_retry`, `get_lag`, `stats`). `ids-replication-stream` consumes these types and contracts — it does not redefine them.

A skeleton `ids-replication-stream` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-replication-stream/`. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned Kafka partitioned log + consumer-controlled offset + acknowledgement semantics (exactly-once via producer ID + sequence number), PostgreSQL logical replication slots (resumable LSN position, checkpoint-confirmed flush LSN, crash-safe persistence), MongoDB change streams (resume token, total ordering via global logical clock, driver auto-reconnect), Debezium exactly-once delivery (at-least-once baseline, deduplication requirement on failure/restart), delta-CRDT anti-entropy convergent replication (deltas tolerate duplicates/reordering; lost deltas retransmitted), vector clocks and dotted version vectors for partial/causal ordering, hybrid logical clocks for versioned stream ordering, stream delivery semantics & resumability (sequence numbers, acks, replay windows, snapshot resync beyond window), replication lag observability (consumer lag max, bytes-behind, alert thresholds), Flink coordinated checkpointing (exactly-once state restore from latest checkpoint + input offset), Raft log replication (leader→follower append, committed index), SCTP/RFC 9260 sequenced delivery within streams (stream sequence numbers, ordered vs unordered delivery modes), gRPC server-streaming resumption (continuation tokens, token journal, replay from cursor), XEP-0198 stream management (ack elements c/b, resume with previd + last-received seq), NATS JetStream delivery & acknowledgment (ack floor, in-flight, redeliver after Ack Wait), Durable Streams protocol (append-only offset-ordered byte streams, catch-up reads, live tailing, explicit EOF), Azure Event Sourcing (append-only immutable event stream, entity event version, replay/rehydration), Cassandra consistency levels (quorum R+W>N overlap guarantee).

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-replication-stream` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a stream-management layer: it sequences outgoing changes into versioned per-stream logs, tracks each consumer's delivery position, manages acks/nacks and in-flight state, repairs gaps after interruptions, observes lag, and recovers from checkpoints. It never sends bytes itself; it produces framed `Vec<u8>` datagrams addressed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets that the caller (or `ids-carrier`) transmits.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ids-* LAYER (stream users: store, crdt, sync, …)          │
│  submit_change(dataset, payload, version) → StreamManager                    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 062: ids-replication-stream (THIS CRATE)                 │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ stream           │ │ stream           │ │ acknowledgement  │ │ lag     │ │
│  │ creation         │ │ versioning       │ │ tracking (in-    │ │ observ- │ │
│  │ (StreamId,       │ │ (StreamVersion,  │ │ flight/acked/    │ │ ability │ │
│  │  targets, source)│ │  resume token)   │ │  nacked)         │ │         │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ resumable        │ │ interruption     │ │ stream recovery  │ │ crypto  │ │
│  │ delivery         │ │ handling (gap    │ │ (checkpoint      │ │ surface │ │
│  │ (watermark +     │ │  detect/repair)  │ │  restore +       │ │ (type-   │ │
│  │  resume token)   │ │                  ││  replay)         │ │ level)   │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                                          │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                          ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                    │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])│
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                      │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a versioned change:** caller submits `Change{payload, dataset_id}` → `StreamManager` assigns monotonically increasing `StreamVersion` (u64) + `StreamId`, appends to the append-only versioned log for that stream, frames `StreamFrame{stream_id, version, payload, checksum}` as opaque `Vec<u8>` → dispatched to targets via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` → each target's consumer tracks `last_delivered_version` (watermark) + `resume_token` → target acks version → ack recorded in acknowledgement tracker → in-flight entry cleared → lag recomputed per target.

**Data flow of resumable delivery after interruption:** consumer reconnects presenting `resume_token` (= last acked version + stream id) → server replays from `resume_token + 1` up to stream head, or instructs full snapshot/resync if beyond retention window → gap-free ordered redelivery.

**Stream states (from ids-000-aa `StreamState`):** Pending → Active → Paused → (Stopped | Failed | Completed). `Paused` supports interruption handling; `Failed` triggers recovery path; `Completed` is terminal.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing stream checkpoints and resume tokens; sha256/blake3 for frame checksums, stream-version hashing, checkpoint chaining; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt stream state payloads at rest when confidentiality required. No other crypto.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Ordered change-propagation stream core

An ordered stream is an append-only, versioned sequence of changes consumed positionally. Every change receives a monotonically increasing `StreamVersion` (u64) at append time; consumers track `last_delivered_version` and resume from `last_delivered_version + 1`. Ordering is per-stream (total order within a stream), matching Kafka's per-partition commit offset, PostgreSQL LSN, and EventStoreDB commit position. Sources: Kafka design (partitioned log, consumer-controlled offset), PostgreSQL logical decoding (LSN position, checkpoint), Azure Event Sourcing (append-only event stream, per-entity version).

#### 3.2 Stream creation

`start_stream(dataset_id, source, targets)` allocates a `StreamId`, initializes an empty versioned log (head version = 0), creates per-target consumer state (watermark = 0, resume token = genesis), sets `StreamState::Pending`, then `activate()` moves to `Active`. Returns `ReplicationStream` (from ids-000-aa). Stream creation is idempotent per `StreamId`: re-creating an existing `StreamId` returns `StreamAlreadyExists`. The crate never redefines `StreamId`/`ReplicationStream` — both live in `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/replication.rs`.

#### 3.3 Stream versioning

Each stream carries a `StreamVersion` (u64) that advances by exactly 1 per appended change. Versions are the resume/cursor unit: a consumer presents `last_acked_version` to resume. Stream versions are independent of `ids-000-aa` `ProtocolVersion`/`EdgeCaseBits` (wire-contract gating) — stream versions are intra-stream logical positions, not protocol versions. Checkpointing snapshots the head version at a point in time (`ReplicationCheckpoint.position` of type `OrderingPos` from ids-000-aa). Version skew between replicas is detected by comparing head versions; divergence triggers gap repair or resync.

#### 3.4 Resumable delivery

Resumability requires (a) a durable resume token (stream id + last acked version + optional epoch), (b) server-side retention of the versioned log long enough to replay from the token, and (c) a policy for when the token is beyond the retention window (instruct full snapshot/resync). Sources: MongoDB change streams (resume token = `_id`; auto-reconnect with cached token; persist token across app restarts), PostgreSQL logical slots (persist slot independently of connection; resume from LSN; client records last LSN seen), XEP-0198 stream management (resume with `previd` + last received seq `b`), gRPC streaming lessons (continuation token; server journals every token; replay from `resume_from_token` with original indices), Durable Streams protocol (catch-up reads from offset; live tailing).

#### 3.5 Acknowledgement tracking

Each delivered change enters an in-flight state keyed by `(stream_id, version, target)` until the target acks. On ack, the watermark advances and the entry is cleared. Nack or timeout → redeliver (at-least-once baseline). Idempotent delivery is achieved by consumer-side dedup on `(stream_id, version)` — a duplicate delivery is a no-op if `version <= last_acked_version`. Sources: Kafka idempotent producer (PID + sequence; broker rejects ≤ highwater mark, accepts exactly last+1), NATS JetStream (ack floor; in-flight; redeliver after Ack Wait; ack exactly once), XEP-0198 (ack element `b` removes all stanzas ≤ value; unacked queue drained), Cloud Pub/Sub exactly-once (ack ID versioning; only latest ack ID valid), Debezium (at-least-once → duplicates possible on restart; dedup required).

#### 3.6 Lag observability

Per-target lag = `head_version - last_acked_version` (version lag) plus `bytes_behind` (unacked bytes) and `time_behind` (ms since last ack). `LagInfo` (from ids-000-aa) carries `target`, `lag_ms`, `bytes_behind`, `last_heartbeat_ms`, `recovered`. `is_stale(threshold_ms)` flags `lag_ms > threshold`. Sources: Kafka monitoring (`records-lag-max`, bytes-behind, alert on sustained growth not non-zero), PostgreSQL replication slot lag (`pg_wal_lsn_diff(current, restart_lsn)`), Cassandra under-replicated partitions.

#### 3.7 Stream interruption handling

Interruptions (carrier pause, target unreachable, consumer crash) move a stream to `Paused` or `Failed`. Gap detection: on resume, if `resume_token + 1 < head_version`, the missing range `[resume_token+1, head_version]` is repaired by replay. If the gap exceeds the retention/replay window, the server instructs a full snapshot/resync. Buffer limits are in bytes and version span (not item count) to bound memory; an attacker sending a far-future version must not exhaust memory. Sources: systemoverflow delivery semantics (reorder buffer, gap repair when age/bytes exceed policy; replay window 5–15 min then resync), gRPC streaming (continuation token resume), XEP-0198 (session discarded if not resumed in time; unacked stanzas handled as offline).

#### 3.8 Stream recovery

Recovery restores a stream from a `ReplicationCheckpoint` (from ids-000-aa: checkpoint_id, dataset_id, position/OrderingPos, node_id, created_at_ms, size_bytes, verified, restored). `restore_checkpoint` verifies the checkpoint (sha256/blake3 chain + ed25519 signature), resets the stream head to `position`, replays pending changes after the checkpoint, and returns `StreamState::Active`. Recovery is bounded: replay only changes after the checkpoint position; idempotent dedup prevents double-apply. Sources: Flink coordinated checkpointing (rollback to latest checkpoint + reset inputs to offset; exactly-once), PostgreSQL logical slot crash recovery (slot returns to earlier LSN on crash; clients idempotent), Kafka exactly-once (checkpoint + offset restore).

#### 3.9 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

`ids-replication-stream` uses: ed25519 to sign stream checkpoints and resume tokens (proof of stream position integrity); sha256 for frame checksums and checkpoint chain links; blake3 for fast content hashing of stream frames and causal-context hashing (parallel, SIMD); xchacha20poly1305 to encrypt stream state at rest (24-byte nonce, random nonces safe); chacha20poly1305 to encrypt session/payload datagrams (12-byte nonce, counter-based bounded use). Crypto operations live in `ids-crypto`; this crate declares only type-level surface and references primitive IDs via `ids-000-aa`. Sources: RFC 8032 Ed25519; RFC 7539 ChaCha20-Poly1305; libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305; NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256; BLAKE3 spec.

#### 3.10 Causality and version vectors (optional causal stream mode)

For causally-ordered streams, changes carry a dotted version vector (DVV) causal dependency; a consumer gates delivery until its causal past is satisfied. This is weaker than linearizability but available under partition. Dots `(node_id, counter)` enable compact causality comparison. Sources: Princeton vector clocks (partial ordering), ACM DL dotted version vectors (10.1145/2332432.2332497), Bernstein write-fast-read-in-past causal consistency, CRDT delta-state (arXiv 1603.01529) — deltas tolerate duplicates/reordering and converge.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|-------------|-------------------------|
| Out-of-order / duplicated change delivery | Stream ordering correctness | Per-stream `StreamVersion` + consumer watermark; dedup on `version <= last_acked_version`; gap buffer with byte/span limits |
| Lost change on carrier/target failure | Delivery durability | In-flight tracking + ack/nack; redeliver on timeout (at-least-once); idempotent dedup upgrades to exactly-once semantics |
| Resume token beyond retention window | Resumability | Server instructs full snapshot/resync; documented boundary |
| Memory exhaustion from far-future versions | Availability | Buffer limits in bytes + version span; reject out-of-window versions |
| Stale/lagging target | Lag SLO | `LagInfo.is_stale(threshold)`; `LagTooHigh` error; backpressure signal to caller |
| Stream interruption losing in-flight changes | Delivery guarantee | In-flight queue persisted until ack; `Paused`/`Failed` states; replay from `resume_token + 1` on recovery |
| Checkpoint tampering / replay attack | Recovery integrity | sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints; verify before restore |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent version dedup tolerates duplicates; sequence gaps detected |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | Allowlist unit test; only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via ids-crypto |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation (std::net/tokio::net/IP/etc.) | Architecture | `Endpoint` sole address type; dependency audit bans networking crates |

The carrier is never trusted: stream positions and checkpoints are signed/hashed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Stream creation** — `start_stream(dataset_id, source, targets)` → allocate `StreamId`, empty versioned log (head=0), per-target consumer state (watermark=0, resume token genesis), `StreamState::Pending` → `activate()` → `Active`. Idempotent per `StreamId`; `StreamAlreadyExists` on duplicate.

2. **Versioned log append** — `append(change)` assigns `head_version + 1`, appends `StreamFrame{stream_id, version, payload, checksum}`, advances head. `read(version)` returns frame at position; `read_range(from, to)` replays `[from, to]`.

3. **Resume token** — `ResumeToken{stream_id, last_acked_version, epoch}`; issued on ack watermark advance; validated against log on resume; replay starts at `last_acked_version + 1`; beyond retention → full snapshot/resync.

4. **Acknowledgement tracking** — `AckRecord{stream_id, version, target, state: InFlight|Acked|Nacked, delivered_at_ms, acked_at_ms}`. Ack advances per-target watermark; clears in-flight. Nack/timeout → redeliver. Dedup: `version <= last_acked_version` ⇒ no-op.

5. **Lag computation** — `lag_versions = head_version - last_acked_version`; `bytes_behind` = unacked payload bytes; `time_behind` = now − last_acked_at_ms; `LagInfo.is_stale(threshold)` ⇒ `lag_ms > threshold`.

6. **Gap detection & repair** — on resume, missing = `[resume_token+1, head_version]`; if span ≤ replay window → replay gap; else → resync instruction. Buffer caps in bytes + version span bound memory.

7. **Stream recovery** — `restore_checkpoint(checkpoint_id)` verifies (hash chain + ed25519), sets head to `position`, replays changes after `position`, returns `Active`. Idempotent dedup prevents double-apply.

8. **Stream state machine** — `Pending → Active → Paused → (Stopped | Failed | Completed)`; `is_terminal()` for Stopped/Failed/Completed; `is_active()` for Active; interruption moves Active→Paused/Failed; recovery moves Failed→Active.

9. **Frame codec** — `StreamFrame::encode()`/`decode()` (stream_id u8[32], version u64, payload_len u32, payload Vec<u8>, checksum [u8;32]); version-tagged for forward compatibility.

10. **Dotted version vector (causal mode)** — `DVV{dot: (node_id, counter), vv: Vec<(node_id, counter)>}`; `a < b` iff `dot_a.counter ≤ vv_b[node_a]`; concurrent iff neither precedes; read gate delivers only when `causal_past ⊆ applied`.

`ids-replication-stream/Cargo.toml`:
- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`StreamId`, `CheckpointId`, `LagInfo`, `StreamState`, `ReplicationStream`, `ReplicationCheckpoint`, `RetryPolicy`, `StreamStateTracker`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `Error`) and sealed `Replication` trait.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — frame transport only; crate never sends directly.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `ids-time` — monotonic `IdsTime` ticks for timestamps, heartbeats, lag_ms.
- `thiserror` — error enum derive.
- `serde` + `serde_bytes` — frame/envelope serialization.
- `blake3` — content hashing (type-level surface; ops in ids-crypto).

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, TCP/IP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS implementations in or under `ids-replication-stream`. No crypto beyond the allowed list; all crypto ops via `ids-crypto`.

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-62.1 | Stream creation: `start_stream` allocates unique `StreamId`, head version = 0, state Pending→Active | `StreamId` unique; `ReplicationStream.state == Active` after activate |
| AC-62.2 | Ordered delivery: changes delivered in strictly increasing `StreamVersion` per stream; no gaps in applied sequence | per-stream version sequence contiguous; dedup rejects `version <= last_acked` |
| AC-62.3 | Stream versioning: head advances by exactly 1 per append; version skew between replicas detectable | `head_version == prior + 1`; skew = head_A − head_B reported |
| AC-62.4 | Resumable delivery: resume token (`stream_id`, last acked version) replays from `token+1`; gap-free | replay covers `[token+1, head]`; beyond window → resync instruction |
| AC-62.5 | Acknowledgement tracking: ack clears in-flight, advances watermark; nack/timeout redelivers (at-least-once) | in-flight count → 0 after ack; redelivery on nack/timeout |
| AC-62.6 | Exactly-once via dedup: duplicate `version <= last_acked_version` is a no-op | duplicate deliveries produce no state change |
| AC-62.7 | Lag observability: per-target `LagInfo` (lag_ms, bytes_behind, last_heartbeat_ms); `is_stale(threshold)` flags lag | `LagInfo` matches `head − last_acked`; stale flag accurate |
| AC-62.8 | Stream interruption: Active→Paused/Failed on interruption; gap detect/repair on resume | Paused/Failed states; missing range replayed or resync instructed |
| AC-62.9 | Stream recovery: restore verified checkpoint, reset head to position, replay after, return Active | checkpoint verified (hash chain + ed25519); head == position; replay idempotent |
| AC-62.10 | Stream states: `Pending→Active→Paused→(Stopped|Failed|Completed)`; terminal states flagged | `is_terminal()`/`is_active()` correct per StreamState |
| AC-62.11 | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 B); zero refs to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh | dependency audit test (`cargo tree`) passes; source grep zero matches |
| AC-62.12 | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 in crypto surface | allowlist unit test passes |
| AC-62.13 | Every checkpoint signed/hashed: sha256/blake3 chain + ed25519 signature; verify before restore | verify() returns false on tampered checkpoint |
| AC-62.14 | Crate compiles cleanly | `cargo check -p ids-replication-stream` exits 0 |
| AC-62.15 | Conformance tests pass | `cargo test -p ids-replication-stream` passes all stream/version/ack/lag/recovery tests |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **Replay window size:** bytes + version span bound for the gap-repair buffer; workload-dependent, unquantified.
- **Retention window vs resume token age:** how long the versioned log is retained before instructing full resync; deployment-tuned.
- **Ack timeout value:** in-flight redelivery timeout trades redelivery storm vs latency; to be validated at integration with `ids-carrier`/`ids-replication`.
- **Causal stream mode (DVV):** whether to ship the optional dotted-version-vector causal gating in Phase 062 or defer to a later phase; design decision pending.
- **Interaction with `ids-sync-checkpoint` (Phase 063):** shared `CheckpointId`/`ReplicationCheckpoint` types already exist in ids-000-aa; exact handshake (checkpoint → sync point) to be validated at integration.
- **Interaction with `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060):** stream writes tagged with profile; profile quorum/durability evaluated before ack; exact admission handshake pending.
- **Stream head persistence:** whether head version and consumer watermarks are checkpointed durably or held in-memory with periodic snapshots; durability/performance tradeoff unquantified.
- **Multi-target fan-out:** per-target watermark state scales with target count; bounded-state strategy for large target sets undecided.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-replication-stream` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear stream-management boundary |
| Per-stream `StreamVersion` (u64) as resume/cursor unit | Matches Kafka commit offset, PostgreSQL LSN, EventStoreDB commit position; simple, gap-free resume |
| At-least-once baseline + consumer-side dedup → exactly-once | Kafka idempotent producer / Pub/Sub ack-ID versioning pattern; dedup on `version <= last_acked` |
| Resume token = `stream_id + last_acked_version + epoch` | Mirrors MongoDB change-stream resume token and XEP-0198 resume (`previd` + `b`) |
| Lag = `head − last_acked` versions + bytes_behind + time_behind | Matches Kafka `records-lag-max` and PostgreSQL slot lag observability |
| Gap repair on replay window; resync beyond window | systemoverflow delivery semantics: replay window then full resync; bounds memory |
| Checkpoints: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519 signature, verify before restore | Tamper-evident, offline-verifiable recovery |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate never sends directly | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in trust base |
| Allowed crypto only; ops in `ids-crypto`, type surface here | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
| `ids-time` monotonic ticks for timestamps/lag; never wall-clock for ordering | Correct under arbitrary delays; no clock manipulation |
| Stream states reuse `ids-000-aa` `StreamState` | Single canonical definition; no redefinition |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 063 creates `ids-sync-checkpoint`, the IDS crate that owns verified sync points for resumable replication. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by checkpoint concern. `ids-sync-checkpoint` provides checkpoint creation, checkpoint verification, resume-from-checkpoint, reconciliation reference, checkpoint versioning, and checkpoint garbage collection — all carrier-agnostic.

**Core design:** a checkpoint is a verified, self-describing snapshot of replication state at a durable position. Each checkpoint carries: a checkpoint ID (BLAKE3-256 content hash), the replicated state root (BLAKE3 Merkle root), the last-applied operation position (`OpRef`/`OrderingPos`), a parent checkpoint link (for incremental/differential chains), an ed25519 signature over the checkpoint header, a sha256/blake3 hash chain entry, and an optional xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305-encrypted payload section. Checkpoints are never sent by this crate; it produces and verifies checkpoint envelopes that callers ship as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

**Scope boundary:** `ids-sync-checkpoint` manages sync points; it does not open sockets, drive transports, or implement replication itself. It returns `CheckpointResult`, `ResumePosition`, and `VerificationResult` values that the replication layer consumes. Thresholds (checkpoint interval, retention count, GC age) are configurable budgets, not hard-coded limits.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshots (consistent cuts, marker-based channel state, 1985 ACM TOCS); coordinated vs uncoordinated checkpointing and two-phase checkpoint protocol; PostgreSQL WAL checkpoints (checkpoint records, crash recovery starting from checkpoint, replication slots); Raft snapshotting (InstallSnapshot RPC, last-included index/term anchor, log compaction, snapshot transfer as separate operation); Apache Flink checkpointing (consistent snapshot of operator state + stream position, exactly-once, checkpoint interval trades overhead vs recovery time, asynchronous state writeback); Apache Spark Streaming checkpointing (metadata + data checkpointing to fault-tolerant storage); Apache Kafka consumer offset checkpointing (periodic offset commit, rewind to old offset); RocksDB incremental backup (share table files, verify backup); event sourcing snapshots (rehydrate aggregate from snapshot + post-snapshot events, snapshot frequency vs replay cost tradeoff); read-write quorum systems (R+W>N intersection, every read quorum intersects every write quorum); anti-entropy Merkle tree repair (Cassandra Merkle trees, digest exchange, reconcile divergent replicas); dotted version vectors (causal precedence, compact causality tracking); vector clocks (Lamport, Mattern/Fidge); LSM compaction and tombstone GC; state machine replication checkpoint-based recovery (PBFT signed checkpoints, 2f+1 quorum, state transfer from checkpoint + log suffix); checkpoint interval optimization (Young/Daly, utilization model, failure rate vs checkpoint cost); incremental/differential checkpointing (copy only changed blocks since base); two-phase commit checkpointing for distributed transactions; Byzantine fault-tolerant checkpoint verification (signed checkpoints, stable checkpoint from quorum digests); CRDT checkpoint anti-entropy convergence (state-based vs op-based, strong convergence, tombstone GC at causal stability); BLAKE3 (Merkle-tree parallel hashing, KDF, XOF, keyed hash); SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4); ed25519-dalek (RFC 8032 EdDSA sign/verify); xchacha20poly1305 (libsodium 192-bit nonce, random nonces safe); chacha20poly1305 (RFC 7539 AEAD, 96-bit nonce).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-sync-checkpoint` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a checkpoint management layer: given a replication position and state digest, it creates a verified checkpoint envelope; given a stored checkpoint, it verifies integrity and authenticity; given a resume request, it computes the resume position and the post-checkpoint operation range. It never sends bytes itself; it returns checkpoint envelopes and resume decisions that callers frame into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    REPLICATION / SYNC LAYER (checkpoint users)               │
│  ids-replication, ids-sync, ids-recovery — create/consume sync checkpoints   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 063: ids-sync-checkpoint (THIS CRATE — checkpoint mgmt) │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌────────┐ │ │
│  │ checkpoint       │ │ checkpoint       │ │ resume           │ │ GC     │ │ │
│  │ creation         │ │ verification     │ │ from checkpoint  │ │ policy │ │ │
│  │ (envelope build) │ │ (sig+hash verify)│ │ (position+range) │ │ (retain│ │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ /age)  │ │ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ └──────────────────┘ └────────┘ │ │
│  │ versioning       │ │ reconciliation   │ │                    │         │ │ │
│  │ (chain+format)   │ │ reference        │ │                    │         │ │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                    │         │ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │                    │         │ │
│  │ crypto surface   │ │ envelope store   │ │                    │         │ │ │
│  │ (ed25519/sha256/ │ │ (index+metadata) │ │                    │         │ │ │
│  │  blake3/xchacha/ │ └──────────────────┘ │                    │         │ │ │
│  │  chacha)         │                      │                    │         │ │
│  └──────────────────┘                      │                    │         │ │
└───────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────┴──────────┘
                                            │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                            ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                    │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload)      │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                     │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of checkpoint creation:** replication layer submits `CreateCheckpoint{state_root, last_position, causal_context}` → `ids-sync-checkpoint` builds `CheckpointEnvelope{header, signature, hash_chain_link, optional_encrypted_payload}` → returns envelope → caller ships as opaque datagram(s) to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets and collects acks → checkpoint marked stable when quorum of replicas confirm receipt.

**Data flow of resume from checkpoint:** replication layer submits `ResumeFrom{checkpoint_id}` → `ids-sync-checkpoint` verifies signature + hash chain + state root → returns `ResumePosition{checkpoint_id, last_position, post_checkpoint_op_range, causal_past}` → caller replays operations after the checkpoint position via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

**Checkpoint semantics (research-verified):**
- **Consistent cut / global snapshot:** Chandy-Lamport marker-based snapshot guarantees no effect is in the past while its cause is in the future; every message received in the snapshot's past was sent in the past (consistent cut).
- **Checkpoint anchor:** last-included index/term pair anchors the checkpoint into the log's coordinate system (Raft); snapshot + log suffix suffices for catch-up.
- **Quorum-certified checkpoint:** PBFT-style — signed checkpoints collected from 2f+1 replicas form a stable checkpoint; only then prune below the low watermark.
- **Exactly-once resume:** restore state from checkpoint, replay operations strictly after checkpoint position; duplicates suppressed via idempotent application.
- **Incremental/differential checkpoints:** checkpoint chain where each checkpoint references its parent; only changed state since parent is stored (differential backup pattern).
- **Garbage collection:** retain-by-count and retain-by-age policies; mark-and-sweep reachability from live roots (active checkpoints, pinned resume positions); GC cannot remove a checkpoint still referenced by an in-flight resume or the latest stable checkpoint.
- **Anti-entropy reconciliation:** Merkle tree digest exchange between replicas identifies divergent ranges; checkpoint versioning detects stale checkpoints; reconciliation reference guides repair.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing checkpoint headers and audit checkpoints; sha256/blake3 for checkpoint IDs, state roots, hash-chain links, Merkle digests; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 for encrypting checkpoint payload at rest when confidentiality required.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Chandy-Lamport distributed snapshots (consistent cuts)

**Source:** Chandy & Lamport, "Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems," ACM Transactions on Computer Systems, Vol 3, No 1 (1985); Princeton COS418 lecture notes on distributed snapshots; UMass 590CC lecture notes on global state recording.

The Chandy-Lamport algorithm captures a consistent global state of a distributed system using marker messages on FIFO channels. A process records its local state, then sends a marker on each outgoing channel before sending further messages. On receiving a marker, if the process hasn't snapshotted, it records its state and sends markers; otherwise it records channel state. The result is a consistent cut: for any event recorded, all events that happened-before it are also recorded. `ids-sync-checkpoint` adopts the consistent-cut principle: a sync checkpoint must represent a causally closed state — no operation whose effects are partially included. Marker-equivalent logic is expressed as barrier positions in the replication log (last-applied `OpRef`/`OrderingPos`).

#### 3.2 Coordinated vs uncoordinated checkpointing

**Source:** "Checkpointing Techniques in Distributed Systems: A Synopsis of Diverse Strategies Over the Last Decades" (SBC WTF journal); Springer "Implementing Rollback-Recovery Coordinated Checkpoints" (ISSADS 2005).

Coordinated checkpointing: all processes agree on a safe execution point via a two-phase checkpoint protocol (prepare phase: processes block and notify readiness; commit phase: initiator signals all to checkpoint). Ensures a consistent global checkpoint (recovery line) but causes latency spikes. Uncoordinated checkpointing: each process checkpoints independently; may produce inconsistent global states requiring rollback-dependency analysis. `ids-sync-checkpoint` supports both: coordinated checkpoints for strong consistency (quorum-signed, stable checkpoints) and uncoordinated local checkpoints for opportunistic local save points, with consistency validation at verification time.

#### 3.3 WAL-based checkpointing and crash recovery

**Source:** PostgreSQL 19 documentation: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL), WAL configuration, continuous archiving and point-in-time recovery.

WAL's central concept: data file changes are written only after WAL records describing them are flushed to permanent storage. Crash recovery always starts from the last checkpoint record; only WAL records after the checkpoint need replaying. A checkpoint record stores metadata about the current database state. `ids-sync-checkpoint` adopts the same structure: a checkpoint is a durable position marker; recovery replays operations strictly after the checkpoint position. Checkpoint interval trades off WAL/log growth against recovery replay time.

#### 3.4 Raft snapshotting and InstallSnapshot

**Source:** Ongaro & Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm" (Raft paper); hashicorp/raft snapshot.go; MerceMay "Snapshot Install and the Cost of Compacting a Consensus Log"; openraft docs on snapshot replication.

Raft snapshots compact the log: the state machine writes current state to a snapshot, then committed log entries up to the snapshot boundary are discarded. A snapshot carries last-included index and term (the anchor). InstallSnapshot is a separate RPC, not a large AppendEntries; followers install chunks in order, then reset their state machine from the snapshot. A node behind the snapshot edge cannot catch up via log entries alone — it needs a snapshot transfer. `ids-sync-checkpoint` models sync points as Raft-style anchors: last-applied position + term/epoch, with snapshot transfer via opaque carrier datagrams.

#### 3.5 Apache Flink checkpointing (exactly-once state snapshots)

**Source:** Apache Flink docs: Stateful Stream Processing, Tuning Checkpoints and Large State; "An Overview of End-to-End Exactly-Once Processing in Apache Flink with Apache Kafka."

Flink checkpoints mark a specific point in each input stream plus operator state. A streaming dataflow resumes from a checkpoint with exactly-once semantics by restoring operator state and replaying records from the checkpoint position. Checkpoints are written asynchronously to persistent storage; the checkpoint interval trades fault-tolerance overhead against recovery time. Incremental checkpointing: operators start from the latest full snapshot and apply incremental updates. `ids-sync-checkpoint` adopts exactly-once resume semantics and the interval-overhead/recovery-time tradeoff model.

#### 3.6 Kafka consumer offset checkpointing

**Source:** Apache Kafka design document.

Kafka consumer position is a single integer offset per partition; state can be periodically checkpointed. A consumer can rewind to an old offset and re-consume — essential for bug recovery. Offset checkpoints are small (one number per partition) and cheap. `ids-sync-checkpoint` uses the offset-checkpoint pattern: a resume position is a compact coordinate (last applied `OpRef`/`OrderingPos` per replication stream) enabling cheap rewind and replay.

#### 3.7 RocksDB incremental backup / verify

**Source:** facebook/rocksdb wiki "How to backup RocksDB."

RocksDB backups are normally incremental (share table files): `CreateNewBackup` copies only new data; `VerifyBackup` validates backup integrity. `ids-sync-checkpoint` adopts incremental checkpoint creation (only state changed since parent checkpoint) and built-in verify (signature + hash chain + state root re-check).

#### 3.8 Event sourcing snapshots

**Source:** CodeOpinion "Snapshots in Event Sourcing for Rehydrating Aggregates"; EventSourcingDB "Snapshots and Performance"; Azure Architecture Center "Event Sourcing Pattern"; Axon Framework "Snapshots."

An entity's state is reconstructed by replaying its event stream; snapshots capture state at a stream position. Rehydration loads the latest snapshot, then replays only post-snapshot events. Snapshot frequency balances storage cost vs replay time. Snapshots are an optimization, not a replacement — full replay remains the fallback if a snapshot is unavailable or unusable. `ids-sync-checkpoint` treats checkpoints the same: resume from checkpoint + replay post-checkpoint ops; full replication from genesis is the fallback path.

#### 3.9 Read-write quorum systems (R+W>N)

**Source:** arXiv 2104.04102 "Read-Write Quorum Systems Made Practical"; Atlas of Engineering "Quorum, Read/Write Intersection and Split-Brain Prevention"; UMass CS677 lecture notes on quorum-based protocols; AWS Aurora quorum blog.

A read-write quorum system (R, W) over replica set X requires every read quorum to intersect every write quorum (r ∩ w ≠ ∅). R + W > N guarantees read/write intersection — a read always contacts at least one replica holding the latest write. Write/write intersection requires W > N/2. Availability: writes tolerate N−W failures, reads tolerate N−R. `ids-sync-checkpoint` uses quorum intersection for checkpoint stability: a checkpoint is stable when a quorum of replicas have signed it; resume requires quorum agreement on the checkpoint position.

#### 3.10 Anti-entropy Merkle tree repair

**Source:** Cassandra docs "Anti-entropy repair" (Merkle trees, depth-15 compact trees); Zenoh blog "Keeping storages aligned in Zenoh" (era-based hash trees, fingerprint comparison); Database Internals Ch. 12 (Merkle trees, read repair, hinted handoff); ACM "Efficient reconciliation and flow control for anti-entropy protocols."

Anti-entropy: background process compares replicas via digest exchange (Merkle trees or version vectors) and reconciles divergent ranges. Cassandra builds a Merkle tree per replica (leaf = row hash), compares trees top-down, streams only differing leaves. Zenoh slices time into eras with era-based hash trees; replicas publish fingerprints, compare, identify missing data. `ids-sync-checkpoint` uses Merkle roots as checkpoint state roots and supports anti-entropy reconciliation reference: given two checkpoints, the Merkle proof path identifies which sub-ranges diverge, enabling targeted repair rather than full resync.

#### 3.11 Dotted version vectors and causal tracking

**Source:** Riak "Vector Clocks Revisited Part 2: Dotted Version Vectors"; ACM DL 10.1145/2332432.2332497 "Efficient causality tracking with dotted version vectors"; UMass DS-2-time lecture notes on logical/vector clocks.

Version vectors track per-node causality but grow with node count. Dotted version vectors (DVV) compact this: a dot is (node_id, counter); a DVV is a set of dots plus a version vector covering the causal past. Causal precedence: dot_a < dot_b iff dot_a.counter ≤ vv_b[dot_a.node]; concurrent iff neither precedes. `ids-sync-checkpoint` stores a DVV as the checkpoint's causal context, enabling resume to verify that all causally-preceding operations are included before the checkpoint position.

#### 3.12 Idempotent replay and exactly-once semantics

**Source:** Apache Flink exactly-once overview; stripe/idempotency-key documentation; CheckMate "Evaluating Checkpointing Protocols for Streaming Dataflows."

Exactly-once processing: each event affects results exactly once even under failure. Flink uses two-phase commit (pre-commit = checkpoint barrier, commit = external state commit). Idempotency keys give exactly-once at the application layer. `ids-sync-checkpoint` guarantees exactly-once resume: state restored from checkpoint, then each post-checkpoint operation applied exactly once via idempotent application keys derived from `OpRef`.

#### 3.13 Checkpoint garbage collection

**Source:** SlateDB docs "Checkpoints" (manifest version pinning, GC keeps reachable manifests/SSTs, checkpoint expiration); OriginTrail SWM public snapshot GC (pressure-based, age + free-space watermarks); RetainZ "Reclaim-Time-Aware Placement for AI Checkpoints" (reclaim epochs); GC-CR decentralized garbage collector for checkpointing.

GC strategies: retain-by-count (keep N most recent), retain-by-age (keep checkpoints newer than T), pressure-based (evict when disk below watermark), reachability-based (mark-and-sweep from live roots: active checkpoints + pinned resume positions). SlateDB: a checkpoint pins a manifest version; GC cannot remove manifests/SSTs reachable from active checkpoints. `ids-sync-checkpoint` implements retain-by-count, retain-by-age, and reachability-based GC with a grace period; a checkpoint referenced by an in-flight resume or the latest stable checkpoint is never collected.

#### 3.14 Checkpoint interval optimization

**Source:** ScienceDirect "A utilization model for optimization of checkpoint intervals in distributed stream processing systems" (FGCS 2020); CPE-05-0002 "Performance and effectiveness trade-off for checkpointing"; ACM TECS "Optimal Checkpointing Strategy for Real-time Systems"; ACM TOPC "Checkpointing Workflows à la Young/Daly Is Not Good Enough."

Young/Daly formula: optimal checkpoint interval balances checkpoint overhead against expected re-execution after failure. Excessive checkpointing degrades performance; deficient checkpointing incurs expensive recovery. Utilization model incorporates checkpoint interval, failure rate, checkpoint cost, failure detection, restart cost, topology depth, message delay. `ids-sync-checkpoint` exposes a configurable interval with guidance: interval = sqrt(2·checkpoint_cost/failure_rate) as a starting point, tunable per deployment.

#### 3.15 Incremental / differential checkpointing

**Source:** Microsoft Learn "Differential Backups (SQL Server)"; SlateDB checkpoints (pin manifest version, cheap metadata-only checkpoint); RocksDB incremental backup (share table files).

A differential/incremental checkpoint is based on a previous full checkpoint and captures only changed state since the base. Much faster than full checkpoints; chains of differentials accumulate until a new full checkpoint is taken. `ids-sync-checkpoint` supports full checkpoints (complete state root) and differential checkpoints (parent link + changed-ranges Merkle proof), with chain length limits to bound resume replay.

#### 3.16 State machine replication checkpoint-based recovery

**Source:** Scixa "Checkpoints and Log Compaction in State-Machine Replication Lifecycle"; jack-vanlightly "VR Revisited - Checkpoint-Based Replica Recovery"; ETH "State Machine Replication Scalability Made Simple" (PBFT signed checkpoints, 2f+1 quorum, stable checkpoints, state transfer from checkpoint + log suffix).

SMR checkpoints: application state snapshots at op-number boundaries; a stale replica recovers by obtaining state from another replica (checkpoint + small log suffix), then switches back to log replication. PBFT: replicas broadcast signed checkpoints after each checkpoint period; 2f+1 matching checkpoints form a stable checkpoint; only then prune below the low watermark. `ids-sync-checkpoint` adopts quorum-signed stable checkpoints and state-transfer-from-checkpoint-plus-suffix recovery.

#### 3.17 Two-phase commit checkpointing for distributed transactions

**Source:** Oracle Database "Distributed Transactions Concepts" (two-phase commit: prepare phase, commit phase).

2PC: coordinator asks participants to prepare (promise to commit/rollback); if all prepare, coordinator sends commit; otherwise rollback. Checkpoints can be taken at prepare/commit boundaries for distributed transaction recovery. `ids-sync-checkpoint` provides the checkpoint primitive at transaction boundaries; the 2PC orchestration lives in higher-layer crates (ids-saga, ids-coordinator).

#### 3.18 Byzantine fault-tolerant checkpoint verification

**Source:** ACM DL 10.1145/3436728 "Byzantine Fault-tolerant State-machine Replication from a Systems Perspective"; ETH SMR scalability paper.

BFT checkpoints: replicas broadcast signed checkpoints; a stable checkpoint requires 2f+1 signatures from distinct replicas; a trailing replica can verify a checkpoint from a single correct source because the proof contains 2f+1 signatures. `ids-sync-checkpoint` supports BFT verification mode: checkpoint header signed by the creating replica, stable when quorum of signatures collected; verification checks signature validity and quorum count.

#### 3.19 CRDT checkpoint anti-entropy convergence

**Source:** ACM Computing Surveys "Approaches to Conflict-free Replicated Data Types" (state-based vs op-based); arXiv 1603.01529 delta-CRDTs.

CRDTs guarantee strong convergence: replicas receiving the same update set converge to the same state, regardless of delivery order. State-based CRDTs merge full state (join-semilattice least upper bound); op-based propagate operations with causal delivery. Checkpoints of CRDT state are mergeable; anti-entropy exchanges Merkle digests of CRDT state and reconciles divergences. `ids-sync-checkpoint` stores CRDT-opaque state roots and supports CRDT merge as the reconciliation reference.

#### 3.20 Vector clocks and Lamport timestamps

**Source:** UMass DS-2-time lecture notes; Wikipedia causal consistency; MIT 6.824 linearizability notes.

Lamport clocks satisfy e → e′ ⇒ TS(e) < TS(e′); vector clocks satisfy e → e′ ⇔ V(e) < V(e′) and detect concurrency. `ids-sync-checkpoint` uses logical timestamps only (never wall-clock) for checkpoint ordering; wall-clock is never used for causality or resume decisions.

#### 3.21 LSM compaction and tombstone GC

**Source:** VLDB 2021 "Constructing and Analyzing the LSM Compaction Design Space."

LSM trees compact sorted runs to reclaim space from overwrites and tombstones. Compaction strategies (leveling, tiering) trade write amplification vs space amplification. `ids-sync-checkpoint` models checkpoint GC analogously: old checkpoints are "compacted" (garbage collected) when their state is covered by newer checkpoints, bounded by retention policy.

#### 3.22 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** RFC 8032 (Ed25519); libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305 construction (192-bit nonce, random nonces safe); RFC 7539 (ChaCha20-Poly1305 AEAD, 96-bit nonce); NIST FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256); BLAKE3-team README (Merkle-tree parallel hash, KDF, XOF, keyed hash); docs.rs sha2, docs.rs ed25519-dalek.

`ids-sync-checkpoint` uses: ed25519 for signing checkpoint headers (64-byte signatures over canonical envelope bytes); sha256 for hash-chain entries and checkpoint ID domain separation; blake3 for checkpoint IDs (content hash of state root + position + parent), Merkle roots, and KDF-derived sub-keys; xchacha20poly1305 for encrypting checkpoint payload at rest with random 192-bit nonces; chacha20poly1305 for encrypting small session/state payloads with 96-bit nonces. No other crypto.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|--------------------------|
| Torn / partial checkpoint write | Checkpoint integrity | Write to temp file, fsync, atomic rename; verify signature + hash chain before accepting |
| Checkpoint forgery / tampering | Decision authenticity | ed25519 signature over canonical envelope bytes; quorum of signatures for stable checkpoints |
| Replay of stale checkpoint | Resume correctness | Hash chain prevents replay of superseded checkpoints; resume validates checkpoint is ancestor of current position |
| Checkpoint chain fork (divergent parents) | Consistency | Single parent link per checkpoint; verification rejects checkpoints whose parent chain doesn't converge to genesis |
| Causal gap in checkpoint (missing dependency) | Causal correctness | DVV causal context stored; resume rejects checkpoint if causal past not satisfied |
| Checkpoint DoS via excessive creation | Storage exhaustion | Configurable max checkpoints; GC enforces retain-by-count/age/reachability |
| Encryption key extraction | Payload confidentiality | Keys never leave node; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 at rest; zeroized on shutdown |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Clock manipulation for checkpoint order | Ordering correctness | Logical positions (OpRef/OrderingPos) only; never wall-clock for checkpoint ordering |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent checkpoint application; idempotency keys from OpRef; carrier is opaque |
| Checkpoint version skew (incompatible format) | Interoperability | Checkpoint format version in header; verification rejects unknown/unsupported versions |

The carrier is never trusted: checkpoint integrity is cryptographic (signature + hash chain), surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-sync-checkpoint |
|-------|------|----------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; sealed trait contracts mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All checkpoint traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns envelopes, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing checkpoint headers; hash chains; Merkle roots; encrypting payload at rest |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization (primary user) | Creates checkpoints at positions; consumes checkpoints for state transfer and catch-up |
| `ids-sync` | Resumable replication (primary user) | Resumes from checkpoint; replays post-checkpoint operations |
| `ids-recovery` | Crash recovery / WAL replay | Uses checkpoints as recovery start points; replays WAL after checkpoint position |
| `ids-crdt` | CRDT state (mergeable checkpoints) | CRDT state roots stored in checkpoints; CRDT merge as reconciliation reference |
| `ids-fault` | Fault detection / failure domains | Failure events trigger checkpoint-based recovery; fault layer consults checkpoints |
| `ids-membership` | Replica membership / region topology | Quorum calculations for checkpoint stability; region-scoped checkpoints |

Integration points: `ids-sync-checkpoint` produces `CheckpointEnvelope` and `ResumePosition` values; consumers frame them into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. The crate never reaches into dependent crate internals and never sends bytes itself.

ids-sync-checkpoint/
