### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

**1. Checkpoint envelope construction**
```
CheckpointEnvelope {
  header: CheckpointHeader { version, id, parent_id, position, term, state_root, causal_ctx, created_at },
  signature: ed25519 Signature over canonical(header) bytes,
  hash_chain_entry: sha256(header || prev_chain_hash),
  encrypted_payload: Optional<xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 ciphertext>
}
CheckpointID = blake3(state_root || position || parent_id || created_at)
```

**2. Consistent-cut checkpoint rule**
A checkpoint is valid iff its state is causally closed: for every operation included in the state, all operations that happened-before it (per DVV causal context) are also included. Equivalent to Chandy-Lamport consistent cut: no effect in the past while its cause is in the future.

**3. Quorum-stable checkpoint (BFT mode)**
A checkpoint becomes stable when `2f+1` distinct replicas have signed identical envelope headers. Verification checks signature validity and quorum count. Only stable checkpoints may serve as resume bases or GC roots.

**4. Resume position computation**
```
ResumePosition { checkpoint_id, last_position (OpRef/OrderingPos), post_checkpoint_op_range, causal_past (DVV) }
Resume is valid iff: checkpoint verified + causal_past ⊆ applied_ops + last_position < current_head
```

**5. Idempotent replay guard**
Each post-checkpoint operation carries an idempotency key derived from `OpRef`. Replay applies each operation at most once; duplicates are detected and skipped. Guarantees exactly-once resume semantics.

**6. Merkle-based reconciliation reference**
Given checkpoint A and checkpoint B with divergent state roots: compare Merkle roots; if equal, states identical; if different, descend the tree comparing child hashes to identify divergent leaf ranges; transfer only differing ranges via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams.

**7. Garbage collection (mark-and-sweep)**
1. Enumerate live roots: active checkpoints, pinned resume positions, latest stable checkpoint per region.
2. Traverse reachable checkpoints via parent links; mark reachable.
3. Sweep: delete unmarked checkpoints older than retain-by-age or beyond retain-by-count.
4. Grace period: checkpoints referenced by in-flight resumes are never collected.

**8. Atomic checkpoint persistence**
Write envelope to temp file → fsync → atomic rename to final location. Verification reads final location only; temp files never visible to readers. Prevents torn checkpoints.

**9. Checkpoint chain validation**
Walk parent links from a checkpoint to genesis; reject if: cycle detected, fork detected (two checkpoints claim same child), missing parent, or format version unsupported.

**10. Interval optimization (Young/Daly-derived)**
Suggested checkpoint interval: `sqrt(2 · checkpoint_cost / failure_rate)` as a deployment starting point; trades checkpoint overhead against expected re-execution after failure. Configurable per deployment.

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list; `ids-sync-checkpoint` imports no crypto directly — all via `ids-crypto`.

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-63.1 | Checkpoint creation produces a signed, hash-chained envelope with BLAKE3-256 ID | Envelope contains ed25519 signature, sha256/blake3 hash-chain entry, BLAKE3 ID |
| AC-63.2 | Checkpoint verification validates signature + hash chain + state root + causal context | Verification returns Verified/Rejected with reason; 100% detection of tampered envelopes |
| AC-63.3 | Resume from checkpoint returns correct ResumePosition + post-checkpoint op range | Resume position = checkpoint's last position; replay starts strictly after checkpoint |
| AC-63.4 | Exactly-once resume: no operation applied twice after resume | Idempotency-key dedup; property test proves at-most-once application |
| AC-63.5 | Consistent-cut invariant: checkpoint state is causally closed | DVV causal past ⊆ operations included in checkpoint state |
| AC-63.6 | Quorum-stable checkpoints (BFT mode): 2f+1 signatures required | Stable checkpoint rejected unless quorum signatures verified |
| AC-63.7 | Checkpoint chain linear: no forks, converges to genesis | Chain validator walks parent links; rejects cycles/forks/missing parents |
| AC-63.8 | Garbage collection: retain-by-count, retain-by-age, reachability enforced | GC collects only unmarked checkpoints beyond policy limits; live roots never collected |
| AC-63.9 | Atomic persistence: temp + fsync + rename; no torn checkpoints | Crash-during-write test: recovery never observes partial envelope |
| AC-63.10 | Merkle reconciliation: divergent sub-ranges identified via proof path | Merkle proof descent identifies changed leaves; only differing ranges transferred |
| AC-63.11 | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh | Dependency audit test (`cargo tree`) + source grep passes |
| AC-63.12 | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 in crypto surface | Allowlist unit test passes |
| AC-63.13 | Every checkpoint decision recorded in append-only, hash-chained, ed25519-signed audit log | Audit chain verifies end-to-end |
| AC-63.14 | Logical positions only (OpRef/OrderingPos); never wall-clock for checkpoint ordering or resume decisions | No `SystemTime`/`Instant` used for causality/ordering |
| AC-63.15 | Full-replay-from-genesis fallback works when checkpoint unavailable | Fallback path replays all operations from genesis |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **Checkpoint interval default:** the optimal interval depends on failure rate and checkpoint cost (Young/Daly model); concrete defaults to be tuned per deployment at integration with `ids-replication`/`ids-sync`.
- **Quorum size for stable checkpoints:** `2f+1` for BFT mode; non-BFT mode may use simple majority. Deployment-dependent.
- **Differential checkpoint chain length limit:** unbounded differential chains increase resume time; max chain length before forcing a full checkpoint is unquantified.
- **GC grace period duration:** how long to retain a checkpoint referenced by an in-flight resume before collection; tradeoff between storage and resume success.
- **Encryption of checkpoint payload:** optional (`encrypted` feature); key management and rotation for at-rest encryption not yet designed.
- **Interaction with `ids-crdt` (checkpoint of CRDT state):** CRDT merge as reconciliation reference; exact merge-audit interface to be validated at integration.
- **Cross-region checkpoint consistency:** region-scoped checkpoints and cross-region stable checkpoints need quorum-per-region semantics; unquantified latency impact.
- **Checkpoint format migration:** rules for migrating between envelope format versions undefined; migration path TBD.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-sync-checkpoint` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear checkpoint boundary |
| Checkpoint = consistent cut (Chandy-Lamport principle) | Guarantees causally closed state; no effect in past while cause in future |
| Anchor = last-applied position (OpRef/OrderingPos) + term/epoch | Raft-style anchor positions checkpoint in the log coordinate system |
| Quorum-signed stable checkpoints (2f+1 for BFT) | PBFT pattern; trailing replica can verify from single correct source |
| Exactly-once resume via idempotency keys (OpRef-derived) | Exactly-once processing semantics under failure; duplicates suppressed |
| Merkle root as state root + Merkle proof for reconciliation | Efficient divergence detection; transfer only differing ranges (Cassandra anti-entropy pattern) |
| DVV causal context stored per checkpoint | Compact causality tracking; resume validates causal past before applying |
| Atomic persistence (temp + fsync + rename) | Prevents torn checkpoints; crash-safe writes |
| GC = mark-and-sweep from live roots + retain-by-count/age | SlateDB/OriginTrail patterns; never collect checkpoints referenced by in-flight resumes |
| Logical positions only; never wall-clock for ordering | Clock manipulation cannot break checkpoint order or resume correctness |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns envelopes, never sends | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Only allowed crypto; `ids-crypto` exposes primitives via `ids-000-aa` | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 064 creates `ids-reconciliation`, the IDS crate responsible for reconciling divergent replicas. Its job is to detect divergence between replicas, compare versions and operation histories, apply conflict and authority rules, resolve conflicts through CRDT merge semantics, and prevent silent overwrites — all carrier-agnostic. `ids-reconciliation` does not open sockets or drive any transport directly; it takes two (or more) replica states as opaque inputs, produces a `MergeDecision` (accept / reject / merge / tombstone / quarantine), and the caller ships it as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

Contents per prompts.txt entry 64: version comparison, operation history comparison, conflict and authority rules, merge semantics, CRDT integration, conflict detection, conflict resolution, silent overwrite prevention.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned the Shapiro et al. 2011 CRDT paper (INRIA RR-7687 / Hal comprehensive study) proving strong eventual consistency via join-semilattice merge (commutative, associative, idempotent); the delta-CRDT paper (Almeida/Shoker/Baquero, arXiv:1603.01529) for incremental delta-state anti-entropy; state-based vs operation-based CRDT comparison (CvRDT vs CmRDT); version vectors and dotted version vectors for causal ordering and conflict detection (Baquero/Preguiça DVV paper, Riak KV docs); Merkle tree anti-entropy (Dynamo/Cassandra/DSE docs) for digest-based replica comparison; anti-entropy digest exchange (systemoverflow/scalecube-prism) for healing divergent state after partitions; LWW register semantics and its lost-update / silent-overwrite hazard (semantic conflict model paper); OR-set (observed-remove / add-wins) semantics; PN-counter and MV-register semantics; CRDT convergence theorem (ACID: associative, commutative, idempotent, distributed); hinted handoff / sloppy quorum (Dynamo paper); read repair (ScyllaDB/Cassandra); read repair and sibling explosion (Riak DVV vs vector clocks); fencing tokens / write fence (Kleppmann stale-write analysis, ETag/If-Match, leader epoch); tombstone garbage collection via causal stability (USENIX OSDI'26 Treedoc); IBLT / invertible bloom filters for set reconciliation (MIT, rateless Bloom filters arxiv 2510.27614); causal consistency session guarantees (read your writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads); OP/ROSEMBLE-style replication protocol (EPFL infoscience); MELD anti-entropy digest under lossy routing (arxiv 2608.16357).

A skeleton `ids-reconciliation` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-reconciliation/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, plus sealed trait contracts and error types. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-reconciliation` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a pure reconciliation layer: given replica states (each tagged with version, operation history, causality metadata), it produces a `ReconcileResult` — the decision about what to keep, what to merge, what to tombstone, what to quarantine, and whether any silent overwrite was blocked. It never sends bytes itself; the caller frames decisions into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   REPLICA OWNERS (ids-store, ids-replication)                │
│  hold local replica state; initiate reconciliation after partition heal      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 064: ids-reconciliation (THIS CRATE — pure logic)       │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ │\\
│  │ version         │ │ op-history      │ │ conflict        │ │ authority│ │ │\\
│  │ comparison      │ │ comparison      │ │ detection       │ │ rules    │ │ │ │\\
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘ │ │\\
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ │\\
│  │ merge semantics │ │ CRDT integration│ │ conflict        │ │ silent   │ │ │ │\\
│  │ (CvRDT/CmRDT)   │ │ adapters        │ │ resolution      │ │ overwrite│ │ │ │\\
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘ │ │\\
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ │                 │ │tombstone │ │ │ │\\
│  │ quarantine      │ │ merkle/digest   │ │                 │ │ / GC     │ │ │ │\\
│  │ buffer          │ │ comparison      │ │                 │ │          │ │ │ │\\
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │                 │ │          │ │ │ │\\
└─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┴──────────────┘\\                                          │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams (MergeDecision payload)│                                          │                                          ▼│┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                   ││  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType≤1024B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload: &[u8])   ││  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                    ││  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS    ││  / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh                               │└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of one reconciliation cycle:**
1. Replica A detects partition heal or receives a peer's digest (merkle/version-vector) indicating divergence.
2. `version_comparison` compares protocol versions and replica state versions; rejects incompatible versions before merge.
3. `op_history_comparison` compares operation histories (OpRef, OrderingPos, dots) to find missing/concurrent operations.
4. `conflict_detection` flags concurrent writes to the same record (incomparable VV/DVV), lost-update candidates, and silent-overwrite risks.
5. `authority_rules` decide which replica's write wins (fencing token, epoch, LWW tie-break, or authority-by-region) — never a silent overwrite.
6. `merge_semantics` applies CRDT merge (join-semilattice LUB) or delta-CRDT delta merge; falls back to quarantine for non-commutative conflicts.
7. `tombstone_GC` marks removed entries with tombstones, garbage-collects only at causal stability.
8. `ReconcileResult` (accept/merge/reject/tombstone/quarantine) is returned; caller ships it via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing reconcile decisions and audit checkpoints; sha256/blake3 for version hashing, digest comparison, audit-chain links; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt reconcile state at rest when confidentiality required.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 13.

#### 3.1 Strong eventual consistency and CRDT convergence theorem

**Source:** Shapiro et al. 2011, "Conflict-free Replicated Data Types" (INRIA RR-7687 / comprehensive study); arxiv 1806.10254 CRDT overview; arxiv 2504.05398 CRDT emulation/simulation; arxiv 2505.19373 CRDT compliance definition; arxiv 2504.01141 coordination-free consistency (ACID = associative, commutative, idempotent, distributed is necessary and sufficient for SEC).

A CRDT is strongly eventually consistent iff: (i) eventual delivery — every update reaches every replica; (ii) strong convergence — replicas that have received the same set of updates (in any order, possibly with duplicates) are in the same state. The merge operator `⊔` must be commutative (`a⊔b = b⊔a`), associative (`(a⊔b)⊔c = a⊔(b⊔c)`), and idempotent (`a⊔a = a`). `ids-reconciliation` enforces these three laws as compile-time/runtime invariants on every CRDT merge adapter it integrates. State-based CRDTs (CvRDT) ship full state and merge via join-semilattice LUB; operation-based CRDTs (CmRDT) ship individual operations requiring causal delivery and commutativity. `ids-reconciliation` supports both modes but defaults to state-based (more robust under lossy/unordered carrier).

#### 3.2 State-based vs operation-based CRDT (CvRDT vs CmRDT)

**Source:** arxiv 1603.01529 (delta-CRDT); arxiv 1710.04469 (pure op-based CRDTs); arxiv 2504.05398; CMU 17-350 lecture 10.

- CvRDT: replica state space is a join-semilattice; local updates are inflationary (`s ≤ update(s)`); merge = join. No special delivery precondition; robust under unordered/lossy delivery. Preferred default for `ids-reconciliation` because the carrier is opaque and unordered by design.
- CmRDT: each operation individually broadcast; requires reliable causal delivery (exactly-once, causal order) and commutative concurrent operations. Smaller messages but stronger transport assumptions. Supported as an optional mode; `ids-reconciliation` documents that CmRDT mode requires the carrier layer to provide causal delivery (which ids-carrier::Endpoint does not guarantee by itself).
- δ-CRDT (arXiv:1603.01529): delta-mutators return a small delta-state joined with both local and remote states; anti-entropy re-sends undelivered deltas. Best-of-both-worlds; `ids-reconciliation` plans a `delta_merge` path for large states.

#### 3.3 Version comparison

**Source:** plan-001/plan-048/plan-060 (ids-000-aa `ProtocolVersion`, `EdgeCaseBits`, `OrderingPos`, `OpRef`); CRDT literature on version vectors.

`ids-reconciliation` compares:
- `ProtocolVersion` (semver MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) from `ids-000-aa` — rejects replicas speaking incompatible wire versions before any state merge.
- `EdgeCaseBits` (u128 bitfield) — one bit per protocol invariant; mismatched invariant bits → quarantine rather than merge.
- Per-record version vectors / dotted version vectors — `VV_1 < VV_2` (dominates), `VV_1 == VV_2` (equal), `VV_1 ∥ VV_2` (concurrent/incomparable → conflict).
- `OrderingPos` — total order position; `OpRef` — 9-byte operation reference (36^9 namespace).
Comparison outputs: `Ordered` (one dominates), `Equal`, `Concurrent` (conflict), `Incompatible` (version skew → reject).

#### 3.4 Operation history comparison

**Source:** OpSets (arxiv 1805.04263); PO-Log pure op-based CRDTs (arxiv 1710.04469); dot-based causality (eribeiro vv-dvv blog; Riak KV causal context).

Each operation carries `(OpRef, OrderingPos, dot=(NodeId, seq), causal_past: VV)`. `ids-reconciliation` compares two replicas' operation histories:
- Missing ops: present on one side, absent on the other → must be exchanged (delta or full-state catch-up).
- Concurrent ops: same record, incomparable dots → conflict (kept as siblings or resolved by authority rule).
- Duplicate ops: same OpRef/OrderingPos → idempotent, applied once.
- Out-of-order delivery: idempotent + commutative merge tolerates any order.
Output: `OpHistoryDiff { missing: Vec<OpRef>, concurrent: Vec<(OpRef, OpRef)>, duplicates: Vec<OpRef> }`.

#### 3.5 Conflict and authority rules

**Source:** semantic conflict model arxiv 2602.19231 (lost updates, silent overwrite); LWW register (arxiv 1806.10254; CMU slides); fencing token / write fence (thecolony.ai; morling.dev S3 leader election; etcfs Kleppmann analysis; redlease; insightful-data-lab fencing token).

Conflict types:
- Concurrent write-write on same record (incomparable VV/DVV) → siblings or authority resolution.
- Lost update: write A based on stale state overwrites write B → flagged by DVV comparison; prevented by fencing.
- Silent overwrite: a later-arriving write clobbers newer state without detection → blocked by version comparison + fencing token check.

Authority rules (decide winner when conflict must be resolved):
- Fencing token / epoch: writer carries a strictly increasing token (lease epoch, fencing token, or `OrderingPos`); store rejects writes with token below its high-water mark. Never a silent overwrite — rejected writes return `Conflict`.
- LWW tie-break: highest `(timestamp, NodeId)` wins; documents the lost-write risk explicitly.
- Authority by region: designated region is authoritative for a record; other regions' concurrent writes are tombstoned or quarantined.
- Application-supplied resolver: hook for domain-specific merge (e.g., three-way merge).

`ids-reconciliation` makes the authority rule explicit and configurable per record/region; default = fencing-token + LWW-with-conflict-flag (never silently discard).

#### 3.6 Merge semantics

**Source:** Shapiro 2011 join-semilattice; delta-CRDT arxiv 1603.01529; CRDT convergence theorem (ACID); OR-set CMU slides; LWW-Element-Set github junjizhi/roshi; MV-register arxiv 1710.04469 / crdt-kit docs.

Merge strategies per data kind:
- Register: LWW (timestamp + NodeId tie-break) — keeps one value, flags conflict if concurrent.
- MV-register: keeps all concurrent values as siblings; application resolves.
- G-counter / PN-counter: component-wise max (GCounter) or inc/dect pair (PNCounter) — always converges.
- Set: OR-set (add-wins, observed-remove, dot-based tombstones) — concurrent add beats concurrent remove.
- Map: OR-map whose values are themselves CRDTs; per-key merge recursion.
- Custom: application-supplied join function (must satisfy commutativity/associativity/idempotence; verified by property tests).

`ids-reconciliation` exposes `MergeSemantics` enum and a `MergeEngine` trait (sealed) with adapters per CRDT kind. Merge result: `Merged(state, conflicts_resolved: Vec<Conflict>, tombstones: Vec<Tombstone>)`.

#### 3.7 CRDT integration

**Source:** delta-CRDT arxiv 1603.01529 anti-entropy; join decompositions for CRDT sync after partition (dl.acm 10.1145/2957319.2957374); Merkle-CRDTs arxiv 2004.00107; OR-set/mv-register implementations.

`ids-reconciliation` does not implement every CRDT itself; it integrates CRDT adapters:
- Each adapter wraps an opaque CRDT state (`Vec<u8>` or typed), exposes `merge(local, remote) -> MergeResult`, `is_conflicted()`, `causal_context() -> DVV`.
- Adapters registered in `CRDTRegistry` keyed by `RecordId` type.
- Delta path: `delta_mutate(op) -> DeltaState` (small), joined locally and gossipped; anti-entropy re-sends undelivered deltas.
- Integration with `ids-crdt` (later phase) via the sealed `CRDT` contract in `ids-000-aa`; `ids-reconciliation` depends on the contract, not the implementation.

#### 3.8 Conflict detection

**Source:** version vectors (Wikipedia; eribeiro vv-dvv); dotted version vectors (Riak KV; gsd.di.uminho.pt DVV paper); MV-register sibling detection (crdt-kit docs); OP protocol (EPFL infoscience).

Detection inputs: two replica states + their DVVs. Output: `ConflictSet`.
- `VV_1 ∥ VV_2` (incomparable) → concurrent updates → conflict.
- Dot not in other's causal past → the writing replica hasn't seen the other's state → potential lost update.
- Same OpRef applied twice → duplicate (idempotent, not a conflict).
- Version skew (ProtocolVersion or EdgeCaseBits mismatch) → incompatibility, not a mergeable conflict → quarantine.
Detection is deterministic and order-independent: comparing A vs B yields the same ConflictSet as B vs A.

#### 3.9 Conflict resolution

**Source:** LWW register (silent overwrite hazard documented in semantic conflict model); OR-set add-wins; MV-register deferred resolution; fencing token (Kleppmann; etcfs; redlease).

Resolution strategies:
- `AuthorityWins` — designated authority (fencing token / epoch / region) wins; loser is tombstoned, not silently dropped.
- `LWW` — highest `(timestamp, NodeId)` wins; conflict flag set so the application can audit.
- `KeepAll` (MV-register style) — all concurrent values kept as siblings; application resolves later.
- `Quarantine` — conflict held in quarantine buffer; no state change until manual or policy resolution.
- `Reject` — incoming write rejected with `Conflict` error; caller retries with newer state.

`ids-reconciliation` never performs a silent overwrite: every resolution that discards a write is recorded (tombstone or quarantine) and audited (ed25519-signed checkpoint).

#### 3.10 Silent overwrite prevention

**Source:** semantic conflict model arxiv 2602.19231 (lost update = silently overwritten); fencing token articles (thecolony.ai write fence; morling.dev; etcfs Kleppmann; insightful-data-lab); Riak DVV vs vector clocks (sibling explosion reduction).

Silent overwrite = a write arriving later clobbers newer state because the store lacks causality metadata. Prevention mechanisms in `ids-reconciliation`:
- Every write carries its causal context (DVV) and a fencing token (epoch/`OrderingPos`).
- Before applying, `ids-reconciliation` checks: incoming causal context ≥ stored causal context? If not, and the incoming write is not an ancestor, it is a stale/silent-overwrite candidate → rejected or quarantined.
- Fencing token check: token must be ≥ store's high-water mark for that record; older token → `StaleFence` rejection.
- LWW with conflict flag: if timestamps tie or are concurrent, both values kept (siblings) unless an explicit authority rule selects one — never silently discard.
- Every discarded/tombstoned write is recorded in the audit chain (sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoint) so silent overwrites are detectable offline.

#### 3.11 Digest-based replica comparison (Merkle / anti-entropy)

**Source:** systemoverflow anti-entropy digests; scalecube-prism anti-entropy merkle; DSE anti-entropy repair docs; arxiv 2608.16357 MELD digest; dl.acm join decompositions CRDT sync after partition.

Instead of shipping full state, replicas exchange compact digests:
- Merkle tree over hashed keyspace (bucketized by FNV-1a-64 hash into fixed-shape complete binary tree; same shape regardless of which keys each replica holds). Root-hash equality ⇒ in sync; mismatch → descend only differing branches; exchange O(k·log n) hashes for k divergent keys.
- Version-vector digest: per-record DVV summary; compare entry-wise; mismatched entries trigger op-history comparison.
- IBLT / rateless Bloom filter (arxiv 2510.27614; MIT set reconciliation) for small-difference set reconciliation: insert one set, remove the other, retrieve difference keys with high probability.
`ids-reconciliation` defines the `Digest` trait (sealed) with `MerkleDigest`, `VVDigest`, `IBLTDigest` implementations; digest comparison is the entry point to reconciliation (cheap common case: roots match → no work).

#### 3.12 Gossip / anti-entropy delivery

**Source:** dl.acm gossip robustness (Demers et al. 1987); systemoverflow anti-entropy post-partition healing; arxiv 2608.16357 MELD anti-entropy under lossy routing.

- Push/pull gossip rapidly disseminates recent changes; anti-entropy (periodic digest exchange) is the backstop that heals divergence missed by gossip or during partitions.
- After partition heal: gossip spreads joins/suspicions in seconds; anti-entropy runs later, exchanges digests, detects mismatched entries, reconciles only the drift.
- `ids-reconciliation` is transport-agnostic: digests and merge decisions are shipped as opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; retry/re-delivery and anti-entropy scheduling are owned by `ids-replication`/`ids-gossip` (later phases), not this crate.
- Convergence guarantee: if every delta/mutation eventually reaches every replica (directly or transitively) and merge is a join, all replicas converge (δ-CRDT Proposition 1).

#### 3.13 Tombstone garbage collection

**Source:** USENIX OSDI'26 Treedoc (tombstone GC via causal stability); CMU slides OR-Set tombstone problem; arxiv 1608.03960 JSON CRDT GC requirement.

- Removes are recorded as tombstones (never silently delete) so concurrent adds can be correctly arbitrated (add-wins).
- Tombstone is garbage-collectable only at causal stability: an operation/tombstone `o` is stable when `VV_o ≤ VV_u` for every replica `u` (everyone has seen it).
- `ids-reconciliation` exposes `TombstoneGC` with `is_stable(tombstone, global_VV_min) -> bool`; actual GC triggered by `ids-replication`/`ids-gc` (later phases).
- Unbounded tombstone growth is a documented risk; bounded by causal-stability window + optional compaction.

#### 3.14 Causal consistency session guarantees

**Source:** Wikipedia causal consistency; arxiv 2211.03501 tunable causal consistency; MongoDB causal consistency docs.

Causal consistency = read your writes + monotonic reads + monotonic writes + writes follow reads. `ids-reconciliation` supports these via DVV gating:
- A read returns only after its observed causal context is satisfied at the serving replica (read your writes).
- Successive reads observe monotonically non-decreasing write sets (monotonic reads).
- Writes on the same session observed in session order (monotonic writes / writes follow reads).
Available under partition (causal consistency is the strongest partition-available model); weaker than linearizability — documented.

#### 3.15 Allowed crypto only

**Source:** ed25519-dalek docs.rs (RFC 8032); chacha20poly1305 docs.rs (RFC 8439, XChaCha20); sha2 RustCrypto (FIPS 180-4 SHA-256); BLAKE3-team README.

`ids-reconciliation` uses:
- ed25519: signing reconcile decisions, authority checkpoints, audit-chain links.
- sha256: version hashing, digest leaf hashing, audit-chain links.
- blake3: fast content hashing for Merkle digests, causal-context hashing, checkpoint chaining (preferred for speed/parallelism).
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypt reconcile state at rest (24-byte nonce, random safe).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypt session/state payloads (12-byte nonce, counter-based).
No other crypto; `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs; `ids-reconciliation` references via `ids-000-aa` only.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation |
|--------|---------------|------------|
| Silent overwrite (stale write clobbers newer state) | Data correctness | DVV + fencing-token pre-check; reject/quarantine stale writes; never discard without tombstone/audit |
| Lost update (concurrent write discarded) | Data correctness | OR-set add-wins; MV-register keeps siblings; LWW with conflict flag; authority rule explicit |
| Sibling explosion (unbounded concurrent values) | Memory / read cost | DVV de-duplication (vs plain vector clocks); tombstone GC at causal stability; compaction |
| Version skew / incompatible merge | Convergence safety | ProtocolVersion + EdgeCaseBits pre-check; quarantine on mismatch |
| Replay of merge decisions | Decision integrity | ed25519-signed audit checkpoints; OpRef idempotency; bounded replay cache |
| Clock manipulation for causality | Causality correctness | Logical clocks (DVV dots/counters + monotonic IdsTime); never wall-clock for ordering |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent merge (idempotence law); OpRef deduplication; carrier-agnostic boundary |
| Partition-induced divergence | Convergence | Anti-entropy digest backstop; δ-CRDT re-send of undelivered deltas; CRDT join convergence |
| Key extraction (signing key) | Decision authenticity | Keys encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Unbounded state growth (tombstones, history) | Memory | Causal-stability tombstone GC; digest-based comparison (no full-state ship) |
| Prohibited crate in dependency tree | Architecture | CI dependency audit; `cargo tree` asserts no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/QUIC/HTTP/DNS |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | ids-crypto is sole crypto surface; allowlist unit test |

The carrier is never trusted: reconcile decisions and audit entries are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-reconciliation |
|-------|------|---------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `Checksum`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; sealed contracts mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All reconcile traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing decisions/audit; encrypting reconcile state at rest; hashing versions and digests |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (replica owner) | Initiates reconciliation on partition heal; applies `ReconcileResult` to local state |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization / anti-entropy | Drives digest exchange, delta re-send, tombstone GC scheduling; uses reconcile decisions |
| `ids-crdt` | CRDT implementations (later phase) | Adapters registered in `CRDTRegistry`; `ids-reconciliation` depends on the sealed `CRDT` contract only |

Integration points: `ids-reconciliation` exposes a pure `reconcile(local, remote) -> ReconcileResult` API; callers frame the result into opaque datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on ids-discovery/ids-session/ids-cli beyond what the contracts expose.

```
│   ├── reconcile_contract.rs           # trait Reconcile: reconcile(local, remote) -> ReconcileResult
│   ├── carrier_adapter.rs              # opaque Vec<u8> framing to ids-carrier::Endpoint (decision carrier only)
│   └── mod.rs
├── invariants/                         # compile-time/runtime invariants (~10 files)
│   ├── mod.rs
│   ├── merge_commutative.rs
│   ├── merge_associative.rs
│   ├── merge_idempotent.rs
│   ├── no_silent_overwrite.rs

├── tests/                              # property/verification tests (~30 files)

```

Total: ~90–1000 files across `src/`, `src/contracts/`, `src/invariants/`, `src/audit/`, `tests/`, `benches/`, `docs/`, organized by subsystem so each concern is a separate file — consistent with the "separate crates instead of more folders" directive applied intra-crate as separate modules/files.

---

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **Version comparison**: `compare_versions(a, b) -> VersionCmp{Ordered, Equal, Concurrent, Incompatible}` using `ProtocolVersion`, `EdgeCaseBits`; `Incompatible` → quarantine before merge.
- **Op-history comparison**: `compare_histories(local, remote) -> OpHistoryDiff{missing, concurrent, duplicates}`; dot `(NodeId, seq)` + causal-past VV; idempotent on duplicates.
- **Conflict detection**: `VV_1 ∥ VV_2` (incomparable) → conflict; dot not in other's causal past → lost-update candidate; same OpRef twice → duplicate (not conflict).
- **Authority resolution**: fencing token high-water mark check → `Accept|Reject|Stale`; LWW tie-break `(timestamp, NodeId)`; region authority; application resolver hook. Every discard → tombstone or quarantine, never silent.
- **Merge semantics**: join-semilattice LUB `merge(a,b)` commutative/associative/idempotent; adapters: LWW-register, OR-set (add-wins), PN-counter, MV-register, OR-map; `MergeResult{state, conflicts_resolved, tombstones}`.
- **CRDT integration**: `CRDTRegistry` keyed by record type; `delta_mutate(op) -> DeltaState` (small) joined locally and remotely; δ-CRDT convergence: if every delta reaches every replica, states equalize.
- **Digest comparison**: Merkle tree over FNV-1a-64-bucketed keyspace; root equality ⇒ in sync; mismatch → descend only differing branches, O(k·log n) for k divergent keys; VVDigest and IBLTDigest variants.
- **Tombstone GC**: tombstone `o` stable iff `VV_o ≤ VV_min` (entry-wise min across all replicas); GC only at stability; bounded by GC window.
- **Audit chain**: each reconcile decision = sha256/blake3-chained entry + ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.
- **Reconcile engine**: pipeline `version_gate → op_history_diff → conflict_detection → authority → merge → tombstone_gc → ReconcileResult`.

### 8. Dependencies

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `Checksum`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — decision transport only; crate never sends directly.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `serde` — serialization of reconcile envelopes, digests, audit entries.
- `thiserror` — error types.
- `blake3` — content hashing for Merkle digests (type-level surface; crypto ops in ids-crypto).

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. No async runtime.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete authority rule defaults per record/region:** fencing token vs LWW vs region authority — deployment-tuned; validated at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-replication`.
2. **Digest choice per workload:** Merkle tree depth (bucket granularity) vs VVDigest vs IBLT; trade-off between detection precision and digest size unquantified.
3. **Anti-entropy interval:** gossip vs anti-entropy scheduling owned by `ids-replication`/`ids-gossip`; interval affects convergence speed vs bandwidth.
4. **Tombstone GC window size:** causal-stability window affects memory growth vs GC frequency; workload-dependent.
5. **MV-register application resolver:** interface for deferred conflict resolution not yet defined; hook reserved in `conflict_resolution.rs`.
6. **Interaction with `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060):** profile-based quorum gating before merge; exact handshake defined here, validated at integration.
7. **Interaction with `ids-immutable` (Phase 040):** reconcile must respect holds/retention; guard handshake defined here, validated at integration.
8. **Interaction with `ids-session` (Phase 050):** session-bound causal context cross-referencing to be validated at integration.
9. **CmRDT mode transport assumption:** operation-based CRDTs require causal/exactly-once delivery; `ids-carrier::Endpoint` doesn't guarantee it — mode gating decision pending.

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-reconciliation` (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear convergence boundary |
| State-based (CvRDT) default, δ-CRDT optional | Robust under unordered/lossy opaque carrier; delta path optimizes large states |
| Merge = join-semilattice LUB (commutative, associative, idempotent) | Shapiro 2011 SEC theorem; order-independent convergence without coordination |
| DVV for causal tracking (not plain VV) | Riak DVV: de-duplicates updates, reduces sibling explosion, avoids lost writes/false conflicts |
| Authority rule explicit + configurable (fencing token / LWW / region) | Never silently overwrite; every discard tombstoned/quarantined + audited |
| Silent overwrite prevention via fence + causal pre-check | Blocks stale writes clobbering newer state; audit trail makes discarded writes detectable |
| Digest-based comparison entry point (Merkle/VV/IBLT) | Anti-entropy backstop: cheap common case (roots match → no work), localized repair on mismatch |
| Tombstone GC at causal stability only | OR-set tombstone problem solved; bounded by GC window + compaction |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence for discarded/tombstoned writes |
| Carrier-agnostic boundary via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Only allowed crypto; `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs via `ids-000-aa` | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 065 creates `ids-mvcc`, the IDS crate that implements snapshot isolation for reads and writes as a separate crate (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule). It is a concurrency-control layer: every write produces a new version tagged with a commit timestamp / transaction ID; reads are served from a stable snapshot taken at transaction start and never block writers; writers conflict only on write-write to the same key and abort the later committer (first-committer-wins). The crate owns version management (per-key version chains), snapshot reads, write visibility rules, garbage collection of old (expired) versions, transaction isolation levels (read committed / repeatable read / snapshot / serializable), phantom-read prevention, and serialization-anomaly prevention via Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) monitoring of read-write dependencies ("dangerous structures" of two adjacent rw-conflict edges).

`ids-mvcc` never opens a socket or drives any transport directly. It evaluates visibility, conflict, and snapshot decisions locally and returns them as decisions; all bytes cross a node only as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). It depends on `ids-000-aa` (canonical types, sealed contracts, invariants, errors) and consumes only the allowed crypto set (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305) via `ids-crypto`.

A skeleton `ids-mvcc` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-mvcc/`. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-mvcc` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a pure concurrency-control/policy crate: it decides what a transaction may read, whether a write may commit, which versions are expired, and whether an anomaly pattern is forming. It never sends bytes itself; callers (`ids-store`, `ids-write`, `ids-read`, `ids-replication`, …) frame decisions into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (txn drivers)                   │
│  ids-store, ids-write, ids-read, ids-replication — begin/read/write/commit   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                Phase 065: ids-mvcc (THIS CRATE — concurrency control)        │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ version mgr      │ │ snapshot mgr     │ │ visibility       │ │ gc      │ │
│  │ (version chains, │ │ (read view at    │ │ (xmin/xmax/xip,  │ │ (expired│ │
│  │  commit ts alloc)│ │  txn start)      │  own-writes first) │ │  old ver│ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ conflict mgr     │ │ isolation levels │ │ phantom          │ │ ssi     │ │
│  │ (ww first-committer││ RC/RR/SI/Serializable│ │ prevention (predicate│ │ │monitor│ │
│  │   wins / abort)  │ │   read views)    │ │   / index locks) │ │(rw edges)│ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┘
                                               │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                  │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload)     │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS    │
│  / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh anywhere in this crate        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Lifecycle of one snapshot-isolation transaction:**
1. `begin()`: allocate a unique transaction ID + snapshot timestamp from the monotonic commit-timestamp allocator; snapshot = (xmin = oldest active txn, xmax = next txn to be assigned, xip = active txn IDs at snapshot time).
2. Reads: walk the per-key version chain; pick the newest version whose creating txn committed before the snapshot and whose deleting txn (if any) is either not-yet-committed or post-snapshot. Own uncommitted writes are visible first (self-consistency).
3. Writes: buffered in the transaction's private workspace; no lock held for the transaction's lifetime; at `commit()`, allocate a commit timestamp and run first-committer-wins write-write conflict detection on every written key. If another transaction committed a newer version of any written key after this snapshot began → abort.
4. Commit success: new versions published atomically; become visible to transactions whose snapshot timestamp is > this commit timestamp.
5. GC: a version is reclaimable when no active snapshot can see it (created by aborted txn, or superseded and older than the oldest active snapshot). Tuple-level (background vacuuming) and transaction-level GC strategies; protected-timestamp (PTS) records can hold GC back for long-running snapshots (CockroachDB pattern).

**Isolation levels implemented:**
- Read Committed: new snapshot per statement; sees commits up to each statement start.
- Repeatable Read / Snapshot: one snapshot at transaction start (first read or explicit BEGIN); stable for the whole transaction.
- Serializable (SSI): snapshot isolation plus runtime rw-conflict dependency tracking ("dangerous structure" detection) to prevent write skew and serialization anomalies; aborted transactions are retryable.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 signs commit decisions and audit checkpoints; sha256/blake3 hash version-vector entries and version IDs; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 encrypt version payloads at rest when confidentiality is required. Nothing else.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to targeted searches executed in parallel. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 MVCC theory — Bernstein & Goodman (1983), Adya et al. (2000)

Foundational theory: each write produces a new version; correctness = equivalence to some serial execution. Snapshot isolation first described in Berenson et al. (1995); generalized isolation-level definitions by Adya, Liskov, O'Neil (ICDE 2000) define phenomena (dirty reads, fuzzy/non-repeatable reads, phantoms, write skew) in terms of read/write dependencies. Bernstein & Goodman's MVCC theory underpins the version-visibility rules used here: a version is visible iff its create-commit precedes the read time and its delete-commit (if any) does not.

#### 3.2 Snapshot reads and version visibility (PostgreSQL xmin/xmax/xip model)

A snapshot is not a physical copy; it is defined by numbers: xmin (oldest active txn; all older XIDs visible unconditionally), xmax (all XIDs >= xmax invisible), xip[] (in-progress txns between xmin and xmax). Tuple visibility: version created by xid < xmin → visible; xmin ≤ xid < xmax → visible iff that txn is not in xip (i.e., committed before snapshot); xid ≥ xmax → invisible. Own transaction's writes always visible. Read view captured at first read (repeatable read: stable for whole transaction; read committed: new per statement).

#### 3.3 Write visibility and first-committer-wins

A transaction's writes are buffered privately and published atomically at commit with a new commit timestamp larger than any existing start/commit timestamp. First-committer-wins: T1 commits only if no transaction T2 with a commit timestamp in T1's execution interval [start_ts, commit_ts] wrote a key that T1 also wrote. If such a T2 exists → T1 aborts (write-write conflict). Lost updates prevented (phenomenon P4). Reads never block writers and writers never block readers; conflicts detected at commit time, not with long-held locks.

#### 3.4 Transaction isolation levels and SQL phenomena

SQL-92 phenomena: dirty read (reads uncommitted), non-repeatable read (re-read differs due to concurrent commit), phantom read (re-executed query sees new/removed rows matching a predicate), serialization anomaly (committed group inconsistent with any serial order). Levels: Read Uncommitted (all allowed), Read Committed (no dirty), Repeatable Read (no dirty/non-repeatable; phantoms possible in standard, prevented in PG via SSI), Serializable (none). `ids-mvcc` implements RC, RR/Snapshot, and Serializable via SSI; document exactly which phenomena each prevents.

#### 3.5 Phantom read prevention

A phantom occurs when a transaction re-runs a predicate query and the matching set changed due to another committed transaction. Pure snapshot isolation prevents phantoms within a stable snapshot (snapshot taken at start), but the write-skew / serialization anomaly remains. Prevention options researched: predicate locks (Eswaran/Gray/Lorie/Traiger 1976 — the original predicate-lock notion), index range locks, and SI's weaker guarantee. `ids-mvcc` design: snapshot reads inherently see a stable predicate set for the transaction's lifetime (no phantom inside one snapshot); cross-snapshot phantoms addressed by SSI's rw-conflict tracking (a read that later conflicts with a concurrent write can be rolled back). Predicate/index-locking as an optional stronger mode, documented as such.

#### 3.6 Serialization anomaly prevention — Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI)

Cahill, Röhm, Fekete (SIGMOD 2008 / TODS 2011): SI permits anomalies (write skew, read-only anomaly). SSI keeps SI's benefits (no reader/writer blocking) while detecting anomaly cycles at runtime. Core insight: each SI anomaly corresponds to a cycle in the dependency graph containing a "dangerous structure" of two adjacent rw-conflict edges: Tin →(rw) Tpivot →(rw) Tout. SSI tracks only rw-conflicts between concurrent transactions (not wr/ww), rolls back a transaction when a dangerous structure is detected. Optimizations: only roll back if Tout commits before Tpivot/Tin; read-only transactions can only be in a cycle if Tout committed before Tin took its snapshot. PostgreSQL 9.1+ implementation (README-SSI in postgres source). `ids-mvcc` implements SSI monitoring as the serializable level: maintain rw-conflict edges, detect dangerous structures, abort one member (retryable serialization failure).

#### 3.7 Write skew anomaly

Two transactions read overlapping state, write disjoint sets, commit; result inconsistent with any serial order (classic: two doctors on-call, each reads count ≥ 2, each marks self off-call → zero on-call). SI allows it because write sets are disjoint (no ww conflict). Prevented only by SSI (track the read→write anti-dependency / rw-conflict edges) or by explicit locking/promotion. `ids-mvcc` SSI level prevents write skew; snapshot level documents it as an allowed anomaly (matching Jepsen's SI model).

#### 3.8 Garbage collection of old versions

MVCC creates new versions on every write; unbounded growth unless reclaimed. Version reclaimable when no active transaction can see it AND it was not created by an in-flight/aborted transaction. Two GC approaches (CMU 15-721/15-445, VLDB '12 main-memory MVCC survey):
- Tuple-level GC: background vacuuming threads scan tables/version chains for expired versions (works with any storage; "dirty page bitmap" optimization skips unchanged pages); cooperative cleaning — workers identify reclaimable versions while traversing version chains (only O2N append-only chains; risk of "dusty corners" if a chain is never traversed).
- Transaction-level GC: each transaction tracks its own old versions; when it completes, all its versions become reclaimable once no snapshot needs them.
Granularity: single-version vs timestamp-based (global minimum timestamp / high-water mark = oldest active snapshot start; versions committed before it are obsolete) vs interval-based (SAP HANA, HyPer — can excise middle of chains). Block compaction: reclaim index entries too. The "vicious cycle": long-running transactions block GC, version chains grow, reads slow down. Mitigation: protected timestamps (CockroachDB PTS holds GC for a timestamp), TiDB GC safe point with max wait cap so one stuck transaction cannot block forever.

#### 3.9 Version chain storage and read path

Per logical key, versions form a chain sorted by commit timestamp (append-only O2N or N2O). A read at snapshot timestamp RT walks the chain and picks the newest version with begin ≤ RT and (end = ∞ or end > RT / end's txn aborted or post-snapshot). If begin/end fields temporarily contain in-progress transaction IDs, resolve that txn's state without blocking (or register a commit dependency). Index management: index entries point to version heads; GC must unlink index entries for reclaimed versions; index-only scans need visibility info (PostgreSQL visibility map pattern) or heap fetch to check visibility.

#### 3.10 Commit timestamp allocation and ordering

Timestamps from a global monotonically increasing counter (atomic fetch-add). Transaction start ts = latest commit ts at begin; commit ts assigned at commit, strictly increasing. FoundationDB pattern: proxy contacts other proxies to get most recent commit version; concurrency-control processes process requests in strict commit-version order. In a single-node `ids-mvcc`, a single atomic counter suffices; distributed extension (later phases) can use HLC or per-shard counters. Never wall-clock for ordering (clock skew).

#### 3.11 Hybrid logical clocks (optional distributed timestamp ordering)

For future multi-node deployment, HLC (Hybrid Logical Clock) combines physical time with logical counter: bounded growth, real-time correlation, causal ordering. Research: hybridclocktxn snapshot isolation with HLC. `ids-mvcc` Phase 065 uses a single monotonic counter; HLC integration noted as a future uncertainty, not adopted now.

#### 3.12 Rust MVCC implementations (reference, not dependencies)

- `mvcc_cell` (gitlab.com/2e71828/mvcc_cell): STM-style MVCC cells; each txn sees a fixed snapshot at start; first committer wins; concurrent commits to accessed cells abort others.
- `txn_db` (docs.rs/txn-db): MVCC transaction layer over a VersionStore trait; versions tagged with commit timestamp; snapshot isolation; retryable conflicts.
- `kovan-mvcc` (github.com/vertexclique/kovan): Percolator-model MVCC using Kovan epoch-based memory reclamation.
- `mvcc-core` (docs.rs/mvcc-core): `db.begin_with::<Snapshot>()` example showing snapshot read unaffected by concurrent commits; serializable write-skew example.
These are research references only — `ids-mvcc` is a fresh crate and does not depend on them.

#### 3.13 Production MVCC systems (reference)

- RocksDB: LSM never modifies in-place; every write = new version; transactions layer on top (Artem Krylysov blog).
- CockroachDB: revision/timestamp-based MVCC KV layer; tombstones for deletes; read "as of" timestamp; GC TTL default 25h; protected timestamps hold GC.
- TiDB/TiKV: Percolator-inspired distributed transactions with snapshot isolation; GC safe point; `tidb_gc_life_time` default 10m, `tidb_gc_max_wait_time` default 86400s.
- FoundationDB: strict serializable by default via conflict ranges (read + write key ranges); snapshot reads omit read conflict ranges (relaxed isolation, no conflict on concurrent writes); snapshot() gives consistent point-in-time view.
- PostgreSQL: xmin/xmax/xip snapshots; SSI since 9.1; VACUUM for GC; XID wraparound (32-bit) mitigations.
These are design references only.

#### 3.14 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

`ids-mvcc` uses: ed25519 to sign commit decisions and GC/audit checkpoints; sha256 and blake3 to hash version IDs and version-chain entries (blake3 preferred for speed/parallelism); xchacha20poly1305 (24-byte nonce, random-safe) and chacha20poly1305 (12-byte nonce, counter-bounded) to encrypt version payloads at rest when confidentiality required. All via `ids-crypto`, referenced through `ids-000-aa` primitive IDs. Nothing else.

#### 3.15 Concurrency control protocol choice (optimistic / MVCC vs locking vs 2PL)

MVCC is a form of optimistic concurrency control: conflicts detected at commit, no read locks, no writer/reader blocking. Pessimistic 2PL holds locks and serializes but blocks readers/writers. `ids-mvcc` chooses optimistic MVCC per the IDS goal of high concurrency; write-write conflicts abort the later committer (retryable). Documented tradeoff: higher abort rates under heavy write contention, higher version-storage/GC cost.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Dirty read (reads uncommitted txn) | Read correctness | Visibility rules exclude uncommitted creators; own-writes visible only within same txn |
| Non-repeatable read | Repeatable-read guarantee | Stable snapshot at txn start (RR/SI); new snapshot per statement only at RC |
| Phantom read | Predicate stability | Snapshot at start freezes predicate set for txn lifetime; SSI covers cross-snapshot cases |
| Write skew / serialization anomaly | Data consistency | SSI rw-conflict "dangerous structure" detection → abort one txn (retryable) |
| Lost update (P4) | Write correctness | First-committer-wins write-write conflict detection at commit |
| Long-running txn blocks GC → version bloat | Storage/memory, read perf | Protected timestamps with max-wait cap; interval GC excising middle of chains; vacuums |
| Aborted-txn versions never reclaimed | Storage leak | Aborted txn's versions marked reclaimable immediately on abort |
| Timestamp counter overflow | Ordering correctness | u64 monotonic counter; saturating semantics documented; wrap handled like PG XID (not in scope) |
| Clock skew (distributed extension) | Snapshot correctness | Logical counters only in Phase 065; HLC noted as future, never wall-clock for ordering |
| GC reclaiming a version still needed by a snapshot | Read correctness / data loss | Reclaim only when version older than oldest active snapshot start; PTS records hold GC |
| Carrier duplication/delay/reordering | Replay/ordering | Decisions are deterministic functions of local state; idempotent version application tolerates duplicates |
| Prohibited crate/dependency | Architecture violation | Dependency audit; Cargo.toml contains only allowed crates; no networking stack |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | Allowlist enforced; only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via ids-crypto |
| Signing-key extraction | Decision authenticity | Signing keys never leave node; encrypted at rest; zeroized on shutdown |

The carrier is never trusted: visibility/commit/GC decisions are pure functions over local version state; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) keeps no network stack in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-mvcc ||
|-------|------|--------------------------|--------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpState`, `CommitState`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; sealed contracts mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) via `Carrier` trait | All traffic to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends bytes itself |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Sign commit decisions/GC checkpoints; hash version IDs; encrypt payloads at rest |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic `IdsTime` source | Commit-timestamp and snapshot timestamps derived from monotonic ticks, never wall-clock |
| `ids-store`, `ids-write`, `ids-read` | Primary record store / txn drivers | Use ids-mvcc for begin/read/write/commit/visibility decisions |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization | Replicates committed versions via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; applies MVCC visibility on replay |
| `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060) | Profile (R/W quorum, durability) | Profile gates write admission; MVCC enforces isolation within the admitted write |

**Integration points:** `ids-mvcc` exposes a public API (`begin`, `read`, `write`, `commit`, `abort`, `snapshot_at`, `gc_safe_point`, `is_version_visible`) called by store/write/read crates. It does not reach into crate internals. All cross-node traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli` beyond exposed contracts.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Snapshot and version visibility (xmin/xmax/xip)

```
Snapshot { xmin: TxnId, xmax: TxnId, xip: BitSet<TxnId> }
is_visible(version, snapshot):
  if version.create_txn == self_txn: return true        # own writes
  if version.create_txn < snapshot.xmin: return true    # committed before snapshot
  if version.create_txn >= snapshot.xmax: return false  # started after snapshot
  if version.create_txn in snapshot.xip: return false   # in-flight at snapshot
  return true                                           # committed before snapshot
  # deletion: version invisible if delete_txn committed ≤ snapshot
```

Applied per version while walking the per-key chain; newest visible version wins.

#### 7.2 First-committer-wins write-write conflict

```
commit(txn):
  for each key k in txn.write_set:
    latest = latest_committed_version(k)
    if latest.commit_ts in (txn.start_ts .. txn.commit_ts):
       abort(txn)   # another txn wrote k in our execution interval
  commit_ts = next_monotonic_ts()
  publish versions with commit_ts
```

Prevents lost updates (P4); abort is retryable.

#### 7.3 Serializable Snapshot Isolation — dangerous structures

Track rw-conflict edges: edge T1 → T2 if T1 read a version that T2 later overwrote (T1's read precedes T2's write in version order). A "dangerous structure" = two adjacent rw edges Tin → Tpivot → Tout. Abort one member (prefer Tout if it committed before Tpivot/Tin; read-only Tin only at risk if Tout committed before Tin's snapshot). Breaks cycles → serializability.

#### 7.4 Garbage collection — safe point

```
safe_point = min(start_ts of all active transactions)
version reclaimable iff version.commit_ts < safe_point AND no active snapshot references it
PTS(ts): hold GC above ts until record removed (protects long-running snapshots)
max_wait cap: single stuck txn cannot block GC past configured deadline (TiDB pattern)
```

Two strategies: tuple-level (background vacuuming + cooperative cleaning on O2N chains) and transaction-level (per-txn version lists reclaimed on commit/abort).

#### 7.5 Phantom prevention

Within one snapshot: predicate set frozen at snapshot start → no phantom. Cross-snapshot: SSI rw edges abort a transaction whose read set was invalidated by a concurrent commit. Predicate/index locking optional stronger mode (documented, not default).

#### 7.6 Version chain data structure

```
VersionChain { head: Option<Version>, versions: Vec<Version> }  # append-only, sorted by commit_ts
read_at(chain, rt): walk from head; first version with visible(rt) wins
write(chain, new_version): append; old version gets end_ts = new.commit_ts
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Commit-timestamp allocator distribution:** single atomic u64 counter for Phase 065; distributed extension (per-shard counters / HLC) deferred to a later phase; HLC integration noted but not adopted.
2. **GC strategy mix:** tuple-level background vacuuming vs transaction-level per-txn tracking; ratio and scheduling to be tuned at integration with `ids-store`.
3. **Version-chain length cap and compaction:** max chain length before forced compaction unquantified; long chains degrade read walk cost.
4. **Phantom prevention strength:** snapshot-level prevents phantoms within a transaction; whether to add optional predicate/index locking for stronger guarantees is a design decision pending.
5. **SSI abort rate under contention:** dangerous-structure detection may abort more than pure SI; acceptable false-positive rate unmeasured for IDS workloads.
6. **Interaction with `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060):** profile quorum/durability gates write admission; exact handshake (profile → MVCC admission) defined here, validated at integration.
7. **Protected-timestamp max-wait default:** CockroachDB-style PTS with TiDB max-wait cap; default value workload-dependent.
8. **Index visibility management:** whether reclaimed versions unlink index entries eagerly or lazily; index-only scan visibility map pattern (PostgreSQL) considered but not mandated.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-mvcc`, not a folder | Project rule: separate crates for new capabilities; clear concurrency-control boundary |
| Optimistic MVCC, first-committer-wins | Readers never block writers, writers never block readers; conflicts at commit time; retryable aborts |
| Snapshot at txn start (xmin/xmax/xip) | Proven PostgreSQL model; simple, well-understood visibility rules |
| Serializable via SSI (dangerous structures) | Prevents write skew + serialization anomalies while keeping SI performance; tracks rw edges only |
| Phantom prevented via snapshot stability + SSI | Predicate set frozen for txn lifetime; cross-snapshot handled by rw-conflict abort |
| GC safe point = oldest active snapshot start | Simple, correct reclaimability; protected timestamps + max-wait cap prevent indefinite GC block |
| Two GC strategies (tuple-level + transaction-level) | Covers all storage schemes; cooperative cleaning for O2N chains, vacuuming as fallback |
| Monotonic u64 commit timestamps, never wall-clock | Clock-skew-safe ordering; distributed HLC deferred |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in trust base |
| Allowed crypto only, via `ids-crypto` / `ids-000-aa` | IDS crypto policy; ed25519/signing, sha256/blake3/hashing, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305/encryption |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable commit/GC decision log |
| Fresh crate, no dependency on existing Rust MVCC crates | `mvcc_cell`, `txn_db`, `kovan-mvcc`, `mvcc-core` are research references only |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 066 creates `ids-vector-clock`, the IDS crate that owns causality tracking and conflict detection. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by logical-clock variant. `ids-vector-clock` implements: (a) standard vector clocks (Mattern/Fidge, 1988) for exact happens-before / concurrent detection, (b) version vectors (per-replica entry, bounded by replication degree) for object-version causality in replicated stores, (c) dotted version vectors (DVV / DVVSet, Almeida et al. 2012) for O(1) causality verification with metadata bounded by degree of replication rather than number of clients, (d) clock pruning / causal-stability garbage collection for bounded metadata growth, (e) hybrid logical clock (HLC, Kulkarni et al. 2014) integration — physical + logical time combination for near-physical timestamps with causality preservation, and (f) conflict detection (concurrent sibling identification) for multi-version replica states.

The crate never opens a socket, never touches `std::net` / `tokio::net` / libp2p / any carrier by name, and never routes traffic itself. It is pure logic + data structures: given two clocks it returns `Before | After | Equal | Concurrent`; given a local clock and an incoming message timestamp it merges (element-wise max) and returns the updated clock plus the causal relationship. All cross-node traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`, ≤ 1024-byte address) as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams framed by the caller. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` (this crate declares type surface / references primitives, implements no crypto).

A skeleton `ids-vector-clock` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-vector-clock/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, plus sealed trait contracts and error types. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned Mattern & Fidge vector clocks (1988, "Virtual Time and Global States of Distributed Systems", INRIA RR; strong clock condition `a → b ⇔ VC(a) < VC(b)`), Princeton COS418 vector-clock comparison algebra (`V(a) < V(b)` iff `∀k: a[k] ≤ b[k] ∧ ∃j: a[j] < b[j]`; concurrent iff neither dominates), dotted version vectors (ACM DL 10.1145/2332432.2332497; O(1) causality check `na ≤ vb[ia]`; size bounded by replication degree; integrated in Riak), DVVSet / dotted version vector sets (haslab.uminho.pt), Bloom clock (arXiv 2011.11744; probabilistic constant-size causality with false positives), plausible clocks (Springer 1999; constant-size logical clocks), interval tree clocks (Almeida/Baquero/Fonte 2008; dynamic membership, fork/event/join), Dynamo version vectors (DeCandia et al. SOSP 2007; siblings, read repair, anti-entropy, pruning can cause false conflicts), hybrid logical clock (Buffalo CSE tech report 2014-04; physical + logical, 64-bit, monotonic, close to NTP), causal stability / garbage collection (USENIX OSDI'26 Treedoc; locally causally stable tombstones; VVmin component-wise minimum), Rust clock crates (`asupersync` vclock, `crdts::vclock`, `uhlc-rs`, `hlc-gen`, `hybrid_logical_clock`), causal consistency session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads; arXiv 2211.03501), sequential vs linearizable (Attiya SPAA'91), anti-entropy digests / Merkle tree reconciliation (systemoverflow; Cassandra), and the IDS plans/format references.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-vector-clock` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a pure logic crate: it takes clocks and timestamps as input and returns ordering decisions, merged clocks, and conflict sets. It never sends bytes itself; the caller frames clock metadata into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```

│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-crdt, ids-sync — attach clocks to versions │

│  │ (Mattern/Fidge)  │ │ (per-replica VV) │ │ vector (DVV)     │ │ (phys+  │ │
│  │ VClock<A>        │ │ VV<A>            │ │ DVV<A> / DVVSet  │ │ logical)│ │
│  │ compare/merge    │ │ compare/merge    │ │ O(1) causality   │ │ now()/  │ │
│  │ tick/send/recv   │ │ tick/send/recv   │ │ tick/send/recv   │ │ update  │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ pruning /        │ │ conflict         │ │ causal           │ │ clock   │ │
│  │ causal stability │ │ detection        │ │ stability (GC)   │ │ factory │ │
│  │ GC / bounds      │ │ siblings         │ │ VVmin / tombstone│ │ registry│ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                      │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams (clock metadata)
                                      ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                    │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])│
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                      │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │

```

**Data flow of a vector-clock update:** local event → `vclock.tick(node)` increments own counter → send: attach clock to message → receive: `vclock.merge(received_clock)` (element-wise max) then `tick(self)` → compare: `vclock.causal_order(a, b)` → `Before | After | Equal | Concurrent`.

**Data flow of conflict detection:** two versions of the same key carry clocks VC1, VC2 → `VC1 || VC2` (concurrent) → both kept as siblings → conflict set emitted → caller (ids-crdt/ids-replication) reconciles via CRDT merge or application resolver.

**Clock kinds supported (sealed, via `ClockKind` enum):**
- `VectorClock<NodeId>` — full vector clock, O(n) space, exact causality, strong consistency of the partial order.
- `VersionVector<NodeId>` — version vector, entries only for replicas that touched the object, bounded by replication degree.
- `DottedVersionVector<NodeId>` — DVV: dot `(node, counter)` + causal-past VV; O(1) causality check.
- `DottedVersionVectorSet<NodeId>` — DVVSet: compact set of DVVs, prevents false conflicts, merge = join of DVV sets.
- `HybridLogicalClock` — HLC: 64-bit physical+logical timestamp, monotonic, causality-preserving, close to wall time.
