### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Vector clock fundamentals (Mattern / Fidge, 1988)

**Source:** Friedemann Mattern, "Virtual Time and Global States of Distributed Systems" (1988/1989); Colin Fidge, "Timestamps in Message-Passing Systems That Preserve the Partial Ordering" (1988); Princeton COS418 L5-vc lecture notes.

Vector clocks were proposed independently by Mattern and Fidge in 1988. A vector clock `VC` is an n-dimensional vector of non-negative integer counters, one per process/replica. Update rules:
- On a local event (or send) at process pi: `VC[i] += 1`.
- On send: attach the current `VC` to the message.
- On receive of message with timestamp `ts`: `VC[k] = max(VC[k], ts[k])` for all k, then `VC[i] += 1` for the receiving process.

Comparison algebra (strong clock condition):
- `VC(a) = VC(b)` iff `∀k: a[k] = b[k]` (same event).
- `VC(a) < VC(b)` (a happened-before b) iff `∀k: a[k] ≤ b[k]` and `∃j: a[j] < b[j]`.
- `VC(a) || VC(b)` (concurrent) iff `¬(a ≤ b) ∧ ¬(b ≤ a)` — neither dominates.

The strong clock condition: `a → b ⇔ VC(a) < VC(b)` — vector clocks capture causality precisely in both directions, unlike Lamport scalar clocks which only guarantee the forward implication.

#### 3.2 Clock comparison & causality detection

**Source:** Princeton COS418 L5-vc; systemoverflow "What Are Vector Clocks and How Do They Encode Causality"; `asupersync` vclock `causal_order()` returning `Before | After | Equal | Concurrent`; `crdts::vclock` `concurrent()`; `like-a-clockwork` `CausalityRelation`.

`ids-vector-clock` exposes:
- `compare(a, b) -> CausalOrder { Before, After, Equal, Concurrent }` — componentwise ≤ check over the union of keys (absent = 0).
- `happens_before(a, b) -> bool` — `a < b`.
- `concurrent(a, b) -> bool` — `a || b`.
- `is_equal(a, b) -> bool`.

Absent keys are treated as 0 (missing counter = never observed that replica), so `{A:1}` and `{A:1, B:0}` are Equal.

#### 3.3 Merge / join (componentwise max)

**Source:** vector clock receive rule `VC = max(VC, ts)`; CRDT join-semilattice (pointwise max = least upper bound); G-Counter as version vector.

`merge(a, b) -> VectorClock` = element-wise max over the union of keys. This is the join (least upper bound) in the join-semilattice of vector clocks: commutative, associative, idempotent. Used on message receipt and on anti-entropy state exchange.

#### 3.4 Version vectors (per-replica, bounded by replication degree)

**Source:** Dynamo paper (DeCandia et al. SOSP 2007); MIT 6.824 Dynamo notes ("version vectors indicate v1 supersedes v2"; `[a:1] -> [a:1,b:2]`); eribeiro "Connecting the Dots: Version Vectors vs. Dotted Version Vectors".

A version vector `VV` maps replica ID → highest sequence number observed from that replica. Unlike a full vector clock (one entry per system process), a version vector has one entry per replica that has touched the object — bounded by the replication degree (typically N=3–5), not the total cluster size. Dynamo uses VVs per object key; a version that is dominated (`VV1 < VV2`) is superseded and dropped; concurrent versions (`VV1 || VV2`) are kept as siblings.

`ids-vector-clock` provides `VersionVector<NodeId>` with:
- `contains(dot) -> bool` — `n ≤ vv[node]`.
- `dominates(other) -> bool` — `self < other`.
- `merge(other)` — pointwise max.
- `conflict(other) -> bool` — concurrent.

#### 3.5 Dotted version vectors (DVV / DVVSet) — O(1) causality

**Source:** ACM DL 10.1145/2332432.2332497 (Preguiça, Baquero, Almeida, Fonte, Gonçalves, "Dotted Version Vectors: Efficient Causality Tracking for Distributed Key-Value Stores", 2012); gsd.di.uminho.pt PDF; `ricardobcl/Dotted-Version-Vectors` (DVVSet); eribeiro vv-dvv blog.

A DVV = `(dot, vv)` where `dot = (node_id, counter)` is the single event being described and `vv` is the causal past (traditional version vector). Causality: event a `((ia, na), va)` causally precedes event b `((ib, nb), vb)` iff `na ≤ vb[ia]` — the dot of a is reflected in b's causal past. O(1) check instead of O(n) componentwise comparison. Size bounded by number of servers storing a replica (degree of replication), not number of clients — solved the client-id explosion of earlier VV schemes. Integrated in Riak (~10% of the space of current VV implementations with unsafe pruning).

DVVSet (compact dotted version vector sets): prevents false conflicts that occur with plain VVs; smaller representation similar to VV size; API `update`, `event`, `join`, `sync` suited to get/put KV interfaces.

`ids-vector-clock` provides:
- `DottedVersionVector<NodeId>` — `dot: Dot<NodeId>`, `past: VersionVector<NodeId>`; `precedes(&self, other) -> bool` (O(1)); `merge`.
- `DottedVersionVectorSet<NodeId>` — set of DVVs; join = least upper bound of sibling contexts; prevents false conflicts.

#### 3.6 Clock pruning & causal-stability garbage collection

**Source:** MIT 6.824 Dynamo notes (Dynamo deletes entries for nodes modified long ago; can cause false conflicts — `[b:7]` pruned then `[b:8]` conflicts with derived `[b:7]`); systemoverflow Dynamo pruning (timestamp per `(node, counter)` pair, oldest removed after threshold — GC not causal ordering, false conflicts possible); USENIX OSDI'26 Treedoc (causal stability: operation o is causally stable if `VV(o) ≤ VV(min)` where `VV(min)` = component-wise minimum over all users; locally causally stable implies global; causally stable tombstones prunable; GarbageCollect protocol with `VVgc`); CRDT tombstone GC at causal stability (Shapiro et al. 2011; arxiv 2310.18220 survey).

Pruning strategies evaluated:
- **Time-based pruning** (Dynamo): drop old entries — simple but can create false conflicts (a real ancestor looks concurrent). Documented as a known hazard; `ids-vector-clock` will NOT prune by wall-clock time by default.
- **Causal-stability pruning**: prune only entries ≤ `VV(min)` (component-wise minimum across all known replicas) — safe, preserves causality, requires knowledge of the minimum vector (gossip/anti-entropy to disseminate).
- **Bounded-size pruning with conflict false-positive tracking**: cap entries, track "possible false conflict" flag when pruning removes potentially-relevant history.

`ids-vector-clock` provides a `PruningPolicy` enum: `None | CausalStability { min_vv } | BoundedSize { max_entries, track_false_conflicts: bool }`, plus `prune(&mut self, policy) -> PruneReport { entries_removed, false_conflict_risk: bool }`.

#### 3.7 Hybrid logical clock (HLC) integration

**Source:** Kulkarni et al., "Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases" (Buffalo CSE tech report 2014-04); `uhlc-rs` (Unique Hybrid Logical Clock for Rust); `hlc-gen` (lock-free HLC, 42-bit wall + 22-bit logical, 64-bit); `hybrid_logical_clock` crate (no_std); Okapi causally consistent geo-replicated KV store (arXiv 1702.04263; HLC + Universal Stable Time stabilization).

HLC combines physical and logical time: each timestamp = `(physical_wall_time, logical_counter)`. On local event: if physical > last physical, set physical and reset logical to 0; else increment logical. On receive of remote timestamp: take max of physicals, merge logicals. Result: monotonic 64-bit timestamps close to NTP wall time, preserving happens-before (`a → b ⇒ HLC(a) < HLC(b)`), but the converse does NOT hold (HLC < HLC does not imply causality — concurrent events can still be ordered). HLC is weaker than vector clocks for causality but constant-size (64 bits) and useful for snapshots, MVCC, and debugging.

`ids-vector-clock` provides `HybridLogicalClock` with `now() -> HlcsTimestamp`, `send() -> Timestamp`, `receive(remote: &Timestamp)`, `compare(a, b) -> Ordering` (wall first, logical second), and `is_causally_possible(a, b)` — HLC ordering is a *necessary but not sufficient* condition for causality; use vector clock / DVV for the definitive check.

#### 3.8 Conflict detection & sibling management

**Source:** Dynamo version vectors (siblings `[a:1]`, `[a:1,b:2]`, `[a:2]`; client must merge); `crdts` survey (dot IDs, vector clock compression, concurrent detection); arXiv 1511.05010 "Eventually Consistent Register Revisited" (multi-value register returns concurrent values as a conflict set; LWW variant with timestamp); systemoverflow vector clocks (attach clocks to object versions; concurrent → siblings; application logic reconciles).

Conflict detection: two versions of the same object with clocks VC1, VC2 → if `VC1 || VC2` (concurrent), both are siblings = a true conflict requiring resolution. Resolution strategies (delegated to caller crates):
- Last-write-wins (LWW) using HLC/physical timestamp as tiebreak.
- CRDT merge (OR-Set, LWW-register, MV-register).
- Application-specific resolver.

`ids-vector-clock` provides `detect_conflicts(versions: &[(Clock, Value)]) -> ConflictSet { concurrent: Vec<Version>, dominated: Vec<Version> }` and `siblings(clocks: &[VectorClock]) -> Vec<Vec<usize>>` (groups of mutually concurrent clocks).

#### 3.9 Causal consistency session guarantees

**Source:** arXiv 2211.03501 "Tunable Causal Consistency" (four session guarantees: read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads; causal consistency = conjunction of the four); MongoDB causal consistency docs (majority read + majority write = all four guarantees); Wikipedia causal consistency (weaker than sequential/linearizable, available under partition).

`ids-vector-clock` supports tracking a per-session causal context: the session's observed DVV/VV is sent with each read (read context) and each write carries its causal dot. A read is gated: deliver only when `causal_past ⊆ applied` (the replica has applied all dependencies). This gives read-your-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads without linearizability.

#### 3.10 Rust clock crate landscape

**Source:** docs.rs `asupersync::trace::distributed::vclock::VectorClock` (BTreeMap<NodeId,u64>, `causal_order()`, manual PartialEq with absent-is-zero); docs.rs `crdts::vclock::VClock` (actors + counters, `concurrent()`); `uhlc-rs` (HLC + unique u128 ID, NTP64 64-bit, update_with_timestamp drift guard); `hlc-gen` (lock-free HLC, 42-bit wall + 22-bit logical); `hybrid_logical_clock` (no_std, `is_concurrent()`).

`ids-vector-clock` will be a fresh IDS crate (not wrapping these directly, to avoid non-IDS dependencies and to keep the type system aligned with `ids-000-aa` `NodeId`), but the design borrows their proven APIs: `tick`, `send`, `receive`, `merge`, `compare/causal_order`, `concurrent`.

#### 3.11 Clock serialization & wire format

Clock metadata is serialized as opaque `Vec<u8>` for the carrier. Encoding: serde/bincode or a custom compact binary (node id as `NodeId` bytes + counter as u64/u128 varint). DVV/DVVSet serialized as `(dot, past)` pairs. HLC as 64-bit. Size bounds: vector clock O(n) entries; version vector bounded by replication degree; DVV/DVVSet bounded similarly; HLC constant 8 bytes. No crypto ops inside this crate — but clock envelopes may be signed with ed25519 or hashed with sha256/blake3 by `ids-crypto` at the caller layer when audit/integrity is required.

#### 3.12 Interaction with ids-000-aa types

`ids-vector-clock` imports `NodeId` (as the actor/replica identifier), `IdsTime` (for HLC physical basis and timeouts), `CarrierType` (not used directly — the crate never addresses endpoints), `Checksum` (for clock-hash digests if needed), and `Error` from `ids-000-aa`. It never redefines these. It references sealed trait contracts only as trait bounds where relevant (e.g. a `Clock` trait could be sealed in a later phase; for Phase 066 the concrete clock types are the API).

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| False conflicts from unsafe pruning | Causality correctness | No time-based pruning by default; causal-stability pruning only (`VV ≤ VV(min)`); `PruneReport` flags `false_conflict_risk` when bounded-size pruning removes possibly-relevant history |
| Clock size growth unbounded (O(n) vector clock) | Memory / bandwidth | Version vector and DVV/DVVSet bounded by replication degree; `BoundedSize` pruning policy with explicit risk flag; HLC constant-size alternative for non-critical ordering |
| Clock manipulation / forged causality | Causal integrity | Clock envelopes can be ed25519-signed / sha256/blake3-hashed by `ids-crypto` at the carrier layer; this crate never trusts remote clocks blindly — merge is idempotent and max-based (monotonic, no regression) |
| Wall-clock dependence for causality | Causality correctness | HLC uses wall time as a component but causality decisions use vector clock / DVV; HLC alone never asserted as causal proof; monotonic `IdsTime` only for timeouts, never for ordering |
| Concurrent siblings silently dropped | Data correctness | `detect_conflicts` returns all concurrent versions as siblings; dominated versions only dropped when strictly `VV1 < VV2`; application must resolve siblings |
| Missing counter treated as 0 vs explicit zero | Comparison correctness | Manual `PartialEq`/`Ord` with absent-is-zero rule (as in `asupersync` fix) — `Eq` coherence with `partial_cmp` maintained |
| Carrier duplication/reordering of clock metadata | Causal correctness | Merge is commutative/associative/idempotent — duplicates and reordering are safe; causal gate (DVV `precedes`) blocks delivery until dependencies applied |
| Non-IDS crate sneaking into dependency tree | Carrier-agnostic / crypto policy | Dependency audit in CI; `cargo tree` asserts no `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p/any networking crate; crypto allowlist test asserts only the five algorithms reachable |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-vector-clock |
|-------|------|------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId` (actor ID), `IdsTime` (HLC physical basis), `Checksum` (clock digest), `Error` — consumed, never redefined |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive | Clock metadata rides as opaque `Vec<u8>` in `Endpoint` payloads; crate never sends/receives directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Optional signing/hashing of clock envelopes at caller layer; this crate implements no crypto |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store | Attaches vector clock / version vector to object versions; consults `ids-vector-clock` for sibling detection |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization / anti-entropy | Exchanges clock digests; uses `compare`/`merge` to determine what to replicate |
| `ids-crdt` | Conflict-free replicated data types | Version vectors / DVV as CRDT metadata; `merge` = join; causal delivery for op-based CRDTs |
| `ids-sync` | Replica synchronization | Causal context piggybacked on sync messages; `ids-vector-clock` validates ordering |
| `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060) | Read/write behavior per profile | Uses DVV causal context for `CausallyConsistent` profile; quorum profiles use version vectors for freshness |
| `ids-hlc` (Phase 067) | Hybrid logical clock for ordering | `ids-vector-clock` HLC integration is the logical-clock half; `ids-hlc` may build on or mirror it |

**Integration points:** `ids-vector-clock` exposes pure functions and data structures; callers frame clock metadata into `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams. No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli`. No crate-internal reaching.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Vector clock (Mattern/Fidge)

```
VectorClock<NodeId> { entries: BTreeMap<NodeId, u64> }

tick(node): entries[node] += 1                          // local event
send():   return clone(entries)                         // piggyback on message
receive(ts):                                            // message with timestamp ts
    for (node, c) in ts: entries[node] = max(entries[node], c)
    tick(self)

compare(a, b) -> CausalOrder:
    all_nodes = keys(a) ∪ keys(b)   // absent = 0
    a_le_b = ∀n: a[n] ≤ b[n]
    b_le_a = ∀n: b[n] ≤ a[n]
    (true, true)  → Equal
    (true, false) → Before   (a happened before b)
    (false, true) → After    (b happened before a)
    (false, false) → Concurrent
```

Strong clock condition: `a → b ⇔ compare(a,b) == Before`.

#### 7.2 Version vector

```
VersionVector<NodeId> { entries: Map<NodeId, u64> }   // one entry per replica that touched object

dominates(other) = self < other   // componentwise ≤ with at least one strict
conflict(other)  = ¬dominates(other) ∧ ¬other.dominates(self)
contains(dot)    = dot.counter ≤ entries[dot.node]
merge(other)     = pointwise max
```

Bounded by replication degree (entries only for replicas that wrote the object).

#### 7.3 Dotted version vector (DVV)

```
Dot<NodeId> = (node: NodeId, counter: u64)
DottedVersionVector<NodeId> { dot: Dot<NodeId>, past: VersionVector<NodeId> }

precedes(a, b) -> bool:   // O(1) — does a causally precede b?
    a.dot.counter ≤ b.past.entries[a.dot.node]
```

`a < b` iff `na ≤ vb[ia]` (the dot of `a` is in `b`'s causal past). Concurrent iff neither precedes.

#### 7.4 Dotted version vector set (DVVSet)

```
DottedVersionVectorSet<NodeId> { dvvs: Set<DottedVersionVector<NodeId>> }

join(a, b):  // least upper bound — merge sibling contexts
    result = a.dvvs ∪ b.dvvs
    prune dominated DVVs (where one's past dominates another's and dot is subsumed)
```

Prevents false conflicts of plain version vectors; compact representation similar to VV size.

#### 7.5 Hybrid logical clock (HLC)

```
HlcTimestamp { physical: u64 (wall ms), logical: u16, ... }   // 64-bit total

now():  if wall > last_wall: physical = wall, logical = 0
        else: physical = last_wall, logical += 1
send(): now() + increment logical
receive(remote):
    physical = max(local_wall, remote.physical)
    logical  = max(local_logical, remote.logical) + (if equal then 1 else 0)

compare(a, b): physical first, then logical   // total order
is_causally_possible(a, b): a < b in HLC order  // necessary, NOT sufficient for causality
```

#### 7.6 Pruning / causal-stability GC

```
VV(min) = component-wise minimum over all known replica version vectors
op o is locally causally stable  ⇔  VV(o) ≤ VV(min)_local
prune(policy):
    CausalStability: remove entries ≤ VV(min); false_conflict_risk = false
    BoundedSize:     cap entries; if evicted entry might be an ancestor → false_conflict_risk = true
PruneReport { entries_removed, false_conflict_risk }
```

#### 7.7 Conflict detection

```
detect_conflicts(versions: &[(Clock, Value)]) -> ConflictSet:
    for each pair (i, j):
        if compare(clock_i, clock_j) == Concurrent:
            add i, j to same sibling group
    ConflictSet { sibling_groups: Vec<Vec<index>>, dominated: Vec<index> }
```

Merge is commutative/associative/idempotent (join-semilattice) — duplicate and out-of-order delivery safe.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Actor identifier type:** `NodeId` from `ids-000-aa` is the natural actor/replica ID; confirm it fits as `VectorClock<NodeId>` key (it is `Copy + Hash + Ord`).
2. **Counter width:** u64 vs u128 for vector-clock counters — u64 sufficient for expected operation rates; u128 if extreme scale needed.
3. **Serialization format:** serde/bincode vs custom compact binary (varint counters) — tradeoff between interoperability and wire size; decision deferred to implementation.
4. **HLC physical clock source:** `IdsTime` (monotonic ticks) vs wall-clock ms — HLC needs a physical basis; `IdsTime` provides monotonic ticks but HLC ideally tracks wall-clock closeness; source to be confirmed at integration with `ids-hlc` (Phase 067).
5. **Pruning default:** `None` (no pruning) is the safe default; whether `CausalStability` becomes default depends on `VV(min)` dissemination mechanism (gossip/anti-entropy in `ids-replication`).
6. **DVV vs DVVSet default:** DVVSet prevents false conflicts but is more complex; default may be DVV for simplicity, DVVSet as opt-in.
7. **Interaction with `ids-hlc` (Phase 067):** whether HLC lives in `ids-vector-clock` or `ids-hlc`; Phase 066 includes HLC integration, Phase 067 may refine or extract it.
8. **Sealed `Clock` trait:** whether to seal the clock trait in `contracts/` (matching `ids-000-aa` pattern) or keep concrete types public; decision pending.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-vector-clock` (not a folder) | "Separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear causality boundary |
| Multiple clock kinds (VC, VV, DVV, DVVSet, HLC) | Different tradeoffs: VC exact but O(n); VV/DVV bounded by replication degree; DVV O(1) causality; HLC constant-size 64-bit |
| Absent key = 0 in comparison (manual PartialEq) | Restores `Eq`/`Ord` coherence with `partial_cmp` (fixes `asupersync` deserialization mismatch) |
| No time-based pruning by default | Dynamo-style time pruning causes false conflicts; causal-stability pruning is the safe alternative |
| HLC ordering = necessary not sufficient for causality | HLC < HLC does not imply happens-before; vector clock / DVV for definitive causality |
| Merge = element-wise max (join-semilattice) | Commutative/associative/idempotent → safe under duplicate/out-of-order carrier delivery |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate never sends | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in the crate |
| Allowed crypto only; no crypto implemented here | IDS policy; `ids-crypto` implements, this crate only references primitive IDs / optionally hashes |
| `NodeId` as actor/replica key | Canonical type from `ids-000-aa`; never redefined |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 067 creates `ids-hlc`, a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), providing the hybrid logical clock (HLC) used for ordering events across the IDS workspace. An HLC timestamp combines a physical time component with a logical counter: it stays close to wall-clock time (human-readable, usable for TTLs and snapshot reads) while preserving the happened-before causality relation of logical clocks — if event `e` happened before event `f`, then `hlc.e < hlc.f` (Kulkarni et al., "Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases," OPODIS 2014 / SUNY Buffalo TR 2014-04).

`ids-hlc` is **local clock logic only**: it generates, merges, compares, and packs HLC timestamps. It never opens a socket and imports no networking crate. Any HLC-stamped payload exchanged between nodes rides as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 bytes); the framing and transport belong to `ids-carrier` / the caller, never to `ids-hlc`.

**Contents (per prompts.txt entry 67):** HLC implementation, physical+logical time combination, clock skew handling, ordering guarantees, fallback to IDS standard time. The fallback means: when the physical clock source is unavailable or untrusted (backward wall-clock jump, no NTP), `ids-hlc` derives its physical component from `ids-time` (`IdsTime`, monotonic u64 ticks defined via `ids-000-aa`), degrading gracefully to a logical-clock-over-monotonic-ticks mode while staying monotonic and ordered.

**Constraints:** carrier-agnostic (no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh); allowed crypto only `ed25519`, `xchacha20poly1305`, `sha256`, `blake3`, `chacha20poly1305` (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-hlc` consumes primitive IDs/types from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only, or stays crypto-free); `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding canonical types (`NodeId`, `IdsTime`, `Error`, …) and sealed trait contracts.

A skeleton `ids-hlc` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-hlc/`. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-hlc` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types, sealed contracts, errors) and `ids-time` (IDS standard time fallback). It is a pure, local, sync-first clock module: every node holds its own HLC instance; timestamps are minted locally, merged on message receipt, compared lexicographically, and optionally packed into a fixed-width integer for wire storage. The crate itself never sends or receives bytes — stamped data is framed by the caller into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams addressed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      CALLER LAYER (ids-*, clients)                           │
│  ids-store (MVCC version timestamps), ids-consistency-profile (Phase 060)   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 067: ids-hlc (THIS CRATE — local clock)             │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌────────────────┐   │
│  │ clock source │ │   hlc core   │ │ ordering /      │ │  fallback to   │   │
│  │ (physical)   │ │  (l, c, id)  │ │ total-order tie │ │  IdsTime ticks │   │
│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └────────────────┘   │
│  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐                       │
│  │   encode     │ │   skew bound │ │   crypto surf.  │                       │
│  │   (64/u128)  │ │   (epsilon)  │ │   (optional)    │                       │
│  └──────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └─────────────────┘                       │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              NO std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC /     │
│              HTTP / DNS — HLC math is local; no network stack in trust base  │
│  HLC-stamped bytes leave the node only as opaque Vec<u8> via                 │
│  ids-carrier::Endpoint (CarrierType + Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B), sent by the caller  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**HLC data model** (Kulkarni et al. 2014): each node maintains `(l, c)` where `l` is the highest physical time observed (from the node's own clock or received messages) and `c` is a bounded logical counter. Comparison is lexicographic: `l` first, then `c`; a `node_id` (from `ids-000-aa`) breaks remaining ties for a total order.

**Core rules (research-verified):**
- Local event / send: `l' = max(l, pt)` where `pt` is the current physical time; if `l' == l` then `c += 1` (physical stalled — break tie logically), else `c = 0`.
- Receive with remote stamp `(lm, cm)`: `l' = max(l, pt, lm)`; counter update by source of the maximum: if `l' == l == lm` → `c = max(c, cm) + 1`; elif `l' == l` → `c += 1`; elif `l' == lm` → `c = cm + 1`; else `c = 0`.
- Strict monotonicity: the physical component never decreases, so backward wall-clock jumps (NTP steps, leap seconds) are absorbed into the logical counter rather than moving time backward.
- Bounded skew assumption `ε`: `|l − pt| ≤ ε`; production systems (CockroachDB) use a max clock offset of ~500 ms; outliers beyond the guard are clamped or rejected.
- Counter bounded in practice (O(n·ε) in theory); if the counter ceiling is reached while physical time stalls, the clock blocks or raises a defined overflow error (never wraps silently).

**Fallback to IDS standard time:** when the physical source is missing or distrusted, `ids-hlc` sources `pt` from `ids-time::IdsTime` (monotonic u64 ticks, never wall-clock), so ordering guarantees survive total loss of physical time — the clock degrades to a pure logical counter over monotonic ticks. Fallback entry/exit conditions and hysteresis are configurable per node.

**Crypto surface:** `ids-hlc` performs no cryptography by default. If a caller wants timestamps signed or hashed (audit checkpoints on profile decisions), it uses only `ed25519` (signing), `blake3`/`sha256` (digesting timestamps), via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs exposed through `ids-000-aa`. `xchacha20poly1305`/`chacha20poly1305` are available for encrypting clock state at rest. No other algorithm may enter the crate.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline; full list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 HLC fundamentals (Kulkarni et al., 2014)

**Source:** S. Kulkarni, M. Demirbas, D. Madeppa, B. Avva, M. Leone, "Logical Physical Clocks and Consistent Snapshots in Globally Distributed Databases," OPODIS 2014 (LNCS 8878) / SUNY Buffalo Tech Report 2014-04. https://cse.buffalo.edu/tech-reports/2014-04.pdf ; https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-319-14472-6_2

HLC bridges logical clocks (causality tracking, no physical time) and physical clocks (real-time correspondence, best-effort NTP). Properties:
- **Causality preservation:** `e hb f ⇒ hlc.e < hlc.f` (one-way happened-before captured).
- **Close to physical time:** `l` stays within clock-skew bound `ε` of NTP/pt; HLC substitutable for physical clocks in applications such as snapshot reads in MVCC globally distributed databases.
- **Strictly monotonic:** tolerates NTP kinks — non-monotonic POSIX updates, leap seconds — without time going backward.
- **Compact:** fits in a 64-bit NTP timestamp format; masking-tolerant to NTP uncertainties.
- **Benefits:** wait-free transaction ordering; consistent snapshots without waiting out clock-sync uncertainty or prior coordination (a posteriori snapshot identification).

`ids-hlc` adopts this as its core contract: causality + bounded real-time proximity + monotonicity.

#### 3.2 HLC data structure and bit packing

**Sources:** https://github.com/glycerine/hlc (int64: upper 48 bits physical ≈ 0.1 ms resolution, lower 16 bits logical counter); https://lib.rs/crates/hlc-gen (lock-free Rust, AtomicU64, 42-bit wall-clock from 2024-01-01 epoch + 22-bit logical, ~4M events/ms, no_std compatible); https://docs.rs/hlc (wall time + logical component); https://docs.rs/crate/uhlc (unique HLC, u128 node id, max-delta drift guard); https://docs.rs/meridian-core (wall_ms u64, logical u16, node_id u64, `Ord` by field order); https://arxiv.org/html/1702.04263v1 (Okapi: 64-bit hybrid timestamp, 48 MSB physical microsecond + 16 LSB logical); https://pingcap.com/blog/time-in-distributed-systems (TiDB TSO centralized HLC: 46-bit physical + 18-bit logical, 262M timestamps/s, sleeps 50 ms when logical ceiling reached).

Common packing: a single `u64` = physical high bits + logical low bits. For `ids-hlc` the natural representation is the unpacked tuple `(physical: u64, logical: u64, node_id: Option<NodeId>)` with optional pack/unpack to `u64` (configurable split, default 48/16) or `u128` (full 64-bit physical + logical + id). Decision deferred (see Section 10).

#### 3.3 Local event / send algorithm

**Sources:** https://singhajit.com/distributed-systems/hybrid-clock ; https://martinfowler.com/articles/patterns-of-distributed-systems/hybrid-clock.html ; Kulkarni 2014 Algorithm 1.

```
now = max(l, pt)          // pt = physical clock read
if now == l:   c += 1     // physical did not advance → break tie logically
else:          c = 0      // physical advanced → reset counter
l = now
return (l, c[, node_id])
```

The attached stamp travels with every outgoing message/datagram. Sender and receiver each maintain independent HLC state — no centralized timestamp oracle (contrast TiDB TSO / Percolator), so no single point of failure and no round-trip per timestamp (research: unmeshjoshi/hybridclocktxn).

#### 3.4 Receive / merge algorithm (four-branch)

**Sources:** Kulkarni 2014; https://singhajit.com/distributed-systems/hybrid-clock ; https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/master/pkg/util/hlc/hlc.go.

On receiving remote stamp `(lm, cm)` with local physical `pt`:
```
l' = max(l, pt, lm)
if   l' == l  == lm: c = max(c, cm) + 1
elif l' == l:        c = c + 1
elif l' == lm:       c = cm + 1
else:                c = 0
l = l'
```

This is the Lamport-style `max` generalized to include physical time: the receiver never moves its clock backward, and every received message that carries newer knowledge pulls the local clock forward. Merge is idempotent: applying the same stamp twice yields the same state as applying it once.

#### 3.5 Ordering guarantees

- **Lexicographic compare:** `(l1, c1, id1) < (l2, c2, id2)` iff `l1 < l2`, or `l1 == l2 ∧ c1 < c2`, or `l1 == l2 ∧ c1 == c2 ∧ id1 < id2`. The `node_id` tie-break gives a deterministic total order even for concurrent events on different nodes (arbitrary but consistent — same convention as Lamport/vector-clock total-order tie-breaks).
- **Causality:** `e → f` (program order or send/receive chain) ⇒ `hlc(e) < hlc(f)`. One-way causality — `hlc.e < hlc.f` does NOT imply `e hb f` (concurrent events can compare either way); that is inherent to scalar clocks.
- **NOT linearizable/external consistency by itself:** HLC gives causal ordering and monotonicity; real-time (external) consistency additionally needs bounded skew + uncertainty windows / read restarts (CockroachDB max-offset 500 ms, follower-read staleness ~4 s; Spanner TrueTime needs GPS/atomic hardware + commit wait — out of scope for IDS commodity assumption).
- **Snapshot reads:** a read at HLC `t` returns a consistent cut across replicas — the core benefit cited in Kulkarni 2014 and used by CockroachDB/YugabyteDB MVCC.

#### 3.6 Clock skew handling

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/html/2104.15099v2 (PWC paper: HLC overview, `|l.e − pt.e| ≤ ε`, counter bound linear in n and ε in theory, small in practice; 48-bit packing stores `l − pt` (12 bits) + `c` (4 bits)); https://yugabyte.com/blog/evolving-clock-sync-for-distributed-databases (NTP typical accuracy 5 ms–100 ms+; CockroachDB/YugabyteDB observe 100–250 ms max skew; 500 ms safe default max offset); https://docs.cockroachlabs.com (max clock offset, uncertainty interval `[T, T + max offset]`, read restart above ambiguous values).

- **Assumption:** physical clocks of any two nodes differ by at most `ε` (loosely synchronized via NTP/PTP; correctness of ordering does not depend on precision, only on the bound existing).
- **Guard:** `max_offset` — how far ahead of the local physical clock/cluster time the wall time may advance; remote stamps beyond the guard are logged as skew violations (clamped or rejected per policy).
- **Backward jumps:** physical component of HLC = max(observed physical times); a wall clock that steps backward simply fails to advance `l`, so the logical counter absorbs the events — time never regresses.
- **Counter bound:** `c` ceiling; when reached and physical time has not advanced, the clock must wait (Okapi) or raise — configurable, never silent wraparound.
- **Drift observation:** krabka-hlc reports clock drift on the data path (records pulling the clock forward = measured skew).

#### 3.7 Fallback to IDS standard time (`ids-time` / `IdsTime`)

**Prompt requirement (entry 67 line 1004):** "fallback to IDS standard time." `ids-000-aa` defines `IdsTime`; `ids-time` (Phase 005) builds the proprietary `Idstime` on it. `ids-hlc`'s physical clock source is injectable:
- Primary: system physical time (NTP-disciplined wall clock, monotonicized via max()).
- Fallback: `IdsTime` monotonic ticks when the physical source is absent, untrusted (backward jump beyond tolerance), or explicitly disabled.
- In fallback mode the clock degenerates to a Lamport-style logical counter over monotonic ticks — still strictly ordered, still causality-preserving, just no real-time correspondence until physical time returns.
- Fallback entry/exit: hysteresis to avoid flapping; timestamped log of fallback duration (observable, not silent).

#### 3.8 Physical + logical time combination

The combination rule is exactly the local-event and receive rules above: `l` tracks the maximum physical time ever observed (own or remote), `c` captures ordering that physical time cannot express (same-tick events, skew-absorbed events). `|l − pt|` stays bounded by `ε` provided messages carry stamps and clocks are loosely synchronized — this bounded distance is what makes HLC timestamps meaningful for humans, TTLs, and log correlation, unlike pure Lamport counters.

#### 3.9 HLC vs Lamport clocks vs vector clocks vs TrueTime

**Sources:** https://cs.stackexchange.com/questions/101496 (Lamport vs vector clocks; total order via node ID tie-break; linearizability stronger than either); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logical_clock; https://martinfowler.com/articles/patterns-of-distributed-systems/hybrid-clock.html.

| Clock | Real-time meaning | Causality | Size | Linearizable? |
|-------|-------------------|-----------|------|---------------|
| Physical (NTP) | Yes (best effort) | No | 64 bits | No (skew) |
| Lamport | No | Yes (one-way) | 1 counter | No |
| Vector clock | No | Yes (exact, concurrent detectable) | O(n) | No |
| HLC | Yes (bounded by ε) | Yes (one-way) | 64–128 bits | No (needs uncertainty windows) |
| TrueTime | Yes (bounded ε, hardware) | Yes | interval | Yes (commit wait) |

IDS adopts HLC because it needs both ordering and human-meaningful timestamps without GPS/atomic hardware and without a centralized timestamp oracle.

#### 3.10 Production precedent

- **CockroachDB:** HLC = transaction timestamps for MVCC; `maxOffset` 500 ms default; uncertainty interval on reads; follower reads with bounded staleness (~4 s closed timestamp). https://docs.cockroachlabs.com/docs/stable/architecture/transaction-layer
- **YugabyteDB:** 64-bit HLC (physical microseconds + logical counter); xCluster last-writer-wins picks greater HLC; monotonic per node. https://docs.yugabyte.com/stable/architecture/transactions/transactions-overview/#hybrid-logical-clocks
- **TiDB:** centralized TSO hybrid logical clock (PD), 46+18-bit packing. https://pingcap.com/blog/time-in-distributed-systems
- **MongoDB:** HLC/ClusterTime as read and commit timestamps; causal consistency sessions; operationTime propagated in every message; NTP not enforced between nodes. https://mongodb.com/company/blog/engineering/casual-guarantees-anything-casual ; https://arxiv.org/html/2111.14946v3
- **Okapi:** HLC for causally consistent geo-replication; responds immediately despite skew by advancing HLC to snapshot time. https://arxiv.org/html/1702.04263v1

#### 3.11 Testing: clock skew injection and fault injection

**Sources:** https://onenoughtone.com/learn/failure-injection/5 (clock skew causes silent correctness violations; skew injection makes nodes disagree about time); CockroachDB HLC tests for backward jumps and `maxOffset` violations.

`ids-hlc` tests must inject: backward wall-clock jumps, per-node skew (±ε), message delay/reordering/duplication (idempotent merge), counter-ceiling reach, fallback entry/exit, and monotonicity assertions under adversarial schedules. Deterministic injectable physical clock (like CockroachDB's `physicalClock func()` or Flynn's injectable clock) makes this reproducible.

#### 3.12 Crypto surface (allowed set only)

**Sources:** https://docs.rs/ed25519-dalek ; https://docs.rs/chacha20poly1305 ; https://docs.rs/sha2 ; https://github.com/BLAKE3-team/BLAKE3.

`ids-hlc` is crypto-free by default. Optional, declared-only surface (implemented in `ids-crypto`, referenced via `ids-000-aa` primitive IDs):
- `ed25519`: signing HLC-stamped decisions/audit checkpoints.
- `blake3` / `sha256`: digesting timestamps, timestamped state hashing.
- `xchacha20poly1305` / `chacha20poly1305`: encrypting clock state at rest (bounded nonce use).
No other algorithm; allowlist enforced by unit test and CI dependency audit.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
||--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------||
|| Clock skew between nodes > ε | Ordering correctness | Bounded-skew assumption; `max_offset` guard; remote outliers clamped/rejected and logged ||
|| Wall clock jumps backward (NTP step, leap second) | Monotonicity | Physical component = max(observed); never decreases; logical counter absorbs ||
|| Logical counter ceiling reached | Liveness / correctness | Defined overflow policy (wait for physical advance or configurable error); never wrap silently ||
|| Duplicate/delayed datagram (carrier replays) | Idempotence | Receive merge is idempotent; applying same stamp twice == once ||
|| Node-id tie-break collision | Total order determinism | `NodeId` from `ids-000-aa` (32-byte, collision-resistant); tie-break arbitrary but fixed ||
|| Fallback hides loss of physical time forever | Observability | Timestamped fallback entry/exit with hysteresis; metrics on fallback duration ||
|| Unchecked drift | Real-time correspondence | `|l − pt| ≤ ε` enforced; drift observed on data path (krabka-style observation seam) ||
|| Prohibited crate sneaking in | Carrier-agnostic rule | CI dependency audit (`cargo tree`); grep bans `std::net`, `tokio::net`, `libp2p`, `IpAddr`, `SocketAddr`, `TcpStream`, `UdpSocket` — zero matches ||
|| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | Only `ed25519`, `xchacha20poly1305`, `sha256`, `blake3`, `chacha20poly1305` reachable; via `ids-crypto` only; allowlist unit test ||
|| Timestamp forgery / replay | Decision authenticity | Optional `ed25519`-signed audit checkpoints over stamped bytes (survives carrier re-framing) ||

The carrier is never trusted: HLC ordering is enforced by the clock math, and stamped bytes are self-describing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (`Endpoint = CarrierType + Vec<u8>`) keeps the network stack out of the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-hlc ||
||-------|------|--------------------------|--------------------------------------||
|| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types, sealed trait contracts, invariants, errors | `NodeId` (tie-breaker), `Error`, sealed contracts consumed — never redefined ||
|| `ids-time` | IDS standard time: `IdsTime` monotonic u64 ticks | Fallback physical source when wall clock untrusted ||
|| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`), `send_datagram`/`receive_datagram` | HLC-stamped payloads ride `Endpoint` datagrams; `ids-hlc` never sends/receives directly ||
|| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only | Optional signing/digest of HLC-stamped decisions; `ids-hlc` declares type surface only ||
|| `ids-store` (later phase) | MVCC versioned store | HLC as version/timestamp component for MVCC ordering ||
|| `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060) | Read/write behavior per profile | HLC as causality input for profile admission decisions ||
|| `ids-replication` (later phase) | Replica synchronization | Ships HLC-stamped ops as `Endpoint` datagrams ||
|| All other `ids-*` | Consumers of timestamps | Import `ids-hlc::HlcTimestamp` via public API; never reach into internals ||

**Integration points:** `ids-hlc` exposes `HlcClock` (`now()`, `send_stamp()`, `receive(stamp)`), `HlcTimestamp` (comparable, encodable), and `HlcConfig` (skew bound, overflow policy, fallback toggle). All traffic that leaves a node is opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-hlc` has no `send`/`receive` of its own and depends on no transport crate.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **HLC timestamp tuple** — `HlcTimestamp { physical: u64, logical: u64, node_id: Option<NodeId> }`; `NodeId` from `ids-000-aa` breaks final ties.
2. **Local tick / send stamp** — `now = max(l, pt)`; if `now == l` then `c += 1` else `c = 0`; `l = now`. Physical advance resets counter; stall bumps it.
3. **Receive merge** — `l' = max(l, pt, lm)`; counter set by source of the max (four-branch, Kulkarni 2014). Monotonic, idempotent, no backward movement.
4. **Total order** — compare `l`, then `c`, then `node_id`; yields a deterministic total order consistent with causality without a central coordinator.
5. **Monotonic physical enforcement** — `l := max(l, new_physical)`; backward wall-clock jumps absorbed into `c`; never decreases.
6. **Bounded skew guard** — `|l − pt| ≤ ε`; `max_offset` rejects/clamps remote stamps too far ahead; monotonicity error counter for observability.
7. **Counter overflow policy** — bounded `c`; at ceiling with stalled physical time: block or raise `HlcError::CounterCeiling` (configurable); never silent wraparound.
8. **Fixed-width encoding** — pack `(physical, logical)` into `u64` (default 48-bit physical / 16-bit logical per CockroachDB/Okapi precedent; configurable split) or `u128` (full 64-bit physical + logical + id); packed `u64` comparison equals tuple comparison.
9. **IDS standard-time fallback** — injectable clock source; on physical-source failure/untrust, `pt := IdsTime` ticks (monotonic); ordering guarantees preserved, real-time proximity suspended until physical time returns.
10. **Idempotent merge** — receiving an already-seen stamp leaves state unchanged; safe under carrier duplication/reordering.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Physical clock source abstraction:** injectable function pointer (CockroachDB `physicalClock fn`), trait object, or `IdsTime`-only? Affects testability and fallback design.
2. **Bit allocation:** 64-bit packed (`u64`, e.g. 48/16 or 52/12 per YugabyteDB; 42/22 per `hlc-gen`) vs `u128` (full 64-bit physical + logical + node id)? Trade wire size vs timestamp longevity vs node-id inclusion.
3. **Fallback trigger thresholds:** how far behind / how many consecutive backward jumps before switching to `IdsTime`, and hysteresis for switching back — workload-dependent, unquantified.
4. **Counter overflow policy:** block, error, or forcibly advance physical? Depends on latency SLAs of consumers (ids-store MVCC, ids-consistency-profile).
5. **Node ID inclusion:** is `node_id` part of `HlcTimestamp` itself or appended by the caller at comparison time? Affects wire encoding size.
6. **Interaction with `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060):** does the profile consume `HlcTimestamp` directly or through a wrapper? Defined here, validated at integration.
7. **`IdsTime` tick resolution:** sufficient for sub-millisecond ordering needs of MVCC/read paths? To be confirmed against `ids-time` spec.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------||
|| Separate `ids-hlc` crate (not a folder) | Project rule: separate crates for new capabilities; keeps clock logic independent of stores ||
|| Tuple `(physical, logical, node_id)` | Total order without central coordinator; node_id tie-break per Lamport/vector-clock convention and HLC implementations (meridian-core, uhlc) ||
|| Kulkarni four-branch receive merge | Research-verified algorithm; monotonic, idempotent, skew-absorbing ||
|| Bounded-skew assumption `ε` + `max_offset` guard | Matches production (CockroachDB 500 ms max offset, YugabyteDB 100–250 ms observed skew); ordering correct under the bound ||
|| Fallback to `ids-time::IdsTime` | Prompt requirement (fallback to IDS standard time); monotonic ticks preserve ordering without physical time ||
|| Sync core, no async runtime | Clock math is CPU-local; no runtime needed; optional async adapters downstream ||
|| Allowed crypto only, via `ids-crypto` | IDS crypto policy; `ids-hlc` crypto-free by default ||
|| No networking types in crate | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; timestamps leave only as `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams framed by caller ||

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 068 creates `ids-total-order-broadcast`, the IDS crate that delivers uniform agreement on message delivery: every correct node delivers the same set of messages in the same order (total order), and if any node delivers a message then every correct node eventually delivers it (uniform agreement). It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per project rule). It is carrier-agnostic: all traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 bytes); the crate never opens a socket, imports no networking crate, and never references `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh.

`ids-total-order-broadcast` owns: total-order assignment (sequence numbers), uniform agreement delivery, atomic broadcast primitives (broadcast/deliver), validity, uniform integrity (at-most-once, only if previously broadcast), FIFO-total order option, consensus-based ordering integration (sequencer / leader-based / quorum-based), state-machine replication hook (deliver to deterministic state machine in the same order at every node), duplicate suppression, crash-recovery with stable storage + checkpoint, epoch/view change on leader failure, and an audit chain (sha256/blake3 chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 — consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`, never implemented here.

A skeleton `ids-total-order-broadcast` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-total-order-broadcast/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts; this crate imports them and never redefines them. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned the atomic broadcast / total order broadcast four-property definition (Validity, Uniform Agreement, Uniform Integrity, Uniform Total Order) from Hadzilacos & Toueg and ACM taxonomy survey; equivalence of atomic broadcast and consensus (FLP impossibility applies: deterministic consensus impossible in asynchronous systems with one crash); Zab (ZooKeeper atomic broadcast: leader + quorum + recovery); Viewstamped Replication (Oki/Liskov; viewstamp = ⟨view-number, op-number⟩; primary assigns op-number = total order; view-change on primary failure; tolerates f crashes with N ≥ 2f+1); Multi-Paxos / Raft log replication (leader assigns consecutive sequence numbers; commit on majority; state machine replication); PBFT 3-phase total order broadcast (3f+1 replicas, pre-prepare/prepare/commit); DAG-BFT / DAG-Rider (dissemination layer reliably broadcasts blocks in rounds; ordering layer derives total order from DAG leaders via perfect coin); Lamport logical clocks (partial order; total order by tie-breaking with process ID); Hybrid Logical Clock (total order with bounded physical-skew); quorum intersection R + W > N (read/write quorum overlap guarantees latest-read); logic-only Rust consensus crates (`raft-lite`, `raft-consensus`, `simple-raft-rs`, `hotstuff_rs`) that produce `Vec<u8>` protocol messages with no networking — ideal carrier-agnostic model; allowed crypto specs (RFC 8032 Ed25519, RFC 7539 ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305 192-bit nonce libsodium, NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256, BLAKE3 256-bit SIMD).

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-total-order-broadcast` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives), and `ids-time` (monotonic ticks). It is an ordering/agreement layer: given a broadcast request it assigns a total-order sequence number, runs agreement with the other nodes, and delivers messages to the local state machine in that exact order. It never sends bytes itself; it returns protocol `Vec<u8>` datagrams addressed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets that the caller (or the carrier adapter) transmits.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CALLER LAYER (ids-* broadcast users)                      │
│  ids-state-machine, ids-replication, ids-fragment — TO-broadcast(message)   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 068: ids-total-order-broadcast (THIS CRATE — ordering)   │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌────────────┐ │
│  │ sequencer/      │ │ agreement       │ │ delivery        │ │ state-machine│ │
│  │ leader-orderer  │ │ (quorum/consensus)│ │ buffer + dedup  │ │ hook       │ │
│  │ (assigns seqno) │ │ (uniform agree) │ │ (seqno-ordered) │ │ (deliver in │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │ same order)     │ │ order)     │ │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └────────────┘ │
│  │ stable storage  │ │ epoch/view      │ │                 │                │ │
│  │ (checkpoint,    │ │ change on       │ │                 │                │ │
│  │  recovery log)  │ │ leader failure  │ │                 │                │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │                 │                │ │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ │                 │                │ │
│  │ audit chain     │ │ duplicate       │ │                 │                │ │
│  │ (sha256/blake3  │ │ suppression     │ │                 │                │ │
│  │  chain + ed25519│ │ (msg-id set)    │ │                 │                │ │
│  │  checkpoints)   │ │                 │ │                 │                │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │                 │                │ │
└─────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┴──────────────┘
                                          │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                          ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                    │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])│
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                      │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │

```

**Data flow of one broadcast:** caller invokes `TO-broadcast(m)` → orderer assigns `seqno = next_sequence()` and stamps message `{msg_id, sender: NodeId, seqno, payload}` → message sent as opaque datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets → agreement protocol collects acks/quorum → once ordered and agreed, `TO-deliver(m)` delivered to local state machine → stable-storage checkpoint + audit-chain entry (sha256/blake3 chain + ed25519 signature) → duplicate suppressed on retransmission by `msg_id` set. FIFO-total order variant preserves per-sender send order within the global total order.

**Uniform agreement properties (research-verified):**
- **Validity:** if a correct node broadcasts m, it eventually TO-delivers m.
- **Uniform Agreement:** if any node (correct or faulty) TO-delivers m, all correct nodes eventually TO-deliver m.
- **Uniform Integrity:** every node TO-delivers m at most once, and only if m was previously TO-broadcast by sender(m).
- **Uniform Total Order:** if nodes p and q both TO-deliver m and m′, then p delivers m before m′ iff q delivers m before m′.

**Equivalence to consensus:** TO broadcast solvable ⇒ consensus solvable (broadcast initial values; decide first delivered value). Therefore FLP impossibility applies: no deterministic TO broadcast guarantees termination in a fully asynchronous system with even one crash. Practical designs evade FLP via partial synchrony (timeouts), failure detectors, or randomization — reflected in this plan's epoch/view-change and leader-failover design.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Atomic broadcast four properties (Hadzilacos & Toueg / ACM taxonomy)

Sources: ACM DL 10.1145/1041680.1041682 (Total order broadcast and multicast algorithms: Taxonomy and survey); Wikipedia Atomic broadcast; TUM lecture DS-6 atomic broadcast.

Formal primitives: `TO-broadcast(m)` / `TO-deliver(m)`. Every message uniquely identified with sender identity. Properties:
- **Validity:** correct broadcaster eventually TO-delivers its own message.
- **Uniform Agreement:** any delivery ⇒ all correct nodes eventually deliver.
- **Uniform Integrity:** at-most-once delivery; only previously broadcast messages.
- **Uniform Total Order:** all nodes agree on relative order of any two delivered messages.

`ids-total-order-broadcast` implements exactly these four properties; uniform agreement (vs non-uniform agreement) is the IDS requirement — a faulty node's delivery must still propagate to all correct nodes.

#### 3.2 Equivalence to consensus; FLP impossibility

Sources: Chandra & Toueg unreliably failure detectors paper (Consensus and Atomic Broadcast reducible to each other); TUM DS-6 lecture; arXiv 2607.24095 (Consensus In Asynchrony); FLP 1985.

Consensus ⇔ atomic broadcast reduction:
- Consensus from broadcast: every process broadcasts its input; decides the first value TO-delivered (all decide same by total order).
- Broadcast from consensus: run one consensus instance per log slot to assign sequence numbers.

FLP: no deterministic protocol solves consensus (hence atomic broadcast) with guaranteed termination in a fully asynchronous system with one crash. Practical escape hatches: partial synchrony + timeouts (Zab/Raft/Paxos), failure detectors (Chandra-Toueg ♦S, ♦P), or randomization (Ben-Or, DAG-BFT perfect coin). `ids-total-order-broadcast` adopts partial synchrony with epoch/view change and bounded retry; termination is "eventual under synchrony," not guaranteed under asynchrony — documented as an uncertainty.

#### 3.3 Sequencer / leader-based ordering (single sequencer assigns sequence numbers)

Sources: TUM DS-6 lecture (sequencer assigns seqno, sends (m, i) to all); JavaGroups TOTAL protocol design (sequencer-based total order); Weave / Multi-Ring Paxos / CORFU geo-replication papers (central sequencer assigns log slots).

Simplest TO broadcast: a designated sequencer `s` receives broadcasts, assigns monotonically increasing sequence numbers, and multicasts `(m, seqno)` to all. Recipients buffer and deliver in seqno order. Single point of ordering (low latency, simple), single point of failure → mitigated by sequencer failover via epoch/view change (Section 3.6). `ids-total-order-broadcast` supports pluggable orderer strategies: `SequencerOrderer` (single sequencer), `LeaderOrderer` (rotating leader, Zab/Raft style), `QuorumOrderer` (quorum-assigned sequence numbers).

#### 3.4 Consensus-based total order: Zab, Viewstamped Replication, Multi-Paxos/Raft, PBFT

Sources: Zab (IEEE 5958223; ZooKeeper primary-backup; recovery on primary crash; quorum support for primary); Viewstamped Replication (Oki/Liskov PODC 1988; viewstamp ⟨view, op-number⟩; primary assigns op-number; view-change on failure; N ≥ 2f+1); VR Revisited (Liskov/Cowling 2012); MIT 6.824 / Princeton COS418/518; Raft (leader log replication, commit on majority, state machine replication); Multi-Paxos (log = sequence of consensus instances); PBFT (Castro/Liskov SOSP 1999; 3-phase pre-prepare/prepare/commit; 3f+1 replicas; Byzantine).

- **Zab:** primary receives all client requests, propagates transactions as Zab broadcast; on primary crash, recovery agrees on common consistent state and elects new primary (quorum support). `ids-total-order-broadcast` Zab-style: leader assigns epoch + sequence, followers ack, commit on quorum, recovery reconciles logs before new leader.
- **VR:** view = leadership period; viewstamp = ⟨view-number, op-number⟩ totally ordered; primary assigns op-numbers; view change requires quorum of DoViewChange; new primary adopts most up-to-date log.
- **Multi-Paxos/Raft:** replicated log; each entry = (index, term, command); committed on majority; all state machines execute same entries in same order.
- **PBFT:** Byzantine variant; 3f+1; client → primary pre-prepare (seqno), prepare phase (consistent ordering within view), commit phase; view change on primary misbehavior.

IDS choice: crash-fault-tolerant (CFT) leader-based (Zab/Raft/VR family) as default; Byzantine option (PBFT family) as a feature-gated variant using ed25519 signatures. Both map to the same `ids-total-order-broadcast` broadcast/deliver interface.

#### 3.5 FIFO-total order vs causal total order vs total order

Sources: Yale Aspnes Broadcast wiki (single-source FIFO vs totally ordered vs causally ordered); EPFL DA total-order-broadcast slides (reliable vs causal vs total order; total order need not respect causality); Cornell CS5414 Dynamo notes (sloppy quorum, hinted handoff).

- **Single-source FIFO:** messages from one sender delivered in send order. Weakest.
- **Causal broadcast:** if m1 causally precedes m2, all deliver m1 before m2. Partial order; different nodes may deliver concurrent messages in different orders.
- **Total order broadcast:** all nodes deliver all messages in one identical order; no constraint on relation to send/causal order (can be layered on top: FIFO-total = total order that also respects per-sender FIFO; causal-total = total order extending causality).

`ids-total-order-broadcast` implements total order; FIFO-total order is a configuration flag (per-sender sequence preserved inside global order). Causal ordering is delegated to `ids-causal-broadcast` (Phase 069) layering on top.

#### 3.6 Leader election, epochs, view change, crash recovery

Sources: VR / VR Revisited (view change; StartViewChange/DoViewChange/StartView; new primary adopts most up-to-date log); Zab recovery (agree on consistent state before new primary); Raft leader election (term, vote, majority); DAG-BFT seamless reconfiguration (multi-configuration, well-spaced transitions).

Design: monotonically increasing `Epoch` (u64) + `ViewId`. Leader of epoch e is deterministic (e.g., `e % N`). On leader timeout, nodes increment epoch, broadcast view-change with their log state; new leader elected by quorum, adopts the log with the highest (epoch, last_seqno), reconciles missing entries, then resumes ordering. Stable storage: last delivered seqno, epoch, committed log prefix persisted before ack (crash recovery). Checkpoint + garbage collection: once a prefix is delivered at all nodes (quorum-acknowledged stable checkpoint), older log entries and buffered messages may be garbage collected.

#### 3.7 Logical clocks for ordering: Lamport timestamps, Hybrid Logical Clocks

Sources: Princeton COS418 Lamport timestamps (total order by (clock, pid)); UCSB/Rochester logical clocks (totally ordered multicast with queue + ack-from-all); Kulkarni HLC paper (cse.buffalo.edu tech report 2014-04); sergeiturukin HLC explainer; CS StackExchange Lamport vs vector clocks; IETF YANG-Push draft (HLC adoption).

- **Lamport timestamp:** per-node counter incremented on events; message tagged; receiver sets `max(local, received)+1`. Gives causal-consistent partial order; tie-break by node ID → total order. Compact (O(1) per message, independent of N).
- **Hybrid Logical Clock:** (physical, logical) pair; close to wall-clock (bounded skew epsilon) + causal ordering; O(1) state; used in CockroachDB/MongoDB.

`ids-total-order-broadcast` assigns sequence numbers via the leader/sequencer (the authoritative total order), and uses Lamport timestamps or HLC as tie-breakers / causal metadata inside messages (consumed from `ids-time`/`ids-000-aa` types). Wall-clock is never used for ordering decisions (monotonic `IdsTime` only).

#### 3.8 State machine replication integration

Sources: Schneider SMR (1990); arXiv 1904.04098 (SMR = same initial state + total-order broadcast + deterministic execution); arXiv 2203.05681 (SMR scalability, epochs/segments); arxiv 2407.01720 (linearizability vs SMR).

SMR contract: all replicas start identical; every replica receives the same client requests in the same total order; deterministic execution ⇒ identical state transitions ⇒ identical responses. `ids-total-order-broadcast` exposes `deliver_to_state_machine(seqno, message)` hook; the caller's state machine applies deliveries in seqno order. Determinism requirement is on the caller (ids-state-machine), not this crate.

#### 3.9 Duplicate suppression, integrity, at-most-once

Sources: atomic broadcast definitions (uniform integrity: at-most-once, only if broadcast); PBFT no-duplication (same seqno ⇒ same request); DAG-BFT integrity.

Mechanism: every broadcast carries `msg_id` (unique, e.g., blake3(sender || counter) or ed25519-signed nonce). Each node keeps a bounded `DeliveredMsgId` set (recent window, checkpoint-evicted). Redelivery of a known `msg_id` is suppressed; a message never broadcast by its claimed sender is rejected (integrity). Signed broadcasts (ed25519) give sender authentication; unsigned broadcasts rely on carrier-layer trust.

#### 3.10 Stable storage, checkpoint, garbage collection

Sources: Pilotfish checkpoint garbage collection (quorum of CheckpointedMessage ⇒ delete prior checkpoints/buffered messages); VR recovery (disk write before state change); Zab recovery (stable log).

Design: each node persists `(epoch, last_seqno, committed_prefix_hash)` to stable storage before acknowledging a commit. Periodic checkpoints (sha256/blake3 hash of state-machine state + seqno) are broadcast; once a checkpoint is quorum-stable, all log entries and buffered messages ≤ checkpoint seqno are garbage collected. Recovery on restart: load last checkpoint, replay committed log entries from stable storage or fetch missing from peers via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams.

#### 3.11 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

Sources: RFC 8032 (Ed25519/EdDSA); RFC 7539 (ChaCha20-Poly1305, 96-bit nonce); libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305 (192-bit nonce, random nonces safe); NIST FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256); BLAKE3 spec (256-bit, SIMD, keyed hash, KDF, XOF).

Usage in `ids-total-order-broadcast`:
- **ed25519:** sign broadcast messages (sender authentication, integrity), sign audit checkpoints, sign view-change/epoch messages.
- **sha256:** message IDs (blake3 preferred for speed; sha256 where NIST-conformant hashing required), audit-chain links.
- **blake3:** message dedup IDs, content addressing of log entries, fast checkpoint hashing (preferred for speed/parallelism).
- **xchacha20poly1305:** encrypt broadcast payloads at rest/in-transit confidentiality (24-byte random nonce safe per message).
- **chacha20poly1305:** encrypt session/state payloads (12-byte counter nonce, bounded use).

No other crypto. `ids-crypto` is the sole crypto surface; this crate references primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`.

#### 3.12 Quorum-based agreement and fault tolerance

Sources: quorum R + W > N (thecodeforge, medium double-pointer, arxiv 2002.06098, deepengineering staleness SLOs); PBFT quorum (2f+1 of 3f+1); VR quorum (majority, f+1).

Fault model: crash-stop / crash-recovery, f < N/2 (majority quorums intersect). Write/ack quorum: a sequence number is committed when a quorum (⌊N/2⌋+1) of nodes have stored it. Read/deliver quorum intersects write quorum ⇒ delivered order is consistent. Byzantine option: 3f+1, PBFT quorums (2f+1), ed25519 signatures to filter equivocation.

#### 3.13 Batching and pipelining for throughput

Sources: "Optimizing Paxos with batching and pipelining" (EPFL TCS); MultiPaxos Made Complete (arxiv 2405.11183, concurrent handlers); Weave geo-replication.

Batching: multiple client messages batched under one sequence number / one consensus instance; amortizes agreement cost. Pipelining: multiple outstanding consensus instances without waiting for commit; increases throughput under WAN latency. `ids-total_order_broadcast` exposes configurable batch size and pipeline depth; batch boundary is an audit event.

#### 3.14 Logic-only Rust consensus crates as carrier-agnostic reference

Sources: docs.rs raft-lite (logic-only Raft, messages are `Vec<u8>`, guarantees total-order delivery); docs.rs raft-consensus (logic-only, no networking, caller passes messages); simple-raft-rs (no_std, alloc, returns `Vec<u8>` unicast messages to retransmit); hotstuff_rs (BFT SMR in Rust, BlockTree).

These crates confirm the carrier-agnostic pattern: consensus logic is pure functions over `Vec<u8>` messages; the caller is responsible for sending/receiving over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. `ids-total-order-broadcast` follows the same pattern — pure ordering logic over opaque datagrams, no networking imports.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Two nodes deliver different orders | Total order correctness | Single leader/sequencer assigns seqno; quorum commit; uniform total order property |
| Message delivered twice | Uniform integrity | `msg_id` dedup set; bounded replay cache; at-most-once |
| Delivered message never broadcast | Uniform integrity | Sender authentication (ed25519); reject unsigned/unverified |
| Correct node's broadcast never delivered | Validity / Uniform agreement | Retransmission until quorum ack; recovery fetches missing log entries |
| Leader crash stalls ordering | Liveness | Epoch/view change; new leader by quorum; reconciles log before resuming |
| Asynchronous network (FLP) | Termination guarantee | Partial synchrony + timeouts; termination eventual under synchrony (documented) |
| Replay of old broadcast | Replay attack | Epoch + seqno window; dedup set rejects stale seqnos |
| Leader equivocates (two seqnos for one slot) | Order safety | Quorum intersection guarantees at most one value per slot; signed proposals |
| Clock manipulation for order | Causality/total order | Leader-assigned seqno (not wall-clock); Lamport/HLC as metadata only; monotonic IdsTime |
| Carrier duplicates/delays/reorders datagrams | Ordering/recovery | Seqno-based rebuffering; dedup; idempotent delivery |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Signing key extraction | Message authenticity | Keys never leave node; encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
| Prohibited networking crate sneaks in | Carrier-agnostic rule | Dependency audit (CI `cargo tree`); crate imports no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | Only five allowed primitives; CI allowlist test |

The carrier is never trusted: order, agreement, and audit entries are signed/sequenced over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing, reordering, or duplication.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Total-order sequence assignment** — `Orderer::next_seqno(&self, msg_id) -> SeqNo`: monotonically increasing per epoch; leader/sequencer assigns; stored with message before broadcast.
2. **Uniform agreement (quorum commit)** — `commit(epoch, seqno)` when quorum (⌊N/2⌋+1) acks; commit certificate = set of ack signatures (ed25519 in Byzantine mode).
3. **Uniform total order** — all nodes deliver messages in ascending `(epoch, seqno)` order; out-of-order messages buffered until prefix is contiguous.
4. **FIFO-total order** — per-sender send sequence preserved inside the global total order (sender seqno + global seqno).
5. **Duplicate suppression** — `DedupSet<MsgId>` bounded sliding window; redelivery of known `msg_id` suppressed; checkpoint evicts old entries.
6. **Integrity check** — deliver only if `verify_signature(sender, msg_id, payload)` or unsigned-but-carrier-trusted; reject messages never broadcast by claimed sender.
7. **View change / leader failover** — on timeout: `epoch += 1`; broadcast view-change with `(epoch, last_seqno, log_hash)`; new leader (deterministic `epoch % N`) elected by quorum, adopts log with highest `(epoch, last_seqno)`, reconciles missing entries.
8. **Stable storage + checkpoint** — persist `(epoch, last_seqno, committed_hash)` before ack; periodic sha256/blake3 checkpoint; quorum-stable checkpoint ⇒ GC log entries ≤ checkpoint.
9. **Recovery** — load last checkpoint; replay committed log from stable storage; fetch missing entries via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams to peers.
10. **Audit chain** — entry = `(seqno, msg_id, blake3(payload), prev_hash)`; chain = sha256/blake3 hash chain; periodic ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.
11. **Batching + pipelining** — batch boundary = one audit event; pipeline depth = outstanding uncommited instances; configurable.

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpRef`, `OrderingPos`, `Endpoint`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — datagram transport only; crate never sends directly.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `ids-time` — monotonic ticks for leader-election timeouts.
- `serde` — serialization of broadcast envelopes, commit certificates, audit entries.
- `thiserror` — error types.
- `blake3` — message-ID and checkpoint hashing.

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. `ids-total-order-broadcast` imports no crypto directly — all via `ids-crypto`.

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-68.1 | Total order: all nodes deliver same messages in same order | 100% of delivered seqno sequences identical across nodes |
| AC-68.2 | Uniform agreement: any delivery ⇒ all correct nodes eventually deliver | Delivery propagation test; 100% delivery under no-partition |
| AC-68.3 | Uniform integrity: at-most-once, only if broadcast | Dedup test; zero duplicate deliveries; reject unsigned/unverified |
| AC-68.4 | Validity: correct broadcaster eventually self-delivers | Self-delivery test |
| AC-68.5 | FIFO-total order option: per-sender send order preserved | Per-sender seqno monotonic within global order |
| AC-68.6 | View change: leader failover elects new leader by quorum | Kill leader; new leader elected; delivery resumes |
| AC-68.7 | Crash recovery: restart from checkpoint + replay | Restore test; state matches pre-crash |
| AC-68.8 | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) | Zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/etc. |
| AC-68.9 | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 in crypto surface | Allowlist unit test passes |
| AC-68.10 | Audit chain: sha256/blake3 chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints, offline verifiable | Verifier test passes on generated chain |
| AC-68.11 | Quorum commit: commit on ⌊N/2⌋+1 acks; intersection guarantees consistency | Quorum calc test |
| AC-68.12 | Batching/pipelining configurable; batch boundary = audit event | Config test |
| AC-68.13 | Logic over `Vec<u8>` datagrams only; no networking imports | Dependency audit test (`cargo tree`) passes |
| AC-68.14 | Compiles cleanly: `cargo check -p ids-total-order-broadcast` exits 0 | Build test |

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Orderer strategy default:** sequencer vs leader vs quorum — default to leader-based (Zab/Raft) for fault tolerance; sequencer for low-latency single-sequencer deployments; validated at integration.
2. **Byzantine mode:** PBFT-style 3f+1 with ed25519 is feature-gated; default is CFT (crash-fault-tolerant) majority quorums.
3. **Quorum size formula:** ⌊N/2⌋+1 majority vs configurable R/W-style quorum from `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060); to be aligned at integration.
4. **Checkpoint interval & GC policy:** checkpoint frequency and garbage-collection aggressiveness are workload-dependent; unquantified.
5. **Dedup window size:** bounded `DeliveredMsgId` window trades memory vs duplicate-detection range; workload-dependent.
6. **Termination under asynchrony:** FLP ⇒ no deterministic termination guarantee with one crash; "eventual under synchrony" is the best achievable — documented limitation.
7. **Batch size / pipeline depth defaults:** throughput vs latency tradeoff; unquantified pending benchmarks (ids-bench, Phase 048).
8. **Interaction with `ids-state-machine`:** deterministic-execution requirement on the caller; hook contract to be validated at integration.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-total-order-broadcast` (not a folder) | "Separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear ordering boundary |
| Four atomic-broadcast properties (Validity, Uniform Agreement, Uniform Integrity, Uniform Total Order) | Hadzilacos & Toueg / ACM taxonomy; uniform = IDS requirement |
| Leader/sequencer assigns total-order seqno | Simplest correct TO broadcast (TUM DS-6; JavaGroups TOTAL); Zab/Raft/VR for fault tolerance |
| Quorum commit (⌊N/2⌋+1 acks) | Majority quorums intersect ⇒ consistent order; tolerates f < N/2 crashes |
| View change / epoch on leader failure | Zab recovery + VR view change; new leader adopts most up-to-date log |
| Stable storage before ack; checkpoint + GC | Crash recovery; bounded memory (Pilotfish GC pattern) |
| `msg_id` dedup set + signed messages | Uniform integrity; at-most-once; sender authentication |
| Lamport/HLC as metadata only; leader seqno is the order | Wall-clock never used for ordering (clock manipulation cannot break total order) |
| Allowed crypto only; `ids-crypto` surface via `ids-000-aa` | IDS crypto policy |
| Logic over `Vec<u8>` datagrams; no networking imports | Carrier-agnostic; matches logic-only Rust consensus crates (raft-lite, raft-consensus, simple-raft-rs, hotstuff_rs) |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision/delivery log; tamper evidence |
