### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline; the full source list is in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Chandy-Lamport marker algorithm (original, 1985)

**Source:** Chandy & Lamport, "Distributed Snapshots: Determining Global States of Distributed Systems", ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 3(1), Feb 1985, pp. 63–75. https://lamport.org/pubs/chandy.pdf ; mirror https://cs.cmu.edu/~gibbons/15-712/papers/chandy85.pdf

Assumptions (base algorithm): no process or channel failures; all messages arrive intact, exactly once; channels are unidirectional and FIFO ordered; a communication path exists between any two processes; any process may initiate the snapshot; the algorithm does not interfere with normal execution; each process records only its own local state and the states of its incoming channels.

Rules:
- Marker sending rule (initiator and on first marker at a process): record local state, then send a marker on each outgoing channel before any further application message on that channel.
- Marker receiving rule (first marker at process p): record p's local state; mark the state of the channel the marker arrived on as empty; send markers on all outbound channels; start recording messages on all other inbound channels.
- Marker receiving rule (subsequent marker on channel c at p): record the state of c as all messages received on c since p recorded its local state and before this marker; stop recording on c.
- Termination: the snapshot is complete when every process has received a marker on every inbound channel.

Marker messages are control messages distinct from application messages and participate in the same FIFO ordering; a marker on a channel separates pre-snapshot ("white") messages from post-snapshot ("red") messages. A process can snapshot without stopping the application, and multiple processes may initiate snapshots concurrently without interfering.

#### 3.2 Consistent global state and consistent cuts

**Source:** Illinois ECE428, "Consistent Cuts / The Snapshot Algorithm" slides. https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/ECE428/ECE428/sp2018/snapshots.pdf ; Princeton COS418 lecture L4 (vector clocks + marker idea). https://cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall18/cos418/docs/L4-vc.pdf ; Cornell CS6410, Lamport ordering and consistent cuts. https://cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs6410/2011fa/lectures/19-lamport.pdf

A cut `C` of a distributed computation is consistent iff it is left-closed under happens-before: `e ∈ C ∧ f → e ⇒ f ∈ C`. Graphically, every channel arrow crossing the cut must cross forward (send before cut, receive after cut); a message received in the cut without its send in the cut is inconsistent (an effect without its cause). A global state is consistent iff it corresponds to a consistent cut.

Chandy-Lamport guarantees every run produces a consistent cut: if receive event `e_j` is in the cut then send event `e_i` (`e_i → e_j`) is also in the cut, by FIFO ordering (markers on each link precede later application messages). The recorded global state is "possible": there need not be a single instant at which it occurred, but some reachable reordering of the execution passes through it. This reachable-state semantics is exactly what checkpoint/restore needs: restore reinstalls a state the system could have reached.

#### 3.3 Channel state and in-flight messages

**Source:** Chandy-Lamport 1985 paper; IISc distributed-systems slides on Chandy-Lamport. https://cds.iisc.ac.in/wp-content/uploads/DS256.2018.L4.Global.Snapshot.pdf ; decomposition.al worked example. https://decomposition.al/blog/2019/04/26/an-example-run-of-the-chandy-lamport-snapshot-algorithm

The state of channel `c = (p, q)` recorded at process `q` is `M(c) = sent(c, t_p) − received(c, t_q)`: messages sent on `c` up to `p`'s snapshot time, minus messages received on `c` up to `q`'s snapshot time — equivalently, the messages recorded on `c` between `q`'s local-state save and `q`'s receipt of the marker on `c` (empty if the marker arrived before any post-save message). These are exactly the messages in flight across the cut. The crate records channel state incrementally per channel: a per-channel recording buffer started at local-state save and closed at marker receipt (first marker → empty; subsequent marker → buffer contents).

#### 3.4 Stable property detection

**Source:** Chandy-Lamport 1985 (stable properties: "computation has terminated", "the system is deadlocked", "all tokens in a token ring have disappeared"); Springer, "Efficient detection of a class of stable properties". https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/bf02280830 ; JPdc 2006, "Efficient detection of a locally stable predicate in a distributed system". https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jpdc.2006.12.004

A stable property is a predicate that, once true, remains true forever. Detection: repeatedly take consistent snapshots and test the predicate over the collected local + channel states; once the property holds, every later snapshot also satisfies it, so repeated snapshots eventually detect it. Examples: computation termination, deadlock, quiescence, token disappearance. The crate exposes `StableProperty` evaluation (predicate over `GlobalSnapshot`) plus a re-snapshot scheduler; it does not decide which properties to track — that is configured by the consumer crate. Locally stable predicates can in principle be detected with weaker assumptions than full Chandy-Lamport (no control messages, possibly-inconsistent snapshots) — noted as a research alternative, not the default.

#### 3.5 Checkpoint/restore foundation

**Source:** Chandy-Lamport 1985 ("Global state detection can also be used for checkpointing"); etcd snapshot/restore docs. https://github.com/etcd-io/etcd/blob/v3.4.14/Documentation/op-guide/recovery.md ; Open MPI interconnect-agnostic checkpoint/restart (ACM DL 1551609.1551619). https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1551609.1551619 ; arxiv 2510.06404, "Asynchronous Checkpoint for Eventually Consistent Databases" (DTCS/MuFASA, overhead of traditional snapshots). https://arxiv.org/html/2510.06404v2

Checkpoint/restore built on consistent global state: save `GlobalSnapshot` (all local states + all channel states) plus a snapshot identifier to durable storage; restore reinstalls every process's state and every channel's in-flight messages, then resumes execution from that consistent cut. Because the cut is consistent, no restored receive lacks its send — restored execution is causally sound. The crate defines the save/restore contract (serialized snapshot envelope, checksum, restore validation) but not the storage backend (bytes only, shipped via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; durable-store crate TBD — see Section 10).

#### 3.6 Flink-style barrier snapshotting integration

**Source:** Apache Flink docs, "Fault Tolerance via State Snapshots" (asynchronous barrier snapshotting). https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-1.11/learn-flink/fault_tolerance.html ; Flink docs, "Checkpointing" (aligned vs unaligned checkpoints, exactly-once vs at-least-once). https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-master/docs/dev/datastream/fault-tolerance/checkpointing ; Flink docs, "Savepoints". https://nightlies.apache.org/flink/flink-docs-release-1.5/ops/state/savepoints.html ; Flink blog, "From Aligned to Unaligned Checkpoints – Part 1". https://flink.apache.org/2020/10/15/from-aligned-to-unaligned-checkpoints-part-1-checkpoints-alignment-and-backpressure

Flink uses a Chandy-Lamport variant called asynchronous barrier snapshotting (ABS): the checkpoint coordinator injects numbered checkpoint barriers at sources; barriers flow through the operator graph with the data stream and mark the before/after parts of each stream for a checkpoint. On receiving a barrier: aligned mode buffers each input until barriers from all inputs arrive (barrier alignment), then snapshots state; unaligned mode stores in-flight data into the operator state so the barrier proceeds immediately, trading checkpoint state size for latency under backpressure (Flink 1.11+). Exactly-once guarantees require replayable sources and transactional/idempotent sinks (e.g., two-phase commit with Kafka: pre-commit at checkpoint start, commit at completion). Checkpoints are automatic recovery snapshots (can be incremental); savepoints are user-triggered for operational redeploy/upgrade/rescaling and are always complete.

The crate's barrier adapter mirrors ABS: `BarrierId` numbered barriers injected at entry points, per-operator barrier alignment state, aligned/unaligned modes selectable per checkpoint, `CheckpointRef` + durable envelope, and an exactly-once restore contract (rewind inputs to barrier position, replay from sources). The IDS stack has no streaming job graph yet, so the barrier adapter is specified as a pluggable layer with operator boundaries supplied by consumer crates — see Section 10.

#### 3.7 Algorithm variants and relaxations

**Source:** McGill snapshot-algorithm notes (no-control-message, non-FIFO algorithm). https://cs.mcgill.ca/~carl/distsnaply.pdf ; IEEE, "Fast and Message-Efficient Global Snapshot Algorithms for Large-Scale Distributed Systems" (Chandy-Lamport O(n²) control messages; survey of variants). https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/5401156 ; PODC '90 StableSnap self-stabilizing iterated snapshot. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/93385.93405 ; Retroscope HLC-based consistent cuts (cut consistent iff vector-clock condition K(i) = V_i(i) ∀i). https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8693529 ; arxiv 2008.11837 crash-tolerant atomic snapshot via lattice agreement. https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.11837v1

Variants researched (documented, not default): Mattern — non-FIFO channels with explicitly colored messages; Lai-Yang — non-FIFO channels with sent/received-set exchange (higher overhead); Spezialetti-Kearns — concurrent snapshot initiation optimizations; causal-order snapshot algorithms using existing causal-delivery metadata with no extra control messages; Retroscope-style hybrid-logical-clock consistent cuts for retrospective snapshots; crash-tolerant atomic snapshots via lattice agreement. The IDS crate defaults to Chandy-Lamport over assumed-FIFO carrier channels; variant selection is a deployment decision captured in Section 10.

#### 3.8 Lattice theory of consistent cuts (stable detection support)

**Source:** Garg et al., lattice-theoretic monitoring of distributed computations (consistent cuts form a distributive lattice; order ideals = consistent global states). https://users.ece.utexas.edu/~garg/dist/rv14-slides.pdf ; formal consistent-cut definition and predicate detection. https://cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs5414/2010fa/publications/BM93.pdf

The set of all consistent cuts of a computation forms a distributive lattice under set inclusion; each consistent global state is an order ideal of the happens-before poset. Predicate detection over this lattice underpins stable property detection (repeated snapshots sample cuts of the lattice). StableSnap-style self-stabilizing iteration (round numbers, prod messages, repeated snapshots from process 0) is the reference pattern for repeated snapshot detection. The crate exposes a `CutLattice` interface (cut validity, join/meet of consistent cuts) consumed by the stable property detector.

#### 3.9 Carrier-agnostic transport mapping

**Source:** IDS plan format references (plan-060.md, plan-048.md) — carrier-agnostic absolute rule from prompts.txt entry 1; Flink barrier flow as logical streams (no IP assumptions in the algorithm itself).

All snapshot traffic is mapped onto `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`): each logical channel between two nodes is an ordered datagram stream over an `Endpoint` pair; markers are a distinct datagram type framed inside the opaque payload; snapshots and checkpoints are serialized envelopes sent as datagrams. The crate depends on `ids-carrier` only for `Endpoint` and the `Carrier` trait (`send_datagram`/`receive_datagram`); it never constructs addresses, never touches `std::net`/`tokio::net`, and assumes nothing about the underlying carrier (loopback, serial, optical, radio, custom). FIFO per channel is assumed for the base algorithm (consistent-cut guarantee); non-FIFO carrier behavior falls back to the variant algorithms of Section 3.7.

#### 3.10 Allowed crypto usage

**Source:** RFC 8032 (Ed25519) / ed25519-dalek docs.rs; RFC 7539 / chacha20poly1305 docs.rs (ChaCha20-Poly1305 + XChaCha20-Poly1305); NIST FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256) / sha2 RustCrypto docs; BLAKE3-team README (BLAKE3-256, SIMD, keyed hash, KDF, XOF).

Allowed set only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305. In `ids-chandy-lamport`: ed25519 signs snapshot envelopes and audit checkpoints (proof that a recorded cut was taken at a given barrier); sha256 and blake3 digest channel states and snapshot IDs and chain audit entries; xchacha20poly1305 (random 192-bit nonces) and chacha20poly1305 (12-byte nonces, bounded use) encrypt snapshot state at rest when confidentiality is required. Crypto operations are implemented in `ids-crypto`; this crate consumes primitive IDs and envelope types from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` and performs no raw cryptography itself.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Marker lost, duplicated, or delayed by carrier | Snapshot consistency / termination | First-marker gate makes duplicate markers harmless; markers carry per-snapshot sequence ids; termination waits for markers on all inbound channels with bounded timeouts; carrier-agnostic boundary means no network stack in trust base |
| Non-FIFO carrier channel | Consistent-cut guarantee | Base algorithm assumes FIFO per Endpoint channel (documented assumption); if violated, use colored-message (Mattern) or sent/received-set (Lai-Yang) variants from Section 3.7 |
| Recorded global state never actually occurred | Restore correctness | Documented reachable-state semantics: some execution reordering passes through the cut; restore is causally sound |
| Stable property not detected promptly (false negative) | Detection soundness | Repeated snapshots over the lattice of consistent cuts; once a stable property holds, all later cuts satisfy it |
| Restore resurrects stale or causally incomplete state | Recovery correctness | Consistent-cut closure (every receive's send is present); Flink-style barrier completion + rewind; exactly-once contract needs replayable sources and idempotent sinks (consumer crates) |
| Barrier alignment blocked by backpressure | Checkpoint latency | Unaligned mode: buffer in-flight data in operator state (Flink 1.11+ pattern) so checkpoints proceed under backpressure |
| Snapshot/checkpoint envelope tampering | Snapshot authenticity | ed25519-signed envelopes and audit checkpoints; sha256/blake3 hash chain over audit entries; offline verifiable |
| Snapshot state read at rest | Confidentiality | xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 encryption of snapshot state at rest; keys never leave the node |
| Checkpoint/restore replay attacks | Replay integrity | Nonce-bound barrier ids; bounded replay cache; monotonic `IdsTime` (never wall-clock) for timestamps |
| Carrier re-framing or reordering datagrams | Ordering/duplication | Idempotent marker and message recording; duplicate messages tolerated by channel-state reconstruction |
| Snapshot initiation storm (many concurrent snapshots) | Resource exhaustion | Snapshot IDs namespace; concurrent snapshots allowed (per Chandy-Lamport) but rate-limitable via config |

The carrier is never trusted: snapshot decisions and audit entries are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **Marker protocol**: initiator records local state then sends a marker on each outbound channel before any further message on that channel; first-marker rule at a process (record state, channel empty, propagate markers, record other inbound channels); subsequent-marker rule (channel state = recorded messages since state save; stop recording).
- **ChannelState**: incremental per-channel buffer of messages received between local-state save and marker receipt; equals in-flight messages at the cut (`sent up to sender's save − received up to receiver's save`).
- **LocalState**: application state snapshot hook (serialized via serde; consumer defines what state is captured).
- **GlobalSnapshot**: `{local_state(p) ∀p} ∪ {channel_state(c) ∀c}`; a consistent cut under FIFO; reachable state (not necessarily an actually-occurred instant).
- **Consistent cut**: left-closed under happens-before (`e ∈ cut ∧ f → e ⇒ f ∈ cut`); validator checks every cross-cut channel arrow crosses forward.
- **Cut lattice**: order ideals of the happens-before poset; join/meet of consistent cuts for stable detection support.
- **Stable property**: predicate over `GlobalSnapshot` that stays true once true; examples termination, deadlock, quiescence; detected via repeated snapshots.
- **Barrier (Flink ABS)**: numbered `BarrierId` injected at entry points, flows with data; aligned mode waits for barriers from all inputs; unaligned mode buffers in-flight data in state; checkpoint completes when all operators ack or is discarded.
- **Checkpoint/restore**: save `GlobalSnapshot` + `BarrierId` as signed envelope; restore reinstalls all states and channel messages, rewinds input positions to the barrier, resumes; exactly-once needs replayable sources + idempotent/transactional sinks.
- **Audit**: each snapshot/barrier/checkpoint decision = sha256/blake3-chained entry + ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.
- **Crypto**: ed25519 signatures on envelopes/checkpoints; sha256/blake3 digests and snapshot IDs; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 at-rest encryption of snapshot state.

### 8. Dependencies

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts; master crate, consumed only.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait (`send_datagram`/`receive_datagram`); transport boundary only; crate never sends bytes itself.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `serde` — serialization of marker/snapshot/checkpoint envelopes and audit entries.
- `thiserror` — unified `SnapshotError` contract.
No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. `ids-crypto` does not depend on `ids-000-aa` to avoid a circular dependency (pattern established in plan-048).

---

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

1. Marker initiation: any node may initiate; initiator records local state, then sends a marker on each outbound channel before any further message on that channel.
2. First-marker rule: on first marker, record local state, mark inbound channel empty, propagate markers on all outbound channels, record all other inbound channels.
3. Subsequent-marker rule: channel state = messages recorded since local state save; recording stops on that channel.
4. Termination: snapshot complete iff every node has received a marker on every inbound channel.
5. Consistent cut: 100% of recorded cuts satisfy happens-before left-closure (if a receive is in the cut, the matching send is in the cut) — under the FIFO channel assumption.
6. Channel state correctness: recorded channel state equals in-flight messages at the cut (`sent(c, t_p) − received(c, t_q)`).
7. Stable property detection: termination/deadlock/quiescence predicates evaluated on recorded `GlobalSnapshot`; repeated snapshots eventually detect any stable property that becomes true.
8. Barrier snapshotting: numbered barriers flow end-to-end; aligned mode blocks until all-input barriers arrive; unaligned mode stores in-flight data; checkpoints complete or are discarded cleanly.
9. Checkpoint/restore: `GlobalSnapshot` saved as signed envelope via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` opaque datagrams; restore reinstates snapshot state and rewinds inputs to barrier position; exactly-once restore with replayable sources/idempotent sinks.
10. Carrier-agnostic: zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh; all traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 B).
11. Crypto allowlist: only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 in the crate's crypto surface; snapshot envelopes and audit checkpoints ed25519-signed.
12. Audit: every snapshot/barrier/checkpoint decision recorded in an append-only, sha256/blake3 hash-chained, ed25519-signed audit log with `NodeId` + `IdsTime`; offline verifiable.

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **FIFO channel assumption over `ids-carrier`:** the base Chandy-Lamport guarantee requires FIFO per channel; IDS datagram channels over `Endpoint` may not guarantee FIFO — confirm or adopt colored-message (Mattern) / sent-received-set (Lai-Yang) variants (Section 3.7).
- **Marker framing:** whether markers travel as a distinct datagram type or are piggybacked on application traffic; affects `ids-carrier` framing contract (TBD with `ids-carrier` Phase 002).
- **Snapshot storage backend:** durable store for `GlobalSnapshot` envelopes is out of scope here (bytes only via `ids-carrier`); backend crate TBD at integration with `ids-checkpoint`/`ids-restore`.
- **Multi-initiator coexistence:** original algorithm permits any number of concurrent initiators; interaction with barrier checkpoints (single coordinator) needs definition.
- **Termination timeouts:** bounded wait values for marker completion under carrier delay — deployment-tuned, validated at integration.
- **Flink job graph mapping:** IDS has no streaming job graph/operator model yet; barrier adapter boundaries supplied by consumer crates — design decision pending.
- **Exactly-once sink contract:** transactional/idempotent sink requirements for restore to be defined by downstream crates (ids-store/ids-query).
- **Snapshot granularity:** full state vs incremental checkpoints (Flink incremental checkpoints) — sizing and delta strategy TBD.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-chandy-lamport` (not a folder inside an existing crate) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear recording-layer boundary |
| Chandy-Lamport base algorithm (FIFO, no failures) as default | Original 1985 algorithm; simple, proven consistent-cut guarantee; well-documented assumptions |
| Non-FIFO variants (Mattern coloring, Lai-Yang) documented, not default | Carrier FIFO behavior unconfirmed; variants kept as research alternatives for integration |
| Flink-style barrier snapshotting as separate barrier submodule | Numbered barriers, aligned/unaligned modes, exactly-once restore; operator boundaries pluggable since IDS has no job graph yet |
| Recorded state = consistent cut / reachable state, not necessarily an actually-occurred instant | Matches Chandy-Lamport semantics; sufficient and sound for checkpoint/restore |
| Stable property detection via repeated snapshots + predicate evaluation over the cut lattice | Stable properties persist once true; repeated sampling eventually detects them |
| Marker as first-class control datagram via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Keeps snapshot traffic distinguishable; FIFO per Endpoint channel assumed |
| Crypto: ed25519 signatures (envelopes/checkpoints), sha256/blake3 digests, xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 at-rest encryption | Complies with allowed-crypto rule; crypto implemented in `ids-crypto`, type surface from `ids-000-aa` |
| `ids-000-aa` types only; no redefinition of canonical types | Single canonical definition per type; downstream crates import `ids_000_aa::X` |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence for snapshots |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 075 creates `ids-swim`, the IDS crate for scalable weak-membership failure detection. It implements the SWIM protocol (Das, Gupta, Motivala, Cornell, IEEE SRDS 2002/2004): a membership service built from two separated components — a **failure detector** (peer-to-peer periodic randomized probing via ping/ping-ack, with indirect probing through k other nodes when a direct ping fails) and a **dissemination component** (infection-style gossip that piggybacks membership updates — joins, voluntary leaves, failures — on the ping/ack datagrams). Suspicion is used before declaring failure (a suspected node is gossiped as suspicious; an `alive` multicast clears the suspicion label), which keeps the false-positive rate low while guaranteeing eventual detection of every crash. Expected detection time and per-member message load are independent of group size, which is what lets SWIM scale to thousands of nodes where all-to-all heartbeating fails quadratically.

`ids-swim` is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule). It is a policy/state-machine crate: it maintains the local membership list (`NodeId` → state + incarnation + last-heard timestamp), runs probe rounds, decides suspicion/failure transitions, and emits membership-update envelopes. It never opens a socket or addresses IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS; every outbound message is an opaque `Vec<u8>` datagram handed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 bytes), and every inbound message arrives from the carrier boundary. Allowed crypto only: ed25519 (signed failure/suspicion announcements and audit checkpoints), sha256 and blake3 (membership-list digests, anti-entropy reconciliation, audit-chain links), xchacha20poly1305 and chacha20poly1305 (membership state encrypted at rest where confidentiality is required). Crypto operations live in `ids-crypto`; `ids-swim` consumes only the type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto`. `ids-000-aa` remains the master crate holding canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, `Error`, …) and sealed trait contracts; `ids-swim` imports them and never redefines them.

A skeleton `ids-swim` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-swim/`. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned the original SWIM paper (cs.cornell.edu/projects/Quicksilver/public_pdfs/SWIM.pdf — randomized probing, ping/ping-ack, indirect probes via k nodes, suspicion, infection-style dissemination, round-robin probe targets, detection time independent of group size), the IEEE SRDS record (ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1028914), the Wikipedia SWIM Protocol summary (ping every T′, suspect→fail after T′, strong completeness, detection time T′/(1−e^{−qf})), Lifeguard (arxiv.org/html/1707.00788v2 — local health awareness, more accurate failure detection over gossip), HashiCorp Consul memberlist/serf gossip internals (hashicorp.com, github.com/hashicorp/serf), SWIM vs Phi accrual comparison (systemoverflow.com), Illinois CS425 SWIM lecture notes (courses.grainger.illinois.edu), dkmccandless "SWIM for Implementers" (probe-round pseudocode), Apple swift-cluster-membership SWIM (github.com/apple/swift-cluster-membership), Tarantool swim module (tarantool.io), brianstorti.com SWIM explainer, prakhar.me SWIM article, builddistributedsystem.com SWIM detector task, Mochi SWIM backend (mochi.readthedocs.io), Vanlightly TLA+ SWIM model, medium.com Rust SWIM build.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-swim` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types, sealed contracts, invariants, errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a failure-detection and membership-dissemination state machine: it runs periodic probe rounds, sends pings, handles ping-acks, escalates to indirect probes (ping-req via k other nodes), transitions members through ALIVE → SUSPECT → FAILED → LEFT, gossips membership changes (piggybacked on pings/acks), and returns signed audit entries. It never sends bytes itself — it produces datagram envelopes and `AckDecision`/`FailureVerdict` objects that the caller frames into `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                 MEMBERSHIP CONSUMERS (ids-*, application layer)               │
│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-placement — read local membership list      │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 075: ids-swim (THIS CRATE — policy/state)           │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ membership      │ │ probe scheduler │ │ ping engine     │ │ suspicion│   │
│  │ list (NodeId →  │ │ (random +       │ │ (ping, ping-ack,  │ │ state    │   │
│  │  state+incarn)  │ │  round-robin)   │ │  indirect probe)  │ │ machine  │   │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ failure         │ │ dissemination   │ │ carrier adapter │ │ crypto   │   │
│  │ confirmation    │ │ (piggyback on   │ │ (opaque Vec<u8> │ │ surface  │   │
│  │ (k-node indirect││  pings/acks)      ││  to Endpoint)     ││ (allowed │   │
││  verify)          │ │                 │ │                   ││  set)    │   │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘   │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                                           │ opaque Vec<u8> datagram envelopes
                                           ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                    │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])│
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                      │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
│  / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh anywhere in ids-swim            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of one probe round:**
1. `probe_scheduler` picks a target: random selection (SWIM default) or round-robin (bounds worst-case detection time); every protocol period T′ each node pings one other member of its list.
2. `ping_engine` builds a ping envelope: opaque `Vec<u8>` containing probe id, sender `NodeId`, incarnation, and piggybacked membership updates (joins/leaves/failures/suspicions pending dissemination). Handler sends it via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.
3. Target replies `ping-ack` (opaque datagram back to sender's endpoint). On ack: target marked ALIVE, "last heard from" refreshed.
4. On no response: `indirect_probe` contacts k other list members (ping-req: "ping this suspect for me"); each replies ping-ack or confirms silence.
5. After T′ with no successful response (direct or indirect): `suspicion` state machine moves target ALIVE → SUSPECT; suspicion is gossiped to all members. If target responds before suspicion timeout, an `alive` update is gossiped and the suspicion label is cleared.
6. If still unresponsive after SUSPECT → FAILED transition: `failure_confirmation` marks target FAILED; the failure is disseminated infection-style to the whole group via subsequent pings/acks.
7. `crypto_surface`: ed25519 signs failure/suspicion announcements and periodic audit checkpoints; sha256/blake3 hash membership-list digests for anti-entropy reconciliation; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 encrypt sensitive membership state at rest.

**SWIM semantics (research-verified):**
- Strong completeness: every crash is eventually detected by all live nodes.
- Expected detection time ≈ T′ / (1 − e^{−qf}) where qf is the fraction of non-faulty nodes — detection time and per-member message load do not grow with group size.
- Weak consistency: membership lists at different nodes need not be identical at the same instant; convergence via gossip.
- No central server: fully peer-to-peer, no single point of failure or bottleneck.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline; full list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 SWIM paper: randomized probing instead of all-to-all heartbeating
**Source:** SWIM paper, Das/Gupta/Motivala, Cornell (cs.cornell.edu/projects/Quicksilver/public_pdfs/SWIM.pdf); IEEE SRDS 2002/2004 (ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/1028914).

Traditional heartbeating does not scale: heartbeats to a central server create a hot spot; heartbeats to all members (multicast or gossip) impose message load quadratic in group size; ring heartbeating has unpredictable detection time under multiple failures. SWIM's design insight: fuse nothing — separate **failure detection** (efficient non-multicast randomized probing) from **membership-update dissemination** (used only when a change occurs). Every T′ time units, each node pings one random other node from its membership list. Mathematical analysis shows expected failure-detection time, false-positive rate, and per-member message load are all independent of group size — enabling thousands of nodes. `ids-swim` adopts this separation as its core architecture: probe rounds run continuously; dissemination runs only on membership changes, piggybacked on probe traffic.

#### 3.2 Ping / ping-ack exchange
**Source:** Wikipedia "SWIM Protocol"; SWIM paper; dkmccandless "SWIM for Implementers" (dkmccandless.github.io/2022/06/27/swim-for-implementers.html).

Node N1 picks target N2 and sends a ping. If N2 replies with ping-ack, N2 is healthy: N1 updates N2's "last heard from" timestamp to now. If no reply within T′, N1 escalates to indirect probing (Section 3.4). The ping envelope carries: probe id, sender NodeId, sender incarnation, target NodeId, and piggybacked membership deltas. `ids-swim` frames ping/ping-ack as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams addressed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets; the carrier is never consulted about addresses.

#### 3.3 Ping-ack datagram framing (carrier-agnostic)
All traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 bytes). `ids-swim` defines only the envelope payload layout (probe id, sender/target NodeId, incarnation, state, membership delta, optional ed25519 signature, optional AEAD nonce+tag). No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, `SocketAddr`, `IpAddr`, `TcpStream`, `UdpSocket`, or any transport concept appears in the crate. The carrier adapter converts `ids-swim` envelopes to/from `Endpoint` datagrams; routing and delivery are the carrier's responsibility.

#### 3.4 Indirect probing (ping-req via k other nodes)
**Source:** SWIM paper; Wikipedia; Lifeguard (arxiv.org/html/1707.00788v2); Mochi SWIM backend (mochi.readthedocs.io/en/latest/flock/09_backends_swim.html).

When N1's direct ping to N2 gets no response, N1 contacts k other members {N3…N3+k} and asks each to ping N2 on its behalf. If any indirect probe succeeds, N2 is alive (the initial failure was likely packet loss). If none succeed within T′, N1 suspects N2. Indirect probing amortizes the cost of lost packets: one suspected node triggers k probes but those k probes are normal pings to other members, so total load stays bounded and independent of group size. `ids-swim` makes k and the indirect-probe timeout configurable per deployment.

#### 3.5 Suspicion mechanism (suspect before declaring failed)
**Source:** SWIM paper ("suspect a process before declaring it as failed — allows the system to discover and rectify false failure detections"); Wikipedia extensions (suspicion + alive multicast); Lifeguard.

Unresponsive nodes are not immediately marked FAILED: they enter SUSPECT, and the suspicion is gossiped to all members (piggybacked on pings/acks). If the suspected node responds to a subsequent ping before the suspicion timeout, an `alive` announcement is gossiped and the suspicion label is cleared — false positives self-heal without coordinator intervention. Suspicion also limits the blast radius of a mistaken failure declaration: a suspected-but-alive node is treated with degraded trust rather than evicted immediately. `ids-swim` implements a three-valued suspicion outcome per probe: `clear` (responded), `sustain` (still silent), `escalate` (timeout → FAILED).

#### 3.6 Failure confirmation and dissemination
**Source:** SWIM paper; HashiCorp Consul memberlist/serf gossip internals (github.com/hashicorp/serf; hashicorp.com "Everybody Talks: Gossip, Serf, memberlist, Raft, and SWIM in Consul"); builddistributedsystem.com SWIM detector task.

Once N2 is FAILED, N1 multicasts (infection-style, piggybacked) the failure to the whole group; every member that learns of the failure re-gossips it, so the failure spreads epidemically until all live members know. Voluntary joins/leaves are disseminated the same way. Failure confirmation requires either direct evidence (N1's indirect probes all failed) or corroborating gossip from another member (another member reports N2 FAILED — N1 can adopt the report subject to incarnation checks, Section 3.9). `ids-swim` records each state transition (ALIVE→SUSPECT→FAILED→LEFT) in its local membership list with an incarnation number and timestamp.

#### 3.7 Infection-style dissemination and round-robin probe targets
**Source:** SWIM paper (infection-style/epidemic/gossip dissemination piggybacked on pings and acks; round-robin probe target selection bounds worst-case detection time without degrading average); Wikipedia extensions.

Instead of a separate multicast for every membership change, updates are piggybacked on ping/ping-ack datagrams — dissemination rides the probe traffic that already exists, adding near-zero marginal load. Optionally, probe targets are chosen round-robin across the list rather than at random, which gives a deterministic upper bound on detection time (every member is probed within a bounded number of rounds) while keeping the average detection time unchanged. `ids-swim` supports both target-selection policies as a configurable switch; random is the SWIM default, round-robin is offered for bounded-latency deployments.

#### 3.8 Scalability to thousands of nodes
**Source:** SWIM paper abstract ("Both the expected time to first detection of each process failure, and the expected message load per member, do not vary with group size"); Wikipedia detection-time formula T′/(1−e^{−qf}); Lifeguard; Illinois CS425 SWIM lecture notes (courses.grainger.illinois.edu/CS425/fa2020/L6.FA20.pdf).

All-to-all heartbeating: message load per member grows O(N) and detection time or false-positive rate grows with N. SWIM: each member sends one ping per period T′ to one target → O(1) load per member per period, O(N) total network load but O(1) per node; indirect probing adds at most k extra pings per suspicion, still O(1) per node per period. Expected detection time is independent of N (depends on T′ and fault fraction qf, not group size). `ids-swim` is designed for thousands of nodes: bounded per-node state (membership list of known members), O(1) messages per probe round per node, gossip convergence of membership changes in O(log N) rounds.

#### 3.9 Member states, incarnation numbers, and stale-entry suppression
**Source:** SWIM paper; Tarantool swim module (tarantool.io/docs/reference_lua_swim); Apple swift-cluster-membership (github.com/apple/swift-cluster-membership/Sources/SWIM/SWIMInstance.swift); Lifeguard member states (joined/failed/suspect/left).

Each list entry: `{NodeId, state ∈ {ALIVE, SUSPECT, FAILED, LEFT}, incarnation: u64, last_heard: IdsTime, address: Endpoint}`. Incarnation (generation counter) increments on every state change; gossip carries the incarnation so members ignore stale reports (a late SUSPECT with an older incarnation than a known ALIVE entry is discarded). LEFT is set when a node voluntarily departs (gossiped leave). Rejoining after FAILED/LEFT requires a higher incarnation and re-introduction via gossip; `ids-swim` validates incarnation monotonicity before applying any remote update — this is how the crate prevents replayed or forged membership changes from resurrecting dead nodes or killing live ones. Crypto binding: failure/suspicion announcements are ed25519-signed by the reporting node so recipients can verify the reporter (Section 3.14).

#### 3.10 Anti-entropy reconciliation and membership-list digests
**Source:** Lifeguard (arxiv.org/html/1707.00788v2 — gossip robustness); SWIM paper anti-entropy component (tarantool swim anti-entropy patch discussion); systemoverflow anti-entropy digests/gossip reconciliation.

Periodically (anti-entropy interval), members exchange compact digests of their membership lists (sha256/blake3 hashes of `(NodeId, state, incarnation)` entries) instead of full lists. Mismatched digests trigger reconciliation: members exchange the differing entries and converge. Anti-entropy heals divergence caused by lost datagrams, partitioned suspicion gossip, or clock skew in last-heard timestamps. Digest size is O(number of members) but compressed via hashing; reconciliation transfers only deltas. `ids-swim` defines the digest format and reconciliation policy; transport is via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams.

#### 3.11 Detection time, false positives, and configuration knobs
**Source:** Wikipedia SWIM detection-time formula T′/(1−e^{−qf}); SWIM paper experimental results (stable detection time, stable false-positive rate, low per-member load); Lifeguard false-positive reduction.

Configurable knobs exposed by `ids-swim` (all plan-level, no values hard-coded as product decisions): protocol period T′, indirect-probe fanout k, suspicion timeout, ping timeout, anti-entropy interval, target-selection policy (random/round-robin). Trade-offs: smaller T′ → faster detection, more load; larger k → fewer false positives, more indirect-probe load; longer suspicion timeout → fewer false positives, slower detection. `ids-swim` documents the trade-off surface; concrete defaults are set at integration with `ids-membership`/deployment.

#### 3.12 SWIM vs Phi accrual failure detector (related work — Phase 076)
**Source:** systemoverflow "SWIM and Phi Accrual: Two Approaches to Failure Detection Over Gossip"; arxiv.org/html/2603.03736 (failure detector taxonomy).

SWIM is a binary-ish detector (ALIVE/SUSPECT/FAILED) driven by probe timeouts and suspicion. Phi accrual (Phase 076, `ids-phi-accrual`) outputs a continuous suspicion level φ from inter-arrival time distributions with adaptive thresholds. They are complementary: `ids-swim` provides membership + failure detection; `ids-phi-accrual` provides adaptive suspicion thresholds that can feed `ids-swim`'s suspicion escalation decision. `ids-swim` does not implement phi accrual; its suspicion/timeout knobs are static per deployment until Phase 076 integration is defined. This plan records the integration point (uncertainty in Section 10).

#### 3.13 Reference implementations
**Source:** HashiCorp memberlist (github.com/hashicorp/memberlist), serf gossip internals (github.com/hashicorp/serf/docs/internals/gossip.html.markdown), Consul (hashicorp.com "Everybody Talks…"); Mochi SWIM backend (mochi.readthedocs.io); Tarantool swim module; Apple swift-cluster-membership SWIM; brianstorti.com and prakhar.me explainers; builddistributedsystem.com SWIM detector task; medium.com "Building a SWIM Gossip Membership Protocol from Scratch in Rust"; Vanlightly TLA+ formal model of SWIM.

These confirm the production shape of SWIM: ping/ping-ack, indirect probes, suspicion, piggybacked dissemination, incarnation lists, gossip-based convergence, and memberlist-style SWIM running over unreliable datagrams. `ids-swim` adopts the same datagram-centric shape, adapted to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` instead of UDP sockets. memberlist/serf's security documentation (github.com/hashicorp/memberlist/SECURITY.md) notes gossip membership is unauthenticated by default — `ids-swim` closes that gap with ed25519-signed announcements (IDS allowed crypto only).

#### 3.14 Allowed crypto surface only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)
**Source:** RFC 8032 Ed25519; RFC 7539/RFC 8439 ChaCha20-Poly1305; libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305; NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256; BLAKE3 specification; ed25519-dalek/chacha20poly1305/sha2/blake3 Rust crate docs.

`ids-swim` crypto usage (all via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`; `ids-swim` implements no crypto itself):
- ed25519: sign failure/suspicion announcements and audit checkpoints (proves which node reported a failure; prevents forged failure reports).
- sha256: membership-list digest entries, audit-chain links.
- blake3: fast membership-list digest hashing for anti-entropy, preferred for speed/parallelism.
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypt membership state at rest (24-byte nonce, random nonces safe).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypt session/state payloads (12-byte nonce, counter-based bounded use).
No other algorithm may enter the crate; a compile-time allowlist test asserts this (Section 9).

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|---|---|---|
| Forged failure report (node claims another failed) | Membership correctness | ed25519-signed failure/suspicion announcements; recipients verify signer; unsigned reports dropped |
| Replayed suspicion/failure gossip resurrects/kills nodes | Membership integrity | Incarnation numbers per entry; remote update applied only if incarnation > stored; replay cache per sender |
| Suspicion spam (constant re-suspecting) | Control-plane load | Suspicion state machine (ALIVE→SUSPECT→FAILED→LEFT monotonic); suspicion gossip dedup; per-sender rate budget |
| Lost ping mistaken for failure | False positives | Indirect probing via k nodes; suspicion-before-failure; `alive` multicast clears suspicion |
| Partition splits membership views | Availability vs consistency | Weak consistency by design; lists converge after partition heals via gossip + anti-entropy digests |
| Carrier delays/duplicates/reorders datagrams | Ordering/replay | Idempotent state-machine transitions; incarnation checks tolerate duplicates; no carrier in trust base |
| Clock manipulation skews last-heard / suspicion | Causality correctness | Logical timestamps from `ids-time` (monotonic ticks); never wall-clock for suspicion decisions |
| Key extraction (announcement signing key) | Decision authenticity | Signing keys never leave node; encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Prohibited crate sneaks into dependency tree | Carrier-agnostic rule | CI dependency audit (`cargo tree`): no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS crate |

The carrier is never trusted: announcements and audit entries are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) keeps the network stack out of the trust base.

| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-swim |
|---|---|---|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types, sealed trait contracts, invariants, errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; sealed contracts mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All ids-swim traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns envelopes, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signed announcements, digests, encrypted state at rest |

| `ids-identity` (Phase 004) | `StableNodeId`/`RotatingNodeId` on `NodeId` | Node identities in membership list; rotation handled via incarnation bump |
| `ids-phi-accrual` (Phase 076) | Phi accrual suspicion with adaptive thresholds | Optional input to ids-swim suspicion escalation (integration point TBD) |
| `ids-membership` (future) | Group membership service built on failure detection | Consumes ids-swim's failure detector output as its membership source |
| `ids-fault` / `ids-backpressure` | Failure handling, bounded recovery bandwidth | Failure verdicts from ids-swim feed fault handling |

**Integration points:** ids-swim evaluates suspicion/failure and returns `FailureVerdict`/`MembershipDelta`; the caller frames envelopes into `ids-carrier::Endpoint` datagrams. ids-swim never reaches into dependent-crate internals and never addresses a transport by name.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Membership list** — `HashMap<NodeId, MemberEntry>` where `MemberEntry { state: ALIVE\|SUSPECT\|FAILED\|LEFT, incarnation: u64, last_heard: IdsTime, endpoint: Endpoint }`. One canonical definition; consumers read via `ids-swim` query API.
2. **Probe round (every T′)** — pick target (random from list, or round-robin for bounded worst-case); build ping envelope (probe id, sender NodeId + incarnation, target NodeId, piggybacked deltas); send via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.
3. **Ping / ping-ack** — on ping-ack: `entry.state = ALIVE; entry.last_heard = now`. On silence: escalate to indirect probe (Section 4).
4. **Indirect probe (ping-req)** — on direct-ping failure, contact k other members asking each to ping the suspect; collect ping-acks or silence; any success ⇒ suspect alive; all silent after T′ ⇒ sustain suspicion.
5. **Suspicion state machine** — `ALIVE → SUSPECT` (after T′ silence, direct + indirect) → `FAILED` (suspicion timeout, still silent or corroborated by gossip) → `LEFT` (voluntary leave gossip). SUSPECT is gossiped; `alive` multicast clears suspicion before timeout.
6. **Failure confirmation** — FAILED requires direct evidence (k indirect probes silent) OR corroborating gossip from another member with `incarnation > stored`. Failure announcement gossiped infection-style until convergence.
7. **Dissemination** — membership deltas (join/leave/fail/suspect/alive) piggybacked on ping/ping-ack; no separate multicast channel. O(log N) epidemic convergence.
8. **Anti-entropy digest** — sha256/blake3 hash of sorted `(NodeId, state, incarnation)` tuples; periodic exchange; mismatches trigger delta reconciliation.
9. **Incarnation monotonicity** — remote update applied iff `remote.incarnation > local.incarnation` for the same NodeId; equal/lower incarnations discarded (anti-replay, anti-stale-resurrection).
10. **Detection-time bound** — expected detection ≈ T′ / (1 − e^{−qf}); per-node load = 1 ping + piggyback per T′ (+ k indirect pings per suspicion) — O(1) per node, independent of group size.
11. **Signed announcement** — ed25519 signature over `{reporter: NodeId, target: NodeId, verdict, incarnation, timestamp}`; verifiable offline.
12. **Audit chain** — sha256/blake3-chained entries of every state transition; ed25519-signed checkpoint every N entries.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete knob values:** protocol period T′, indirect-probe fanout k, suspicion timeout, ping timeout, anti-entropy interval — deployment-tuned; no product-level defaults decided in this plan.
2. **Target-selection default:** random (SWIM default, simplest) vs round-robin (bounded worst-case detection); to be confirmed at `ids-membership` integration.
3. **Interaction with `ids-phi-accrual` (Phase 076):** whether phi suspicion feeds ids-swim's suspicion escalation, or runs alongside; integration point undefined.
4. **WAN extension:** SWIM paper discusses extensibility to WAN-wide scale; gossip period and failure-detection trade-offs over high-latency links unquantified.
5. **Leave handling:** voluntary LEFT gossip vs silent failure — graceful-leave protocol and leave confirmation details TBD.
6. **Membership list size at scale:** thousands of nodes × per-entry state is O(N) memory per node; sharding or region-scoped lists may be needed (deferred to later phases).
7. **Corroborating-gospel trust policy:** how many independent FAILED reports are required before adopting another member's verdict without direct evidence — unquantified.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Separate `ids-swim` crate (not a folder) | User directive: "separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones"; clear failure-detection boundary |
| Failure detection + dissemination separated | SWIM paper core insight; dissemination only on change, piggybacked on probe traffic |
| Ping/ping-ack + indirect probes via k nodes | SWIM paper mechanism; bounds false positives from packet loss |
| Suspicion before failure (SUSPECT state) + `alive` clear gossip | SWIM paper extension; false positives self-heal, no coordinator |
| Random probe targets (default) + optional round-robin | SWIM defaults; round-robin bounds worst-case detection time |
| Infection-style dissemination piggybacked on pings/acks | Zero marginal dissemination load; O(log N) convergence |
| Incarnation numbers + monotonicity checks | Anti-replay, anti-stale-resurrection, weak consistency convergence |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` opaque datagrams | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in ids-swim |
| Crypto only via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` | Allowed set: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 |
| ed25519-signed failure/suspicion announcements | memberlist/serf gossip is unauthenticated by default; IDs close the forgery gap |
| sha256/blake3 anti-entropy digests | Compact reconciliation of divergent membership lists |
| Monotonic `IdsTime` ticks only; no wall-clock for suspicion | Clock manipulation cannot break failure detection |
| Research only: plan document, no code, no source modifications | Per prompts.txt entry 75 |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 076 creates `ids-phi-accrual`, the IDS crate implementing phi (φ) accrual suspicion with adaptive thresholds. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by statistical-monitoring concern.

`ids-phi-accrual` implements the accrual failure detector described by Hayashibara et al. (2004), "The φ Accrual Failure Detector": instead of a binary alive/dead timeout, it outputs a continuous suspicion level φ on a logarithmic scale. φ is computed as `-log10(P_later)`, where P_later is the probability that a heartbeat would arrive at least as late as the current silence, given the historical distribution of heartbeat inter-arrival times. Each unit of φ represents another factor of ten in implausibility: φ=1 ≈ 10% chance of a transient delay, φ=8 ≈ 1-in-100-million. The crate never declares a node dead on its own — it publishes φ continuously, and consumers (membership, lease, replication paths) apply their own thresholds.

**Core design per crate:** each monitored peer gets an independent `PhiDetector` instance holding:
- a bounded sliding window (ring buffer) of recent inter-arrival intervals (default 1000 samples, matching Cassandra and Akka),
- running mean and standard deviation estimated via Welford's online algorithm or recomputed from the window,
- timestamp of the last received heartbeat,
- configurable `acceptable_heartbeat_pause` (margin to survive GC pauses / scheduling hiccups; Akka default 3 s),
- configurable `min_std_deviation` floor (prevents φ exploding to infinity on a perfectly steady sender),
- configurable `first_heartbeat_estimate` (bootstrap for cold start; Cassandra seeds with 2× heartbeat interval),
- configurable `phi_threshold` (default 8; cloud/WAN deployments raise to 10–12).

The crate is **pure computation**: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. Heartbeats arrive as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams at the carrier boundary via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); the crate records arrival timestamps and computes φ but never sends bytes itself. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 — used only for signing/digesting suspicion checkpoints and audit entries; `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs, `ids-phi-accrual` consumes them via `ids-000-aa` only.

**Scope boundary:** `ids-phi-accrual` estimates suspicion; it does not evict, remap, or reconfigure. It publishes φ and lets the caller decide. Thresholds are configurable per peer/profile, not hard-coded, so a noisy path degrades gracefully rather than falsely convicting.

A skeleton `ids-phi-accrual` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-phi-accrual/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned Hayashibara/Défago/Yared/Katayama 2004 SRDS paper (intercontinental link study, window size 1000, mistake rate vs window size), Akka `PhiAccrualFailureDetector.scala` (φ = -log10(1-CDF), logistic approximation `1/(1+exp(-y*(1.5976+0.070566*y*y)))`, error 0.00014 at ±3.16, acceptable-heartbeat-pause, firstHeartbeatEstimate, clock abstraction for testing), Apache Pekko docs (default threshold 8, cloud EC2 = 12), Cassandra `FailureDetector.java` + `ArrivalWindow` (bounded circular buffer 1000 intervals per endpoint, `PHI_FACTOR = 1/ln(10)`, MAX_INTERVAL clamped to rpc_timeout to avoid window poisoning during long partitions, seeds new peers with 2× gossip interval), Hazelcast docs (default threshold 10, sample size 200, min std dev millis floor), Rust crates `phi-accrual-failure-detector`, `atomr-remote`, `phi-accrual-detector`, `phi_detector` (EWMA variants, constant-memory two-value estimators, `PingWindow`/`NormalDist`), `suspect_machines` (Ruby, warming-up state when below min_samples, monotonic nanosecond clock), SWIM vs phi-accrual comparison (continuous suspicion vs binary suspect/dead with indirect probing), threshold tuning guidance (φ=8 = 1-in-100M false positive; φ=5 ≈ 1-in-100k; detection time 8–12 s LAN, 15–25 s WAN/GC), window-size tradeoffs (small W adapts fast but false-positives on gradual degradation; large W smooths but sluggish; sweet spot 500–2000), GC-pause handling (acceptable pause margin; never age out window entries during silence — that inflates variance and suppresses φ when most needed), adaptive-accrual alternatives (Satzger et al., no normal-distribution assumption).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-phi-accrual` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a per-peer statistical estimation layer: every time a heartbeat datagram arrives from a peer, the caller records the arrival timestamp; on demand the crate returns φ for that peer. It never sends bytes itself — it consumes timestamps and publishes suspicion.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CALLER LAYER (membership / lease / replication)            │
│  ids-membership, ids-lease, ids-replication — record heartbeat arrivals,      │
│  read φ, apply per-consumer threshold (aggressive φ>3 vs conservative φ>8)    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 076: ids-phi-accrual (THIS CRATE — estimation)           │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ ││
│  │  phi_detector    │ │  interval_window │ │  distribution    │ │  clock   │ ││
│  │  (φ = -log10 P)  │ │  (ring buffer    │ │  (normal approx, │ │  (monotonic│ ││
│  │  per peer        │ │   1000 samples)  │ │   Welford/EWMA)  │ │   ticks) │ ││
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────┘ ││
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │            │ ││
│  │  thresholds      │ │  pause_margin    │ │  audit/checkpoint│ │            │ ││
│  │  (φ_threshold    │ │  (GC pause       │ │  (signed φ log   │ │            │ ││
│  │   per peer)      │ │   tolerance)     │ │   entries)       │ │            │ ││
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │            │ ││
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────┘│
                                       │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                       ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                    │
│  Heartbeats arrive as opaque Vec<u8> to Endpoint{CarrierType, addr ≤1024 B} │
│  ids-phi-accrual receives arrival timestamps only; never sends, never opens  │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of one heartbeat cycle:**
1. Peer P sends a heartbeat datagram (opaque `Vec<u8>`) via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.
2. Caller (e.g. `ids-membership`) receives it, notes arrival tick `t_now` from `ids-time` (monotonic, never wall-clock), and calls `detector.record_heartbeat(P, t_now)`.
3. `ids-phi-accrual` computes interval `Δ = t_now - t_last`, appends to P's bounded ring window, updates running mean/variance, stores `t_last = t_now`.
4. On suspicion query `detector.phi(P, t_now)`: computes `elapsed = t_now - t_last`; if window empty → return 0.0 (warming-up); otherwise `y = (elapsed - mean - pause_margin) / stddev`; φ via logistic approximation of the normal CDF tail; φ grows monotonically with silence.
5. Caller compares φ against its own per-consumer threshold (lease path φ>3, membership eviction φ>8, alerting φ>12) and acts. `ids-phi-accrual` never evicts.

**Phi formula (research-verified):**
- `φ(t) = -log10(1 - F(t))` where `F` is the CDF of `N(mean, stddev)` estimated from historical inter-arrival times.
- `F(t)` approximated by the β Mathematics Handbook logistic form: `1 / (1 + exp(-y*(1.5976 + 0.070566*y*y)))`, `y = (t - mean)/stddev`, error 0.00014 at ±3.16.
- Cassandra variant: `φ = (1/ln(10)) * (elapsed / mean)` (exponential approximation, no σ) — noted as a divergent implementation; ids-phi-accrual follows the paper/Akka normal-distribution form.
- `acceptable_heartbeat_pause` shifts the mean: `effective_mean = mean + pause` so GC pauses don't trigger suspicion.
- `min_std_deviation` floor prevents divide-by-zero / infinite φ on steady senders.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing φ checkpoint entries; sha256/blake3 for digesting suspicion logs and checkpoint chaining; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt per-peer suspicion state at rest when confidentiality required. No other crypto.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources cited inline; full list in Section 13.

#### 3.1 Phi accrual failure detector (Hayashibara et al., 2004)

**Source:** Hayashibara, Défago, Yared, Katayama, "The φ Accrual Failure Detector," SRDS 2004 (IEEE), also available as JAIST IS_RR_2004_010 / HDY04.pdf. Analyzed over an intercontinental link for a week; φ performs equally well as other adaptive failure detectors with improved flexibility.

An accrual failure detector outputs a continuous suspicion level rather than binary trust/suspect. The φ detector samples heartbeat arrival times, maintains a sliding window of recent samples, estimates the distribution of future arrivals from past samples, and computes φ on a dynamically adjusted scale matching recent network conditions. Higher φ = higher chance the monitored process has crashed. If the process actually crashes, φ is guaranteed to accrue toward infinity. Applications set their own threshold per QoS requirements: low threshold → many false suspicions but quick detection; high threshold → fewer mistakes but slower detection.

Window size experiments: mistake rate improves as window size increases; curve flattens for large values (diminishing returns). Default window 1000 samples; analysis excluded warmup period (before window fills).

#### 3.2 Phi computation: normal CDF and logistic approximation

**Source:** Akka `PhiAccrualFailureDetector.scala`; Pekko docs; Apache Pekko `PhiAccrualFailureDetector`; `atomr-remote` Rust source; `phi_accrual_detector` Rust crate docs.

`φ = -log10(1 - F(timeSinceLastHeartbeat))`, `F` = CDF of normal distribution with mean and standard deviation estimated from historical heartbeat inter-arrival times.

Logistic approximation (β Mathematics Handbook): `F(y) ≈ 1 / (1 + exp(-y*(1.5976 + 0.070566*y*y)))`, `y = (x - mean)/stddev`. Error 0.00014 at ±3.16. Equivalent to `-log10(1 - CDF(y))`.

Akka adds two operational knobs:
- `acceptableHeartbeatPause`: margin (default 3 s) added to the mean so sudden GC pauses / network drops don't raise suspicion. Warning logged when heartbeat interval exceeds 2/3 of the pause.
- `firstHeartbeatEstimate`: bootstrap duration with high stddev when environment unknown at start.
- `Clock` abstraction returning milliseconds, faked for testing.

Threshold: default 8; cloud environments (EC2) raise to 12. Sweet spot 8 ≤ φ < 12 per Satzger et al.; detection time rises sharply beyond threshold 10–11.

#### 3.3 Inter-arrival time distribution and sliding window

**Source:** Cassandra `FailureDetector.java` + `ArrivalWindow`; Hazelcast docs (sample size 200, min std dev millis); systemdesignsimulator.org phi-accrual internals; padho-wiki phi accrual.

Each peer maintains a bounded sliding window (ring buffer) of recent inter-arrival intervals — default 1000 samples (Cassandra/Akka), 200 (Hazelcast). The window tracks a running sum so `mean = sum/count` is O(1); when full, oldest entry evicted. Mean reflects ~last 1000 seconds of heartbeat history at 1 s cadence.

Critical discipline: the window is updated **only on heartbeat arrival** — no entries added during silence, no entries aged out by time. Aging out entries during long silence artificially inflates variance and suppresses φ exactly when needed most.

Cassandra clamps `MAX_INTERVAL_IN_MS` to `rpc_timeout`: during a long partition, intervals longer than the RPC timeout are ignored rather than recorded, preventing the detector from adapting to a dead peer and delaying conviction.

Bootstrap: new peer seeded with `2 × heartbeat_interval` as a conservatively high initial mean so it isn't immediately suspected before the window fills.

#### 3.4 Welford online statistics vs recompute-from-window

**Source:** systemdesignsimulator.org; multiple implementations.

Running mean/variance updated online (Welford) or recomputed from the window when a sample is evicted. Welford: O(1) per sample, numerically stable; mergeable partitions. Recompute-from-window: O(window) on eviction but simple and exact. Both acceptable; window ≤ 1000 makes recompute cheap.

#### 3.5 GC pause handling and acceptable heartbeat pause

**Source:** Akka acceptableHeartbeatPause (default 3 s); dipach.github.io Cassandra analysis (stop-the-world GC pause → false positive vs slow detection tradeoff); systemoverflow SWIM vs phi-accrual (detection stretches to 15–25 s during 2–5 s GC pauses); padho-wiki (σ floor prevents infinite φ on first delayed packet).

The `acceptable_heartbeat_pause` is the key production knob: it represents the number of potentially lost/delayed heartbeats accepted before considering it an anomaly. Without it, any GC pause causes false suspicion. A minimum stddev floor (`min_std_deviation`) is equally important: a perfectly steady sender has σ → 0, and any silence shoots φ to infinity. Floor stddev (e.g. 1 ms, or 25% of first_heartbeat_estimate) bounds sensitivity.

#### 3.6 Cold start and warming-up state

**Source:** seuros/suspect_machines (warming-up: reports samples + required + silence until min_samples intervals); Akka firstHeartbeatEstimate; Cassandra seed 2× interval.

Until a peer has `min_samples` intervals, there is no basis for φ. Options: return φ=0 (treat as healthy, Akka behavior), return a `WarmingUp` state (suspect_machines), or bootstrap with `first_heartbeat_estimate` and a high stddev (Akka). A peer sending one heartbeat then vanishing stays warming up forever unless a warm-up ceiling is configured; `scan` names it once silence passes the ceiling.

#### 3.7 Threshold tuning: false positive vs detection latency

**Source:** Hazelcast docs (φ=1 ≈ 10% mistake, φ=2 ≈ 1%, φ=3 ≈ 0.1%, default 10); systemoverflow (φ=8 = 1-in-100M, LAN detection 8–12 s, WAN/GC 15–25 s); padho-wiki (φ=5 ≈ 1-in-100k; φ=8 crossing at ~1.85 s for μ=100 ms cadence); manuel.bernhardt.io (sweet spot 8 ≤ φ < 12; sharp detection-time increase beyond 10–11).

Per-consumer thresholds: same φ stream can feed an aggressive lease-renewal path (φ>3) and a conservative remove-from-membership path (φ>8) simultaneously. Two-tier alerting: auto-failover at φ=8, page humans at φ=10–12.

#### 3.8 Window size adaptation tradeoffs

**Source:** padho-wiki (W=50 chases jitter aggressively; W=5000 sluggish to regime changes; sweet spot 500–2000, upper bound for fast cadence ≤100 ms, lower bound for slow cadence ≥1 s); Hayashibara 2004 (mistake rate improves with window size, flattens for large values).

Small W: fast adaptation to current jitter, but gradual deterioration (slowly failing NIC adding 20 ms/packet) never raises σ enough → false positives accumulate. Large W: smooths jitter but slow to react to network recovery; cluster pays latency tax for a full window after recovery.

#### 3.9 Phi accrual vs SWIM vs fixed timeouts

**Source:** systemoverflow SWIM vs phi-accrual; dipach.github.io; learn.padho.ai.

Fixed timeout conflates estimation and decision. SWIM: alive/suspect/dead states, indirect probing via 3–5 random members, reduces false positives from transient issues but adds gossip rounds. Phi accrual: continuous suspicion, decouples monitoring from interpretation — multiple consumers apply different thresholds to the same stream. No indirect probing in the detector itself; that is a membership-layer concern (`ids-membership`, not `ids-phi-accrual`).

#### 3.10 Rust implementations and API patterns

**Source:** docs.rs `phi_accrual_failure_detector`, `phi_accrual_detector`, `phi_detector`, `atomr_remote` source; lib.rs `phi-accrual-failure-detector`.

Common Rust API: `heartbeat(timestamp)` records arrival; `phi(timestamp)` returns f64 suspicion; `is_available()` = φ < threshold; `Clock` trait abstracts time for deterministic testing; config fields: threshold, max_samples, min_std_deviation, acceptable_heartbeat_pause, first_heartbeat_estimate. `phi_detector` uses constant memory (two values: sum and count) instead of storing all pings.

#### 3.11 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** ed25519-dalek docs.rs (RFC 8032 EdDSA over Curve25519); chacha20poly1305 docs.rs (RFC 8439 AEAD + XChaCha20 192-bit nonce); sha2 RustCrypto (SHA-256); BLAKE3-team README (256-bit output, SIMD, keyed hash, KDF, XOF).

`ids-phi-accrual` uses:
- ed25519: signing φ checkpoint entries (tamper-evident suspicion log).
- sha256: checkpoint chaining, suspicion-entry hashing.
- blake3: fast content hashing for suspicion-state snapshots, parallel-friendly.
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypt per-peer suspicion state at rest (24-byte nonce, random nonces safe).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypt session/state payloads (12-byte nonce, counter-based bounded use).
All via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`; `ids-phi-accrual` implements no crypto itself.

#### 3.12 Determinism and testing

**Source:** sir-teo.github.io "The Heartbeat Is a Suspicion Score" (deterministic lab for a given seed; Clock abstraction faked for testing; default run 26 heartbeats before crash, φ crosses threshold after ~1.80 s silence with threshold 4.0 and 250 ms pause margin).

Deterministic testing requires a faked/injectable clock (`ids-time` monotonic ticks). Property tests: φ resets toward 0 after a heartbeat arrives; φ grows monotonically during silence; φ=0 when no heartbeats received; window eviction bound; min_stddev floor prevents infinite φ.

#### 3.13 Carrier-agnostic boundary

**Source:** IDS prompts.txt entry 76; plan-001/plan-048/plan-060 format; `ids-carrier::Endpoint` = CarrierType + Vec<u8> (max 1024 bytes); CarrierType: Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom(u16).

`ids-phi-accrual` receives heartbeat arrival timestamps only. It never constructs an `Endpoint`, never calls `send_datagram`, and imports no networking crate. The caller wires heartbeats (which arrive over `ids-carrier::Endpoint`) into the detector. No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| False positive suspicion (GC pause, scheduling hiccup) | Availability | `acceptable_heartbeat_pause` margin; `min_std_deviation` floor; per-consumer thresholds |
| Slow detection of real failures | Liveness | Threshold tuning per path (aggressive φ>3 for lease, conservative φ>8 for eviction); two-tier alerting |
| Window poisoning during long partition | Detection accuracy | Clamp max recorded interval to rpc_timeout (Cassandra pattern); never age out window during silence |
| Cold-start false suspicion | Availability | Bootstrap with `first_heartbeat_estimate` + high stddev; warming-up state until min_samples |
| σ → 0 on steady sender → infinite φ | False positives | `min_std_deviation` floor; never return infinite φ |
| Clock manipulation / wall-clock jump | Suspicion correctness | Monotonic `ids-time` ticks only; injectable `Clock` for tests |
| Audit/tampering of suspicion log | Accountability | ed25519-signed checkpoint entries; sha256/blake3 hash chain |
| Prohibited crate in dependency tree | Carrier-agnostic rule | CI dependency audit (`cargo tree`); imports no networking crate |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via ids-crypto; allowlist unit test |
| φ stream used as binary verdict | Semantic misuse | Detector never decides; publishes φ only; consumer applies threshold |
| Correlated multi-node failure | Membership accuracy | Out of scope for this crate (membership layer handles); φ is per-peer independent |

The carrier is never trusted: φ is computed from locally observed arrival timestamps, surviving any carrier re-framing or delay; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-phi-accrual ||
|-------|------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `Endpoint`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; `Clock` built on `IdsTime` monotonic ticks |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram transport | Heartbeats arrive as opaque `Vec<u8>` over `Endpoint`; crate never sends or constructs endpoints |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing φ checkpoints, digesting suspicion state, encrypting per-peer state at rest |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic IDS standard time source | All interval/elapsed measurements keyed to `IdsTime` ticks; never wall-clock |
| `ids-membership` (later phase) | Cluster membership / failure detection primary consumer | Records heartbeat arrivals per peer, reads φ, applies per-consumer threshold |
| `ids-lease` (later phase) | Lease renewal path | Aggressive φ threshold (e.g. φ>3) on the same heartbeat stream |
| `ids-replication` (later phase) | Replica liveness for quorum decisions | Conservative φ threshold (e.g. φ>8) before evicting a replica |

**Integration points:** `ids-phi-accrual` is a pure library — `record_heartbeat(peer_id, tick)` and `phi(peer_id, tick) -> f64`. It holds no sockets, spawns no tasks, opens no files. All cross-peer traffic is the caller's responsibility via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on `ids-discovery`, `ids-session`, or `ids-cli`.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Phi computation** — `φ(elapsed) = -log10(1 - F(elapsed))`; `F` = normal CDF `N(mean, stddev)` estimated from the interval window; logistic approximation `1/(1+exp(-y*(1.5976+0.070566*y*y)))`, `y=(elapsed-mean)/stddev`, error 0.00014 at ±3.16. Equivalent to `-log10(1-CDF(y))`. Guard: if tail probability `p <= 0`, return `f64::INFINITY` (saturated suspicion).

2. **Sliding interval window** — Fixed ring buffer of `max_samples` (default 1000) inter-arrival intervals. Running sum for O(1) mean; variance from sum of squares or Welford. On eviction, subtract outgoing sample from running stats. Window updated only on heartbeat arrival; never aged during silence.

3. **Welford online statistics** — `state = (n, mean, M2)`; `push(x): n+=1; delta=x-mean; mean+=delta/n; M2 += delta*(x-mean)`; `variance = M2/n`. Mergeable partitions for parallel stats.

4. **Acceptable heartbeat pause adjustment** — `effective_mean = mean + acceptable_pause`; `adjusted_elapsed = max(0, elapsed - pause_margin)`. Shifts the suspicion curve right so GC pauses don't trigger φ.

5. **Min stddev floor** — `stddev = max(computed_stddev, min_std_deviation)`. Prevents σ→0 → infinite φ on perfectly steady senders.

6. **Cold start / warming-up** — Until `min_samples` intervals collected: bootstrap with `first_heartbeat_estimate` mean and high stddev (25% of estimate), or report `WarmingUp{samples, required, silence}`. No φ guess before min_samples.

7. **Per-peer detector state** — `PeerDetectorState { window, last_tick: Option<Tick>, mean, stddev, phi_threshold }`. One `PhiDetector` per monitored peer (NodeId keyed), all independent.

8. **Threshold bands / hysteresis** — `Suspect` when `phi > suspect_threshold`; `Recover` when `phi < recover_threshold` (recover < suspect to prevent flapping). Bands: Healthy (φ<3), Elevated (3–8), Suspect (>8), Dead (configurable high).

9. **Suspicion audit chain** — Each φ checkpoint: `CheckpointEntry { peer: NodeId, tick: IdsTime, phi: f64, prev_hash: [u8;32] }`; chain via sha256/blake3; periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable.

10. **Clock abstraction** — `Clock { timestamp() -> Tick; elapsed(before, after) -> Duration }`; implementations: `IdsTimeClock` (monotonic ids-time ticks) and `FakeClock` (deterministic tests).
