### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Exact default `max_samples`:** 1000 (Cassandra/Akka) vs 200 (Hazelcast) — affects adaptation speed vs memory; to be validated at integration with `ids-membership`.
2. **`min_samples` for warming-up:** How many intervals before φ is trusted; Akka returns 0.0 with no history; suspect_machines requires min_samples. Undecided.
3. **Distribution choice:** Normal (paper/Akka) vs exponential (Cassandra `PHI_FACTOR * t/mean`) vs lognormal (some productions). Normal with logistic approximation selected; alternatives noted.
4. **`acceptable_heartbeat_pause` default:** Akka 3 s; deployment-dependent (GC pause profile). Tuning guide required.
5. **Per-peer threshold defaults:** Lease path φ>3, membership eviction φ>8, alerting φ>10–12 — deployment-tuned, validated at integration.
6. **Window eviction during long silence:** Never age out (discipline confirmed) vs bounded max interval clamp (Cassandra clamps to rpc_timeout). Both documented; decision pending integration.
7. **`ids-time` tick resolution:** Must be sufficient for sub-millisecond heartbeat cadences; clock source to be confirmed.
8. **Persistence of detector state across restarts:** Cold start after restart loses history; state persistence (encrypted at rest) out of scope for Phase 076, noted as future work.
9. **Correlated multi-node failure handling:** φ is per-peer independent; correlated failures (whole rack down) produce simultaneous φ rises — membership layer interprets, not this crate.

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-phi-accrual` crate, not a folder | "Separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear statistical-estimation boundary |
| φ = -log10(1-CDF) with normal distribution + logistic approximation | Hayashibara 2004 paper; Akka/Pekko reference implementation; error 0.00014 at ±3.16 |
| Bounded sliding window (default 1000 intervals) per peer | Matches Cassandra/Akka; O(1) mean via running sum; adapts to regime changes |
| Window updated only on heartbeat arrival; never aged during silence | Aging during silence inflates variance and suppresses φ when most needed (observed bug) |
| `acceptable_heartbeat_pause` margin + `min_std_deviation` floor | Survives GC pauses; prevents infinite φ on steady senders (Akka operational knobs) |
| `first_heartbeat_estimate` bootstrap + warming-up state | Conservative cold start; no false suspicion before min_samples |
| Per-peer independent `PhiDetector` | Each peer's heartbeat history differs; φ crosses threshold at different times (Cassandra observation) |
| Detector never decides; publishes φ only; consumer applies threshold | Decouples monitoring from interpretation; lease path φ>3 vs membership φ>8 on same stream |
| Monotonic `ids-time` ticks; injectable `Clock` for tests | Deterministic testing; clock manipulation cannot break suspicion |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate never sends bytes | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in trust base |
| Allowed crypto only: ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via ids-crypto | IDS crypto policy; type-level surface + primitive IDs only |
| Audit chain: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable, tamper-evident suspicion log |

# PHASE 077:

## Phase 077 — Create the ids-quorum-intersection crate: Guarantee read/write quorum intersection. Research Findings & Implementation Blueprint

**Research complete (30 targeted searches executed). No code written, no files created, no repository changes made. This document is the blueprint for implementation.**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 077 creates `ids-quorum-intersection`, the IDS crate that guarantees read/write quorum intersection — the fundamental safety property ensuring that every read quorum overlaps every write quorum by at least one replica, so a read always sees the latest acknowledged write. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by quorum domain. The crate owns: quorum system validation (R + W > N), intersection proof generation, fault tolerance calculation (write tolerance N−W, read tolerance N−R), quorum size optimization, minimum-overlap computation (W + R − N), strict vs partial quorum distinction, weighted quorum support, and Byzantine quorum intersection. `ids-quorum-intersection` never sends bytes itself; it evaluates quorum configurations, proves intersection, and returns decisions (`QuorumDecision`, `IntersectionProof`) that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`).

Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-quorum-intersection` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-quorum-intersection` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-quorum-intersection/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error`, sealed traits, invariants incl. `QuorumIntersection`). Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned Gifford's weighted voting (SOSP 1979, r + w > v), Thomas majority consensus (TODS 1979), quorum consensus algorithm (Lynch-Merritt PODC 87), strict quorum definition (any two quorums intersect), minimum overlap formula W + R − N, pigeonhole principle proof of intersection, Dynamo R + W > N (N=3, W=2, R=2 default), Cassandra consistency levels (QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, EACH_QUORUM), PBS (Probabilistically Bounded Staleness) for partial quorums, Flexible Paxos (phase-cross quorum intersection only), PBFT/BFT quorum intersection (n=3f+1, quorum 2f+1 → intersection ≥ f+1, at least one correct), quorum leases (fast reads without sacrificing writes), k-quorum systems (return one of last k values), read-write quorum systems formalism (Q = (R, W) where every r ∈ R intersects every w ∈ W), masking quorum systems (intersect in ≥ correct servers despite Byzantine), anti-entropy + Merkle trees for eventual convergence, quorum-based mutual exclusion, dynamic/adaptive quorum systems (Orca), heterogeneous quorum systems (Satrapy), weighted quorum systems (WHEAT, Swiper, Cabinet), read repair + hinted handoff for sloppy quorums, CAP/PACELC tradeoff, linearizability vs quorum intersection (W+R>N is not linearizability).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-quorum-intersection` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a policy/validation layer: given N replicas and desired read/write quorum sizes R and W, it (a) validates the quorum configuration (R + W > N for strict quorum), (b) generates an intersection proof (certificate that every read quorum intersects every write quorum), (c) computes fault tolerance (write tolerance = N − W, read tolerance = N − R), (d) optimizes quorum sizes for a target availability/latency tradeoff, and (e) supports weighted and Byzantine quorum variants. It never sends bytes itself; it returns `QuorumDecision`/`IntersectionProof` that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (quorum users)                  │
│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-consistency-profile — quorum-configured ops │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 077: ids-quorum-intersection (THIS CRATE — validation)  │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌────────┐ │ │\n│  │ quorum config    │ │ R+W>N validation │ │ intersection     │ │ fault  │ │ │\\n│  │ (N, R, W, scope) │ │ strict vs partial│ │ proof generation │ │ tolerance│ │ │\\n│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ (certificate)    │ │ calc       │ │ │\\n│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └────────┘ │ ││\n│  │ quorum size      │ │ weighted quorum  │ │                  │                │ │ │\\n│  │ optimization     │ │ Byzantine quorum │ │                  │                │ │ │\\n│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                  │                │ │ │\\n│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │                  │                │ │ │\\n│  │ decision types   │ │ audit/logging    │ │                  │                │ │ │\\n│  │ (QuorumDecision) │ │ (signed+chained) │ │                  │                │ │ │\\n│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                  │                │ │ │\\n└──────────────────────────────┬─────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────┘\\n                              │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams\\n┌──────────────────────────────▼──────────────────┐\\n│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only│\\n│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType≤1024B addr, Vec<u8>},│\\n│  payload: &[u8])                                          │\\n│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                    │\\n│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP /     │\\n│  QUIC / HTTP / DNS / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN   │\\n└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a quorum-validated write:** client submits `Write{record_id, payload, quorum_config}` → `ids-quorum-intersection` validates `R + W > N` (or weighted/Byzantine equivalent), generates `IntersectionProof`, computes fault tolerance, returns `QuorumDecision{admit: bool, required_w: W, required_r: R, min_overlap: W+R−N, proof, fault_tolerance}` → caller sends the write to W replicas as opaque datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets and collects acks → quorum re-validates ack count against W → returns `WriteResult{committed, durable, intersection_verified}`.

**Quorum semantics (research-verified):**
- **Strict quorum** (R + W > N): every read quorum intersects every write quorum → strong read-your-writes; minimum overlap = W + R − N ≥ 1.
- **Partial quorum** (R + W ≤ N): read and write quorums may be disjoint → eventual consistency only; staleness possible.
- **Majority quorum** (W = R = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1): symmetric balanced case; tolerates ⌊N/2⌋ failures.
- **Write-all/read-one** (W = N, R = 1): fast reads, writes blocked by any single failure.
- **Write-one/read-all** (W = 1, R = N): fast writes, reads need all nodes.
- **Dynamo default** (N=3, W=2, R=2): 2+2>3, overlap=1, tolerates 1 failure each way.
- **Weighted quorum**: replicas carry votes; read weight + write weight > total weight → intersection; generalizes NWR.
- **Byzantine quorum** (n = 3f+1, quorum = 2f+1): any two quorums intersect in ≥ f+1 nodes, at least one correct → safety under Byzantine faults.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing quorum decisions and intersection proofs; sha256/blake3 for quorum config IDs, version-vector hashing, proof-chain links; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt quorum state at rest when confidentiality required.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

#### 3.1 Quorum intersection: R + W > N (strict quorum)

**Source:** Gifford "Weighted Voting for Replicated Data" (SOSP 1979); Thomas "A Majority Consensus Approach to Concurrency Control for Multiple Copy Databases" (ACM TODS 1979); Quorum Consensus (Lynch-Merritt, PODC 1987); Wikipedia Quorum (distributed computing); Stanford CS145; UMD/MIT 6.033 Quorum Consensus notes; arxiv 2002.06098.

Given N replicas, a write succeeds when W replicas ack; a read succeeds when R replicas respond. If R + W > N, then by the pigeonhole principle, any read quorum (size R) and any write quorum (size W) must overlap in at least W + R − N ≥ 1 nodes. That overlapping node carries the latest acknowledged write, so a read always contacts at least one replica with the current value — strong read-your-writes (freshness, not linearizability). If R + W ≤ N, quorums may be disjoint → stale reads possible → eventual consistency. `ids-quorum-intersection` implements strict-quorum validation with the `R + W > N` guard and minimum-overlap computation `W + R − N`.

#### 3.2 Pigeonhole principle proof of intersection

**Source:** Multiple system-design references (thecodeforge.io, onenoughtone.com, sdepedia.com, hld.handbook.academy).

Proof: N total slots; write fills W slots; remaining unfilled = N − W. A read set of R nodes can avoid the write set only if R ≤ N − W, i.e. R + W ≤ N. Contrapositive: if R + W > N, the read set cannot avoid the write set — at least one node is in both. Minimum overlap size = W + R − N. Examples: N=3, W=2, R=2 → overlap = 1; N=5, W=3, R=3 → overlap = 1; N=5, W=4, R=3 → overlap = 2. Edge case W + R = N exactly → quorums could be complementary with zero overlap, which is why strict inequality `>` is required, not `≥`.

#### 3.3 Fault tolerance calculation

**Source:** deepengineering.net staleness SLOs; hld.handbook.academy quorums/replication; ironclad.academy quorum/read-repair; BEE-19014 NWR consistency.

- Write availability: write succeeds iff ≥ W replicas available → tolerates N − W write failures.
- Read availability: read succeeds iff ≥ R replicas available → tolerates N − R read failures.
- W = N, R = 1: 0 write failures tolerated, N − 1 read failures tolerated.
- W = 1, R = N: N − 1 write failures tolerated, 0 read failures tolerated.
- W = R = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1: ⌊N/2⌋ failures tolerated each way (balanced).
- `ids-quorum-intersection` exposes `write_tolerance() = N − W` and `read_tolerance() = N − R`, and validates that configured tolerances meet deployment requirements.

#### 3.4 Quorum size optimization

**Source:** systemoverflow tuning quorum parameters; JavaAtoll quorum cheat sheet; hld.handbook.academy config table.

Optimization trades off latency, availability, and consistency:
- Smaller W → lower write latency, higher write availability, weaker durability (fewer replicas have the write).
- Smaller R → lower read latency, higher read availability, weaker freshness.
- Larger overlap (W + R − N) → stronger consistency but higher latency on both sides.
- Recommended defaults: N=3, W=2, R=2 (balanced, tolerates 1 failure); N=3, W=3, R=1 (read-heavy); N=3, W=1, R=3 (write-heavy telemetry); N=5, W=3, R=3 (mission-critical larger cluster).
- `ids-quorum-intersection` provides an optimizer that, given N and a target fault tolerance f, computes minimal W and R satisfying R + W > N and N − W ≥ f, N − R ≥ f.

#### 3.5 Strict vs partial quorum

**Source:** arxiv 2002.06098 (Consistency Analysis of Replication-Based Probabilistic KV Stores); arxiv 1804.00742 (Minimizing Content Staleness); PBS paper (arxiv 2104.04102 / CACM); Berkeley EECS-2012-4.

- Strict quorum (R + W > N): strong consistency, every read sees the latest write; higher latency, lower availability.
- Partial quorum (R + W ≤ N): eventual consistency, lower latency, higher availability, staleness unbounded without anti-entropy.
- Expanding partial quorums: write quorum grows post-ack via anti-entropy; eventual intersection.
- `ids-quorum-intersection` classifies configurations as strict/partial and enforces the crate's guarantee (strict by default; partial requires explicit opt-in with documented staleness SLO).

#### 3.6 Weighted quorum systems

**Source:** Gifford SOSP 1979 (fractional weights, v_r + v_w > v); arxiv 2307.15561 (Swiper); arxiv 2609.39715 (adaptive Byzantine quorum, WHEAT); arxiv 2512.20485 (Cabinet dynamic weights); arxiv 1403.5128 (wheel quorum protocol).

Each replica i carries weight w_i; total weight V = Σ w_i. Read requires weight ≥ v_r; write requires weight ≥ v_w; intersection guaranteed iff v_r + v_w > V. Weighted quorums generalize NWR and let operators tune per-replica influence (failure domains, capacity, responsiveness). `ids-quorum-intersection` supports weighted configs with `v_r + v_w > V` validation and weighted overlap computation.

#### 3.7 Byzantine quorum intersection

**Source:** Princeton COS 418 BFT lecture; arxiv 2609.39715 (adaptive Byzantine quorum); Satrapy (heterogeneous quorum systems, 2026); arxiv 2104.04102 masking quorums; Malkhi-Reiter Byzantine quorum survey.

With n = 3f + 1 replicas and quorum size 2f + 1, any two quorums intersect in ≥ f + 1 nodes, hence ≥ 1 correct node → safety under f Byzantine faults. Masking quorums: read quorum intersects last write quorum in ≥ correct servers, enabling the reader to identify correct up-to-date data. Heterogeneous quorum systems: each participant has its own quorum set; quorum intersection + weak availability + quorum subsumption are sufficient for consensus. `ids-quorum-intersection` supports Byzantine quorum validation with `n = 3f + 1`, quorum = `2f + 1`, intersection ≥ `f + 1`, correct-intersection ≥ 1.

#### 3.8 Flexible Paxos / phase-cross quorum intersection

**Source:** arxiv 1608.06696 (Flexible Paxos); arxiv 2203.03058; blog.acolyer.org.

Paxos traditionally requires all quorums (all phases/rounds) to intersect. Flexible Paxos shows only phase-1 and phase-2 quorums of a given round need intersect: |Q1| + |Q2| > N. Within a phase, disjoint quorums are safe. This trades larger leader-election quorums for smaller replication quorums. `ids-quorum-intersection` documents this as an advanced optimization; the crate enforces the simpler universal rule (all read/write quorums intersect) by default.

#### 3.9 Quorum leases

**Source:** cs.cmu.edu quorum leases (Paxos Quorum Leases: Fast Reads Without Sacrificing Writes).

Quorum leases let a majority of replicas perform strongly consistent local reads without contacting the leader, reducing read latency by orders of magnitude in WAN. Leases are time-bounded; a leader grants lease to a quorum; reads within lease are local and linearizable. Writes still need quorum. `ids-quorum-intersection` documents quorum leases as a read-path optimization; lease management lives in `ids-time`/`ids-leader` (later phases).

#### 3.10 k-quorum systems

**Source:** Cornell DISC 2005 / DISC 2006 (Byzantine and Multi-writer K-Quorums).

k-quorums guarantee a read returns one of the last k written values, even under adversarial scheduling. Write propagates tuples for preceding k−1 writes; reads collect quorum, pick latest valid tuple, write back to make it visible at more locations. Trade: higher availability than strict quorums at cost of bounded staleness (k values). `ids-quorum-intersection` documents k-quorum as a relaxed-consistency option; not the default guarantee.

#### 3.11 Read-write quorum systems (formalism)

**Source:** arxiv 2104.04102 (Read-Write Quorum Systems Made Practical); arxiv 2610.00702 (Ditto: generalized reconfigurable linearizable reads).

Formal definition: Q = (R, W) over node set X; R = set of read quorums (subsets of X), W = set of write quorums; every r ∈ R intersects every w ∈ W (r ∩ w ≠ ∅). Upward closure: supersets of quorums are quorums. Ditto: shrinking read quorums forces write quorums to grow and vice versa; local reads (read quorums of size 1) require write quorums containing at least one process from every read quorum. `ids-quorum-intersection` implements the formal relation `∀r∈R, ∀w∈W: r ∩ w ≠ ∅` as an exhaustive checker for small N and a sufficient-condition checker (R + W > N) for uniform quorums.

#### 3.12 CAP / PACELC and availability

**Source:** CAP theorem; PACELC (Abadi); Wikipedia PACELC; CockroachDB fundamental tradeoffs.

CAP: under partition P, choose Consistency C or Availability A. PACELC: elsewhere (no partition) choose Latency L or Consistency C. `ids-quorum-intersection` encodes this: strict quorum chooses C (rejects below quorum); partial quorum chooses A (progress with possible staleness); quorum leases choose L in the common case. Failure behavior matrix per configuration.

#### 3.13 Anti-entropy and eventual convergence (partial quorum backstop)

**Source:** HLD Handbook Merkle trees/anti-entropy; HotShard anti-entropy & read repair; jepemo read repair/anti-entropy; Dynamo paper (SOSP 2007) Merkle trees + hinted handoff; Cassandra read repair.

Partial quorums converge via anti-entropy (Merkle-tree digest exchange, O(K log N) comparisons for K differences) and read-repair (quorum read detects digest mismatch, returns newest, pushes back to stale replicas). Hinted handoff: writes to sloppy nodes are replayed when the intended target recovers. `ids-quorum-intersection` documents the backstop but delegates repair execution to `ids-replication`/`ids-anti-entropy` (later phases) via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

#### 3.14 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** ed25519-dalek (RFC 8032); chacha20poly1305 (RFC 8439 + XChaCha20); sha2 (FIPS 180-4); blake3 (BLAKE3-team).

- ed25519: signing quorum decisions, intersection proofs, audit checkpoints.
- sha256: quorum config IDs, version-vector entry hashing, proof-chain links.
- blake3: fast content hashing for quorum-state fingerprints, checkpoint chaining (parallel, SIMD).
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypt quorum state at rest (24-byte nonce, random nonces safe).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypt session/state payloads (12-byte nonce, counter-based).
No other crypto. `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs; `ids-quorum-intersection` references them via `ids-000-aa` only.

#### 3.15 Linearizability boundary

**Source:** Jepsen (Cassandra QUORUM write loss under partition); JavaAtoll quorum cheat sheet; Attiya SPAA'91; CockroachDB linearizability notes.

W + R > N guarantees the read set and write set intersect → never read a stale *committed* value. It does NOT guarantee linearizability: concurrent writes, partially failed writes, and read-modify-write races can still yield non-linear states. True linearizability needs consensus (Paxos/Raft) or ABD write-back. `ids-quorum-intersection` documents this boundary explicitly: it provides freshness (read-your-writes via intersection), not linearizability.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Stale read below quorum (R + W ≤ N) | Read correctness | `R + W > N` enforced for strict quorum; partial quorum requires explicit opt-in + documented staleness SLO |
| Lost write (W replicas fail) | Write durability | `write_tolerance() = N − W`; deployment must provision N such that N − W ≥ required failure tolerance |
| Split-brain / disjoint quorums | State consistency | Intersection proof certificate required before any quorum-configured operation is admitted |
| Byzantine intersection node | Correctness under faults | Byzantine quorum mode: n = 3f+1, quorum 2f+1 → intersection ≥ f+1, ≥1 correct |
| Clock manipulation for quorum state | Causality correctness | Logical version numbers only (Gifford pattern), never wall-clock; monotonic `IdsTime` for timeouts |
| Quorum config downgrade attack | Consistency integrity | Config is immutable per record/region; changes require signed governance decision, audited |
| Key extraction (quorum signing key) | Decision authenticity | Signing keys never leave node; encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent intersection checks; replay protection via nonces and bounded replay cache |
| Partial quorum masquerading as strict | Safety violation | Compile-time/runtime flag `Strict` vs `Partial`; `Partial` cannot be silently promoted to `Strict` |

The carrier is never trusted: quorum decisions and proofs are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-quorum-intersection ||
|-------|------|--------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; `QuorumIntersection` invariant mirrored here |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All quorum traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing quorum decisions/proofs; hashing quorum configs and proof chains; encrypting quorum state at rest |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (quorum user) | Tags writes/reads with quorum config; consults `ids-quorum-intersection` before admitting |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization / anti-entropy | Runs repair backstop for partial quorums; uses this crate's quorum validation |
| `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060) | Read/write behavior per profile | Profiles map to quorum configs (R, W, N); this crate validates and proofs them |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic time source | Quorum lease timeouts and `IdsTime` timestamps on decisions (never wall-clock for causality) |

**Integration points:** `ids-quorum-intersection` is a pure validation/proof layer. It imports canonical types and contracts from `ids-000-aa`, emits `QuorumDecision`/`IntersectionProof` values, and relies on callers (`ids-store`, `ids-replication`, `ids-consistency-profile`) to frame them into opaque datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. It does not depend on `ids-discovery`, `ids-session`, or any carrier implementation.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 QuorumConfig / QuorumMode
`QuorumConfig { n: u32, r: u32, w: u32, mode: QuorumMode, scope: QuorumScope, weights: Option<Vec<u32>> }` where `QuorumMode = Strict | Partial | Weighted | Byzantine | KQuorum { k }` and `QuorumScope = Local | Region | CrossRegion`. Re-exports `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum` from `ids-000-aa`.

#### 7.2 Strict quorum validation
```
admit(N, R, W) -> bool iff R + W > N
classify(N, R, W) -> Strict if R + W > N else Partial
validate(config) -> QuorumDecision { admit, required_r, required_w, min_overlap, proof, fault_tolerance }
```

#### 7.3 Intersection proof (certificate)
For uniform quorums (all subsets of size R/W): proof = certificate that `R + W > N` holds, signed (ed25519) and hash-chained (sha256/blake3). For arbitrary quorum sets Q = (R_set, W_set): exhaustive checker `∀r∈R_set, ∀w∈W_set: r ∩ w ≠ ∅` (exponential, feasible for small N); result `Some(true)`/`Some(false)`/`None` with safe fallback on `None`.

#### 7.4 Minimum overlap
```
min_overlap(R, W, N) = W + R − N   (when R + W > N; else 0 / no guarantee)
```
Examples: N=3, W=2, R=2 → 1; N=5, W=3, R=3 → 1; N=5, W=4, R=3 → 2.

#### 7.5 Fault tolerance
```
write_tolerance(N, W) = N − W
read_tolerance(N, R) = N − R
```
Balanced majority: W = R = ⌊N/2⌋ + 1 → tolerates ⌊N/2⌋ failures each way.

#### 7.6 Quorum size optimizer
Given N and target fault tolerance f: find minimal W, R such that `R + W > N`, `N − W ≥ f`, `N − R ≥ f`. Returns (W, R) minimizing max(W, R) (latency-balanced) or minimizing W (write-optimized) / R (read-optimized) per objective.

#### 7.7 Weighted quorum
Weights w_i, total V = Σ w_i; read threshold v_r, write threshold v_w; admit iff `v_r + v_w > V`; weighted overlap computed per config.

#### 7.8 Byzantine quorum
n = 3f + 1; quorum = 2f + 1; any two quorums intersect in ≥ f + 1 nodes; ≥ 1 correct node in intersection → safety under f Byzantine faults.

#### 7.9 Audit chain
Each quorum decision (admit/reject/reconfigure) = SHA-256/BLAKE3-chained entry + ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts; `QuorumIntersection` invariant.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — decision transport only; crate never sends directly.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `serde` — serialization of quorum configs, decisions, proofs, audit entries.
- `thiserror` — error types.

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. `ids-quorum-intersection` imports no crypto directly — all via `ids-crypto`.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete quorum defaults per deployment:** N/R/W defaults (e.g., N=3, W=2, R=2) are deployment-tuned; to be validated at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-consistency-profile`.
2. **Anti-entropy interval for partial quorum backstop:** convergence schedule for partial-quorum staleness healing; workload-dependent.
3. **Quorum lease integration:** lease grant/renewal flow with `ids-time`/`ids-leader` (later phases) not yet designed.
4. **Weighted quorum weight assignment:** how weights are derived from failure domains/capacity; policy pending.
5. **Byzantine fault model scope:** whether IDS assumes Byzantine faults at all; crash-fault-only would simplify to n=2f+1.
6. **k-quorum adoption:** whether k-quorum (bounded staleness) is offered as a profile or deferred.
7. **Relation checker scalability:** exhaustive checker is exponential; sufficient-condition (R+W>N) used for uniform quorums; arbitrary quorum-set checking for large N needs sampling/approximation.
8. **Audit chain performance:** signed checkpoints per decision may be hot-path expensive; batching interval TBD.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Separate crate `ids-quorum-intersection` (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear validation boundary |
| Strict quorum default (`R + W > N`), partial requires explicit opt-in | Guarantee is the crate's purpose; partial quorum weakens it intentionally |
| Minimum overlap = W + R − N; strict inequality `>` (not `≥`) | Pigeonhole principle; W + R = N allows complementary disjoint quorums |
| Intersection proof certificate (signed + hash-chained) | Auditability and offline verifiability of every quorum decision |
| Fault tolerance: write = N − W, read = N − R | Direct from quorum definition; exposes availability tradeoff |
| Quorum optimizer for minimal W/R given target fault tolerance | Automates config tuning; balances latency vs availability |
| Weighted quorum support (`v_r + v_w > V`) | Generalizes NWR; lets operators tune per-replica influence |
| Byzantine quorum (n = 3f+1, quorum = 2f+1, intersection ≥ f+1) | Standard BFT quorum intersection; ≥1 correct in intersection |
| Logical versions only, no wall-clock for causality; monotonic IdsTime for timeouts | Clock manipulation cannot break quorum correctness |
| Freshness guarantee only, not linearizability | W + R > N ≠ linearizability; consensus needed for linearizability (later phases) |
| Carrier-agnostic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Only allowed crypto; via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs through `ids-000-aa` | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 078 creates `ids-circuit-breaker`, the IDS crate for failure isolation via circuit breakers. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by breaker scope (per-peer, global, handshake). It implements the classic three-state circuit breaker (CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN → CLOSED) with configurable failure threshold, success threshold, timeout/reset timeout, and backoff strategy. Per-peer circuit breakers isolate one failing peer while breakers for healthy peers stay closed; global circuit breakers trip on aggregate failure rate or when every per-peer breaker is open; handshake circuit breakers protect protocol handshakes from hanging on unresponsive peers. All protected traffic rides opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); the crate never touches `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh, and never sends bytes itself — it returns an admit/reject/probe decision that the caller frames to an `Endpoint`.

**Core design:** a state machine per circuit keyed by `NodeId` (per-peer) plus a global aggregator. In CLOSED, calls pass through and outcomes are recorded; on crossing the failure threshold (consecutive failures or sliding-window failure rate) the breaker trips to OPEN and fails fast for the reset timeout; after the timeout it enters HALF-OPEN and admits a limited number of probe calls; all-probe success closes the circuit, any probe failure re-opens it with backoff applied. Backoff strategies: fixed, exponential, and exponential-with-jitter (full/equal/decorrelated) to avoid thundering herds on recovery. Failure classification is predicate-based so only breaker-worthy outcomes (timeouts, transport failures, 5xx-equivalent errors) count; everything else passes through untyped. Observability emits state (closed/open/half-open), success/failure/rejection counters, and transition events.

**Scope boundary:** `ids-circuit-breaker` decides; it does not execute, send, or retry. Callers (ids-store, ids-replication, ids-fragment, ids-session, etc.) route every outbound datagram through the breaker for the target `Endpoint`, then act on the decision. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` (breaker state-transition audit entries are signed/hash-chained; crypto ops live in `ids-crypto`).

A skeleton `ids-circuit-breaker` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-circuit-breaker/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts, consumed but never redefined. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned Martin Fowler's Circuit Breaker bliki (3 states, fail-fast, monitor alert), Azure Architecture Center Circuit Breaker pattern (open/half-open flows, short-circuit, retry vs breaker distinction), Resilience4j `CircuitBreakerConfig` (sliding window count-based/time-based, failure rate threshold 50% default, success threshold, wait duration, minimum calls), SmallRye Fault Tolerance circuit breaker (rolling window, `delay`/open→half-open, `successThreshold` probe count), arXiv 1609.05830 "Circuit Breakers, Discovery, and API Gateways in Microservices" (client-side vs proxy deployment, fail fast, stability), AWS "Exponential Backoff and Jitter" (full/equal/decorrelated jitter, thundering herd), AWS Step Functions + DynamoDB circuit breaker (Michael Nygard *Release It* popularization, callee recovery detection), docs.rs `breaker` Rust crate (state machine, sliding-window failure-rate tripping, consecutive-failure tripping, half-open probe permits with stampede protection, backoff strategies Fixed/Exponential/ExponentialJitter, typed errors, failure predicate), tower-resilience-circuitbreaker (Rust, async, metrics, health check), pyresilience CircuitBreaker (consecutive failures, recovery timeout, success threshold, doubled-timeout backoff on repeated failure), per-replica vs global breaker layering (per-replica ejects one degraded node; global trips only when all per-peers are open), OpenTelemetry circuit breaker observability metrics (state gauge, transitions, rejection rate, flapping alert), Go `bjaus/breaker` (failure threshold, success threshold, open duration, half-open requests, OnReject hook), *Release It* (Michael Nygard, stability patterns: circuit breaker, timeouts, bulkheads, handshaking), Hystrix circuit breaker (rolling counters, circuit open → short-circuit → fallback).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-circuit-breaker` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types, sealed contracts, errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives), and `ids-time` (monotonic ticks for timeouts). It is a decision layer: given a call targeted at a peer (`NodeId` → `Endpoint`), it returns `Admit | RejectFast | Probe` and records outcomes. It never opens a socket, never dials an address, and never sends bytes — the caller frames the datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only when the breaker admits.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CALLER LAYER (ids-store, ids-replication, …)                   │
│  build datagram → call breaker.admit(peer: NodeId) → send or reject             │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 078: ids-circuit-breaker (THIS CRATE — decision layer)      │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ breaker_registry │ │ per_peer         │ │ global           │ │ handshake│   │
│  │ (keyed by NodeId)│ │ breakers (one    │ │ breaker (aggregate│ │ breaker  │   │
│  │                  │ │ per peer target) │ │ failure rate)    │ │ (handshake│  │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ deadline)│   │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ └──────────────────┘ └──────────┘   │
│  │ backoff_strategy │ │ failure_classifier│ │                  │           │   │
│  │ (fixed/exp/jitter│ │ (predicate-based)│ │                  │           │   │
│  │  state machine)  │ │                  │ │                  │           │   │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                  │           │   │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │                  │           │   │
│  │ metrics          │ │ audit            │ │                  │           │   │
│  │ (state, counts,  │ │ (signed+chained  │ │                  │           │   │
│  │  transitions)    │ │  state changes)  │                  │           │   │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                  │           │   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
                                            │ Admit → caller sends opaque Vec<u8>
                                            │ RejectFast → caller fails fast
                                            ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                        │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])   │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                          │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS /        │
```

**Per-peer circuit lifecycle:** `CLOSED` (pass through, count outcomes; threshold reached → OPEN) → `OPEN` (reject fast, reset timeout running; timeout elapsed → HALF-OPEN) → `HALF-OPEN` (admit `success_threshold` probe calls; all succeed → CLOSED; any fail → OPEN with backoff-applied reset timeout).

**Global circuit breaker:** aggregates per-peer state; trips to OPEN when the fleet-wide failure rate exceeds its threshold or every per-peer breaker for a scope is open; callers consult the global breaker first (cheap gate), then the per-peer breaker.

**Handshake circuit breaker:** a per-handshake breaker keyed by handshake ID (`HandshakeId` from `ids-000-aa`); bounds the handshake deadline with `IdsTime` monotonic ticks; trips on handshake timeout/failure so one unresponsive peer cannot stall the handshake pipeline.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 to sign breaker state-transition audit entries; sha256/blake3 to hash-chain the audit log and derive breaker IDs; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt breaker state at rest where confidentiality is required.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 13.

#### 3.1 Circuit breaker state machine (CLOSED / OPEN / HALF-OPEN)

**Source:** Martin Fowler Circuit Breaker bliki; Azure Architecture Center Circuit Breaker pattern; SmallRye Fault Tolerance circuit breaker reference; pyresilience CircuitBreaker; Go `bjaus/breaker`.

The breaker is a three-state finite state machine. `CLOSED` is the initial state: calls execute, outcomes (success/failure) are recorded, and crossing the failure threshold trips the breaker to `OPEN`. In `OPEN`, every call is rejected immediately without executing the protected operation (fail fast); after the reset timeout elapses, the breaker moves to `HALF-OPEN` to probe recovery. In `HALF-OPEN`, a limited number of probe calls are admitted; if all probes succeed the breaker returns to `CLOSED`, otherwise it returns to `OPEN` (typically with backoff applied to the next reset timeout). This is the reference lifecycle `ids-circuit-breaker` implements for every circuit.

#### 3.2 Failure threshold: consecutive failures vs sliding-window failure rate

**Source:** Resilience4j `CircuitBreakerConfig` (failureRateThreshold, slidingWindowSize, slidingWindowType COUNT_BASED/TIME_BASED, minimumNumberOfCalls); SmallRye circuit breaker (rolling window ratio); async-concurrency tuning guide (consecutive count vs rate threshold simulation); Go `500px/circuitbreaker` (ConsecutiveBreaker vs RateBreaker); `breaker` Rust crate docs (trips on whichever fires first: consecutive failures or sliding-window failure rate).

Two tripping policies are supported, configured per circuit:
- **Consecutive failures:** opens after `failure_threshold` failures in a row; any success resets the streak. Simple, fast, detects a hard-down dependency; fragile under alternating fail/success (degraded dependency never trips).
- **Sliding-window failure rate:** opens when `failures / outcomes ≥ failure_rate_threshold` within a window of `window_size` outcomes (count-based or time-based), once `minimum_calls` outcomes are recorded. Scale-independent: 5% failure at 10 req/s and at 10k req/s are treated identically. Recommended default for high-throughput IDS paths.

`ids-circuit-breaker` supports both policies (whichever fires first, matching the `breaker` Rust crate design), with defaults: `failure_threshold = 5` consecutive, `failure_rate_threshold = 0.50` (50%), `minimum_calls = 10`, `window_size = 100` outcomes.

#### 3.3 Success threshold and half-open probe logic

**Source:** SmallRye (`successThreshold`: number of probe invocations, default 1); Resilience4j (`permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState`, `automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled`); pyresilience (`success_threshold` consecutive successes to close); Go `bjaus/breaker` (`successThreshold`, `halfOpenRequests`); Tencent Cloud circuit breaker policy (success threshold ≤ probing requests).

In `HALF-OPEN`, the breaker admits at most `half_open_max_calls` concurrent probes (stampede protection: the rest are rejected instantly without counting as failures). The circuit closes when `success_threshold` probes succeed; any probe failure re-opens the circuit. `ids-circuit-breaker` defaults: `success_threshold = 2`, `half_open_max_calls = 3`. Probes are the only calls allowed through an OPEN→recovering breaker, preventing recovery traffic from re-overloading a just-recovering peer.

#### 3.4 Timeout / reset timeout and backoff strategy

**Source:** Resilience4j (`waitDurationInOpenState`, default 30s; `resetTimeout`); opossum (`resetTimeout: 30000` ms, timeout default 10s); AWS "Exponential Backoff and Jitter" (full/equal/decorrelated jitter; capped exponential backoff); pyresilience (doubled timeout on repeated failure, 2h TTL so stale breakers self-heal); arrow-kt circuit breaker (`resetTimeout` multiplied by `exponentialBackoffFactor` up to `maxResetTimeout`); `breaker` Rust crate (backoff strategies Fixed, Exponential, ExponentialJitter applied per trip via attempt counter).

- `reset_timeout`: time the breaker stays OPEN before moving to HALF-OPEN. Default 30 s.
- **Backoff strategy** applied per trip: `Fixed` (constant reset timeout), `Exponential` (reset timeout multiplied by factor per consecutive trip, capped at `max_reset_timeout`), `ExponentialJitter` (exponential with full/equal/decorrelated jitter so recovering peers don't retry in lockstep). Repeated trips lengthen the open duration (10s → 15s → 22.5s …) until success, then reset. A per-circuit TTL (e.g. 2 h of inactivity) auto-closes stale breakers so historical failures cannot penalize future traffic.
- A per-call `timeout` (optional, via `ids-time` ticks, never wall-clock) counts timed-out calls as failures.

#### 3.5 Per-peer circuit breakers (isolation / bulkhead per peer)

**Source:** arXiv 1609.05830 (client-side circuit breakers: one breaker per external service per client); A2A circuit breaker architecture (per-peer breakers create bulkheads; one failing peer cannot consume resources needed for healthy peers); database-read-replicas.com (per-replica breaker ejects one degraded node while healthy peers keep serving).

One independent breaker instance per peer target (`NodeId` → `Endpoint`). The breaker for a failing peer opens and sheds that peer's calls; breakers for healthy peers stay closed and traffic continues unaffected. This bounds the blast radius to the actually-failing peer and prevents a single bad dependency from saturating shared resources. Per-peer breakers are the default scope in `ids-circuit-breaker`.

#### 3.6 Global circuit breakers (aggregate / derived all-open signal)

**Source:** Resilient Circuit documentation (distributed, shared state across instances); database-read-replicas.com (global breaker trips only when every per-replica breaker is open → degraded read mode); Polly distributed circuit breaker issue (state shared between instances); `blackblacktigerHQ/resilience-circuitbreaker` (Redis-shared circuits per resource key, tenant-aware keys).

A global breaker sits above the per-peer layer and trips on an aggregate signal (fleet-wide failure rate, or every per-peer breaker in a scope open). It switches the whole affected path into a degraded mode (fallback target, load shedding). Running only a global breaker is a coarse-grained mistake: one slow peer would trip traffic for the entire fleet. `ids-circuit-breaker` implements both layers; callers consult global first (cheap gate), then per-peer.

#### 3.7 Handshake circuit breakers

**Source:** *Release It* stability patterns (handshaking, defensive integration points); arrow-kt (one request as test in half-open); Webhook architecture circuit breaker patterns (TLS handshake failure classified separately as unreachable/non-self-healing).

A handshake circuit breaker protects protocol handshakes: one breaker per handshake (`HandshakeId`), bounded by a handshake deadline (`IdsTime` monotonic). On handshake timeout or repeated failure it trips, so one unresponsive peer cannot stall the handshake pipeline or exhaust handshake slots. After the reset timeout it probes with a single lightweight handshake attempt. Handshake breakers are keyed separately from data-plane per-peer breakers so a failing data path does not interfere with control/handshake paths and vice versa.

#### 3.8 Circuit breaker vs retry vs bulkhead

**Source:** Azure Architecture Center (breaker prevents calls likely to fail; retry expects eventual success; they combine — retry through a breaker); *Release It* (circuit breaker, timeouts, bulkheads, handshaking as complementary stability patterns); async-concurrency guide (circuit breaker + bulkhead).

Circuit breakers stop calls to a likely-failing dependency; retries re-attempt with expectation of eventual success; bulkheads isolate resources (thread pools, connection pools). They compose: retry logic sits *through* the breaker (breaker trips → retries fail fast). `ids-circuit-breaker` defines the breaker boundary; retry/backoff and bulkhead concerns live in companion crates (ids-bulkhead, Phase 079) and are referenced, not implemented, here.

#### 3.9 Observability: state, transitions, rejections

**Source:** OneUptime circuit breaker monitoring (OpenTelemetry metrics: state gauge 0=closed/1=open/2=half-open, transitions, rejection rate, flapping alert); breaker_machines observability (opened/closed/half_opened/rejected/success/failure events); stackpractices circuit breaker monitoring (Prometheus metrics per service/endpoint).

`ids-circuit-breaker` emits per-circuit metrics: current state, total/success/failure/rejected call counts, state-transition count and timestamps, open duration, probe outcomes. Alerts: breaker stuck open beyond N reset timeouts; flapping (rapid OPEN↔HALF-OPEN cycling); sustained high rejection rate. Metrics are structured over `ids-000-aa` types (`NodeId`, circuit ID) and feed `ids-observability`.

#### 3.10 Rust circuit breaker implementations and sealed-trait style

**Source:** docs.rs `breaker` crate (state machine, sliding-window failure-rate tripping, consecutive-failure tripping, half-open probe permits, backoff strategies, typed errors, failure predicate, Tower layer); tower-resilience-circuitbreaker (async Rust, `state_sync()`, `is_open()`, `metrics()`); docs.rs/axum-conf circuit breaker (per-target organization: one breaker per database, one per external HTTP service).

`ids-circuit-breaker` follows the sealed-trait contract style of `ids-000-aa`: `trait Breaker: private::Sealed` with `admit(&self, key: CircuitKey) -> Decision`, `record(&self, key, outcome)`, `state(&self) -> CircuitState`. Downstream crates use as bounds but cannot implement. Sync state inspection (`state_sync`, `is_open`) for health checks; async metrics via `ids-time`-keyed snapshots.

#### 3.11 Failure classification (what counts as a breaker failure)

**Source:** Resilience4j (`recordExceptions`/`ignoreExceptions`); opencode/gomodel resilience config (`CIRCUIT_BREAKER_FAILURE_ON_STATUSES`: 429, 5xx; client cancellation ignored; local timeouts count); async-concurrency guide (timeouts and 5xx count as failures; declines don't).

A `FailurePredicate` classifies outcomes: transport timeout, transport error, and protocol-level error responses count as failures; business-logic rejections (e.g. invalid payload) and caller cancellations do not. Timeouts are measured against `ids-time` ticks, never wall-clock. The predicate is configurable per circuit so idempotent control-plane calls and latency-sensitive data-plane calls can classify differently.

#### 3.12 Distributed circuit breaker coordination considerations

**Source:** arXiv 1609.05830 (client-side vs proxy deployment); Resilient Circuit (shared PostgreSQL state, coordinated failure handling, fail-open on storage read failure); Polly distributed breaker (shared state between instances so other nodes break earlier).

`ids-circuit-breaker` is per-node local state by design (no shared storage, no carrier dependency). Breaker state is not synchronized across nodes — each node trips independently on its own observed failures. This matches IDS's carrier-agnostic, no-central-coordinator philosophy. Coordination (if ever needed) is an integration-layer concern outside this crate; this plan explicitly does not implement distributed breaker state.

#### 3.13 Carrier-agnostic enforcement (Endpoint only)

**Source:** IDS prompts.txt entry 78; existing `ids-000-aa` skeleton (`Endpoint { CarrierType, address: Vec<u8> }`, `MAX_ADDRESS_SIZE = 1024`); HX-241 carrier-agnostic socket abstraction research.

`ids-circuit-breaker` imports no networking crate. `CircuitKey` = `NodeId` (peer identity from `ids-000-aa`), not an address; the breaker's decision is applied before the caller sends to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. CI test asserts zero references to `std::net`, `tokio::net`, `libp2p`, `IpAddr`, `SocketAddr`, `TcpStream`, `UdpSocket` in the crate.

#### 3.14 Crypto surface for breaker decisions (allowed set only)

**Source:** IDS allowed-crypto rule (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305); RFC 8032 Ed25519; RFC 7539 ChaCha20-Poly1305; libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305; NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256; BLAKE3 spec.

- ed25519: sign breaker state-transition audit entries (proof that a trip/close decision was made locally).
- sha256: breaker ID derivation, audit-chain links.
- blake3: fast hash-chaining of audit entries, circuit key hashing.
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypt breaker state at rest (random 192-bit nonces).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypt session/breaker payloads (96-bit nonces, counter-based, bounded use).
No other crypto. `ids-crypto` is the sole implementation surface; `ids-circuit-breaker` references primitive IDs via `ids-000-aa`.

#### 3.15 Integration surface with ids-000-aa types

**Source:** `ids-000-aa` canonical types and sealed trait contracts (types.rs, contracts/, errors.rs); existing IDS plan format precedents (plan-001, plan-048, plan-060).

Consumed types: `NodeId` (circuit key / peer identity), `Endpoint` (carrier target the decision is applied to), `CarrierType`, `IdsTime` (monotonic ticks for timeouts and reset deadlines), `Checksum` (audit chain), `Error` (unified error contract, wrapped as `BreakerError` variants). Sealed trait contracts mirrored: `trait Breaker: private::Sealed` declared here; impl crates (`ids-carrier`-adjacent consumers) implement at integration time.

---

### Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Cascading failure: one failing peer drains caller resources | System stability | Per-peer breaker isolates the failing peer; healthy peers' breakers stay closed |
| Global breaker tripping all traffic due to one slow peer | Availability | Global breaker trips only on aggregate rate or all-per-peers-open; per-peer layer is the first decision |
| Recovery stampede re-overloading a just-recovered peer | Peer recovery | HALF-OPEN admits at most `half_open_max_calls` probes; rest rejected instantly |
| Threshold too sensitive (flapping on noise) or too lax (sends traffic into outage) | Correctness | Rate-based threshold with `minimum_calls`; defaults tuned above normal error rates (50%) |
| Stale breaker penalizing traffic long after recovery | Liveness | Per-circuit TTL auto-closes after inactivity; backoff caps max reset timeout |
| Clock manipulation for timeout/deadline | Correctness | `ids-time` monotonic ticks only; no wall-clock for breakers |
| Replay/forgery of breaker state transitions | Decision integrity | ed25519-signed, sha256/blake3 hash-chained audit log; offline verifiable |
| Breaker keyed by network address (couples to carrier) | Carrier-agnosticism | Keyed by `NodeId`; decision applied to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` by caller; crate never addresses sockets |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Policy compliance | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via ids-crypto; allowlist test |
| Breaker rejecting calls it should admit (false positive) | Availability | `minimum_calls` gate prevents tripping on low traffic; failure predicate excludes business rejections |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Breaker is idempotent on outcomes; duplicates counted once per admit call |

The carrier is never trusted: breaker decisions are local observations over outcomes the caller reports; no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-circuit-breaker ||
|-------|-------|-----------------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, `Error` consumed, never redefined; `trait Breaker: private::Sealed` contract declared here |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | Breaker decision is applied before caller sends to an `Endpoint`; crate never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Sign/hash-chain breaker audit entries; encrypt breaker state at rest |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic IDS standard time source | Reset timeouts, handshake deadlines, backoff scheduling — never wall-clock |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (breaker user) | Wraps writes/reads to a peer `Endpoint` with that peer's breaker |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization (breaker user) | Replica-to-peer datagrams gated by per-peer breakers |
| `ids-fragment` | Record fragments/shards (breaker user) | Fragment send path gated by target-peer breaker |
| `ids-session` (Phase 050) | Client-session binding | Handshake circuit breaker protects session handshakes with `HandshakeId` keys |
| `ids-bulkhead` (Phase 079) | Resource isolation (companion) | Composes with circuit breaker: breaker fails fast, bulkhead caps concurrent calls |
| `ids-observability` | Metric/trace sinks | Consumes breaker state/transition/rejection metrics |

**Integration points:** `ids-circuit-breaker` declares the sealed `Breaker` contract and breaker types; consumers call `admit(key)` then `record(key, outcome)` around each protected operation, and route admitted traffic only to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli` beyond exposed contracts.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Three-state breaker** — `CircuitState { Closed, Open, HalfOpen }`; `admit(key)` returns `Decision { Admit | RejectFast | Probe }`; closed passes through and records outcomes; open rejects fast until reset timeout; half-open admits probes only.

2. **Failure counting (two policies)** — consecutive-failure streak (opens at `failure_threshold` in a row; success resets) and sliding-window failure rate (`failures / min(window_size, outcomes) ≥ failure_rate_threshold` once `minimum_calls` recorded); breaker trips on whichever fires first.

3. **Half-open probe with stampede protection** — at most `half_open_max_calls` concurrent probes; excess calls rejected instantly without counting as failures; `success_threshold` consecutive probe successes → CLOSED; any probe failure → OPEN with backoff-applied reset timeout.

4. **Backoff strategies** — `Fixed` (constant `reset_timeout`), `Exponential` (`reset_timeout × factor` per consecutive trip, capped at `max_reset_timeout`), `ExponentialJitter` (full/equal/decorrelated jitter so recovering peers don't retry in lockstep); per-trip attempt counter; TTL auto-closes stale breakers.

5. **Per-peer breaker map** — `HashMap<NodeId, Breaker>`; one breaker per peer target; per-peer outcomes never leak into other peers' breakers (blast-radius isolation).

6. **Global breaker aggregation** — roll up per-peer outcomes into fleet-wide failure rate; global trips on rate threshold or derived all-open signal; callers consult global gate first, then per-peer.

7. **Handshake breaker with deadline** — per-`HandshakeId` breaker bounded by `IdsTime` monotonic deadline; handshake timeout/failure trips; single probe on recovery; separate key space from data-plane breakers.

8. **Failure predicate** — `classify(outcome) -> BreakerWorthy | NotCounted`: timeouts and transport errors count; business rejections and caller cancellations do not; timeouts keyed to `ids-time`.

9. **Breaker metrics** — per-circuit state gauge, success/failure/rejected counters, transition timestamps, open duration; alert rules for stuck-open and flapping.

10. **Audit chain** — each state transition = `{from, to, reason, NodeId, IdsTime}` entry, blake3/sha256 hash-chained, periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable.

### 8. Dependencies

|| Crate | Purpose ||
|-------|---------|---------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Canonical types (`NodeId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts |
| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` type only — decision is applied before caller sends to an `Endpoint` |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic ticks for reset timeouts, handshake deadlines, backoff |
| `serde` | Serialization of breaker envelopes, audit entries, metrics |
| `thiserror` | Error types |

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, TCP/IP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS implementations in or under `ids-circuit-breaker`. No crypto beyond the allowed list; all crypto via `ids-crypto`. No async runtime (sync state machine; consumers drive timing through `ids-time`).

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete thresholds per circuit:** defaults (`failure_threshold=5`, `failure_rate_threshold=0.50`, `minimum_calls=10`, `window_size=100`, `success_threshold=2`, `reset_timeout=30s`) are starting points; production tuning requires observed error-rate baselines from `ids-store`/`ids-replication` integration.
2. **Backoff factor and cap:** exponential factor (1.5–2.0) and `max_reset_timeout` unquantified; trade-off between recovery speed and peer protection.
3. **Half-open probe count vs success threshold:** whether `half_open_max_calls` equals `success_threshold` or allows multiple windows (per Tencent Cloud config where attempts < required successes spans multiple sleep windows).
4. **Distributed breaker state:** whether breaker state should ever be shared across nodes (Redis/PostgreSQL-backed) — explicitly out of scope for Phase 078; per-node local state is the design.
5. **Interaction with `ids-bulkhead` (Phase 079):** breaker fails fast; bulkhead caps concurrency; exact composition order (bulkhead around breaker vs breaker around bulkhead) TBD at integration.
6. **Interaction with `ids-session` (Phase 050):** handshake breaker keyed by `HandshakeId`; session-handshake handshake off TBD at integration.
7. **Metrics export format:** Prometheus/OpenTelemetry vs IDS-native `ids-observability` sink; to be decided at integration.
8. **Per-call timeout source:** whether per-call timeout uses `ids-time` ticks directly or a deadline wrapper passed by the caller.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Separate `ids-circuit-breaker` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear failure-isolation boundary |
| Three-state machine (Closed/Open/HalfOpen) | Industry-standard pattern (Fowler, Azure, Resilience4j, SmallRye); fail fast + automatic recovery detection |
| Key circuits by `NodeId`, not network address | Carrier-agnostic; breaker is a peer-scoped decision applied before sending to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` |
| Per-peer breakers as default scope | Isolates one failing peer; blast-radius bounded (A2A architecture, per-replica breaker research) |
| Global breaker on aggregate/all-open signal | Complements per-peer layer without the "one slow node trips the fleet" anti-pattern |
| Rate-based + consecutive failure thresholds | Rate-based is scale-independent (50% default); consecutive catches hard-down dependencies fast |
| `success_threshold` probes + `half_open_max_calls` stampede protection | Half-open probes test recovery without re-overloading (SmallRye, bjaus/breaker) |
| Backoff: Fixed/Exponential/ExponentialJitter | Jitter breaks retry synchrony (AWS backoff-and-jitter research); cap prevents runaway open durations |
| `ids-time` monotonic ticks only, no wall-clock | Clock manipulation cannot corrupt timeouts or deadlines |
| Failure predicate for classification | Business rejections/cancellations must not trip the breaker (Resilience4j record/ignore exceptions) |
| Per-node local state, no distributed sync | Matches IDS no-central-coordinator philosophy; carrier-agnostic; no shared storage dependency |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence for trip/close decisions |
| Allowed crypto only via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
| Sealed `Breaker` trait via private supertrait | Rust API Guidelines C-SEALED; consistent with `ids-000-aa` contracts |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 079 creates `ids-bulkhead`, the IDS crate for resource isolation to prevent cascade failure. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by isolation dimension: thread-pool isolation, connection-pool isolation, memory isolation, CPU isolation, failure-domain isolation, and blast-radius limitation. `ids-bulkhead` implements the bulkhead pattern — isolating resources into independent compartments so that failure or overload in one compartment cannot drain resources needed by other compartments. All protected operations ride opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); the crate never touches `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh, and never sends bytes itself — it returns an admit/reject/defer decision that the caller frames to an `Endpoint`.

**Core design:** a registry of named bulkheads, each backed by a bounded resource pool with admission control. Each bulkhead enforces a hard concurrency limit (semaphore-style permits) plus an optional bounded wait queue. Admission strategies: immediate rejection (fail-fast), bounded FIFO queue with timeout, priority-based admission with reserved capacity, and load shedding. Bulkheads compose with circuit breakers (ids-circuit-breaker, Phase 078): the breaker fails fast, the bulkhead caps concurrency. Composition order is circuit-breaker → bulkhead → call so doomed calls never consume a bulkhead permit.

**Scope boundary:** `ids-bulkhead` decides admission; it does not execute, send, or retry. Callers (ids-store, ids-replication, ids-fragment, ids-session, ids-circuit-breaker consumers) route every outbound datagram through the relevant bulkhead for the target resource pool, then act on the decision. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` (bulkhead audit entries are signed/hash-chained; crypto ops live in `ids-crypto`).

A skeleton `ids-bulkhead` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-bulkhead/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, `Error`, `FailureDomain`) and sealed trait contracts, consumed but never redefined. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned Michael Nygard's *Release It!* bulkhead pattern (2007, watertight-compartment ship analogy); Wikipedia Bulkhead pattern (failure compartmentalization, combined with circuit breakers/retries); Microsoft Azure Architecture Center bulkhead pattern (cell-based architecture, per-consumer connection pools, QoS levels); systemoverflow bulkhead pattern (isolating failures through resource partitioning, blast radius); Hystrix bulkhead (per-dependency thread pools vs semaphore isolation); resilience4j Bulkhead (SemaphoreBulkhead maxConcurrentCalls/maxWaitDuration; FixedThreadPoolBulkhead maxThreadPoolSize/coreThreadPoolSize/queueCapacity/keepAliveDuration; default maxConcurrentCalls 25, maxWaitDuration 0); bulkhead vs circuit breaker composition order (breaker first so bulkhead capacity isn't wasted on doomed requests); admission-control strategies (immediate rejection, bounded queue, timeout admission, priority admission, load shedding); bounded-queue backpressure (tail drop vs head drop, Little's Law L=λ×W, coordinated omission); M/M/1 queueing theory and saturation; adaptive concurrency limiting (AIMD, Vegas, Gradient2 — Envoy adaptive concurrency filter, tower-resilience); priority-based rejection with reserved capacity; weighted concurrency + strict FIFO bounded waiting (go-bulkhead); Rust implementations: reliakit-bulkhead (no_std, zero dependencies, try_acquire/release, no RAII guard, saturating arithmetic), tower-resilience-bulkhead (tokio-based BulkheadLayer, max_concurrent_calls, max_wait_duration), tokio::sync::Semaphore async concurrency limiting; rate-limiting vs concurrency-limiting distinction.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-bulkhead` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types, sealed contracts, errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives), and `ids-time` (monotonic ticks for timeouts). It is an admission-control layer: given an operation targeted at a named resource pool, it returns `Admit | Reject | Defer` and records pool occupancy. It never opens a socket, never dials an address, and never sends bytes — the caller frames the datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` only when the bulkhead admits.

```
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CALLER LAYER (ids-store, ids-replication, …)                         │
│  build datagram → call bulkhead.admit(pool) → send or reject/defer                     │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 079: ids-bulkhead (THIS CRATE — admission layer)               │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐  │
│  │ bulkhead_registry│ │ thread_pool      │ │ connection_pool  │ │ memory           │  │
│  │ (keyed by PoolId)│ │ isolation        │ │ isolation        │ │ isolation        │  │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘  │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐  │
│  │ cpu              │ │ failure_domain   │ │ blast_radius     │ │ admission        │  │
│  │ isolation        │ │ isolation        │ │ limitation       │ │ control          │  │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ (reject/queue/   │  │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ └──────────────────┘ │  priority/shed)  │  │
│  │ backoff_strategy │ │ metrics          │                      │                  │  │
│  │ (fixed/exp/jitter│ │ (occupancy,      │                      │                  │  │
│  │  retry attempts) │ │ rejections, waits│                      │                  │  │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘                      │                  │  │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │                  │  │
│  │ audit            │ │ priority/reserve │ │ cpu_limiter      │ │                  │  │
│  │ (signed+chained  │ │ capacity         │ │ (token bucket)   │ │                  │  │
│  │  decisions)      │ │                  │ │ mem_limiter      │ │                  │  │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ (watermark)      │                  │  │
└───────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┴──────────────────┘
                                            │ Admit → caller sends opaque Vec<u28>
                                            │ Reject → caller fails fast
                                            │ Defer  → caller queues/retry later
                                            ▼
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                               │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])          │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                                 │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS /               │
│  Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh                                             │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Per-bulkhead admission lifecycle:** `OPEN` (admit up to `max_concurrent`; queue up to `max_queued` if configured; reject beyond) → on permit release, admit next queued waiter (FIFO) → saturated pool rejects new arrivals immediately (or after `max_wait`). Each resource dimension (thread pool, connection pool, memory, CPU, failure domain) is a separate named bulkhead so overload in one dimension starves none of the others.

**Failure-domain isolation:** each bulkhead is tagged with a `FailureDomain` (from `ids-000-aa`); correlated-failure domains share no permits, so a domain-wide failure drains only that domain's pool.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 to sign bulkhead admission/audit entries; sha256/blake3 to hash-chain the decision log and derive bulkhead IDs; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt bulkhead state at rest where confidentiality is required.
