### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Bulkhead pattern origin and ship analogy

**Source:** Michael Nygard *Release It!* (2007, stability patterns incl. bulkhead); Wikipedia Bulkhead pattern; Microsoft Azure Architecture Center bulkhead pattern; systemoverflow bulkhead pattern.

The bulkhead pattern is named after the watertight compartments of a ship's hull: a hull breach floods only the breached compartment, not the whole vessel. In software, resources are partitioned into independent compartments so that failure, latency, or resource exhaustion in one compartment cannot drain resources needed by other compartments. Without bulkheads, a single slow dependency (e.g. a slow database query) can exhaust all threads in a shared pool, blocking unrelated requests that never touch that dependency — a classic cascade failure. `ids-bulkhead` implements this compartmentalization per resource dimension.

#### 3.2 Thread pool isolation

**Source:** Hystrix bulkhead (per-dependency thread pools, semaphore isolation); resilience4j FixedThreadPoolBulkhead (maxThreadPoolSize, coreThreadPoolSize, queueCapacity, keepAliveDuration); systemoverflow bulkhead (separate thread pools per dependency, 50 threads each).

Each downstream dependency gets its own thread pool. Requests to resource-pool A execute on Pool A; requests to Pool B execute on Pool B. When Pool A is exhausted, new A requests are rejected/queued within Pool A only; Pool B continues operating. Per-pool queue size trades latency for throughput: longer queues absorb bursts but increase wait time; for latency-sensitive paths use small queues (5–10) or no queue (fail immediately when pool exhausted). `ids-bulkhead` models thread-pool isolation as a bounded-concurrency bulkhead per pool keyed by `PoolId`.

#### 3.3 Connection pool isolation

**Source:** Microsoft Azure Architecture Center bulkhead (per-service connection pools; one failing service affects only its own pool); Hystrix bulkhead (connection-pool per dependency).

A consumer that calls multiple services is assigned a separate connection pool per service. If one service begins to fail, only its connection pool is affected; the consumer continues using other services. `ids-bulkhead` models connection-pool isolation identically to thread-pool isolation — a bounded pool of "connection slots" per target pool, with admission control deciding whether a new connection attempt may proceed.

#### 3.4 Memory isolation

**Source:** resource-governor / resource-bulkhead research (partition memory so one workload cannot consume all memory); geeksforgeeks bulkhead resource-bulkhead (partition system resources incl. memory).

Memory is a shared, unbounded-by-default resource: one workload allocating unboundedly can trigger OOM for all workloads. Memory isolation partitions memory into per-bulkhead budgets (watermark-based: soft limit triggers load shed, hard limit rejects). `ids-bulkhead` exposes a `mem_limiter` per bulkhead with watermarks; allocations beyond the hard watermark are rejected before touching storage/downstream services.

#### 3.5 CPU isolation

**Source:** resource-bulkhead research (partition CPU so one workload cannot saturate CPU); lean-ctx process-guard (fixed concurrent-slot limit).

CPU isolation limits the number of CPU-bound operations running concurrently per bulkhead (a token-bucket or semaphore over CPU slots). A CPU-hungry workload cannot starve latency-sensitive work because each bulkhead caps its own concurrent CPU operations. `ids-bulkhead` exposes a `cpu_limiter` per bulkhead backed by bounded permits; excess CPU work is queued or rejected.

#### 3.6 Failure domain isolation

**Source:** ids-000-aa `FailureDomain` type and `correlated_failure` invariant; correlated-failure modeling; failure-domain boundaries containing failures.

A failure domain is a boundary (power, facility, network segment, operator, geography) inside which failures are correlated. Bulkheads tagged with distinct `FailureDomain`s share no permits and no state, so a domain-wide failure drains only that domain's pool. `ids-bulkhead` integrates `FailureDomain` from `ids-000-aa` so domain isolation is enforced at the type level.

#### 3.7 Blast radius limitation

**Source:** blast-radius research (bulkhead limits blast radius to one compartment); Azure well-architected reliability (segmentation contains faults to one bulkhead).

Blast radius = the set of components affected by a single failure. Bulkheads bound blast radius to the compartment where the failure occurs. `ids-bulkhead` quantifies blast radius per bulkhead (max concurrent ops × max queued ops) and enforces it as a hard cap; no single overload can exceed its compartment's budget.

#### 3.8 Bulkhead variants: semaphore vs thread-pool/bounded-queue

**Source:** resilience4j Bulkhead (SemaphoreBulkhead vs FixedThreadPoolBulkhead); systemoverflow bulkhead implementation (thread pools, connection pools, semaphores); stackoverflow Hystrix bulkhead Q&A (thread isolation vs semaphore isolation).

Two canonical implementations:
- **Semaphore bulkhead:** limits concurrent executions on the calling thread; acquire/release a permit; full ⇒ immediate reject (or wait up to `maxWaitDuration`). Low overhead, no extra threads.
- **Thread-pool/queue bulkhead:** bounded queue + dedicated thread pool; caller submits and returns; pool exhaustion ⇒ reject. Caller thread is freed immediately.

`ids-bulkhead` supports both variants behind a sealed `AdmissionPolicy` trait; the semaphore variant is the default (no runtime threads, carrier-agnostic friendly).

#### 3.9 Admission control strategies

**Source:** onenoughtone bulkhead admission control; systemoverflow bulkhead failure handling/rejection strategies; go-bulkhead (RejectImmediately vs Wait with FIFO).

When a bulkhead is full, the system must decide:
- **Immediate rejection (fail-fast):** reject instantly, sub-millisecond; caller retries/uses fallback. Best for latency-sensitive paths.
- **Bounded queue:** queue up to `max_queued`, then reject. Absorbs brief spikes but adds latency; queue timeout must be shorter than caller timeout.
- **Timeout-based admission:** wait up to `max_wait` for a permit; reject on timeout.
- **Priority-based admission:** higher-priority requests admitted first; low-priority rejected first near capacity; reserved capacity for VIP/health checks.
- **Load shedding:** proactively reject before saturation based on leading indicators (rising latency, error rate).

`ids-bulkhead` supports all five strategies via `AdmissionPolicy`; default = immediate rejection with optional bounded queue.

#### 3.10 Head-of-line blocking and lane isolation

**Source:** gojek engineering per-bank consumer lanes (bulkhead killed head-of-line blocking); per-bank lanes with priority vs bulk traffic.

Without lane separation, bursty "bulk" traffic starves sporadic "priority" traffic sharing the same consumers. Full isolation per lane (per bank, transfer type, priority) contains failure completely and allows independent throughput tuning. `ids-bulkhead` supports per-lane bulkheads so priority vs bulk traffic never contend.

#### 3.11 Backpressure, bounded queues, tail drop vs head drop

**Source:** readpipe network queues (tail drop vs backpressure; head drop better than tail drop in many cases); ironclad backpressure/flow control (bounded buffer forces backpressure; block/reject/drop-oldest); task-queues backpressure strategies; leaky-bucket overflow.

An unbounded queue absorbs everything until OOM; a bounded queue exerts backpressure. Overflow choices: block producer, reject work, or drop. Drop variants: tail drop (newest), head drop (oldest — better for stale work), priority-based (sacrifice low priority first), random. Queue depth should be sized from max acceptable latency: `capacity = max_latency × drain_rate` (Little's Law). Reject early and cheaply beats rejecting after expensive work. `ids-bulkhead` makes queue depth a deliberate, configurable number and offers tail/head/priority drop.

#### 3.12 Queueing theory: M/M/1 saturation and Little's Law

**Source:** MIT urban_or M/M/1 finite capacity; LibreTexts queueing (saturation λ vs μ); arxiv Erlang Redux M/M/m (iron law R=S+W; Little's Law Q=λR).

Little's Law: at fixed throughput, bounding queue length strictly bounds latency. As λ approaches μ (saturation), queue length and wait time grow without bound. Finite-capacity queues reach steady state even when oversaturated — excess users are turned away (blocking probability = probability queue is full). `ids-bulkhead` uses finite-capacity pools precisely so saturation turns into controlled rejection, not unbounded latency.

#### 3.13 Bulkhead vs circuit breaker composition

**Source:** onenoughtone bulkhead vs circuit breaker; systemoverflow bulkhead vs circuit breakers; Azure circuit breaker vs bulkhead; Release It stability patterns.

- **Circuit breaker** detects failures and stops calls (fails fast on known-bad destination).
- **Bulkhead** contains damage while detection happens (limits concurrency even on slow-but-successful calls).
- Composition order matters: circuit-breaker → bulkhead → call. If bulkhead is evaluated first, a circuit-open call still consumes a permit, wasting capacity under sustained failure.
- A circuit breaker takes 10–30s to trip; without bulkheads that window can exhaust all resources. `ids-bulkhead` explicitly composes with ids-circuit-breaker (Phase 078) in breaker-first order.

#### 3.14 Adaptive concurrency limiting

**Source:** Envoy adaptive concurrency filter (minRTT, headroom, AIMD/gradient); tower-resilience adaptive limiter (AIMD/Vegas/Gradient2); resile adaptive limiter (TCP-Vegas style, RTT-based multiplicative decrease/additive increase).

Static bulkheads pick a fixed number; adaptive limiters tune the concurrency limit in real time from observed latency/error. `ids-bulkhead` provides static bulkheads by default and documents an optional `AdaptiveLimiter` extension (AIMD/Vegas) for dynamic environments; the adaptive layer is explicitly future work, not Phase 079 scope.

#### 3.15 Rust bulkhead implementations and no_std style

**Source:** reliakit-bulkhead (no_std, zero deps, no unsafe, try_acquire/release, Copy type, saturating arithmetic); tower-resilience-bulkhead (tokio-based BulkheadLayer); tokio::sync::Semaphore docs (fair FIFO permits, acquire_owned for task boundaries).

- `reliakit-bulkhead`: counting semaphore, no blocking/queueing/clock/allocation, `no_std`, `Copy`, permits paired manually (no RAII). Ideal carrier-agnostic foundation.
- `tower-resilience-bulkhead`: tokio async, `max_concurrent_calls` + `max_wait_duration`, callbacks on permit/reject.
- `tokio::sync::Semaphore`: fair FIFO async semaphore; permits movable across tasks via `acquire_owned`.

`ids-bulkhead` follows the `reliakit-bulkhead` style: `no_std`-compatible core, zero dependencies beyond `ids-000-aa`/`ids-time`/`ids-crypto`, no unsafe, saturating arithmetic, manual permit pairing. Async waiting (if any) is opt-in via a feature gated on `ids-time` deadlines, never `tokio::net`.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
||--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
|| Cascade failure: one overloaded dependency drains shared resources | System stability | Per-resource-pool bulkhead isolates the overloaded pool; healthy pools keep admitting |
|| Bulkhead saturation wastes capacity on doomed calls | Availability | Circuit-breaker → bulkhead → call order (breaker first); doomed calls never acquire a permit |
|| Recovery stampede re-overloading a just-recovered pool | Peer/pool recovery | Bounded wait queue + max_wait; FIFO admission; no permit hoarding |
|| Threshold too sensitive (flapping) or too lax (sends traffic into outage) | Correctness | Configurable max_concurrent/max_queued/max_wait per bulkhead; defaults tuned above normal load |
|| Unbounded queue → OOM and unbounded latency | Stability/Liveness | Hard queue capacity; deliberate bound sized via Little's Law; no unbounded queues |
|| Memory/CPU starvation by one workload | Stability | Separate mem_limiter/cpu_limiter bulkheads with hard watermarks |
|| Failure domain drains unrelated domains | Stability | FailureDomain-tagged bulkheads share no permits/state |
|| Clock manipulation for wait/deadline | Correctness | ids-time monotonic ticks only; no wall-clock |
|| Replay/forgery of admission decisions | Decision integrity | ed25519-signed, sha256/blake3 hash-chained audit log; offline verifiable |
|| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Policy compliance | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 via ids-crypto; allowlist test |
|| Bulkhead keyed by network address (couples to carrier) | Carrier-agnosticism | Keyed by PoolId/FailureDomain; decision applied to ids-carrier::Endpoint by caller; crate never addresses sockets |
|| Bulkhead rejecting calls it should admit (false positive) | Availability | max_queued + max_wait absorb bursts; failure classification excludes non-overload rejections |
|| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Bulkhead is idempotent on occupancy; duplicates counted once per admit |

The carrier is never trusted: bulkhead decisions are local observations of pool occupancy; no network stack is in the trust base.

No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli` beyond exposed contracts.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

1. **Bulkhead admission** — `admit(pool) -> Decision { Admit | Reject | Defer }`; `release(pool)` frees a permit; occupancy = in-flight + queued; admit succeeds iff occupancy < max_concurrent (or queue has space for Defer).
2. **Semaphore bulkhead** — bounded permits; acquire on admit, release on complete; full ⇒ immediate reject (default) or bounded wait; no RAII guard (permit paired manually), `no_std`-friendly.
3. **Thread-pool/queue bulkhead** — bounded queue + permit pool; caller submits and returns; pool exhaustion ⇒ reject; caller thread freed immediately.
4. **Admission policies** — immediate rejection (fail-fast), bounded FIFO queue with `max_wait` deadline, timeout-based admission, priority-based admission with reserved capacity, load shedding; selected per bulkhead via `AdmissionPolicy`.
5. **Per-pool registry** — `HashMap<PoolId, Bulkhead>`; one bulkhead per resource pool; per-pool occupancy never leaks into other pools (blast-radius isolation).
6. **Failure-domain tagging** — each bulkhead tagged with `FailureDomain`; distinct domains share no permits/state; domain-wide failure drains only that domain's pool.
7. **Memory limiter** — watermark-based: soft watermark triggers load shed, hard watermark rejects; budget tracked in bytes; no unbounded allocation.
8. **CPU limiter** — token bucket over `ids-time` ticks; bounded concurrent CPU operations; excess queued/rejected.
9. **Backoff strategies** — `Fixed` (constant delay), `Exponential` (factor × delay per retry, capped), `ExponentialJitter` (full/equal/decorrelated jitter so retries don't synchronize); per-retry attempt counter.
10. **Wait queue** — bounded FIFO with `max_queued` capacity and `max_wait` deadline; head-drop/tail-drop/priority-drop overflow policies; waiters admitted in FIFO order on permit release.
11. **Bulkhead metrics** — per-bulkhead occupancy gauge, success/rejection/wait counters, saturation ratio; alert rules for stuck-full and high rejection.
12. **Audit chain** — each admission decision = `{decision, PoolId, FailureDomain, IdsTime}` entry, sha256/blake3 hash-chained, periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable.

---

### 8. Dependencies

|| Crate | Purpose ||
||-------|---------|---------|
|| `ids-000-aa` | Canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `IdsTime`, `Checksum`, `Error`, `FailureDomain`) and sealed trait contracts |
|| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` type only — decision applied before caller sends to an `Endpoint` |
|| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 |
|| `ids-time` | Monotonic ticks for wait timeouts, deadlines, backoff |
|| `serde` | Serialization of bulkhead envelopes, audit entries, metrics |
|| `thiserror` | Error types |

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, TCP/IP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS implementations in or under `ids-bulkhead`. No crypto beyond the allowed list; all crypto via `ids-crypto`. No async runtime (sync admission state machine; consumers drive timing through `ids-time`; optional async-wait feature gated on `ids-time` deadlines only).

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete limits per pool:** defaults (`max_concurrent`, `max_queued`, `max_wait`) are starting points; production tuning requires observed load baselines from `ids-store`/`ids-replication` integration.
2. **Async-wait feature:** whether `max_wait` > 0 requires an async runtime or can be implemented with `ids-time`-deadline polling; opt-in feature gating TBD.
3. **Adaptive limiter:** whether to include an optional AIMD/Vegas adaptive concurrency limiter (future work; explicitly out of Phase 079 scope).
4. **Interaction with `ids-circuit-breaker` (Phase 078):** breaker-first composition order confirmed, but exact wrapping (bulkhead around breaker vs breaker around bulkhead per call site) TBD at integration.
5. **Interaction with `ids-backpressure` (Phase 080):** bulkhead caps concurrency, backpressure signals queue full; combined admission+backpressure flow TBD at integration.
6. **Metrics export format:** Prometheus/OpenTelemetry vs IDS-native `ids-observability` sink; to be decided at integration.
7. **Memory/CPU accounting granularity:** whether limits are per-bulkhead or per-pool-plus-domain; cross-product cardinality impact on registry size.
8. **Overflow drop policy default:** tail-drop vs head-drop vs priority-drop as the default when queue is full; head-drop better for stale work, tail-drop simpler.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| Separate `ids-bulkhead` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear resource-isolation boundary |
|| Semaphore bulkhead as default variant | Low overhead, no runtime threads, carrier-agnostic-friendly; matches `reliakit-bulkhead` no_std style |
|| Admission policies: reject/queue/defer/priority/shed | Covers fail-fast, burst absorption, timed wait, priority reservation, proactive shed (onenoughtone/systemoverflow/go-bulkhead research) |
|| Bounded queues only, sized via Little's Law | Unbounded queues → OOM + unbounded latency; finite capacity turns saturation into controlled rejection (M/M/1, Little's Law research) |
|| Key bulkheads by `PoolId`, not network address | Carrier-agnostic; decision applied before sending to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` |
|| Per-pool bulkheads as default scope | Isolates one overloaded pool; blast-radius bounded to compartment |
|| FailureDomain-tagged bulkheads | Domain-wide failures drain only that domain's pool; type-level integration with `ids-000-aa` |
|| Circuit-breaker → bulkhead → call order | Prevents bulkhead capacity wasted on doomed calls; breaker fails fast, bulkhead caps concurrency (onenoughtone/systemoverflow research) |
|| `ids-time` monotonic ticks only, no wall-clock | Clock manipulation cannot corrupt waits or deadlines |
|| Backoff: Fixed/Exponential/ExponentialJitter | Jitter breaks retry synchrony (AWS backoff-and-jitter research); cap prevents runaway delays |
|| Permit pairing manual (no RAII), `no_std`-compatible core | Keeps crate minimal, allocation-free in steady state, usable from sync and async contexts |
|| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence for admit/reject/defer |
|| Allowed crypto only via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
|| Sealed `Bulkhead` trait via private supertrait | Rust API Guidelines C-SEALED; consistent with `ids-000-aa` contracts |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 080 creates `ids-backpressure`, the IDS crate for flow control under load. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by flow-control mechanism. `ids-backpressure` provides: credit-based flow control (per-endpoint credit windows, credit reservation, credit return), blocked signal emission (backpressure signals propagate upstream through opaque datagrams), queue management (bounded queues with configurable overflow policy), load shedding (drop/priority shed when overloaded), adaptive rate limiting (PID + gradient-based rate adjustment), and congestion detection (queue-delay, loss, ECN-style signals). All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` address ≤ 1024 bytes); `ids-backpressure` never opens a socket, never imports a networking crate, and never touches `std::net`/`tokio::net`/libp2p/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS or any carrier by name. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` only; `ids-backpressure` implements no crypto itself.

`ids-backpressure` is a policy/admission layer above `ids-000-aa` (types, sealed contracts, invariants, errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It does not send bytes itself; it returns credit grants, backpressure signals, admit/drop/shed decisions, and rate limits that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

**Core design:** a per-endpoint credit window (`Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)`, credit-grant/credit-return/credit-reserve protocol) plus an adaptive rate limiter (PID/gradient on queue delay + RTT) plus a load shedder (criticality-ranked drop when queue depth crosses watermarks). Congestion is detected from queue sojourn time (CoDel-style, target ~5 ms), loss-rate, and ECN-style marks carried inside opaque datagram envelopes. Backpressure signals ("blocked" emission) travel as opaque datagrams on `ids-carrier::Endpoint`, never on any network stack.

**Scope boundary:** `ids-backpressure` admits, credits, sheds, and rates; it does not implement transport reliability, retransmission, or ordering (those live in `ids-transport`/`ids-carrier`). It never trusts the carrier: credit decisions and audit entries are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing. Skeleton `ids-backpressure` does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-backpressure/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned Reactive Streams (demand signaling `request(n)`, non-blocking backpressure, publisher bounded by demand), DLEP RFC 9893 (credit-window flow control, per-flow credit windows, Credit Window Grant/Status/Request data items), Kung & Morris IEEE Network 1995 / ATM credit-based flow control (`Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)`, credit cell per forwarded cell, receiver-oriented adaptive buffer allocation), Flink credit-based flow control (1 buffer = 1 credit, channel credits, backlog reporting), Google SRE load shedding (observe local load, drop fraction of traffic, stack-rank by criticality), Netflix concurrency-limits `Gradient2Limit` (adaptive concurrency from RTT gradient vs EWMA base RTT), Uber Cinnamon (PID rate limiter, dynamic priority threshold, load shedding), BBR (bandwidth-delay product, min RTT, PROBE_BW/PROBE_RTT), CoDel RFC 8289 (queue sojourn time as congestion signal, TARGET 5 ms, control law), RED (random early detection, average queue size thresholds), ECN (explicit congestion notification marking), HTTP/2 RFC 9113 (WINDOW_UPDATE credit-based flow control, 65,535 octet initial window), SCTP/WebRTC advertised receiver window credit, tokio mpsc bounded channels with `reserve`/`Permit` (credit-like admission), actor bounded mailboxes (drop-new/drop-head/reject), Little's law (L = λW), token bucket / leaky bucket.

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-backpressure` sits above `ids-000-aa`, `ids-carrier`, and `ids-crypto`. It is an admission/flow-control layer: given an inbound datagram destined for an `ids-carrier::Endpoint`, it decides (a) whether the sender holds sufficient credit, (b) whether to admit, delay, or shed the datagram, (c) what rate limit applies, and (d) what backpressure/blocked signal to emit upstream. It never sends bytes itself; it returns `CreditDecision`, `AdmitDecision`, `ShedDecision`, `RateLimit`, and `BackpressureSignal` that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (flow-control users)               │
│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-fragment — send datagrams with credit tag     │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 080: ids-backpressure (THIS CRATE — policy/admission)      │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ │\\n│  │ credit window    │ │ credit           │ │ queue          │ │ load       │ │ │\\n│  │ (per endpoint)   │ │ reservation/     │ │ management     │ │ shedding     │ │ │\\n│  │ Crd_Bal formula  │ │ credit return    │ │ bounded queues   │ │ (criticality │ │ │\\n│  │ grant/return/reserve│ │                  │ │ overflow policy  │ │ ranked drop) │ │ │\\n└──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────┘ │ │\\n│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │                │ │ │\\n│  │ adaptive rate    │ │ congestion       │ │ blocked signal   │ │                │ │ │\\n│  │ limiter (PID/    │ │ detection (delay │ │ emission (opaque │ │                │ │ │\\n│  │  gradient/token bucket)│ │  sojourn/loss/ECN)│ │  datagram)      │ │                │ │ │\\n│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                │ │\\n│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │                │                │ │ │\\n│  │ audit/logging    │ │ crypto surface   │ │                │                │ │ │\\n│  │ (signed+chained) │ │ (allowed set only)│ │                │                │ │ │\\n│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │                │                │ │\\n└─────────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┴──────────────┘\\n                                              │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams\\n┌─────────────────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────┐\\n│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only      │\\n│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType≤1024B addr, Vec<u8>}, payload)│\\n│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                        │\\n│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC /   │\\n│  HTTP / DNS / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh        │\\n└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a credit-gated send:** caller submits `Send{endpoint, payload, priority, credit_cost}` → `ids-backpressure` checks the endpoint's credit window: if `Crd_Bal ≥ credit_cost`, reserve credit, decrement `Crd_Bal`, return `Admit{reserved_credit, rate_limit, deadline}` → caller sends the datagram as opaque bytes to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` → on receiver processing/forwarding, receiver emits `CreditReturn{fwd_cnt}` as opaque datagram → sender updates `Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)`. If `Crd_Bal < credit_cost`, return `Backpressure{blocked_until, signal}` → caller emits a blocked/backpressure signal upstream as opaque datagram and waits.

**Data flow of load shedding:** when queue depth crosses high watermark, `load_shedder` ranks incoming datagrams by criticality and drops/sheds lower-priority traffic; emits `ShedDecision{dropped, reason, backpressure_signal}`; when depth falls below low watermark, resume admission (XON/XOFF-style hysteresis).

**Congestion detection:** per-endpoint queue sojourn time, loss rate, and ECN-style marks inside envelopes feed `congestion_detector`; when sojourn > TARGET for interval, enter drop state and increase drop probability (CoDel control law `t + INTERVAL / sqrt(count)`); when below target, cancel drops.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing credit/backpressure/audit decisions; sha256/blake3 for credit-window IDs, envelope hashing, audit-chain links; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt credit state / backpressure state at rest when confidentiality required.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Credit-based flow control (credit window, grant/return/reserve)

**Source:** DLEP RFC 9893 (credit-window flow control, per-flow credit windows, Credit Window Grant/Status/Request/Initialization/Association data items); Kung & Morris IEEE Network 1995 (ATM credit-based flow control, `Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)`, credit cell per forwarded cell, receiver-oriented adaptive buffer allocation); Flink credit-based flow control (1 buffer = 1 credit, channel credits, backlog reporting, backpressure on a logical channel only).

Credit-based flow control: before forwarding any datagram, the sender must hold credits for the endpoint's credit window. The receiver sends credits indicating available buffer space. Each sent datagram decrements `Crd_Bal` by its cost; each processed/forwarded datagram returns a credit. `Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cint)` guarantees the receiver buffer never overflows: overflow is impossible even under abrupt stop/start because buffer ≥ Rate × RTT (one BDP). Lost/delayed feedback does not hurt — the sender uses the previous allowance; transmission can be stopped completely (rate → 0). Credit windows may be shared or dedicated per endpoint/destination. `ids-backpressure` implements `CreditWindow{Buf_Alloc, Tx_Cnt, Fwd_Cnt, Crd_Bal, MaxSize}` per endpoint, with `credit_reserve(cost)`, `credit_return(fwd_cnt)`, `credit_grant(increment)` operations. Credit values are octet counts (include framing overhead, as in DLEP where credit value includes MAC headers).

#### 3.2 Blocked signal emission (backpressure signal)

**Source:** Reactive Streams spec (demand signaling `request(n)`, non-blocking backpressure, publisher never signals more than demand); Actor bounded mailboxes (bounded mailbox caps consumer memory; backpressure expressed through the messaging protocol, e.g. `bufferedAmountLow` threshold, dead-letter on reject).

When `Crd_Bal` hits 0 or queue depth crosses the high watermark, `ids-backpressure` emits a `BackpressureSignal{endpoint, reason, blocked_until, credit_needed}` as an opaque `Vec<u8>` datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. The upstream sender slows/stops emission until credits return or the signal clears. Blocked emission is non-blocking: the producer hands the signal to the carrier boundary and is not stalled on a thread. Backpressure propagates hop-by-hop through opaque datagrams, never through `std::net`/`tokio::net`.

#### 3.3 Queue management (bounded queues, overflow policy)

**Source:** Actor bounded mailbox patterns (drop-new/drop-head/reject, capacity sizing by worst-case burst and latency budget); Datadog Observability Pipelines (buffer on-full behavior: block vs drop-newest); Flink network stack (exclusive vs floating buffers, channel credits, backlog).

`ids-backpressure` manages bounded per-endpoint queues. Overflow policy is configurable: `DropNew` (discard incoming, preserve queued — critical work), `DropHead` (discard oldest, newest wins — telemetry), `Reject` (refuse and dead-letter — refusal on record), `Block` (propagate backpressure). Queue capacity is sized by worst-case burst size, per-message memory (`capacity × bytes`), and latency budget (`capacity / drain_rate`). Queue depth feeds the load shedder and congestion detector.

#### 3.4 Load shedding (criticality-ranked drop under overload)

**Source:** Google SRE load shedding (observe local load like CPU/memory/queue length; when above safe level, drop a fraction of incoming traffic; stack-rank requests by criticality, shed least-critical first); Netflix concurrency-limits (adaptive concurrency limit sheds excess load); RAJOMON (market-based overload control, tokens + prices).

`ids-backpressure` implements a load shedder: observe local load (queue depth, CPU, memory), and when it crosses a safe threshold, drop a fraction of incoming datagrams. Criticality is established per traffic class (control-plane vs data-plane, high-priority vs bulk). Shedding starts at `drop_fraction = 1/10` and ramps up as load stays high, ramps down as load returns to safe. Shedded datagrams are recorded in the audit log; `ShedDecision{dropped, reason, criticality, backpressure_signal}` is emitted.

#### 3.5 Adaptive rate limiting (PID / gradient / token bucket / leaky bucket)

**Source:** Uber Cinnamon (PID rate limiter, dynamic priority threshold, self-correction); Netflix `Gradient2Limit` (adaptive concurrency from RTT gradient vs EWMA base RTT); APNIC rate vs credit-based flow control (absolute vs differential rate adjustment, XON/XOFF); token bucket / leaky bucket (GeeksforGeys, Wikipedia, Cloudflare); Uber-go ratelimit (leaky bucket).

`ids-backpressure` implements adaptive rate limiting: a PID controller adjusts the sending rate based on error = target_latency − measured_latency (queue sojourn); a gradient-based limiter (Netflix style) adjusts concurrency from RTT gradient vs smoothed base RTT; token bucket (`rate` + `burst`) permits bursty traffic with a long-term average cap; leaky bucket smooths to a constant rate. Rate is adjusted dynamically (differential: speed-up/slow-down by Δ%) rather than absolute replacement, to avoid overreaction. `RateLimit{rate, burst, priority_threshold, adjustment_interval}` per endpoint.

#### 3.6 Congestion detection (queue delay, loss, ECN)

**Source:** CoDel RFC 8289 (queue sojourn time as congestion signal, TARGET 5 ms, control law `t + INTERVAL / sqrt(count)`, parameterless AQM); RED (random early detection, average queue size min/max thresholds, mark/drop probability); ECN (explicit congestion notification, CE marking instead of dropping); BBR (bandwidth-delay product, min RTT, BDP-based inflight bound); RFC 8085 UDP usage guidelines (UDP applications must employ congestion control to prevent collapse).

`ids-backpressure` detects congestion per endpoint from: (1) queue sojourn time (dequeue − enqueue) — CoDel-style, if min sojourn > TARGET for INTERVAL, enter drop state; (2) loss rate — lost datagrams / sent datagrams; (3) ECN-style marks inside opaque datagram envelopes (carrier-agnostic: marks are envelope fields, not IP ECN). Congestion state drives the rate limiter (reduce rate) and load shedder (increase drop fraction). BDP = bandwidth × min_RTT bounds in-flight data; `ids-backpressure` tracks BDP per endpoint to size credit windows.

#### 3.7 Credit reservation and return

Credit reservation: before constructing a datagram, the sender calls `credit_reserve(endpoint, cost)`; if `Crd_Bal ≥ cost`, credit is reserved (`Crd_Bal −= cost`, reservation recorded with timeout). If the datagram is never sent, the reservation is released (`credit_return` of the reserved amount). Credit return: when the receiver processes/forwards a datagram, it sends `CreditReturn{fwd_cnt, endpoint}`; sender updates `Fwd_Cnt` and recomputes `Crd_Bal`. Credit grant: receiver proactively grants additional credits (`CreditWindowGrant{additional_credits, endpoint}`) when buffer availability exceeds the window. All credit messages are opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

#### 3.8 Determinism and reproducibility

Every flow-control decision is recorded with `ids-time` ticks (monotonic, never wall-clock for ordering) and `NodeId`. Runs are deterministic given the same seed, payload pattern, and congestion scenario. Run manifest records git revision, dirty state, toolchain, host, config, and results (schema-versioned JSON). No wall-clock or RTT-derived timeouts for correctness; `ids-time` only for timeouts and measurement.

#### 3.9 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** ed25519-dalek (RFC 8032 EdDSA); chacha20poly1305 docs (RFC 8439 AEAD + XChaCha20Poly1305 192-bit nonce); sha2 RustCrypto (SHA-256); BLAKE3-team README (BLAKE3-256, SIMD, keyed hash, KDF, XOF).

`ids-backpressure` uses: ed25519 for signing credit/backpressure/audit decisions; sha256 for credit-window IDs and audit-chain links; blake3 for fast envelope/content hashing and credit-state checkpoint chaining; xchacha20poly1305 to encrypt credit/backpressure state at rest (24-byte nonce, random nonces safe); chacha20poly1305 for session/state payloads (12-byte nonce, counter-based). No other crypto. `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs; `ids-backpressure` references them via `ids-000-aa` only.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Buffer overflow / receiver memory exhaustion | Receiver memory | Credit window bounds in-flight data: `Crd_Bal ≥ 0` enforced; buffer ≥ Rate × RTT (one BDP); no datagram sent without credit |
| Lost/delayed credit feedback | Flow-control liveness | Sender uses previous allowance on lost/delayed feedback; bounded liability; credit windows re-initialized on re-sync |
| Credit theft / forgery | Decision integrity | ed25519-signed credit/backpressure decisions; signed audit checkpoints |
| Congestion collapse | Network stability | Congestion detection (sojourn/loss/ECN) reduces rate + sheds load; BDP bounds in-flight |
| Queue-induced tail latency | Latency SLO | CoDel-style drop on persistent sojourn > TARGET; bounded queues prevent unbounded buffering |
| Load-shedding unfairness | Request fairness | Criticality-ranked shedding; least-critical traffic shed first; audit records every shed |
| Rate oscillation / instability | Rate stability | Differential (not absolute) rate adjustment; PID damping; gradient vs smoothed base RTT |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Replay protection at flow-control layer; idempotent credit return tolerates duplicates |
| Prohibited crate in dependency tree | Carrier-agnostic rule | CI dependency audit; `cargo tree` asserts no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/QUIC/HTTP/DNS crate |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy | Only the five allowed primitives; `ids-crypto` is sole crypto surface; allowlist unit test |
| Clock manipulation for congestion | Congestion correctness | Logical/monotonic `ids-time` only; never wall-clock for flow-control decisions |
| Credit-window DoS (reservation exhaustion) | Availability | Reservations carry timeouts; unreserved after `reservation_ttl`; per-endpoint reservation caps |

The carrier is never trusted: credit and backpressure decisions are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Credit window
```
CreditWindow { Buf_Alloc, Tx_Cnt, Fwd_Cnt, Crd_Bal, MaxSize }
Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)   (credit balance, never negative)
credit_reserve(endpoint, cost): if Crd_Bal ≥ cost { Crd_Bal −= cost; record reservation } else → Backpressure
credit_return(endpoint, fwd_cnt): Fwd_Cnt += fwd_cnt; Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)
credit_grant(endpoint, increment): Crd_Bal += increment (capped at MaxSize)
```
Guarantee: no datagram sent without credit ⇒ receiver buffer never overflows ⇒ zero loss due to buffer overflow (credit-based advantage over rate-based).

#### 7.2 Blocked / backpressure signal emission
```
BackpressureSignal { endpoint, reason, blocked_until, credit_needed }
emitted as opaque Vec<u8> datagram to ids-carrier::Endpoint when Crd_Bal = 0 or queue depth ≥ high watermark
non-blocking: producer hands signal to carrier boundary, not stalled on a thread
```

#### 7.3 Load shedding
```
observe load L (queue depth, CPU, memory)
if L > safe_threshold: drop_fraction = min(1, drop_fraction × ramp_up); start at 1/10
if L < safe_threshold: drop_fraction = max(floor, drop_fraction × ramp_down)
shed least-critical traffic first (criticality-ranked)
ShedDecision { dropped, reason, criticality, backpressure_signal }
```

#### 7.4 Adaptive rate limiting
```
PID: error = target_latency − measured_sessions; rate += Kp·error + Ki·∫error + Kd·d(error)
Gradient2Limit: concurrency adjusts from RTT gradient vs EWMA base RTT
Token bucket: tokens += rate·Δt (capped at burst); conform iff tokens ≥ cost
Leaky bucket: water += cost; leak at constant rate; conform iff water ≤ capacity
Differential adjustment (speed-up/slow-down by Δ%), not absolute replacement
```

#### 7.5 Congestion detection (CoDel-style)
```
cur_qdelay = dequeue_time − enqueue_time
track min sojourn over interval (~1 RTT)
if min_sojourn > TARGET (5 ms) for INTERVAL: enter drop state; next_drop = t + INTERVAL / sqrt(count)
if min_sojourn ≤ TARGET: cancel drops, reset interval
loss_rate = lost / sent; ECN marks from envelopes → congestion state
BDP = bandwidth × min_RTT; bounds in-flight data per endpoint
```

#### 7.6 Audit chain
Each flow-control decision (admit/reserve/return/shed/rate-change/congestion) = SHA-256/BLAKE3-chained entry + ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.

| `ids-carrier` | `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — decision transport only; crate never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic time source for all flow-control timeouts and measurements |
| `serde` | Serialization of credit envelopes, backpressure signals, audit entries |
| `thiserror` | Error types |

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list. `ids-backpressure` imports no crypto directly — all via `ids-crypto`.

---

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| AC-80.1 | Credit window per endpoint: `Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)`, never negative | CreditWindow unit tests; invariant `credit_nonnegative` |
| AC-80.2 | Credit reservation/return/grant protocol | reservation grants when `Crd_Bal ≥ cost`; return recomputes `Crd_Bal`; grant caps at `MaxSize` |
| AC-80.3 | Blocked signal emission when `Crd_Bal = 0` or queue ≥ high watermark | `BackpressureSignal` emitted as opaque datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; non-blocking |
| AC-80.4 | Bounded queue with configurable overflow policy (DropNew/DropHead/Reject/Block) | overflow policy unit tests; capacity sized by burst/bytes/latency |
| AC-80.5 | Load shedding: criticality-ranked drop, fraction ramps 1/10 → up/down with load | shedder tests; least-critical dropped first; audit records every shed |
| AC-80.6 | Adaptive rate limiting: PID + gradient + token bucket + leaky bucket | rate limiter converges to target latency; differential adjustment (no oscillation) |
| AC-80.7 | Congestion detection: queue sojourn (CoDel TARGET 5 ms), loss rate, ECN marks | detector enters/exits drop state; `t + INTERVAL / sqrt(count)` control law |
| AC-80.8 | BDP bounds in-flight data per endpoint | `BDP = bandwidth × min_RTT`; credit window sized ≥ one BDP |
| AC-80.9 | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh | dependency audit test (`cargo tree`) + source grep — zero matches |
| AC-80.10 | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 in crypto surface | allowlist unit test passes |
| AC-80.11 | Every flow-control decision in append-only, hash-chained, ed25519-signed audit log with `NodeId` + `IdsTime` | audit chain verifiable offline |
| AC-80.12 | Determinism: same seed + scenario ⇒ identical decisions | determinism tests pass |
| AC-80.13 | No wall-clock for flow-control correctness; `ids-time` only | monotonic clock usage enforced |

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Credit granularity:** credits in octets (incl. framing overhead, DLEP-style) vs per-datagram credits; unquantified for IDS payload sizes.
2. **Credit window defaults per endpoint:** `Buf_Alloc`, `MaxSize`, reservation TTL are deployment-tuned; validated at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-replication`.
3. **Load-shedding criticality taxonomy:** exact traffic classes and drop-fraction ramp curve are workload-dependent.
4. **PID tuning constants (Kp/Ki/Kd) and gradient EWMA alpha:** latency-vs-stability tradeoff; unquantified on target host.
5. **Congestion TARGET/INTERVAL:** CoDel TARGET 5 ms / INTERVAL ~1 RTT is Internet-default; IDS carrier latency characteristics may require retuning.
6. **Credit feedback on lossy/unreliable carriers:** lost credit datagrams must not stall the sender indefinitely; re-sync protocol details pending.
7. **Interaction with `ids-transport` (reliability/ordering):** credit flow control is orthogonal to transport reliability; exact handshake to be validated at integration.
8. **Audit signing overhead per decision:** ed25519 sign per credit decision may be heavy at high throughput; batching/checkpoint interval TBD.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-backpressure` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear flow-control boundary |
| Credit-based flow control (`Crd_Bal = Buf_Alloc − (Tx_Cnt − Fwd_Cnt)`) | Receiver-oriented, guarantees zero buffer-overflow loss, bounded by one BDP (Kung & Morris; Flink; DLEP RFC 9893) |
| Blocked signal as opaque datagram to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Non-blocking backpressure; carrier-agnostic; no `std::net`/`tokio::net` |
| Bounded queues with DropNew/DropHead/Reject/Block | Bounded memory; overflow policy per traffic criticality (actor mailbox patterns) |
| Load shedding: criticality-ranked, drop fraction 1/10 ramping | Google SRE load shedding; shed least-critical first under overload |
| Adaptive rate limiting: PID + gradient + token bucket + leaky bucket | Uber Cinnamon / Netflix Gradient2Limit; dynamic rate from queue latency + RTT; differential adjustment avoids overreaction |
| Congestion detection: CoDel-style sojourn (TARGET 5 ms) + loss + ECN | RFC 8289; queue delay as congestion signal; parameterless |
| BDP bounds in-flight data | BBR; credit window ≥ one BDP keeps link loss-free at full use |
| Audit: SHA-256/BLAKE3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable flow-control decision log; tamper evidence |
| Logical/monotonic `ids-time` only; no wall-clock for decisions | Clock manipulation cannot break flow control |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Only allowed crypto; via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 081 creates `ids-graceful-degradation`, a separate IDS crate (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities). It defines ordered fallback states between health and failure: a degradation hierarchy with named, ordered intermediate states, each trading capability for availability, plus fallback behavior per state, a recovery path back to health, capability-reduction bookkeeping, availability tradeoff documentation, and operator notification of degraded state.

The crate is a policy/decision layer: it observes health signals (from ids-health or equivalent), computes the current degradation state, decides which capabilities are reduced or disabled, and emits a `DegradationDecision` (state transition + capability mask + operator notice). It never sends bytes itself; every protection-relevant message rides opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). All traffic is carrier-agnostic: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh.

Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto`; never implemented in this crate). `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpState`, `Endpoint`, `FailureDomain`, …) and sealed trait contracts; this crate imports them as `ids_000_aa::X`.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned the ordered-degradation-hierarchy model (named intermediate states between healthy and down, each trading capability for availability), circuit-breaker three-state machine (Closed/Open/Half-Open) from Nygard's Release It! and Azure/AWS guidance, fallback chains (ordered alternatives: fresh → cached → simplified → static default → error), load shedding (reject early, reject cheap, tiered by priority), retry storms / thundering herd and exponential backoff + jitter prevention, graceful-degradation mode from Azure self-preservation and Google Cloud reliability guidance, fail-safe defaults (Saltzer & Schroeder 1975; de-energize-to-safe), degraded mode entry/exit rules with hysteresis (Atlas of Engineering), operator notification patterns, anti-patterns (silent degradation; fallback hard to prove/test — AWS Builder Library), and degrade-from-the-edges-inward tiering.

A skeleton `ids-graceful-degradation` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-graceful-degradation/`. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-graceful-degradation` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a degradation-state machine with an ordered hierarchy of states and a fallback engine that maps each state to a capability mask. It observes health/failure signals, computes transitions, and emits `DegradationDecision`s that callers frame into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. It never sends or receives datagrams directly.

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    CALLER LAYER (ids-*, operators, health monitors)         │
│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-session — report health, consume decisions │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 081: ids-graceful-degradation (THIS CRATE — policy)     │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐│
│  │ degradation      │ │ state machine    │ │ fallback engine  │ │ recovery││
│  │ hierarchy        │ │ (Healthy→…→Failed│ │ (per-state fallback│ │ path    ││
│  │ (ordered states) │ │  ordered chain)  │ │   chain)         │ │ (hysteresis││
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘│
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐│
│  │ capability       │ │ operator         │ │ audit log        │ │ carrier ││
│  │ reduction mask   │ │ notification     │ │ (signed+chained) │ │ adapter ││
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ └─────────┘│
└──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘
                                           │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                           ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                   │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload)      │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                     │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS /   │
│  Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh                                  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Ordered degradation hierarchy** (states between full health and complete failure, each trading capability for availability — research-verified pattern from Sujeet Jaiswal's graceful-degradation catalog and the HLD Handbook):

| Level | State | Behavior | Capability reduction | Availability tradeoff |
|-------|-------|----------|----------------------|----------------------|
| 0 | Healthy | Full functionality, real-time data, all writes accepted | None | None (baseline) |
| 1 | Degraded | Serve cached/stale data where fresh is unavailable; non-critical features on | Staleness | Higher availability under dependency slowness |
| 2 | Limited | Disable Tier-3 (non-critical) features; critical path preserved | Functionality | Stability preserved for core flows |
| 3 | Minimal | Read-only mode; reject writes; serve from local/cached replicas | Writes lost | Reads preserved during write-path failure |
| 4 | Static | Return default/static responses; no personalization or dynamic data | Personalization | Uptime preserved with no dynamic backend |
| 5 | Failed | Reject all operations; emit terminal failure to callers | Everything | Safe fail-safe default; operator intervention required |

**Data flow:** health signal arrives → state machine evaluates transition rules → if state changes, fallback engine computes capability mask for the new state → operator notification emitted → `DegradationDecision{from_state, to_state, capability_mask, reason, timestamp, operator_notice}` returned → caller frames it into opaque datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets. Recovery path: state only exits downward when hysteresis/confirmation conditions are met (persist ≥ T_confirm, no fault recurrence), preventing rapid chatter.

**Key research-verified patterns applied:**
- Ordered intermediate states with explicit recovery paths (Sujeet Jaiswal; HLD Handbook).
- Circuit-breaker semantics per dependency (Closed/Open/Half-Open) to isolate failing components (Nygard; Azure/AWS).
- Fallback chain per capability: fresh → cached → simplified → static default → error (sujeet.pro; Tetrate; nRouter).
- Load shedding by priority tier; reject non-critical first (Google SRE; HLD Handbook; Uber Cinnamon).
- Fail-safe defaults: on uncertainty, transition to a predefined safe state and signal operators (arc42; Saltzer & Schroeder).
- Degraded-mode entry/exit with hysteresis to prevent chatter (Atlas of Engineering degraded-mode entry/exit rules).
- Operator notification on every state transition (Azure self-preservation degraded UX; HLD Handbook banners).
- Anti-pattern awareness: silent degradation is dangerous; fallback code paths are rarely exercised and must be tested (AWS Builder Library "Avoiding fallback"; Google SRE "code path you never use").

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources cited inline; full list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Ordered degradation hierarchy (named intermediate states between Healthy and Failed)

**Sources:** sujeet.pro "Graceful Degradation" (ordered intermediate states between full health and complete failure, each trading capability for availability); HLD Handbook "Graceful Degradation: When Partial Service Beats No Service" (critical-path tiering, three-tier model); antimetal glossary (explicit ranking of functionality by importance; fallbacks, feature flags, load shedding).

The crate defines an ordered chain of degradation states `Healthy → Degraded → Limited → Minimal → Static → Failed`. Each state has: a name, an ordinal severity, a capability mask (which capabilities are on/off), entry conditions, exit conditions, entry/exit actions, and an operator-notice template. States are totally ordered by severity so there is always a well-defined "next worse" and "next better" state. Degradation proceeds from the edges inward: non-critical capabilities shed first; the critical path is the last to degrade.

#### 3.2 Fallback behavior per state (fallback chains)

**Sources:** sujeet.pro fallback chains (fresh → cached → simplified → static default → error); Tetrate Agent Router fallback policy (ordered backends, advance on recoverable error); nRouter provider fallback chains (ordering is deterministic; advance conditional on retryable-only failures; exhaustion is an error); Frontier Engineering circuit-breaker + fallback chain (degrade through progressively simpler alternatives).

Each capability in the system has a fallback chain: an ordered list of fallback behaviors, tried in order on failure. The chain terminates when an attempt succeeds; if every fallback is exhausted, the result is an explicit error (never a silent stub). Failure classification decides whether to advance: retryable failures (timeout, 5xx-equivalent, capacity) advance; terminal failures (malformed request, auth failure) fail fast. Each fallback level is tagged with its quality impact so degradation is observable and honest.

#### 3.3 Recovery path (return from degraded to healthy)

**Sources:** Azure self-preservation degraded mode (failure detection → automated initiation → alternative paths); Atlas of Engineering degraded mode (entry conditions explicit; exit requires evidence the degraded condition cleared + hysteresis/persistence rules; transition time budget T_rev = T_detect + T_decide + T_transition ≤ T_req); Google SRE cascading failures (degraded code path must be exercised regularly or it rots).

The recovery path is the reverse transition chain: `Failed → Static → Minimal → Limited → Degraded → Healthy`. Exit from a degraded state requires: (a) the failure condition cleared, (b) a confirmation window `T_confirm` elapsed without recurrence (hysteresis, prevents chatter), (c) a bounded transition time `T_rev` checked against a requirement `T_req`. Recovery actions are logged and notified to operators. The crate enforces that recovery cannot skip states (must traverse the ordered chain back up) to avoid re-exciting a flapping dependency.

#### 3.4 Capability reduction (what is shed at each state)

**Sources:** HLD Handbook critical-path tiering (Google's four fixed criticality levels CRITICAL_PLUS/CRITICAL/SHEDDING_PLUS/SHEDDING; tie tiers to SLOs); alivedise BEE-12005 graceful degradation (critical vs non-critical feature classification; per-feature fallback); Defcon (Meta graceful feature degradation; essential vs fungible features; knob-driven runtime degradation).

Every capability (read path, write path, replication, rebalancing, anti-entropy, telemetry verbosity, personalization, etc.) is assigned to a tier. At each degradation state, a capability-reduction mask specifies which tiers are disabled or degraded. Tier 0 (critical) is disabled only at `Failed`; Tier 3 (non-critical) is disabled at `Limited`. Reduction is deterministic: given the same state, the same capabilities are reduced. No ad-hoc shedding.

#### 3.5 Availability tradeoff (documented per state)

**Sources:** antimetal graceful degradation vs failover (degradation handles capability failure where no equivalent exists; failover handles infrastructure failure with redundancy); AWS REL05-BP01 (transform hard dependencies into soft dependencies; component functions minimally impeded); Google Cloud graceful degradation (system continues with reduced performance/accuracy; resumes full functionality when load eases).

For each state the crate documents: what capability is lost, what SLA/SLO no longer applies, what error callers receive, and what the operator must do. The tradeoff is explicit: availability is bought with reduced capability, never silently. This documentation is part of the crate's public contract so downstream crates (ids-store, ids-replication) can rely on it.

#### 3.6 Operator notification of degraded state

**Sources:** Azure self-preservation (degraded UX: notification mechanism tells users what functionality remains/changed; banners by severity); HLD Handbook (Tier 3 shed → no banner; Tier 2 shed → yellow banner; database-down → red banner with status page link); New Relic four considerations (shed workload, time shift, reduce quality, add capacity — user-impact ordering).

Every state transition emits an operator notification: from-state, to-state, reason, capabilities affected, estimated recovery, and recommended action. Notifications are severity-graded (info for Degraded, warning for Limited/Minimal, critical for Failed) and routed through the carrier as opaque datagrams so downstream observability crates can consume them. Silent degradation is treated as a bug.

#### 3.7 Circuit-breaker integration per dependency

**Sources:** Martin Fowler Circuit Breaker (Closed/Open/Half-Open; failure threshold trips; half-open permits trial requests); Azure circuit breaker (Closed → Open on threshold; Half-Open after timeout; closed again on success); AWS circuit breaker (prevents retrying a failing callee; detects recovery).

Each dependency wrapped by the crate has a circuit breaker. Closed: calls proceed; failures counted. Open: calls short-circuit, fallback used immediately. Half-Open: limited trial requests; success closes, failure re-opens. The breaker state feeds the degradation state machine: an open breaker on a critical dependency can push the system down one degradation level.

#### 3.8 Load shedding by priority tier

**Sources:** Google SRE cascading failures (load shedding drops load as server approaches overload; per-task throttling; queue-length limiting); HLD Handbook load shedding (reject at earliest layer with cheap 503 + Retry-After; shed non-critical first; criticality propagates across RPC hops); Uber Cinnamon (priority-tagged requests; PID-controller rejection threshold).

When overload is detected, the crate sheds load by rejecting the lowest-criticality requests first with a fast, cheap response. Shedding decisions use the same tiered criticality as the degradation hierarchy so shedding and degradation are consistent. Health checks are given priority over other requests (New Relic).

#### 3.9 Retry storm / thundering herd prevention

**Sources:** Azure retry storm antipattern (limit attempts; pause with exponential backoff; circuit breaker; honor retry-after); Google SRE (randomized exponential backoff with jitter; retry budget 10%; cap amplification); gronex (jitter desynchronizes clients; retry budget; circuit breaker + retry budget combined).

The crate bounds retries: capped exponential backoff with full jitter, a per-operation deadline, and a retry budget tied to successful request volume. When the budget is exhausted, retries are shed. Circuit breakers and retry budgets are used together: the breaker stops traffic entirely past a hard threshold; the budget prevents amplification during partial degradation.

#### 3.10 Fail-safe defaults and safe-state transitions

**Sources:** arc42 Fail-Safe Defaults (define explicit safe state per component/mode; unrecognized inputs denied by default; atomic transition; alert operators); Saltzer & Schroeder 1975 (fail-safe defaults; base decisions on permission not exclusion); Nguyen "Designing Defaults That Fail Safely" (name the failure mode; what does the user see if dependency is down).

Every state transition defines a safe state: if the crate cannot determine the correct action, it degrades rather than proceeding optimistically. Transitions are atomic where possible (no partial states that are neither operational nor safe). Safe states are documented explicitly so operators know what to expect and what recovery steps are required.

#### 3.11 Degradation hysteresis and anti-chatter

**Sources:** Atlas of Engineering degraded mode (exit requires evidence condition cleared + `t_valid ≥ T_confirm`; prevents rapid mode chatter); Google SRE cascading failures (degraded mode won't be exercised in steady state; exercise it regularly or it rots).

The state machine enforces hysteresis: a state change downward requires the fault condition to persist; a change upward requires the healthy condition to persist for `T_confirm`. This prevents flapping when a dependency hovers near a threshold. The crate also schedules periodic exercises of degraded paths (canary) so the rarely-used code stays working.

#### 3.12 Degradation vs failover distinction

**Sources:** antimetal (failover replaces failed component with healthy equivalent — full functionality preserved; degradation reduces functionality when no equivalent exists); New Relic (networks re-route traffic if path unavailable; enterprise apps shed/reduce quality).

The crate is explicitly about degradation (capability reduction when no redundant equivalent exists), not failover (switching to a healthy replica). Failover is handled by ids-stonith / ids-replication; this crate owns the degradation policy when failover is exhausted or unavailable.

#### 3.13 Audit trail for degradation decisions

**Sources:** MongoDB causal consistency (read/write concerns); AWS REL05-BP01 (failure modes seen as normal operation; predictable and recoverable states); Azure self-preservation (audit/logging of degraded mode).

Every degradation decision (enter state, exit state, shed load, trip breaker) is recorded in an append-only, hash-chained audit log with `NodeId` + `IdsTime`, sha256/blake3 chaining, and periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints. Offline-verifiable; tamper-evident. This makes degradation visible and auditable — addressing the "silent degradation is dangerous" anti-pattern.

#### 3.14 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Sources:** RFC 8032 (ed25519); RFC 7539 (ChaCha20-Poly1305, 96-bit nonce); libsodium (XChaCha20-Poly1305, 192-bit nonce); NIST FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256); BLAKE3 spec.

The crate uses: ed25519 for signing degradation decisions and audit checkpoints; sha256 for profile/state IDs and audit-chain links; blake3 for fast content hashing of degradation state and capability masks; xchacha20poly1305 for encrypting degradation state at rest (random 192-bit nonces); chacha20poly1305 for encrypting session/state payloads (12-byte nonces). All via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs; no other crypto.

#### 3.15 Carrier-agnostic transport

**Sources:** HX-241 carrier-agnostic socket abstraction; IDS prompts.txt entry 1 (Endpoint = CarrierType + Vec<u8>; no IP/TCP/UDP).

All degradation notifications, audit events, and state transitions are shipped as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 bytes). The crate imports no networking crate and never references `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
||--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
|| Silent degradation (operators unaware) | Operability / trust | Every state transition emits operator notification; silent degradation treated as bug; audit log |
|| Degradation chatter (rapid state flapping) | Stability | Hysteresis: entry requires persistence; exit requires `T_confirm` without recurrence |
|| Fallback code path rot (rarely exercised code breaks) | Reliability | Periodic canary exercise of degraded paths; degradation tests in CI |
|| Fallback harder to prove/test than primary path | Reliability | Fallback paths are simpler than primary (AWS guidance); covered by property tests |
|| Retry storm amplifying overload | Availability | Capped exponential backoff + jitter; retry budget; circuit breaker |
|| Circuit breaker trips too early/late | Stability | Tunable failure threshold, reset timeout, success threshold; documented defaults |
|| Operator override disables fail-safe | Safety | Fail-safe defaults documented; overrides require signed governance decision, audited |
|| Clock manipulation affecting recovery timing | Causality correctness | Monotonic `IdsTime` only for timeouts/hysteresis; no wall-clock for state decisions |
|| Partial state transition (neither safe nor operational) | Safety | Atomic transitions where possible; intermediate states documented |
|| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
|| Key extraction (degradation signing key) | Decision authenticity | Keys never leave node; encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
|| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent state application; replay cache per degradation decision |
|| Degradation below safe threshold | Safety | Each state documents minimum viable capability; `Failed` is the safe default |
|| Crypto beyond allowed list | Policy compliance | CI allowlist test; only five primitives reachable |

The carrier is never trusted: degradation decisions and audit entries are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-graceful-degradation ||
||-------|------|--------------------------|--------------------------------------|
|| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `OpState`, `Endpoint`, `FailureDomain`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined |
|| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All degradation notifications/audit ship to `Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends directly |
|| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing decisions/audit; encrypting degradation state at rest; hashing state/capability masks |
|| `ids-health` | Health/failure signal source (probe results, dependency health) | Feeds health signals into the degradation state machine |
|| `ids-store` | Primary record store (degradation consumer) | Reads capability mask; disables/reduces capabilities per degradation state |
|| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization | Respects degradation state: reduces replication frequency under degradation |
|| `ids-session` | Client-session binding | Sessions carry degradation context; operator notifications routed per session |
|| `ids-fault` | Fault injection / failure detection | Fault events can trigger degradation transitions |
|| `ids-backpressure` | Backpressure / load shedding | Load-shedding decisions coordinated with degradation tiers |
|| `ids-observability` | Metric/trace sinks | Degradation state and transitions exported as metrics/traces |

**Integration points:** `ids-graceful-degradation` is a pure policy crate: it consumes health signals and produces `DegradationDecision`s; it never opens a transport. All cross-node traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli` beyond what the contracts expose.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Degradation state machine (ordered chain)

```
DegradationState { level: u8 (0..5), name, severity, capability_mask, entry_conditions, exit_conditions }
Chain: Healthy(0) → Degraded(1) → Limited(2) → Minimal(3) → Static(4) → Failed(5)
next_worse(state)  = state.level + 1  (capped at Failed)
next_better(state) = state.level - 1  (capped at Healthy)
can_transition_to(a, b) = |a.level - b.level| == 1  (no skipping states)
```

Transitions downward require fault persistence; transitions upward require `T_confirm` without recurrence (hysteresis).

#### 7.2 Fallback chain resolution

```
FallbackChain { links: [FallbackLink; N] }  // ordered by quality, best first
execute(input): for link in links:
  if link.breaker.is_open(): continue
  try link.fn(input) → result
    if success: return { result, source: link.name, degraded: true }
    if failure is terminal: return error (do not advance)
    if failure is retryable: continue to next link
return error { exhausted: true, last_error }  // never a silent stub
```

Each link tagged with `QualityImpact` (documented degradation). Circuit breaker per link skips open breakers.

#### 7.3 Circuit breaker (three-state machine)

```
state: Closed | Open | HalfOpen
Closed:  call proceeds; failure_count++ ; if ≥ threshold → Open, start reset_timeout
Open:    calls short-circuited; fallback used; after reset_timeout → HalfOpen
HalfOpen: limited trial requests; success → Closed; failure → Open
```

Parameters: `failure_threshold`, `reset_timeout`, `success_threshold` (tunable, documented defaults).

#### 7.4 Capability reduction mask

```
CapabilityMask { bit per CapabilityId; tier: u8 }
apply(state): mask = default_mask AND NOT disabled_tiers(state)
disabled_tiers(Degraded) = {}; (Limited) = {Tier3}; (Minimal) = {Tier2, Tier3, writes}; ...
```

Deterministic: same state ⇒ same mask. Tier 0 (critical) disabled only at `Failed`.

#### 7.5 Load shedding by tier

```
shed(request): if system.overloaded():
  reject lowest criticality tier first with cheap 503 + Retry-After
  health-check requests never shed
return request  // admitted
```

Criticality propagates: the tier of the calling request sets the tier of downstream calls (per HLD Handbook).

#### 7.6 Retry policy (storm prevention)

```
retry(attempt): delay = min(base * 2^attempt, cap) * random_jitter(0..1)
if attempt ≥ max_attempts or deadline exceeded: shed (fail fast)
if retry_budget exhausted: shed
```

Jitter desynchronizes clients; budget caps amplification (Google SRE).

#### 7.7 Audit chain

```
entry_i = { decision, node_id, ids_time, prev_hash, payload_hash }
chain_hash_i = blake3(entry_i)
checkpoint_k = ed25519_sign(chain_hash at checkpoint interval)
```

Offline-verifiable: recompute chain, verify signatures.

#### 7.8 Operator notification

```
notify(transition): { from, to, reason, capabilities_affected, severity, recommended_action }
severity: Degraded=info, Limited=warning, Minimal=warning, Static=critical, Failed=critical
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **Concrete per-state capability masks:** which capabilities belong to which tier and are disabled at which state — deployment-tuned; to be validated at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-replication`.
- **T_confirm / T_rev defaults:** hysteresis confirmation window and transition time budget are workload-dependent; unquantified pending integration.
- **Fallback chain per capability:** the exact ordered fallback list (fresh/cached/simplified/static) per capability must be defined by product teams; this crate provides the mechanism, not the policy content.
- **Circuit-breaker parameter defaults:** failure_threshold, reset_timeout, success_threshold need production tuning.
- **Load-shedding threshold:** the overload signal (queue length, CPU, latency) that triggers shedding is not yet defined.
- **Interaction with ids-health:** health signal format and frequency feeding the state machine to be confirmed at integration.
- **Audit checkpoint interval:** how often ed25519-signed checkpoints are written; trades audit granularity against cost.
- **Canary exercise frequency:** how often degraded paths are exercised in production without causing real degradation.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
||----------|-----------|-------------|
|| Separate `ids-graceful-degradation` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear policy boundary |
|| Six-state ordered chain (Healthy→…→Failed) | Named intermediate states between health and failure; each trades capability for availability (research-verified) |
|| No state skipping (adjacent transitions only) | Prevents re-exciting flapping dependencies; well-defined next-worse/next-better |
|| Fallback chain: fresh → cached → simplified → static default → error | Ordered alternatives preserve forward progress with reduced quality (Tetrate/nRouter research) |
|| Exhaustion = error, never silent stub | Silent degradation is dangerous (AWS/Azure guidance); every path must be observable |
|| Circuit breaker per dependency (Closed/Open/Half-Open) | Isolates failing components; prevents cascade (Nygard; Azure/AWS) |
|| Recovery path = reverse chain + hysteresis (T_confirm) | Prevents chatter; exit requires evidence condition cleared (Atlas of Engineering) |
|| Capability mask deterministic per state | Same state ⇒ same reduction; operators and downstream crates can rely on it |
|| Tier 0 (critical) disabled only at Failed | Critical path preserved as long as possible (degrade from edges inward) |
|| Operator notification on every transition | Silent degradation treated as bug; severity-graded notices (Azure/HLD Handbook) |
|| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable, tamper-evident degradation log |
|| Carrier-agnostic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
|| Allowed crypto only; via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs | Complies with IDS crypto policy |
|| Retry: capped backoff + jitter + deadline + budget | Prevents retry storms / thundering herd (Google SRE; Azure) |
|| Fail-safe defaults; atomic transitions | On uncertainty, degrade safely (arc42; Saltzer & Schroeder) |
|| Canary exercise of degraded paths | Prevents fallback code-path rot (Google SRE: "code path you never use") |

6. Google SRE, "Addressing Cascading Failures" — load shedding; graceful degradation; randomized exponential backoff + jitter; retry budget; degraded code path must be exercised. https://sre.google/sre-book/addressing-cascading-failures/
7. Google Cloud Architecture Center, "Design for graceful degradation" — system continues with reduced performance/accuracy; throttling; drop excess requests early; handle partial errors. https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability/graceful-degradation

10. Antimetal, "Graceful Degradation" — explicit ranking of functionality; degradation vs failover distinction; silent degradation is dangerous. https://antimetal.com/glossary/graceful-degradation
11. Atlas of Engineering, "Degraded Mode, Fallback Operation and Validation" — entry conditions explicit; exit requires evidence + hysteresis `t_valid ≥ T_confirm`; transition time budget `T_rev ≤ T_req`. https://atlasofengineering.com/industrial-and-management-engineering/degraded-mode
