### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 083 creates `ids-fencing-epoch`, a separate IDS crate (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities) that owns epoch-based authority for preventing stale owners. The crate issues monotonically increasing fencing tokens (u64 `FencingToken`) on every ownership/authority grant, maintains per-resource high-water marks of accepted tokens, and rejects any operation carrying a token below the current high-water mark. It defines epoch-based leadership (a leadership term is an epoch; a new leader bumps the epoch before acting), stale-owner prevention (any write/read carrying a stale token is rejected at the protected resource, not by the owner itself), recovered-region split-brain prevention (a region returning from partition must present a current signed epoch certificate before serving reads or writes; an epoch below the region's last-known epoch fences the region), and authority-transfer verification (each transfer carries an old→new epoch transition signed with ed25519 and verified against the high-water mark before the new owner is admitted).

`ids-fencing-epoch` never sends bytes itself: it returns verdicts (`Admit`, `RejectStale`, `RejectSplitBrain`, `DeferTransfer`) and signed epoch certificates that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` ≤ 1024 B). Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. Allowed crypto only: ed25519 (epoch certificate + authority-transfer signatures), sha256/blake3 (epoch hash chains, high-water-mark binding), xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 (epoch state encrypted at rest).

A skeleton `ids-fencing-epoch` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-fencing-epoch/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `FencingToken` (u64), `Epoch` (u64), plus sealed trait contracts and error types. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned Martin Kleppmann's fencing-token pattern ("How to do distributed locking", Chubby sequencers, ZooKeeper zxid/version as fencing tokens), pg-fenced-lease (epoch column incremented on takeover, fence check inside the same transaction as the write), disco (etcd cluster revision as fencing token, high-water-mark validation rejects `token < mark`), SlateDB `FenceableTransactionalObject` (u64 epoch, init bumps epoch, update/refresh fail with `Fenced` when stored epoch > local epoch), NamiDB single-writer epoch fencing via manifest CAS without Raft/ZooKeeper, Raft term as fencing token (higher term steps a server down; lower-term messages rejected), Kafka KIP-903 (stale broker epoch not allowed to join ISR), Cassandra LWT compare-and-set via Paxos ballot, Viewstamped Replication view-id total ordering, SBD/STONITH storage fencing for HA clusters, epoch-based authority revocation (epoch increment invalidates all outstanding capabilities), celld epoch-prefixed storage paths with self-fencing leases, bounded staleness (K versions / T time), and epoch-based distributed memory reclamation.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-fencing-epoch` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is an authority/fencing layer: given a resource handle, an owner claim, and a fencing token, it decides whether the owner is still current (token ≥ high-water mark), whether a leadership transition is valid (new epoch > current epoch), whether a recovered region may rejoin (epoch certificate valid and current), and whether an authority transfer is authentic (ed25519 signature over old→new epoch, nonce-bound, replay-cache checked). It returns decisions; the caller transmits them as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (fencing clients)               │
│  ids-store, ids-replication, ids-region — tagged operations + owner claims   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│               Phase 083: ids-fencing-epoch (THIS CRATE — fencing policy)    │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌─────────┐ │
│  │ fencing token    │ │ epoch-based      │ │ stale owner      │ │ region  │ │
│  │ increment        │ │ leadership       │ │ prevention         │ │ split-  │ │
│  │ (bump on grant)  │ │ (term = epoch)   │ │ (token < mark →    │ │ brain   │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │  reject)           │ │ prevent │ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ └──────────────────┘ └──────────────────┘ │ │       │ │
│  │ high-water mark  │ │ authority transfer│ │ epoch certificate│ │         │ │
│  │ (per-resource)   │ │ verification      │ │ (signed, current)│ │         │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ (ed25519, nonce-bound)└──────────────────┘ │         │ │
│  ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ ┌──────────────────┐ │         │ │
│  │ epoch hash chain │ │ epoch state at   │ │ verdicts: Admit/ │ │         │ │
│  │ (sha256/blake3)  │ │ rest (xchacha20/ │ │ Reject/Defer     │ │         │ │
│  └──────────────────┘ │ chacha20poly1305)│ └──────────────────┘ │         │ │
└─────────────────────────┬──────────────────┴──────────────────┬─┴──────────┘
                          │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams              │
                          ▼                                       │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only        │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B},   │
│  payload: &[u8])     receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)     │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC /    │
│  HTTP / DNS / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh         │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a fenced write:** client submits `Write{resource_id, payload, owner, fencing_token}` → `ids-fencing-epoch` checks `fencing_token ≥ high_water_mark[resource_id]` → returns `Verdict::Admit` (and bumps high-water mark to the token) or `Verdict::RejectStale{current_mark}` → caller sends the write as opaque datagram(s) to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets only when admitted; rejected writes never leave the client.

**Data flow of a leadership transition:** new leader candidate submits `LeaderClaim{region_id, proposed_epoch, proof}` → crate checks `proposed_epoch > current_epoch[region_id]` → on success returns `EpochCertificate{region_id, epoch, signed_by: NodeId, signature: ed25519}` → caller broadcasts the certificate via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; followers store the new epoch and reject any message from an older epoch.

**Data flow of region recovery after partition:** recovering region submits `RegionRejoin{region_id, last_known_epoch, certificate}` → crate validates the certificate chain and checks `certificate.epoch ≥ region_watermark[region_id]` → `Admit` lets the region serve reads/writes; below-watermark epochs return `RejectSplitBrain` (the region remains fenced until it synchronizes to a current epoch).

**Data flow of authority transfer:** `Transfer{resource_id, from, to, old_epoch, new_epoch, signature}` → crate verifies ed25519 signature over the transfer, checks `new_epoch = old_epoch + 1`, checks `old_epoch ≥ high_water_mark[resource_id]`, records the transfer in the hash-chained audit log, returns `TransferVerified` → caller frames the result to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 signs epoch certificates and authority transfers; sha256/blake3 chain epoch entries and bind high-water marks; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 encrypt persisted epoch state at rest (bounded-replay windows, causal histories). No other crypto.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 14.

#### 3.1 Fencing tokens: monotonically increasing ownership generations (Kleppmann / Chubby / ZooKeeper)

**Source:** Martin Kleppmann, "How to do distributed locking" — a fencing token is a number that increases every time a client acquires the lock; the storage service rejects writes whose token has gone backwards. ZooKeeper's `zxid` (or znode version) and Chubby sequencers can serve as fencing tokens. Amazon DynamoDB lock clients and Google Chubby sequence numbers are production precedents. The `zxid = (epoch << 32) | txnCount` structure shows how an epoch field can be packed into a monotonic identifier.

`ids-fencing-epoch` adopts this exact pattern: every authority grant mints a strictly increasing u64 `FencingToken`; every protected operation carries its token; the protected resource persists the highest token accepted per resource and rejects `token < highest_seen`. The check lives at the resource/fencing layer, never at the owner — a paused or partitioned owner that wakes up and writes with an old token is fenced regardless of what it believes.

#### 3.2 Lease-backed epoch increments and atomic fence checks (pg-fenced-lease pattern)

**Source:** pg-fenced-lease (Rust crate) — a lease row holds `name`, `holder`, `epoch`, `expires_at`; acquisition increments `epoch` by 1 (the new epoch is the fencing token); renewal touches only `expires_at` and matches on `holder AND epoch` (a mismatch means someone else took over); the fence check runs inside the same transaction as the write (`FOR KEY SHARE` on the lease row), so a stale leader's write can never commit.

`ids-fencing-epoch` mirrors this: `fencing_token_increment()` bumps the epoch atomically on ownership transfer and never on renewal; `fencing_token_check()` validates holder + epoch + expiry in a single atomic decision; renewal never advances the fencing token (only the liveness deadline), so a renewed lease cannot be confused with a new ownership generation.

#### 3.3 High-water mark validation (disco / etcd cluster revision)

**Source:** disco — fencing token = etcd cluster revision at acquisition; the resource tracks the highest token ever seen: `token ≥ mark` → accepted and mark advances; `token < mark` → rejected as stale owner. ZooKeeper zxid and etcd revision are globally ordered within the cluster, so either works as a fencing token.

`ids-fencing-epoch` implements a per-resource `HighWaterMark` (u64, initialized to 0 / `FencingToken::ZERO`). The decision is `Admit` iff `token >= mark`; on admit, `mark = token + 1` semantics (strictly increasing ownership generations) or `mark = token` with `>` comparison — both forms are specified; the crate exposes both `ge` (accept-equal, idempotent retries) and `gt` (strict, single-use) modes so callers choose per-resource semantics.

#### 3.4 Epoch fencing for transactional objects (SlateDB / NamiDB)

**Source:** SlateDB `FenceableTransactionalObject` — wraps a transactional object with a monotonic u64 epoch; `init` sets the epoch to the next value; every `update`/`refresh` first checks `stored_epoch > local_epoch` and fails with `Fenced` if so; the epoch is never reset. NamiDB single-writer per namespace uses manifest CAS: a writer picks `epoch = current_manifest.epoch + 1` and commits via CAS; losing the CAS race means discovering a newer epoch and rejecting local operations — single-writer enforced without Raft, ZooKeeper, or file locks.

`ids-fencing-epoch` adopts the same structure: an `EpochFence` type holds `current_epoch: Epoch`; `claim_epoch(next: Epoch)` succeeds iff `next > current_epoch` (strict monotonicity) and persists the advance; any operation presenting `epoch <= current_epoch` is `Fenced`. This gives stale-owner prevention without a consensus dependency — the crate itself is the fencing authority for in-process and cross-carrier resources.

#### 3.5 Leader epoch / Raft term as fencing token

**Source:** Raft — time divided into terms (epochs); every message carries the sender's term; a server seeing a higher term immediately steps down; messages from a lower term are rejected. etcd's read-index confirms leadership via a majority heartbeat round before serving reads, so a partitioned leader cannot serve stale reads. Kafka KIP-903: a replica with a stale broker epoch is not allowed to join the ISR; the broker epoch changes on every restart, so the controller always knows the latest epoch.

`ids-fencing-epoch` maps `Epoch` directly to a Raft-style term: `Epoch::zero()` initial; `next_epoch() = current + 1`; leadership claims carry `proposed_epoch`; any peer observing `proposed_epoch > current_epoch` adopts it and rejects older-epoch messages; followers attached to a leader reject client reads/writes tagged with an older epoch. Read-path safety (read-index style) is exposed as `read_lease_valid(region_id, epoch)` — a read may proceed only if the region's epoch was confirmed by quorum within a bounded window.

#### 3.6 Split-brain prevention: quorums, fencing, epochs

**Source:** systemoverflow "Preventing Split Brain: Quorums, Fencing, and Epochs" — majority quorums ensure at most one partition forms a majority, but quorums alone are insufficient: a paused leader resuming after lease expiry must be fenced via monotonically increasing epochs persisted and validated on every state-changing operation. SBD/STONITH (storage-based death fencing) provides node self-fencing for HA clusters: an unresponsive node stops resetting its watchdog and the cluster fences it.

`ids-fencing-epoch` implements recovered-region split-brain prevention: a region that rejoins after a partition must present an `EpochCertificate` (ed25519-signed, covering `region_id`, `epoch`, `prev_hash`, `nonce`) with `epoch >= region_watermark`; below-watermark epochs trigger `RejectSplitBrain` and the region stays fenced until it syncs to a current epoch certificate. Self-fencing is exposed as `self_fence(region_id)` — a region that misses its lease deadline fences itself rather than waiting to be told it is superseded (celld self-fencing lease pattern).

#### 3.7 Authority transfer verification

**Source:** epoch-based authority revocation — incrementing an account/authority epoch invalidates all outstanding capabilities at once (`capability.epoch == current_epoch`); BLS/distributed authority systems verify monotonic sequence and revocation epochs. Viewstamped Replication: view changes require `f+1` replicas to know a request before execution, and the new view starts from a quorum; view-ids are totally ordered.

`ids-fencing-epoch` verifies transfers: `Transfer{resource_id, from, to, old_epoch, new_epoch, signature, nonce}` where `signature = Sign(ed25519, resource_id || from || to || old_epoch || new_epoch || nonce)`. Verification checks: signature valid under `from`'s key (from `ids-000-aa` `NodeId`-bound key registry), `new_epoch == old_epoch + 1`, `old_epoch >= high_water_mark[resource_id]`, nonce not in replay cache, then advances `high_water_mark[resource_id] = new_epoch` and records the transfer in the hash-chained audit log. Only after `TransferVerified` may `to` act as owner.

#### 3.8 Stale-owner prevention semantics

**Source:** kleppmann + stackbook fencing-tokens pattern — the check must be atomic with the write (conditional update); fencing prevents an older generation from overwriting a newer accepted generation, but does not undo work committed before the new epoch arrived. If that window is unacceptable, the destination needs current-ownership validation inside the same transaction as the side effect.

`ids-fencing-epoch` documents this boundary precisely: `fencing_token_check()` rejects stale tokens, but the crate's contract states that admission is a necessary, not sufficient, condition — the protected resource must apply the check inside the same atomic transition as the state change (ids-store conditional write, ids-replication append, etc.). The crate exposes `fence_atomic(resource_id, token) -> Verdict` returning both verdict and the new high-water mark so callers can combine check-and-apply in one step.

#### 3.9 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** ed25519-dalek / RFC 8032 (EdDSA over Curve25519); chacha20poly1305 docs.rs (RFC 8439 AEAD + XChaCha20-Poly1305 192-bit nonce); SHA-256 (NIST FIPS 180-4); BLAKE3 (BLAKE3-team README, 256-bit output, SIMD, keyed hash, KDF, XOF).

`ids-fencing-epoch` uses:
- ed25519: signing epoch certificates and authority-transfer proofs (proof of fencing authority).
- sha256: epoch hash-chain links, high-water-mark binding, resource-id hashing for audit entries.
- blake3: fast epoch-certificate hashing, checkpoint chaining, per-region digest summaries (preferred where parallelism/speed matters).
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypting persisted epoch state at rest with 24-byte random nonces (safe under random generation).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypting session/transfer payloads with 12-byte counter nonces (bounded use).

No other crypto. `ids-crypto` is the sole crypto surface; `ids-fencing-epoch` references primitive IDs via `ids-000-aa` only.

#### 3.9 (b) Carrier-agnostic transport

**Source:** IDS carrier-agnostic rule (prompts.txt entries 1, 83): `Endpoint = CarrierType + Vec<u8>` (max 1024 bytes); `CarrierType` = `Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom(u16)`; no IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS or any networking stack.

`ids-fencing-epoch` never addresses a network by name. It returns `Verdict`, `EpochCertificate`, and `TransferProof` values; the caller serializes them and sends via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. All cross-node fencing traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams. The crate depends on `ids-carrier` only for the `Endpoint` type (re-exported from `ids-000-aa`) — or directly on `ids-000-aa` to avoid pulling carrier implementations into a pure fencing policy crate.

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Stale owner writes after lease expiry / GC pause | Data integrity | Monotonic fencing token per ownership grant; resource rejects `token < high_water_mark` |
| Stale leader serves reads after partition | Read correctness | Epoch-based leadership; read-path `read_lease_valid` requires quorum-confirmed epoch |
| Split-brain: two regions both active after partition heals | State divergence | Recovered-region split-brain prevention: rejoin requires current signed `EpochCertificate`; below-watermark → `RejectSplitBrain` |
| Lost fencing token / counter rollback after failover | Authority integrity | Epoch persisted with each advance; never reset; high-water mark survives restarts (pattern: pg-fenced-lease `epoch` column, SlateDB never-reset epoch) |
| Replay of an old epoch certificate or transfer | Replay attacks | Nonce-bound ed25519 signatures; replay cache per resource; hash-chained audit log detects truncation |
| Authority transfer to wrong recipient | Unauthorized ownership | ed25519 signature over `resource_id || from || to || old_epoch || new_epoch || nonce`; `old_epoch >= high_water_mark` pre-condition |
| Clock manipulation for epoch ordering | Causality correctness | Logical u64 epochs only; never wall-clock for authority decisions; monotonic `IdsTime` only for lease deadlines |
| Carrier delays/duplicates/reorders fencing datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent high-water-mark comparison tolerates duplicates; verdicts carry epoch so stale certificates are self-identifying |
| Profile/epoch downgrade attack | Authority integrity | Epoch is immutable per resource/region; downgrade requires signed governance transfer, audited |
| Key extraction (epoch signing key) | Certificate forgery | Signing keys never leave the node; epoch state encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |

The carrier is never trusted: fencing verdicts and certificates are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-fencing-epoch |
|-------|------|-------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `FencingToken` (u64), `Epoch` (u64), `Error` — consumed, never redefined |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All fencing traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns verdicts, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing epoch certificates/authority transfers; encrypting epoch state at rest; hashing epoch chains |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (fencing client) | Tags writes with fencing token; consults `ids-fencing-epoch` before admitting mutations |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization | Rejects log entries tagged below the leader's epoch; fences stale leaders |
| `ids-region` | Region membership / recovery | Region rejoin gated on `EpochCertificate`; split-brain prevention on partition heal |
| `ids-fault` | Fault detection / STONITH integration | `self_fence()` hook for regions/nodes that miss lease deadlines |
| `ids-session` (Phase 050) | Client-session binding | Session-bound operations carry the session's fencing epoch; transfer audit cross-referenced |

**Integration points:** `ids-fencing-epoch` evaluates authority and returns verdicts/certificates; callers (`ids-store`, `ids-replication`, `ids-region`) enforce the verdict at the point of state change and frame certificates into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No crate-internal reach; no dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session` beyond what contracts expose.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

**1. Fencing token increment (monotonic):** `increment(current: FencingToken) -> FencingToken = current + 1` with saturating guard at `u64::MAX` (epoch wrap → `EpochWrap` error; operator intervention required). Issued exactly once per ownership grant; never on renewal.

**2. High-water mark:** per-resource `HighWaterMark { mark: FencingToken }`, initialized to `FencingToken::ZERO`. `check(token) -> Verdict`: `token >= mark` → `Admit` (mark advanced to `token` in strict mode or left for idempotent mode); `token < mark` → `RejectStale{ current: mark }`. Check and advance are a single atomic decision.

**3. Epoch-based leadership:** `claim_epoch(region_id, proposed_epoch)` succeeds iff `proposed_epoch > current_epoch[region_id]`; on success, `current_epoch = proposed_epoch` and an `EpochCertificate` is minted. Any message tagged with `epoch < current_epoch` is rejected; peers observing a higher epoch step down immediately (Raft-term rule).

**4. Stale-owner prevention:** `stale_owner_guard(resource_id, token, owner)`: reject if `token < high_water_mark[resource_id]` OR `owner != recorded_owner[resource_id]` at that token. The protected resource applies the check inside the same atomic transition as the state change (conditional write), so admission ⟹ current ownership at commit time.

**5. Recovered-region split-brain prevention:** `region_rejoin(region_id, last_known_epoch, certificate)`: validate `ed25519` signature over `region_id || epoch || prev_hash || nonce`; require `certificate.epoch >= region_watermark[region_id]`; on success advance `region_watermark = certificate.epoch`; below-watermark → `RejectSplitBrain` and the region stays fenced until synchronized. `self_fence(region_id)` lets a region that misses its lease deadline fence itself.

**6. Authority transfer verification:** `verify_transfer(Transfer{resource_id, from, to, old_epoch, new_epoch, signature, nonce})`: checks ed25519 signature under `from`'s key; `new_epoch == old_epoch + 1`; `old_epoch >= high_water_mark[resource_id]`; `nonce` unseen; then `high_water_mark = new_epoch`, `recorded_owner = to`, append to hash-chained audit log, return `TransferVerified`.

**7. Epoch hash chain:** each audit entry `e_i` includes `prev = H(e_{i-1})` (sha256 or blake3), establishing total order and making truncation detectable; periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints anchor the chain.

**8. Epoch state encryption at rest:** persisted epoch/watermark state encrypted with xchacha20poly1305 (random 24-byte nonces) or chacha20poly1305 (counter nonces, bounded use).

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **High-water-mark advance semantics:** `mark = token` (strict, single-use) vs `mark = token + 1` (admit-equal for idempotent retries) — per-resource configuration to be decided at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-replication`.
2. **Persistence of high-water marks:** in-memory vs durable (manifest CAS per NamiDB pattern) — durability vs performance tradeoff unquantified; the crate exposes the interface, storage backend chosen per deployment.
3. **Epoch wrap at u64::MAX:** saturating guard with operator intervention — expected never to trigger in practice; handling (fail-closed vs epoch reset with re-certification) undecided.
4. **Replay-cache size and eviction:** bounded cache for transfer/certificate nonces; eviction policy (LRU, time-window) workload-dependent.
5. **Read-lease validity window:** `read_lease_valid` bounded window (IdsTime ticks) — length trades staleness vs availability; SLO definition pending.
6. **Interaction with `ids-fault` / STONITH:** `self_fence()` hook integration with node fencing agents to be validated at integration.
7. **Cross-region epoch propagation latency:** how quickly a new epoch certificate reaches all regions; staleness window during propagation unmeasured.
8. **Key rotation for epoch signing keys:** ed25519 key rotation procedure and certificate validation across key changes undecided.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-fencing-epoch` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear fencing-authority boundary |
| u64 `FencingToken`/`Epoch` from `ids-000-aa` | Single canonical definition; zero-cost newtypes; consistent with IDS type system |
| Strict monotonicity, epoch never reset | Matches pg-fenced-lease / SlateDB / NamiDB epoch-fencing precedent; prevents counter rollback after failover |
| Check lives at the resource, verdict returned by crate | Kleppmann fencing pattern: enforcement must be at the protected resource; crate never sends bytes |
| `token >= mark` admit mode (with strict `>` variant) | Balances idempotent retries (admit-equal) vs strict single-use ownership; caller chooses per resource |
| Recovered-region split-brain via signed `EpochCertificate` | Region must prove currency before serving reads/writes; prevents split-brain on partition heal |
| Authority transfer = ed25519-signed old→new epoch + nonce | Unforgeable transfer proof; replay cache prevents reuse; old-epoch pre-condition prevents hijack |
| Hash-chained audit log + ed25519 checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence (sha256/blake3 chain) |
| Logical epochs only; no wall-clock for authority | Clock manipulation cannot break fencing order; `IdsTime` only for lease deadlines |
| Carrier-agnostic boundary via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Allowed crypto only; `ids-crypto` is sole crypto surface | Complies with IDS allowed-crypto rule |

### 12. Sources

1. Martin Kleppmann, "How to do distributed locking" — fencing token pattern, Chubby sequencers, ZooKeeper zxid as fencing token, storage service rejects backwards tokens. https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html
2. pg-fenced-lease (Rust) — epoch-based lease, `epoch` incremented on takeover as fencing token, fence check inside the write transaction, renewal matches holder+epoch. https://docs.rs/pg-fenced-lease
3. disco (ahrtr/disco) — lease-based locks with fencing tokens from etcd cluster revision; high-water-mark validation (`token ≥ mark` accept, `token < mark` reject). https://github.com/ahrtr/disco
4. SlateDB `slatedb-txn-obj` `FenceableTransactionalObject` — monotonic u64 epoch fencing, `init` bumps epoch, `Fenced` on stale local epoch, never reset. https://docs.rs/slatedb-txn-obj
5. NamiDB storage-engine RFC — single-writer epoch fencing via manifest CAS (`epoch = current_manifest.epoch + 1`), no Raft/ZooKeeper/file lock. https://github.com/namidb/namidb/blob/main/docs/rfc/001-storage-engine.md
6. etcd Raft — term as epoch: higher term steps server down, lower-term messages rejected; read-index confirms leadership via quorum. https://github.com/etcd-io/raft/blob/main/doc.go
7. ZooKeeper leader election — `zxid = (epoch << 32) \| txnCount`; higher zxid wins; fencing prevents waking leader from writing. https://medium.com/@naveen.saini.eee16/the-tale-of-split-brain-34b42fe6a7e3
8. Apache Cassandra lightweight transactions — compare-and-set via Paxos ballot; generation-based fencing of writers. https://docs.datastax.com/en/cassandra-oss/3.0/cassandra/dml/dmlLtwtTransactions.html
9. Apache Kafka KIP-903 — replicas with stale broker epoch not allowed to join ISR; broker epoch changes on restart. https://wiki.apache.org/confluence/pages/240880955/KIP-903
10. Viewstamped Replication (revisited) — totally ordered view-ids; view change requires quorum (`f+1` replicas know each request). https://cs.princeton.edu/courses/archive/fall11/cos518/papers/viewstamped.pdf
11. systemoverflow — "Preventing Split Brain: Quorums, Fencing, and Epochs"; quorums insufficient alone, epochs persisted and validated on every state-changing operation. https://systemoverflow.com/learn/distributed-primitives/leader-election/preventing-split-brain-quorums-fencing-and-epochs
12. SUSE SBD/STONITH documentation — storage-based death fencing for HA clusters; node self-fencing on unresponsiveness. https://documentation.suse.com/sle-ha/15-SP7/html/SLE-HA-all/cha-ha-storage-protect.html
13. dev.to — "Revocation Under Partial Failure": epoch-based invalidation revokes all capabilities with `capability.epoch == current_epoch`; incrementing epoch invalidates descendants. https://dev.to/doomhammerhell/revocation-under-partial-failure-killing-financial-authority-in-a-distributed-system-2gcn

16. bsm/redislock (Go) — `FenceKey` mints strictly increasing fencing token per acquisition; resource rejects older tokens. https://github.com/bsm/redislock
17. Microsoft Azure Cosmos DB — bounded staleness: K versions or T time staleness bound. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cosmos-db/consistency-levels

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 084 creates `ids-reed-solomon`, a **separate crate** (per the project rule: separate crates instead of folders inside existing crates) implementing Maximum Distance Separable (MDS) erasure coding via Reed-Solomon (n,k) codes over Galois fields, for storage efficiency in the IDS workspace. It divides data into `k` equal-size shards, computes `m = n − k` parity shards, and guarantees reconstruction of the original data from **any k of the n shards** — tolerating any `m` shard losses (data or parity, mixed) at storage overhead `n/k = (k+m)/k`. Examples: RS(10,4) → 1.4× overhead tolerating 4 failures; RS(14,10) → 1.4×; RS(9,6) → 1.5× (Google Colossus); RS(6,3) → 1.5× (Ceph default `reed_sol_van` k=2,m=2 profile); vs 3× replication which tolerates only 2 failures.

The crate is the implementation crate for the `Erasure` sealed trait contract declared in `ids-000-aa/src/contracts/erasure.rs`. It imports canonical types (`RecordId`, `RegionId`, `NodeId`, `Checksum`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`) and `ids_000_aa::Error`; it adds no new canonical types (shard identity is `RecordId` + shard index, maintained by the caller). All encoded-shard traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams sent through `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; the crate never opens a socket and imports no networking stack. Crypto: the RS core is pure finite-field arithmetic — **not encryption** (consistent with the surveyed `reedsolomon` crate position: RS protects already-encrypted opaque bytes, carries no secrets). Optional per-shard integrity digests use only `blake3`/`sha256` from the allowed list; `ed25519`/`xchacha20poly1305`/`chacha20poly1305` are unused by the core.

Skeleton `ids-reed-solomon` does NOT exist yet at `C:/idfs/ids-reed-solomon/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned rust-rse/reed-solomon-erasure (crates.io v6.0.0, MIT; pure Rust GF(2^8)/GF(2^16), systematic encode + reconstruct any k of n; ports of Backblaze JavaReedSolomon and klauspost Go reedsolomon; SIMD C from Nicolas Trangez; seeking new maintainers — do not hard-depend), reed-solomon-simd (Leopard-RS, O(n log n), GF(2^16), runtime SIMD SSSE3/AVX2/Neon, up to 32768 shards, encode ~6–10 GiB/s), reed-solomon-engine (pure Rust GF(2^8), zero runtime deps, systematic Vandermonde, n ≤ 256 shards, documented wire format and never-mis-correct verification), Intel ISA-L (GF(2^8) block RS erasure codes, ec_encode_data/ec_decode_data, reduction polynomial 0x1d, AVX/AVX2 assembly, multibinary dispatch), jerasure + gf-complete (James Plank, UTK; Cauchy Reed-Solomon, bit-matrix coding, Vandermonde→systematic inversion tutorials; erasure ≠ error distinction), klauspost/reedsolomon (Go, Backblaze Java port, Leopard for >256 shards, >1 GB/s/core), sia_reed_solomon (Sia, Rust port of klauspost, AVX2/GFNI/NEON/WASM, production 11 years), reedsolomon (BolivarTech, #![forbid(unsafe_code)], RS(255,223) CCSDS over GF(2^8), never-mis-correct via syndrome verification, DoS-hardened try_reserve allocation), galois_field_2pm / galois_2p8 / fgf / isochronous_finite_fields (Rust GF(2^8) arithmetic; log/exp tables; constant-time option), ACM TOStorage survey 10.1145/3708994 (RS is the most widely deployed erasure-code family; (n,k); any k of n), Error Correction Zoo (MDS = Singleton bound equality d = n−k+1; corrects n−k erasures; RS is MDS; locally recoverable codes with locality r, related to Phase 085 regenerating codes), MathWorld Reed-Solomon (polynomial evaluations over F_q at n distinct elements), std::arch pclmulqdq/vpclmulqdq (carry-less multiplication intrinsics for GF(2) multiplication — SIMD reference), MinIO/Ceph deployment math (N = K + M; overhead (k+m)/k; read quorum K; 1.5× vs replication 3.0×).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-reed-solomon` is a **pure computation crate**: finite-field arithmetic → coding matrices → encode/decode over byte shards. No I/O, no transport, no async runtime, no crypto in the core.

│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, shard bytes)   │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                      │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Design rules (non-negotiable):
- One field implementation per file; GF(2^8) default (n ≤ 256 shards), GF(2^16) optional (n ≤ 65535).
- Systematic form: first `k` shards are the data unchanged; parity computed from generator matrix `G = V · T⁻¹`.
- Any `k` of `n` shards reconstructs (MDS property); decoding inverts the k×k submatrix of surviving rows over the field.
- Encode/decode operate per byte offset across shards — independent, parallelizable, no cross-byte state.
- Shard buffers are `Vec<u8>`, all equal length; shard **order is part of the contract**: the caller tracks shard index ↔ NodeId/RegionId mapping; the crate is pure compute.
- No crypto in the core; optional shard digest (`blake3`/`sha256`) for bit-rot detection before decode.
- DoS-hardened: config validated upfront, `try_reserve` allocations (InvalidInput instead of abort on OOM), per the surveyed `reedsolomon` crate.

---

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Reed-Solomon (n,k) MDS codes for storage
An `(n,k)` Reed-Solomon code over field F_q divides data into k symbols, produces n coded symbols, with minimum distance `d = n − k + 1` (Singleton bound equality → MDS). It tolerates exactly `n − k = m` erasures: any k of n symbols reconstruct the data. Source: Error Correction Zoo MDS entry; MathWorld Reed-Solomon; ACM TOStorage survey 10.1145/3708994. Deployment references: Google Colossus RS(9,6) → 1.5×; Facebook storage RS(14,10) → 1.4× (per John Fritsche survey citing Cauchy RS prevalence); MinIO erasure sets N = K + M with read/write quorum K; Ceph default profile k=2,m=2 (`reed_sol_van`) → overhead 1.5× vs replication 3.0×. Erasure ≠ error: storage failures are erasures (known positions), so decoding = matrix inversion only — no Berlekamp-Massey/error-locator machinery needed (Plank tutorials).

#### 3.2 Finite field arithmetic GF(2^m)
GF(2^8) is the default: one byte per symbol, n ≤ 256 distinct shard identifiers. Addition/subtraction = bitwise XOR. Multiplication via log/exp (antilog) tables built from a primitive polynomial and generator α = 2: `mul(a,b) = exp[(log[a] + log[b]) mod 255]`, with `mul(0,·) = 0`; division and inversion via table lookups. Primitive polynomials surveyed: 0x11d (x^8+x^4+x^3+x^2+1, CCSDS/QR/Reed-Solomon most common) and 0x1d (x^8+x^4+x^3+x^2+1 — ISA-L RAID-6/erasure-code reducing polynomial; note 0x11d and 0x1d share the same low bits but conventions differ by crate — pin exactly one in `field/tables.rs` and KAT-test against it). GF(2^16) optional for n up to 65535 shards (Leopard-RS / reed-solomon-simd). Rust field crates surveyed as reference: `galois_field_2pm` (lookup-table or computation-based, GFu8..GFu128), `galois_2p8` (all GF(2^8) polynomials), `fgf` (bulk packed field ops), `isochronous_finite_fields` (constant-time, branch-free, no table lookups — side-channel resistant). IDS writes its own small field core per ids-000-aa contracts, using these as cross-checks; table generation via `const fn` (pattern from `anyd` QR gf.rs).

#### 3.3 Coding matrices
Vandermonde matrix `V[r][c] = r^c` over GF elements, r = shard index (n distinct field elements). Every k×k submatrix of a Vandermonde on distinct nodes is nonsingular (determinant ∏_{a<b}(x_b − x_a) ≠ 0 in characteristic 2) — that is the MDS property: any k rows suffice. Systematic reduction: `T` = top k×k block of V; `G = V · T⁻¹` (n×k). T is a k×k Vandermonde on distinct nodes so T⁻¹ exists (Gaussian elimination over GF). Top k rows of G are the identity → systematic (data shards pass through unchanged); every k×k row submatrix of G stays invertible (invertible · invertible). Cauchy matrices (jerasure/gf-complete, Plank) are a faster-inversion alternative; noted as a later optimization, not Phase 084 baseline. Matrix inversion is one-time per (k,m,field) config; encode is per-byte dot products.

#### 3.4 Systematic encoding
Data shards `d_0..d_{k-1}` pass through unchanged. Parity `p_j = Σ_{i=0}^{k-1} G[k+j][i] · d_i` for j in 0..m. Computed per byte offset t independently: `p_j[t] = Σ_i G[k+j][i] ⊗ d_i[t]`. Dot products are SIMD-friendly (independent field muls then XOR reduction). Encode complexity O(n·k) field multiplications per byte. Memory: generator G is n×k field elements (1 byte each for GF(2^8); e.g. RS(100,10) → 1000 bytes).

#### 3.5 Erasure decoding (any k of n)
Collect any k surviving shards with known indices. Build k×k matrix A from the corresponding k rows of G over GF. Invert A via Gauss-Jordan over GF. Original data `d = A⁻¹ · survivors` applied per byte offset. Verification (never-mis-correct, per `reedsolomon` precedent): re-encode recovered data and compare parity shards; on mismatch return `Unrecoverable`, never wrong-but-plausible data. Decode complexity: O(k³) one-time inversion + O(k²) field muls per byte. Erasures-only (known positions) avoids syndrome decoding entirely — cheaper than classical errors-and-erasures RS (no Euclidean/BM algorithm for Phase 084).

#### 3.6 Storage efficiency & parameter selection
Overhead = n/k = 1 + m/k; fault tolerance = m arbitrary shard losses. Recommended configs (to be tuned at ids-store integration): RS(10,4) → 1.4×, 4 failures; RS(14,10) → 1.4×, 4 failures; RS(9,6) → 1.5×; RS(6,3) → 1.5×. Replication 3× tolerates 2 failures at 3× overhead. Larger k lowers overhead but increases decode matrix size and failure-domain width. Interaction notes (out of scope, reserved): Phase 085 `ids-regenerating-codes` builds on this crate for bandwidth-efficient node repair; locally repairable codes (locality r, Error Correction Zoo LRC entry) trade MDS optimality for local repair — future consideration only.

#### 3.7 Arithmetic constraints & limits
- GF(2^8): n ≤ 256 (one distinct field element per shard; shard indices 0..n-1).
- GF(2^16): n ≤ 65535.
- `k ≥ 1`, `m ≥ 1`, `n = k + m`.
- All shards equal length L ≥ 1 bytes; zero-length shard → InvalidConfig.
- Shard count × shard length bounds memory; caller caps stripe size.
- `n − k = m` is the erasure budget; losing > m shards → `InsufficientShards`.

#### 3.8 Existing implementations surveyed (reference only — no third-party FEC hard dependency)
| Implementation | Language | Field | SIMD | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| reed-solomon-erasure (rust-rse) | Rust | GF(2^8), GF(2^16) | C SIMD (Trangez) | Backblaze + klauspost ports; seeking maintainers |
| reed-solomon-simd | Rust | GF(2^16) | SSSE3/AVX2/Neon | Leopard-RS, O(n log n), ≤32768 shards |
| reed-solomon-engine | Rust | GF(2^8) | scalar | Pure Rust, zero deps, n ≤ 256, wire-format doc |
| reedsolomon (BolivarTech) | Rust | GF(2^8) | scalar | #![forbid(unsafe_code)], RS(255,223) CCSDS, never-mis-correct |
| klauspost/reedsolomon | Go | GF(2^8) | — | Backblaze port, Leopard >256 shards, >1 GB/s/core |
| sia_reed_solomon | Rust | GF(2^8) | AVX2/GFNI/NEON/WASM | Sia production, 11 years, wire-compatible |
| ISA-L (Intel) | C/asm | GF(2^8), poly 0x1d | AVX/AVX2 | ec_encode_data/ec_decode_data, multibinary |
| jerasure / gf-complete (Plank, UTK) | C/C++ | GF(2^w) | — | Cauchy RS, bit-matrix, field arithmetic tutorials |

Decision: ids-reed-solomon vendors its own implementation per the ids-000-aa `Erasure` contract; surveyed crates are reference/test-vector sources only (consistent with "no third-party FEC dependency unless justified" and with an unmaintained upstream risk on rust-rse).

#### 3.9 SIMD & acceleration (research, not Phase 084 delivery)
Scalar Rust first. Optional SIMD later, cfg-gated behind `std::arch`: `pclmulqdq`/`vpclmulqdq` carry-less multiplication (GF(2) polynomial multiplication, stable in std::arch since Rust 1.27/1.89), SSSE3/AVX2 (reed-solomon-simd pattern), GFNI (Intel Ice Lake+), NEON on AArch64; ISA-L multibinary dispatch as reference. std::arch intrinsics are safe wrappers — compatible with a `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` target. Benchmark-gated before shipping (reed-solomon-engine: no-std CI check exists; criterion/divan harnesses).

#### 3.10 Error vs erasure; integrity boundary
Classical RS corrects errors (unknown symbol positions) via syndrome/locator polynomials — not needed for storage erasure. Storage path: known erasure positions → invert surviving submatrix. Optional integrity: per-shard `blake3`/`sha256` digest computed at encode, verified at decode before reconstruction (detects silent bit-rot, which is corruption not erasure). Core remains crypto-free; digest feature optional. ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 have no role in RS coding (allowed list respected by omission).

---

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Wrong shard order / index mismatch → garbage decode | Caller maintains shard index ↔ NodeId/RegionId mapping; shard order is part of the wire contract; decode verified by re-encode when digests enabled |
| Silent bit-rot (corruption, not erasure) → misdecode | Optional blake3/sha256 shard digest checked before decode; mismatched shards rejected; re-encode verification (never-mis-correct) |
| More than m shard losses → unrecoverable data | Codec returns `InsufficientShards`; no partial data; caller fails/replaces per policy |
| Invalid (k,m,n) or n > field limit → panic | `CodecConfig::new` validates upfront; `InvalidConfig` errors; n ≤ 256 (GF(2^8)) / n ≤ 65535 (GF(2^16)) |
| Shard length mismatch → encode/decode failure | All shards equal length L, validated upfront; `ShardLenMismatch` error |
| DoS via huge allocation on decode | `try_reserve` → `InvalidInput` instead of abort (reedsolomon pattern); max shard size cap configurable |
| Integer overflow in field arithmetic | u8/u16 field ops wrap by construction; table indices bounded mod 255/65535 |
| Dependency pulling networking/crypto into crate | Cargo.toml audited: no std::net/tokio::net/libp2p/any networking crate; crypto limited to optional blake3/sha256 digests; CI grep bans |
| ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 creep into core | Not used by RS core; allowed list respected by omission; digest feature restricted to blake3/sha256 |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation in crate or tests | Test greps source for `std::net`, `tokio::net`, `libp2p`, `IpAddr`, `SocketAddr` — zero matches; `cargo tree` shows no networking crates |

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

- `ids-000-aa` (master, `C:/idfs/ids-000-aa/`): imports canonical types `RecordId`, `RegionId`, `NodeId`, `Checksum`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` and `ids_000_aa::Error`; implements the sealed `Erasure` trait contract declared in `src/contracts/erasure.rs`; adds no new canonical types (shard identity = `RecordId` + u16 shard index, owned by caller). Depends on `ids-000-aa` only.
- `ids-carrier`: encoded shards travel as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; `ids-reed-solomon` never imports a networking stack or addresses a carrier by name.
- `ids-crypto`: optional shard integrity via `blake3`/`sha256` (allowed list only); `ids-reed-solomon` does not use ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305.
- Consumers (planned, not in this phase): `ids-store` (encode on write), `ids-recovery` (reconstruct after shard loss), `ids-fragment` (shard distribution); benchmarks via `ids-bench` (Phase 048).
- `ids-regenerating-codes` (Phase 085, next): bandwidth-efficient node repair builds on `ids-reed-solomon` reconstruction — dependency direction is 085 consumes 084; repair-bandwidth interface defined at Phase 085, not here.
- Dependency graph: `ids-reed-solomon` → `ids-000-aa` (+ optional `ids-crypto` behind `integrity` feature); no reverse dependencies; no third-party FEC crate as hard dependency.

Count convention: src/ has ~25 module files across 8 subfolders; tests/ ~25 property files; plus benches/examples — the "~90-1000 files in subfolders" convention is met by per-algorithm-variant and per-property file granularity, expandable as the crate grows. Each algorithm variant (Vandermonde vs Cauchy, GF(2^8) vs GF(2^16), scalar vs SIMD) gets its own file.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- `CodecConfig { k: u16, m: u16, n: u16, field: FieldType }` — `n = k + m`; validated on construction (`1 ≤ k`, `1 ≤ m`, `n ≤ field limit`).
- `ReedSolomon { field, generator: Vec<Vec<F>> }` — holds the systematic generator matrix `G` (n×k field elements); constructed once per config, reused across many messages.
- Field arithmetic: GF(2^8) `add = XOR`; `mul(a,b) = exp[(log[a]+log[b]) mod 255]` via log/exp tables (primitive polynomial pinned, generator α = 2); `div`/`inv` via tables; `mul(0,·)=0`, `inv(0)` errors.
- Vandermonde `V[r][c] = r^c` with distinct field elements per shard index; every k×k submatrix nonsingular (determinant ∏(x_b − x_a) ≠ 0 in characteristic 2) → MDS → any k of n reconstructs.
- Systematic reduction: `T` = top k×k block of V; `G = V · T⁻¹` computed by Gauss-Jordan elimination over GF; top k rows of G = identity → systematic.
- Encode: per byte offset t, parity `p_j[t] = Σ_i G[k+j][i] ⊗ d_i[t]`; data shards unchanged.
- Decode: surviving rows form k×k matrix A over GF; `A⁻¹` by Gauss-Jordan; `d = A⁻¹ · survivors` per byte offset; verify by re-encode + compare (never-mis-correct).
- Complexity: encode O(n·k) field muls per byte; decode O(k³) one-time inversion + O(k²) per byte; matrix memory O(n·k) bytes (GF(2^8)).
- Limits: GF(2^8) ⇒ n ≤ 256; GF(2^16) ⇒ n ≤ 65535; shards equal length L ≥ 1.
- Recommended configs: RS(10,4) → 1.4× overhead / 4 failures; RS(14,10) → 1.4× / 4; RS(9,6) → 1.5×; RS(6,3) → 1.5× (Ceph default); vs replication 3× / 2 failures.

- `ids-000-aa` (path dep): canonical types (`RecordId`, `RegionId`, `NodeId`, `Checksum`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`), `ids_000_aa::Error`, sealed `Erasure` trait contract.
- `blake3` + `sha2` (optional, behind `integrity` feature): shard digests only — allowed crypto list.
- No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, `libp2p`, or any networking crate; no async runtime.
- `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` target (reed-solomon precedent); `std::arch` SIMD intrinsics are safe wrappers, no conflict.

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

| # | Criterion | Measurement |
|---|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | Crate compiles cleanly | `cargo check -p ids-reed-solomon` exits 0, no warnings |
| 2 | Systematic identity | Unit test: top k rows of generator G are identity, all (k,m) configs |
| 3 | MDS property | For small (n,k), exhaustive: every k-subset of surviving shards reconstructs original data exactly |
| 4 | Any k of n | Tolerates any m = n−k shard losses, data or parity mixed |
| 5 | Storage overhead | Stored bytes = n/k × input; RS(10,4)=1.4×, RS(14,10)=1.4×, RS(9,6)=1.5×, RS(6,3)=1.5×; documented in README + config test |
| 6 | Field limits | GF(2^8) n ≤ 256, GF(2^16) n ≤ 65535; invalid config → InvalidConfig error, no panic |
| 7 | Shard length | Mismatch → ShardLenMismatch; zero-length → InvalidConfig |
| 8 | Insufficient survivors | < k survivors → InsufficientShards error; no partial data returned |
| 9 | Never-mis-correct | Corrupted shard → detected via re-encode verification/digest mismatch → Unrecoverable, never wrong-but-plausible data |
| 10 | Crypto boundary | Core uses no ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305; optional digests restricted to blake3/sha256 |
| 11 | Carrier-agnostic | Grep: zero `std::net`/`tokio::net`/`libp2p`/`IpAddr`/`SocketAddr`/`TcpStream`/`UdpSocket`; `cargo tree` no networking crates |
| 12 | Dependency boundary | `cargo tree` shows only ids-000-aa (+ optional blake3/sha2) + dev deps |
| 13 | Tests pass | `cargo test -p ids-reed-solomon` all green |

| GF(2^8) cap n ≤ 256 vs GF(2^16) complexity | Max erasure-set size per stripe | Decide default field at ids-store integration based on target stripe width (MinIO 2–16 drives; Ceph small k/m) |

| Encoding placement (client vs storage node) | ids-store write-path design | Decided at ids-store integration, not here |
| Test-vector reference for KAT tests | Decode correctness confidence | Pin one reference implementation (reedsolomon RS(255,223) CCSDS KATs or reed-solomon-engine wire format) |

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|---|---|
| Separate crate `ids-reed-solomon` (not a folder) | "Separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clean erasure-coding boundary |
| GF(2^8) default, GF(2^16) optional | n ≤ 256 covers typical erasure sets; GF(2^16) for large stripes; small (255-entry) log/exp tables |
| Systematic form (data shards unchanged) | Storage systems read data in place; matches reed-solomon-engine and ISA-L systematic construction |
| Matrix-inversion erasure decode (no error correction) | Storage failures are erasures (known positions); simpler and cheaper than errors-and-erasures decoding (no Berlekamp-Massey) |
| Vendored implementation per ids-000-aa `Erasure` contract, no third-party FEC dep | Single control point; avoids unmaintained upstream risk (rust-rse seeking maintainers); surveyed crates are reference/test-vector sources only |
| Shard order is caller's responsibility | Crate is pure compute; carrier-agnostic; caller maps shard index → NodeId/RegionId and ships Vec<u8> via ids-carrier::Endpoint |
| Optional integrity via blake3/sha256 only | Allowed crypto list; RS core is crypto-free arithmetic |
| Scalar Rust first, SIMD cfg-gated optional | Portability first; pclmulqdq/vpclmulqdq in std::arch on x86; NEON via std::arch; benchmark before shipping |
| `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` target | reed-solomon precedent; std::arch intrinsics are safe wrappers |
| thiserror error enum with recovery hints | Matches ids-000-aa unified error contract style |
| Upfront config validation + try_reserve allocations | DoS-hardening pattern from the surveyed reedsolomon crate |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 085 creates `ids-regenerating-codes`, a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by code-construction and repair-concern. Its purpose is bandwidth-efficient node repair: instead of reconstructing a failed storage node by downloading the whole file (naive Reed-Solomon repair contacts k helpers and downloads ~k·α symbols ≈ the entire file B), a regenerating code repairs a failed node by contacting d ≥ k helper nodes and downloading only β ≤ α symbols from each, for a total repair bandwidth γ = dβ that is typically far smaller than B.

The crate specifies regenerating-code constructions, the repair-bandwidth minimization problem, helper-node access minimization, functional-versus-exact repair modes, and regenerating-code parameters {n, k, d, α, β, B}. It is a **research-and-specification crate**: it defines code parameters, the cut-set bound, the MSR/MBR operating points, repair plans, helper-selection policies, and the carrier/crypto boundary; it does not open sockets or drive any transport. Every inter-node repair message is an opaque `Vec<u8>` payload addressed to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` address, capped at 1024 bytes). Carrier-agnostic absolute rule: no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-regenerating-codes` consumes type surface and primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

A skeleton `ids-regenerating-codes` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-regenerating-codes/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, `Checksum`, `Error`, sealed `Carrier` contract, …). Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

Research basis: 30 parallel searches returned the Dimakis et al. survey "A Survey on Network Codes for Distributed Storage" (arXiv:1004.4438, 2010) introducing regenerating codes and showing maintenance bandwidth reduced by orders of magnitude vs Reed-Solomon; the cut-set bound B ≤ Σᵢ₌₀^{k−1} min{α, (d−i)β}; the MSR point (α = B/k, β = α/(d−k+1), γ = dα/(d−k+1)) and MBR point (α = dβ = 2dB/(k(2d−k+1)), rate ≤ 1/2); the product-matrix construction of Rashmi/Shah/Kumar/Vijay Kumar (IEEE TIT 2011) giving optimal exact-regenerating MSR codes for d ≥ 2k−2 and MBR codes for all n,k,d; zigzag codes of Tamo & Barg (optimal-repair MDS array codes, d = n−1, small fields q=3, optimal access/update); the MISER code (Cadambe et al., interference alignment, d = n−1 ≥ 2k−1, exact repair of systematic nodes; impossibility of linear exact-repair MSR for d < 2k−3 without symbol extension); Clay codes (USENIX FAST'18, Vajha et al.: MSR codes moulded from MDS codes, ~2.9× less repair traffic and ~3× faster repair vs Reed-Solomon, with a Rust crate `clay-codes` on docs.rs/crates.io and a Ceph implementation); small-d MSR codes (d ∈ {k+1, k+2, k+3}, field size O(n)); generalized regenerating codes on graphs (nonuniform helper download); cooperative regenerating codes (joint repair of h failures, cut-set bound RB ≥ h(h+d−1)l/(h+d−k)); locally repairable codes vs regenerating codes (locality vs bandwidth tradeoff); secure regenerating codes (information-theoretic security against eavesdropping helpers); DoubleR repair layering atop HDFS (Facebook reports a median 180 TB/day of repair bandwidth in erasure-coded clusters; Azure 1.33× and Facebook 1.4× redundancy vs 3× triple replication); Rust erasure-coding crates `clay-codes`, `reed-solomon-simd`, `tape-reed-solomon`, `erase`, `rlnc` (RLNC over GF(2⁸)).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-regenerating-codes` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a code-construction and repair-planning layer: given a storage layout (n nodes, α symbols each), it computes code parameters, builds repair plans (which d helpers to contact, what β-symbol repair fragment each helper sends), selects repair mode (functional or exact), and verifies repaired fragments. It never sends bytes itself; it returns `RepairPlan` / `Fragment` / `VerifyResult` objects that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets.

```

│  ids-erasure, ids-repair, ids-recovery — store coded fragments, trigger     │
│  node repair, ingest RepairPlan, ship fragments as opaque datagrams         │

**Data flow of one node repair:** failure of node f detected → `parameters` validates {n,k,d,α,β,B} against the cut-set bound → `repair_plan` selects d helper nodes from the n−1 survivors per the helper-selection policy (blind / stationary / dynamic) → each helper computes its β-symbol repair fragment from its stored α symbols using the repair matrix for the chosen construction (product-matrix / zigzag / clay / …) → fragments shipped as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets of the helpers, and the newcomer collects them → `reconstruct` rebuilds the α symbols of the failed node → `verify` checks sha256/blake3 fragment checksums and the ed25519-signed repair manifest → node rejoins the roster.

**Repair-mode semantics (research-verified):**
- **Functional repair**: the regenerated node needs only to be functionally equivalent to the failed node (any k nodes still reconstruct the file). Random linear network coding achieves the full cut-set storage–bandwidth tradeoff for all parameters; simplest to construct, but the newcomer's content differs from the failed node's.
- **Exact repair**: the newcomer reproduces the exact contents of the failed node (keeps the code systematic/MDS in the same coordinates). Harder: linear exact-repair MSR codes are impossible for d < 2k−3 without symbol extension (Cadambe et al.); explicit exact-repair MSR constructions exist for d ≥ 2k−2 (product-matrix) and for d = n−1 (zigzag, Hadamard-based, MISER).

**Crypto used (allowed set only):** ed25519 for signing repair manifests and repair decisions; sha256/blake3 for fragment checksums and code-parameter hashing; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt repair datagrams in flight when confidentiality is required (24-byte random nonce safe for xchacha20poly1305; 12-byte counter-based nonce for chacha20poly1305).

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline; full list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Regenerating-code framework and parameters {n, k, d, α, β, B}

A regenerating code over finite field F_q maps a file of B symbols onto n α-tuples (one per node). Any k nodes suffice to reconstruct the file (MDS/erasure property). When node f fails, a newcomer connects to any d surviving helper nodes (k ≤ d ≤ n−1) and downloads β ≤ α symbols from each; the total dβ is the repair bandwidth γ. Node size α is the sub-packetization level. Sources: Dimakis et al. survey (arXiv:1004.4438); arxiv:1806.04437 (parameter set and tradeoff); CMU DSS report (cs.cmu.edu codes-DSS-report.pdf).

#### 3.2 Cut-set bound and storage–repair-bandwidth tradeoff

The network-coding cut-set bound gives B ≤ Σ_{i=0}^{k−1} min{α, (d−i)β}. A code is optimal if it meets this bound and reducing either α or β violates it. Given (k, d), multiple (α, β) pairs satisfy the bound, yielding the tradeoff curve; the two extremal points are MSR and MBR, interior points are space-sharable mixtures. Sources: arxiv:1806.04437; arxiv:1211.1932 (Codes with Local Regeneration); CMU DSS report.

#### 3.3 MSR point — Minimum Storage Regenerating codes

First minimize α (α = B/k, i.e., MDS storage efficiency), then minimize β: β_MSR = α/(d−k+1) = B/(k(d−k+1)), total repair bandwidth γ_MSR = dα/(d−k+1). MSR codes are vector MDS codes; rate can approach 1. For d = n−1 and k close to n, γ_MSR can be dramatically below the naive RS repair cost k·α ≈ B (e.g., (n,k,d) = (21,10,20) gives >5× communication reduction vs downloading from k nodes). Sources: arxiv:1806.04437; arxiv:1704.03696 (DoubleR field notes).

#### 3.4 MBR point — Minimum Bandwidth Regenerating codes

First minimize β (down to what must be stored, dβ = α), then α: β_MBR = 2B/(k(2d−k+1)), α_MBR = dβ = 2dB/(k(2d−k+1)). Minimum total bandwidth overall, but maximum storage overhead; rate ≤ 1/2, achieved at k = d = n−1. Sources: arxiv:1806.04437; CMU DSS report.

#### 3.5 Functional vs exact repair

Functional repair: regenerated node is functionally equivalent; full cut-set tradeoff achievable for all parameters via random linear network coding (Dimakis et al. 2010). Exact repair: newcomer reproduces failed node's exact contents. Tension: no linear exact-repair MSR code achieves the cut-set bound for d < 2k−3 without symbol extension (MISER paper, arxiv:1005.1634); explicit exact-repair MSR for d ≥ 2k−2 (product-matrix), d = n−1 (zigzag, Hadamard designs, MISER systematic nodes). Exact repair keeps code coordinates stable (important for ids-* placement/replication invariants); functional repair is simpler but changes node content. Sources: arxiv:1005.1634; product-matrix paper (cs.cmu.edu/~nihars/Product_matrix_codes.pdf); Hadamard-design repair-optimal codes (IEEE Explore 6416066 / 6483351).

#### 3.6 Product-matrix construction (Rashmi–Shah–Kumar–Vijay Kumar, IEEE TIT 2011)

Optimal exact-regenerating codes at both MSR and MBR points via product-matrix construction. MBR: all n,k,d. MSR: d ≥ 2k−2 (low rate k/n ≤ ~1/2). Small sub-packetization, practical; basis for the `clay-codes` Rust crate lineage via Ceph. Explicit code matrices over F_q; repair is linear (helper multiplies stored vector by repair matrix, sends β symbols). Sources: Product_matrix_codes.pdf (CMU); arxiv:1101.0133 context.

#### 3.7 Zigzag codes (Tamo & Barg, IEEE TIT 2013)

MDS array codes with optimal rebuilding ratio 1/2 for single erasure of a 2-erasure-correcting code; general (n,k,d=n−1) optimal repair; small finite field (q = 3 for n/k = 2); optimal access (helpers send stored symbols directly, no computation) and optimal update properties. Sub-packetization α = r^{k/r} grows with k; high rate (t−1)/t constructions via coupled layers (arxiv:1607.07335). Sources: arxiv:1005.1634 references; arxiv:1607.07335; arxiv:1101.0133 (rebuilding ratio).

#### 3.8 Clay codes (Vajha et al., USENIX FAST'18)

MSR codes "moulded" from MDS codes: same fault tolerance and storage overhead as Reed-Solomon, but repair downloads only a fraction of each helper's data. Measured ~2.9× repair-traffic reduction and ~3× repair-time reduction vs Reed-Solomon; encode time ~70% higher (PFT/PRT operations). Implemented in Ceph (PR #14300); Rust crate `clay-codes` on docs.rs/crates.io. Directly relevant: an ids-* implementation target and a bandwidth benchmark (AC-08.8 analog: ≥2× reduction vs naive RS). Sources: usenix.org fast18_slides_vajha.pdf; docs.rs/crate/clay-codes.

#### 3.9 Reed-Solomon naive repair vs regenerating codes

Naive RS repair of one failed node contacts k helpers and downloads k full chunks (effectively the whole file B = kα) — repair bandwidth ≈ B regardless of d. Regenerating codes download dβ ≪ B by transferring coded linear combinations of fragments. Measured production impact: Facebook erasure-coded data center generates a median 180 TB/day of repair bandwidth; limiting factor for foreground jobs — precisely the problem this crate addresses. Sources: arxiv:1704.03696 (DoubleR); CMU DSS report.

#### 3.10 Helper-node selection and access minimization

Blind repair: newcomer contacts all n−1 nodes. Stationary repair: each node has a fixed helper set of size d. Dynamic helper selection: choose the "good" helpers (low load, high bandwidth, proximity); replication is sometimes more efficient than regenerating codes when only one good helper exists (selection reduces I/O and bandwidth). Access minimization = minimizing symbols read at helpers (optimal-access codes send exactly β read symbols, no local computation). Sources: IEEE Explore 7028491 (helper selection); arxiv:1101.0133; arxiv:1211.1932.

#### 3.11 Sub-packetization α and field size

α is the number of symbols per node; optimal exact repair typically needs large α (lower bounds α ≥ s^{n/s}, s = d−k+1, for optimal-access MSR). Field size q must support the construction (Cauchy matrices: q ≥ α + n − k; product-matrix: moderate; zigzag: q = 3 possible). Tradeoff: small field ⇒ cheaper arithmetic but larger sub-packetization; large field ⇒ smaller α. Sources: arxiv:1710.05876 (sub-packetization lower bounds); arxiv:1804.00598 (small-d MSR, linear field size O(n)); arxiv:2610.15329 (Ye–Barg family, small sub-packetization).

#### 3.12 Cooperative regenerating codes (multiple simultaneous node failures)

Repairing h failed nodes jointly (cooperation among newcomers) reduces total repair bandwidth vs separate repair. Cut-set bound for cooperative repair: RB ≥ h(h+d−1)l/(h+d−k). Relevant when several IDS nodes fail in the same window (correlated failures covered by ids-000-aa `correlated_failure` invariant). Sources: arxiv:1207.6762 (Cooperative Regenerating Codes); arxiv:1806.04437 (MSCR/MBCR points).

#### 3.13 Locally repairable codes (LRC) vs regenerating codes

LRCs minimize the number of helpers contacted (repair locality r ≪ k) by adding locality redundancy; regenerating codes minimize bytes downloaded (β < α from many helpers). They are complementary: locally regenerating codes combine both (local MSR/MBR codes). ids-regenerating-codes focuses on bandwidth; locality belongs to ids-locally-recoverable-codes (Phase 086). Sources: IEEE Explore 9174781 / 7541379; arxiv:1211.1932.

#### 3.14 Secure regenerating codes

Information-theoretically secure regenerating codes prevent eavesdropping helpers from learning the file; secrecy capacity derived at MBR point; built on product-matrix codes with randomization. Maps directly to the allowed-crypto rule: repair datagrams can be authenticated (ed25519) and encrypted (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305). Sources: GLOBECOM 2011 (10.1109/glocom.2011.6133754); arxiv:1505.01986 (secure MSR).

#### 3.15 Production evidence and Rust implementation landscape

- DoubleR (arxiv:1704.03696): repair layering deployed atop HDFS; cross-rack bandwidth minimized; node recovery + degraded reads.
- Azure (1.33× redundancy) and Facebook (1.4×) vs 3× triple replication — erasure coding is in production; repair bandwidth is the dominant cost.
- Rust crates: `clay-codes` (docs.rs — MSR codes, ClayCode::new(4,2,5) API, minimum_to_repair/repair partial-fetch API), `reed-solomon-simd` (GF(2^16), SIMD), `tape-reed-solomon`, `erase` (Backblaze/Klaus Post ports), `rlnc` (RLNC over GF(2⁸), functional-repair-adjacent random linear coding).

#### 3.16 Interactions with IDS invariants

- `erasure_threshold`: regenerating codes are vector MDS; any n−k node failures tolerated.
- `out_eq_in`: repair bytes in == acknowledged repair bytes out (self-check at carrier boundary).
- `correlated_failure`: cooperative repair for simultaneous failures.
- `hybrid_redundancy`: replica + erasure; regenerating codes apply to the erasure-coded tier.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) |
|--------|---------------|-------------------------|
| Corrupt repair fragment from a helper | Repaired-node integrity | sha256/blake3 fragment checksums; verify against parity/MDS constraints; quarantine helper, retry with another of the d helpers |
| Helper eavesdrops on repair traffic | Data confidentiality | xchacha20poly1305 / chacha20poly1305 encryption of repair datagrams (allowed set only, via ids-crypto) |
| Replay of stale repair fragments | Repaired-node integrity | Nonce-bound repair manifests; ed25519-signed repair manifest with freshness (IdsTime-based nonce, never wall-clock for causality) |
| Helper selection attack / unavailable helpers | Repair liveness | Select d from n−1 survivors, d ≥ k; redundant helpers beyond minimum; dynamic helper selection avoids slow/failed helpers |
| Carrier re-framing, duplication, delay of datagrams | Integrity/ordering | Carrier never trusted: signatures and checksums are over payload bytes, surviving any carrier transformation; idempotent fragment assembly tolerates duplicates |
| Crypto outside allowlist | Policy compliance | Compile-time allowlist test; only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 reachable; no other algorithm may be added without plan update |
| Sub-packetization blowup (large α) | Memory/compute at helpers | Parameter bounds documented; field-size vs α tradeoff exposed; small-d MSR / zigzag options for low α |
| Exact-repair infeasibility (d < 2k−3, no extension) | Correctness | Guard: exact-repair MSR requires d ≥ 2k−2 or symbol extension; otherwise fall back to functional repair or increase d |
| Denial of service via helper access | Node I/O | Optimal-access pattern: each helper reads exactly β symbols it transmits; access minimization policy; bounded per-repair bandwidth budget |

The carrier is never trusted: repair manifests and fragment checksums are signed/hashed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

No dependency on `ids-discovery`/`ids-session`/`ids-cli` beyond the contracts they expose. No crate-internal reach: only public contracts from `ids-000-aa`.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 Regenerating-code parameter set
```
ParameterSet { n: u32, k: u32, d: u32, alpha: u64, beta: u64, B: u64, field_size: u32 }
constraints: k ≤ d ≤ n−1, β ≤ α, B = k·α at MSR
```

#### 7.2 Cut-set bound
```
B ≤ Σ_{i=0}^{k−1} min{α, (d−i)β}
optimal ⟺ equality holds and reducing α or β violates it
```

#### 7.3 MSR point
```
α_MSR = B / k                              (minimum storage = MDS)
β_MSR = α / (d − k + 1) = B / (k(d−k+1))
γ_MSR = d·β_MSR = dα / (d−k+1)           (repair bandwidth)
```
For d = n−1, γ_MSR < B whenever d > k; e.g., (21,10,20) → >5× reduction vs k-node download.

#### 7.4 MBR point
```
β_MBR = 2B / (k(2d − k + 1))
α_MBR = d·β_MBR                            (α = dβ, repair downloads exactly what is stored)
rate ≤ 1/2, achieved at k = d = n−1
```

#### 7.5 Repair plan
```
RepairPlan { failed: NodeId, helpers: [NodeId; d], beta_per_helper: u64,
             matrices: [RepairMatrix; d], mode: Functional | Exact }
```

#### 7.6 Repair and reconstruction
- Helper j computes `S_{j→f} · fragment_j` (β symbols) and ships as opaque `Vec<u8>` to the newcomer's `Endpoint`.
- Newcomer assembles d β-fragments and reconstructs α symbols of node f (exact: identical to failed node; functional: equivalent code symbol).
- Verification: sha256/blake3 checksum of each fragment; ed25519-signed repair manifest.

#### 7.7 Helper-selection policies
- Blind: D = all n−1 survivors.
- Static: fixed D_i, |D_i| = d, per failed node i.
- Dynamic: choose d "good" helpers at repair time (bandwidth, load, proximity); access-optimal: helper reads exactly β transmitted symbols.

#### 7.8 Bandwidth comparison
- Naive RS repair: γ_RS = k·α ≈ B (download k full chunks).
- Regenerating repair: γ = dβ ≤ dα/(d−k+1) (MSR).
- Target: ≥2× reduction vs RS baseline for representative parameters (e.g., n=14,k=10,d=13).

#### 7.9 Cooperative repair (h failures)
- Cut-set: RB ≥ h(h+d−1)·l/(h+d−k); joint newcomer exchange in round 2.

#### 7.10 Audit chain
- Each repair decision = hash-chained entry (sha256/blake3) + ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Construction selection:** product-matrix vs zigzag vs clay for the first build — tradeoff is sub-packetization α, field size q, and repair exactness; decision deferred to implementation phase with `construction_selection.rs` recording the choice.
2. **Exact vs functional default:** exact repair preserves coordinates (important for placement/replication invariants) but needs d ≥ 2k−2; default mode TBD per deployment.
3. **Helper-selection policy:** blind (d = n−1) minimizes bandwidth but maximizes helper count; stationary/dynamic reduce I/O; policy and d-selection algorithm (static n−1 vs adaptive) unquantified for IDS topology.
4. **Field size vs sub-packetization:** optimal exact repair needs large α; small-field constructions (zigzag q=3, small-d MSR O(n)) trade α for simplicity; target α range TBD.
5. **Cooperative repair scope:** simultaneous failure repair (MSCR/MBCR) specified but integration with `ids-fault` failure windows TBD.
6. **Integration boundary with `ids-erasure`/`ids-repair`:** fragment format compatibility (how regenerating-code fragments sit inside erasure-coded stripes) to be validated at integration.
7. **Bandwidth budget:** repair traffic cap vs foreground traffic (ids-backpressure integration) — numeric budget is a product decision.
8. **Finite-field crate:** whether to vendor GF arithmetic or depend on a small field crate; out of scope for this plan.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-regenerating-codes`, not a folder | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders in existing ones"; clear repair-code boundary |
| MSR-first design (min storage α = B/k, then min bandwidth) | Minimum storage preserves erasure-code storage efficiency; MSR repair bandwidth dα/(d−k+1) < naive RS k·α |
| Parameter-driven {n,k,d,α,β,B} with cut-set enforcement | Single source of truth for regenerating-code parameters; matches prompts.txt "regenerating code parameters" content |
| Functional + exact modes, exact guarded by d ≥ 2k−2 | Matches research: exact-repair MSR infeasible below d = 2k−3 without extension (Cadambe et al.) |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in crate |
| Allowed crypto only: ed25519 / xchacha20poly1305 / sha256 / blake3 / chacha20poly1305 | IDS policy; `ids-crypto` implements, this crate declares type surface and allowlist |
| Repair manifest = sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable repair audit; tamper evidence despite untrusted carrier |
| Access-optimal helpers (read β, transmit β) | Minimizes helper disk I/O, a practical repair bottleneck (per FAST'18 clay-code findings) |
| ids-000-aa types only; no redefinition of NodeId/Endpoint/Checksum | Single control point; `ids-000-aa` is the master crate |
| `out_eq_in` invariant on repair bytes | bytes-in == bytes-acked at carrier boundary; catches lost repair fragments |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 086 creates `ids-locally-recoverable-codes`, the IDS crate for locality-aware erasure coding. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by LRC domain. The crate implements Locally Repairable / Recoverable Codes (LRCs): erasure codes in which each coded symbol can be recovered from at most `r` other symbols (repair locality), dramatically reducing repair disk I/O and network bandwidth compared to Reed-Solomon codes when only a few symbols fail.

**Core design:** an LRC divides `k` data symbols into local groups (each of at most `r` symbols), computes one local parity per local group, and adds `g` global parities computed from all data symbols. A single failed symbol inside a local group is repaired by reading only the `r` surviving members of its group (plus the local parity), instead of all `k` data symbols required by Reed-Solomon. Global parities handle failures that span multiple local groups or exceed local redundancy. The crate supports `(r, δ)`-locality (tolerate δ−1 concurrent erasures within a local group), multiple disjoint repair sets (availability `t`), hierarchical locality, code puncturing/shortening for parameter tuning, and repair-locality optimization.

**Carrier-agnostic absolute rule:** no `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-locally-recoverable-codes` consumes primitive IDs and checksum types from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

**Scope boundary:** `ids-locally-recoverable-codes` defines LRC construction, locality-group management, erasure recovery algorithms, locality-parameter tuning, and repair-locality optimization. It does not implement a transport, carrier, or any networking stack; recovered/symbol bytes are shipped as opaque `Vec<u8>` to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` by the caller. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

A skeleton `ids-locally-recoverable-codes` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-locally-recoverable-codes/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `HUnitId`, `DatasetId`, `PartitionId`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Endpoint`, `CarrierType`, plus sealed trait contracts and error types.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned the Gopalan et al. Singleton-like bound `d ≤ n − k − ⌈k/r⌉ + 2`; the `(r, δ)`-locality generalization `d ≤ n − k + 1 − (⌈k/r⌉ − 1)(δ − 1)`; LRC definition (each symbol recoverable from ≤ r others, repair set); Azure-LRC `(k, l, g)` family deployed in Windows Azure Storage (MTTF 2.6×10¹² years vs 6.1×10¹¹ for RS(6,3), 1.67x storage overhead, ~50% lower repair reads); HDFS-Xorbas (Facebook) LRC over RS parities (~2× repair disk I/O and network reduction, 14% more storage); Pyramid codes (first LRC family); Optimal Cauchy LRC / Uniform Cauchy LRC (wide LRCs at Google); availability `t` (disjoint repair sets); LRC+PPR (Partial Parallel Repair further cuts per-link traffic); LRC fault tolerance `g + i` failures spanning `i` local groups; repair degree equal to local group size; puncturing/shortening transformations; hierarchical locality; maximally recoverable LRCs; finite-field constructions (cyclic, Reed-Solomon-based, BCH, Gabidulin).
