### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-locally-recoverable-codes` sits above `ids-000-aa` (canonical types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is an erasure-coding layer: given a data stripe and locality parameters, it constructs an LRC codeword, partitions symbols into locality groups, computes local and global parities, and, on erasure, recovers failed symbols locally (within group) or globally (across groups). It never sends bytes itself; it returns encoded fragments and recovery plans that the caller ships as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (LRC users)                      │
│  ids-erasure, ids-recovery, ids-ppr-reconstruction — encode/decode stripes   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│             Phase 086: ids-locally-recoverable-codes (THIS CRATE)            │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ lrc_construction│ │ locality_groups │ │ erasure_recovery │ │ locality│ │
│  │ (encode/decode) │ │ (partitioning)  │ │ (single/double)  │ │ params  │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ repair_opt      │ │ r_delta_locality│ │ availability_t  │ │ puncturing│ │
│  │ (optimization)  │ │ (multi-erasure) │ │ (disjoint sets) │ │ shortening│ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐   │
│  │ hierarchical    │ │ maximally_recov │ │ finite_field    │ │ codecs    │ │
│  │ locality        │ │ (MR-LRC)        │ │ (RS/cyclic/BCH) │ │ (XOR/GF) │ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──────────┘   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┘
                                              │ opaque Vec<u8> fragments + plans
                                              ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                     │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])│
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                      │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of an LRC encode:** caller supplies `k` data symbols + locality parameters `(r, l, g)` → `lrc_construction` partitions `k` data symbols into `l = ⌈k/r⌉` local groups of ≤ `r` symbols each → computes one local parity per group (XOR or GF-linear combination) → computes `g` global parities over all `k` data symbols → returns codeword of `n = k + l + g` symbols partitioned into locality groups.

**Data flow of a single-symbol recovery:** failed symbol `c_i` belongs to local group `R_j` → `erasure_recovery` reads the `r` surviving symbols in `R_j` (excluding `c_i`) + the local parity of `R_j` → reconstructs `c_i` via the local code (single-parity-check or MDS local code) → returns recovered symbol.

**Data flow of a double-erasure recovery within a locality:** two symbols fail in the same local group → requires `(r, δ=3)`-locality (local code distance ≥ 3) → recover both from the local group using the extended local parity structure, or fall back to global parities if local redundancy insufficient.

**LRC parameter semantics (research-verified):**
- `(n, k, r)` LRC: length `n`, dimension `k`, locality `r`. Each symbol recoverable from ≤ `r` others.
- Data blocks grouped into local groups of at most `r`; one local parity per group; `g` global parities over all data.
- Local group size ≤ `r + 1` (data + local parity). Single failure in a group needs `r` reads.
- `n = k + ⌈k/r⌉ + g` (Azure-LRC form). Fault tolerance: any `g + 1` failures; up to `g + i` failures spanning `i` local groups.
- Singleton-like bound: `d ≤ n − k − ⌈k/r⌉ + 2`. Distance-optimal LRC meets equality.
- Rate bound: `k/n ≤ r/(r+1)`.
- `(r, δ)`-locality: local code distance ≥ `δ`, tolerates `δ−1` erasures per group. Bound: `d ≤ n − k + 1 − (⌈k/r⌉ − 1)(δ − 1)`.
- Availability `t`: `t` disjoint repair sets per symbol; enables parallel/concurrent recovery.

**Crypto used:** sha256/blake3 for fragment checksums and locality-group IDs; ed25519 for signing encode/decode audit entries; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt symbol fragments at rest when confidentiality required. No other crypto.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 LRC definition and basic parameters

**Source:** Error Correction Zoo (errorcorrectionzoo.org/c/locally_recoverable); Gopalan et al. (2012 ISIT); Tamo & Barg (IEEE TIT 2014); Papailiopoulos & Dimakis (2012 ISIT).

A code `C` of length `n` over alphabet `Q` is locally recoverable with locality `r` if for every coordinate `i ∈ [n]` there exists a subset `R_i ⊆ [n] \ {i}`, `|R_i| ≤ r`, and a function `φ_i` such that for every codeword `c ∈ C`, `c_i = φ_i({c_j : j ∈ R_i})`. `R_i` is called a repair set. An `(n, k, r)` LRC has length `n`, dimension `k`, locality `r`. The Singleton-like bound (Gopalan et al.): `d ≤ n − k − ⌈k/r⌉ + 2`. An LRC meeting this bound is distance-optimal. Rate bound: `k/n ≤ r/(r+1)`.

#### 3.2 LRC construction: local groups, local parity, global parity

**Source:** USENIX ATC'12 "Erasure Coding in Windows Azure Storage" (Huang et al.); USENIX ATC'18 "On Fault Tolerance, Locality, and Optimality in Locally Repairable Codes" (Kolosov et al.); VLDB'13 "XORing Elephants" (Sathiamoorthy et al.); ACM ToS 2025 survey "A Survey of the Past, Present, and Future of Erasure Coding for Storage Systems".

An `(k, l, g)` LRC divides `k` data fragments into `l` local groups of `⌈k/l⌉` (≤ `r`) fragments each. It encodes one local parity per local group and `g` global parities over all `k` data fragments. Total `n = k + l + g`. Any single fragment failure in a local group is decoded from the `k/l` fragments within its group (plus local parity). LRC achieves Maximally Recoverable property: tolerates up to `g + 1` arbitrary fragment failures, and `g + i` failures spanning `i` local groups.

- **Azure-LRC:** variation of Pyramid codes, used in Windows Azure Storage. `(12, 2, 2)` LRC chosen for 1.33x storage overhead target; MTTF 2.6×10¹² years; ~50% fewer blocks read per repair vs RS.
- **Xorbas / HDFS-RAID:** Facebook HDFS module replacing RS with LRC; 4 RS parities + local XOR parities; ~2× repair disk I/O and network reduction, 14% more storage.
- **Pyramid codes:** first LRC family, based on RS codes.

#### 3.3 Single erasure recovery within a locality

**Source:** USENIX ATC'18 (Kolosov et al.); ACM ToS 2025 survey; VLDB'13 Xorbas.

When one block fails in a local group of size `r + 1` (r data + 1 local parity), the missing block is recovered by reading the `r` surviving blocks in the group and computing the local parity equation. Repair degree = `r` (number of helper nodes), vs `k` for Reed-Solomon. For `(12, 2, 2)` Azure-LRC: repair reads 6 blocks vs 12 for RS(12,4). Degraded read similarly local.

#### 3.4 Double erasure recovery within a locality — (r, δ)-locality

**Source:** arXiv 1701.07340 "Locally Repairable Codes with Unequal Local Erasure Correction"; arXiv 1702.05741 "LRCs with Multiple (r_i, δ_i)-Localities"; arXiv 1507.02796 "LRCs with Functional Repair and Multiple Erasure Tolerance"; arXiv 2106.03302 "Rack-Aware Regenerating Codes".

An `(r, δ)`-LRC: every symbol has a local repair set of size `r + δ − 1` such that the code restricted to that set has distance ≥ `δ`, tolerating `δ − 1` concurrent erasures within the group. Singleton-like bound: `d ≤ n − k + 1 − (⌈k/r⌉ − 1)(δ − 1)`. For `δ = 2` this degenerates to the basic LRC bound. Double erasure within a locality requires `δ ≥ 3`. Sequential repair of multiple failures: order newcomers so each is repaired from live nodes plus previously repaired newcomers.

#### 3.5 Code with locality parameters (n, k, r, l, g, δ, t)

**Source:** ACM ToS 2023 "Practical Design Considerations for Wide Locally Recoverable Codes"; USENIX ATC'12 Azure; Error Correction Zoo; arXiv 1810.08510 "Alphabet-Dependent Bounds for Linear LRCs".

Parameter space:
- `n`: code length (total symbols), `k`: dimension (data symbols), `r`: locality.
- `l = ⌈k/r⌉`: number of local groups; `g`: number of global parities; `n = k + l + g`.
- `δ`: local distance (δ=2 → single-erasure local tolerance; δ≥3 → multi-erasure).
- `t`: availability (number of disjoint repair sets per symbol).
- Storage overhead: `n/k`. Fault tolerance `f = g + 1` (single-group) up to `g + i` spanning `i` groups.
- Rate: `k/n ≤ r/(r+1)`; distance-optimal when Singleton-like bound met with equality.

Wide-LRC examples (rate ≥ 0.85): 24-of-28 (n=28,k=24,r=2), 48-of-55 (n=55,k=48,r=3), 72-of-80 (n=80,k=72,r=4), 96-of-105 (n=105,k=96,r=5).

#### 3.6 Repair locality optimization

**Source:** USENIX ATC'18 (Kolosov et al.); USENIX FAST'19 OpenEC; SRDS'24 "Harmonizing Repair and Maintenance in LRC-Coded Storage"; arXiv 2106.03302; arXiv 2505.06819 "New Wide LRCs with Unified Locality".

Repair locality `r̄` = average number of blocks read to repair a block. Optimization targets:
- Minimize `r̄` by balancing local group sizes and placing local groups within fault domains / clusters (one local group per cluster → zero cross-cluster traffic for local repairs).
- Azure-LRC+1: treats global parities as a local repair group too, improving locality and avoiding cross-zone transfers.
- Uniform Cauchy LRC: lowest locality `⌈n/p⌉` by uniformly dividing `n` blocks into `p` groups.
- Trade-off: repair performance vs maintenance (upcoding/downcoding) performance cannot be simultaneously optimized; configurable data placement navigates the trade-off.
- LRC+PPR: Partial Parallel Repair applied to LRC reduces per-link chunks (e.g., 6 → 3 chunks for (12,2,2) LRC).

#### 3.7 Availability `t` and multiple disjoint repair sets

**Source:** Error Correction Zoo; arXiv 2004.06770 "Cyclic and convolutional codes with locality" (Barg, Chen); terpconnect.umd.edu "On codes with the locality property" (Barg newsletter); MDPI Mathematics 2026 "Optimal Binary LRCs with Locality and Availability from Latin Squares".

A symbol has `(r, t)`-availability if it has `t` disjoint repair sets `R_1(i), …, R_t(i)`, each `|R_j(i)| ≤ r`, pairwise disjoint. Enables `t` independent simultaneous recovery processes → high availability for hot data. Orthogonal partitions (from coprime-order subgroups of multiplicative/additive field groups) yield disjoint repair sets. MOLS-based binary constructions achieve distance-optimal LRCs with availability.

#### 3.8 Puncturing and shortening of LRCs

**Source:** arXiv 1909.10553 "Error Decoding of Locally Repairable and Partial MDS Codes"; arXiv 2105.11271 "Constructions of Optimal Binary LRCs via Intersection Subspaces"; Yonsei IWSDA'20 "concatenated binary LRC with locality 2 using puncturing".

- Shortening: decrease length and dimension simultaneously; `n' = n − a(r+1)`, `k' ≥ k − ar`, `d' ≥ d` (remove `a` full local groups).
- Puncturing: decrease length, keep dimension; removing a column from each distinct submatrix of the parity-check matrix yields `[n' = n − τ, k' = k − τ, d' = d]`.
- Used to tune LRC parameters to target `n`, `k`, `r` when exact divisibility `(r+1) | n` or `r | k` does not hold.

#### 3.9 Hierarchical locality and H-LRCs

**Source:** arXiv 2004.06770 (Barg, Chen); ISCDS monograph "Codes for Distributed Storage" (Section 13 hierarchical locality).

Hierarchical locality: layers of local codes with increasing block length and erasure-recovery capability. Permits graceful degradation in repair degree as the number of erasures increases — when one local code is overwhelmed, fall back to the next layer. Cyclic constructions characterize zeros supporting hierarchical locality; quasicyclic form enables tail-biting convolutional LRCs.

#### 3.10 Maximally recoverable LRCs (MR-LRCs)

**Source:** Dagstuhl LIPIcs ICALP'2019 "Constructions of Maximally Recoverable LRCs via Function Fields"; arXiv 2012.07804 "Improved MR-LRCs using Skew Polynomials"; ISCDS monograph Section 14.

An MR-LRC corrects all erasure patterns information-theoretically correctable given local recovery groups: `a` erasures per local group plus up to `h` additional erasures anywhere. Guarantees maximal fault tolerance under locality constraints. Field size is exponential in `h` or `a` in known constructions; minimizing field size is an open research area. MR-LRCs maximize mean time to data loss.

#### 3.11 Finite-field constructions

**Source:** arXiv 1502.01414 "Cyclic LRC Codes and their Subfield Subcodes"; arXiv 2007.14752 "New Constructions of Optimal Cyclic (r, δ)-LRCs from Their Zeros"; arXiv 1810.08510; arXiv 2112.02569 "Optimal Quaternary (r, δ)-LRCs"; Springer 2026 "Cyclic (r, δ) LRCs from constacyclic/negacyclic subcodes".

- Reed-Solomon-based: polynomial evaluation; locality via partition of evaluation points into subsets of size `r+1` where a polynomial is constant.
- Cyclic LRCs: zeros of generator polynomial contain cosets of `ν`-th roots of unity; cyclic shifts partition support into disjoint recovery sets of size `r+1`.
- Small-field / binary: cyclic codes, Reed-Muller, Simplex-based, tensor-product constructions.
- Quaternary `(r, δ)`-LRCs: complete classification via projective geometry over F₄.

#### 3.12 LRC vs Reed-Solomon and deployment evidence

**Source:** USENIX ATC'12 Azure; VLDB'13 Xorbas; USENIX ATC'18 Kolosov; DIMACS slides "Coding for Distributed Storage" (Dimakis); ACM ToS 2025 survey.

- RS(12,4): repair reads 12 chunks; Azure-LRC(12,2,2): reads 6 chunks (~50% reduction).
- Storage overhead: LRC 1.67x vs RS 1.5x for comparable params; Xorbas 14% more storage than RS.
- Repair disk I/O and network: ~2× reduction (Xorbas); 30–40% faster repairs in some cases.
- MTTF: Azure-LRC(6,2,2) 2.6×10¹² years vs RS(6,3) 6.1×10¹¹ vs 3-replication 3.5×10⁹.
- Deployed: Windows Azure Storage, Facebook HDFS-RAID/Xorbas, Ceph LRC plugin, OpenEC middleware.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Local group overwhelm (δ−1+ erasures in one group) | Data loss within group | `(r, δ)`-locality with δ≥3; fall back to global parities; hierarchical locality for graceful degradation |
| Global parity bottleneck | Repair of global parities needs all k data | Treat global parities as local group (Azure-LRC+1); locality-aware placement |
| Correlated failure across local groups | Multiple groups fail simultaneously | Fault tolerance `g + i` spanning `i` groups; rack/rack-aware placement via ids-topology |
| Locality-distance tradeoff (sacrificed d) | Reduced fault tolerance vs MDS | Distance-optimal construction target; MR-LRC option for maximal patterns |
| Parameter mismatch (r ∤ k, (r+1) ∤ n) | Invalid group partitioning | Puncturing/shortening transformations; parameter validation at construction |
| Symbol fragment corruption | Silent data corruption | sha256/blake3 checksums per fragment; verify before use in recovery |
| Replay of encoded fragments | Stale data | ed25519-signed encode/decode audit entries; nonce/version binding |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying fragment datagrams | Reordering/duplication | Carrier-agnostic; idempotent XOR/GF reconstruction tolerates duplicates |
| Prohibited crypto/networking | Policy violation | Allowed-crypto allowlist; dependency audit bans std::net/tokio::net/libp2p |
| Key extraction (fragment signing key) | Decision authenticity | Signing keys never leave node; encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305) |

The carrier is never trusted: LRC fragments and recovery plans are signed/checksummed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 LRC construction (encode)
```
LrcParams { n, k, r, l=⌈k/r⌉, g, δ, t, field }
partition(data[0..k], l groups of ≤ r) → groups[0..l-1]
for each group j: local_parity[j] = XOR or GF-combination of group j
for i in 0..g: global_parity[i] = GF-linear-combination of all data[0..k]
codeword = data + local_parities + global_parities   (n = k + l + g symbols)
```

#### 7.2 Single erasure recovery within locality
```
failed symbol c_i ∈ group j
read surviving r symbols in group j (excluding c_i) + local_parity[j]
c_i = local_parity[j] XOR/GF-sum(survivors)   (single-parity local code, δ=2)
repair degree = r  (vs k for Reed-Solomon)
```

#### 7.3 Double erasure recovery within locality — (r, δ≥3)
```
two failures c_i, c_j in group j
requires local code distance ≥ 3 (δ=3)
recover both from local group using extended local parity structure
if insufficient local redundancy → fall back to global parities (read k symbols)
```

#### 7.4 Singleton-like bound check
```
d ≤ n − k − ⌈k/r⌉ + 2   (basic LRC)
d ≤ n − k + 1 − (⌈k/r⌉ − 1)(δ − 1)   ((r, δ)-locality)
distance-optimal iff equality
```

#### 7.5 Rate bound
```
k/n ≤ r/(r+1)
storage overhead n/k ≥ (r+1)/r
```

#### 7.6 Fault tolerance
```
tolerates any g + 1 arbitrary failures
tolerates g + i failures spanning i local groups (1 ≤ i ≤ l)
failures beyond → unrecoverable (data loss)
```

#### 7.7 Availability t (disjoint repair sets)
```
t disjoint repair sets R_1(i)…R_t(i) per symbol, each ≤ r, pairwise disjoint
enables t independent simultaneous recoveries of symbol i
```

#### 7.8 Puncturing / shortening
```
shorten: remove a full local groups → n' = n − a(r+1), k' ≥ k − ar, d' ≥ d
puncture: remove τ columns from parity-check submatrices → n' = n − τ, k' = k − τ, d' = d
```

#### 7.9 Repair-locality optimization
```
repair_locality r̄ = average helpers per repair
balance local group sizes; place one local group per fault domain/cluster
Azure-LRC+1: global parities as local group → zero cross-cluster traffic for parity repair
```

#### 7.10 Fragment checksum
```
checksum = sha256(fragment) or blake3(fragment) per symbol
verify before including in recovery; checksum chain in audit log
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete `(n, k, r, l, g)` defaults:** deployment-tuned per workload (e.g., Azure `(12,2,2)`, Xorbas `(16,10,5)`); to be validated at integration with `ids-erasure`/`ids-recovery`.
2. **Field size vs locality tradeoff:** optimal LRC constructions require specific field sizes (MR-LRCs exponential in `h`/`a`); small-field binary/cyclic options trade distance for field size — selection pending.
3. **`(r, δ)`-locality δ default:** δ=2 (single-erasure local) vs δ≥3 (multi-erasure) affects storage overhead and field size; workload-dependent.
4. **Availability `t` default:** number of disjoint repair sets; higher `t` improves concurrent-repair availability at storage cost — unquantified.
5. **Hierarchical locality layer count:** number of layers and per-layer block length trade graceful degradation against complexity — design decision pending.
6. **MR-LRC inclusion:** maximally recoverable LRCs give maximal fault tolerance but large field sizes; feature-gated, inclusion decision pending.
7. **LRC+PPR integration:** PPR applied on LRC (Phase 087) further reduces per-link traffic; exact integration interface with `ids-ppr-reconstruction` to be defined.
8. **Checksum algorithm choice per fragment:** sha256 vs blake3 trade security vs speed; per-fragment configuration pending.
9. **Placement locality vs fault-domain constraints:** one-local-group-per-cluster optimizes repair locality but may conflict with rack/region fault-tolerance placement — resolved via `ids-topology` integration.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate crate `ids-locally-recoverable-codes` (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear erasure-coding boundary |
| `(k, l, g)` Azure-LRC form: `n = k + l + g`, `l = ⌈k/r⌉` local groups, `g` global parities | Proven in production (Azure, HDFS-Xorbas); simple XOR local parities + RS global parities |
| Locality `r` = max helpers for single-symbol repair | Directly minimizes repair degree; `r << k` vs Reed-Solomon's `k` |
| Singleton-like bound `d ≤ n − k − ⌈k/r⌉ + 2` as distance ceiling | Gopalan et al. information-theoretic bound; distance-optimal target |
| `(r, δ)`-locality for double-erasure within locality | Generalizes single-erasure; δ≥3 tolerates δ−1 concurrent erasures per group |
| Availability `t` via disjoint repair sets | Enables parallel/concurrent recovery; hot-data availability |
| Puncturing/shortening for parameter tuning | Handles non-divisible `(r+1) ∤ n`, `r ∤ k` cases; preserves distance |
| Hierarchical locality for graceful degradation | Layers of local codes; fall back when one layer overwhelmed |
| XOR local parities (binary) + GF global parities | Azure-LRC/Xorbas pattern; XOR avoids GF multiplication cost locally |
| All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns fragments/plans, never sends | Carrier-agnostic absolute rule; no network stack in trust base |
| Allowed crypto only; via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs | IDS crypto policy |
| sha256/blake3 fragment checksums + ed25519-signed audit log | Fragment integrity + tamper-evident encode/decode audit |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 087 creates `ids-ppr-reconstruction`, the IDS crate for distributed erasure-coded storage repair. It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by repair domain. The crate implements the design surface for Partial Parallel Repair (PPR): dividing a reconstruction operation into partial operations executed in parallel across storage nodes, aggregated through a reduction tree (binomial reduction tree), plus m-PPR scheduling for concurrent failures and network-pressure-reduction mechanics.

`ids-ppr-reconstruction` does not open sockets or drive any transport directly; it computes reconstruction schedules, partial-operation trees, helper selection, and bandwidth budgets, and ships every protection-relevant message as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 (implemented in `ids-crypto`; `ids-ppr-reconstruction` consumes primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`/`ids-crypto` only).

**Core results from research** (Mitra, Panta, Ra, Bagchi, "Partial-Parallel-Repair (PPR): A Distributed Technique for Repairing Erasure Coded Storage," EuroSys 2016): PPR completes network transfer in ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps vs k timesteps for conventional (k,m) Reed-Solomon repair, reducing maximum bandwidth per server by ~50–67% depending on code params ((6,3) 50%, (8,3) 62.5%, (10,4) 60%, (12,4) 66.6%) and reconstruction time by up to 59% for RS(12,4). m-PPR schedules multiple concurrent reconstructions to minimize contention for shared network/disk resources.

A skeleton `ids-ppr-reconstruction` crate does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-ppr-reconstruction/`. `ids-000-aa` already declares canonical types referenced by this crate but never redefined: `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, plus sealed trait contracts and error types. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

---

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-ppr-reconstruction` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a **reconstruction scheduler/planner**: given a failed chunk/stripe and a set of surviving helper nodes, it (a) selects helpers, (b) decomposes the repair into partial operations, (c) arranges participants into a reduction tree, (d) schedules timesteps and bandwidth, (e) handles concurrent failures via m-PPR, and (f) caps network pressure so foreground traffic is not starved. It never sends bytes itself; it returns a `RepairPlan` that the caller executes through `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```

│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (repair drivers)                │
│  ids-erasure, ids-recovery, ids-rebuild — trigger repair with failed chunk   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│              Phase 087: ids-ppr-reconstruction (THIS CRATE — planner)       │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ │\n│  │ helper          │ │ partial-op      │ │ reduction-tree    │ │ m-PPR    │ │ │\n│  │ selection       │ │ bandwidth/      │ │ failure-state   │ │                 │                │ │ │\n│  │ pressure caps   │ │ tracker         │ │                 │                │ │ │\n│  │ (foreground     │ │ (per-chunk,     │ │                 │                │ │ │\n│  │  protection)    │ │ per-node)       │ │                 │                │ │ │\n│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │ │ emission        │ │ (signed+chained)│ │                 │                │ │ │\n│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ │                 │                │ Vec<u8>},  │\\n│  payload: &[u8])                                           │\\n│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                    │\\n│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP /      │\\n│  QUIC / HTTP / DNS / Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN    │\\n└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a single-chunk PPR repair:** driver submits `RepairRequest{failed_chunk, stripe_id, k, m}` → `ids-ppr-reconstruction` selects k helper nodes, decomposes into partial operations, arranges them in a binomial reduction tree with ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps, computes per-node bandwidth and pressure caps, returns `RepairPlan{partial_ops, tree, timesteps, bandwidth_caps}` → caller executes partial ops as opaque datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets, collectors aggregate up the tree, final reconstructed chunk delivered to requestor.

**Data flow of concurrent-failure (m-PPR) repair:** driver submits multiple `RepairRequest`s → m-PPR scheduler interleaves/schedules reconstruction jobs to minimize contention for shared network/disk IO, returns per-job `RepairPlan`s with coordinated bandwidth allocations.

**Research-verified performance characteristics:**
- PPR network transfer: ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps vs k timesteps conventional; total transfer time ~2×C/BN for small k examples.
- PPR per-server max traffic: each participating server transfers only ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ chunks vs k chunks in traditional repair (e.g., 4 vs 8 for RS(8,3)).
- Reported gains: up to 59% reconstruction-time reduction for RS(12,4); 8.25× degraded-read throughput improvement; m-PPR 31–47% total repair-time reduction for simultaneous failures vs traditional RS repair.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 PPR — Partial Parallel Repair (Mitra et al., EuroSys 2016)

**Source:** Purdue DCSl / AT&T Labs Research, "Partial-Parallel-Repair (PPR): A Distributed Technique for Repairing Erasure Coded Storage," EuroSys 2016. https://engineering.purdue.edu/dcsl/publications/papers/2016/final_erasurecodedrepair_eurosys16_cameraready.pdf ; https://about.att.com/ecms/dam/sites/labs_research/content/publications/SDN_Partial-Parallel-Decoding_PPR.pdf

PPR is a distributed reconstruction technique for erasure-coded storage. It divides the reconstruction of a failed chunk into partial operations and schedules them to execute in parallel on multiple servers already involved in the reconstruction. A distributed protocol progressively combines partial results, overlaying a binomial reduction tree over the helper servers. Theoretically, PPR completes network transfer in ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps vs k timesteps needed for a conventional (k,m) Reed-Solomon repair.

Key insight: conventional repair has the requestor fetch k chunks from k helpers, congesting the requestor's incoming link. PPR distributes bandwidth usage across helper links so no single link is overloaded; even the incoming link to the destination gets approximately as much traffic as the first aggregator server.

Reported advantages (Table 1 of the paper):
- (6,3): 50% network transfer reduction, 50% max BW/server reduction
- (8,3): 50% network transfer reduction, 62.5% max BW/server reduction
- (10,4): 60% network transfer reduction, 60% max BW/server reduction
- (12,4): 66.6% network transfer reduction, 66.6% max BW/server reduction

Experimental: up to 59% reconstruction-time reduction for RS(12,4); 8.25× degraded-read throughput improvement.

#### 3.2 m-PPR — Multiple Concurrent PPR

**Source:** Same EuroSys 2016 paper, Section 5.

In a data center, multiple chunk failures occur concurrently (transient failures, maintenance, upgrades, disk failures). Naive overlapping reconstructions contend for shared network and disk IO. m-PPR schedules multiple reconstruction jobs in parallel while minimizing competition for shared resources. Each repair job uses the main PPR algorithm; m-PPR apportions load across concurrent reconstructions. Evaluation: 31–47% total repair-time reduction for simultaneous failures vs traditional RS repair (RS(12,4), 64MB chunks, BIGSITE testbed with 83 chunk servers); benefit decreases with higher numbers of simultaneous failures.

#### 3.3 Reduction tree / binomial reduction tree aggregation

**Source:** PPR paper Section 4.2 ("Reduction in network transfer time"); HPC binomial reduction tree references.

PPR overlays a tree-like reduction structure (binomial reduction tree) over servers holding relevant chunks. Reconstruction takes logarithmic timesteps (⌈log₂(k+1)⌉) instead of linear (k). Partial results are progressively combined up the tree until the requestor holds the fully reconstructed chunk. This fully utilizes available network resources and significantly reduces repair time.

#### 3.4 Repair pipelining (ECPipe) and follow-up techniques

**Source:** Li et al., "Repair Pipelining for Erasure-Coded Storage," USENIX ATC 2017; "Repair Pipelining for Erasure-Coded Storage: Algorithms and Evaluation," arXiv:1908.01527.

ECPipe partitions a chunk into slices and pipelines repair across storage nodes in units of slices; achieves O(1) single-block repair time vs O(log k) for PPR and O(k) for conventional. ECPipe integrates as middleware into HDFS and QFS. Follow-ups: PPT/PPCT (Parallel Pipeline Tree / Cross-Tree, non-uniform traffic), SMFRepair/MSRepair (bandwidth-aware scheduling), RAN (aggregation repair with programmable switches), NetEC (in-network aggregation), SelectiveEC (balanced recovery load), FastPR (proactive repair via migration + reconstruction), CORE (concurrent failure recovery for regenerating codes), InaPR/FinRepair (in-network aggregation).

#### 3.5 Regenerating codes (MSR/MBR) and repair bandwidth

**Source:** Dimakis et al. regenerating codes; Goparaju et al. "Minimum Storage Regenerating Codes for All Parameters" (IEEE TIT 2017); ACM TOS survey 2025.

Regenerating codes minimize repair bandwidth (network traffic during repair) via sub-packetization. MSR codes minimize storage overhead then repair bandwidth; MBR minimize bandwidth then storage. For single-node failures (>98% of stripe failures in Facebook's warehouse cluster), MSR can reduce repair bandwidth by close to 50% vs RS. Clay codes support general (n,k) and are state-of-the-art MSR codes. PPR is compatible with repair-friendly codes and compounds savings.

#### 3.6 Concurrent failure handling

**Source:** CORE (Li, Lin, Lee, TC 2014 / arXiv:1302.3344); m-PPR section of EuroSys 2016; survey § "Failure repair."

Concurrent failures (t failed nodes, t ≤ n−k) require reconstructing multiple lost chunks. Conventional multi-block repair takes k + f − 1 timeslots with skewed bandwidth (requestor downlink congested). PPR + m-PPR distribute load. CORE extends regenerating codes to concurrent failures with 36–64% bandwidth savings (optimal cases). PPR's m-PPR minimizes contention across simultaneous reconstructions.

#### 3.7 Network pressure reduction

**Source:** PPR paper (key insight, Section 4); Rashmi et al. arXiv:1309.0186 (Facebook warehouse cluster: >100 TB/day recovery traffic); SelectiveEC; SMFRepair/MSRepair.

PPR reduces network pressure by (i) reducing total transfer time from k to ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps, (ii) capping max bandwidth per server to ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ chunks vs k, (iii) distributing traffic across helper links instead of concentrating on the requestor's downlink. m-PPR adds coordinated scheduling across concurrent jobs. SelectiveEC balances recovery load via bipartite-graph task selection; SMFRepair/MSRepair use idle nodes and bandwidth-aware link scheduling in heterogeneous networks.

#### 3.8 Carrier-agnostic transport

**Source:** IDS prompts.txt entry 1 / plan-001/048/060; ids-000-aa `trait Carrier` contract.

All traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` = `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` (max 1024 bytes). `CarrierType`: Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom(u16). No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. `ids-ppr-reconstruction` returns repair plans; the caller frames partial operations as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to endpoints.

#### 3.9 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** RFC 8032 (Ed25519); RFC 7539/8439 (ChaCha20-Poly1305, XChaCha20-Poly1305); NIST FIPS 180-4 (SHA-256); BLAKE3 spec.

`ids-ppr-reconstruction` uses:
- ed25519: signing repair plans, reduction-tree aggregation proofs, audit checkpoints.
- sha256/blake3: chunk/stripe checksums, reduction-tree node hashes, repair plan IDs, audit-chain links.
- xchacha20poly1305: encrypt repair state at rest (24-byte nonce, random-safe).
- chacha20poly1305: encrypt session/state payloads (12-byte nonce, counter-based).
No other crypto. Consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa`.

#### 3.10 Failure models and fault tolerance

**Source:** PPR paper (single chunk failure ≈99% of cases; f ≤ n−k concurrent); CORE (concurrent failure patterns); regenerating codes.

`ids-ppr-reconstruction` must handle: single-chunk degraded read, single-node full recovery, f ≤ n−k concurrent chunk failures in a stripe, partial helper availability, helper failure mid-repair (fallback to alternate helpers or re-schedule), straggler helpers (timeout and re-issue), correlated failures (same rack/region). Repair scope bounded by redundancy: t ≤ n−k or data unrecoverable.

---

### Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Requestor downlink congestion (conventional repair) | Repair latency | PPR reduction tree: ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps, traffic distributed across helpers |
| Helper link overload / incast | Network pressure | Max per-server traffic capped to ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ chunks; m-PPR coordinates concurrent jobs |
| Concurrent reconstruction contention | Repair performance | m-PPR scheduler apportions load across jobs, minimizes shared-resource competition |
| Helper failure mid-repair | Repair completion | Alternate helper selection; re-schedule partial ops; bounded retry |
| Straggler helper | Tail latency | Timeout + re-issue to alternate helper; cancellation tokens |
| Replay of repair plan / partial op | Decision integrity | ed25519-signed repair plans; nonce-bound partial ops; bounded replay cache |
| Clock manipulation for scheduling | Causality | Logical timesteps + IdsTime monotonic ticks; never wall-clock for scheduling |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent partial-op application; idempotent reduction-tree merge |
| Unauthorized repair initiation | Access control | Repair plan signed by authorized coordinator; ed25519 verification |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Disallowed crypto in repair path | Policy compliance | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305; CI allowlist test |
| Carrier-agnostic rule violation | Architecture | `Endpoint` sole address type; dependency audit bans networking crates |

The carrier is never trusted: repair plans and partial-op messages are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary means no network stack is in the trust base.

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-ppr-reconstruction ||

| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error` — consumed, never redefined; sealed trait contracts mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All repair traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns plans, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing plans/partial ops/audit; encrypting repair state at rest; hashing chunks and tree nodes |

| `ids-recovery` | Recovery orchestration | Triggers PPR repairs on failure detection; consumes `RepairPlan` |
| `ids-rebuild` | Node rebuild | Full-node recovery uses PPR per-chunk; m-PPR for concurrent chunks |
| `ids-fragment` | Record fragments/shards | Fragment reads/writes governed by parent record's redundancy; PPR repairs fragments |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store | Source of surviving chunks for repair; checksum verification on reconstructed chunks |

**Integration points:** `ids-ppr-reconstruction` is a pure planner: it emits `RepairPlan` structures; callers (`ids-recovery`, `ids-rebuild`) execute via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on ids-discovery/ids-session/ids-cli beyond what contracts expose. Never touches crate internals — public contracts only.

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

#### 7.1 PPR partial-op decomposition

```
decompose(stripe, failed_chunk, k_helpers, erasure_params) -> Vec<PartialOp>
  - Split each helper's surviving chunk into sub-chunks (sub-packetization)
  - Form linear combinations over GF(2^w) per erasure code coefficients
  - Each PartialOp: {source_helper, target_aggregator, sub_chunk_id, coefficients, payload: Vec<u8>}
  - Partial ops are independent → parallelizable across helpers
```

#### 7.2 Binomial reduction tree

```
BinomialTree { nodes: Vec<TreeNode>, root: NodeId, timesteps: ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ }
  - Arrange k helpers + requestor as a binomial tree
  - Timestep t: nodes at distance t send partial results to parent
  - Each node transfers ≤ ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ chunks total vs k in conventional repair
  - Root (requestor) reconstructs failed chunk from aggregated partial results
  - Merge at each node: idempotent, commutative, associative (linear combination)
```

#### 7.3 Timestep scheduling

```
assign_timesteps(tree, bandwidth_caps) -> Vec<TimestepBatch>
  - Timestep 0..T where T = ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉
  - Each batch contains partial ops whose links don't share a congested endpoint
  - Logical timesteps keyed to IdsTime ticks; never wall-clock
```

#### 7.4 m-PPR concurrent scheduling

```
m_ppr_schedule(jobs: Vec<RepairRequest>) -> Vec<ScheduledJob>
  - Apportion network/disk load across concurrent reconstruction jobs
  - Minimize competition for shared resources (per EuroSys 2016 §5)
  - Return per-job RepairPlan with coordinated bandwidth allocations
  - Benefit decreases as number of simultaneous failures grows
```

#### 7.5 Bandwidth caps / network pressure reduction

```
BandwidthCap { per_server: bytes/timestep, per_link: bytes/timestep, foreground_budget: bytes/s }
  - Per-server cap: ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ chunks vs k conventional
  - Foreground traffic protected: repair bandwidth ≤ configured budget
  - Throttle/backpressure when links approach cap
```

#### 7.6 Failure handling

```
FailureTracker { chunk_state: Map<ChunkId, ChunkState>, node_state: Map<NodeId, NodeState> }
  - ChunkState: Pending / InProgress / Reconstructed / Failed / Fallback
  - On helper failure: select alternate, re-schedule partial op, bounded retry
  - On straggler: timeout, cancel, re-issue to alternate
  - Scope: t ≤ n−k concurrent failures; beyond → unrecoverable (signal ids-recovery)
```

#### 7.7 Audit chain

```
AuditEntry { op_id, node_id, timestamp(IdsTime), decision, prev_hash: [u8;32], signature: Signature }
  - sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints
  - Offline verifiable; tamper-evident repair decision log
```

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

1. **Concrete (n,k) defaults per deployment:** PPR gains vary by code params ((6,3) 50% … (12,4) 66.6%); defaults to be validated at integration with `ids-erasure`/`ids-recovery`.
2. **Sub-packetization level:** number of sub-chunks per chunk trades parallelism vs overhead; unquantified for IDS chunk sizes.
3. **m-PPR load-apportionment heuristic:** exact algorithm for coordinating concurrent jobs (greedy vs LP) to be selected at implementation.
4. **Bandwidth cap values:** per-server/per-link caps and foreground budget are deployment-tuned; SLO pending.
5. **Straggler timeout bound:** trades tail latency vs re-issue overhead; workload-dependent.
6. **Helper failure fallback chain:** how many alternates before declaring a chunk unrecoverable mid-repair; policy pending.
7. **Interaction with regenerating codes (MSR/Clay):** PPR compounds with repair-bandwidth-reducing codes; combined savings unquantified for IDS.
8. **Audit checkpoint frequency:** tradeoff between audit granularity and signing overhead; to be tuned.
9. **Cross-rack/region repair:** PPR reduction tree assumes helper reachability; cross-rack bandwidth constraints need network-aware tree construction (cf. PPT/PPCT, SMFRepair) — deferred.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

| Decision | Rationale |
|----------|-----------|
| Separate `ids-ppr-reconstruction` crate (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear repair-planning boundary |
| PPR reduction tree with ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ timesteps | EuroSys 2016: logarithmic vs linear transfer time; 50–67% bandwidth reduction |
| m-PPR for concurrent failures | EuroSys 2016 §5: schedules multiple reconstructions, minimizes shared-resource contention |
| Crate is a pure planner (emits RepairPlan, never sends bytes) | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base; caller executes via ids-carrier::Endpoint |
| Binomial reduction tree aggregation | Distributes traffic across helper links; no single congested requestor downlink |
| Logical timesteps keyed to IdsTime; no wall-clock | Clock manipulation cannot break repair scheduling |
| ed25519-signed repair plans + sha256/blake3 audit chain | Tamper-evident, offline-verifiable repair decision log |
| Only allowed crypto; consumed via ids-crypto primitive IDs | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
| Failure scope t ≤ n−k enforced | Beyond redundancy, data is unrecoverable; signal rather than fabricate recovery |
| Per-server bandwidth cap ⌈log₂(k+1)⌉ chunks | Caps network pressure; protects foreground traffic |
| Idempotent/commutative/associative tree merge | Tolerates carrier-duplicated datagrams and re-tries |

### 1. Executive Summary

Phase 089 creates `ids-warm-tier`, the IDS crate for warm storage — the tier that holds moderately accessed data: less frequently accessed than hot data, but still actively used and requiring immediate availability, sitting between the hot tier (frequently accessed, highest performance) and the cold tier (infrequently accessed, lowest cost). It is a **separate crate** (not a folder inside an existing crate, per the project rule of separate crates for new capabilities), organized into subfolders by warm-tier concern: placement, promotion/demotion, cost modeling, capacity management, and access-pattern tracking.

**Core design:** `ids-warm-tier` owns warm-tier data lifecycle — admission into the warm tier, temperature scoring of records, promotion back to hot and demotion down to cold based on access frequency and recency, warm-tier capacity watermarks (low/high), cost-per-byte accounting for warm storage, and access-pattern histogram tracking. Every decision it returns is a policy decision; it never opens a socket or drives any transport directly. All cross-node warm-tier traffic flows as opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` address ≤ 1024 bytes). Allowed crypto only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305, consumed via `ids-crypto` primitive IDs from `ids-000-aa` (ids-crypto does not depend on ids-000-aa to avoid circular dependency; ids-warm-tier depends on both).

**Scope boundary:** `ids-warm-tier` decides placement, promotion/demotion, capacity, and cost; it does not store bytes itself. Warm-tier storage nodes are served by other crates (ids-store, ids-erasure, ids-replication); `ids-warm-tier` tells them *where* and *when* data belongs. Thresholds are configurable budgets (watermark ratios, temperature scores, cost-per-byte caps), not hard-coded limits, so a capacity-constrained platform degrades gracefully rather than failing.

Skeleton `ids-warm-tier` does NOT yet exist at `C:/idfs/ids-warm-tier/`. `ids-000-aa` is the master crate holding every canonical type and sealed trait contract. Research only — no code, no source modifications, only this plan document.

**Research basis:** 30 parallel searches returned f4: Facebook's Warm BLOB Storage System (USENIX OSDI'14, Reed-Solomon(10,4) warm storage, effective replication factor 3.6 → 2.8/2.1); Elasticsearch data tiers (hot/warm/cold/frozen, ILM migration after weeks); HDFS storage policies (Hot/Warm/Cold with replica placement); Ceph cache tiering (cache pool + backing pool, writeback/read-only cache modes); S3 Intelligent-Tiering (automatic access-pattern-based moves, monitoring + automation charge); Azure blob access tiers (hot/cool/cold); Google Cloud Storage classes (Standard/Nearline/Coldline/Archive); Dropbox Magic Pocket warm/cold tiers (warm tier 1+1 replication, async cold migration); ELECT erasure-coding tiering for LSM-trees (hotness-aware redundancy transition, storage saving target α); Alluxio tiered storage (memory/SSD/HDD tiers, LRU/LFU/Greedy evictors, TTL, annotation policies); GlusterFS tiering volume watermark-hi/watermark-low with promote/demote frequency thresholds; IBM Easy Tier warm/cold demotion and warm promotion (extent-level heat values, 80% capacity threshold); HSM hierarchical storage management (migration policy, LRU/STP/STEP algorithms, file grooming); DITIS tiered storage simulator (tier placement, migrate up/down, deletion policies); Mole tier-specific hotness profiling (reaccess-interval histograms, targeted promotion, staging demotion); HotRAP hot-record retention and promotion for LSM tiered storage; CloudJump III eviction-centric engine-aware tiering; storgatech PLC SSD warm-tier SLOs (read p99 < 20ms, TTL 30–90 days).

### 2. Architecture Overview

`ids-warm-tier` sits above `ids-000-aa` (types + sealed contracts + invariants + errors), `ids-carrier` (opaque `Endpoint` datagram transport), and `ids-crypto` (allowed primitives). It is a policy/decision layer: given a record's access history, current tier, tier capacity, and workload SLO, it decides (a) whether the record belongs in the warm tier, (b) whether to promote it to hot or demote it to cold, (c) how much warm-tier capacity to reserve, (d) what warm-tier cost-per-byte applies, and (e) what placement topology to use. It never sends bytes itself; it returns a `PlacementDecision` / `PromotionDecision` / `DemotionDecision` that the caller frames into opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    APPLICATION / ids-* LAYER (tier users: ids-store, ids-erasure, …)     │
│  read/write with temperature tag, admission to warm tier, migration requests             │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                    Phase 089: ids-warm-tier (THIS CRATE — policy)                        │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌──┐   │
│  │ access-pattern  │ │ temperature     │ │ placement       │ │ promotion/      │ │cost│ │
│  │ tracking        │ │ scoring         │ │ (warm tier)     │ │ demotion policy │ │model│ │
│  │ (frequency/     │ │ (hot/warm/cold) │ │ admission,      │ │ hysteresis,     │ │per │ │
│  │  recency)       │ │ per record      │ │ topology hints  │ │ thrashing prev. │ │byte│ │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └──┘   │
│  ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐ ┌─────────────────┐                            │
│  │ capacity        │ │ crypto surface  │ │ audit/logging   │                            │
│  │ management      │ │ (allowlist only)│ │ (signed+chained)│                            │
│  │ (watermarks,    │ │                 │ │                 │                            │
│  │  reservations)  │ │                 │ │                 │                            │
│  └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘ └─────────────────┘                            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                           │ opaque Vec<u8> datagrams
                                           ▼
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              CARRIER BOUNDARY: ids-carrier::Endpoint only                                │
│  send_datagram(Endpoint{CarrierType, addr: Vec<u8> ≤ 1024 B}, payload: &[u8])            │
│  receive_datagram → (Endpoint, Vec<u8>)                                                  │
│  No std::net / tokio::net / libp2p / IP / TCP / UDP / QUIC / HTTP / DNS /                │
│  Wi-Fi / Bluetooth / cellular / VPN / mesh                                               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Data flow of a warm-tier admission decision:** client submits `Admit{record_id, size, access_history, current_tier}` → `ids-warm-tier` scores temperature (frequency × recency weight), checks warm-tier capacity watermark and reservation, returns `AdmitDecision{admit_to_warm: bool, topology_hint, reservation_bytes, cost_per_byte}` → caller places the record via `ids-store`/`ids-erasure` and sends migration as opaque datagram(s) to `ids-carrier::Endpoint` targets.

**Data flow of a promotion/demotion cycle:** `temperature_scanner` sweeps warm-tier records on a tick (monotonic `ids-time`, never wall-clock for ordering); records whose temperature falls below the demote threshold for N consecutive ticks become demotion candidates → `DemoteDecision{target_tier: Cold, bytes, migration_bandwidth_cap}`; records whose temperature rises above the promote threshold become promotion candidates → `PromoteDecision{target_tier: Hot, bytes}`. Hysteresis (separate promote/demote thresholds + minimum dwell time) prevents thrashing.

**Temperature semantics (research-verified):**
- **Hot data**: frequently accessed, highest performance tier (SSD/NVMe), small fraction of total data (the "20% most important" rule observed in tiered-storage literature).
- **Warm data**: accessed less frequently than hot but still actively used — the moderately accessed tier this crate owns; balanced performance/cost (HDD or cost-optimized SSD), typically holds recent-weeks data (Elasticsearch warm pattern) or data accessed monthly or less (Google Nearline pattern).
- **Cold data**: infrequently accessed, lowest cost, higher retrieval latency (object storage / archive), minimum retention durations.

**Crypto used:** ed25519 for signing placement/promotion/demotion decisions and audit checkpoints; sha256/blake3 for temperature hashing, access-pattern digest, audit-chain links; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt warm-tier state at rest (temperature tables, reservation records) when confidentiality required.

### 3. Detailed Research Dimensions

Each dimension maps to one or more of the 30 targeted searches executed. Sources are cited inline with the source list in Section 12.

#### 3.1 Warm tier definition and the three-tier model (hot / warm / cold)

**Source:** Elasticsearch data tiers documentation (elastic.co/docs/manage-data/lifecycle/data-tiers); Aerospike tiered storage guide; Purestorage tiered data storage overview; Cloud storage tier optimization through storage object classification (Springer, Computing 2024); storgatech PLC SSD tiered storage strategy.

The three-tier model orders storage by access frequency: hot (frequent, fast, expensive), warm (moderate, balanced, mid-cost), cold (infrequent, slow, cheap). Warm tier sits between hot and cold: "data that is important to retain and use occasionally, but not frequently enough to justify the cost of premium storage" (Aerospike). Elasticsearch warm tier holds data from recent weeks, queried less frequently than hot, updates allowed but infrequent. Azure cool/cold tiers are for data accessed less frequently but still immediately available. `ids-warm-tier` owns the warm tier: admission, temperature scoring, promotion/demotion, capacity, cost.

#### 3.2 Data temperature classification (access frequency + recency)

**Source:** Data Temperature Informed Streaming for Optimising Large-Scale Multi-Tiered Storage (Big Data Mining and Analytics, 2024); Mole: Tier-Specific Hotness Profiling Driven Memory Tiering (arXiv:2610.12164); Automating Distributed Tiered Storage Management in Cluster Computing (PVLDB 2019); Harnessing Page Access Frequency Distribution for Efficient Memory Tiering (ACM TOCS).

Data temperature combines access frequency and recency: existing solutions classify hot/cold primarily on age and usage frequency, but research shows age alone assumes new data has priority and usage is purely reactive — additional variables (reaccess interval, unaccessed duration, user-defined weights) improve placement. Mole builds hotness histograms from reaccess intervals (not just access counts) and derives capacity-based tier thresholds. `ids-warm-tier` scores temperature as a weighted combination of access frequency, recency (last access age), and record size, with configurable per-class weights.

#### 3.3 Warm tier placement and admission policy

**Source:** HDFS Archival Storage / storage policies (Hot/Warm/Cold/All_SSD/One_SSD); Apache Ozone storage policies (Hot→SSD, Warm→DISK, Cold→ARCHIVE with fallback); DITIS tiered storage simulator (tier placement policies); Alluxio tiered storage block allocation.

Placement decides the initial tier for new data and the target tier for migrated data. HDFS warm policy stores some replicas on DISK and some on ARCHIVE (partially hot, partially cold). Ozone warm data goes to DISK (not SSD, not ARCHIVE), with fallback to warm/cold if hot is full. Alluxio allocates new blocks to the top tier by default, spilling to the next tier when full. `ids-warm-tier` admission policy: new writes may be admitted directly to warm (bypassing hot) based on size/class; placement considers tier capacity watermarks, replica topology, and cost-per-byte budget.

#### 3.4 Promotion and demotion policy (hysteresis, thrashing prevention)

**Source:** IBM Easy Tier automatic processing (warm demotion, cold demotion, warm promotion); GlusterFS tiering volume (watermark-hi/watermark-low, promote/demote frequency, access-count threshold); Mole staging demotion and targeted promotion; f4 warm BLOB storage (asynchronous background migration as data becomes cold).

Promotion moves warm→hot when temperature exceeds the promote threshold; demotion moves warm→cold when temperature falls below the demote threshold. Hysteresis (separate thresholds + minimum dwell time / cooldown) prevents thrashing — the "three movements up, three movements back down" wasted-movement problem documented in data-temperature research. Easy Tier: warm demotion triggered when a higher tier exceeds bandwidth capacity; warm promotion when a lower tier exceeds IOPS capacity; 80% capacity threshold on tier assignment. GlusterFS: watermark-low/hi govern promote/demote likelihood; promote/demote frequency and read/write access-count threshold mark files HOT/COLD. `ids-warm-tier` implements promote threshold > demote threshold with a minimum dwell time and per-record migration budget.

#### 3.5 Warm tier capacity management (watermarks, reservations, spill)

**Source:** IBM Easy Tier (80% tier capacity threshold, pending assignments above threshold); Alluxio tiered storage management (eviction when tiers full, watermark-based eviction deprecated in favor of annotation policies); HSM (migration policy controls tier transfers to keep response time short); Ceph cache tiering (flush objects from cache to backing tier).

Capacity management keeps warm tier within budget: low watermark (stop demotions, allow promotions), high watermark (stop promotions, trigger demotions), spill to cold when warm exceeds high watermark. Reservations: warm tier reserves bytes for expected promotions so hot-tier spill doesn't overflow warm. When warm tier is full, admission of new warm data is rejected or redirected to cold with a `CapacityExceeded` decision. `ids-warm-tier` tracks `tierStorageUsed` per tier and exposes `isFull`/`availableBytes`.

#### 3.6 Warm tier access-pattern tracking (histograms, scoring)

**Source:** Mole tier-specific hotness profiling (reaccess-interval histogram, tier thresholds from capacity boundaries); Automating Distributed Tiered Storage Management (tracking and predicting file access patterns with incremental learning); Harnessing Page Access Frequency Distribution (page access frequency distribution for tiering); DITIS (caching + tiering policies driven by access patterns).

Access-pattern tracking records per-record access frequency, recency, and access pattern (sequential vs random, read vs write ratio) in bounded histograms. Mole constructs hotness histograms from reaccess intervals and unaccessed durations, deriving tier thresholds when bucket counts reach tier capacity boundaries. `ids-warm-tier` maintains a per-record `AccessProfile` (access count, last-access tick, first-access tick, access-size histogram, sequentiality score) and recomputes temperature on each access and on each scanner tick.

#### 3.7 Warm tier cost modeling (cost per byte, cost per access)

**Source:** storgatech PLC SSD tiered storage strategy (SLOs: warm read p99 < 20ms, TTL 30–90 days); Amazon S3 Intelligent-Tiering (monitoring + automation charge per object); Google Cloud Storage cost guidance (Standard vs Nearline vs Coldline pricing, retrieval fees, early deletion); Cloud storage tier optimization through storage object classification (performance/cost trade-off per tier).

Cost model: warm tier cost per byte (storage) + cost per access (read/write operations) + migration cost (bytes moved × migration bandwidth cost). S3 Intelligent-Tiering charges a small monthly object monitoring and automation fee; Google Nearline/Coldline charge per-GB access and early-deletion fees. `ids-warm-tier` computes warm-tier cost per byte per record class and compares against hot/cold alternatives to recommend the cost-minimizing tier for each record, subject to SLO constraints (latency, availability).

#### 3.8 Warm tier durability and replication (replica vs erasure coding)

**Source:** f4: Facebook's Warm BLOB Storage System (OSDI'14, Reed-Solomon(10,4), effective replication factor 3.6 → 2.8/2.1); Dropbox Magic Pocket warm tier (1+1 replication scheme, 2× internal region replication); ELECT erasure-coding tiering for LSM (hybrid redundancy, storage saving target α); HDFS erasure coding (EC overhead ~50% vs 200% for 3× replication); Ceph erasure-coded pools (4+2 overhead 1.5× vs replication 3.0).

Warm data tolerates higher latency than hot, so warm tier can use erasure coding for storage efficiency where hot tier uses replication. f4 reduced warm BLOB effective replication factor from 3.6 to 2.1 using RS(10,4) across racks plus XOR wide-area. Magic Pocket warm tier uses 1+1 replication. ELECT selectively converts data from replication to erasure coding based on hotness and a configurable storage-saving target α. `ids-warm-tier` exposes redundancy policy per warm record (replication factor or erasure-code K/M) and durability scope (local/region), enforced jointly with `ids-consistency-profile`.

#### 3.9 Warm tier migration mechanics (bandwidth caps, background migration)

**Source:** f4 (asynchronous background migration as data becomes cold); Alluxio (tier management tasks back off under user I/O load, align/promote tasks respectful to user I/O); ELECT (redundancy transitioning and data offloading incur performance overhead, balanced by storage-saving target α); IBM Easy Tier (moves measured amount of extents at regular intervals without negatively impacting performance).

Migration moves bytes between tiers in the background, bounded by a migration bandwidth cap so foreground traffic is not starved. f4 migrates warm→cold asynchronously in the background. Alluxio tier management tasks (align/promote) back off whenever a worker or disk is under load. ELECT balances storage savings vs access performance via α. `ids-warm-tier` returns `MigrationPlan{bytes, bandwidth_cap_bytes_per_s, throttle_under_load: bool}` and the executor (ids-store/ids-replication) performs the actual datagram movement via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`.

#### 3.10 Warm tier consistency with cold/hot tiers (read-your-writes across tiers)

**Source:** ids-consistency-profile (Phase 060) profiles; Elasticsearch warm tier (updates still allowed, likely infrequent); Cloud Jump III eviction-centric engine-aware tiering (logical ownership decoupled from physical placement).

A record may move tiers while being read/written. Consistency across tier moves: logical ownership (which record belongs to which logical key) is decoupled from physical placement (which tier holds the bytes). Reads route to the current tier; writes go to the admission tier. During migration, reads are served from the source tier until the copy is acknowledged at the target, then ownership flips. `ids-warm-tier` coordinates with `ids-consistency-profile` so a record's profile quorum/durability requirements hold across tier transitions (e.g., warm tier demotion must not drop below the profile's durability requirement).

#### 3.11 Warm tier access SLOs (latency, availability targets)

**Source:** storgatech PLC SSD warm tier (read p99 < 20ms, write p99 < 50ms, 99.5% availability, accessed 0.05%–0.5% of objects/day); Elasticsearch warm tier (nodes don't need to be as fast as hot, replicas for resiliency); Google Cloud Storage Nearline (once per month or less) vs Standard (regular access).

Warm tier SLOs are looser than hot but tighter than cold: read p99 in the tens of ms, availability 99–99.5%, access frequency monthly-or-less to weekly. `ids-warm-tier` carries per-record SLO targets (max read latency, min availability, max cost per byte) and uses them in admission/promotion/demotion decisions — a record whose access pattern violates its warm SLO is promoted to hot; one that cools below the warm floor is demoted to cold.

#### 3.12 Warm tier and lifecycle management (TTL, retention, grooming)

**Source:** HSM hierarchical storage management (migration policy, file grooming = deletion from higher level after move to lower); Alluxio TTL (time-to-live with FREE/DELETE actions, periodic expiration check); Google Cloud Storage lifecycle (object transitions between storage classes, minimum storage durations Nearline 30 days / Coldline 90 days / Archive 365 days); Azure lifecycle management (hot 30 days → cool 90 days → archive 1 year).

Lifecycle: records have a warm-tier TTL or retention; after expiry they are groomed (deleted from warm after being moved to cold) or transitioned per a lifecycle policy. Minimum storage durations prevent premature demotion (e.g., 30-day Nearline minimum). `ids-warm-tier` exposes `warm_ttl` and `retention_policy` per record class, enforced by the capacity/scanner loop.

#### 3.13 Carrier-agnostic transport boundary (ids-carrier::Endpoint)

**Source:** IDS carrier-agnostic rule (prompts.txt entries 1, 89); HX-241 carrier/socket abstraction (Carrier/Socket/Endpoint traits with no networking-stack references); ids-000-aa `trait Carrier` sealed contract.

All warm-tier migration, replication, and placement traffic rides `ids-carrier::Endpoint` = `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>` (≤ 1024 bytes). `CarrierType` enum: Loopback, Serial, Optical, Radio, Custom(u16). No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, IP, TCP, UDP, QUIC, HTTP, DNS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, VPN, or mesh. `ids-warm-tier` never touches the carrier directly; it returns decisions that other crates frame into datagrams.

#### 3.14 Allowed crypto only (ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305)

**Source:** IDS allowed-crypto policy (prompts.txt); RFC 8032 Ed25519; RFC 7539/8439 ChaCha20-Poly1305; libsodium XChaCha20-Poly1305 (192-bit nonce); NIST FIPS 180-4 SHA-256; BLAKE3 spec.

`ids-warm-tier` uses: ed25519 to sign placement/promotion/demotion/audit decisions; sha256 for temperature/access-pattern digest and audit-chain links; blake3 for fast content hashing of warm-state checkpoints; xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305 to encrypt warm-tier state at rest (temperature tables, reservations) with random/counter nonces. No other crypto. `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs; `ids-warm-tier` references them via `ids-000-aa` only.

### 4. Threat Model & Mitigations

|| Threat | Asset at risk | Mitigation (this crate) ||
|--------|-----------|-------------------------------|--------------------------|
| Thrashing (repeated promote/demote of same record) | Warm tier stability, migration bandwidth | Hysteresis: separate promote/demote temperature thresholds + minimum dwell time; per-record migration cooldown |
| Warm tier capacity overflow | Warm tier availability | High-watermark demotions, low-watermark promotion gating, spill-to-cold, `CapacityExceeded` admission decision |
| Stale temperature score (record heats up but stays cold) | Read latency, SLO violation | Periodic temperature scanner tick (monotonic ids-time), access-frequency decay, promote threshold re-evaluation |
| Migration storms (too many records moving at once) | Foreground traffic starvation | Migration bandwidth cap, per-tick migration byte budget, backoff under load (Alluxio pattern) |
| Durability drop below profile requirement on demotion | Data durability | `ids-consistency-profile` coordination: demotion only if target tier meets the record's profile durability scope |
| Replay of placement/promotion/demotion decisions | Decision integrity | ed25519-signed audit checkpoints, nonce-bound decisions, bounded replay cache per decision type |
| Temperature table tampering | Placement correctness | sha256/blake3 hash chain of temperature snapshots + periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints |
| Key extraction (warm-tier signing key) | Decision authenticity | Signing keys never leave node; encrypted at rest (xchacha20poly1305/chacha20poly1305); zeroized on shutdown |
| Audit log tampering | Accountability | sha256/blake3 hash chain + periodic ed25519-signed checkpoints; offline verifiable |
| Carrier duplicating/delaying datagrams | Replay/ordering | Idempotent placement decisions tolerate duplicates; carrier-agnostic boundary keeps no network stack in trust base |
| Disallowed crypto algorithm | Crypto policy compliance | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305; CI allowlist test |

The carrier is never trusted: placement decisions and audit entries are signed over bytes, surviving any carrier re-framing; the carrier-agnostic boundary (opaque `Endpoint`, `CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) means no network stack is in the trust base.

### 5. Integration with Existing Crates

|| Crate | Role | Relevance to ids-warm-tier ||
|-------|------|--------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| `ids-000-aa` | Master crate: canonical types + sealed trait contracts + invariants + errors | `NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `Error`, `PlacementDecision` — consumed, never redefined; sealed trait contracts mirrored |
| `ids-carrier` | Opaque `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) datagram send/receive via `Carrier` trait | All warm-tier traffic flows to/from `Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends directly |
| `ids-crypto` | Allowed primitives: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305 | Signing decisions/audit; encrypting warm-tier state at rest; hashing temperature tables and access digests |
| `ids-store` | Primary record store (warm-tier consumer) | Receives admission/placement decisions; stores records on the tier `ids-warm-tier` assigns |
| `ids-erasure` | Erasure coding for warm-tier storage efficiency | Warm-tier redundancy (K/M) per `ids-warm-tier` redundancy policy; RS-style coding like f4 |
| `ids-replication` | Replica synchronization / migration | Performs warm↔hot↔cold data movement as opaque `Endpoint` datagrams per `MigrationPlan` |
| `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060) | Read/write behavior per profile | Demotion must not violate a record's profile durability/quorum requirement; profile tags records |
| `ids-cost` / `ids-accounting` | Cost tracking | Warm-tier cost per byte per record class; feeds cost model |
| `ids-time` | Monotonic time source | All temperature/scanner ticks keyed to `IdsTime`, never wall-clock |

**Integration points:** `ids-warm-tier` drives public contracts declared in `ids-000-aa`; it does not reach into crate internals. All cross-node traffic is opaque `Vec<u8>` datagrams to `ids-carrier::Endpoint`. No dependency on ids-discovery/ids-session/ids-cli beyond what the contracts expose.

Total: ~90–1000 files across `src/`, `src/contracts/`, `src/invariants/`, `src/audit/`, `tests/`, `benches/`, `docs/`, organized by subsystem so each concern is a separate file — consistent with the "separate crates instead of more folders" directive applied intra-crate as separate modules/files.

---

### 7. Key Algorithms & Data Structures

- **AccessProfile / temperature score**: `AccessProfile { access_count: u64, last_access_tick: IdsTime, first_access_tick: IdsTime, size_bytes: u64, sequentiality: f64 }`; `temperature_score = w_freq·log(1+access_count) + w_recency·decay(now − last_access_tick) + w_size·size_class`, weights configurable per record class.
- **Classifier**: `classify(score) → HotZone | WarmZone | ColdZone` using hot_threshold ≥ warm_threshold; warm zone = score ∈ [warm_threshold, hot_threshold).
- **Admission decision**: `admit(record, warm_available) → AdmitToWarm | RedirectToCold | Reject(CapacityExceeded)`; considers warm watermark, cost budget, redundancy feasibility.
- **Promotion/demotion with hysteresis**: `promote_if(score ≥ hot_threshold && dwell ≥ min_dwell)`; `demote_if(score ≤ warm_threshold − margin && dwell ≥ min_dwell)`; margin prevents thrashing at the boundary.
- **Watermark capacity**: `low_watermark ≤ tierStorageUsed ≤ high_watermark`; above high → stop promotions + trigger demotions; below low → allow promotions; reservation reserves bytes for expected promotions.
- **Migration plan**: `MigrationPlan { bytes: u64, bandwidth_cap: u64/s, throttle_under_load: bool }`; per-tick byte budget; backoff when foreground I/O saturated (Alluxio tier-management pattern).
- **Cost model**: `cost_per_byte = storage_price_per_gb/month + access_price_per_op × access_freq + migration_price_per_gb × migration_rate`; compares warm vs hot vs cold for cost-minimizing tier subject to SLO.
- **Redundancy policy**: replication factor N (warm: 1+1 like Magic Pocket) or erasure K/M (warm: RS(10,4) like f4, overhead 1.4× vs 3× replication); durability scope local/region.
- **Audit chain**: each placement/promotion/demotion decision = SHA-256/BLAKE3-chained entry + ed25519-signed checkpoint; offline verifiable.

---

### 8. Dependencies

- `ids-000-aa` — canonical types (`NodeId`, `RegionId`, `IdsTime`, `CarrierType`, `RecordId`, `Checksum`, `PlacementDecision`, `Error`) and sealed trait contracts.
- `ids-carrier` — `Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`) and `Carrier` trait — decision transport only; crate never sends directly.
- `ids-crypto` — allowed primitives only: ed25519, xchacha20poly1305, sha256, blake3, chacha20poly1305.
- `ids-time` — monotonic time source for temperature scanner ticks and dwell-time measurement.
- `serde` — serialization of warm-tier envelopes, temperature profiles, audit entries.
- `thiserror` — error types.

No `std::net`, `tokio::net`, libp2p, or any networking stack. No crypto beyond the allowed list.

### 9. Measurable Acceptance Criteria

|| # | Criterion | Measurement ||
|---|-----------|-----------|-------------|
| AC-089.1 | Access-pattern tracking: per-record frequency, recency, size recorded | `AccessProfile` populated on every access; scanner tick recomputes temperature |
| AC-089.2 | Temperature classification: hot/warm/cold zones with configurable thresholds | Classifier returns correct zone per score; unit tests cover boundary values |
| AC-089.3 | Warm tier admission: admit/redirect/reject decisions | `AdmitDecision` correct under below/above/at capacity watermarks |
| AC-089.4 | Promotion/demotion with hysteresis: no thrashing at boundary | Promote threshold > demote threshold + min dwell time; thrash test passes |
| AC-089.5 | Capacity watermarks: low < high; spill to cold above high | `isFull`/`availableBytes` correct; spill decision triggered above high watermark |
| AC-089.6 | Cost model: cost per byte per record class vs hot/cold | Cost model output matches pricing formula; budget enforcement rejects over-budget placements |
| AC-089.7 | Migration plan: bandwidth cap + per-tick budget | `MigrationPlan.bandwidth_cap` enforced; per-tick migration bytes ≤ budget |
| AC-089.8 | Lifecycle: TTL with FREE/DELETE; retention minimum duration | TTL expiry triggers action; minimum storage duration blocks premature demotion |
| AC-089.9 | Redundancy: replication factor or erasure K/M per record | Redundancy policy output matches configured replication/erasure scheme |
| AC-089.10 | All traffic via `ids-carrier::Endpoint` (`CarrierType` + `Vec<u8>`); zero references to `std::net`/`tokio::net`/IP/TCP/UDP/QUIC/HTTP/DNS/Wi-Fi/Bluetooth/cellular/VPN/mesh | Dependency audit test passes |
| AC-089.11 | Only ed25519/xchacha20poly1305/sha256/blake3/chacha20poly1305 in crypto surface | Allowlist unit test passes |
| AC-089.12 | Every placement/promotion/demotion decision in append-only, hash-chained, ed25519-signed audit log | Audit chain verifies offline; checkpoints signed |

---

### 10. Remaining Uncertainties

- **Concrete temperature thresholds:** hot/warm/cold score thresholds are deployment-tuned; to be validated at integration with `ids-store`/`ids-erasure`.
- **Weights in temperature score:** frequency vs recency vs size weights are workload-dependent; unquantified defaults needed.
- **Watermark ratios:** low/high warm-tier watermark values (e.g., 70%/85%) are capacity-planning decisions; Easy Tier uses 80% as a reference point.
- **Migration bandwidth cap:** default bytes-per-second cap trades warm-tier rebalancing speed vs foreground latency; unquantified.
- **Minimum dwell time:** cooldown between promote/demote cycles prevents thrashing; value (in `IdsTime` ticks) unquantified.
- **Redundancy default for warm tier:** replication (1+1, Magic Pocket) vs erasure coding (RS(10,4), f4) vs hybrid (ELECT α); selection is a deployment decision.
- **Interaction with `ids-consistency-profile` (Phase 060):** demotion must not drop below the record's profile durability scope; exact guard handshake defined here, validated at integration.
- **Dwell time vs access burstiness:** a record with bursty access may oscillate near the boundary; decay function shape (linear vs exponential) unquantified.

---

### 11. Engineering Decisions Summary

|| Decision | Rationale ||
|----------|-----------|-------------|
| Separate crate `ids-warm-tier` (not a folder) | Follows "separate crates instead of more folders" directive; clear policy boundary |
| Temperature score = frequency + recency + size, weighted | Data temperature research (Big Data Mining & Analytics 2024; Mole) shows age+frequency alone insufficient; weights configurable |
| Hysteresis: separate promote/demote thresholds + min dwell time | Prevents thrashing documented in data-temperature research (wasted movement up/down tiers) |
| Low/high watermarks + spill to cold | IBM Easy Tier / Alluxio / HSM capacity management pattern; keeps warm tier within budget |
| Strongest durability on warm tier: replication or erasure (RS(10,4)) | f4 reduced warm effective replication factor 3.6→2.1 with RS(10,4); Magic Pocket warm uses 1+1 replication |
| Migration bounded by bandwidth cap + per-tick budget | f4 asynchronous background migration; Alluxio tier tasks back off under user I/O load |
| Audit: sha256/blake3 hash chain + ed25519-signed checkpoints | Offline-verifiable decision log; tamper evidence |
| Logical clocks only (IdsTime ticks); no wall-clock for temperature/dwell | Clock manipulation cannot break temperature or dwell-time correctness |
| Carrier-agnostic boundary via `ids-carrier::Endpoint`; crate returns decisions, never sends bytes | Preserves IDS architecture; no network stack in trust base |
| Only allowed crypto; `ids-crypto` exposes primitive IDs via `ids-000-aa` | Complies with allowed-crypto rule |
